records.l: The Diary of Samuel Pepys, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, JUNE, JULY & AUGUST 1661 June 1st.
records.s: From June 1 to June 5, the diarist and Sir W. Pen inspect ships at Woolwich and Deptford and conduct business connected with an impending voyage. The diarist discusses Wardrobe responsibilities with my Lord, who expresses confidence in him and promises him first refusal of Mr. Young’s place for his father if it becomes vacant. The diarist and Mr. Creed obtain financial imprests and seek ammunition for my Lord’s ships, while the Navy Office conducts its regular business. The diarist also spends time with family and colleagues, attends church and the theatre, and takes part in social and musical activities.

records.l: Sir W. Pen, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, JUNE, JULY & AUGUST 1661 June 1st.
records.s: Sir W. Pen accompanied the diarist by water to Woolwich and Deptford on June 1 to inspect ships and give orders concerning their readiness to go forth. He later attended the Navy Office, went bowling with Sir R. Slingsby, and returned home with the diarist.

records.l: Lord Sandwich, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, JUNE, JULY & AUGUST 1661 June 1st.
records.s: My Lord instructed the diarist about Wardrobe business during his absence and said that he intended to join the diarist and Mr. Moore in managing it if Mr. Townsend died. He expressed great confidence in the diarist and promised to give him the refusal of Mr. Young’s place in the Wardrobe if it became vacant. The diarist also obtained my Lord’s imprest of L1000 and sought ammunition for his ships.

records.l: Mr. Creed, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, JUNE, JULY & AUGUST 1661 June 1st.
records.s: Mr. Creed’s imprest of L10,000 was signed against the voyage. He dined with the diarist, accompanied him to the Tower to seek ammunition for my Lord’s ships, and walked with him around the Tower.

records.l: the Wardrobe, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, JUNE, JULY & AUGUST 1661 June 1st.
records.s: The Wardrobe was the subject of my Lord’s instructions to the diarist concerning its management during his absence. My Lord proposed joining the diarist and Mr. Moore in its business if Mr. Townsend died, and promised the diarist first refusal of Mr. Young’s place for his father if it became vacant.

records.l: the Navy Office, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, JUNE, JULY & AUGUST 1661 June 1st.
records.s: The diarist attended the Navy Office on several days to conduct and sit over official business. The office was also involved in arrangements concerning nearby lodgings, though the houses considered by the Comptroller and the diarist did not suit them.

records.l: the voyage, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, JUNE, JULY & AUGUST 1661 June 1st.
records.s: Imprests for my Lord and Mr. Creed were signed against the voyage. The diarist and others inspected ships and made preparations for their going forth.

records.l: ships, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, JUNE, JULY & AUGUST 1661 June 1st.
records.s: On June 1, the diarist, Sir W. Pen, and Mr. Gauden went from ship to ship at Woolwich and Deptford to give orders and assess their readiness to go forth. The diarist and Mr. Creed later sought ammunition at the Tower for my Lord’s ships.

records.l: The Diary of Samuel Pepys, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The diarist spends these days visiting Greenwich, Whitehall, the Wardrobe, the office, and the Theatre, while dining and drinking with various acquaintances. Lieutenant Lambert, now Captain of the Norwich, explains ships to him during a water journey to Greenwich. The diarist learns from my Lord that Mr. Townsend is to reveal the whole mystery of the Wardrobe and that he may become Townsend's deputy. He sees Bartholomew Faire at the Theatre, visits the Wardrobe with his wife, and discusses ecclesiastical matters with Dean Fuller.

records.l: Lieutenant Lambert, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Lieutenant Lambert has been made Captain of the Norwich. He takes the diarist by water to Greenwich, explains various matters concerning ships, and later accompanies him to Mr. Holland's house.

records.l: Whitehall, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The diarist goes to Whitehall several times, seeking my Lord and later meeting Dean Fuller there. He also returns to Whitehall after visiting Mr. Pierce and drinks with Mr. Symons at the Swan tavern.

records.l: Lord Sandwich, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: My Lord tells the diarist to go to Mr. Townsend, who is to disclose the whole mystery of the Wardrobe to him. He also says that the diarist will be made deputy to Mr. Townsend in case Townsend dies during my Lord's absence.

records.l: the Wardrobe, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The diarist visits the Wardrobe, where he dines with my Lady and is kindly treated. He later brings his wife there to dine, and she is received with considerable attention.

records.l: Mr. Townsend, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Mr. Townsend has been ordered by my Lord to reveal the whole mystery of the Wardrobe to the diarist and no one else. The diarist is to become his deputy because of the possibility of Townsend's death during my Lord's absence.

records.l: the Wardrobe business, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The diarist is promised an important role in the Wardrobe administration: my Lord intends to make him deputy to Mr. Townsend. Townsend is to explain the administration's whole mystery to him.

records.l: the Theatre, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The diarist goes to the Theatre with Mr. Shepley and Mr. Creed and sees Bartholomew Faire. He considers the play admirable and well acted, though excessively profane and abusive.

records.l: Bartholomew Faire, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Bartholomew Faire is performed at the Theatre for the first time in the present day. The diarist finds it most admirable and well acted, but too profane and abusive.

records.l: the narrator's wife, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The diarist's wife wears a black silk gown laced all over with black gimp lace and looks very pretty in it. She walks with him to the Wardrobe, dines there, and remains with my Lady after the diarist leaves.

records.l: The Diary of Samuel Pepys, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The narrator's lord is to go to Algier to settle business, put the fleet in order, and return to Lisbone with three ships to meet the following fleet. He entrusts the narrator with overseeing the great preparation during his absence under orders from my Lord Chancellor and Edward Montagu. The office agrees to write to the Duke of York about its severe shortage of money and inability to obtain supplies without personal security. The office's credit has fallen so low that suppliers will no longer sell to it without such security.

records.l: fleet, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The fleet is to be put in order at Algier. The narrator's lord is to return to Lisbone with three ships and meet the fleet that is to follow him.

records.l: my Lord Chancellor, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: My Lord Chancellor is to give the narrator orders concerning the great preparation during the narrator's lord's absence.

records.l: Edward Montagu, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Edward Montagu is to give the narrator orders concerning the great preparation during the narrator's lord's absence.

records.l: Lord Sandwich, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The narrator's lord is to go to Algier to settle business and put the fleet in order there, then return to Lisbone with three ships. He entrusts the narrator with overseeing the great preparation during his absence.

records.l: great preparation, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The great preparation is to be overseen by the narrator during the narrator's lord's absence, under orders from my Lord Chancellor and Edward Montagu.

records.l: the Navy Office, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The office agrees to write to the Duke of York about its sad condition and lack of money. Its men are unable to serve it further without money.

records.l: Sir George Carteret, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Sir G. Carteret attends the office and joins in agreeing on a letter to the Duke of York about the office's financial difficulties.

records.l: Duke of York, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The office is to receive a letter informing him of its lack of money, its inability to obtain further supplies, and the low state of its credit.

records.l: money, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The office lacks money, and its men are not able to serve it more without some money.

records.l: the office's credit, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The office's credit has fallen so low that no one will sell it anything without personal security from those involved.

records.l: The Diary of Samuel Pepys, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The narrator spends time with Captain Rolt, Ferrers, and others before arranging a cloth purchase for my Lord and obtaining an advance through Alderman Backwell. On the 13th, the narrator accompanies my Lord from Whitehall to Deptford and boards the Dutch yacht with him. My Lord becomes angry when W. Howe delays bringing his things, but they eventually sail, and the narrator takes leave of my Lord with expressions of respect and a five-gun salute. The narrator then returns toward London by boat with Captain Ferrers.

records.l: Samuel Pepys, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The narrator visits Lambeth, works at home, and writes a letter to the Duke. He arranges for £300 of cloth to be purchased for my Lord through Alderman Backwell, accompanies my Lord to Deptford, and takes leave of him aboard the Dutch yacht before returning toward London with Captain Ferrers.

records.l: Lord Sandwich, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: My Lord requires £300 worth of cloth to give as presents among the Turks in Barbary. He travels from Whitehall to Deptford, boards the Dutch yacht, becomes angry when W. Howe is late with his things, and then sails after taking leave of the King and his friends.

records.l: the cloth, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The cloth is intended for presents to the Turks in Barbary. Mr. Shaw offers the narrator £300 for my Lord to purchase it with, and my Lord orders Mr. Creed to advance that amount through Alderman Backwell.

records.l: Dutch yacht, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The Dutch yacht is boarded by my Lord and the narrator at Deptford. It waits while W. Howe brings my Lord's things, then sails from Erith after dinner.

records.l: The Diary of Samuel Pepys, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The diarist manages the purchase and shipment of cloth for my Lord, arranging scarlet, purple, and black cloth and linen, and eventually sending it by a Margate Hoy after other plans fail. He recovers from a painful cold and spends several days overseeing painters who finish work on his stairs. He visits friends and relatives, including my father, my Lady, Captain Lambert's household, and Jack Cole, and attends to office and financial business. By the end of the unit, he is pleased with the completed stairs and relieved of his illness and household troubles.

records.l: Samuel Pepys, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The diarist arranges the purchase and delivery of cloth for my Lord, attends to office, household, and financial matters, and visits family and friends. He recovers from his illness, supervises the painters' work on his stairs, and is pleased when it is completed.

records.l: the diarist's father, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: My father advises and assists with the cloth business. He visits the diarist, drinks his morning draft with him, discusses the cloth, and helps resolve on two pieces each of scarlet, purple, and black, with £50 in linen.

records.l: Lord Sandwich, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: My Lord is the intended recipient of the cloth. The diarist writes to him to report what has been arranged.

records.l: the painters, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The painters work on the diarist's stairs. Their progress causes the diarist some vexation because of delays, but they finish the work by the 20th, to his great content.

records.l: a Margate Hoy, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: A Margate Hoy is hired to carry the cloth and related goods. The diarist sends the things aboard it late at night, hoping they will reach the Downs by the following night.

records.l: the cloth, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The cloth is being bought for my Lord and consists of two pieces of scarlet, two of purple, and two of black, together with £50 in linen. The diarist struggles to find a reliable way to send it.

records.l: garden stairs, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The stairs are being painted by the diarist's workmen. The work is finished by the 20th and pleases the diarist greatly.

records.l: the cloth shipment, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The cloth shipment is delayed when the purser of the King's yacht does not come for it and the diarist learns that the Duke of York has already departed. After considering sending it by carrier or by a vessel hired for the purpose, he sends it by a Margate Hoy.

records.l: the diarist's illness, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The diarist's illness is a painful cold caused by playing in the water. He stays home, keeps warm, breaks wind, and gains relief; by the 19th he reports that he is very well again.

records.l: the painters' work, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The painters' work on the stairs is delayed and troubles the diarist for much of the 18th and 19th. It is completed on the 20th, leaving him greatly content.

records.l: The Diary of Samuel Pepys, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The narrator met uncle Wight at the Exchequer and went home with him to dinner. At dinner, the narrator and Mr. Norbury discussed Mr. Norbury's wife's house and land at Brampton, which the narrator found too much to buy. The narrator later went to the office and was pleased to see the house beginning to be clean. On the 22nd, the narrator dined with Lord Crew and was very much made of by Lord Crew and his lady.

records.l: uncle Wight, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The narrator met uncle Wight at the Exchequer and went home with him to dinner.

records.l: Mr. Norbury, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Mr. Norbury discussed his wife's house and land at Brampton with the narrator over dinner.

records.l: Mr. Norbury's house and land at Brampton, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The narrator learned about Mr. Norbury's wife's house and land at Brampton and found it too much to buy.

records.l: Lord Crew, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The narrator dined with Lord Crew on the 22nd and was very much made of by Lord Crew and his lady.

records.l: The Diary of Samuel Pepys, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Pepys spent time with Luellin and Blirton, attended church, socialized with Sir W. Batten and others, and visited Islington. He was pleased that his house had become very clean and neat, and his father came to see it on Midsummer-day. Elizabeth Pepys was unwell, with a sore belly that she believed had become dangerous. At Graye’s Inn Walks, Pepys considered Mrs. Frances Butler the greatest beauty he had ever seen.

records.l: the narrator's house, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Pepys found his house very clean and was greatly pleased with it. On Midsummer-day, his father came to see it after it was finished and found it very neat.

records.l: the narrator's wife, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Elizabeth Pepys was not well, so Pepys went with Sir W. Batten to dinner instead of remaining at home. Dr. Williams came to see her, as her sore belly had grown dangerous in her opinion.

records.l: Sir W. Batten, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Sir W. Batten accompanied Pepys home to dinner and later spent time with him at his own house. He was among the company who went to church after dinner.

records.l: Mrs. Frances Butler, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Pepys saw Mrs. Frances Butler at Graye’s Inn Walks and described her as the greatest beauty he had ever seen. She was identified as Monsieur L'Impertinent’s sister.

records.l: Pepys's wife's illness, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Pepys’s wife was unwell, and her sore belly was described as having become dangerous as she thought. Dr. Williams came to see her.

records.l: The Diary of Samuel Pepys, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The diarist begins singing lessons with Mr. Mage and spends time with family and visitors. He learns from a letter from his aunt that Robert has become ill with dizziness, prompting his father to travel to attend to Robert's business. The diarist discusses with his father how to present a proposed land purchase to Robert, offering £600 immediately and £150 annually for land yielding £50 per year. He later attends a performance of "Bartholomew Fayre" with Lady Batten, Mrs. Rebecca Allen, Mrs. Thompson, and others.

records.l: the diarist's father, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The diarist's father learns from the letter from the diarist's aunt that Robert is seriously unwell and needs help with his business. He plans to travel to Robert, and the diarist advises him on how to discuss the proposed land purchase.

records.l: Sir W. Batten, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Sir William Batten sits with the diarist and others until late, and the diarist provides a substantial collation. Later, the diarist stays late at Sir William Batten's house after attending "Bartholomew Fayre."

records.l: the letter from the diarist's aunt, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The letter informs the diarist's father that Robert has been taken with dizziness in his head and that his help is wanted with Robert's business. The letter leads the diarist's father to plan a journey to Robert.

records.l: Aunt Fenner, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The diarist's aunt writes to the diarist's father that Robert is seriously unwell and requires his assistance.

records.l: uncle Robert, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Robert is suffering from dizziness in his head, and his condition is considered serious. His business requires the diarist's father's attention, and the diarist wants his father to discuss buying land with him.

records.l: land, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The diarist is considering buying land that would yield £50 per year. He proposes paying £600 immediately and £150 annually for the remainder.

records.l: the land-purchase plan, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The diarist plans to have his father present the purchase as an offer of £600 in ready money followed by £150 per year until the price is complete. He wants Robert to think he is a greater saver than he really is, since he has no more than £500 in ready money.

records.l: Bartholomew Faire, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: "Bartholomew Fayre" is performed very well, and the diarist attends the performance with Lady Batten, Mrs. Rebecca Allen, Mrs. Thompson, and others in two coaches.

records.l: The Diary of Samuel Pepys, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The writer spent the 28th practising singing, visiting his Lady, working at the office, and going with Sir W. Pen to Moorefields to watch wrestling. On the 29th, the writer and both Sir Williams examined delays in preparing ships at Deptford, then met Mr. Chetwind, Gregory, Hartlibb, and Mr. Kipps at the Bell at the Maypole in the Strand. Mr. Chetwind, formerly consumptive, had become very fat and sallow from chewing tobacco and praised Hooker's Ecclesiastical Polity as the book that made him a Christian. On the 30th, the writer observed that the trade of briefs had become so constant that he and others resolved to give no more to them.

records.l: Sir W. Pen, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Sir W. Pen accompanied the writer in his coach to Moorefields, where they walked and watched wrestling between north and west countrymen.

records.l: our old club, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Several members of the writer's old club, including Mr. Chetwind, Gregory, and Hartlibb, met with the writer at the Bell at the Maypole in the Strand and talked and drank with much pleasure.

records.l: Mr. Chetwind, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Mr. Chetwind had become very fat and sallow from chewing tobacco, whereas he had previously been consumptive. He commended Hooker's Ecclesiastical Polity as the best book and the only one that had made him a Christian.

records.l: the Bell at the Maypole in the Strand, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The Bell at the Maypole in the Strand was the place where the writer met Mr. Chetwind, Gregory, Hartlibb, and Mr. Kipps for drinking and conversation.

records.l: Hooker's Ecclesiastical Polity, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Hooker's Ecclesiastical Polity was praised by Mr. Chetwind as the best book and the only one that had made him a Christian. The writer decided to buy it shortly.

records.l: trade of briefs, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The trade of briefs had become a constant practice every Sunday. The writer and others resolved to give no more to it.

records.l: The Diary of Samuel Pepys, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The speaker attended a sermon, had dinner with his wife, and went to Whitehall with Sir Williams to report to the Duke of York about why the ships had not been sent out. The ships could not leave the river because the wind was against them. The speaker later walked alone in Graye's Inn Walk, returned home tired, and found his wife out of order but not sick. The Portuguese Embassador came to White Hall to take leave of the King before ending matters with the Queen and sending her over.

records.l: Duke of York, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The Duke of York met the speaker and Sir Williams at Whitehall to receive an account of where the fault lay in the failure to send out the ships.

records.l: Whitehall, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The speaker went to Whitehall with Sir Williams and met the Duke of York there. The Portuguese Embassador also came to White Hall to take leave of the King.

records.l: Portuguese Embassador, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The Portuguese Embassador came to White Hall to take leave of the King.

records.l: Queen, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The Portuguese Embassador was going to end all with the Queen and send her over. The speaker hoped to make up his expenses by helping prepare things to send with the next fleet to the Queen.

records.l: order to report on the ships, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: An order had been sent to the speaker and Sir Williams the previous day to give the Duke of York an account of where the fault lay in the ships not being sent out.

records.l: ships, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The ships could not get out of the river because the wind had been against them.

records.l: failure to send out the ships, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The failure to send out the ships was attributed solely to the wind being against them, which prevented them from leaving the river.

records.l: Portuguese ambassador's departure and arrangements for the Queen, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The Portuguese Embassador came to take leave of the King and was going to end all with the Queen and send her over.

records.l: fleet, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The speaker hoped to recover his recent expenses during the summer by helping get things ready to send with the next fleet to the Queen.

records.l: The Diary of Samuel Pepys, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, JULY 1661 July 1st.
records.s: The diarist bought household goods, including a chest of drawers and an Indian gown, attended to office and domestic affairs, and continued singing lessons with Theodore Goodgroome. He visited Sir William Davenant's Opera, where the second part of "The Siege of Rhodes" was performed for the King and the Queen of Bohemia, though the Eunuch was hissed off the stage. He also learned of the serious illness of his uncle and the death of Mr. Saml. Crew from spotted fever. On July 4th, he saw "Claracilla" at the Theatre and noted that the house was unusually empty because of the Opera.

records.l: Samuel Pepys, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, JULY 1661 July 1st.
records.s: The diarist bought a chest of drawers for his chamber and an Indian gown, attended to business at Westminster and the office, and took singing lessons with Theodore Goodgroome. He visited Sir William Davenant's Opera and the Theatre, wrote letters to his Lord at sea, and learned of his uncle's illness and Mr. Saml. Crew's death.

records.l: the Theatre, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, JULY 1661 July 1st.
records.s: The Theatre presented "Claracilla" on July 4th, which the diarist saw for the first time and considered well acted. The house, formerly very crowded, was unusually empty because the Opera had begun.

records.l: the Opera, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, JULY 1661 July 1st.
records.s: Sir William Davenant's Opera had begun four days earlier when the diarist attended it on July 2nd. The performance was delayed while waiting for the King and the Queen of Bohemia, and a broken board caused dust to fall on the ladies and men. The scene was described as very fine and magnificent, and the acting was generally good.

records.l: The Siege of Rhodes, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, JULY 1661 July 1st.
records.s: The second part of "The Siege of Rhodes" was acted at Sir William Davenant's Opera on July 2nd. The Eunuch performed so poorly that he was hissed off the stage.

records.l: Claracilla, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, JULY 1661 July 1st.
records.s: "Claracilla" was performed at the Theatre on July 4th. The diarist saw it for the first time and thought it well acted.

records.l: The Diary of Samuel Pepys, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The narrator travels from London to Brampton after learning that his uncle Robert has died, finding his father well and the corpse awaiting burial. He and his father read uncle Robert's will, arranged the burial, and spent the following week sorting his papers and investigating the estate, which proved less substantial and more disorganized than expected. Tom Trice entered a caveat on behalf of his mother, while the missing surrenders of the copyhold land created further legal trouble. The narrator later visits Cambridge and travels on to Impington to see his elderly uncle Talbot Pepys.

records.l: uncle Wight, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The narrator visited uncle Wight after learning of uncle Robert's death and told him the news. Earlier, uncle Wight had been merry with the narrator at the Mitre, though he was offended that the narrator's father had gone to Brampton without informing him.

records.l: uncle Robert, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Uncle Robert died on the 5th, and the narrator traveled to Brampton for his funeral and to examine his affairs. His will was found to provide reasonably well for the narrator's family and other relatives, although his estate and papers were less satisfactory than expected.

records.l: Brampton, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The narrator rode to Brampton after uncle Robert's death and found his father there. He remained there through the following week while the family arranged the burial, sorted papers, and dealt with disputes over the estate.

records.l: the diarist's father, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The narrator found his father well at Brampton and stayed with him there. They read uncle Robert's will together, examined the property, and worked through the deceased man's papers, while the narrator tried not to increase his father's troubles.

records.l: uncle Robert's corpse, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Uncle Robert's corpse was in a coffin on joint-stools in the hall at Brampton. Because it began to smell, the narrator had it moved into the yard for the night, where two men watched it.

records.l: aunt (uncle Robert's widow), The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The narrator found his aunt in bed in a condition he described as extremely dirty and unpleasant. He was repeatedly troubled by what he called her ugly and disagreeable humours during the week at Brampton.

records.l: the will, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The narrator and his father read uncle Robert's will on the morning after his arrival. Although the narrator received little immediately and would receive more only after his father's death, he was pleased that the will provided well for the family and other relatives.

records.l: burial of uncle Robert, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Uncle Robert was buried at the church on Sunday after the family prepared ribbons and gloves. Mr. Taylor conducted the burial, and Mr. Turners preached a funeral sermon praising the deceased's widely known honesty.

records.l: Tom Trice, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Tom Trice put in a caveat on behalf of his mother, who had received nothing from uncle Robert's will. This development troubled the narrator and his father.

records.l: caveat against the estate, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: A caveat was entered against the family in behalf of Tom Trice's mother, who was excluded from uncle Robert's will for reasons expressed there. The caveat added to the family's uncertainty about the inheritance.

records.l: uncle Robert's estate, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The estate appeared to be worth much less than the narrator and the general public had expected. The family also faced difficulty because the surrenders of the copyhold land could not be found, and they sought legal advice from Mr. Philips.

records.l: uncle Robert's papers, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The narrator's father examined uncle Robert's papers while the narrator worked through them during the week. The papers were badly disorganized, making them difficult to understand and causing the narrator considerable distress.

records.l: copyhold land, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The surrenders for uncle Robert's copyhold land were missing. Without them, the land would pass to the heir at law rather than to the intended beneficiaries.

records.l: Cambridge, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The narrator rode to Cambridge on the 15th and arrived early in the morning. He visited Christ College, King's College chapel, the Rose tavern, and friends connected with the university before riding onward.

records.l: Impington, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: After leaving Cambridge, the narrator rode to Impington. There he found his elderly uncle Talbot Pepys.

records.l: Talbot Pepys, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The narrator visited his old uncle Talbot Pepys at Impington after traveling through Cambridge. The text identifies him as the sixth son of John Pepys of Impington, a former Cambridge-educated barrister and public official.

records.l: The Diary of Samuel Pepys, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Samuel Pepys spends 16–31 October arranging his uncle’s will and estate with his father, the Trices, Sir Robert Bernard, Mr. Moore, and others. An agreement is reached for Pepys’s aunt to leave the house in return for £10, while other disputes are left to the law, but Pepys remains worried that debts and legal claims will reduce the inheritance. He returns from Brampton to London, resumes work at the Navy Office, manages family and household affairs, and visits theatres, friends, and relatives. In London he follows disputes between Parliament’s Houses and hears reports about King Charles II, the Lord Chancellor, and national politics.

records.l: Samuel Pepys, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Samuel Pepys reviews and manages his uncle’s will, papers, debts, surrenders, and property with advice from Dr. John Pepys, Sir Robert Bernard, Mr. Moore, and others. He travels from Brampton to London, resumes business at the Navy Office, visits friends and theatres, and worries that the estate will yield less than expected.

records.l: the will, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The will is read and reviewed with Dr. John Pepys, Sir Robert Bernard, Mr. Moore, and several family members. Mr. Moore advises that the three witnesses, although legatees, do not invalidate it, but Pepys continues to expect trouble over its interpretation and execution.

records.l: Pepys family estate, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The estate includes land, crops, copyhold interests, houses, money, debts, and surrenders. Pepys learns that about £500 has been found and that the estate may contain more, but he fears that debts and legal claims will substantially reduce the inheritance; he publicly says it amounts to £200 a year in land besides money.

records.l: the diarist's father, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Samuel Pepys’s father works with him at Brampton to put the estate in order, including letting the crop and arranging for Stankes to manage the business. He participates in discussions with the Trices and others about the will, remains alone at Brampton after Samuel’s return to London, and causes concern over whether he will profit from his London house rather than leave it to Tom.

records.l: uncle Robert's corpse, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Samuel Pepys’s uncle’s will and papers become the central business of the unit. His estate is believed by Thomas Pepys to contain more than the roughly £500 already found but little money overall; a debt of £164 from Piggott may pass with the debts to the heir at law, and his surrender of Sturtlow is delivered to Samuel through William Luffe.

records.l: Mr. Moore, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Mr. Moore advises Samuel Pepys that the will’s three witnesses being legatees does not harm the will. He later reads the will with Samuel, gives further opinions, accompanies him to an ordinary and the Theatre, and walks with him in London.

records.l: Brampton, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Brampton is where Samuel Pepys and his father organize the uncle’s affairs, inspect and manage lands, negotiate with relatives, and settle an agreement concerning the aunt’s departure from the house. Samuel leaves Brampton for London on the 22nd, while his father remains there afterward.

records.l: London, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Samuel Pepys returns to London on the 22nd and resumes his household, social, theatrical, and official activities there. He visits Whitehall, Westminster Hall, the Exchange, the Wardrobe, the City, and the Navy Office while continuing to investigate the uncle’s estate.

records.l: the narrator's wife, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Samuel Pepys’s wife accompanies him by water to Whitehall and assists with household and family visits. She tells him that their silver tankard has been stolen, later gives him his linen to keep in his own custody, and visits Sir William Pen’s daughter.

records.l: King Charles II, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: King Charles II is seen traveling by barge to adjourn Parliament. Samuel hears that the King may be forced to favor Presbytery or lose the City’s support, and that although the King does not love the Lord Chancellor as a companion, he needs him for policy and service.

records.l: Parliament, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Parliament is in disorder and is expected to be adjourned for several months, though the adjournment is delayed. The two Houses dispute the Lords’ privilege not to have their houses searched, preventing agreement on the Commons’ bill concerning pamphlets and seditious books.

records.l: the Navy Office, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Samuel Pepys returns to work at the Navy Office and takes pleasure in speaking with persons of quality and exercising authority. He attends to official business there, including matters concerning Tangier, and helps consider whether Sir Robert Ford’s house could be added to the office.

records.l: will litigation, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The will dispute produces negotiations among Samuel Pepys, his father, the Trices, Mr. Greene, and others. They agree that Samuel’s aunt will leave the house in return for £10, while other matters will be left to the law; Samuel also seeks counsel about debts, surrenders, the heir at law, and the forthcoming assizes.

records.l: The Diary of Samuel Pepys, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, AUGUST 1661 August 1st.
records.s: On August 1, Sir Williams both, the narrator, the narrator’s wife, and Mrs. Margarett Pen went by coach to Walthamstow to visit Mrs. Browne. The narrator gave Mrs. Browne six silver spoons for her boy, and the party ate a venison pasty and were merry. They heard an allegation that Lady Batten had been a man’s whore and tried unsuccessfully to reconcile the matter. On August 2, Dr. Thos. Pepys dined with the narrator, and Tom visited before the narrator prepared to travel on horseback to Cambridge.

records.l: Sir Williams both, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, AUGUST 1661 August 1st.
records.s: Sir Williams both went by coach with the narrator, the narrator’s wife, and Mrs. Margarett Pen to Walthamstow on August 1.

records.l: the narrator's wife, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, AUGUST 1661 August 1st.
records.s: The narrator’s wife went by coach with the narrator, Sir Williams both, and Mrs. Margarett Pen to visit Mrs. Browne at Walthamstow.

records.l: Mrs. Margarett Pen, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, AUGUST 1661 August 1st.
records.s: Mrs. Margarett Pen accompanied the narrator and the others to Walthamstow. It was the first time the narrator had seen her since she came from Ireland.

records.l: Mrs. Browne, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, AUGUST 1661 August 1st.
records.s: Mrs. Browne was visited at Walthamstow by the narrator and the others. The narrator gave her six silver spoons for her boy, and the party ate a venison pasty and were merry.

records.l: Lady Batten, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, AUGUST 1661 August 1st.
records.s: Lady Batten was the subject of a report that she had been a man’s whore. She was known to have left her estate to the person connected with the report, and an attempt to reconcile the matter failed.

records.l: Samuel Pepys's uncle Thomas, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, AUGUST 1661 August 1st.
records.s: Dr. Thos. Pepys dined with the narrator on August 2 after the narrator had spent the morning at the office.

records.l: Tom, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, AUGUST 1661 August 1st.
records.s: Tom, the narrator’s brother, came to the narrator after Dr. Thos. Pepys’s dinner on August 2.

records.l: Walthamstow, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, AUGUST 1661 August 1st.
records.s: Walthamstow was the destination of the August 1 coach journey, where the narrator and the others visited Mrs. Browne.

records.l: Cambridge, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, AUGUST 1661 August 1st.
records.s: Cambridge was the narrator’s intended destination after he prepared to travel there on horseback on August 2.

records.l: the allegation about Lady Batten, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, AUGUST 1661 August 1st.
records.s: The allegation was that Lady Batten had been a man’s whore. The narrator believed the story was true, but an attempt to reconcile the matter failed.

records.l: the visit to Walthamstow, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, AUGUST 1661 August 1st.
records.s: The visit to Walthamstow took place on August 1, with Sir Williams both, the narrator, the narrator’s wife, and Mrs. Margarett Pen traveling by coach to see Mrs. Browne. The party ate a hot venison pasty, were merry, and returned home at night.

records.l: the journey to Cambridge, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, AUGUST 1661 August 1st.
records.s: The narrator prepared for a journey to Cambridge on horseback after Tom came to him on August 2.

records.l: The Diary of Samuel Pepys, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Samuel Pepys travels through Cambridge, Huntingdon, Brampton, and surrounding places to consult Roger Pepys, his father, relatives, tenants, and others about his uncle's will and related family business. Roger Pepys explains his concerns about young men's conduct in Parliament and the risk of renewed war. After returning to London, Pepys attends to Privy Seal business, visits Whitehall, and works with Mr. Moore and Lord Roberts while waiting for delayed proceedings. He also manages social and family matters, including his wife's assistance to Mrs. Hater, his father's affairs, and an outing to the theatre with my Lady's household.

records.l: Roger Pepys, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Roger Pepys accompanies Pepys from Cambridge to Impington and gives him a respectful welcome. He explains the expected difficulties concerning the uncle's will and later discusses his serious concerns about Parliament, young men's opposition to serious business, profanity, and the possibility of renewed war.

records.l: Cambridge, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Pepys reaches Cambridge after riding with a letter-carrier and attends the Assizes at Castle Hill. He dines at Trinity Hall, drinks with Mr. Pechell and others at the Rose, and observes tensions between older university doctors and better scholars whom they had found there.

records.l: Parliament, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Roger Pepys reports that young men in Parliament have opposed measures advanced by serious men. He considers their profane conduct a danger that could spoil affairs and bring the country into war again.

records.l: Huntingdon, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Pepys travels to Huntingdon but finds that the judges have not arrived. He drinks there with Thomas Trice and Mr. Phillips before returning to Brampton.

records.l: Brampton, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Pepys finds his father well at Brampton and is glad that his aunt has left, although her departure costs the family £10. He returns there after visiting Yelling and Graveley, and later leaves from Brampton to ride toward London.

records.l: the diarist's father, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Pepys finds his father well at Brampton and later returns with him to Gorum's to speak with Thomas Trice. His father notices that Pepys has been drinking, something he had never seen or heard of before, and later returns from Brampton to London in good health.

records.l: Quakers, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Pepys observes that the Quakers continue to be present in Baldwick and elsewhere, and that they seem to be increasing rather than diminishing.

records.l: London, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Pepys returns to London after traveling from Brampton through Baldwick and finds everyone well at home, at his father's, and at my Lady's. He resumes his office and Privy Seal duties there.

records.l: Lady Sandwich, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Pepys visits my Lady after returning to London and finds her household merry and well. He later takes two young gentlemen, two ladies, and Captain Ferrers to the Theatre and then brings them home for fruit and wine.

records.l: Mr. Moore, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Mr. Moore tells Pepys that he is needed for the next day's Seal day because it is Pepys's month to attend Lord Roberts. He works with Pepys at the Privy Seal and reads over the bills when Lord Roberts finally arrives.

records.l: the Privy Seal, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The Privy Seal business is delayed because Lord Roberts does not appear during the morning or afternoon of the 8th. On the 9th, Lord Roberts arrives after four o'clock, questions Pepys about his deputation, and then allows the bills to be read and the business to conclude successfully.

records.l: Whitehall, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Pepys goes to Whitehall early on the 8th and waits there for Lord Roberts at the Privy Seal. He returns there on the 9th, and after Lord Roberts arrives they go to his chamber over the gate.

records.l: Lord Privy Seal, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Lord Roberts, the Lord Privy Seal, fails to attend during the morning and afternoon of the 8th, frustrating Pepys and causing concern about delays and the treatment of the Privy Seal clerks. On the 9th he asks Pepys what deputation he has from his lord, accepts Pepys's explanation, and completes the business.

records.l: Sir George Carteret, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Sir George Carteret had invited some officers to dine at Deptford. Pepys goes out when he hears Carteret is coming to see whether he will invite him, but Carteret does not send for him, which troubles Pepys somewhat.

records.l: the narrator's wife, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Pepys's wife goes with Mr. Hater when he comes to fetch her because his wife is falling into labour. She is also expected to return from Brampton in about three weeks, possibly traveling with Pepys's father.

records.l: Pepys family business, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Pepys travels through Brampton, Yelling, and Graveley to investigate family business and property matters. He consults his father, Roger Pepys, his cousin Nightingale, Chancler, Jackson, and others, gaining information about the Graveley lands and related obligations.

records.l: the will, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Pepys discusses his uncle's will at length with Roger Pepys at Impington. Roger gives him useful information about what to expect and do, warns that the matter will bring considerable trouble, and later agrees to read the Captain's will with Pepys's uncles for their satisfaction.

records.l: Privy Seal business, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Pepys is required to attend Lord Roberts at the Seal because it is his month of duty. After delays on the 8th, he and Mr. Moore complete the reading of the bills on the 9th; Mons. Eschar is also waiting there for a warrant for £5,000 for the Earl of Sandwich's preparation for Portugal.

records.l: Parliamentary conflict, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Roger Pepys describes conflict in Parliament between young men who opposed measures and serious men who advanced them. He also reports that the young men were exceptionally profane and might cause renewed war.

records.l: Quaker movement, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Pepys reports that the Quaker movement continues in Baldwick and in every other place he visits. He believes it is growing rather than declining.

records.l: The Diary of Samuel Pepys, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Samuel Pepys records concern over Lord Hinchingbroke’s illness and Lord Sandwich’s sickness at Alicante, along with the effects on Lord Sandwich’s family. Lord Hinchingbroke develops a severe illness feared to be smallpox but improves, while Lord Sandwich is reported to have recovered from pain and fever and expects to go aboard. Pepys and other Navy officials report the Navy’s lack of money to the Duke of York, as the Navy Office’s bills are being offered at a 20 percent loss. The unit also describes widespread sickness, anxiety about the Court, and Pepys’s visits to plays, taverns, and family and official gatherings.

records.l: Samuel Pepys, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Samuel Pepys visits Lord Hinchingbroke during his illness, consults with Lady Sandwich, and helps house her three younger sons to protect them from possible smallpox. He reports the Navy’s financial difficulties to the Duke of York with Sir W. Batten and Sir W. Pen, follows news of Lord Sandwich’s health, attends plays and social gatherings, and worries that his fondness for plays is distracting him from business.

records.l: Lord Hinchingbroke, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Lord Hinchingbroke becomes very ill and is feared to have smallpox after Pepys gives fruit to his family. He improves over the following days, eventually sitting up and walking about his chamber.

records.l: Lady Sandwich, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Lady Sandwich consults with Samuel Pepys about Lord Hinchingbroke’s illness and sends her three other sons, Sidney, Oliver, and John, to Pepys’s house for fear of smallpox. She later has the children fetched to dine with her.

records.l: Lord Sandwich, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Lord Sandwich is reported to be sick ashore at Alicante, causing Pepys serious concern about his health and his family’s condition. A letter from Mr. Creed says that Lord Sandwich has been relieved of his pain and fever and hopes to go aboard within a day or two.

records.l: Sir W. Batten, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Sir W. Batten joins Samuel Pepys and Sir W. Pen in waiting on the Duke of York to report the Navy’s lack of money. He later meets Pepys and Sir W. Pen at the Dolphin.

records.l: Sir W. Pen, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Sir W. Pen joins Pepys and Sir W. Batten in reporting the Navy’s financial condition to the Duke of York. He later takes Pepys and Captain Ferrers from the Theatre, visits the Dolphin, and helps take Captain Ferrers home.

records.l: Lord Sandwich's family, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Lord Sandwich’s family is placed under strain by his illness at Alicante. Lady Sandwich sends Sidney, Oliver, and John to Pepys’s house while Lord Hinchingbroke is ill, and Pepys expresses relief that he can provide this service.

records.l: the Navy Office, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: At the Navy Office, Pepys and the other officials have little business because clerks are attending the burial of Tom Whitton. The officials report the Navy’s financial condition and the severe losses on the Office’s bills to the Duke of York.

records.l: Alicante, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Alicante is where Lord Sandwich is reported to be sick ashore before his recovery is communicated by letter.

records.l: the smallpox, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The smallpox is feared to be the cause of Lord Hinchingbroke’s severe illness. Because of this fear, Lady Sandwich sends Sidney, Oliver, and John to stay at Pepys’s house.

records.l: the fever, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Lord Sandwich is reported to have recovered from his fever. A widespread fever is also said to be affecting people throughout the City and country.

records.l: Lord Sandwich's illness, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Lord Sandwich’s illness at Alicante causes Pepys to fear for the future of his family. Mr. Creed later reports that the pain and fever have left him and that he may soon return aboard.

records.l: Lord Hinchingbroke's illness, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Lord Hinchingbroke’s illness is initially severe, with great fear that it is smallpox. He steadily improves and is described as sitting up and walking about his chamber.

records.l: the Navy's financial crisis, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The Navy is suffering from a lack of money, and its bills are being offered on the Exchange at a 20 percent loss. The Duke of York is troubled by the situation and says he will speak to the King and Council.

records.l: the sickness in City and country, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: A severe and unusually widespread sickness, described as a sort of fever, is affecting both the City and the country. Tom Fuller and Dr. Nichols, Dean of Paul's, have died from it, and Lord General Monk is dangerously ill.

records.l: the Court, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Ned Pickering complains openly about the Court’s lewdness and beggary. Pepys fears that such conditions may bring everything to ruin again.

records.l: The Diary of Samuel Pepys, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The narrator attends to sealing business, office affairs, family matters, and social visits from the 19th through the 24th. He helps negotiate the addition of Sir R. Ford’s house to the office, agreeing to pay him £200 per year, and spends time arranging a possible marriage between his brother Tom and Mrs. Whately’s daughter. He visits relatives and associates, takes his wife to the Opera, and observes family tensions, mourning, and the death of his aunt Fenner. He also sees a baboon brought from Guiny and receives a visit from Captain Isham before his voyage to Portugal.

records.l: Samuel Pepys, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The narrator conducts sealing business at Worcester House and with the Lord Privy Seal, walks home after losing his coach, and spends time with Mr. Marsh and others. He organizes papers, visits family and associates, assists with proving his uncle’s will, takes his wife to see "The Witts" at the Opera, and attends to various office and household matters. He is troubled by his parents’ discontent and by losing the company of the children, who his Lady keeps at home. He views a baboon brought from Guiny and believes it may understand English and perhaps be taught to speak or make signs.

records.l: the Navy Office, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The office reaches an agreement with Sir R. Ford to add his house to its quarters, completing the arrangement for £200 per year. The narrator spends the morning of the 24th at the office conducting business.

records.l: the diarist's father, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The narrator’s father accompanies him to Dr. Williams and to Mrs. Whately’s household while discussing a possible marriage for Tom. He helps examine and prove his uncle’s will with Tom Trice and Dr. Williams. He is present with the narrator and uncle Wight at an overheated gathering at his brother’s house, and later he and the narrator find the narrator’s mother discontented and unquiet.

records.l: the narrator's wife, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The narrator’s wife accompanies him to his uncle Fenner’s house and to his aunt Wight’s house, where they supped on Westphalia ham. She meets the narrator by appointment at W. Joyce’s, goes with him to the Opera to see "The Witts," and then visits his Lady at the Wardrobe.

records.l: the proposal of marriage, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The proposal concerns Mrs. Whately’s daughter as a possible wife for the narrator’s brother Tom. The narrator and his father discuss it with Mrs. Terry and Mrs. Whately; Mrs. Whately is eager for it to proceed but worries that her daughter is too young and that her portion is insufficient, although she offers £200 down. The daughter is described as well-favoured, modest, and very young, and the narrator thinks she would suit his brother; the matter awaits word from her father, who is at Hatfield.

records.l: The Diary of Samuel Pepys, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The diarist manages family, household, legal, and financial affairs while attending theatres, taverns, and social gatherings. He arranges for Pall to go into the country, bids farewell to Jane as she leaves for her mother, and worries about his father’s finances, Tom’s future, and his wife’s brother Balty. Lord Sandwich has recovered from a severe fever at Alicante, while Lord Hinchingbrooke and his brother depart for France. The diarist ends the month concerned about his borrowing, indulgence in plays and pleasure, court disorder, and clerical conduct.

records.l: Samuel Pepys, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The diarist handles family accounts, legal business, household changes, and arrangements concerning Pall and Jane. He attends several theatre performances and social gatherings, but recognizes that his spending and pleasure-seeking are interfering with business and resolves to amend this.

records.l: the narrator's wife, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The diarist's wife is treated coldly by Lady Batten and her daughter because she does not seek their acquaintance. She is distressed about her brother Balty's condition and urges the diarist to help him, telling his story with tears.

records.l: the diarist's father, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The diarist's father helps confront Pall and agrees that she should go into the country with the diarist's mother. His accounts show that he has only £45 owed to him and owes about the same amount, and he goes to Brampton to settle matters before the diarist's mother arrives.

records.l: Pall, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Pall is reprimanded before the diarist's father for her conduct and high spirit. The diarist arranges for her to go into the country with his parents for a time, and she is left responsible for the household work until she departs.

records.l: Jane, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Jane completes three years as the diarist's maid and leaves to go into the country to her mother. Although the diarist considers her lazy and spoiled by Pall's arrival, he regards her as harmless and unusually pleasing, pays her wages, gives her an additional 2s. 6d., and is deeply troubled by her departure.

records.l: Tom, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Tom Pepys, identified as the Executor, hosts the diarist, family members, and several ladies at dinner. The diarist also deals with discussions about possible marriages for Tom, including proposals involving a broker's daughter and Mr. Evans's daughter.

records.l: Lord Sandwich, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Lord Sandwich writes that he is well again after his fever but remains at Alicante. He is expected to proceed toward Portugal, and the diarist is concerned about how Edward Montagu will dispose of £5,000 intended for Lord Sandwich's departure.

records.l: the clergy, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The diarist reports that the clergy are regarded as excessively high by many people he meets. He says that people broadly protest against their practice.

records.l: the Court, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The Court is described as being in very poor condition, marked by emulation, poverty, drinking, swearing, and loose amours. The diarist fears that these conditions will end in confusion.

records.l: Brampton, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Brampton is where the diarist's father goes to settle matters concerning the family estate and arrangements before the diarist's mother arrives.

records.l: Alicante, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Alicante is where Lord Sandwich lay sick with a fever and was twice let blood. He has recovered there but has not yet departed.

records.l: theatre performances, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The diarist sees performances of "The Antipodes" and "The Joviall Crew," finding the former amusing but lacking much else and the latter full of mirth. He also attends a French comedy that he considers poorly performed, dirty, disordered, and unpleasant.

records.l: Lord Sandwich's illness, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Lord Sandwich's illness was a serious fever at Alicante, during which he was twice let blood. By the time of his letter, he had recovered but remained at Alicante.

records.l: Jane's departure to the country, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Jane leaves the diarist's service to go to her mother in the country after he settles her wages and gives her an additional 2s. 6d. Her departure causes him considerable sadness because he believes he will not find another maid who pleases him as well.

records.l: Pall's removal to the country, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: After the diarist rebukes Pall and threatens to keep her no longer, his father agrees that she should go into the country with the diarist's mother and remain there for a time. The diarist views this arrangement as bringing relief from the trouble she causes.

records.l: the Pepys family estate and finances, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The diarist examines his father's accounts and finds that his father is owed only £45 in money and owes about the same sum. He is concerned about what would have happened to his mother if his father had died before his uncle Robert, and he works to settle the family's affairs.

records.l: court corruption and disorder, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The diarist sees the Court as afflicted by emulation, poverty, drinking, swearing, and loose amours. He concludes that its condition is likely to produce confusion.

records.l: clerical conduct, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The diarist reports widespread criticism of the clergy's conduct and says that people protest against their practice. He also records hearing a strong sermon from Mr. Mills on the necessity of restitution.

records.l: financial debt and borrowing, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The diarist says that no money is coming in and that he has been forced to borrow heavily for his own expenses and to furnish his father. He also seeks advice about a £200 bond connected with his aunt Pepys and doubts whether interest will not have to be paid.

records.l: The Diary of Samuel Pepys, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The writer considers subscribing L20 and reports that the Office is quiet because of a lack of money. The Office's bills have been offered for sale on the Exchange at a 10 per cent. loss. The Office may add Sir R. Ford's house, but difficulties over dividing it and personally guaranteeing the L200 annual rent may prevent this. The season is described as sickly everywhere because of strange and fatal fevers.

records.l: the Navy Office, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The Office is quiet because of a lack of money. It may add Sir R. Ford's house, though difficulties over dividing the house and personally guaranteeing the rent may prevent the arrangement.

records.l: money, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: A lack of money has left the Office quiet.

records.l: bills, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The bills have been offered for sale on the Exchange at a 10 per cent. loss.

records.l: Sir R. Ford, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Sir R. Ford's house is being considered for addition to the Office.

records.l: Sir R. Ford's house, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Sir R. Ford's house may be added to the Office, but difficulties in dividing it may prevent this.

records.l: rent, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The rent would be L200 per annum, and the parties would become personally bound to pay it.

records.l: the sickness in City and country, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: The season is very sickly everywhere.

records.l: strange and fatal fevers, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, opening
records.s: Strange and fatal fevers are causing the season to be very sickly everywhere.

records.l: Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering, Abstract
records.s: The abstract proposes Generation-Augmented Retrieval (GAR) for open-domain question answering. GAR generates diverse, heuristically discovered relevant contexts without external resources as supervision and uses them to augment queries. GAR with BM25 achieves performance comparable to or better than dense retrieval methods such as DPR, and combining GAR with DPR improves performance further. GAR achieves state-of-the-art results on Natural Questions and TriviaQA under extractive question answering and consistently outperforms other retrieval methods with the same generative reader.

records.l: GAR, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering, Abstract
records.s: Generation-Augmented Retrieval (GAR) augments queries by generating heuristically discovered relevant contexts without external resources as supervision. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on Natural Questions and TriviaQA with an extractive reader and consistently outperforms other retrieval methods when the same generative reader is used.

records.l: BM25, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering, Abstract
records.s: BM25 is used with GAR as a sparse representation and achieves performance comparable to or better than state-of-the-art dense retrieval methods such as DPR. Fusing results from diverse generated contexts consistently improves retrieval accuracy.

records.l: DPR, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering, Abstract
records.s: Dense passage retrieval methods, including DPR, are compared with GAR using sparse representations. GAR achieves comparable or better performance, and combining GAR with DPR produces further improvements because sparse and dense representations are often complementary.

records.l: Natural Questions, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering, Abstract
records.s: Natural Questions is one of the datasets on which GAR achieves state-of-the-art performance under the extractive question answering setup with an extractive reader.

records.l: TriviaQA, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering, Abstract
records.s: TriviaQA is one of the datasets on which GAR achieves state-of-the-art performance under the extractive question answering setup with an extractive reader.

records.l: Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering, Introduction
records.s: The unit concerns Open-domain question answering (OpenQA) and introduces Generation-Augmented Retrieval (GAR), which expands questions with contexts generated by a pre-trained language model before retrieval. GAR trains sequence-to-sequence models to generate answers, answer-containing sentences, or passage titles, then appends those contexts to the original questions for retrieval. Experiments on Natural Questions and TriviaQA show that GAR with BM25 improves retrieval and question-answering performance, can match or outperform dense methods such as DPR, and can complement DPR when their results are fused.

records.l: OpenQA, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering, Introduction
records.s: Open-domain question answering aims to answer factoid questions without a pre-specified domain, often using large document collections such as Wikipedia. The unit reports that GAR achieves strong retrieval and end-to-end question-answering results on Natural Questions and TriviaQA.

records.l: retriever-reader architecture, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering, Introduction
records.s: The retriever-reader architecture first retrieves a small subset of documents using a question and then uses a reader to extract or generate an answer from the retrieved documents.

records.l: retriever, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering, Introduction
records.s: The retriever selects relevant documents because examining every passage in a large collection is infeasible. Its retrieval accuracy bounds the performance of an extractive reader.

records.l: reader, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering, Introduction
records.s: The reader examines retrieved documents to extract or generate an answer. The reported experiments compare retrieval methods using the same extractive or generative reader.

records.l: sparse representations, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering, Introduction
records.s: Sparse retrieval methods use sparse representations and are lightweight and efficient, but they do not perform semantic matching well when relevant passages lack lexical overlap. With GAR, sparse retrieval can handle semantics before retrieval by enriching queries while retaining exact lexical matching.

records.l: dense retrieval methods, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering, Introduction
records.s: Dense retrieval methods embed queries and passages into a latent vector space, allowing semantic matching beyond lexical overlap. They can retrieve lexically different relevant passages but are more computationally expensive and may lose information by condensing text into fixed-size vectors.

records.l: BM25, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering, Introduction
records.s: BM25 is used as the sparse retrieval model in GAR experiments. GAR combined with BM25 significantly improves over BM25 using original queries or existing unsupervised query expansion and achieves performance comparable to or better than dense retrieval methods.

records.l: GAR, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering, Introduction
records.s: Generation-Augmented Retrieval augments questions with relevant contexts generated by a pre-trained language model rather than rewriting the original query. It generates answers, answer-containing sentences, or passage titles, appends them to the question, and improves retrieval and question-answering performance; combining its results with DPR provides further gains.

records.l: PLMs, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering, Introduction
records.s: A pre-trained language model generates contexts for Generation-Augmented Retrieval. These contexts provide background information and explicitly express search intent that may not appear in the original question.

records.l: query expansion, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering, Introduction
records.s: The unit distinguishes GAR from existing unsupervised query expansion methods. GAR improves queries through generated, heuristically discovered contexts and does not require external resources or downstream reinforcement-learning feedback.

records.l: DPR, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering, Introduction
records.s: DPR is presented as a state-of-the-art dense retrieval method. GAR with BM25 achieves comparable or better results than DPR in several settings, while fusing GAR and DPR retrieval results consistently improves performance over either method alone.

records.l: Natural Questions, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering, Introduction
records.s: Natural Questions is one of the two benchmark datasets used to evaluate GAR. GAR achieves extractive question-answering EM of 41.8, or 43.8 when combined with DPR, and generative question-answering EM of 38.1, or 45.3 when combined with DPR.

records.l: TriviaQA, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering, Introduction
records.s: TriviaQA is one of the two benchmark datasets used to evaluate GAR. GAR achieves extractive question-answering EM of 62.7 and generative question-answering EM of 62.2 on this dataset.

records.l: Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering, Related Work
records.s: The unit compares GAR with conventional query expansion and recent query reformulation methods. GAR expands queries using knowledge stored in PLMs, generated through standard seq2seq learning with in-domain contexts such as passage titles, rather than relying on retrieved passages or external resources. For OpenQA, GAR extends sparse retrieval beyond question information and can achieve comparable or better performance than dense methods while retaining sparse-representation efficiency. The unit also distinguishes GAR from generative QA, which focuses on generating answers or improving the reading stage.

records.l: GAR, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering, Related Work
records.s: GAR expands queries with relevant contexts learned through text generation from knowledge stored in PLMs rather than from retrieved passages. It uses freely accessible in-domain contexts such as passage titles as generation targets and standard seq2seq learning, making it more efficient and effective for OpenQA than the methods discussed. GAR extends sparse retrieval beyond question information and can also be used with dense representations.

records.l: query expansion, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering, Related Work
records.s: Query expansion methods based on pseudo relevance feedback expand queries with relevant terms without external supervision. GAR shares this property but differs by using knowledge stored in PLMs and learning expanded terms through text generation.

records.l: query reformulation, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering, Related Work
records.s: Recent query reformulation studies use generation models for other retrieval tasks. The unit states that they may require external resources or time-consuming training such as reinforcement learning, making them less applicable or efficient for OpenQA.

records.l: OpenQA, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering, Related Work
records.s: OpenQA may lack the external resources required by some query reformulation methods, and those resources can show inferior domain-transfer performance. GAR is presented as an efficient approach for OpenQA that improves sparse retrieval and can achieve comparable or better performance than dense methods.

records.l: retrieval, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering, Related Work
records.s: The unit discusses retrieval for OpenQA and contrasts sparse and dense representations. GAR uses generated relevant contexts to support retrieval and can be combined with dense representations for potentially better performance.

records.l: sparse representations, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering, Related Work
records.s: Existing sparse retrieval methods for OpenQA rely solely on question information. GAR extends them with information extracted from PLMs and helps them achieve comparable or better performance than dense methods while retaining the simplicity and efficiency of sparse representations.

records.l: PLMs, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering, Related Work
records.s: PLMs store knowledge that GAR uses to expand queries with relevant contexts. The unit also states that factual knowledge can be extracted from PLMs in contexts beyond answers.

records.l: DPR, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering, Related Work
records.s: Generative QA studies discussed in the unit directly reuse DPR as the retriever. GAR is presented as distinct from this approach because its goal is to generate retrieval-helpful contexts rather than perfect answers.

records.l: generative OpenQA, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering, Related Work
records.s: Generative QA generates answers through seq2seq learning instead of extracting answer spans, with recent studies focusing on improving the reading stage while reusing DPR as the retriever. GAR is orthogonal to generative QA because it generates pertinent contexts for retrieval rather than perfect answers, and it extracts factual knowledge from PLMs beyond answers alone.

records.l: Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering, Generation-Augmented Retrieval / Task Formulation .. Generative Reader
records.s: The unit describes GAR, a generation-augmented retrieval method for OpenQA using a retriever-reader architecture over a large document collection such as Wikipedia. GAR generates answers, answer-containing sentences, and relevant passage titles as query contexts, appends them to the question, and retrieves passages with BM25 before fusing the results. It evaluates both extractive and generative readers, including a DPR-style extractive reader with passage-level span voting and a BART-large generative reader. The method is intended to improve retrieval effectiveness and efficiency and thereby improve question-answering performance.

records.l: OpenQA, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering, Generation-Augmented Retrieval / Task Formulation .. Generative Reader

GAR generates answer, sentence, and title contexts that increase lexical overlap with relevant passages, and combining these contexts improves retrieval because they are complementary. GAR substantially improves BM25 retrieval, approaches or exceeds DPR at larger retrieval cutoffs, and achieves strong end-to-end extractive and generative QA performance, especially when combined with DPR. GAR is also reported to require substantially less training, indexing, and retrieval computation than DPR.

records.l: Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering, Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering, Conclusion .. Future Extensions
records.s: The unit concludes that Generation-Augmented Retrieval (GAR) uses relevant contexts generated by pretrained language models without external supervision to enrich query semantics and improve retrieval accuracy. GAR with sparse representations performs similarly to or better than state-of-the-art methods using dense representations of the original queries, and combining sparse and dense representations improves results further. GAR achieves state-of-the-art end-to-end performance on extractive OpenQA and competitive performance under the generative setup. Future work includes improving context generation and fusion, jointly optimizing generation and retrieval, tuning hyperparameters, and applying GAR to other text-matching tasks.

records.l: RACE: Retrieval-Augmented Commit Message Generation, RACE: Retrieval-Augmented Commit Message Generation, Abstract
records.s: The paper concerns automatic commit message generation, where neural network-based approaches have shown promising results but may produce repetitive or redundant messages. It proposes RACE, a retrieval-augmented method that uses a retrieved similar commit as an exemplar for generating accurate commit messages. RACE includes an exemplar guider that learns the semantic similarity between the retrieved and current code diff and guides message generation accordingly. Experiments on a large public dataset covering five programming languages show that RACE outperforms all baselines and improves existing Seq2Seq models.
