records.s: Other Day, an educated Dakota Indian who had adopted Christianity and civilized habits, guided sixty-two men, women, and children to safety through Kandiyohi, Hutchinson, Glencoe, and Carver. He later spoke in St. Paul and attributed their escape to the mercy of the Great Spirit.

records.l: Henry Hastings Sibley, Novel-10146, THE GREAT SIOUX OUTBREAK IN 1862.
records.s: Henry Hastings Sibley was placed in command of the troops assembled at St. Peter because of his long familiarity with Indian character. He soon led partially uniformed and poorly supplied forces in offensive operations and relieved Fort Ridgely.

records.l: Fort Ridgely, Novel-10146, THE GREAT SIOUX OUTBREAK IN 1862.
records.s: Fort Ridgely was a lightly protected post defended by about 150 Fifth Regiment men, fifty Renville Rangers, and civilians against an estimated 700 or 800 Sioux. Its garrison endured a siege for more than a week before relief arrived under Col. McPhail, the advance of Sibley’s force.

records.l: New Ulm, Novel-10146, THE GREAT SIOUX OUTBREAK IN 1862.
records.s: New Ulm was attacked by Sioux forces that killed citizens and burned buildings. After a later attack, its defenders evacuated about 1,200 to 1,500 noncombatants to Mankato, and nearly 200 houses had been burned.

records.l: Charles E. Flandrau, Novel-10146, THE GREAT SIOUX OUTBREAK IN 1862.
records.s: Charles E. Flandrau organized volunteers at St. Peter and marched to New Ulm. He commanded about 300 poorly armed and inexperienced men, helped defend the town, and led the evacuation to Mankato after provisions and ammunition became scarce.

records.l: Birch Coulie, Novel-10146, THE GREAT SIOUX OUTBREAK IN 1862.
records.s: Birch Coulie was the site of a camp established by Maj. Joseph R. Brown’s detachment about fifteen miles from Fort Ridgely. The camp’s attractive but exposed location left roughly 150 men vulnerable to a large Sioux attack.

records.l: St. Paul, Novel-10146, THE GREAT SIOUX OUTBREAK IN 1862.
records.s: St. Paul experienced intense anxiety as reports of Sioux attacks and refugees arrived. Residents organized home guards, patrolled the bluffs, assisted refugees, and feared that the city itself might be attacked.

records.l: Birch Coulie battle, Novel-10146, THE GREAT SIOUX OUTBREAK IN 1862.
records.s: The Birch Coulie battle began around 4 a.m. when an estimated 500 or 600 armed and mostly mounted Sioux opened fire on Maj. Brown’s command. The defenders held out for two days, but about half of their force was killed or wounded before relief arrived.

records.l: Sioux massacre, Novel-10146, THE GREAT SIOUX OUTBREAK IN 1862.
records.s: The Sioux massacre began on August 18 with attacks on settlers and spread throughout the reservation and isolated communities. The text reports that about 1,000 people were killed in less than a week, millions of dollars in property were destroyed, and 30,000 people were made homeless.

records.l: Fort Ridgely siege, Novel-10146, THE GREAT SIOUX OUTBREAK IN 1862.
records.s: The Fort Ridgely siege lasted several days and included two attempted assaults by Sioux forces. Defenders improvised ammunition by opening spherical case shot, making cartridges, and cutting nail rods into projectiles until relief arrived.

records.l: New Ulm attacks, Novel-10146, THE GREAT SIOUX OUTBREAK IN 1862.
records.s: The New Ulm attacks included an initial assault that killed citizens and burned homes, followed several days later by a larger encirclement and assault. Flandrau’s defenders drove the Sioux away, but lost ten men killed and about forty wounded before evacuating the town.

records.l: it494-narrative-corpora-raw/graphrag-bench/Novel-10146.txt, Novel-10146, As soon as Gen.
records.s: Gen. Sibley led about 2,000 men in an offensive expedition that culminated in the Wood Lake battle on September 23, 1862, where Col. Marshall routed an approximately equal force of Sioux. His command reached Camp Release, where a large Indian camp surrendered and about 250 mixed bloods and white women and children were freed. A military tribunal convicted 321 Indians, but the President of the United States authorized the execution of only thirty-eight at Mankato on December 26, 1862. Little Crow escaped and was later killed, while the Sioux lost their Minnesota lands and the military struggled to transport supplies to frontier troops.

records.l: Henry Hastings Sibley, Novel-10146, As soon as Gen.
records.s: Gen. Sibley collected about 2,000 men and moved against the Sioux after gathering a sufficient force. He led the command to Camp Release, where he proceeded cautiously until the Indian camp surrendered and the captives were released, then organized a military tribunal to try suspected offenders.

records.l: Wood Lake, Novel-10146, As soon as Gen.
records.s: Wood Lake was the vicinity where foraging parties from the Third regiment were fired upon on the morning of September 23, 1862.

records.l: Battle of Wood Lake, Novel-10146, As soon as Gen.
records.s: About 800 of Gen. Sibley's men fought approximately 800 Indians at Wood Lake. Col. Marshall led about 400 men in a double-quick charge that routed the Sioux; the whites lost four killed and forty or fifty wounded.

records.l: Sioux, Novel-10146, As soon as Gen.
records.s: The Sioux opposed Gen. Sibley's forces at Wood Lake and were routed by Col. Marshall's charge. Many Sioux at Camp Release had been involved in the massacres, and the outbreak caused them to forfeit their Minnesota lands to the government.

records.l: Minnesota, Novel-10146, As soon as Gen.
records.s: Minnesota's people opposed removing the troops after Gen. Pope declared the Indian war over. Public excitement over the condemned Indians became so intense that the governor urged citizens not to commit lawlessness.

records.l: Camp Release, Novel-10146, As soon as Gen.
records.s: Gen. Sibley's command reached Camp Release on September 26, where a large Indian camp surrendered after preliminary consultations. The captives held there were released.

records.l: Indian camp at Camp Release, Novel-10146, As soon as Gen.
records.s: The Indian camp at Camp Release contained many Indians who had participated in the massacres and held about 250 mixed bloods and white women and children. The entire camp surrendered after Gen. Sibley avoided a hostile demonstration that he believed might lead to the prisoners' annihilation.

records.l: mixed bloods and white women and children, Novel-10146, As soon as Gen.
records.s: About 250 mixed bloods and white women and children were held by the Indian camp at Camp Release. They were released when the camp surrendered.

records.l: The Great Sioux Outbreak in 1862, Novel-10146, As soon as Gen.
records.s: After the Wood Lake battle, Gen. Pope telegraphed that the Indian war was over and asked how to dispose of the troops. Minnesota's people opposed removing the troops, and they remained until making two long marches through the Dakotas and to Montana.

records.l: military tribunal, Novel-10146, As soon as Gen.
records.s: Gen. Sibley formed a military tribunal to investigate and try Indians suspected of participating in the recent atrocities. After sittings from September 30 to November 5, it found 321 guilty, sentencing 303 to death and the remainder to imprisonment.

records.l: condemned Indians, Novel-10146, As soon as Gen.
records.s: The condemned Indians were taken to Mankato and confined in a specially constructed jail. The President of the United States reduced the executions to thirty-eight, while the others remained confined until spring and were later transported to Davenport and a point on the Missouri river.

records.l: Mankato, Novel-10146, As soon as Gen.
records.s: Mankato held the condemned Indians in a large jail before the authorized executions. Thirty-eight Dakota prisoners were executed there on December 26, 1862.

records.l: St. Paul, Novel-10146, As soon as Gen.
records.s: St. Paul residents petitioned in favor of removing the condemned Indians to Massachusetts and later prepared to receive prisoners being transported to Davenport. Government officers avoided the city by arranging for the steamer Favorite to pass it during the night.

records.l: Abraham Lincoln, Novel-10146, As soon as Gen.
records.s: After consulting military advisers and receiving remonstrances, the President of the United States authorized the execution of only thirty-eight of the condemned Indians. He directed that they be hanged on December 26, 1862.

records.l: execution of the thirty-eight Dakota prisoners, Novel-10146, As soon as Gen.
records.s: The thirty-eight Dakota prisoners were hanged at Mankato on December 26, 1862. Their bodies were placed together in a sandbar grave and were later taken away by students and others familiar with dissection.

records.l: Little Crow, Novel-10146, As soon as Gen.
records.s: Little Crow, described as the chief instigator of the insurrection, did not surrender at Camp Release. He escaped and was later killed by a farmer named Lamson near Hutchinson; his scalp was held by the state historical society.

records.l: transportation of military supplies, Novel-10146, As soon as Gen.
records.s: Because there were no railroads, military supplies had to be transported by wagon. The authorities impressed teams into government service when volunteers were insufficient, sent Company K of the Eighth regiment to enforce the order, and provided escorts for supply trains.

records.l: Ladies Aid Society, Novel-10146, As soon as Gen.
records.s: The Ladies Aid Society in St. Paul organized to sew for wounded soldiers and assist destitute refugees. Mrs. Stella Selby served as president, and Miss M.O. Holyoke served as secretary and devoted her time to collecting sanitary supplies.

records.l: Dakota lands in Minnesota, Novel-10146, As soon as Gen.
records.s: The Sioux forfeited to the government all lands they held in Minnesota, totaling about 750,000 acres, in addition to an annual annuity of $68,000 for fifty years. The text estimates the land's present value at about $15,000,000.

records.l: it494-narrative-corpora-raw/graphrag-bench/Novel-10146.txt, Novel-10146, FIREMEN AND FIRES OF PIONEER DAYS.
records.s: This unit recounts the development of the St. Paul Fire Department from bucket brigades and volunteer companies to a paid department with steamers and other modern equipment. It describes the organization of Pioneer Hook and Ladder Company No. 1, Hope Engine Company No. 1, and Minnehaha Engine Company No. 2, as well as the department's first parade in 1859. The account also recalls the work of pioneer firemen, the service of Mrs. Bartlett Presley, and an anecdote about Michael E. Ames during a house fire.

records.l: St. Paul fire department, Novel-10146, FIREMEN AND FIRES OF PIONEER DAYS.
records.s: The St. Paul Fire Department developed from volunteer companies organized in the 1850s, including Pioneer Hook and Ladder Company No. 1, Hope Engine Company No. 1, and Minnehaha Engine Company No. 2. Its first annual parade was held in 1859, and after the first steamer arrived on August 11, 1866, the department continued to expand.

records.l: firemen and fires of pioneer days, Novel-10146, FIREMEN AND FIRES OF PIONEER DAYS.
records.s: The unit describes pioneer firemen responding to alarms with hand engines, hooks, ladders, and bucket brigades. Firemen worked the engine brakes, sometimes requiring spectators or people compelled by the police to relieve them, and many enlisted during the war.

records.l: old machine, Novel-10146, FIREMEN AND FIRES OF PIONEER DAYS.
records.s: The old machine is remembered in a poem by Gus Wiliams as a former fire apparatus with which firemen ran through flames and danger. The poem says that only a few of the old firemen remained, while their memories and spirits endured.

records.l: fire engines, Novel-10146, FIREMEN AND FIRES OF PIONEER DAYS.
records.s: Early fire engines included wheeled tanks, hand engines, and engines equipped with pumps, air chambers, suction pipes, and leather hose. St. Paul received its first engine through John McCloud and Thompson Ritchie and later purchased two double-deck hand engines that arrived in August 1858.

records.l: United States, Novel-10146, FIREMEN AND FIRES OF PIONEER DAYS.
records.s: In the United States, bucket fire departments were organized in many cities early in the nineteenth century, while hand engines came into general use about fifty years later. Cincinnati received credit for introducing the first paid steam fire department, and other large cities followed.

records.l: St. Paul, Novel-10146, FIREMEN AND FIRES OF PIONEER DAYS.
records.s: St. Paul required building owners in 1850 to keep marked fire buckets in good repair and later organized volunteer fire companies. The city purchased hand engines and constructed or requested cisterns, held its first fire department parade in 1859, and received its first steamer in 1866.

records.l: R.C. Knox, Novel-10146, FIREMEN AND FIRES OF PIONEER DAYS.
records.s: R.C. Knox made the first attempt to organize a St. Paul fire brigade in the fall of 1851. He raised money by subscription to purchase several ladders and was said to be able to tire out a dozen ordinary men at a fire.

records.l: John McCloud, Novel-10146, FIREMEN AND FIRES OF PIONEER DAYS.
records.s: John McCloud and Thompson Ritchie purchased and brought to St. Paul the first fire engine introduced in the Northwest at their own expense. McCloud was a member of McCloud & Bro., was an original member of Pioneer Hook and Ladder Company No. 1, and was identified as the only surviving member of that original roll living in the city at the time of the account.

records.l: Pioneer Hook and Ladder Company No. 1, Novel-10146, FIREMEN AND FIRES OF PIONEER DAYS.
records.s: Pioneer Hook and Ladder Company No. 1 was organized in November 1854 under the city charter, with members required to respond promptly to fire alarms. In 1856 its accounts were turned over to the city, and it possessed a truck, hooks and ladders, and a fire engine with hose; it participated in the 1859 parade.

records.l: Hope Engine Company No. 1, Novel-10146, FIREMEN AND FIRES OF PIONEER DAYS.
records.s: Hope Engine Company No. 1 was organized in 1857 and petitioned the common council for 500 feet of hose. It received one of the new hand engines in the fall of 1858, was housed first on Franklin and Fourth streets and later on Third street, and disbanded after objecting to the engineer selected for the first steamer.

records.l: Minnehaha Engine Company No. 2, Novel-10146, FIREMEN AND FIRES OF PIONEER DAYS.
records.s: Minnehaha Engine Company No. 2 was organized in the winter of 1857-1858 and received an engine house near Third and Jackson streets. It was described as prosperous, and its engine house served as a lounging and reading room; the company participated in the 1859 parade.

records.l: first parade of the St. Paul fire department, Novel-10146, FIREMEN AND FIRES OF PIONEER DAYS.
records.s: The first parade of the St. Paul fire department took place on September 12, 1859. Pioneer Hook and Ladder Company No. 1, Hope Engine Company No. 1, Minnehaha Engine Company No. 2, and Rotary Independent Company No. 1 participated, totaling 175 men.

records.l: first steamer, Novel-10146, FIREMEN AND FIRES OF PIONEER DAYS.
records.s: The first steamer arrived in St. Paul on August 11, 1866. It was initially lodged with Hope Engine Company, which received an engineer and fireman appointed at a combined salary of $1,600 per year; after the company disbanded, St. Paul Hose Company No. 1 took charge of it.

records.l: Mrs. Bartlett Presley, Novel-10146, FIREMEN AND FIRES OF PIONEER DAYS.
records.s: Mrs. Bartlett Presley was described as a guardian angel of the volunteer fire department. She attended fires in severe weather and personally provided coffee and sandwiches to tired and hungry firemen, earning their lasting gratitude.

records.l: Michael E. Ames, Novel-10146, FIREMEN AND FIRES OF PIONEER DAYS.
records.s: Michael E. Ames escaped from a fire in his sleeping apartment in uppertown after asking the firemen to pause until he had arranged his toilet. His apartments were soon destroyed by fire.

records.l: St. Paul fire department annual parade of 1859, Novel-10146, FIREMEN AND FIRES OF PIONEER DAYS.
records.s: The St. Paul fire department annual parade of 1859 was held on September 12 and included four companies. The 175 participants completed a line of march and were reviewed by the mayor and common council in front of the old city hall.

records.l: paid fire department, Novel-10146, FIREMEN AND FIRES OF PIONEER DAYS.
records.s: The paid fire department followed the volunteer period and expanded as St. Paul grew. At the time described, it had 211 paid men, 15 steamers, 4 chemicals, 8 hook and ladder companies, and 122 horses.

records.l: volunteer fire department, Novel-10146, FIREMEN AND FIRES OF PIONEER DAYS.
records.s: The volunteer fire department was organized through companies such as Pioneer Hook and Ladder Company No. 1, Hope Engine Company No. 1, and Minnehaha Engine Company No. 2. Its members received exemptions from jury duty, poll tax, road work, and state military service for five years, and many prominent citizens served in its ranks.

records.l: firefighting equipment, Novel-10146, FIREMEN AND FIRES OF PIONEER DAYS.
records.s: Firefighting equipment discussed in the unit includes marked buckets, ladders, hooks, hand engines, hose, cisterns, steamers, chemical apparatus, and horses. St. Paul initially had limited equipment, then acquired two double-deck hand engines in 1858 and additional apparatus as the city expanded.

records.l: it494-narrative-corpora-raw/graphrag-bench/Novel-10146.txt, Novel-10146, HOTEL FIRES.
records.s: The unit recounts hotel fires and other major fires during St. Paul’s early history, describing destroyed buildings, causes, rescues, losses, and the development of the fire department. It concerns hotels including the Daniels house, Sintominie hotel, Rice house, Winslow house, American house, Cosmopolitan hotel, International hotel, and others. The account also describes the March 16, 1860 fire, the February 3, 1869 International hotel fire, the May 1870 Concert Hall fire, and several later hotel fires. It names people who fought fires, rescued occupants, managed hotels, or were associated with the buildings and events.

records.l: St. Paul, Novel-10146, HOTEL FIRES.
records.s: St. Paul experienced numerous destructive hotel fires during its early history. In the March 16, 1860 fire, thirty-four buildings were destroyed, while the February 3, 1869 International hotel fire threatened the lower city but caused no deaths.

records.l: St. Paul fire department, Novel-10146, HOTEL FIRES.
records.s: The fire department initially consisted of three engines and one truck, manned by one hundred men. In 1869 the city had no waterworks and relied on cisterns, with water sometimes pumped from the river through more than two thousand feet of hose.

records.l: hotel fires, Novel-10146, HOTEL FIRES.
records.s: The unit lists hotels destroyed by fire during St. Paul’s early history, including the Daniels house, Sintominie hotel, Rice house, New England hotel, Winslow house, American house, International hotel, Cosmopolitan hotel, Central house, Emmert house, Greenman house, Mansion house, Park Place hotel, and Carpenter house.

records.l: Daniels house, Novel-10146, HOTEL FIRES.
records.s: The Daniels house stood on Eagle street near Seven Corners and was destroyed in 1852 shortly after it had been finished and furnished. Strong wind prevented the small group of firemen from saving the structure, though Rev. D.D. Neill, Isaac Markley, Bartlett Presley, and W.M. Stees helped save furniture.

records.l: Sintominie hotel, Novel-10146, HOTEL FIRES.
records.s: The Sintominie hotel stood at Sixth and John streets and was constructed by C.W. Borup. Howard Ward and E.C. Rich were preparing to open it when it was totally destroyed because of inadequate fire protection.

records.l: Rice house, Novel-10146, HOTEL FIRES.
records.s: The Rice house stood on Third street near Market and was commonly considered the first brick building erected in St. Paul. Built by Henry M. Rice, the three-story hotel burned to the ground in early winter 1856 after having served as a principal hotel and a meeting place for the territorial legislature and supreme court.

records.l: New England hotel, Novel-10146, HOTEL FIRES.
records.s: The New England hotel was a two-story log house and one of the first hotels built in St. Paul. It burned in the March 16, 1860 fire; it had been known as the first gubernatorial mansion, where Gov. and Mrs. Ramsey began housekeeping in 1849.

records.l: Winslow house, Novel-10146, HOTEL FIRES.
records.s: The Winslow house at Seven Corners was a four-story brick building constructed in 1854 by J.M. Winslow. A defective stovepipe in the cupola caused its destruction in the fall of 1862, and only a few badly damaged pieces of furniture were saved; its proprietors were arrested for incendiarism but discharged after a preliminary examination.

records.l: American house, Novel-10146, HOTEL FIRES.
records.s: The American house stood at Third and Exchange streets and was built in 1849. It burned on a bitterly cold December night in 1863 before the fire department arrived, and although guests narrowly escaped, thieves carried away jewelry and clothing.

records.l: International hotel, Novel-10146, HOTEL FIRES.
records.s: The International hotel, formerly the Fuller house, stood at Seventh and Jackson streets and was built by A.G. Fuller in 1856. The five-story brick building cost about $110,000 and was regarded for years as the best hotel in the West before it burned on February 3, 1869.

records.l: Cosmopolitan hotel, Novel-10146, HOTEL FIRES.
records.s: The Cosmopolitan hotel occupied a three-story brick building at Third and Franklin streets that Mackubin & Edgerton had erected in 1856. Bechtner & Kottman remodeled it as a European-plan hotel, but it later burned while full of lodgers, many of whom lost all they possessed; its remaining walls later collapsed onto Dr. Schell’s nearby building.

records.l: Central house, Novel-10146, HOTEL FIRES.
records.s: The Central house stood at Bench and Minnesota streets and was described as the first hotel of any pretension built in St. Paul. The first session of the territorial legislature met in its dining room, and after it became a boarding house it was burned in August 1873.

records.l: Emmert house, Novel-10146, HOTEL FIRES.
records.s: The Emmert house stood on Bench street near Wabasha and had been built in territorial times by Fred Emmert. It was no longer used as a hotel when it burned during the winter of 1868, but a family and boarding-house residents occupied it; two people sick with smallpox were rescued by firemen and later taken to safety by W.L. Wilson.

records.l: Greenman house, Novel-10146, HOTEL FIRES.
records.s: The Greenman house stood at Fifth and St. Peter streets and was a three-story frame building built in the early 1870s. Mr. Greenman sold it to John Summers, who owned it when it burned.

records.l: Mansion house, Novel-10146, HOTEL FIRES.
records.s: The Mansion house stood at Wabasha and Fifth streets on the site of the old post office. Nicholas Pottgieser built the three-story frame hotel in early days at a cost of $12,000, and it was a popular resort; in 1866 guest Hawkes accidentally shot and killed his wife there and was later acquitted of murder.

records.l: Park Place hotel, Novel-10146, HOTEL FIRES.
records.s: The Park Place hotel stood at Summit avenue and St. Peter street and was a four-story frame building intended as a family hotel. It was unoccupied when it burned on May 19, 1878, in a fire thought to have been caused by incendiaries; four firemen were seriously injured but recovered.

records.l: Carpenter house, Novel-10146, HOTEL FIRES.
records.s: The Carpenter house stood at Summit avenue and Ramsey street and was built by Warren Carpenter, who envisioned attracting millions of tourists. The panic of 1857 and the Civil war thwarted his plans, and the hotel burned on January 26, 1879 after having passed beyond his control.

records.l: Fuller house, Novel-10146, HOTEL FIRES.
records.s: The Fuller house was the former name of the International hotel. A.G. Fuller erected the five-story brick building in 1856, and it later became the International hotel under Samuel Mayall.

records.l: 1852 Daniels house fire, Novel-10146, HOTEL FIRES.
records.s: The 1852 Daniels house fire was the first hotel fire of importance described in the unit. A strong wind prevented the small group of firemen from saving the newly finished building, though furniture was rescued.

records.l: March 16, 1860 St. Paul fire, Novel-10146, HOTEL FIRES.
records.s: The March 16, 1860 St. Paul fire began in a small wooden building on Third street near Jackson and became the city’s most destructive fire to that time. Thirty-four buildings burned, including the New England hotel and Hotel to the Wild Hunter, but firemen prevented the flames from crossing Robert street and destroying lower town.

records.l: Winslow house fire, Novel-10146, HOTEL FIRES.
records.s: The Winslow house fire occurred in the fall of 1862 and was caused by a defective stovepipe in the cupola. The four-story brick hotel was beyond control when firemen arrived, and only a few badly damaged pieces of furniture were saved.

records.l: Cosmopolitan hotel fire, Novel-10146, HOTEL FIRES.
records.s: The Cosmopolitan hotel fire destroyed a hotel full of lodgers, many of whom lost all they owned. The walls remained standing afterward despite being declared dangerous, and a later collapse crushed Dr. Schell’s nearby frame building, though he survived with no serious injury.

records.l: Emmert house fire, Novel-10146, HOTEL FIRES.
records.s: The Emmert house fire occurred during the winter of 1868. Two occupants suffering from smallpox were rescued by firemen but were left in the street until W.L. Wilson learned of their situation the next day and took them to safety.

records.l: February 3, 1869 International hotel fire, Novel-10146, HOTEL FIRES.
records.s: The February 3, 1869 International hotel fire began in the basement, probably from a laundry lamp, during an intensely cold night with a strong northwest gale. More than two hundred guests escaped, aided by night watchman Pete O’Brien, and no lives were lost, although the hotel and four other buildings were destroyed.

records.l: May 1870 Concert Hall fire, Novel-10146, HOTEL FIRES.
records.s: The May 1870 Concert Hall fire began beneath the sidewalk, where combustible materials were stored, and rapidly engulfed the building. Charles and August Mueller leaped from an upper-floor window and survived after months of suffering, while McClellan, who operated a dressmaking establishment there, was burned to death.

records.l: St. Paul Concert Hall, Novel-10146, HOTEL FIRES.
records.s: Concert Hall was a three-story building in front and six or seven stories on the river side, located on Third street near Market. Built by J.W. McClung in 1857, it contained one of the city’s largest halls and was destroyed in May 1870.

records.l: firemen, Novel-10146, HOTEL FIRES.
records.s: Firemen fought numerous St. Paul fires despite strong winds, bitter cold, limited equipment, and a lack of waterworks. They saved furniture at the Daniels house, rescued guests and smallpox patients, and at the International hotel were aided by the calm direction of Pete O’Brien.

records.l: hotel guests, Novel-10146, HOTEL FIRES.
records.s: Hotel guests faced narrow escapes during several fires. At the American house they escaped in bitter cold while thieves stole their belongings, and at the International hotel more than two hundred guests fled in nightclothes without any lives being lost.

records.l: fire, Novel-10146, HOTEL FIRES.
records.s: The unit describes fires caused or suspected to have been caused by strong winds, defective stovepipes, lamps, and possible incendiarism. Fires destroyed hotels and other buildings, threatened entire sections of St. Paul, and sometimes required rescues from severe cold, smoke, flames, or collapsing walls.

records.l: it494-narrative-corpora-raw/graphrag-bench/Novel-10146.txt, Novel-10146, THE FIRST AMUSEMENT HALLS IN ST.
records.s: The unit recounts the early amusement halls and musical entertainment venues of St. Paul, including Irvine hall, Concert hall, the Athenaeum, Market hall, and Ingersoll block. Dan Emmet performed at Irvine hall, later wrote "Dixie," and sent it to his friend R.C. Munger, whose music store hosted its first Western performance. The Hutchinson family frequently performed in St. Paul and was known for patriotic and abolitionist songs. The text also describes political meetings, speeches, concerts, military activity, and library fundraising held in the city's halls.

records.l: St. Paul, Novel-10146, THE FIRST AMUSEMENT HALLS IN ST.
records.s: St. Paul had several early amusement and assembly halls that hosted minstrels, dramatic companies, musical performances, political meetings, military drills, lectures, and charitable events. The city was visited by performers and speakers including Dan Emmet, the Hutchinson family, Tom Marshall, Edward Everett, Ralph Waldo Emerson, and John B. Gough.

records.l: Irvine hall, Novel-10146, THE FIRST AMUSEMENT HALLS IN ST.
records.s: Irvine hall, later called Melodeon hall, occupied a three-story, three-cornered building on Third street at Seven Corners. Dan Emmet's minstrel company performed there during 1857 and 1858, and the Hutchinson family gave an entertainment there in the summer of 1858.

records.l: Dan Emmet, Novel-10146, THE FIRST AMUSEMENT HALLS IN ST.
records.s: Dan Emmet led a minstrel company at Irvine hall in 1857 and 1858, with performers including Frank Lombard, Max Irwin, and Johnny Ritter. He organized the first traveling minstrel troupe in the United States in 1843, later wrote popular melodies including "Dixie," and was the brother of Lafayette S. Emmett. He and his brother did not spell their surname alike.

records.l: Hutchinson family, Novel-10146, THE FIRST AMUSEMENT HALLS IN ST.
records.s: The Hutchinson family frequently visited St. Paul and performed its own music, and the town of Hutchinson, McLeod county, was named after the family. During the Civil War, the family was ordered out of the Army of the Potomac by Gen. McClellan because of abolitionist sentiments expressed in its songs. John W. Hutchinson was identified in 1902 as the last surviving member of the famous concert-giving family.

records.l: R.C. Munger, Novel-10146, THE FIRST AMUSEMENT HALLS IN ST.
records.s: R.C. Munger was Dan Emmet's friend in St. Paul. Munger encouraged Emmet to publish "Dixie," financially assisted in placing it before the public, and received one of the first printed copies. The composition was first sung in the West in the music store of Munger Bros. in the old concert hall building on Third street.

records.l: Dixie, Novel-10146, THE FIRST AMUSEMENT HALLS IN ST.
records.s: "Dixie" was written by Dan Emmet while he was connected with Bryant's Minstrels in New York City. It quickly became popular, appeared on minstrel programs throughout the country, and became the national air of the Confederate States. The text says that Abraham Lincoln regarded it as national property by capture.

records.l: Confederate States, Novel-10146, THE FIRST AMUSEMENT HALLS IN ST.
records.s: The Confederate States adopted "Dixie" as their national air after it became popular in New Orleans and throughout the South during the Civil War.

records.l: St. Paul Concert Hall, Novel-10146, THE FIRST AMUSEMENT HALLS IN ST.
records.s: Concert hall was built in 1857 by J.W. McClung and held approximately 400 or 500 people. Although its basement location made it somewhat inaccessible and limited demand, it hosted speeches by Horatio Seymour and Tom Marshall, as well as musical gatherings including an election-night performance in 1860.

records.l: Athenaeum, Novel-10146, THE FIRST AMUSEMENT HALLS IN ST.
records.s: The Athenaeum was constructed in 1859 by the German Reading society and for several years was St. Paul's only amusement hall with a stage and drop curtain. It hosted performances by Peter and Caroline Richings, wartime benefits for soldiers, German and English dramatic performances, and Plunkett's Dramatic company with Susan Denin. During the Sioux massacre, it also sheltered maimed refugees brought to the city.

records.l: Market Hall, Novel-10146, THE FIRST AMUSEMENT HALLS IN ST.
records.s: Market hall was built in 1853 at Wabasha and Seventh streets and became one of St. Paul's principal places of amusement. It hosted the Hough Dramatic company and was used by the Wide Awakes as a drill hall in 1860.

records.l: Ingersoll Hall, Novel-10146, THE FIRST AMUSEMENT HALLS IN ST.
records.s: The Ingersoll block on Bridge Square was constructed in 1860, and its third-floor hall was well attended for several years. It hosted speakers including Edward Everett, Ralph Waldo Emerson, John B. Gough, and Mrs. Scott Siddons, and was used by Company C of the First regiment of Minnesota volunteers for military drills and enlistment meetings. A 1861 social and supper held there raised funds for a library that began with about 350 books.

records.l: it494-narrative-corpora-raw/graphrag-bench/Novel-10146.txt, Novel-10146, The People's theater, an old frame building on the corner of Fourth and St.
records.s: The unit describes St. Paul's early theaters, halls, concerts, balls, political meetings, and wartime fundraisers. The People's theater hosted performers including the Wallacks and Col. R.E.J. Miles, while Mazurka hall, Mozart hall, Masonic hall, and the old opera house served as entertainment venues. Adalina Patti performed at the old capitol, and the house of representatives hosted civic meetings, Republican conventions, and other events. The account also covers wartime support for the American government, the activities of the Pioneer Guards, and appearances by Frederick Douglass and James J. Hill.

records.l: People's theater, Novel-10146, The People's theater, an old frame building on the corner of Fourth and St.
records.s: The People's theater was an old frame building at Fourth and St. Peter streets and the only real theatrical building in St. Paul. H. Van Liew managed it with a stock company that included Emily Dow, Harry Gossan, and Azelene Allen; the Wallacks performed Macbeth and The Man in the Iron Mask there in 1858, Col. R.E.J. Miles first produced Mazeppa there, and A.M. Carver acted there. Its gallery charged the shaded gentry the same admission as the parquet, and Joe Rolette's friends sometimes removed him after he had epileptic fits during performances.

records.l: Mazurka hall, Novel-10146, The People's theater, an old frame building on the corner of Fourth and St.
records.s: Mazurka hall occupied the second story of the Elfelt brothers' old frame building at Third and Exchange streets. It was the principal amusement hall of the city for a time, and many swell entertainments of the early 1850s took place there. J.Q.A. Ward met Miss Pratt at a ball there, left with her, and married her after about twenty minutes.

records.l: Mozart hall, Novel-10146, The People's theater, an old frame building on the corner of Fourth and St.
records.s: Mozart hall was built by Charles N. Mackubin in 1860 at the Third Street end of two large buildings on the site of the Metropolitan hotel. It was joined with Masonic hall for a large sanitary-fair entertainment in the winter of 1864.

records.l: Masonic hall, Novel-10146, The People's theater, an old frame building on the corner of Fourth and St.
records.s: Masonic hall was built by Charles N. Mackubin in 1860 on the Fourth Street corner of the site of the Metropolitan hotel. It was joined with Mozart hall for a large sanitary-fair entertainment in the winter of 1864.

records.l: sanitary fair, Novel-10146, The People's theater, an old frame building on the corner of Fourth and St.
records.s: A sanitary fair held in the winter of 1864 combined Mozart hall and Masonic hall for a large entertainment. Its proceeds helped the nearly depleted funds of the sanitary commission, and the event raised several thousand dollars.

records.l: Sanitary Commission, Novel-10146, The People's theater, an old frame building on the corner of Fourth and St.
records.s: The sanitary commission received several thousand dollars from the successful 1864 sanitary fair in St. Paul. The fair was part of a broader practice of holding fairs in principal Northern cities to raise money for the commission.

records.l: Pioneer Guards, Novel-10146, The People's theater, an old frame building on the corner of Fourth and St.
records.s: The Pioneer Guards used Armory hall from its construction in 1859 until the outbreak of the war. Their annual ball was a leading social event, and the organization disbanded shortly after the war began; many members became Union army officers, while two or three joined the Confederate forces.

records.l: Adalina Patti, Novel-10146, The People's theater, an old frame building on the corner of Fourth and St.
records.s: Adalina Patti appeared in St. Paul for the first time in 1857 at about sixteen years of age. She traveled with the Ole Bull Concert company, which used a small steamboat to give concerts in river towns, and she performed in the hall of the house of representatives.

records.l: old capitol, Novel-10146, The People's theater, an old frame building on the corner of Fourth and St.
records.s: The old capitol provided the only available venue for Adalina Patti's 1857 concert. Two boys who had been using the house for smoking and playing cards accidentally caused a fire that nearly burned through its floor.

records.l: house of representatives, Novel-10146, The People's theater, an old frame building on the corner of Fourth and St.
records.s: The hall of the house of representatives hosted Adalina Patti's 1857 concert, Washington's Birthday exercises, a mass meeting supporting the government after the attack on Sumter, and the first Republican state convention after Minnesota entered the Union. The hall was also the scene of speeches, resolutions, and political nominations.

records.l: Sumter, Novel-10146, The People's theater, an old frame building on the corner of Fourth and St.
records.s: After Maj. Anderson was compelled to lower the Stars and Stripes on Sumter's walls, St. Paul citizens held a mass meeting to express indignation at the attempt of the Cotton States to disrupt the government. The meeting pledged support to the government, urged young men to enlist, and promised financial aid for dependents of those who served.

records.l: John S. Prince, Novel-10146, The People's theater, an old frame building on the corner of Fourth and St.
records.s: John S. Prince, mayor of St. Paul, presided over the mass meeting held after the events at Sumter. He was assisted by several prominent citizens serving as vice presidents.

records.l: John M. Gilman, Novel-10146, The People's theater, an old frame building on the corner of Fourth and St.
records.s: John M. Gilman was one of the principal speakers at the mass meeting held after the events at Sumter. Although he had been the Democratic candidate for Congress the previous fall, he expressed hearty sympathy with the meeting's support for the government and received strong approval.

records.l: old opera house, Novel-10146, The People's theater, an old frame building on the corner of Fourth and St.
records.s: The old opera house facing Wabasha Street was completed in the winter of 1866–67 and opened with an entertainment by local talent. Its boxes and some parquet seats were auctioned, and the first regular company was the Macfarland Dramatic Company, featuring Emily Melville. The theater seated about 1,000 people and hosted speakers including Wendell Phillips, Henry Ward Beecher, Theodore Tilton, and Frederick Douglass.

records.l: Frederick Douglass, Novel-10146, The People's theater, an old frame building on the corner of Fourth and St.
records.s: Frederick Douglass addressed a large audience at the old opera house in St. Paul. During his lecture, two Republicans in an upper box applauded loudly while standing behind W.H. Shelley, causing the audience to think Shelley was supporting Douglass and had returned to the Republican fold; Shelley eventually left in disgust.

records.l: James J. Hill, Novel-10146, The People's theater, an old frame building on the corner of Fourth and St.
records.s: James J. Hill took part in a mock reenactment of the Heenan and Sayers prize fight at the Athenaeum. He was to imitate Sayers, but after Theodore Borup made a false pass, Hill knocked Borup out instead of following the prearranged result.

records.l: St. Paul, Novel-10146, The People's theater, an old frame building on the corner of Fourth and St.
records.s: St. Paul had early entertainment venues including the People's theater, Mazurka hall, Mozart hall, Masonic hall, Agony hall, and the old opera house. The city also hosted patriotic meetings, sanitary fairs, concerts, political conventions, and Washington's Birthday celebrations.

records.l: Civil War, Novel-10146, The People's theater, an old frame building on the corner of Fourth and St.
records.s: The unit describes St. Paul's mobilization during the Civil War, including patriotic meetings, enlistment appeals, financial support for soldiers' dependents, and the disbanding of the Pioneer Guards. Many Pioneer Guards members became Union officers, while two or three joined the Confederate forces.

records.l: Republican Party, Novel-10146, The People's theater, an old frame building on the corner of Fourth and St.
records.s: The first Republican state convention after Minnesota entered the Union met in the hall of the house of representatives and nominated Col. Aldrich and William Windom for Congress. Republicans also backed Col. Marshall in the sanitary-fair sword contest and attended Frederick Douglass's lecture, where some teased W.H. Shelley about his association with Andrew Johnson.

records.l: United States government, Novel-10146, The People's theater, an old frame building on the corner of Fourth and St.
records.s: At a mass meeting after the events at Sumter, St. Paul citizens pledged the American government their earnest support. They called on young men to enroll in military companies and promised financial aid for the dependent families of those who served.

records.l: it494-narrative-corpora-raw/graphrag-bench/Novel-10146.txt, Novel-10146, PRINTERS AND EDITORS OF TERRITORIAL DAYS.
records.s: This unit describes territorial printers and editors in Minnesota, focusing especially on Capt. E.Y. Shelly, the first printer to permanently locate in the territory. It recounts Shelly's printing career in St. Paul, his Mexican War service, and his Civil War service with Brackett's battalion. It also discusses other territorial printers who served in the Civil War and notes that few of the original printers remained. The unit provides detailed accounts of printing offices, military service, and the exceptional typesetting speed of Charles R. Stuart.

records.l: Capt. E.Y. Shelly, Novel-10146, PRINTERS AND EDITORS OF TERRITORIAL DAYS.
records.s: Capt. E.Y. Shelly was born in Bucks county, Pa., in 1827, learned printing in Philadelphia, served in the Third United States dragoons during the Mexican War, and arrived in St. Paul in July 1849 as the first printer to permanently locate in Minnesota. He worked for the Register, the Pioneer, and the Daily Democrat, and later organized a company with Major Brackett that served in Brackett's battalion during the Civil War. He was mustered out in 1865 and afterward continued working at printing until within a few years of the account.

records.l: James M. Goodhue, Novel-10146, PRINTERS AND EDITORS OF TERRITORIAL DAYS.
records.s: James M. Goodhue arrived in St. Paul from Lancaster, Wis., in the spring of 1849 with a Washington hand press and several fonts of type to start a paper in the new territory of Minnesota. He employed Capt. E.Y. Shelly and was working with him at the time of Goodhue's tragic death.

records.l: Minnesota, Novel-10146, PRINTERS AND EDITORS OF TERRITORIAL DAYS.
records.s: Minnesota is described as the new territory where James M. Goodhue established a newspaper in 1849 and where Capt. E.Y. Shelly became the first printer to permanently locate. Territorial printers from Minnesota served in numerous Civil War units, including the First, Second, Seventh, Eighth, and Tenth Minnesota regiments.

records.l: St. Paul, Novel-10146, PRINTERS AND EDITORS OF TERRITORIAL DAYS.
records.s: St. Paul was the capital of the new territory of Minnesota and the location of the Pioneer, Register, Chronicle, and Daily Democrat offices. Capt. E.Y. Shelly arrived there in July 1849, and many of the territorial printers later worked in its printing offices or enlisted for military service.

records.l: Fort Donelson, Novel-10146, PRINTERS AND EDITORS OF TERRITORIAL DAYS.
records.s: Brackett's battalion was the only Minnesota force engaged at Fort Donelson during its attack and surrender in February 1862. Capt. E.Y. Shelly's unit performed exhausting service to prevent Gen. Buckner from receiving reinforcements, and the regiment later returned to defend the fort against attacks in August 1862 and February 1863.

records.l: Pioneer, Novel-10146, PRINTERS AND EDITORS OF TERRITORIAL DAYS.
records.s: The Pioneer was the first paper printed in St. Paul. Capt. E.Y. Shelly worked there for James M. Goodhue, and later the Pioneer consolidated with the Daily Democrat.

records.l: Brackett's battalion, Novel-10146, PRINTERS AND EDITORS OF TERRITORIAL DAYS.
records.s: Brackett's battalion consisted of three Minnesota companies and was mustered into service in September 1861. It was assigned to Curtis horse, later changed to the Fifth Iowa cavalry, and served at Fort Donelson, on scouting and railroad protection duty, in the Tennessee campaigns, and later in Gen. Sully's campaign across the Dakotas.

records.l: Civil War, Novel-10146, PRINTERS AND EDITORS OF TERRITORIAL DAYS.
records.s: Many territorial printers served in the Civil War as soldiers and officers, including Capt. E.Y. Shelly, Capt. Henry C. Coates, Jacob J. Noah, Frank H. Pratt, John C. Devereux, Jacob T. McCoy, Martin Williams, Edward Richards, Charles R. Stuart, E.S. Lightbourn, M.J. Clum, and others. Their service included work in infantry, cavalry, artillery, sharpshooter, and other units, with several returning as officers.

records.l: printing and typesetting, Novel-10146, PRINTERS AND EDITORS OF TERRITORIAL DAYS.
records.s: The unit describes printing offices, newspaper work, and the movement of printers among territorial papers. Charles R. Stuart is described as an exceptional compositor who reportedly set 26,000 ems of solid brevier in twenty-four hours and commonly set 2,000 ems of solid bourgeois per hour.

records.l: territorial printers, Novel-10146, PRINTERS AND EDITORS OF TERRITORIAL DAYS.
records.s: The unit lists numerous territorial printers, including E.Y. Shelly, George W. Moore, John C. Devereux, Martin Williams, H.O. Bassford, and many others. It states that only H.O. Bassford, George W. Benedict, David Brock, John C. Devereux, Barrett Smith, J.B.H. Mitchell, David Ramaley, M.R. Prendergast, Jacob T. McCoy, A.S. Diamond, R.V. Hesselgrave, H.P. Coates, J.R. Chaney, and M.J. Clum were then known survivors.

records.l: it494-narrative-corpora-raw/graphrag-bench/Novel-10146.txt, Novel-10146, TERRITORIAL PRINTERS IN CIVIL LIFE.
records.s: The unit profiles territorial printers and editors in Minnesota, especially those connected with St. Paul newspapers and printing offices. It describes their occupations, political and civic careers, artistic interests, personal eccentricities, and notable incidents. The account also explains that early editors and printers worked closely together, sometimes living in their offices, while mechanization diminished the sociability of composing rooms.

records.l: James Mills, Novel-10146, TERRITORIAL PRINTERS IN CIVIL LIFE.
records.s: James Mills came to Minnesota early, worked at the old Pioneer office, and later joined its editorial department. After the war he returned to Pittsburgh and became editor-in-chief of the Pittsburgh Post.

records.l: Minnesota, Novel-10146, TERRITORIAL PRINTERS IN CIVIL LIFE.
records.s: Minnesota attracted many young printers and editors during its early territorial period.

records.l: O.G. Miller, Novel-10146, TERRITORIAL PRINTERS IN CIVIL LIFE.
records.s: O.G. Miller was a well-known musically inclined printer in St. Paul. He belonged to the Great Western band, sang tenor in several churches, and was a 33d Degree Mason; a midnight funeral service was held for him in Masonic hall after his death.

records.l: George W. Moore, Novel-10146, TERRITORIAL PRINTERS IN CIVIL LIFE.
records.s: George W. Moore came to St. Paul in 1850 and briefly served as foreman for Mr. Goodhue. He later partnered with John P. Owens in publishing the Minnesotian, sold his interest to Dr. Foster in 1860, and served as collector of the port of St. Paul for more than twenty years after President Lincoln appointed him in 1861.

records.l: John P. Owens, Novel-10146, TERRITORIAL PRINTERS IN CIVIL LIFE.
records.s: John P. Owens partnered with George W. Moore in publishing the Minnesotian. He was also the first editor of the Minnesotian and later formed a publishing partnership with John O. Terry.

records.l: Minnesotian, Novel-10146, TERRITORIAL PRINTERS IN CIVIL LIFE.
records.s: The Minnesotian was published by George W. Moore and John P. Owens beginning in 1852. George W. Moore sold his interest in it to Dr. Foster in 1860, and J.Q.A. Ward served as its business manager during its prosperous period.

records.l: Louis E. Fisher, Novel-10146, TERRITORIAL PRINTERS IN CIVIL LIFE.
records.s: Louis E. Fisher was foreman of the Commercial Advertiser and later an editor of the Pioneer and Pioneer Press. He was a staunch Democrat, ran for governor on the Democratic ticket, and was described as a potential model governor had he been elected.

records.l: Pioneer, Novel-10146, TERRITORIAL PRINTERS IN CIVIL LIFE.
records.s: The Pioneer employed James Mills in its editorial department, Louis E. Fisher as an editor, and George W. Armstrong as a printer. Marshall Robinson also worked as a compositor there, and Earle S. Goodrich was its editor-in-chief.

records.l: Pioneer Press, Novel-10146, TERRITORIAL PRINTERS IN CIVIL LIFE.
records.s: The Pioneer Press employed Louis E. Fisher as an editor and Richard Bradley as foreman of its job department for many years.

records.l: George W. Armstrong, Novel-10146, TERRITORIAL PRINTERS IN CIVIL LIFE.
records.s: George W. Armstrong was known as the Beau Brummel of the early printers and wore kid gloves while making up forms at the old Pioneer. He was elected state treasurer on the Democratic ticket in 1857 and later entered the real estate business.

records.l: James M. Culver, Novel-10146, TERRITORIAL PRINTERS IN CIVIL LIFE.
records.s: James M. Culver was a fastidious printer and the first delegate from St. Paul to the International Typographical Union. Members of the Sons of Malta remembered his resistance to the canine portion of their third-degree ceremony.

records.l: David Ramaley, Novel-10146, TERRITORIAL PRINTERS IN CIVIL LIFE.
records.s: David Ramaley was described as one of the best-known and most capable printers in the Northwest. He worked as a printer, reporter, editor, publisher, and type founder, and remained active after nearly fifty years in the trade.

records.l: George W. Benedict, Novel-10146, TERRITORIAL PRINTERS IN CIVIL LIFE.
records.s: George W. Benedict was familiar to longtime residents and had served as foreman of the old St. Paul Press. He later became editor and publisher of the Sauk Rapids Sentinel.

records.l: St. Paul Press, Novel-10146, TERRITORIAL PRINTERS IN CIVIL LIFE.
records.s: The old St. Paul Press employed George W. Benedict as foreman. Richard Bradley later held the foreman position in its job department, and the paper moved from Bridge Square to a new building at Third and Minnesota streets in 1869.

records.l: Times, Novel-10146, TERRITORIAL PRINTERS IN CIVIL LIFE.
records.s: The St. Paul Times employed Richard Bradley as foreman of its job department and Jebb as a reporter. Jebb's report about stolen chickens, which ended with a papal bull of excommunication against the thief, marked the end of his reporting career.

records.l: John O. Terry, Novel-10146, TERRITORIAL PRINTERS IN CIVIL LIFE.
records.s: John O. Terry was the first hand pressman in St. Paul and partnered with Col. Owens in publishing the Minnesotian. He later served for a long time as assistant postmaster of St. Paul and held other positions of trust.

records.l: Andrew Jackson Morgan, Novel-10146, TERRITORIAL PRINTERS IN CIVIL LIFE.
records.s: Andrew Jackson Morgan was brought to St. Paul by Col. D.A. Robertson and made foreman of the Democrat. He was a printer-politician and editor who claimed a resemblance to Stephen A. Douglas, carried a silver dollar said to have been given to him by Andrew Jackson, and died in Ohio more than forty years before the account was written.

records.l: William Jebb, Novel-10146, TERRITORIAL PRINTERS IN CIVIL LIFE.
records.s: William Jebb was a fluent and well-informed debater in the old Pioneer composing room and had also been a reporter on the St. Paul Times. After writing about the theft of his prized chickens and ending the report with a papal bull of excommunication, he left reporting.

records.l: Earle S. Goodrich, Novel-10146, TERRITORIAL PRINTERS IN CIVIL LIFE.
records.s: Earle S. Goodrich was editor-in-chief of the Pioneer and was also a printer. When the old Press moved into a new building in 1869, he set the first type there, composing about half a column of editorial without copy; printers later found an error in its first line.

records.l: territorial printers, Novel-10146, TERRITORIAL PRINTERS IN CIVIL LIFE.
records.s: Territorial printers held many roles, including printer, reporter, editor, publisher, foreman, and type founder. They often worked and slept in the same offices because of limited hotel accommodations, and their composing rooms were known for debate, literary quotations, and sociability.

records.l: printing and typesetting, Novel-10146, TERRITORIAL PRINTERS IN CIVIL LIFE.
records.s: The printing business included both technical and editorial work and was closely connected with politics, publishing, theater, and civic service. The introduction of the iron printer reduced the sociability and informal intellectual exchanges formerly associated with composing rooms.

records.l: it494-narrative-corpora-raw/graphrag-bench/Novel-10146.txt, Novel-10146, THE DECISIVE BATTLE OF MILL SPRINGS.
records.s: The Battle of Mill Springs was an early decisive Union victory in the Civil War, fought after the Second Minnesota Infantry Regiment joined George H. Thomas's division near Logan's Cross Roads, Kentucky. The Second Minnesota fought Confederate troops near Beech Grove, using rifle fire and bayonets, and suffered twelve killed and thirty-five wounded. Confederate General Zollicoffer was killed by Colonel Fry, while Bailie Peyton was killed after shooting Lieutenant Stout. The Union victory captured Confederate artillery, wagons, ammunition, and supplies, disrupted the Confederate right flank, and prompted widespread rejoicing in Minnesota, Louisville, and St. Paul.

records.l: The decisive battle of Mill Springs, Novel-10146, THE DECISIVE BATTLE OF MILL SPRINGS.
records.s: The decisive battle of Mill Springs was the first important Union victory in the Southwest after the outbreak of the Civil War. It resulted in Confederate losses of about 600 killed, wounded, and captured, Union losses of 248 killed and wounded, and the capture of twelve cannon and large quantities of equipment.

records.l: American Civil War, Novel-10146, THE DECISIVE BATTLE OF MILL SPRINGS.
records.s: The American Civil War provided the context for the organization and service of the Second Minnesota Infantry Regiment. The Battle of Mill Springs was described as an early Union success in the conflict.

records.l: Union forces, Novel-10146, THE DECISIVE BATTLE OF MILL SPRINGS.
records.s: Union forces under George H. Thomas advanced during the Mill Springs campaign and defeated the Confederate forces near Logan's Cross Roads. They captured twelve cannon, 200 wagons, ammunition, and camp supplies.

records.l: Confederate forces, Novel-10146, THE DECISIVE BATTLE OF MILL SPRINGS.
records.s: Confederate forces held an entrenched camp at Beech Grove and advanced against the Union pickets near Logan's Cross Roads. They were driven from the field and suffered about 600 killed, wounded, and prisoners.

records.l: Second Minnesota Infantry Regiment, Novel-10146, THE DECISIVE BATTLE OF MILL SPRINGS.
records.s: The Second Minnesota Infantry Regiment was organized in 1861 under Colonel H.P. Van Cleve and assigned to George H. Thomas's First Division. At Mill Springs it fought in the center of the engagement, used the bayonet, and suffered twelve killed and thirty-five wounded; its conduct received enthusiastic praise.

records.l: Minnesota, Novel-10146, THE DECISIVE BATTLE OF MILL SPRINGS.
records.s: Minnesota supplied the Second Minnesota Infantry Regiment after citizens volunteered in numbers exceeding the first regiment's quota. The state legislature praised the regiment's heroism at Mill Springs and contrasted its victory with the First Minnesota's service in defeat.

records.l: Louisville, Novel-10146, THE DECISIVE BATTLE OF MILL SPRINGS.
records.s: Louisville became the Second Minnesota's destination after its planned movement to Washington was changed. The regiment later returned there, where Mayor J.M. Dolph presented it with a silk flag in recognition of its conduct at Mill Springs.

records.l: George H. Thomas, Novel-10146, THE DECISIVE BATTLE OF MILL SPRINGS.
records.s: George H. Thomas commanded the First Division that included the Second Minnesota, the Eighteenth United States Infantry, and the Ninth and Thirty-fifth Ohio regiments. His troops began the Mill Springs campaign on January 1, 1862.

records.l: Mill Springs campaign, Novel-10146, THE DECISIVE BATTLE OF MILL SPRINGS.
records.s: The Mill Springs campaign began on January 1, 1862, under George H. Thomas. The troops marched through rain, sleet, and mud before camping near Logan's Cross Roads and engaging the Confederate forces at Beech Grove.

records.l: Logan's Cross Roads, Novel-10146, THE DECISIVE BATTLE OF MILL SPRINGS.
records.s: Logan's Cross Roads was the Union camp where George H. Thomas's troops assembled before the battle. It lay eight miles north of Zollicoffer's entrenched Confederate camp at Beech Grove.

records.l: Beech Grove, Novel-10146, THE DECISIVE BATTLE OF MILL SPRINGS.
records.s: Beech Grove was the site of Zollicoffer's entrenched Confederate camp, located eight miles south of Logan's Cross Roads. Confederate forces withdrew from the area after the battle.

records.l: Bailie Peyton, Novel-10146, THE DECISIVE BATTLE OF MILL SPRINGS.
records.s: Bailie Peyton was a Confederate lieutenant and the son of a prominent Union man in Tennessee. After refusing to surrender, he shot Lieutenant Stout through the body and was immediately killed; Lieutenant Tuttle captured his sword, which had previously been presented to him by citizens of New Orleans.

records.l: Zollicoffer, Novel-10146, THE DECISIVE BATTLE OF MILL SPRINGS.
records.s: Zollicoffer commanded the Confederate forces at Mill Springs and was killed during the battle. Colonel Fry reported that he shot Zollicoffer in the breast after Zollicoffer's companion fired at him; Zollicoffer had previously opposed Tennessee's secession but followed the state after it seceded.

records.l: Colonel Fry, Novel-10146, THE DECISIVE BATTLE OF MILL SPRINGS.
records.s: Colonel Fry of the Fourth Kentucky reported that he killed Zollicoffer during the battle. He described shooting the Confederate general in the breast after Zollicoffer's companion fired at him.

records.l: Union victory at Mill Springs, Novel-10146, THE DECISIVE BATTLE OF MILL SPRINGS.
records.s: The Union victory at Mill Springs broke up the Confederate right flank and opened a route into East Tennessee. It also helped force the withdrawal of Albert Sidney Johnston's troops from Bowling Green to Nashville and caused rejoicing throughout the loyal North.

records.l: Kentucky, Novel-10146, THE DECISIVE BATTLE OF MILL SPRINGS.
records.s: Kentucky was the setting for the Mill Springs campaign and battle, which loyal Kentuckians viewed as a victory over rebel invaders from Tennessee, Mississippi, and Alabama. Kentucky troops, including Wolford's First Cavalry and the Fourth Kentucky Infantry, were among the first to confront the invaders.

records.l: St. Paul, Novel-10146, THE DECISIVE BATTLE OF MILL SPRINGS.
records.s: St. Paul had two full companies in the Second Minnesota and additional residents serving in other companies. Its residents closely followed reports of the battle, and newspaper offices were crowded with relatives and friends seeking news of the soldiers' safety; several surviving veterans later lived and worked in the city.

records.l: it494-narrative-corpora-raw/graphrag-bench/Novel-10146.txt, Novel-10146, THE GREAT BATTLE OF PITTSBURG LANDING.
records.s: The unit describes the Battle of Pittsburg Landing, also called the Battle of Shiloh, fought on April 6–7, 1862, between Ulysses S. Grant's Union forces and the Confederate forces under Albert Sidney Johnston and P. G. T. Beauregard. The Confederates initially drove back parts of the Union army, but Union resistance, gunboat support, and reinforcements under Don Carlos Buell and Lew Wallace prevented their victory. The Union army counterattacked on April 7 and forced the Confederates to retreat toward Corinth. The battle caused heavy losses, including the deaths of Albert Sidney Johnston and William H. L. Wallace, and later became the subject of disputes over Grant, Buell, and the conduct of the campaign.

records.l: The Great Battle of Pittsburg Landing, Novel-10146, THE GREAT BATTLE OF PITTSBURG LANDING.
records.s: The battle was fought on April 6–7, 1862, and was described as one of the greatest and most sanguinary battles of the Civil War. Union forces ultimately drove the Confederate forces from the field, though both sides suffered heavy casualties.

records.l: American Civil War, Novel-10146, THE GREAT BATTLE OF PITTSBURG LANDING.
records.s: The Battle of Pittsburg Landing was presented as one of the most terrific battles of the American Civil War. The text compares it with Waterloo and discusses its wider consequences for Union commanders and military operations.

records.l: Army of the Tennessee, Novel-10146, THE GREAT BATTLE OF PITTSBURG LANDING.
records.s: The Army of the Tennessee, commanded by Ulysses S. Grant, was attacked at Pittsburg Landing before the arrival of much of Don Carlos Buell's army. It resisted the Confederate assault and, after receiving reinforcements, helped drive the enemy toward Corinth.

records.l: Army of the Cumberland, Novel-10146, THE GREAT BATTLE OF PITTSBURG LANDING.
records.s: The Army of the Cumberland, under Don Carlos Buell, was expected to join Grant's forces at Pittsburg Landing. The text states that critics believed Buell could have made the junction earlier and thereby reduced the Union loss of life.

records.l: Confederate forces, Novel-10146, THE GREAT BATTLE OF PITTSBURG LANDING.
records.s: The Confederate forces under Albert Sidney Johnston and P. G. T. Beauregard attacked Grant's army on April 6, expecting to destroy it before reinforcements arrived. They fought fiercely but failed to reach the Tennessee River or prevent the Union counterattack, and retreated toward Corinth on April 7.

records.l: Albert Sidney Johnston, Novel-10146, THE GREAT BATTLE OF PITTSBURG LANDING.
records.s: Albert Sidney Johnston commanded the Confederate forces at Pittsburg Landing. He was killed during the first day's battle while attempting to induce a Confederate brigade to charge the enemy.

records.l: P. G. T. Beauregard, Novel-10146, THE GREAT BATTLE OF PITTSBURG LANDING.
records.s: P. G. T. Beauregard served with Albert Sidney Johnston as a Confederate commander at Pittsburg Landing. He reportedly said that before sundown he would water his horses in the Tennessee River or in hell, and later reported Confederate losses of 10,699.

records.l: Ulysses S. Grant, Novel-10146, THE GREAT BATTLE OF PITTSBURG LANDING.
records.s: Ulysses S. Grant commanded the Union forces at Pittsburg Landing and, despite an injured ankle, rode among the divisions throughout the first day directing their movements. He stopped a general flight toward the river, led the pursuit on the second day, and later argued that an immediate pursuit could have captured prisoners and guns.

records.l: Don Carlos Buell, Novel-10146, THE GREAT BATTLE OF PITTSBURG LANDING.
records.s: Don Carlos Buell commanded the Army of the Cumberland and was criticized for taking nineteen days to move approximately eighty-five miles to the Tennessee River. His troops, including divisions under Nelson and Thomas, reinforced Grant during the battle; Grant did not believe Buell was guilty of the charges later made against him.

records.l: Henry W. Halleck, Novel-10146, THE GREAT BATTLE OF PITTSBURG LANDING.
records.s: Henry W. Halleck suspended Grant from command shortly before the battle and later assumed personal command of the forces at Pittsburg Landing, placing Grant second in command. Halleck constructed extensive fortifications that were never occupied before he was ordered to Washington.

records.l: William Tecumseh Sherman, Novel-10146, THE GREAT BATTLE OF PITTSBURG LANDING.
records.s: William Tecumseh Sherman commanded a Union division whose position saw some of the hardest fighting on the first day. He was wounded slightly twice, had a ball pass through his hat, and lost several horses, while his resistance was important to the Union defense.

records.l: Lew Wallace, Novel-10146, THE GREAT BATTLE OF PITTSBURG LANDING.
records.s: Lew Wallace brought 5,000 Union troops from Crump's Landing after nightfall on the first day. His division appeared on the Confederate left during the retreat and was strongly reinforced on the second day.

records.l: Tennessee River, Novel-10146, THE GREAT BATTLE OF PITTSBURG LANDING.
records.s: The Union forces were positioned near the Tennessee River at Pittsburg Landing. The Confederate plan was to reach the river after defeating Grant, but gunboat fire and Union resistance prevented that result.

records.l: Pittsburg Landing, Novel-10146, THE GREAT BATTLE OF PITTSBURG LANDING.
records.s: Pittsburg Landing was the principal Union position and the site of the April 6–7 battle. Troops and reinforcements arrived there by steamer, and the Union army used the landing and nearby river positions during the fighting.

records.l: Church of Shiloh, Novel-10146, THE GREAT BATTLE OF PITTSBURG LANDING.
records.s: The Church of Shiloh was an old log church about three miles from Pittsburg Landing. Some of the hardest fighting occurred in its vicinity, giving the battle its alternate name, the Battle of Shiloh.

records.l: Grant's command of the Army of the Tennessee, Novel-10146, THE GREAT BATTLE OF PITTSBURG LANDING.
records.s: Grant's command of the Army of the Tennessee was threatened before the battle when Halleck suspended him, but a restoration order arrived before Grant learned of the suspension. After the battle, Halleck placed Grant second in command until Grant later received command of the Department of West Tennessee.

records.l: Grant's military reputation, Novel-10146, THE GREAT BATTLE OF PITTSBURG LANDING.
records.s: Grant's military reputation was damaged by accusations that he was drunk, absent from the battlefield, and unprepared for the Confederate attack. The text rejects those claims by describing his active direction of the battle and noting that his army made a firm resistance.

records.l: Buell's delayed reinforcement, Novel-10146, THE GREAT BATTLE OF PITTSBURG LANDING.
records.s: Buell's delayed reinforcement was criticized as a possible cause of the Union army's terrible first-day losses. The text states that Buell was at Columbia on March 19 and required nineteen days to reach the Tennessee River, although his troops eventually reinforced Grant.

records.l: Union casualties at Shiloh, Novel-10146, THE GREAT BATTLE OF PITTSBURG LANDING.
records.s: The Union casualties in the two days of fighting were reported as 1,754 killed, 8,408 wounded, and 2,885 missing. The first day also saw approximately 2,200 men captured with Prentiss and about 6,000 inexperienced recruits flee toward the river.

records.l: Grant's alleged drunkenness, Novel-10146, THE GREAT BATTLE OF PITTSBURG LANDING.
records.s: Grant's alleged drunkenness was one of several charges made against him after the battle. The text states that he was instead in the saddle from early morning until late at night, directing Union divisions despite severe pain from a sprained ankle.

records.l: it494-narrative-corpora-raw/graphrag-bench/Novel-10146.txt, Novel-10146, At banquet hall, regimental reunion or campfire, whenever mention is made of the
records.s: The unit recounts the service of the First Minnesota battery during the American Civil War, especially its actions at the Battle of Pittsburg Landing. Organized at Fort Snelling under Captain Emil Munch, the battery fought in the Hornet's Nest and suffered several casualties while helping hold the Union lines. The text also memorializes Captain William Henry Acker, a St. Paul military leader who was killed at Pittsburg Landing and later honored through the naming of Acker Post.

records.l: First Minnesota battery, Novel-10146, At banquet hall, regimental reunion or campfire, whenever mention is made of the
records.s: The First Minnesota battery, light artillery, was organized at Fort Snelling in the fall of 1861 and sent to Pittsburg Landing after receiving its equipment in St. Louis. At the Battle of Pittsburg Landing, it fought in Prentiss' division, repeatedly drove off rebel batteries, and helped hold the Union lines at the Hornet's Nest. It suffered three killed and six wounded, with two of the wounded dying later, and received warm commendation for its conduct.

records.l: American Civil War, Novel-10146, At banquet hall, regimental reunion or campfire, whenever mention is made of the
records.s: The American Civil War is described as the great crisis and struggle in which Minnesota volunteers served. The text states that the First Minnesota battery later participated in the siege of Vicksburg, the fighting in front of Atlanta, and the march from Atlanta to the sea.

records.l: Emil Munch, Novel-10146, At banquet hall, regimental reunion or campfire, whenever mention is made of the
records.s: Emil Munch was made the first captain of the First Minnesota battery when it was organized at Fort Snelling in the fall of 1861. During the Battle of Pittsburg Landing, his horse was shot in the head and he was wounded in the thigh, preventing him from continuing in the battle; Lieutenant Pfaender then took command.

records.l: Pittsburg Landing, Novel-10146, At banquet hall, regimental reunion or campfire, whenever mention is made of the
records.s: Pittsburg Landing was the location where the First Minnesota battery arrived in late February 1862 and where it fought on April 6 and 7. The site was also where William Henry Acker was killed, and his remains were later recovered and returned to St. Paul.

records.l: The Great Battle of Pittsburg Landing, Novel-10146, At banquet hall, regimental reunion or campfire, whenever mention is made of the
records.s: The Battle of Pittsburg Landing began for the First Minnesota battery on the morning of April 6, when it was sent against the advancing rebel forces. The battery fought for hours, especially at the Hornet's Nest, and helped prevent the Union lines from being forced back toward the Tennessee River. On April 7, after General Buell arrived, the battery was held in reserve and did not participate in the battle.

records.l: William Henry Acker, Novel-10146, At banquet hall, regimental reunion or campfire, whenever mention is made of the
records.s: William Henry Acker was a captain who was killed at Pittsburg Landing while leading his company and urging his men forward. He had served as adjutant general of Minnesota, organized a company for the First Minnesota regiment, fought at the first battle of Bull Run, and was wounded there. Born in New York State in 1833, he came to St. Paul in 1854, where he became a military leader and was widely respected; after his death, St. Paul's first Grand Army post was named Acker Post in his honor.

records.l: St. Paul, Novel-10146, At banquet hall, regimental reunion or campfire, whenever mention is made of the
records.s: St. Paul is described as the home of William Henry Acker and the community that deeply mourned his death. His remains were returned there, received by citizens at the steamboat landing, displayed at Masonic Hall, and buried after a funeral at St. Paul's church attended by a large concourse. The first Grand Army post formed in St. Paul was named Acker Post to commemorate him.

records.l: it494-narrative-corpora-raw/graphrag-bench/Novel-10146.txt, Novel-10146, THE DEATH OF PRESIDENT LINCOLN.
records.s: Abraham Lincoln was assassinated on April 14, 1865, and news of his death plunged the United States into widespread mourning. In St. Paul, the House of Hope church held a solemn memorial service led by its pastor, Frederick A. Noble, who praised Lincoln’s life, leadership, and commitment to the Union cause. The service also mourned Secretary of State Seward, who had been attacked but survived. The text contrasts the universal grief following Lincoln’s assassination with the less-universal shock caused by the later assassinations of two other presidents.

records.l: Abraham Lincoln, Novel-10146, THE DEATH OF PRESIDENT LINCOLN.
records.s: Abraham Lincoln is described as the martyred president and as an ideal statesman to Frederick A. Noble. He had patiently led the country through more than four years of war and was assassinated just as Union victory appeared near.

records.l: assassination of Abraham Lincoln, Novel-10146, THE DEATH OF PRESIDENT LINCOLN.
records.s: The assassination was announced over the wires on the morning of April 15, 1865, after Lincoln was shot by an assassin. It caused nationwide grief and condemnation and was remembered as an especially appalling event.

records.l: death of Abraham Lincoln, Novel-10146, THE DEATH OF PRESIDENT LINCOLN.
records.s: Lincoln’s death occurred when an assassin’s bullet ended his life shortly after the fall of Richmond and Lee’s surrender. His death plunged the country into mourning and was commemorated in churches, including the House of Hope church.

records.l: United States, Novel-10146, THE DEATH OF PRESIDENT LINCOLN.
records.s: The United States was plunged into mourning after Lincoln’s assassination. Public and private buildings throughout the country were draped in mourning, and churches held memorial services.

records.l: St. Paul, Novel-10146, THE DEATH OF PRESIDENT LINCOLN.
records.s: St. Paul felt Lincoln’s assassination especially deeply. Its public and private buildings were draped in mourning, and memorial services were held throughout the city.

records.l: House of Hope church, Novel-10146, THE DEATH OF PRESIDENT LINCOLN.
records.s: The House of Hope church on Walnut Street held a solemn memorial service on the Sunday following Lincoln’s assassination. The church was heavily draped in mourning and was crowded almost to suffocation.

records.l: Frederick A. Noble, Novel-10146, THE DEATH OF PRESIDENT LINCOLN.
records.s: Frederick A. Noble was the pastor of the House of Hope church and was described as an eloquent, learned, fearless, forcible, and aggressive divine. He delivered an emotional invocation and a memorial discourse praising Lincoln and also eulogizing Secretary of State Seward.

records.l: House of Hope congregation, Novel-10146, THE DEATH OF PRESIDENT LINCOLN.
records.s: The House of Hope congregation was intensely patriotic, and many of its members were serving at the front defending the country. Its members regarded Lincoln’s death as if someone from their own household had been taken, and many wept during the memorial service.

records.l: Union cause, Novel-10146, THE DEATH OF PRESIDENT LINCOLN.
records.s: Frederick A. Noble consistently believed that the Union cause was just and would ultimately triumph. He supported vigorous prosecution of the war even during its darkest days.

records.l: Civil War, Novel-10146, THE DEATH OF PRESIDENT LINCOLN.
records.s: The American Civil War had lasted more than four years when Lincoln was assassinated. At the time of his death, the fall of Richmond, Lee’s surrender, and the probable surrender of Johnston appeared likely to end the war.

records.l: the Union, Novel-10146, THE DEATH OF PRESIDENT LINCOLN.
records.s: The Union was defended during the war by members of the House of Hope congregation and was approaching victory when Lincoln was assassinated. Noble’s sermons repeatedly supported the Union’s war effort.

records.l: William H. Seward, Novel-10146, THE DEATH OF PRESIDENT LINCOLN.
records.s: William H. Seward, referred to in the text as Secretary of State Seward, was believed at first to have been killed by the conspirators’ dagger but survived. Noble eulogized him as the foremost statesman of his time and credited his diplomatic skill with keeping the country free from foreign entanglements.

records.l: assassination conspiracy, Novel-10146, THE DEATH OF PRESIDENT LINCOLN.
records.s: The assassination conspiracy aimed to murder the president, vice president, and entire cabinet. The attempt was fatal only in Lincoln’s case, while Secretary of State Seward survived.

records.l: John Wilkes Booth, Novel-10146, THE DEATH OF PRESIDENT LINCOLN.
records.s: John Wilkes Booth fired the bullet that pierced Abraham Lincoln’s temple and caused his death. His act was remembered as a crime of extraordinary horror.

records.l: Lincoln's assassination memorial sermon, Novel-10146, THE DEATH OF PRESIDENT LINCOLN.
records.s: Lincoln’s assassination memorial sermon was delivered by Frederick A. Noble at the House of Hope church on the Sunday after the assassination. It recounted Lincoln’s early history and presidential achievements, condemned the killing, and eulogized Secretary of State Seward.

records.l: it494-narrative-corpora-raw/graphrag-bench/Novel-10146.txt, Novel-10146, AN ALLEGORICAL HOROSCOPE IN TWO CHAPTERS.
records.s: The unit presents an allegorical prophecy concerning Robert A. Smith, the city that will arise along the Mississippi River, and the political influence of the Okons. A dusky maiden predicts that Robert will become the long-reigning chief of a great city and will preserve political support by avoiding firm positions, withdrawing from controversies, and distributing offices to the Okons and their followers.
