More than eighty years later, the voyageur returns to find the city transformed into a large, modern metropolis, with Robert ruling from a magnificent public building and the Okons controlling every office within his gift. The voyageur leaves in anguish at the Okons’ pervasive power.

records.l: voyageur, Novel-10146, AN ALLEGORICAL HOROSCOPE IN TWO CHAPTERS.
records.s: A solitary voyageur travels along the Mississippi River on a peaceful mission to the red men. More than eighty years later, he returns, witnesses the city’s transformation and the political dominance of the Okons, and quietly departs in anguish.

records.l: Robert A. Smith, Novel-10146, AN ALLEGORICAL HOROSCOPE IN TWO CHAPTERS.
records.s: As a young paleface, Robert is told by the dusky maiden that he will become the mighty chief of the future great city and reign for a long time. In the later scene, a banner identifies him as the candidate for mayor in 1902, and he rules from the magnificent building with the support of the Okons.

records.l: dusky maiden, Novel-10146, AN ALLEGORICAL HOROSCOPE IN TWO CHAPTERS.
records.s: The dusky maiden gives Robert an astrological forecast and administers an elixir said to grant lasting life and power over his enemies. She advises him to avoid definite convictions, withdraw from disputes when danger arises, and reserve offices for the Okons and their followers.

records.l: Okons, Novel-10146, AN ALLEGORICAL HOROSCOPE IN TWO CHAPTERS.
records.s: The Okons are described as descendants of the sea kings from the bogs of Tipperary who will aid Robert when the city becomes too large for him to manage alone. In the later city, they and their followers control every office within Robert’s gift.

records.l: followers of the Okons, Novel-10146, AN ALLEGORICAL HOROSCOPE IN TWO CHAPTERS.
records.s: The followers of the Okons are to receive and retain offices through Robert’s patronage. In the later city, they possess every office within the paleface’s gift alongside the Okons.

records.l: Mississippi River, Novel-10146, AN ALLEGORICAL HOROSCOPE IN TWO CHAPTERS.
records.s: The voyageur travels along the river stretching from the North Star State to the Gulf of Mexico. More than eighty years later, the same grand river, called the Father of Water, still follows its course toward the ocean while the surrounding city has greatly changed.

records.l: St. Paul, Novel-10146, AN ALLEGORICAL HOROSCOPE IN TWO CHAPTERS.
records.s: St. Paul is not named directly in the unit, but the setting describes a great city on the Mississippi River whose residents include people labeled “St. Paul’s finest.”

records.l: great city, Novel-10146, AN ALLEGORICAL HOROSCOPE IN TWO CHAPTERS.
records.s: The dusky maiden predicts that a great city will eventually be built on the ground Robert surveys. When the voyageur returns, it has become a populous and technologically advanced metropolis with enormous buildings and rapid transportation.

records.l: magnificent building, Novel-10146, AN ALLEGORICAL HOROSCOPE IN TWO CHAPTERS.
records.s: A magnificent building erected through the generosity of the people stands in the midst of the transformed city. Robert, supported by the Okons, rules from it.

records.l: offices, Novel-10146, AN ALLEGORICAL HOROSCOPE IN TWO CHAPTERS.
records.s: The dusky maiden instructs Robert to arrange the offices within his gift so that the Okons and their followers remain securely established. In the later city, the Okons and their followers occupy every such office.

records.l: prophecy of the dusky maiden, Novel-10146, AN ALLEGORICAL HOROSCOPE IN TWO CHAPTERS.
records.s: The prophecy states that Robert will become the long-reigning chief of a great city, avoid firm political commitments, and depend on the Okons and their followers. The later events are presented as its fulfillment, including Robert’s mayoral campaign in 1902 and the Okons’ control of the offices.

records.l: city government and political patronage, Novel-10146, AN ALLEGORICAL HOROSCOPE IN TWO CHAPTERS.
records.s: The city government is portrayed as centered on Robert, who preserves support by avoiding decisions that might alienate opposing parties and by relying on the working majority to resolve controversies. Political patronage keeps the Okons and their followers in all offices within his gift.

records.l: transformation of the city, Novel-10146, AN ALLEGORICAL HOROSCOPE IN TWO CHAPTERS.
records.s: When the voyageur returns after more than eighty years, the former wilderness has become a vast modern city. Cultivated fields, steamers, steam-powered and electrically powered transportation, gigantic buildings, and a large population replace the earlier frontier setting.

records.l: it494-narrative-corpora-raw/graphrag-bench/Novel-10146.txt, Novel-10146, SPELLING DOWN A SCHOOL.
records.s: The narrator describes growing up in a small village in northern Pennsylvania before railroads and telegraphs reached the area. At about twelve, the narrator secretly rode under a sleigh seat to attend a grand spelling match involving four schools. The schoolmaster from the narrator's district entered the narrator into the contest, where the narrator correctly spelled "phthisic" and outlasted the other pupils. The narrator's school was declared the champion, and the narrator's reputation as a speller was established.

records.l: narrator, Novel-10146, SPELLING DOWN A SCHOOL.
records.s: The narrator lived in a small village in northern Pennsylvania at about twelve years of age and was considered too young for joint spelling matches. The narrator secretly rode under a driver's seat to attend one contest, correctly spelled "phthisic," and spelled down four schools. Afterward, the narrator's reputation as a speller was established, and the narrator was no longer called last in spelling contests.

records.l: small village, Novel-10146, SPELLING DOWN A SCHOOL.
records.s: The small village was in a mountainous and sparsely settled section of northern Pennsylvania before the arrival of the railroad and telegraph. Its people had limited prosperity and intellectual opportunities compared with the present time described by the narrator.

records.l: school districts, Novel-10146, SPELLING DOWN A SCHOOL.
records.s: The school districts generally offered reading, writing, and arithmetic, with school terms often lasting only six months a year. Older children could not attend during the summer because they were needed for cultivating the soil, and four districts participated in the grand spelling contest.

records.l: our school, Novel-10146, SPELLING DOWN A SCHOOL.
records.s: The narrator's school participated in the grand spelling contest against three other schools. It was declared to have furnished the champion speller after the narrator correctly spelled "phthisic."

records.l: schoolmaster from the narrator's district, Novel-10146, SPELLING DOWN A SCHOOL.
records.s: The schoolmaster from the narrator's district noticed the narrator standing apart and identified the narrator as one of the best spellers in the school. He pronounced the contest words, appeared to expect the narrator to spell "phthisic" correctly, and confirmed the narrator's answer by saying, "Correct."

records.l: pupils and scholars, Novel-10146, SPELLING DOWN A SCHOOL.
records.s: The pupils and scholars from four schools lined up for the spelling contest according to their reputations as spellers. One after another, the older scholars were eliminated by simple words and then by "phthisic," leaving the narrator as the only contestant standing.

records.l: spelling match, Novel-10146, SPELLING DOWN A SCHOOL.
records.s: The spelling match was held on a Saturday night at a country crossroads about four miles from the narrator's village. Four schools participated, and the contest established the narrator's school as the winner.

records.l: phthisic, Novel-10146, SPELLING DOWN A SCHOOL.
records.s: "Phthisic" was a difficult word familiar to the narrator but absent from the spelling book. It was used to eliminate the remaining contestants, but the narrator spelled it correctly as "ph-th-is-ic--phthisic."

records.l: spelling championship, Novel-10146, SPELLING DOWN A SCHOOL.
records.s: The spelling championship among the four districts went to the narrator's school because the narrator outlasted the other contestants. The narrator was thereafter recognized as the champion speller and was no longer placed last in the line.

records.l: it494-narrative-corpora-raw/graphrag-bench/Novel-10146.txt, Novel-10146, HALF A CENTURY WITH THE PIONEER PRESS.
records.s: Frank Moore celebrated the fiftieth anniversary of his connection with the Pioneer Press in 1908 at an informal dinner attended by a dozen former employees. He began working for the Minnesotian in St. Paul in 1858 as a printer’s “devil” and later joined the Pioneer Press when it absorbed the Minnesotian. Moore became superintendent of the composing room and had held that position for about forty years. His service was continuous except for his time as a Civil War volunteer, and he was recognized for his loyalty and efficiency.

records.l: Frank Moore, Novel-10146, HALF A CENTURY WITH THE PIONEER PRESS.
records.s: Frank Moore began working for the Minnesotian on April 17, 1858, at age fifteen, performing duties such as carrying water, retrieving newspapers from arriving steamers, and delivering papers. He joined the Pioneer Press when it absorbed the Minnesotian in 1861 and remained with the merged paper formed when the Press and Pioneer united in 1874. At age sixty-five, he was superintendent of the composing room, a position he had held for about forty years, and was recognized for his loyalty, devotion, and efficiency.

records.l: Pioneer Press company, Novel-10146, HALF A CENTURY WITH THE PIONEER PRESS.
records.s: The Pioneer Press absorbed the Minnesotian in 1861 and united with the Pioneer in 1874. Frank Moore’s service with the paper and its antecedents extended for fifty years, and he celebrated the anniversary in 1908.

records.l: Minnesotian, Novel-10146, HALF A CENTURY WITH THE PIONEER PRESS.
records.s: The Minnesotian employed Frank Moore as a printer’s “devil” beginning April 17, 1858. The Pioneer Press absorbed the Minnesotian in 1861, and Moore continued with the resulting paper.

records.l: St. Paul, Novel-10146, HALF A CENTURY WITH THE PIONEER PRESS.
records.s: Frank Moore came to St. Paul from Tioga county, Pa., when he was fifteen years old. He worked for the Minnesotian there beginning in 1858 and carried newspapers through parts of the city.

records.l: fiftieth anniversary of Frank Moore's connection with the paper, Novel-10146, HALF A CENTURY WITH THE PIONEER PRESS.
records.s: Frank Moore’s fiftieth anniversary of connection with the Pioneer Press was celebrated on April 17, 1908, with an informal dinner at Magee’s attended by a dozen old employees of the paper.

records.l: composing room, Novel-10146, HALF A CENTURY WITH THE PIONEER PRESS.
records.s: Frank Moore served as superintendent of the Pioneer Press composing room for about forty years. He continued to fill the position efficiently at age sixty-five, as the newspaper grew from its early beginnings into a large modern operation.

records.l: Travels in Morocco, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER I.
records.s: The unit describes the social conditions, customs, appearance, religion, and treatment of Jewish communities in Morocco, especially Mogador and the Atlas Mountains. It contrasts the improved position of European and some native Jews with the oppression described by Ali Bey and the continuing fluctuations of imperial policy. It recounts the devastation of Mogador during the French bombardment, the independence and beliefs of the Atlas Jews, and customs involving marriage, polygamy, beauty, superstition, and white brandy. It concludes with anecdotes about the Moroccan Court and the dangers faced by physicians and quacks.

records.l: Morocco, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER I.
records.s: Morocco is presented as a country where Jews, Moors, Berbers, and Arabs live under sharply unequal social and religious conditions. The unit discusses Moroccan marriage customs, superstition, intoxication, imperial policy, and the position of Jewish communities.

records.l: Mogador, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER I.
records.s: Mogador contains a European society in which European and native Jews increasingly mix with European merchants and attend social functions. Its Jewish community suffered massacres, destruction, plunder, homelessness, and starvation during the French bombardment.

records.l: Mogador Jewesses, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER I.
records.s: The European Jewesses of Mogador are described as the belles of society and as attending its balls. They are said to forget religious differences more readily than Jewish men, and some native Jewesses adopt European clothing and seek husbands who wear European hats or coats.

records.l: Moroccan Jews, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER I.
records.s: Moroccan Jews historically endured humiliation, violence, restrictions, and unfavorable treatment before Muslim judges, though their position had reportedly improved during the preceding half century. Some adopted European clothing and habits, while others continued to live under oppression and social constraint.

records.l: European merchants, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER I.
records.s: European Jews in Mogador came principally from London, Gibraltar, and Marseilles. They mixed with European merchants and helped form the European society of the city.

records.l: Moorish subjects, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER I.
records.s: Moors are described as having oppressed Jews, including by violence, legal favoritism, and social humiliation. During the bombardment of Mogador, Moorish rabble plundered Jewish houses and stripped Jewish women, while Moorish men also practiced early marriage, polygamy, and the drinking of white brandy.

records.l: Berbers, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER I.
records.s: Berbers protect certain Atlas Jewish communities, whose standards the Jews follow, and the Atlas Jews share their mountaineer way of life. During the destruction of Mogador, Berber and Arab tribes plundered the city and later pillaged Moors who had fled with booty.

records.l: Atlas Jews, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER I.
records.s: The Atlas Jews live dispersed through the Atlas ranges and enjoy a degree of independence from imperial authority under the protection of Berber chieftains. They bear arms, speak Shelouh, dress like mountaineers, maintain their own sheiks for domestic matters, and rarely descend to the plains or cities.

records.l: Ali Bey, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER I.
records.s: Ali Bey described Jews as suffering continual disputes, violence, legal discrimination, forced removal of shoes, and restrictions on movement. He reported that Jews considered themselves slaves of the Sultan and compensated themselves for mistreatment by cheating Moors.

records.l: Jewish religion, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER I.
records.s: The unit portrays Jewish religious and communal life through Passover, Tabernacle, and wedding festivals, Sabbath observance, and Jewish marriage customs. It also states that Jews in Mahometan countries were occasionally permitted to have four wives.

records.l: religion of the Atlas Jews, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER I.
records.s: The religion of the Atlas Jews is described as differing from that of Jews generally: they are said to resemble Caraaites, to be unacquainted with Ezra or Christ, and to call the Supreme Being Shadai. Their written law is said to omit the deluge, describe distinct human species, and recount God's appearance to Ishmael.

records.l: Atlas Mountains, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER I.
records.s: The Atlas Mountains shelter the main population of Shelouh Jews, especially around Jebel Melge, described as a vast ridge capped with eternal snows. The mountain setting is associated with their physical strength, isolation, independence, and freedom.

records.l: Tangier, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER I.
records.s: Tangier had Jewish residents who sometimes returned from Gibraltar wearing European dress. The Emperor ordered such Jews to be undressed and to resume wearing the black turban so they could not pass as Christians or Europeans.

records.l: French bombardment of Mogador, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER I.
records.s: The French bombardment of Tangier and Mogador brought severe suffering to the Jewish communities. Jews were massacred or buried beneath ruins, their wives were plundered, and survivors wandered naked and starving or hid in the mountains.

records.l: Mogador sack and destruction, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER I.
records.s: The plunder of Mogador was carried out from within while French forces attacked from outside. Moorish rabble targeted Jewish houses and women, while Berbers and Arabs later plundered both Jews and Moors who had escaped with booty.

records.l: Jewish polygamy, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER I.
records.s: Jewish polygamy is portrayed as rare and disorderly. One Jewish silk-merchant in Tunis had four wives whose household was marked by rivalry, quarrelling, neglect of the older wives, and the overattention of all four women to their only child.

records.l: early marriage, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER I.
records.s: Early marriage is common in the unit's account of Mogador, with girls sometimes married at nine and commonly at ten or eleven. A nine-year-old girl was reportedly married to a man over fifty.

records.l: marriage customs, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER I.
records.s: Marriage customs among Jews and Moors are presented as arrangements of sale and barter rather than love. Engagements may be broken over the value of household goods, and wealthy older men are said to be preferred over handsome and amiable young men.

records.l: female beauty and obesity, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER I.
records.s: Jewish women are described as often having fair complexions, delicate features, and expressive eyes, while Moorish standards value extreme size in the lower back, thighs, calves, and knees. Betrothed women may be deliberately fattened with paste and prevented from exercising, and enormous women are treated as especially attractive.

records.l: white brandy, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER I.
records.s: White brandy is described as a stimulant of immorality and intoxication in Moroccan society. Jews are said to produce and distribute it despite government punishment, while Moors drink it on the understanding that it is not grape juice, and Jewish families become excited and troubled by it on the Sabbath.

records.l: Travels in Morocco, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER II.
records.s: The unit traces the succession of Maroquine dynasties from the Edristees in 789 through the Shereefs, who have ruled Morocco for more than three centuries. It describes the Shereefian genealogy and explains the dynasty’s descent from Ali and Fatima, the daughter of Mahomet. It profiles Muley Abd Errahman, who was selected by his uncle Muley Suleiman and strengthened imperial authority through frugal, conservative rule. It also discusses Morocco’s religious and political importance, the status of its Shereefs, and the limits of Abd-el-Kader’s ability to replace the reigning dynasty.

records.l: Morocco, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER II.
records.s: Morocco is described as an immense remnant of the monarchies created by the Saracens and as the only remaining independent Mussulman kingdom founded by the Saracen conquest of North Africa. Its present Shereefian dynasty claims descent from the Prophet through Ali and Fatima and has ruled the country for more than three centuries.

records.l: Maroquine dynasties, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER II.
records.s: The Maroquine dynasties are listed as the Edristees, Fatamites, Zuheirites, Moravedi, Almohades, Merinites, Oatagi, and Shereefs. They succeeded one another from the Edristee accession in 789 until the Shereefs became the reigning dynasty.

records.l: Shereefian dynasty, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER II.
records.s: The Shereefian dynasty originated from a family near Medina in Arabia and gained control of Morocco through successive usurpations. It is divided into the Hoseinee branch and the El Fileli, or Tafilett, branch, with the latter forming the present ruling line.

records.l: Muley Abd Errahman, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER II.
records.s: Muley Abd Errahman was chosen by his dying uncle, Muley Suleiman, instead of Suleiman’s own children. He is portrayed as a frugal and pacific ruler who consolidated imperial authority, preserved the empire through long periods of internal quiet, and generally avoided bloodshed, although he was accused of avarice, confiscations, and imprisonments.

records.l: Muley Suleiman, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER II.
records.s: Muley Suleiman preferred his nephew Muley Abd Errahman as successor because Abd Errahman was considered more suitable to preserve and consolidate the empire. His designation of Abd Errahman was presented as an act of justice because Abd Errahman had been excluded from the succession earlier on account of his youth.

records.l: Shereefs, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER II.
records.s: The Shereefs are presented as descendants of the Prophet’s family and as profoundly venerated by true Mussulmen. Many members of the royal family reside at Tafilett, and the Shereefs there are described as living in a small fortified town in moderate or impoverished circumstances.

records.l: Islam, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER II.
records.s: The Shereefian sultans are portrayed as religious leaders whose claim to head Islam is stronger than that of the Ottoman sultans, according to the text. The Shereefs’ descent from Ali and Fatima is said to give them exceptional authority among Mussulmen.

records.l: Abd-el-Kader, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER II.
records.s: Abd-el-Kader is described as a highly revered marabout warrior and an object of enthusiasm among Mussulmen in North Africa, especially Morocco. The text argues that he could not have successfully dethroned the Shereefian emperor because Moroccans would not deliberately abandon the Prophet’s line for a ruler of different blood.

records.l: Tafilett, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER II.
records.s: Tafilett is identified as the ancient country of the Sherfah, or Shereefs, and as a place especially appropriated for members of the royal family. The present Shereefian branch extended its authority from Tafilett over the provinces of Morocco.

records.l: North Africa, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER II.
records.s: North Africa is described as the region conquered by the Saracens and as the area where Abd-el-Kader was widely revered. Morocco is distinguished from Tunis and Tripoli, which are described as regencies, and from Algeria, which had become an integral part of France.

records.l: Moorish imperial throne, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER II.
records.s: The Moorish imperial throne passed through a succession of dynasties before being held by the Shereefs. Muley Abd Errahman occupied it after Muley Suleiman and is credited with making imperial authority more solid and preserving the empire during his reign.

records.l: Travels in Morocco, Travels in Morocco, [5] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper
records.s: The unit recounts the succession crisis after Sidi Mohammed’s death, the reigns of Yezeed, Muley Hisham, and Muley Suleiman, and Muley Abd Errahman’s succession among the Shereefs. It praises Muley Suleiman’s peaceful rule and abolition of Christian slavery, while discussing Morocco’s relations with France, England, and Europe. It examines the slave trade and the Shereefian justification of it under Islam. It also criticizes the British-Moroccan treaties, especially their provisions for disputes involving British subjects, and describes British influence in Morocco, including at Gibraltar and Mogador.

records.l: Muley Suleiman, Travels in Morocco, [5] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper
records.s: Muley Suleiman was proclaimed Sultan in the north at Fez during the civil war following Yezeed’s death, and later became Sultan of the whole empire after Muley Hisham’s retirement. He is described as a good and patriotic prince who maintained peace and tranquility, remained neutral during European wars, cultivated peace with Europe, and abolished Christian slavery in his States. He died on 28 March 1820 after declaring his nephew, Muley Abd Errahman, his legitimate and hereditary successor.

records.l: Yezeed, Travels in Morocco, [5] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper
records.s: Yezeed was the hereditary prince and succeeded his father, Sidi Mohammed, three days after his death in April 1790 or 1789. He is portrayed as a tyrant whose cruelties caused civil war; he was mortally wounded by a poisoned arrow and died in February 1792 during the 22nd month of his reign. Despite his reputation, he was buried with great solemnities at the mosque of Kobah Sherfah because he was a Shereef.

records.l: Muley Hisham, Travels in Morocco, [5] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper
records.s: Muley Hisham disputed the succession after Yezeed’s death and was proclaimed Sultan in the south at Morrocco and Sous. In 1795 he retired to a sanctuary, where he soon died.

records.l: Muley Abd Errahman, Travels in Morocco, [5] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper
records.s: Muley Abd Errahman was declared by Muley Suleiman to be the legitimate and hereditary successor of the Shereefs. The text later describes him as pursuing a pacific policy with the assistance of his vizier, Bouseilam.

records.l: Shereefs, Travels in Morocco, [5] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper
records.s: The Shereefs are presented as the lineage of Mussulman sovereigns claiming descent from the Prophets of God. Their rulers are described as exercising divine or inviolable Shereefian privileges, and the Shereefian Court defended slavery as authorized by Islamic scripture and tradition.

records.l: Morocco, Travels in Morocco, [5] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper
records.s: Morocco is described as an empire divided by civil war after Yezeed’s death and later governed by Muley Suleiman and Muley Abd Errahman. Its relations with European powers, especially England and France, are discussed through diplomacy, trade, piracy, slavery, and treaties.

records.l: Fez, Travels in Morocco, [5] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper
records.s: Fez was the place where Muley Suleiman was saluted as Emperor in the north during the succession conflict. The text also refers to the war party and diplomatic activity at the Court of Fez.

records.l: Gibraltar, Travels in Morocco, [5] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper
records.s: The peace of Utrecht conceded Gibraltar to England, which the text says more than compensated England for the loss of Tangier. A treaty or arrangement also supplied provisions, especially cattle, to the garrison of Gibraltar.

records.l: Mogador, Travels in Morocco, [5] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper
records.s: Mogador is described as a place where European merchants, including Mr. Saferty, conducted business under the authority of the Moroccan government. The text says merchants there were sometimes prohibited from visiting vessels in or outside the port, despite a treaty provision appearing to permit it.

records.l: England, Travels in Morocco, [5] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper
records.s: England’s influence and trade in Morocco expanded during the eighteenth century, and British influence was strengthened by the battle of Trafalgar and the fall of Napoleon. England concluded treaties with Morocco concerning peace, trade, piracy, and the treatment of British subjects.

records.l: France, Travels in Morocco, [5] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper
records.s: France entered relations with the western Moors shortly after England and began sending its flag to Moroccan ports in 1555 under Francis I. France gained influence while England occupied Tangier, later sought a treaty of peace, and was associated with protection for a Jewish former consul who was decapitated by the Emperor.

records.l: Europe, Travels in Morocco, [5] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper
records.s: Muley Suleiman maintained neutrality while Christian powers in Europe were convulsed with war and cultivated peace with Europe. The text also discusses Morocco’s diplomatic intercourse with European princes and European efforts to influence Morocco.

records.l: Yezeed's succession crisis, Travels in Morocco, [5] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper
records.s: After Sidi Mohammed’s death, Yezeed and Hisham disputed the succession, and Yezeed was proclaimed Sultan at Salee as the hereditary prince. Yezeed’s cruelties provoked civil war, and after his death the empire was divided among three pretenders before Muley Hisham and Muley Suleiman became the principal competitors.

records.l: Muley Suleiman's reign, Travels in Morocco, [5] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper
records.s: Muley Suleiman’s reign lasted about a quarter of a century. The text characterizes it as peaceful and prosperous, noting his just administration, neutrality in European wars, peaceful relations with Europe, and abolition of Christian slavery.

records.l: abolition of Christian slavery, Travels in Morocco, [5] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper
records.s: The abolition of Christian slavery in Muley Suleiman’s States is identified as the most glorious and beneficent act of his reign from the perspective of European nations.

records.l: Christian slavery, Travels in Morocco, [5] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper
records.s: The text says that Moroccan rulers formerly subjected Christian captives to severe bondage, motivated partly by hostility toward Spain and revenge for injuries inflicted on the Moors. It credits Muley Suleiman with abolishing Christian slavery in his States.

records.l: slave trade, Travels in Morocco, [5] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper
records.s: The slave trade is defended in letters from the Sultan to Mr. Hay as a practice accepted since the time of the sons of Adam and confirmed by the Koran and the Sunnat. The correspondence states that Islamic law regulates the treatment, sale, emancipation, and religious transfer of slaves.

records.l: Islam, Travels in Morocco, [5] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper
records.s: The Shereefian correspondence presents Islam as authorizing slavery and the slave trade through the Koran and traditions of the Prophet. It also states that a Muslim, the sacred misshaf, and a young person may not be sold or given to an unbeliever.

records.l: Moorish law, Travels in Morocco, [5] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper
records.s: The British-Moroccan treaties provide that disputes involving British and Moorish subjects are to be decided according to Moorish law in specified circumstances. The text criticizes this arrangement because it could expose British subjects to punishments imposed under the Moorish legal system.

records.l: British influence in Morocco, Travels in Morocco, [5] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper
records.s: British influence in Morocco grew after the peace of Utrecht and was strengthened by Trafalgar and the fall of Napoleon. British diplomacy sought to support Muley Abd Errahman’s pacific policy, counter French influence, and prevent French pretexts for invading Morocco.

records.l: British-Moroccan treaties, Travels in Morocco, [5] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper
records.s: The principal treaty discussed was signed at Fez on 14 June 1801 and confirmed on 19 January 1824 by Muley Suleiman. It addressed consuls, trade, disputes, punishment, religious renegades, and access to vessels, but the text argues that it required immediate revision because it gave excessive authority to the Emperor and insufficient security to British subjects.

records.l: British subjects, Travels in Morocco, [5] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper
records.s: British subjects in Morocco were granted treaty protections concerning consuls, commerce, disputes, punishment, and access to vessels. The text argues that they remained exposed to Moorish punishments and uncertain justice, citing the imprisonment and attempted punishment of Mr. Saferty at Mogador.

records.l: Moors, Travels in Morocco, [5] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper
records.s: The Moors are described as the inhabitants and rulers of Morocco, with historical conflicts involving England, France, Spain, and other European powers. The text says that Moors were subject to severe punishments under Moorish law and that disputes between Moors and Europeans were governed by the Moroccan authorities and treaties.

records.l: Travels in Morocco, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER III.
records.s: The unit describes the Empire of Morocco’s uncertain extent, military and commercial resources, political influence, geography, and population. It reviews the successive settlement and conquest of North Africa by Libyans, Getulians, Phoenicians, Romans, Vandals, and Arabs, and distinguishes Berbers, Arabs, Moors, Jews, and Blacks among Morocco’s inhabitants. It explains that the Sultan’s authority is strong in religious and nominal terms but limited in many southern, northern, and mountainous regions. It also discusses Morocco’s natural boundaries, Atlas mountains, trade, and the mixed origins of its urban population.

records.l: Empire of Morocco, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER III.
records.s: The Empire of Morocco is presented as having either a restricted effective territory or a much wider sphere of nominal influence. Its dependent territory is estimated at about 137,400 square miles, while its population is approximately six million; its army, commerce, and authority over distant provinces are described as limited and uneven.

records.l: Morocco, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER III.
records.s: Morocco is also called El-Gharb, or Mogrel-el-Aksa, meaning the West or Far West, and is sometimes called the Country of the Sultan Muley Abd Errahman. It is bounded by the Mediterranean and Straits of Gibraltar to the north, the Atlantic to the west, the Sahara and southern deserts to the south, and Algeria, the Atlas, and Tafilett to the east.

records.l: Sultan of Morocco, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER III.
records.s: The Sultan of Morocco is the head of the orthodox religion of the Mussulmen of the West and claims authority over territories where his direct power is often only nominal. He can use religious titles and honors, including those associated with the Shereefian Parasol, to set chiefs against one another and strengthen his position.

records.l: Atlas Mountains, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER III.
records.s: The Atlas contains quasi-independent Berber tribes that oppose both the Arabs and the Moorish government. Its eastern and mountainous regions limit the Sultan’s authority, and some inhabitants of its snowy mountains are reported to have European-looking customs.

records.l: North Africa, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER III.
records.s: North Africa is described as having been successively inhabited or conquered by Libyans, Getulians, Phoenicians, Romans, Vandals, and Arabs. Its population is portrayed as religiously homogeneous under Islam, while its peoples include Berbers, Arabs, Moors, Jews, and Blacks.

records.l: Barbary, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER III.
records.s: Barbary is the region in which the aboriginal tribes of North Africa were called Barbarians or Berbers by the Romans and Arabs. The term Barbary States derives from this designation.

records.l: Sahara, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER III.
records.s: The Sahara forms Morocco’s southern boundary and contains distant oases over which the Shereefs formerly claimed, and sometimes still nominally claim, sovereignty. The oases of Touat, Agobli, and Taoudeni are described as having little or no effective dependence on Morocco.

records.l: Romans, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER III.
records.s: The Romans took control of Africa from the Phoenicians or Carthaginians and encountered indigenous peoples whom they called Moors, Berbers, or Barbarians. After being displaced by the Vandals, they later expelled or destroyed the Vandals, but eventually lost North Africa to the Arabs.

records.l: Phoenicians, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER III.
records.s: The Phoenicians successively invaded North Africa and established themselves on its shores around the foundation of Carthage, about 820 years before the Christian era. The Romans later received or wrested control of Africa from them.

records.l: Arabs, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER III.
records.s: The Arabs invaded North Africa from Asia around the middle of the seventh century and fought both the Romans and the indigenous Berbers. Arabs later ruled Morocco and, after being expelled from Spain, many refugees settled in Barbary, contributing to the growth of maritime cities.

records.l: Berbers, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER III.
records.s: The Berbers are presented as descendants or representatives of North Africa’s indigenous peoples, especially the Getulians, and as persistent opponents of foreign domination. They inhabit Morocco’s mountains, while many Arab tribes occupy the plains, and their resistance continued against Roman and Arab conquerors.

records.l: Berber race, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER III.
records.s: The Berber race is described as including the Amayeegh and Shelouh varieties in Morocco. Its members are chiefly located in the mountains and are difficult to distinguish from Arabs or Moors when they adopt urban occupations, dress, or habits.

records.l: Moorish population, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER III.
records.s: The Moorish population is concentrated mainly in Morocco’s towns and cities and consists of a mixture of many races, including descendants of Moors expelled from Spain. Europeans commonly call urban inhabitants Moors, although the population itself distinguishes more specifically between Arabs and Berber tribes.

records.l: Islam, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER III.
records.s: Islam provides the common religion that helps hold Morocco’s diverse populations together. The Sultan’s religious position allows him to claim influence across Western Barbary and Central Africa wherever Muslims are found, and a Christian or other non-Muslim enemy could unite otherwise hostile tribes.

records.l: Arab conquest of North Africa, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER III.
records.s: The Arab conquest of North Africa began around 650, when Arab forces from Asia attacked the declining Roman power. The Berbers initially submitted to the Arabs to escape Roman rule, then revolted and continued the struggle against their new conquerors.

records.l: Arab conquest of Spain, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER III.
records.s: The conquering Arabs crossed from North Africa into Spain in the early eighth century. Because they came from Mauritania, the Spaniards called them Moors, although the text states that they may have had little in common with the indigenous Moors of North Africa.

records.l: Travels in Morocco, Travels in Morocco, The nature of the soil and climate of Morocco are not unlike those of Spain and
records.s: The unit describes Morocco’s climate, geography, agriculture, commerce, mineral resources, and animal life. It compares Morocco’s soil and climate with those of Spain and Portugal and identifies the Atlas Mountains as its dominant geographic feature. Morocco produces grain, fruits, vegetables, timber, and regionally distinctive argan oil, while its northern and southern regions export different staple goods. The unit also reports that Morocco possesses extensive but largely neglected mineral resources and describes the desert horse called sherb-errech.

records.l: Morocco, Travels in Morocco, The nature of the soil and climate of Morocco are not unlike those of Spain and
records.s: Morocco is described as one of the healthiest countries in Africa, except perhaps Tunis, because of its Atlantic exposure, Atlas elevations, varied terrain, and lack of extensive marshes. Its surface consists largely of a central ridge with slopes toward the Atlantic and the Sahara, and its coasts have few well-protected ports.

records.l: Atlantic Ocean, Travels in Morocco, The nature of the soil and climate of Morocco are not unlike those of Spain and
records.s: The Atlantic Ocean borders Morocco to the west and receives the country’s northwestern rivers. The Atlantic coast is characterized mainly by ridges of hills, and its ports offer poor protection from the ocean.

records.l: Atlas Mountains, Travels in Morocco, The nature of the soil and climate of Morocco are not unlike those of Spain and
records.s: The Atlas Mountains traverse Morocco from northeast to southwest, and their highest stated point, Miltsin, rises more than 15,000 feet above sea level. The mountains influence Morocco’s climate, produce numerous rivers, and contain forests, mineral resources, and the highest peaks of the Moroccan portion of the range.

records.l: Sahara, Travels in Morocco, The nature of the soil and climate of Morocco are not unlike those of Spain and
records.s: The Sahara receives the southeastern slopes and streams of Morocco, including waters that feed the Wad Draha and other rivers before disappearing into desert sands. Southern Morocco has more desert heat and less rain because of its proximity to the Sahara.

records.l: Elaeonderron Argan, Travels in Morocco, The nature of the soil and climate of Morocco are not unlike those of Spain and
records.s: Eloeondenron Argan is a tree peculiar to southern Morocco. Its fruit resembles an olive and contains an almond whose crushed kernel produces a rancid oil commonly used instead of olive oil.

records.l: Argan, Travels in Morocco, The nature of the soil and climate of Morocco are not unlike those of Spain and
records.s: Argan trees are bushy and large, sometimes reaching the size of wide-spreading oaks. Several argan forests grow near Mogador.

records.l: climate and soil of Morocco, Travels in Morocco, The nature of the soil and climate of Morocco are not unlike those of Spain and
records.s: The climate and soil of Morocco are described as similar to those of Spain and Portugal. Northern Morocco has a climate nearly like Spain’s, while the south has less rain and more desert heat but greater fertility for valuable commercial staples.

records.l: agriculture of Morocco, Travels in Morocco, The nature of the soil and climate of Morocco are not unlike those of Spain and
records.s: Agriculture centers on wheat and barley in the plains, while vegetables and fruits are cultivated near towns. Irrigation sustains cultivation when rains cease or fail, allowing Southern European fruits and vegetables, as well as plants suited to Africa, to be grown successfully.

records.l: Moroccan commerce, Travels in Morocco, The nature of the soil and climate of Morocco are not unlike those of Spain and
records.s: Northern Morocco exports cattle, grain, bark, leeches, and skins, while southern Morocco exports gums, almonds, ostrich feathers, wax, wool, and skins. Cork, salt, argan oil, leather-related plants, and fish such as the Shebbel also contribute to commerce.

records.l: Moroccan mineral resources, Travels in Morocco, The nature of the soil and climate of Morocco are not unlike those of Spain and
records.s: Morocco possesses deposits of gold, silver, lead, iron, tin, sulphur, mineral salt, antimony, copper, saltpetre, and amethyst. Most mines are neglected or unworked because the government fears encouraging foreign interest, although silver mines in Sous, copper mines between several southern settlements, and other deposits are identified.

records.l: Travels in Morocco, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: The unit describes Morocco’s political, tribal, and natural divisions, distinguishing the northern Rif, the central Atlas, and the southern quasi-Saharan region. It questions the reliability of Moroccan population statistics and surveys coastal towns, ports, and Spanish presidios along the Mediterranean. Particular attention is given to the Jafarine Isles, Melilla, Alhucemas, Penon de Velez, Gomera, Tetouan, and Ceuta, including their populations, strategic positions, commerce, and relations with Spain. It also describes the Berbers of the Rif and Garet and recounts Abd-el-Kader’s refuge among them.

records.l: Morocco, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: Morocco is described as having historically been divided into the kingdoms or provinces of Morocco and Fez, with Tafilett and sometimes Sous attached to Morocco. Its modern divisions include northern Fez, central Morocco, eastern Tafilett, and southern Sous, while its practical administration is based chiefly on tribes and kaidats. Its coastal towns, interior regions, and natural resources are surveyed, although reliable population information is difficult to obtain.

records.l: Fez, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: Fez was historically a powerful independent kingdom extending eastward to the gates of Tlemsen. In the modern geographical division it is identified with the northern kingdom of Fez and is listed among the districts of the central Atlas region.

records.l: Mulweeah, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: The Moulwia, also called Mulweeah or Malwia, forms an important reference point for Morocco’s northern coast. The Rif is described as extending from the river’s mouth toward Tangier, and the Jafarine Isles lie near its mouth; Kalat-el-wad is situated near the river, although its navigability is unknown.

records.l: Rif, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: The Rif is Morocco’s mountainous northern coastal region, extending along the Mediterranean from the Moulwia to Tangier. It contains the districts of Hashbat, Gharet, and Aklaia and is inhabited by warlike Berbers over whom the Sultan exercises precarious authority. The region is fertile and mineral-rich, with cork forests, grazing valleys, and exports of skins, but travel there is described as exceptionally dangerous.

records.l: Atlas Mountains, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: The Atlas is presented as Morocco’s central great mountain chain, called the Deren by the natives, extending from the Algerian frontier to Cape Gheer. It separates the northern regions from the southern quasi-Saharan region and includes or borders districts such as Fez, Morocco, Todla, Dukala, Abda, Haha, and Sous.

records.l: Sahara, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: The Sahara is included in the quasi-Saharan region south of the Atlas, particularly in the area southeast of the mountain chain. The text treats the Sahara as a comparison for the dangers of travel in the Rif, stating that travel in the Rif is more dangerous than in the farthest wastes of the Sahara.

records.l: Berbers, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: Berbers inhabit the provinces of Rif and Garet and are portrayed as warlike, semi-barbarous, and only loosely controlled by the Sultan. They graze herds and flocks in the Rif’s valleys, exploit its forests and resources, and participate in fierce disputes at market gatherings.

records.l: Spanish, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: The Spanish possess the Jafarine Isles and the presidios of Melilla, Alhucemas, Penon de Velez, and Ceuta on the Moroccan coast. Their settlements are described as fortified or penal establishments, and their authority is portrayed as a remnant of Spain’s weakened power.

records.l: Abd-el-Kader, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: Abd-el-Kader sought refuge and support among the tribes of the Rif after withdrawing from Algeria. He resisted the Imperial government there for several months but ultimately chose to confront the Sultan in a pitched battle.

records.l: Jafarine Isles, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: The Jafarine Isles are three islands near the mouth of the Moulwia that belong to Spain. They had recently been additionally fortified, although the text questions the purpose of those fortifications; a small town is said to stand on the mainland opposite them.

records.l: Melilla, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: Melilla, an ancient Carthaginian city near the cape called Rusadir by the Romans, is the capital of Garet and is said to contain about 3,000 inhabitants. It lies amid fertile country rich in minerals and honey. A nearby Spanish presidio, also called Melilla, occupies an island connected to the mainland by a drawbridge and is reported to contain 2,244 people by Spanish figures, though other writers give a lower number.

records.l: Garet, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: Garet is a northern Moroccan province containing Melilla and extending through a rich and highly cultivated region. Like the Rif, it is inhabited by warlike Berbers over whom the Sultan’s authority is precarious.

records.l: Alhucemas, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: Alhucemas is a small Spanish island presidio containing approximately five or six hundred inhabitants. It commands the bay of the same name at the mouth of the Wad Nechor, near the Islet of Ed-Housh; the ruined ancient capital of Mezemma lies nearby.

records.l: Penon de Velez, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: Penon de Velez is a Spanish presidio island and convict settlement situated opposite the mouths of the Gomera River. It is a strong position with a garrison and population of about nine hundred, but it is largely a barren rock and must receive fresh water from the mainland for part of the year.

records.l: Gomera, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: Gomera, or Badis, lies on the mainland opposite Penon de Velez and is identified with several ancient names, including Parientina and possibly the Acra of Ptolemy. Although Count Graberg claimed that it contained 3,000 inhabitants, other and later writers described it as abandoned and inhabited only by serpents and hyenas.

records.l: Tetouan, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: Tetouan, identified with the Roman Yagath, is a large, prosperous, and commercial city of the province of Hasbat, situated several miles inland from the Mediterranean. It has gardens, olive and vine plantations, extensive orange groves, covered bazaars, a Jewish quarter, and a nearby port at Marteen or Marteel. Its population is variously estimated at 9,000 to 12,000, and its fortifications are strong enough mainly to resist hostile Berbers.

records.l: Tangier, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: Tangier marks the western extent of the Rif in the unit’s description of the northern coast. Tetouan lies roughly two-thirds of a day’s journey southeast of Tangier, and the northern intermediate zone extends from Tangier toward Mogador.

records.l: Ceuta, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: Ceuta, or Sebta, is an ancient city and fortress identified with Esilissa of Ptolemy and formerly regarded as the capital of Mauritania Tingitana. Portugal conquered it in 1415, and Spain retained it after Portugal recovered its independence in 1640. It contains a Spanish garrison of roughly 2,000 to 3,000 men, a free population of about 5,000 to 6,000, and a small insecure port.

records.l: Gibraltar, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: Gibraltar is described as lying opposite Ceuta across the Straits of Gibraltar and as the European counterpart of the African Pillars of Hercules. The text also mentions the supposed subterranean passage beneath the straits through which monkeys were fancifully believed to travel between Gibraltar and Africa.

records.l: Straits of Gibraltar, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: The Straits of Gibraltar are the maritime setting of Ceuta, which stands fourteen miles south of Gibraltar and nearly opposite it. The surrounding mountains are identified with the African Pillars of Hercules, facing Gibraltar as the European pillar.

records.l: Spain's North African presidios, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: Spain's North African presidios include the settlements at Melilla, Alhucemas, Penon de Velez, and Ceuta, as well as the fortified Jafarine Isles. They are characterized as garrisons or convict settlements established on islands, peninsulas, or coastal strongpoints, and the text calls them of limited utility apart from their military or penal functions.

records.l: population statistics of Morocco, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: Moroccan population statistics are described as approximate and conjectural because local people resist counting populations and regard such questions as ill-omened, intrusive, or suggestive of espionage. Conflicting estimates for Mazagran, Melilla, Gomera, and other places are offered as evidence of their unreliability. The text nevertheless attempts to provide figures to indicate Morocco’s approximate strength and resources.

records.l: Moroccan coastal towns and ports, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: Moroccan coastal towns and ports on the Mediterranean are said to be important but poorly documented, apart from the Spanish presidios and well-known places such as Tetouan and Tangier. The unit describes Kalat-el-wad, Melilla, Alhucemas, Penon de Velez, Gomera, Tegaza, Tetouan, and Ceuta, noting their trade, fortifications, populations, bays, and varying degrees of accessibility.

records.l: Moroccan tribal administration, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: Moroccan tribal administration is presented as more fundamental than European-style provincial divisions. Districts and mountains are commonly named after their chief tribes, while kaidats provide a jurisdictional structure more comparable to European government. The Sultan’s authority is especially weak among the Berber tribes of the Rif and Garet.

records.l: Travels in Morocco, Travels in Morocco, Passing Tangier after a day's journey, we come to Arzila or Asila, in the provin
records.s: The unit describes towns, rivers, tribes, fortifications, populations, commerce, and historical events along Morocco's Atlantic coast, from Arzila southward to Mogador. It discusses Arzila, El Araish, Mehedia, Salee, Rabat, Fidallah, Dar-el-Beida, Azamor, Mazagran, Saffee, and El-Waladia, including their ports and relations with Portuguese, Spanish, Moorish, and European powers. It also connects ancient sites such as Lixus and Shella with Roman, Phoenician, Carthaginian, and Berber history. The text highlights the activities of the Salee rovers and the historical importance of Almanzor and the Bouragrag River.

records.l: Arzila, Travels in Morocco, Passing Tangier after a day's journey, we come to Arzila or Asila, in the provin
records.s: Arzila, or Asila, is an ancient Berber city in the province of Hasbat, formerly called Zilia and Zulia by the Romans. It lies on the naked Atlantic shore, has a small port, a population of about one thousand, and produces good tobacco; its Portuguese fortifications are rapidly decaying under Moorish possession.

records.l: Atlantic Ocean, Travels in Morocco, Passing Tangier after a day's journey, we come to Arzila or Asila, in the provin
records.s: The Atlantic Ocean borders the Moroccan towns described in this unit, including Arzila, El Araish, and the coastal settlements farther south. Its shores and roadsteads provide ports and anchorages, although many entrances are obstructed by sandbars, rocks, or shallow water.

records.l: Moors, Travels in Morocco, Passing Tangier after a day's journey, we come to Arzila or Asila, in the provin
records.s: The Moors possess or govern many of the towns described, including Arzila, El Araish, Mehedia, Salee, Rabat, and Dar-el-Beida. They have retaken several coastal strongholds from the Portuguese or Spanish, but some Moorish fortifications and ports are described as weak, neglected, or decaying.

records.l: El Araish, Travels in Morocco, Passing Tangier after a day's journey, we come to Arzila or Asila, in the provin
records.s: El Araish, also called Laratsh, replaces the ancient city of Lixus and is the capital and seat of the governor of the district of Azgar. It has a population of about four thousand according to one estimate, a garrison of five hundred troops, a difficult port on the river Cos or Luccos, and exports cork, wool, skins, bark, beans, and grain.

records.l: Azgar, Travels in Morocco, Passing Tangier after a day's journey, we come to Arzila or Asila, in the provin
records.s: Azgar is the district whose capital and governor's residence is El Araish. Its name is connected in the text with a powerful tribe of the Touaricks, and its environs include the Beni-Arous vineyards and the Beni Arasis mountains.

records.l: Lixus, Travels in Morocco, Passing Tangier after a day's journey, we come to Arzila or Asila, in the provin
records.s: Lixus, also called Liscas and Lixa, was the ancient city replaced by El Araish. Its Phoenician coins depict grapes, ears of corn, and fishes, reflecting the area's vineyards, grain fields, and rivers.

records.l: Mauritania, Travels in Morocco, Passing Tangier after a day's journey, we come to Arzila or Asila, in the provin
records.s: Mauritania is described through the ancient Roman frontier and the fertile Atlantic region associated with Lixus. Strabo characterizes most of it as rich, fertile, well watered, and abundant in trees and other products, while Salee is identified as the farthest Roman city on the Atlantic coast of ancient Mauritania Tingitana.

records.l: Mehedia, Travels in Morocco, Passing Tangier after a day's journey, we come to Arzila or Asila, in the provin
records.s: Mehedia, also called Mamora or Nuova Mamora, stands near the mouth of the Sebou on the edge of the Mamora plain and forest. It was captured by the Spaniards in 1614 and retaken by the Moors in 1681; it later became a weak settlement with fishermen, a small garrison, and a crumbling castle.

records.l: Salee, Travels in Morocco, Passing Tangier after a day's journey, we come to Arzila or Asila, in the provin
records.s: Salee, or Sala, is an ancient city on the right bank of the Bouragrag near its mouth and a major commercial and fortified city of Beni-Hassan. It was captured by Alphonso the Wise in 1263, returned to Moorish rule, and later became a center of piracy; its population estimates vary widely, and Christians and Jews were not permitted to reside there.

records.l: Bouragrag River, Travels in Morocco, Passing Tangier after a day's journey, we come to Arzila or Asila, in the provin
records.s: The Bouragrag River flows between Salee on its right bank and Rabat on its left bank before reaching the Atlantic. It is broad near the two cities and is presented as a natural line separating the more humid northern side from the higher and drier southern side.

records.l: Salee rovers, Travels in Morocco, Passing Tangier after a day's journey, we come to Arzila or Asila, in the provin
records.s: The Salee rovers were Moroccan pirates based at Salee and Rabat who formed a nearly independent military republic. They were described as exceptionally ferocious and courageous and once operated as far away as Lundy Island in the British Channel.

records.l: Rabat, Travels in Morocco, Passing Tangier after a day's journey, we come to Arzila or Asila, in the provin
records.s: Rabat, or Er-Rabat, is a large, densely populated, fortified city opposite Salee on the Bouragrag River. It was built by Yakob-el-Mansour as Rabat-el-Fatah, contains wealthy Jewish residents and active merchants, and has gardens, plantations, forts, and a mausoleum associated with Almanzor.

records.l: Jakoub Almanzor, Travels in Morocco, Passing Tangier after a day's journey, we come to Arzila or Asila, in the provin
records.s: Almanzor, also called Elmansor, was a famous and victorious Sultan who intended Rabat to be his capital. The text says that he expelled the Moravedi from Spain and that his untenanted mausoleum stands in Rabat.

records.l: Dar-el-Beida, Travels in Morocco, Passing Tangier after a day's journey, we come to Arzila or Asila, in the provin
records.s: Dar-el-Beida, or Casa-Blanco, is a small Atlantic town built by the Portuguese on the ruins of Anafa, which they destroyed in 1468. It has a small port and a spacious bay capable of sheltering large vessels, but its population is estimated at only about one thousand or as few as two hundred.

records.l: Azamor, Travels in Morocco, Passing Tangier after a day's journey, we come to Arzila or Asila, in the provin
records.s: Azamor, or Azemmour, is an ancient Berber city of Dukaila whose name means olives in the Berber language. It lies near the mouth of the Omm-er-Rbia, has fertile surroundings and a trade in Shebbel salmon, and was captured and fortified by the Portuguese in 1513 before being abandoned about a century later.

records.l: Mazagran, Travels in Morocco, Passing Tangier after a day's journey, we come to Arzila or Asila, in the provin
records.s: Mazagran is an ancient and strong castle on a peninsula at the bottom of a spacious bay, rebuilt by the Portuguese in 1506 as Castillo Real. The Portuguese abandoned it in 1769, making it their last stronghold in Morocco; it has thick walls, a small port, and a population of two or three hundred.

records.l: Saffee, Travels in Morocco, Passing Tangier after a day's journey, we come to Arzila or Asila, in the provin
records.s: Saffee, properly Asafee and formerly Soffia or Saffia, is an ancient city of Abda built by the Carthaginians near Cape Pantin. It has massive walls, a summer roadstead, and a history of European commerce, but its population is about one thousand and the surrounding country is comparatively uncultivated.

records.l: Mogador, Travels in Morocco, Passing Tangier after a day's journey, we come to Arzila or Asila, in the provin
records.s: Mogador is mentioned as the next destination after the description of El-Waladia. The text states that Mogador and Aghadir have already been described.

records.l: Travels in Morocco, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER V.
records.s: The unit describes the imperial cities of Morocco, El-Kesar, Mequinez, Fez, and Morocco, as well as Tafilett, the birthplace of the ruling Shereefian dynasty. It records their locations, populations, defenses, religious and commercial institutions, historical origins, and apparent decline. Fez is presented as the Empire’s principal center of learning and commerce, Mequinez as a fortified royal residence and treasury, Morocco as the southern capital, and Tafilett as a caravan mart and place associated with the Imperial family. The account concludes that the cities and the wider Moorish civilization are declining and may require reconstruction by European hands.
records.t: The unit describes the imperial cities of Morocco—El-Kesar, Mequinez, Fez, and Morocco—as well as Tafilett, the birthplace of the ruling Shereefian dynasty. It records their locations, populations, defenses, religious and commercial institutions, historical origins, and apparent decline. Fez is presented as the Empire’s principal center of learning and commerce, Mequinez as a fortified royal residence and treasury, Morocco as the southern capital, and Tafilett as a caravan mart and place associated with the Imperial family. The account concludes that the cities and the wider Moorish civilization are declining and may require reconstruction by European hands.

records.l: Imperial Cities of Morocco, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER V.
records.s: The Imperial Cities of Morocco are identified as El-Kesar, Mequinez, Fez, and Morocco. They are described as royal or capital cities with important roles in administration, defense, commerce, religion, and learning, although all are said to be in decline.

records.l: Empire of Morocco, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER V.
records.s: The Maroquine Empire contains the royal cities of El-Kesar, Mequinez, Fez, and Morocco, together with Tafilett and its surrounding districts. Its principal cities are portrayed as politically divided, commercially active, and weakened by decay and inadequate defenses.

records.l: El-Kesar, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER V.
records.s: El-Kesar lies in the province of the Gharb on the southern bank of the Luccos. It was enlarged and beautified by Almansor around 1180 as a military magazine and rendezvous, but its narrow streets, ruined houses, inactive mosques, and small population reflect decline. The Battle of the Three Kings took place there in 1578.

records.l: Battle of the Three Kings, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER V.
records.s: The Battle of the Three Kings occurred at El-Kesar in 1578. Don Sebastian, the Portuguese king, and two Moorish princes perished in connection with the battle, while Muley Moluc died secretly in a litter so that the Moorish forces would not lose courage.

records.l: Mequinez, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER V.
records.s: Mequinez, or Miknas, is a royal residence and city of the province of Fez, situated on a hill in a well-watered and pleasant region. It is surrounded by a triple wall, contains much of the Imperial guard, and holds royal treasures estimated at about fifty million dollars. Its inhabitants are described as polished, kind, and hospitable, while its palace is noted for elaborate stucco Arabesque work.

records.l: Berbers, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER V.
records.s: Berbers founded Mequinez through the tribe of Meknasab, a fraction of the Zenatah, in the middle of the tenth century. Berbers also inhabit the mountains near Mequinez and are among the peoples whose revolts or disaffection concern the Sultan.

records.l: Fez, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER V.
records.s: Fez is described as one of the leading cities of Morocco in learning, wealth, industry, commerce, and religious importance. It contains old and new sections, hundreds of mosques, schools, markets, caravans, and manufactures, but its walls and defenses are decayed and its inhabitants are characterized as fanatical. Its population is uncertain, with estimates ranging from about thirty thousand to eighty-eight thousand or more.

records.l: Edris-Ben-Edris, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER V.
records.s: Edris-Ben-Edris inherited the virtues and influence of his father, Edris Ben Abdalluh. He is credited with being the first bona-fide Mussulman sovereign of the Maroquine empire and with founding Fez.

records.l: El-Karoubin, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER V.
records.s: El-Karoubin, also called El-Karouiin, is the most famous mosque of Fez and is supported by three hundred pillars. It is said to contain a celebrated ancient library with Greek and Latin authors and lost books of Titus Livy, although the text treats this claim as conjectural.

records.l: Muley Edris, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER V.
records.s: Muley Edris is identified as the founder of the modern city of Fez, whose ashes rest in a revered mosque mausoleum. The people are said to invoke his name in prayers, treating him with excessive veneration.

records.l: Tafilett, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER V.
records.s: Tafilett consists of fortified towns and villages on the south-eastern side of the Atlas and is inhabited partly by the Imperial family. It is a major caravan rendezvous and market for products from the surrounding countries and the Sahara. The area is also used as a place of exile for troublesome members of the Imperial family.

records.l: Morocco, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER V.
records.s: Morocco, or Maraksh, is the capital of the South and is sometimes called the capital of the Empire, though it is described as a diminished shadow of its former greatness. It has extensive walls, mosques, markets, gardens, an Imperial palace, and caravan trade, but its streets and buildings are decayed and its learning is limited. Its population estimates range from about thirty thousand to one hundred thousand.

records.l: Atlas Mountains, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER V.
records.s: The Atlas lies near Morocco, whose city spreads across a plain at its foot. The Atlas supplies water through streams and aqueducts and forms the geographical setting for Tafilett on its south-eastern side.

records.l: Eastern Province of Tafilett, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER V.
records.s: The Tafilett province was anciently called Sedjelmasa and later took the name Tafilett from an Arab immigrant associated with improved date cultivation. It contains several fortified towns and fertile level districts producing corn, fruits, vegetables, sheep, and woollen and silk manufactures.

records.l: Shereefs, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER V.
records.s: The Shereefs are descendants or family members of the Prophet and inhabit Tafilett, which is called the country of the Shereefs. The ruling family is described as a southern African branch of Shereefs rather than Shereefs of Fez.

records.l: Shereefian dynasty, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER V.
records.s: The present dynasty belongs to Morocco and is identified as a dynasty of Shereefs from the south. Its rulers must favor Fez at times to maintain the allegiance of the northern country, while the dynasty’s authority is threatened by restless tribes and rival political centers.

records.l: Sultan of Morocco, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER V.
records.s: The Sultan of Morocco resides mainly at Fez, Mequinez, and Morocco, using his presence to maintain allegiance and restrain disaffected tribes. He sends troublesome members of his family to Tafilett, and he sometimes retreats to Morocco when relations with European powers become difficult. The text says that the Emperors never visit Tafilett except as dethroned exiles.

records.l: France, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER V.
records.s: France is mentioned in connection with hostilities provoked by the fanatics of Fez and with the possibility of awakening the population’s energies. The text suggests that European intervention, including that of France, might help reconstruct the declining royal cities.

records.l: Moorish civilization, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER V.
records.s: Moorish civilization is portrayed as having entered a period of decline, with ruined cities, decaying fortifications, diminished learning, and weakened institutions. The text calls the royal cities the remnants of a once flourishing civilization and suggests that they may not recover without European reconstruction.

records.l: Travels in Morocco, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: The unit describes towns, cities, rivers, provinces, tribes, and trade routes in Morocco, especially the Kingdom of Fez and the southern regions of Sous, Draha, and Tafilett. It discusses places including Wazen, Muley Driss, Taza, Oushda, Aghmat, and many smaller settlements, noting their populations, commerce, agriculture, fortifications, and political organization. The text emphasizes the influence and near-independence of Amazirgh, Berber, and Shelouh communities, as well as the economic importance of Jews in many towns. It concludes by questioning existing population estimates and describing the uncertainty surrounding the interior geography of Morocco.

records.l: Morocco, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: The unit surveys Morocco's interior towns and cities, including regions of the Kingdom of Fez, Sous, Draha, and Tafilett. It describes Morocco as politically weakened by independent or semi-independent tribes and as having poorly documented geography and population.

records.l: Northern kingdom of Fez, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: The Kingdom of Fez includes places such as Seisouan, Wazen, Muley Driss, Taza, Oushda, Aghla, Nakhila, and Meshra Khaluf. Its districts contain fertile plains, commercial towns, sanctuaries, and areas where local religious or tribal authorities exercise considerable independence.

records.l: Fez, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: Fez is used as a point of reference for the distances of several towns, including Muley Driss, Dubdu, Taza, Oushda, and Aghla. The surrounding kingdom is described as containing important commercial and agricultural districts.

records.l: Atlas Mountains, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: The Atlas range is associated with picturesque mountain scenery, Berber settlements, fertile valleys, and routes toward the southern provinces. Several towns, including Tefza, Pitideb, Ghuer, and Tednest, are situated on or near its mountains.

records.l: Wazen, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: Wazen, in the province of Azgar and the region of the Gharb, is a small city without walls and the residence of the hereditary High Priest or Grand Marabout. Its religious ruler exercises substantial influence, and the district pays no tribute to the imperial government.

records.l: Muley Driss, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: Muley Driss, also called Zawiat-Muley-Driss or Muley Edris, is a renowned city in the province of Fez at the foot of the mountains of Terhoun. It contains a sanctuary dedicated to Edris, founder of the Edrisiti dynasty, and lies in a fertile country producing many necessities and luxuries.

records.l: Taza, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: Taza is the capital of the well-watered district of Haiaina and is described as one of the finest cities in Morocco. Built on a rock surrounded by a river, it has spacious streets, a large mosque, good provisions, hospitable inhabitants, and commerce with Tlemsen and Fez.

records.l: Oushda, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: Oushda is a frontier town in the northeast, protected by a fortress and enclosed by garden walls. Its small population lives among low clay houses and winding streets, while irrigated gardens produce melons, olives, and figs; the surrounding Desert of Angad is extremely arid, especially in summer.

records.l: Sous, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: Sous is a southern region containing towns such as Tagawost, Fedsi, Messa or Assah, Talent, and Shtouka. It has fertile areas, trade with the Sahara and Timbuctoo, divisions among Shelouhs, Moors, and Jews, and districts that are sometimes nearly independent of Morocco.

records.l: Draha, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: Draha is a southern province containing Beni-Sabih, Tatta, and Akka, with caravan routes leading toward the Great Desert. Beni-Sabih, also called Moussabal or Draha, is its small but populated and commercial capital.

records.l: Tafilett, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: Tafilett is identified as a southern destination reached by the road from Aghmat. The unit includes it among the distinguished places of Morocco but provides little further description.

records.l: Amazirghs, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: The Amazirghs are described as an aboriginal population with their own elders, chiefs, and local institutions. Their mountain tribes frequently resist imperial authority, and their leaders may exploit conflicts between Morocco and European powers to avenge old grievances.

records.l: Omm-er-Rbia River, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: The Omm-Erbegh River passes near or through several settlements, including Meshra Khaluf, Tijijet, Bulawan, Soubeit, and Meramer. It provides fords and routes of travel, and the surrounding districts are often fertile and productive in grain and cattle.

records.l: Aghmat, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: Aghmat was formerly a great fortified city and the capital of Rhamna, but it has declined into a village inhabited by about sixty families, including a few Jews. It lies near the Atlas and a river of the same name in a fertile country of orchards and vineyards, and it was the first capital of the Marabout dynasty.

records.l: Sahara, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: The Sahara begins beyond the Mulweeah, more than forty leagues from Tlemsen, and is described as extremely sterile, particularly in summer. Tatta and Akka serve as meeting points for caravans crossing the Great Desert.

records.l: Berber race, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: Shelouhs are presented as a major Berber population in the southern towns and districts, whose presence is suggested by the frequent use of names beginning or ending with the letter T. They inhabit places such as Dimenet, Fronga, and Tagawost, and often trade or live alongside Moors and Jews.

records.l: Berbers, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: Berbers built or inhabited many of the towns described, including Tefza, Pitideb, Meramer, Tednest, Aghmat, and Messa. The text portrays them as an aboriginal population whose mountain communities often retain substantial political independence.

records.l: Arabs, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: Arabs appear among the mixed and nomadic populations of Morocco and inhabit or visit many of the described districts. The author argues that previous writers have overstated their numbers relative to the aboriginal Amazirgh population.

records.l: Moors, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: Moors are described as inhabitants of towns such as Oushda, Messa or Assah, and Akka, and as part of the mixed population estimates for Morocco. The text distinguishes them from Arabs in some demographic classifications and notes that many people called Moors may descend from aboriginal Amazirghs.

records.l: Jews, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: Jews are present in many towns as merchants, artisans, traders, and sometimes farmers. The unit repeatedly describes Jewish quarters or populations in places such as Tefza, Tagodast, Dimenet, Tednest, Akka, Messa, and Ilirgh, and argues that Jewish commerce is important to the economic life of North African Muslims.

records.l: Graeberg de Hemso, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: Graeberg supplies population figures and descriptions for many Moroccan towns. The author considers his total estimate of 8,500,000 exaggerated but more moderate than Jackson's, suggesting that deducting two million may produce a more probable figure.

records.l: population statistics of Morocco, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: The unit questions the reliability of Moroccan population statistics because the towns enumerated appear to contain scarcely one million inhabitants and the tribal population is poorly known. Graeberg estimates 8,500,000 people, while the author considers a total reduced by about two million more plausible and rejects Jackson's estimate of nearly fifteen million as excessive.

records.l: interior geography of Morocco, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: The interior geography of Morocco, particularly in the south, is described as obscure, with multiple names and uncertain locations appearing on maps. The author selects places whose existence is considered certain while acknowledging discrepancies between sources such as Graeberg and Davidson.

records.l: Moroccan tribal independence, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: Many Moroccan districts and tribes operate with substantial independence from the Sultan.
