Religious leaders at Wazen and Tedda, Amazirgh chiefs, and communities in places such as Talent and Shtouka may collect no imperial tribute or govern themselves with only nominal submission to Morocco.

records.l: Travels in Morocco, Travels in Morocco, Of the Maroquine Sahara, I have only space to mention the interesting cluster of
records.s: The Maroquine Sahara includes the oasis cluster of Figheegh, also called Figuiq, which consists of twelve villages. The villages lie along the descent of Wal-el-Khalouf and depend on wells and regulated water for their gardens, where date-palms, fruit trees, madder-root, tobacco, and barley are cultivated. The villages frequently fight over water, despite having commercial relations with Fez, Tafilett, and Touat. The people of Figheegh are generally prosperous through commerce, industry, and mining as well as agriculture.

records.l: Sahara, Travels in Morocco, Of the Maroquine Sahara, I have only space to mention the interesting cluster of
records.s: The Maroquine Sahara contains the oasis cluster of Figheegh, or Figuiq. Its settlements are described as a Saharan district with gardens, wells, agriculture, commerce, and mining.

records.l: Figheegh, Travels in Morocco, Of the Maroquine Sahara, I have only space to mention the interesting cluster of
records.s: Figheegh, also called Figuiq, is an agglomeration of twelve villages known for palm plantations and date production. It has commercial relations with Fez, Tafilett, and Touat, and its people are generally prosperous.

records.l: villages of Figheegh, Travels in Morocco, Of the Maroquine Sahara, I have only space to mention the interesting cluster of
records.s: The twelve villages are generally close together, no more than a quarter of a league apart, and lie on the descent of Wal-el-Khalouf. They have houses, mosques, schools, religious and civil leaders, crenated walls, and defensive towers; the larger villages include Maiz, El-Wadghir, and Zenega.

records.l: Wal-el-Khalouf, Travels in Morocco, Of the Maroquine Sahara, I have only space to mention the interesting cluster of
records.s: Wal-el-Khalouf, meaning "river of the wild boar," is dry except in winter. Its bed contains inexhaustible wells whose water is distributed to the gardens.

records.l: date-palm, Travels in Morocco, Of the Maroquine Sahara, I have only space to mention the interesting cluster of
records.s: Date-palms are abundant in the gardens of Figheegh, and their dates supply the western province of Algeria. The villages' wars are unusually destructive because the inhabitants destroy the fruitful palms, unlike communities elsewhere in the Sahara that spare them during bloodshed.

records.l: water, Travels in Morocco, Of the Maroquine Sahara, I have only space to mention the interesting cluster of
records.s: Water is obtained from wells in the bed of Wal-el-Khalouf and distributed among the gardens by means of a clepsydra, a vessel that releases a measured amount over an hour. Its scarcity and distribution are the immediate causes of discord among the villages.

records.l: strife among the villages, Travels in Morocco, Of the Maroquine Sahara, I have only space to mention the interesting cluster of
records.s: The villages are perpetually in conflict and sometimes take up arms against one another. Their wars are especially cruel, involving the destruction of productive date-palms, and water is identified as the immediate cause of their disputes.

records.l: people of Figheegh, Travels in Morocco, Of the Maroquine Sahara, I have only space to mention the interesting cluster of
records.s: The people of Figheegh cultivate madder-root, tobacco, barley, fruit trees, and date-palms, and they are skilled miners. Although they engage in severe warfare, they also practice commerce and various industries and are generally prosperous.

records.l: Travels in Morocco, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: The narrator describes tensions involving London Jew-boys, Moors, and the British Consul at Mogador, including the imprisonment of a Jewish youth after he cursed a Moor. He visits Saneeates-Sultan, also called the Garden of the Emperor, and describes the barren landscape, the Argan tree, and legends of the Argan forests. In a further interview, the Governor of Mogador says that the Sultan of Morocco will not accept an anti-slavery appeal except under superior force. The narrator also records Moorish opinions that abolition might have gained more support through stronger official representation, gifts, or influence from Tunis and Constantinople.

records.l: London Jew-boys, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: London Jew-boys of the lower lemon-selling class are described as highly resentful of the contempt shown to them by the Moors. One was imprisoned by the British Consul after returning a Moor's curse.

records.l: Moors, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: The Moors are said to treat London Jew-boys with contempt, and some reportedly wished that a fire at a Jewish merchant's house had spread so they could appropriate goods. The Governor says that most Moors oppose abolition, although some favor it.

records.l: Mogador, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: Mogador is the setting for disputes involving London Jew-boys, the British Consul, Jewish merchants, and the Governor. The narrator also distributed Arabic anti-slavery tracts and prepared an anti-slavery circular for British merchants there.

records.l: Saneeates-Sultan, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: Saneeates-Sultan, three or four hours' ride south of Mogador, is visited by the narrator and companions. Its valley contains the Garden of the Emperor, the river Wad-el-Kesab, sandy mounds, palmettos, Argan trees, and little cultivated land.

records.l: Garden of the Emperor, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: The Garden of the Emperor contains a well, a few fruit trees, and a celebrated Argan tree. European visitors carved their names into the bark of a fine fig tree there.

records.l: Morocco, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: A great part of Morocco is described as having a desolate appearance, with uncultivated land and sparse vegetation. The narrator says that European visitors generally adopt Moorish habits rather than promoting Christian intellectual pleasures.

records.l: Argan forests, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: The Argan forests are associated with Moorish legends of enchantresses, magical springs, deceptive fruit, and wicked jinns. According to the tale, a holy man released the forests from enchantment by tying pieces of cork bark bearing the sacred name of the Deity to the trees.

records.l: Elaeonderron Argan, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: The narrator visits a celebrated, ancient Argan tree said by the people to have been planted by Okba. Its broad branches provide shade for many people, and the narrator compares its grandeur with the enchanted wood described by Tasso.

records.l: Governor of Mogador, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: The Governor of Mogador tells the narrator that he has heard nothing improper about his conduct and regrets being unable to assist his anti-slavery work. He says the Sultan will not be persuaded on slavery by argument, though he jokes about his own slaves and asks the narrator what he would pay for them.

records.l: Mr. Treppass, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: Mr. Treppass accompanies the narrator to the interview with the Governor and assists with interpretation. He believes that a larger deputation carrying presents and official authority might have produced a better effect, and that many Moors favor abolition.

records.l: Sultan of Morocco, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: The Governor says that the Sultan of Morocco will never listen to an appeal for abolition, even if presented by another official representative. He says the Sultan might yield only if Christians conquered the country and imposed the matter by superior force.

records.l: anti-slavery mission, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: The anti-slavery mission sought to persuade the Sultan and Moroccan authorities to consider an address against slavery. The narrator is told that the mission might have appeared more effective with stronger official backing, several delegates, presents, and letters from the Bey of Tunis.

records.l: abolition of slavery, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: The Governor says that the Sultan will not accept abolition through persuasion, while Mr. Treppass believes that a considerable number of Moors support it. The narrator suggests that abolition by the Turkish Sultan could influence Morocco.

records.l: slavery, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: The Governor says that the Koran does not command the liberation of slaves, although it commends those who voluntarily free them. He acknowledges divisions among Muslims over the subject and says that most people in his community oppose abolition.

records.l: Bey of Tunis, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: The Bey of Tunis is cited as a Muslim ruler who has entered into engagements with Christians for the suppression of slavery. Moorish advisers say that letters showing what had been done in Tunis might have strengthened the narrator's mission.

records.l: Imaum of Muscat, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: The Imaum of Muscat is cited alongside the Bey of Tunis as a Muslim ruler who has entered into engagements with Christians for the suppression of slavery. The Governor explains that their views differ from those held in Morocco.

records.l: Koran, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: The Governor denies that the Koran commands the abolition of slavery. He says that it commends Muslims who voluntarily liberate their slaves and promises them God's blessing.

records.l: Travels in Morocco, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VIII.
records.s: The unit describes El-Jereed, the Tunisian Sahara, its salt lake El-Sibhah, and its dependence on dates and the date-palm. It explains how date-palms are propagated, cultivated, irrigated, tapped for sap, and used for food, drink, building, and crafts. It also portrays palm-groves, date production and trade, and the importance of tribute collected by the Bey of the Camp. The unit concludes by introducing a forthcoming Tour to the Jereed, including accounts of Toser, Nefta, and Ghafsa.

records.l: Jereed, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VIII.
records.s: El-Jereed, or Belad-el-Jereed, is described as the country of dates and a part of the Sahara near the Great Desert. Its principal resources are dates and palm products, and about twenty thousand people live there for six months of the year entirely on dates. The region is an important part of the Tunisian territory and provides the Government with substantial revenue.

records.l: Sahara, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VIII.
records.s: The Sahara is described as the hot, dry country lying near the Great Desert. El-Jereed is identified as the Tunisian Sahara, while most of the broader region between the Atlantic and Egypt is known among Arabs as the Sahara or Sahra.

records.l: El-Sibhah, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VIII.
records.s: El-Sibhah, literally the salt plain, is a vast salt lake in El-Jereed. It extends about seventy English miles from north-east to south-west and contains dry areas whose number and extent vary with the season. Its salt is weaker than sea salt, has an agreeable flavour, and is not exported or used commercially.

records.l: dates, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VIII.
records.s: Dates are the principal food and resource of El-Jereed. They are stored in bunches suspended from poles and pressed into large earthen jars, where their juice collects as a thick syrup. They may also be dried and ground into meal that keeps indefinitely and serves as a valuable food for desert travellers.

records.l: date-palm, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VIII.
records.s: The date-palm is male and female, and the female requires communication with the male to produce good fruit. Trees propagated from shoots can bear in six or seven years, while those grown from stones require sixteen years; according to Tunisian accounts, they reach greatest vigour at about thirty years and may bear for seventy years. The palm also supplies sap, fruit, leaves, fibres, wood, baskets, ropes, and other useful materials.

records.l: palm-groves, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VIII.
records.s: Palm-groves are described as beautiful plantations whose trees are generally planted in a quincunx or at distances of four or five yards apart. They are commonly situated beside streams or rivulets, and abundant water produces healthier trees and finer fruit. The groves may yield very large quantities of dates, with one plantation producing fifteen hundred camels' loads.

records.l: irrigation, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VIII.
records.s: Irrigation is essential to the date-palm and is carried out in spring and throughout the summer. Small channels carry water from a stream to basins formed around individual trees, where clay embankments hold the water until it soaks into the earth. The palms tolerate water that is salt, sweet, or impregnated with nitre.

records.l: date cultivation, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VIII.
records.s: Date cultivation requires regular watering at the roots every four or five days and the removal of lower branches when they droop or wither. The palms are usually propagated from shoots, and the male plants are hung or shaken over the female plants in February or March to ensure fruitfulness. Excessive rain injures the dates, although the trees thrive in generally dry countries.

records.l: date trade, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VIII.
records.s: Dates are exported from El-Jereed to other parts of the Regency and to foreign countries because of their fine quality. The average annual export is stated as three to four thousand quintals. The produce of a large plantation may be sold for one thousand dollars.

records.l: tribute collection, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VIII.
records.s: Tribute collection is one of the duties associated with governing El-Jereed and the other divisions of the Regency. It is carried out through a yearly visit by a flying camp led by the Bey of the Camp.

records.l: Bey of the Camp, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VIII.
records.s: The Bey of the Camp visits El-Jereed each year with a flying camp to administer affairs and collect tribute. He is described as sovereign in the country and as heir-apparent to the Tunisian throne. On the death of the reigning Bey, he occupies the hereditary beylick and nominates his successor, generally according to seniority within the royal family.

records.l: Tour to the Jereed, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER VIII.
records.s: The Tour to the Jereed is introduced as a narrative extracted from the tourists' notebooks and supplemented with the author's observations. It is intended to provide further details about the region, including Toser, Nefta, and Ghafsa.

records.l: Travels in Morocco, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IX.
records.s: Captain Balfour and Richard Reade joined Sidi Mohammed, Bey of the Camp, on an expedition through the Jereed toward Kairwan. The Bey's camp included Mamelukes, Turkish Infantry, Spahis, Arab camp followers, artillery, attendants, and water-carriers, and followed a formal daily order of march. The tourists observed Tunisian customs, justice, saints' shrines, poor water supplies, ruined bridges, and the severe-looking but often merely formal bastinado. They also hunted partridges, hares, gazelles, wild boar, foxes, wolves, and hyaenas across plains and hills.

records.l: Captain B., Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IX.
records.s: Captain Balfour joined the tour through the Jereed with Richard Reade. A wad from a ceremonial gun nearly struck him on the head, and he later hunted with the Bey's doctor and observed the Turkish Infantry and the camp's daily movements.

records.l: R., Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IX.
records.s: Richard Reade joined Captain Balfour on the expedition and received the skin and head of a hyaena, along with a fine bay horse, as presents from the Bey. He reported that Sidi Mohammed was an exceptionally accurate shot from horseback.

records.l: Sidi Mohammed, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IX.
records.s: Sidi Mohammed, Bey of the Camp, led the expedition from the Bardo across the plain of Manouba toward the Jereed. He regularly paid respects at saints' shrines, hunted daily, saluted the various divisions of the march, received local officers, and treated the tourists with familiarity and kindness.

records.l: Mr. Reade, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IX.
records.s: The tourists traveled with the Bey's expedition, carrying their baggage on three camels and staying in a tent near the Bey's. They visited the Bey, observed the camp's organization and customs, hunted extensively, and received his presents and hospitality.

records.l: the expedition and camp, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IX.
records.s: The Bey's camp contained about 2,660 men, including Mamelukes, Turkish Infantry, Spahis, and Arab camp followers, as well as two artillery pieces. Its tents were arranged around the Bey's central tent, and its attendants included guards of the pipe, gun, coffee, shoes, and water, together with a story-teller and a supply of water brought from Tunis.

records.l: Turkish Infantry, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IX.
records.s: The 300 Turkish Infantry followed the mounted troops by about two hours and were honored by the Bey when they caught up. They were described as highly irregular, performed sham sword fights and music for the Bey, guarded the camp at night, and repeatedly shouted 'Alleya.'

records.l: Arabs, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IX.
records.s: Arab troops and camp followers formed most of the expedition's supporting force, and additional Arab groups joined temporarily as honorary welcomes to the Bey. Arabs were described as eating dogs, foxes, wolves, and other animals, while some were flogged for stealing barley; Arab women saluted the passing camp with shrill looloos.

records.l: Tunis, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IX.
records.s: The tourists began their journey from Tunis and sent baggage to Giovanni, the 'Guarda-pipa.' Water for the Bey was carried from Tunis by camels, and the tourists returned there briefly to obtain neglected supplies before rejoining the expedition.

records.l: Jereed, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IX.
records.s: The Jereed was the destination of Sidi Mohammed's expedition with Captain Balfour and Richard Reade. It was portrayed as a largely flat, dry region with sparse inhabitants, little water, ruins, Arab encampments, and extensive plains suitable for hunting.

records.l: the plain of Manouba, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IX.
records.s: The Bey crossed the plain of Manouba after leaving the Bardo. It was covered by baggage-camels, horses, mules, attendants, and troops moving in what the tourists called glorious confusion.

records.l: Kairwan, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IX.
records.s: Kairwan appeared beyond the hills at the edge of a boundless plain that also extended toward Susa. The expedition approached this broad plain after traveling through hill country with little water and few inhabitants.

records.l: the Bey's expedition, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IX.
records.s: The Bey's expedition traveled southward through the Jereed with mounted guards, Turkish Infantry, artillery, camp followers, baggage animals, and attendants. It followed a set routine of striking camp before daylight, marching, saluting successive groups, hunting, and encamping at places such as Beereen, Tfeefleeah, Heelet-el-Gazlen, Ben Sayden, and Jebanah.

records.l: Tour to the Jereed, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IX.
records.s: The tour took Captain Balfour and Richard Reade across plains and hills toward Kairwan. Along the route they saw ruined towns, ancient bridges and aqueducts, saints' chapels, Arab villages, camels, gazelles, and varied game, while enduring cold mornings and evenings and very hot midday weather.

records.l: the march, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IX.
records.s: The march generally proceeded at about four miles per hour, with mounted troops moving ahead of the Turkish Infantry and camels progressing slowly. The Bey saluted Arab guards, Turkish soldiers, water-carriers, and gunners, then often left the route to hunt before returning to the next encampment.

records.l: the bastinado, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IX.
records.s: The bastinado was used against several Arabs accused of stealing barley, with the culprits tied and beaten on the soles of the feet by inferior Mamelukes. The text says it was usually a formal threat, with many strokes omitted and those delivered often amounting to taps or scratches.

records.l: the water supply, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IX.
records.s: Water was scarce throughout much of the route and limited cultivation and habitation. The Bey's personal water was brought from Tunis by camels, while the camp relied on streams, wells, and water found near Arab encampments; a missing bridge arch could have forced a thirty-mile detour if the stream had risen.

records.l: the hyaena, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IX.
records.s: A hyaena was flushed from brushwood and shot by the Mameluke Si Smyle. The Bey sent Richard Reade its skin and head, and the text records a Moorish belief that eating its brain causes madness, while describing the animal as generally stupid in the woods and not usually dangerous to people.

records.l: the hunting and shooting, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER IX.
records.s: The Bey hunted every day and was described as a highly accurate shot from horseback, killing partridges and other game. The tourists and their companions pursued wild boar, hyaenas, foxes, wolves, hares, partridges, and gazelles, though difficult terrain, the speed of the animals, and poor preparation limited their success.

records.l: Travels in Morocco, Travels in Morocco, Rode to Kairwan.
records.s: R. and his party rode to Kairwan, where they observed the city, its religious figures, the Kaed's household, and the fortress. They encountered Sidi Amour Abeda, a revered but reportedly fanatical Moorish saint, and learned about local beliefs concerning saints and holy places. The Bey of Tunis administered justice, seized camels for government use, inspected Arabs, and received or distributed animals and hunting birds. R. hunted gazelles, was involved in the punishment of an Arab who insulted him, and later secured the man's release from bastinadoing.

records.l: Kairwan, Travels in Morocco, Rode to Kairwan.
records.s: Kairwan was a clean city in which many houses stood in ruins, and a large part of a regiment of the Nitham was quartered there. R. and his party visited its holy well, fortress, the Kaed's house, and the Bey's place of justice.

records.l: famous mosque (Kairwan), Travels in Morocco, Rode to Kairwan.
records.s: R. and his party were not allowed to enter the famous mosque at Kairwan. They heard from Giovanni that many of its marble pillars and other ornaments had been taken from Christian churches and Pagan temples.

records.l: house of the Kaed, Travels in Morocco, Rode to Kairwan.
records.s: The house of the Kaed was described as a good specimen of dwellings in the country. R. and his companions visited it, ate sweetmeats and dinner there, and later returned to it after visiting the holy well.

records.l: the Kaed, Travels in Morocco, Rode to Kairwan.
records.s: The old Kaed was ill and weeping because his son, who commanded part of the camp guards, had arrived. He was described as a great fanatic, and his mamelukes stopped R. from approaching him for fear that R. might be insulted.

records.l: Sidi Amour Abeda, Travels in Morocco, Rode to Kairwan.
records.s: Sidi Amour Abeda was treated by Si Smyle, the Bash-Boab, and others as a man of exceeding sanctity. He accompanied R.'s party to the Kaed's house, blessed the sweetmeats while mumbling bismillas, and was to have a house built for the future deposit of his remains. The renegade doctor of the Bey said that he wished to see English infidels burnt alive.

records.l: Moorish saints, Travels in Morocco, Rode to Kairwan.
records.s: Moorish saints were said to be especially associated with lineal descent from the Prophet and the ability to divine through lucky guesses. They were described as numerous in Kairwan, and as receiving devout obeisance and exploiting poor people.

records.l: Bey of Tunis, Travels in Morocco, Rode to Kairwan.
records.s: The Bey of Tunis administered justice morning and evening while at Kairwan, gave orders concerning plaintiffs, and had camels seized when he needed them. He inspected arriving Arabs, gave Captain B. a handsome black horse and the French officer a grey one, replaced the grey horse after it was criticized, and took part in hunting and hawking.

records.l: Tunis, Travels in Morocco, Rode to Kairwan.
records.s: Tunis was the source of the Bey's extensive camel holdings, which he farmed out through district overseers. A Sicilian nobleman once exported about eighty camels from Tunis to Sicily, with the duty remitted by the Bey.

records.l: the administration of justice, Travels in Morocco, Rode to Kairwan.
records.s: The Bey's administration of justice involved hearing many plaintiffs, though no defendants were brought before him. Some people received orders intended to obtain redress, while others were referred to kadys and chiefs; many plaintiffs were dismissed summarily.

records.l: Bey's ministers and mamelukes, Travels in Morocco, Rode to Kairwan.
records.s: Mamelukes stopped R. when he ran up to shake hands with the old Kaed, fearing that the Kaed might insult him. They also served the Bey and dealt with the French officer's complaint about the grey horse.

records.l: Bey's camel seizure, Travels in Morocco, Rode to Kairwan.
records.s: Because camels had become scarce after a disorder caused heavy mortality, parties acting for the Bey drove in the finest camels they could find. About two hundred animals were marked with the Bey's mark and made government property despite the cries and curses of their former owners.

records.l: camels, Travels in Morocco, Rode to Kairwan.
records.s: The Bey of Tunis possessed many camels and farmed them out through overseers for mills and agricultural work. Camels were also acquired through tribal fines for manslaughter and were considered useful mainly for crossing vast plains, while mules were thought better for the Mediterranean islands.

records.l: Arabs, Travels in Morocco, Rode to Kairwan.
records.s: A hundred Arabs joined the camp and passed before the Bey for inspection, arriving in small groups and firing their long guns. An Arab insulted R. after R. cut the throat of a gazelle in the Moorish manner; the Bey ordered him to receive two hundred bastinadoes and be chained, but R. obtained his release after the whipping began.

records.l: R., Travels in Morocco, Rode to Kairwan.
records.s: R. visited Kairwan with his party, observed its mosque and religious customs, and met Sidi Amour Abeda. He shot a gazelle, reported an Arab's insult to the Bey, and then generously pleaded for the Arab to be spared further punishment. He also took part in gallops after gazelles and visited the Bey's court, fortress, and hunting activities.

records.l: Travels in Morocco, Travels in Morocco, Marched to a place called Gilma, near which the road passes through an ancient t
records.s: The expedition and camp traveled through the desert from Gilma and Wady Tuckah toward Ghafsa, encountering ancient ruins, saline plains, springs, and desert wildlife. The Bey directed the movement of water, received horses and other gifts, hunted, and was accompanied by increasing numbers of Arabs. At Ghafsa, the travelers examined hot springs containing fish and snakes, the ruined Kasbah, local oil-making, domestic life, and surrounding gardens. The account also describes hunting with hawks and dogs, the use of camels, and the neglected agricultural potential of the region.

records.l: Bey of Tunis, Travels in Morocco, Marched to a place called Gilma, near which the road passes through an ancient t
records.s: The Bey ordered the Arabs of the district to release water from Wady Tuckah toward the expedition's camp when it reached Kairwan. He received a hobara, horses including a fine mare, and other presents, and he joined in hunting by shooting a fox. At Ghafsa, he drank water brought from Tunis and maintained a guard of fifty Turks in the ruined Kasbah.

records.l: Ghafsa, Travels in Morocco, Marched to a place called Gilma, near which the road passes through an ancient t
records.s: Ghafsa lies at the foot of hills beside an extensive plain and is surrounded by olive and date trees. It is described as largely ruined and dirty, though it has numerous hot and mineral springs, ancient baths, a ruined Kasbah, gardens, and water sufficient to irrigate the plain and support many palms and olive trees. Local people make oil by grinding olives between stones and separating the oil from water by hand.

records.l: North Africa, Travels in Morocco, Marched to a place called Gilma, near which the road passes through an ancient t
records.s: North African plains are described as often covered with saline and nitrous efflorescence. The account attributes the soil's apparently inexhaustible fertility to these minerals, despite the limited use of manure.

records.l: the Desert, Travels in Morocco, Marched to a place called Gilma, near which the road passes through an ancient t
records.s: The Desert contains abundant but neglected water, including springs and streams that could support extensive irrigation. Its landscape includes hot springs, salt-covered plains, sparse grasses, thorny plants, date groves, and striking scenery.

records.l: the expedition and camp, Travels in Morocco, Marched to a place called Gilma, near which the road passes through an ancient t
records.s: The expedition marched between roughly ten and twenty miles at a time through plains, hills, and salt-covered country, encamping near Wady Tuckah, Ghafsa, Ghorbatah, Furfouwy, and Dra-el-Hammah. The camp traveled with about two thousand camels and was joined by increasing numbers of Arabs. Its members hunted, bathed in a shallow stream, inspected ruins and local houses, and observed animals, birds, locusts, springs, and desert vegetation.

records.l: Arabs, Travels in Morocco, Marched to a place called Gilma, near which the road passes through an ancient t
records.s: Arabs joined the expedition in increasing numbers, brought horses as presents or had them seized for the Bey, and performed displays of horsemanship called playing at powder. They hunted gazelles, hares, hobaras, and foxes, and when an animal was secured they cut its throat while saying, "Bismillah, Allah Akbar." Some chiefs traveled with their wives in enclosed camel palanquins.

records.l: Moors, Travels in Morocco, Marched to a place called Gilma, near which the road passes through an ancient t
records.s: The Moors are described as enjoined by their religion to use the bath constantly, although the account criticizes their clothing and general cleanliness. Their preference for square buildings is associated with religious forms such as the Kaaba, and their domestic and social practices are compared with religious expectations of the afterlife.

records.l: hot springs of Ghafsa, Travels in Morocco, Marched to a place called Gilma, near which the road passes through an ancient t
records.s: The hot springs of Ghafsa include hot, sulphurous, and other mineral waters in which fish and small snakes live together. The fish are described as resembling gudgeons or other small fish, while the snakes feed entirely on them. Ancient bath structures and fragments of inscriptions remain near the springs.

records.l: camels, Travels in Morocco, Marched to a place called Gilma, near which the road passes through an ancient t
records.s: The expedition and camp had about two thousand camels, which carried no supplied provender and survived on coarse grass, weeds, and thorns. The camels were especially fond of sharp prickly thorns despite their apparently tender mouths. Some women traveled in enclosed palanquins mounted on camels, whose bells and rigging made them resemble ships of the Desert.

records.l: gazelles, Travels in Morocco, Marched to a place called Gilma, near which the road passes through an ancient t
records.s: Gazelles were repeatedly encountered and pursued during the marches. Some were caught by Arabs or dogs, one was shot and escaped on three legs, and Captain B. caught one himself; small deer called ebba escaped beyond pursuit.

records.l: hares, Travels in Morocco, Marched to a place called Gilma, near which the road passes through an ancient t
records.s: Hares were found in large numbers in warrens and among tufts of rushy grass, and many were caught with dogs or hawks. When attacked by hawks, a hare sometimes ran briefly, dodged the bird's pounce, or hid in grass or a bush before being driven out by Arabs.

records.l: falconry and hunting, Travels in Morocco, Marched to a place called Gilma, near which the road passes through an ancient t
records.s: Hawks caught hobaras, hares, and other birds during the expedition, although strong wind sometimes prevented them from being flown. Dogs caught hares, gazelles, and a fox, while Arabs and members of the expedition also shot or pursued game. The hawks used in hunting hares had their legs connected by a leather strap to prevent strain when one claw seized the hare and the other caught the ground.

records.l: water management in the desert, Travels in Morocco, Marched to a place called Gilma, near which the road passes through an ancient t
records.s: Water was directed to the camp at Wady Tuckah when the Bey ordered local Arabs to release it from the hills. The travelers used ancient and modern tanks, cisterns, stone ducts, pools, streams, and springs, including hot springs near Ghafsa and Dra-el-Hammah. The account argues that the abundant water could irrigate the neighboring plains and support thousands of palms and olive trees, but that people neglect this resource.

records.l: Travels in Morocco, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER X.
records.s: The travelers reach Toser in the Jereed, describing its mud-and-brick houses, date gardens, inhabitants, crafts, customs, and the Bey’s administration. They visit Nefta, a larger oasis settlement nearer the Sahara, and observe its saints, waterworks, commerce, and social organization. Sheikh Tahid is imprisoned and repeatedly bastinadoed because the Bey’s tribute is not ready, while the travelers witness other punishments, diversions, and snake-charming performances. They also travel to Wedyen, attempt unsuccessfully to hunt deer, and view the Sahara’s salt flats and mirages.

records.l: Toser, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER X.
records.s: Toser, identified with the ancient Tisurus, is described as a town of about six thousand people, surrounded by villages and a mud wall. It contains mosques, schools, baths, inns, markets, detached brick houses, date gardens, and numerous inhabitants engaged in weaving burnouses. The travelers find it poor in appearance but rich in gardens, dates, and some wealthy residents.

records.l: Bey of the Camp, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER X.
records.s: The Bey leaves his tent to occupy a palace at Toser and administers justice morning and evening while in the Jereed. He receives gifts, including a young ostrich, shoots at targets, decorates horses with henna and markings, and punishes or imprisons people over tribute and alleged theft.

records.l: Jereed, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER X.
records.s: The Jereed is a date-growing region containing Toser, Nefta, Wedyen, and other villages and oases. Its settlements rely on palm gardens, warm watercourses, local trade, and tribute collected for the Bey, while its inhabitants include Arabs, merchants, landed proprietors, craftsmen, saints, and slaves’ descendants.

records.l: Sahara, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER X.
records.s: The Sahara appears to the travelers as an immeasurable ocean of sand extending around the Jereed. They observe its heat, blowing sand, salt flats, sparse marshes, rocky hills, and difficult routes where knowledge of hidden wells is essential.

records.l: date cultivation and trade at Toser, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER X.
records.s: Toser’s date gardens are abundantly irrigated, and its dates are considered among the finest. Dates form almost the only food of the inhabitants, their stones cover the streets, and the tribute imposed on the area is equivalent to two bunches from each date-tree.

records.l: Toser's water system, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER X.
records.s: An abundant spring called Meshra rises at a small rocky mountain northwest of Toser. It runs along the city walls, divides into three branches, waters Toser’s gardens and neighboring villages, and eventually disappears into the sand; the town’s wells are insufficient, so inhabitants fetch water from Wad Meshra.

records.l: Santa Maria, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER X.
records.s: Santa Maria returns a horse to the Bey and receives another in exchange, and he is criticized for his delicate feeling and impudence toward the Bey’s officers. He later leaves for Ghabs with an escort of twelve men, although no reliable route to that place is shown on the charts.

records.l: Sheikh Tahid, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER X.
records.s: Sheikh Tahid is imprisoned because he has not prepared the Bey’s tribute. He is repeatedly bastinadoed, including an additional fifty strokes, and is chained after directing searchers to several supposed hiding places where no money is found; he maintains that he cannot pay.

records.l: tribute of the Jereed, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER X.
records.s: The tribute is collected through a system in which the Sheikh gathers dates from the people and pays the Bey a fixed yearly sum when he arrives. At Toser, the tax is described as equivalent to two bunches of dates for each date-tree, and failure to have it ready leads to imprisonment and punishment.

records.l: Nefta, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER X.
records.s: Nefta, the ancient Negeta, lies about fourteen miles from Toser and is the southern frontier town of the Tunisian territories. It consists of villages separated by gardens, has abundant water, mosques, schools, markets, saints, merchants, landed proprietors, and Shereefs, and serves as an entrepôt called the gate of Tunis for commerce toward the Sahara.

records.l: Tunis, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER X.
records.s: Tunis is the source of commerce sent through Nefta toward the Sahara. It is also associated with the Bey’s authority, with Dutch tiles brought from Tunis appearing in Nefta’s houses, and with a decree placing Jews on the same footing of rights and privileges as other subjects.

records.l: Sahara mirage, Travels in Morocco, CHAPTER X.
records.s: The travelers repeatedly mistake the Sahara’s salt-covered or sandy surface for water, seeing apparent shores, inlets, bays, and islands. At Nefta and on the return from Toser, the seemingly liquid expanse is identified as the Palus Libya or a salt plain with sand heaps rather than an actual lake.

records.l: Travels in Morocco, Travels in Morocco, The Sheikh Tahib's gardens were sold for 15,000 piastres, his wife also added to
records.s: Sheikh Tahib's gardens were sold for 15,000 piastres, and his wife added 1,000 more, after which he was set at liberty. Dates were being harvested in the Jereed, with several varieties described, and their superior ripeness was attributed to only one day of rain during the past year. Moorish feastday entertainment included masked men performing lascivious and indecent actions, which the text presents as a negative aspect of the Moors. Sultan Kaed of the Hammama died at an extremely old age, while Sheikh Ali brought in two loteds after being ordered by the Bey to return with some.

records.l: Sheikh Tahid, Travels in Morocco, The Sheikh Tahib's gardens were sold for 15,000 piastres, his wife also added to
records.s: His gardens were sold for 15,000 piastres, and his wife added 1,000 more. He was then set at liberty.

records.l: Sultan Kaed, Travels in Morocco, The Sheikh Tahib's gardens were sold for 15,000 piastres, his wife also added to
records.s: Sultan Kaed, one of the greatest chiefs of the Hammama, died at an extremely old age. During his life he had distinguished himself, including in fighting against the French before Constantina.

records.l: Moors, Travels in Morocco, The Sheikh Tahib's gardens were sold for 15,000 piastres, his wife also added to
records.s: The text describes masked men performing revolting, lascivious, and indecent actions during Moorish feastdays. It presents this behavior as the worst side of the character of the Moors.

records.l: French, Travels in Morocco, The Sheikh Tahib's gardens were sold for 15,000 piastres, his wife also added to
records.s: The text states that Moorish women had never been so profligate as since the arrival of the French in Algeria. Sultan Kaed had also distinguished himself against the French before Constantina.

records.l: Algeria, Travels in Morocco, The Sheikh Tahib's gardens were sold for 15,000 piastres, his wife also added to
records.s: The arrival of the French in Algeria is associated in the text with increased profligacy among Moorish women.

records.l: Jereed, Travels in Morocco, The Sheikh Tahib's gardens were sold for 15,000 piastres, his wife also added to
records.s: The Jereed had received only a single day of rain during the past year. The lack of rain was said to have contributed to the superior ripeness of its dates.

records.l: dates, Travels in Morocco, The Sheikh Tahib's gardens were sold for 15,000 piastres, his wife also added to
records.s: Dates were coming in in large quantities and included several kinds, especially Degalah, Trungah, and Monachah. Degalah was described as very sweet and almost transparent; Trungah as plum-shaped and plum-like in taste; and Monachah as larger, drier, mealier, and less sweet. Rain was said to be bad for dates, although the roots of the date tree could not have too much water.

records.l: loted, Travels in Morocco, The Sheikh Tahib's gardens were sold for 15,000 piastres, his wife also added to
records.s: Sheikh Ali brought in two loteds, a female and its young one, which he had shot. The loted was about the size of a fallow deer, with a head like a deer's but with the eye farther up; the female lacked a goat-like beard and instead had long hair extending from the head to the chest and over the fore-legs.

records.l: sale of Sheikh Tahib's gardens, Travels in Morocco, The Sheikh Tahib's gardens were sold for 15,000 piastres, his wife also added to
records.s: Sheikh Tahib's gardens were sold for 15,000 piastres. His wife added 1,000 piastres, and Sheikh Tahib was set at liberty.

records.l: date harvest, Travels in Morocco, The Sheikh Tahib's gardens were sold for 15,000 piastres, his wife also added to
records.s: The date harvest was coming in in considerable quantity, though the dates were not in very great abundance. Their superior ripeness was attributed to only one day of rain during the past year in the Jereed.

records.l: Moorish feastdays, Travels in Morocco, The Sheikh Tahib's gardens were sold for 15,000 piastres, his wife also added to
records.s: On Moorish feastdays, masked men performed lascivious and indecent actions, sometimes dressing as women and dancing indecently. Such actions were described as an indispensable part of the entertainment.

records.l: death of Sultan Kaed, Travels in Morocco, The Sheikh Tahib's gardens were sold for 15,000 piastres, his wife also added to
records.s: Sultan Kaed, one of the greatest chiefs of the Hammama, died. He was extremely old, and the text remarks that people live to a good old age in the burning climate.

records.l: Travels in Morocco, Travels in Morocco, On our march back to Tunis, we encamped for two days by the foot of a range of h
records.s: The tourists’ return march to Tunis passed through Sheesheeah, Ghortabah, Ghafsa, Byrlafee, Sidi-Mahammedeah, and Momakeeah, amid severe heat, cold, wind, rain, hail, locusts, and heavy losses of men and animals. Santa Maria arrived safely from Ghabs, and the text records information about Ghabs, Toser, the Jereed, ancient ruins, waterworks, and the tribute collected there. After reaching Tunis, the tourists observed the Bardo, discussed their Boab’s account of marriage and divorce, and received or brought home various Jereed objects and animals. The narrator then describes leaving Mogador aboard the Renshaw schooner and enduring a month-long sea voyage marked by successive gales before reaching England.

records.l: Tunis, Travels in Morocco, On our march back to Tunis, we encamped for two days by the foot of a range of h
records.s: The party returned toward Tunis and later arrived there, calling at the Bardo to see the guard mounting and hear a military band. Tunisian prices are given for camels, horses, and sheep, and the city is described as a market where a tolerably good horse sells for 800 to 1000 piastres.

records.l: Ghafsa, Travels in Morocco, On our march back to Tunis, we encamped for two days by the foot of a range of h
records.s: On the return march, the party reached Ghafsa after experiencing rain, hail, high wind, and severe cold. Ghabs was said to be about 130 miles from Ghafsa.

records.l: Ghabs, Travels in Morocco, On our march back to Tunis, we encamped for two days by the foot of a range of h
records.s: Santa Maria arrived safely from Ghabs after traveling much of the way without seeing anyone. Ghabs was described as having better-built towns than Nefta and Toser, a water-filled river, fertile soil, and dates inferior to those of the Jereed.

records.l: Toser, Travels in Morocco, On our march back to Tunis, we encamped for two days by the foot of a range of h
records.s: Santa Maria calculated the distance from Ghabs to Toser at 200 miles. The party later marched from Byrlafee, about ninety-one miles from Toser, and dates collected at Toser formed part of the tribute.

records.l: Jereed, Travels in Morocco, On our march back to Tunis, we encamped for two days by the foot of a range of h
records.s: The Jereed is described as a dry region whose dates are especially good and whose inhabitants supplied tribute in dates, money, woollen goods, blankets, quilts, and animals. The tourists brought home Jereed baskets, dates, woollen articles, skins, and live animals.

records.l: Mogador, Travels in Morocco, On our march back to Tunis, we encamped for two days by the foot of a range of h
records.s: Before leaving Mogador, the narrator formally took leave of the Governor and received civilities from Moorish authorities and European residents. Merchants in Mogador were closely controlled by the Moorish Government and could not even go aboard vessels to supervise the stowing of their goods.

records.l: Bey of the Camp, Travels in Morocco, On our march back to Tunis, we encamped for two days by the foot of a range of h
records.s: The Bey of the Camp’s exactions on the tribes were suggested as a possible reason for Arabs attacking two couriers. He ordered the party to continue marching after reaching Sidi-Mahammedeah, and he owned Momakeeah and much of the surrounding land. The tourists praised his hospitality and kindness, while the tribute collected during the expedition was associated with his camp.

records.l: Santa Maria, Travels in Morocco, On our march back to Tunis, we encamped for two days by the foot of a range of h
records.s: Santa Maria arrived safely from Ghabs and was described as enterprising and worthy of imitation. He had spent many years in North Africa, spoke Arabic fluently, and planned to visit Tripoli and Ghadames the following season. The party took leave of him when he went to Beja to give an account of his espionage.

records.l: railways, Travels in Morocco, On our march back to Tunis, we encamped for two days by the foot of a range of h
records.s: The text suggests that railways could be applied to Tunis and notes that the French were already discussing a line from Algiers to Blidah across the Mitidjah. It argues that railways and accompanying water ducts could distribute water across the country and that developed Tunisian resources could make railways profitable.

records.l: water supply, Travels in Morocco, On our march back to Tunis, we encamped for two days by the foot of a range of h
records.s: The party found bad, salty water at Sheesheeah, brought from some distance. Ancient aqueducts and water-regulating structures were seen at Byrlafee and Gilma, and the text proposes using railway lines and ducts to carry good water from Zazwan to the dry deserts of the Jereed.

records.l: tribute of the Jereed, Travels in Morocco, On our march back to Tunis, we encamped for two days by the foot of a range of h
records.s: The tribute was estimated at forty camel-loads of money, six of burnouses, blankets, quilts, and other woollen goods, and 500 camel-loads of dates, for a total of 529 loads. The goods were valued at about £2,860 and the money was estimated at up to £6,250, producing a possible total of £9,110, excluding additional horses, camels, and other animals.

records.l: return march to Tunis, Travels in Morocco, On our march back to Tunis, we encamped for two days by the foot of a range of h
records.s: The return march involved camps at Sheesheeah, Ghortabah, Ghafsa, Byrlafee, Sidi-Ben-Habeeba, Sidi-Mahammedeah, and Momakeeah before the party reached Tunis. The march was marked by abrupt changes from intense heat to freezing cold, difficult clay roads, strong winds, locusts, and the deaths or disappearance of many people and animals.

records.l: deaths from extreme weather, Travels in Morocco, On our march back to Tunis, we encamped for two days by the foot of a range of h
records.s: Two prisoners and one Turk died from excessive heat near Ghortabah. After the temperature suddenly fell, ten men were brought in dead from cold, eight more were buried soon afterward, three were missing, and many camels and horses also perished.

records.l: sea voyage from Mogador, Travels in Morocco, On our march back to Tunis, we encamped for two days by the foot of a range of h
records.s: After departing Mogador, the vessel soon lost sight of land and spent the next month at sea. The narrator remained in bed for twenty-five days, living on bread, water, and a little biscuit, while a horse and a young vulture died during the voyage; an aoudad survived and was later lodged in Regent’s Park.

records.l: gales at sea, Travels in Morocco, On our march back to Tunis, we encamped for two days by the foot of a range of h
records.s: The voyage encountered successive gales of foul wind from the north and northeast, with huge rising waves and foam. The schooner’s bows were repeatedly under water, and Captain Taylor sometimes rushed on deck to swear at the gale and sea.

records.l: camels, Travels in Morocco, On our march back to Tunis, we encamped for two days by the foot of a range of h
records.s: Many camels could not reach camp over the clayey ground, and 550 died during the camp’s return. Their prices ranged from 60 to 200 piastres; many good camels were sold for eighty piastres, while one near death sold for one and a half piastres.

records.l: Renshaw schooner, Travels in Morocco, On our march back to Tunis, we encamped for two days by the foot of a range of h
records.s: The narrator embarked for the Renshaw schooner after taking leave of the Governor at Mogador. The vessel was a beautiful, flat-bottomed, shallow-draft ship built for Barbary ports and carried the narrator, a horse, a young vulture, and an aoudad through severe Atlantic weather.

records.l: Travels in Morocco, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
records.s: The unit describes the French bombardment and capture of Mogador in August 1844, during which the Moorish authorities and much of the population fled and wild tribes sacked and burned the city. British and other European residents, who had been detained by Sidi Abdallah Deleero, escaped through great danger with assistance from Mr. Lucas and others. It also records the destruction suffered by the Jews and inhabitants of Mogador and summarizes commerce at Tangier, Mogador, Rabat, and Mazagan, including imports, exports, shipping, and trade restrictions.

records.l: Mogador, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
records.s: Mogador was bombarded by the French on 13 August 1844, and its batteries were silenced after sustained fighting. The Governor and most inhabitants fled, after which wild tribes sacked and burned the city, leaving it largely ruined and unoccupied.

records.l: French bombardment of Mogador, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
records.s: The French bombardment began on 13 August 1844 after the Moors fired twenty-one guns, although the French did not return fire until 2 P.M. The bombardment lasted about twenty-eight hours and caused relatively few French casualties, while the Moors suffered heavily.

records.l: French bombarding squadron, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
records.s: The squadron consisted of the ships of the line Gemappes, Suffren, and Triton; the frigate Belle Poule; the steamers Asmodee and Pluton; and some brigs. It silenced the batteries at Mogador before French forces landed on the isle.

records.l: Warspite, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
records.s: The English frigate Warspite reached Mogador on 13 August. Its captain strongly remonstrated with the Moorish authorities but could not obtain permission for the British Consul, his wife, or other Europeans to leave.

records.l: Mr. Willshire, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
records.s: The British Consul was detained in Mogador during the bombardment because of his liabilities to the Emperor. He escaped through the sacked city with his wife and others and later reached the Warspite.

records.l: wife of the British Consul, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
records.s: The wife of the British Consul was refused permission to leave because Sidi Abdallah Deleero claimed that husband and wife were one. During the escape, she spoke Arabic to a marauding band and persuaded them not to kill her or her companions.

records.l: Mr. Robertson, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
records.s: Mr. Robertson escaped with his wife and four children during the sack of Mogador. He narrowly avoided a sabre blow and reached the water-port after one of his daughters was threatened with a dagger for money.

records.l: Mrs. Robertson, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
records.s: Mrs. Robertson escaped with her infant and another child but became separated from Mr. Robertson in the crowd. She later rejoined him at the water-port in a fainting condition.

records.l: Mr. Lucas, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
records.s: Mr. Lucas constructed a raft from deal planks and cordage and paddled alone to the French brig Canard to seek help. He returned in a boat to rescue the detained fugitives, whose transfer to the Warspite was then arranged.

records.l: Governor of Mogador, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
records.s: Sidi Abdallah Deleero was the Moorish Deputy-Governor in command at Mogador. He refused repeated requests to allow the British and other Europeans to depart before the bombardment.

records.l: Moors, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
records.s: The Moors opened fire before the French had taken up position and fought effectively for about two hours. After their best gunner, Omar Ei-Haj, was killed, they became dispirited, abandoned the batteries, and fled.

records.l: Moorish garrison, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
records.s: The Moorish garrison defended Mogador and the isle but was overcome by the French. About five hundred Moors were reported killed on the isle.

records.l: wild tribes, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
records.s: The wild tribes entered Mogador after the Governor and troops fled, sacking, burning, and attacking the inhabitants. They committed murders, assaults, robbery, and other acts of violence against Jews and Europeans.

records.l: Berbers, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
records.s: The Berbers were feared by the escaping Europeans, who believed they might be murdered if discovered. Their attention was chiefly occupied with plundering the city while the fugitives remained near the water-port.

records.l: Europeans of Mogador, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
records.s: The British Consul, his wife, Mr. and Mrs. Robertson, and other Europeans were detained in Mogador during the bombardment. Several escaped through the violence of the sack, aided by Mr. Lucas and others, while some residents were left behind.

records.l: Jews of Mogador, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
records.s: The Jews of Mogador, especially those in the Jewish quarter, were exposed to assault, robbery, stripping, and murder during the sack. Poor Jews were maltreated, and many were left to accompany the natives in misery.

records.l: Moorish authorities, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
records.s: The Moorish government, represented locally by the Governor and Deputy-Governor, detained European residents in the hope that their presence might aid the city's defense or lessen the bombardment. Its authorities later fled or failed to prevent the city's destruction.

records.l: Morocco, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
records.s: Morocco supplied Tangier, Mogador, Rabat, and Mazagan with agricultural products and raw materials for export, while receiving manufactured goods and provisions. The text states that Moroccan commerce could expand greatly under a more liberal government and lower duties.

records.l: isle of Mogador, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
records.s: Nine hundred French troops landed on the isle of Mogador on 16 August. After a rough encounter with the garrison, they captured the isle and its forts.

records.l: Mogador forts and batteries, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
records.s: The Mogador forts and batteries were subjected to the French squadron's fire and were eventually silenced. The Moorish defenders abandoned them after the death of their best gunner.

records.l: Mogador water-port, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
records.s: The Mogador water-port served as the intended place of escape for the Consul's party and the Robertson family. Mr. Lucas reached it by boat after contacting the French fleet, and the fugitives were subsequently rescued from the area.

records.l: Mogador sack and destruction, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
records.s: The sack began after the Moorish authorities and population fled, when wild tribes broke into houses, attacked residents, looted goods, and burned property and records. Mogador was left a heap of ruins, with scarcely any house standing entire.

records.l: escape of the detained Europeans, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
records.s: The detained Europeans escaped during the night through streets filled with fighting and plunder. The British Consul's party and the Robertson family endured attacks, while Mr. Lucas secured rescue by rafting to the French fleet.

records.l: commerce with Morocco, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
records.s: Commerce with Morocco included British and foreign imports of textiles, metals, dyes, foodstuffs, and manufactured goods in exchange for hides, wool, wax, almonds, fruit, grain, oil, and other produce. The unit gives commercial details for Tangier, Mogador, Rabat, and Mazagan and repeatedly attributes limited trade to high duties, monopolies, and restrictive fiscal laws.

records.l: Tangier, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
records.s: Tangier traded almost exclusively with Gibraltar and maintained active intercourse with that port. In 1856 it imported British goods valued at L101,773 6s. and foreign goods valued at L33,793, while exporting goods to British and foreign ports and sending thousands of cattle and other provisions to Gibraltar.

records.l: Gibraltar, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
records.s: Gibraltar was Tangier's principal trading partner and received cattle, poultry, eggs, flour, and other provisions. About 3,000 cattle were annually exported to Gibraltar at a fixed duty, with roughly 2,000 more exported at higher rates.

records.l: Mogador commerce, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
records.s: Mogador exported valuable Moroccan products and imported mainly Manchester cotton goods and other manufactured articles for local and inland consumption. Its trade increased because of strong demand for olive oil, and the text states that more liberal government would greatly expand commerce.

records.l: Mogador exports, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
records.s: Mogador's exports included almonds, gums, wool, olive oil, seeds, skins, ostrich feathers, and occasionally maize. In 1855 exports were valued at L228,112 3s. 2d. for British ports and L55,965 13s. 1d. for foreign ports.

records.l: Mogador imports, Travels in Morocco, APPENDIX.
records.s: Mogador imported Manchester cotton goods, blue salampores, prints, sugar, tea, coffee, iron, steel, spices, drugs, nails, beads, deals, woollen cloth, cotton wool, and mirrors. In 1855 British imports were valued at L136,496 7s. 6d. and foreign imports at L31,222 11s. 5d.

records.l: Travels in Morocco, Travels in Morocco, notes
records.s: The notes discuss the political and religious distinction between the Shereefs and Marabouts, describing the Shereefs as combining regal and sacerdotal authority and the Marabouts as a priestly family. They defend Morocco and the Moors of Barbary against a report of human sacrifice, while recounting the cruelty of Yezeed. The text also describes the peoples, cities, geography, and historical traditions of Barbary, including the Berbers, Algiers, Tunis, Fez, Tangier, the Atlantic System, the Atlas Mountains, and the Sahara.

records.l: Shereefs, Travels in Morocco, notes
records.s: The Shereefs are described as descendants of the Prophet who combine regal and sacerdotal authority, corresponding to the type of Melchizedek rather than to a strictly priestly order. Because they once possessed the throne, they are said to be jealous of the Marabouts.

records.l: Moravedi, Travels in Morocco, notes
records.s: The Marabouts are described as a family of priests who have not forgotten that they once ruled Morocco. They are distinguished from the Shereefs, who combine princely and sacerdotal authority.

records.l: Abd-el-Kader, Travels in Morocco, notes
records.s: Abd-el-Kader is described as uniting princely and sacerdotal authority like the Shereefs, although he is not descended from the Prophet. During a storm on his passage from Oran to Toulon, his companions threw handfuls of salt into the sea to appease its fury.

records.l: human sacrifice, Travels in Morocco, notes
records.s: The text rejects the report that a beautiful young girl was sacrificed before the Sultan of Morocco, calling it an unmitigated libel. It states that human sacrifice is repudiated by every class in Barbary and is unknown to the Moors.

records.l: Tunis, Travels in Morocco, notes
records.s: Tunis is described as containing the hill of Ghamart near Carthage, where a red heifer was sacrificed during a drought. A Bey's frigate returning from Malta also prompted the sacrifice of two sheep to tutelar saints.

records.l: Yezeed, Travels in Morocco, notes
records.s: Yezeed is described as the son of Sidi-Mohammed and the renegade Irish widow of a sergeant of Sappers and Miners. He is portrayed as a ferocious and cruel tyrant who conducted violent practical jokes, made war widely except on the English, and nevertheless received obeisance from European consuls.

records.l: Barbary, Travels in Morocco, notes
records.s: Barbary is described as a region whose inhabitants reject human sacrifice and may sacrifice animals to God or tutelar saints. The notes also discuss its cities, peoples, mountains, deserts, agriculture, and political divisions.

records.l: Algiers, Travels in Morocco, notes
records.s: Algiers is included in the middle Western Region and in the mountain system extending across the Barbary States. The Pass of Teniah, leading from Algiers to Mediah, is treated as part of the principal mountain chain in that area.

records.l: Moors, Travels in Morocco, notes
records.s: The Moors of Barbary are described as having no conception of the enormity of sacrificing human beings to God or to a ruler. The notes also discuss competing explanations for the name Moors and criticize an account that portrays them as a uniformly dirty, lazy, inhuman, and indomitable people.

records.l: Berbers, Travels in Morocco, notes
records.s: The Berbers are described as comprising numerous tribes and subdivisions, including the Amayeegh, Shelouh, Kabyles, Aoures, Shouwiah, and Touarichs. The text gives traditions about their origins and notes that their present divisions do not correspond exactly to the five ancient principal tribes.

records.l: Atlantic System, Travels in Morocco, notes
records.s: The Atlantic System is the name Monsieur Balbi gives to the extensive mountain system of the Maghreb and the elevations scattered through the Sahara. Its principal ridge is said to extend from near Cape Noun on the Atlantic to east of the Great Syrte in Tripoli, with its greatest heights in Morocco.

records.l: Atlas Mountains, Travels in Morocco, notes
records.s: The Atlas Mountains are described as the principal heights of the Barbary region, reaching their greatest elevations in Morocco and diminishing eastward through Algiers, Tunis, and Tripoli. Mount Atlas was called Dyris or Derem by ancient and modern aborigines.

records.l: Sahara, Travels in Morocco, notes
records.s: The Sahara is described as containing elevations and secondary branches of the mountain system, including branches in southern Tripoli and Libya. Ghafsa is identified as the gate of the Tunisian Sahara, where the sands begin to disappear and the land becomes more suitable for growing corn.

records.l: Morocco, Travels in Morocco, notes
records.s: Morocco is described as being ruled by Shereefian princes and as containing the greatest heights of the Atlantic System, especially east of the town of Morocco and southeast of Fez. The text defends its ruler against the allegation that human sacrifice was performed before him.

records.l: Tangier, Travels in Morocco, notes
records.s: Tangier is listed among the places in Barbary that have already been described. The notes also state that England might again need to possess its former garrison there if Morocco became an enemy in a European war.

records.l: Fez, Travels in Morocco, notes
records.s: Fez is described as the capital of the realm of that name and as the court of the king in the west. The notes give conflicting traditions about its foundation and suggest that its true history may remain unknown until its library is examined.

records.l: Novel-10146
records.s: This document is a collection of historical reminiscences and accounts centered on St. Paul and Minnesota from territorial and pioneer years through the Civil War and later developments. Its principal subjects are the city’s newspapers and printers, civic institutions, entertainment, fires, transportation, politics, the 1862 Sioux conflict, and Minnesota’s wartime experience. It opens with the growth and rivalry of St. Paul daily papers, the Pioneer, Minnesotian, Times, Press, North Star, and Weekly Journal, covering state-printing patronage, political campaigns, telegraph and Atlantic-cable news, Minnesota’s admission, and Civil War reporting. Printers and editors emerge as important civic and military figures: Capt. E.Y. Shelly and others served in the war, Charles R. Stuart was celebrated for typesetting, and Frank Moore’s career runs from a Minnesotian printer’s “devil” in 1858 to long service with the Pioneer Press. The accounts trace production from early presses to stereotyping and linotype machinery. Other sections portray a growing river city: busy upper-Mississippi steamboat traffic; the Five Million Loan Election and railroad-bond collapse; the Sons of Malta; volunteer fire companies becoming a paid department; destructive hotel and public-building fires; and halls and theaters that hosted music, political meetings, conventions, military activity, fundraisers, and performers including Dan Emmet, the Hutchinson family, Adalina Patti, Frederick Douglass, and James J. Hill. One political satire imagines Robert A. Smith ruling a transformed Mississippi city while the Okons dominate patronage. The Civil War forms the collection’s central crisis. It records printer patriotism, preparations for draft resistance, Minnesota soldiers at Mill Springs and Pittsburg Landing, the First Minnesota battery, Captain William Henry Acker’s death, and public rejoicing at Union successes. On July 4, 1863, while the Pioneer moved offices, the Press alone issued an extra announcing Gettysburg and Vicksburg, helping ignite celebration in St. Paul. The narrative closes the war with St. Paul’s mourning for Abraham Lincoln and its memorial service led by Frederick A. Noble. A major Minnesota emergency is the Great Sioux Outbreak of 1862: attacks at Fort Ridgely, New Ulm, Birch Coulie, and elsewhere; Alexander Ramsey’s emergency response; Henry Hastings Sibley’s campaign; Other Day’s rescue of refugees; Wood Lake and Camp Release; the liberation of captives; convictions and the execution of thirty-eight Indians; Little Crow’s escape and death; and the loss of Sioux lands. A final personal recollection of winning a school spelling match adds a small-scale memory of life before railroads and telegraphs.

records.l: James M. Goodhue, Novel-10146
records.s: James M. Goodhue was a pioneer printer of Minnesota who arrived in St. Paul from Lancaster, Wis., in spring 1849 with a Washington hand press and fonts of type to start a paper in the new territory. He employed Capt. E.Y. Shelly at the Pioneer; they were working together when Goodhue died tragically. He later presented a retrospective account of St. Paul newspaper production, news gathering, conflicts, labor, politics, and wartime experiences.

records.l: St. Paul, Novel-10146
records.s: St. Paul is a Minnesota place that was the capital of the new territory of Minnesota and grew from a busy upper Mississippi steamboat destination into a “great city.” In its early period it had a levee, hotels, stage and steamboat connections, a population of about 10,000, and an active press. Capt. E.Y. Shelly, its first permanently located printer, arrived in 1849; by the 1850s newspapers, printers, editors, and competing Republican and Democratic enterprises made the city a news center. News first came by steamboats and mail coaches and later by telegraph lines. The city celebrated the Atlantic cable in 1858, supported the Five Million Loan by a majority of more than 4,000, and marked Union victories on July 4, 1863 with cheers, cannon, anvils, and firecrackers. Its civic life combined organizations, entertainment, public meetings, and practical services. A Sons of Malta lodge drew men from many occupations. Halls and theaters hosted performances, lectures, drills, political meetings, charitable events, conventions, concerts, and celebrations; a sanitary fair was held in the winter of 1864. Fire protection developed from required marked buckets in 1850 to volunteer companies, hand engines, cisterns, a 1859 parade, and a first steamer in 1866, amid destructive fires including one that destroyed thirty-four buildings in 1860. The central strain is war and loss. During the Sioux outbreak of 1862, St. Paul received refugees, organized home guards, patrolled the bluffs, and feared attack until the Battle of Wood Lake brought safety. Its residents served in the Second Minnesota, followed the battle of Mill Springs anxiously, and later included surviving veterans. The city mourned William Henry Acker through a public reception, funeral, burial, and Acker Post, its first association of Civil War veterans. It also deeply mourned Lincoln’s assassination, draping public and private buildings and holding memorial services. By the later account, it is presented as a transformed great city on the Mississippi River.

records.l: daily newspapers, Novel-10146
records.s: St. Paul daily newspapers began as small-staff operations using old hand presses, competing to print speeches, messages, telegraphic reports, and breaking news first. After the Winslow line reached St. Paul, they used telegraph news. They often paused around holidays before expanding late in the Civil War with the city’s population.

records.l: Pioneer Press, Novel-10146
records.s: Pioneer Press is a daily newspaper that also publishes a Sunday edition. During the war, while the Pioneer was moving its plant, the Press had the field exclusively on July 4, 1863. It delayed an extra until it received the fullest possible details of Union victories, then sold papers to a large waiting crowd. Its Sunday edition illustrates the labor of large nineteenth-century printing, and its composing room later used the Minnesotian proof press. Louis E. Fisher and Richard Bradley served for many years.

records.l: Minnesotian, Novel-10146
records.s: The Minnesotian was a St. Paul daily morning newspaper, generally printed the evening before, begun in 1852 by George W. Moore and John P. Owens, its first editor. It was a Republican paper and received the 1857 state-printing contract for the Republican constitutional body, printing that convention’s proceedings. Competitive in news and printing, it bought the first Hoe press brought to Minnesota, published an early illustrated local feature, sought the state-printer position after the 1859 election, and was once misled by bogus telegraphic reports circulated by the Pioneer. Moore was part owner and manager in 1858; Dr. Thomas Foster later controlled and edited the paper after Moore sold his interest in 1860. Foster’s bitter rivalry with Thomas M. Newson’s Times led to a temporary Minnesotian and Times consolidation, followed by Foster’s resumed control. The paper opposed the Five Million Loan measure and attacked Gov. Sibley and railroad bonds. After facing the St. Paul Daily Press and Foster’s sale of the plant, it was absorbed by the Pioneer Press in 1861, becoming part of the present Pioneer Press.

records.l: Pioneer, Novel-10146
records.s: The Pioneer was a daily newspaper, the first paper printed in St. Paul and a leading Minnesota paper in 1857. Under its constitutional-convention contract, it printed Democratic body proceedings. It competed with the Minnesotian and Times for political and telegraphic news, secretly gained telegraph service, briefly held a news monopoly, published Minnesota admission news first in 1858, and later deceived the Minnesotian with fabricated dispatches. It employed editors, printers, and compositors including James Mills, Louis E. Fisher, George W. Armstrong, Marshall Robinson, and editor-in-chief Earle S. Goodrich. On July 4, 1863, it moved to Third and Robert and could not issue an extra on Union victories. It united with Press in 1874.

records.l: Times, Novel-10146
records.s: Times was a St. Paul daily, morning Republican paper and one of three competing papers. It competed with the Pioneer and Minnesotian for presidential messages, telegraphic news, and, after the 1859 election, state printer; it also printed and circulated bogus Minnesotian reports before learning of the deception. Managed by Thomas M. Newson, it traded insults with Dr. Foster of the Minnesotian, briefly merged as the Minnesotian and Times, then dissolved. Newson leased its office and material to W. R. Marshall and Thomas F. Slaughter, who started the St. Paul Daily Press. Its job department employed Richard Bradley and reporter Jebb.

records.l: George W. Moore, Novel-10146
records.s: George W. Moore was a printer who came to St. Paul in 1850 and briefly served as foreman of the Pioneer office. He became part owner and manager of the Daily Minnesotian, publishing it with John P. Owens until selling his interest to Dr. Foster in 1860. Appointed collector of the port of St. Paul by Abraham Lincoln in 1861, he held that post for more than twenty years. He was Frank Moore's brother.

records.l: Minnesota, Novel-10146
records.s: Minnesota began as a territory in 1849, a new place that received James Mills and drew young printers and editors; James M. Goodhue established a newspaper there, and Capt. E. Y. Shelly became the first printer to locate permanently. It held a 1857 election for delegates to a constitutional convention, held that convention in preparation for statehood, and entered the Union through a congressional bill; news of admission reached St. Paul by passenger boat in 1858 because telegraphic communication with Washington was lacking. Railroad aid authorized through the Five Million Loan amendment brought grading of nearly 250 miles of road, but company defaults compromised its credit until, under Gov. Pillsbury, it settled by paying half the securities' nominal value. During the Civil War it furnished regiments, including the Second Minnesota Infantry, whose volunteers exceeded the first regiment's quota and whose Mill Springs service was praised. While men were recruited, the Sioux outbreak of 1862 depopulated areas and left thousands homeless, prompting legislative relief and defense. It opposed troop removal, executed thirty-eight Dakota prisoners amid opposition to pardons, and later conducted a draft in counties behind quota.

records.l: constitutional convention, Novel-10146
records.s: The 1857 Minnesota election chose delegates; after a close result, Republicans and Democrats held separate constitutional conventions, with proceedings printed under contract.

records.l: Republican Party, Novel-10146
records.s: The Republican Party held a separate constitutional convention in 1857, with proceedings assigned to the Minnesotian. In 1859 it campaigned for Alexander Ramsey and its legislative ticket, using speakers Galusha A. Grow and Schuyler Colfax. After winning a legislative majority, its newspapers, the Minnesotian and Times, disputed state printing patronage before leaders arranged a temporary consolidation. Its first state convention after Minnesota entered the Union nominated Col. Aldrich and William Windom for Congress; Republicans also backed Col. Marshall and attended Frederick Douglass's lecture.

records.l: Democratic Party, Novel-10146
records.s: hold Democratic body [as a separate constitutional convention] Democrats held a separate constitutional convention in 1857, and the Pioneer received the contract to print its proceedings. Minnesota Democrats later hoped that Stephen A. Douglas would be nominated for president at the Charleston convention.

records.l: James J. Hill, Novel-10146
records.s: James J. Hill participated at the Athenaeum in a mock reenactment of the Heenan and Sayers prize fight, assigned to imitate Sayers; after Theodore Borup made a false pass, Hill knocked him out rather than follow the planned result.

records.l: Mississippi River, Novel-10146
records.s: A grand river, called the Father of Water, stretches from the North Star State to the Gulf of Mexico, following an unmolested course toward the boundless ocean as surrounding city greatly changes.

records.l: Henry Hastings Sibley, Novel-10146
records.s: Henry Hastings Sibley is a governor of Minnesota during the bond dispute and later a military commander. As Gov.
