Sibley, he initially refused to issue railroad bonds until the state's rights were protected, but, following the attorney general's advice and the supreme court's mandate, reluctantly signed them; he later failed to negotiate them in New York. Placed in command at St. Peter, he led poorly supplied troops, relieved Fort Ridgely, assembled about 2,000 men and a battery, reached Camp Release, secured surrender and captives' release, and formed a military tribunal for suspected offenders.

records.l: Pioneer Guards, Novel-10146
records.s: Pioneer Guards was a military company and organization, described as the oldest in the state and the finest in the West. Formed for Washington's birthday celebrations, it received Minie rifles and used Armory hall from 1859 until war began. Its annual ball was a leading social event; it soon disbanded, with members joining Union and Confederate forces.

records.l: Gov. Alexander Ramsey, Novel-10146
records.s: called Minnesota legislature [into extra session to address the outbreak] Gov. Alexander Ramsey called an extra legislative session to arrange arms, equipment, and shelter for refugees. He also tried to calm St. Paul residents by stating that the nearest reported attacks were many miles from the capital.

records.l: People's theater, Novel-10146
records.s: The People's theater was an old frame theatrical building on the corner of Fourth and St. Peter streets, described as the only real theatrical building in St. Paul. H. Van Liew leased and managed it with a stock company including Emily Dow, Harry Gossan, and Azelene Allen. In summer 1858, J.W. Wallack and Mrs. J.W. Wallack appeared for two weeks, performing works including Macbeth and The Man in the Iron Mask; Mrs. Wallack portrayed Lady Macbeth. Col. R.E.J. Miles was a star and first produced Mazeppa there. A.M. Carver often performed, including as Uncle Tom in Uncle Tom's Cabin. Its gallery charged the shaded gentry parquet prices, and Joe Rolette sometimes had epileptic fits during performances.

records.l: James Buchanan, Novel-10146
records.s: James Buchanan exchanged messages with Queen Victoria after the successful laying of the Atlantic cable. In St. Paul's celebration, he was represented by George Folsom, a product of the city.

records.l: Mr. Winslow's telegraph line, Novel-10146
records.s: The Winslow telegraph line, reaching St. Paul, was completed in summer 1860. It ended newspapers’ heavy reliance on steamboats and mail coaches for distant news. Before it, the narrator met arriving boats at the levee by their whistles; afterward, high rates limited use, though the Pioneer secretly obtained service.

records.l: president's message, Novel-10146
records.s: is_competed_for_by Pioneer [among St. Paul daily papers] The Pioneer, Minnesotian, and Times competed intensely to publish the full text of the president's message first. Printers prepared large staffs and distributed type in advance, while one Minnesotian proprietor unsuccessfully traveled to intercept an earlier copy.

records.l: Panic of 1857, Novel-10146
records.s: depresses business [business of every description] The panic of 1857 had a very depressing effect on business. Supporters of the Five Million Loan measure argued that it would employ thousands and revive railroad building, land speculation, and other economic activity.

records.l: Civil War, Novel-10146
records.s: The Civil War began in 1861 and became a desperate conflict lasting more than four years. It placed severe demands on the United States government, contributing in 1862 to delayed Sioux annuity payments and limited readiness for the Sioux outbreak. St. Paul mobilized through patriotic meetings, enlistment appeals, and support for soldiers’ dependents; the Pioneer Guards disbanded, with many members becoming Union officers and two or three joining Confederate forces. Many printers and editors enlisted or served as officers in infantry, cavalry, artillery, sharpshooter, and other units, straining the Press’s staff as it supported vigorous prosecution of the war and faced hostility to the draft. By Lincoln’s assassination, Richmond had fallen, Lee had surrendered, and Johnston’s probable surrender appeared likely to end the war.

records.l: William H. Seward, Novel-10146
records.s: William H. Seward, Secretary of State and foremost statesman of his time, used diplomatic skill during the war to keep the United States free from foreign entanglements. Targeted in an assassination conspiracy and initially believed killed, he survived the dagger attack.

records.l: Earle S. Goodrich, Novel-10146
records.s: Earle S. Goodrich, a printer and Pioneer editor-in-chief, set the first type in the Press’s new building in 1869, composing editorial copy that began with an error.

records.l: First Battle of Bull Run, Novel-10146
records.s: is_a Union reverse [despite earlier reports of victory] Initial reports of the First Battle of Bull Run announced a Union victory, causing James M. Goodhue to feel confident after attending Dan Rice's circus. Later reports revealed a major Union reverse, and Gov. Marshall expressed deep concern about the country's prospects.

records.l: Abraham Lincoln, Novel-10146
records.s: Abraham Lincoln was President of the United States during the Civil War, described as the greatest of all presidents, a martyred president, and an ideal statesman. In 1862 he issued a 600,000-volunteer enlistment, responded to the Minnesota draft, and limited condemned Indians’ executions to thirty-eight cases. He spoke of firmness for the right, led the country through more than four years of war, and was assassinated by John Wilkes Booth as Union victory appeared near.

records.l: Union forces, Novel-10146
records.s: Union forces, a military force under George H. Thomas, advanced in the Mill Springs campaign and defeated Confederate forces near Logan's Cross Roads, capturing cannon, wagons, ammunition, and supplies.

records.l: United States Army draft, Novel-10146
records.s: A draft was ordered in several Minnesota counties behind military quotas; despite bitter opposition and feared riot, fort troops were brought and it proceeded without interruption.

records.l: Fourth of July, Novel-10146
records.s: is_a holiday On July 4, 1863, the Pioneer was moving its plant, while the Press issued an extra containing news of Gettysburg and the surrender of Vicksburg. The day became the occasion of St. Paul's greatest celebration up to that time.

records.l: the surrender of Vicksburg, Novel-10146
records.s: occurred_during the Civil War [on July 4, 1863] The surrender of Vicksburg occurred on July 4, 1863, along with the battle of Gettysburg. News of it was reported in the Press's extra and helped prompt intense public excitement in St. Paul.

records.l: American Civil War, Novel-10146
records.s: The American Civil War was an American civil conflict and a great crisis and struggle in which Minnesota volunteers served. It included early Union success at the Battle of Mill Springs and the exceptionally severe Battle of Pittsburg Landing, with consequences for Union commanders and operations. On July 4, 1863, the battle of Gettysburg and the surrender of Vicksburg occurred. Later, fighting continued before Atlanta and in the march from Atlanta to the sea; enlistment also reduced volunteer fire departments, while daily newspapers expanded during the latter part of the war.

records.l: unnamed narrator, Novel-10146
records.s: A narrator arrived in St. Paul on April 17, 1858, worked for the Daily Minnesotian, and in 1863 helped prepare Press news, distributed papers through a crowd, and sold them at the counting room window.

records.l: the Fourth of July celebration in St. Paul (1863), Novel-10146
records.s: celebrated Union victories [before sundown] The celebration followed the circulation of news about Gettysburg and the surrender of Vicksburg. Cheers, cannon, anvils, firecrackers, and other noises filled the city, and before sundown St. Paul had celebrated what the narrator called the greatest Fourth of July in its history.

records.l: admission of Minnesota into the Union, Novel-10146
records.s: made_minnesota_part_of the Union [by an act of Congress] Congress passed a bill admitting Minnesota into the Union. The Pioneer published the news before the Minnesotian and Times, while the Minnesotian later issued an extra and sent it to subscribers.

records.l: the Union, Novel-10146
records.s: The Union side in the American Civil War was defended by House of Hope members, supported by Noble’s sermons, and approached victory when Lincoln was assassinated.

records.l: Galena, Dunleith, Dubuque and Minnesota Packet company, Novel-10146
records.s: During the steamboat era, Galena, Dunleith, Dubuque and Minnesota Packet company operated steamers on the upper Mississippi, linking St. Louis, Dubuque, Prairie du Chien and La Crosse; arrivals drew people to St. Paul's levee.

records.l: Fuller house, Novel-10146
records.s: The Fuller house was the former name of the International hotel. A.G. Fuller erected the five-story brick building in 1856, and it later became the International hotel under Samuel Mayall.

records.l: Winslow house, Novel-10146
records.s: Winslow house was a four-story brick hotel at Seven Corners, constructed by J.M. Winslow in 1854 and among the city’s largest except Fuller house. In fall 1862, a defective cupola stovepipe caused a fire that entirely destroyed it; proprietors were arrested and discharged.

records.l: American house, Novel-10146
records.s: American house, a city landmark hotel at Third and Exchange streets, was built in 1849 and burned in 1863 before firefighters arrived; guests escaped, but thieves took jewelry and clothing.

records.l: Central house, Novel-10146
records.s: Central house was a hotel at Bench and Minnesota streets, described as the first hotel of any pretension in St. Paul. Its dining room hosted the first territorial legislature session; later a boarding house, it burned in August 1873.

records.l: Five Million Loan Election, Novel-10146
records.s: The Five Million Loan Election was a Minnesota constitutional amendment election authorizing state aid of $10,000 per mile to four railroad companies for road graded and ready to iron. Intended to promote railroad development and employment, it had leading bipartisan support and passed by an immense majority after the panic of 1857.

records.l: railroad companies receiving state bonds, Novel-10146
records.s: demand_bonds_from Henry H. Sibley [after work commenced] Four railroad companies were to receive $10,000 in state bonds for every mile of road graded and ready to iron. They demanded that Gov. Sibley issue the bonds, rejected his restrictions, obtained a peremptory writ from the supreme court, and later defaulted when the railroad construction scheme collapsed.

records.l: Minnesota state bonds, Novel-10146
records.s: fail_to_be_negotiated_in New York [during Henry H. Sibley's attempt to market them] The Minnesota state bonds issued for railroad construction could not be negotiated in the New York market, compromising the state's credit. They were repudiated for more than twenty years before the state compromised with their holders and paid half their nominal value.

records.l: Minnesota Supreme Court, Novel-10146
records.s: orders_issuance_of Minnesota state bonds [by peremptory writ] The Minnesota Supreme Court issued a peremptory writ directing Gov. Sibley to issue the railroad bonds. Judge Flandrau dissented, believing the state's financial reputation would have been greatly improved had his position prevailed.

records.l: Charles E. Flandrau, Novel-10146
records.s: Charles E. Flandrau dissented from the Minnesota Supreme Court bond opinion, organized volunteers at St. Peter during the 1862 Sioux outbreak, commanded New Ulm’s defense, and led its evacuation to Mankato when supplies ran short.

records.l: state of Minnesota, Novel-10146
records.s: forecloses_on railroad development in Minnesota [nearly 250 miles of road were graded] The state of Minnesota faced a compromised credit after the railroad companies defaulted and the bonds could not be sold. It foreclosed on nearly 250 miles of graded railroad and later donated the lines to new organizations before settling with bondholders for 50 percent of the securities' nominal value.

records.l: Shakopee, Novel-10146
records.s: Shakopee is a place near the late-May 1858 battle between Sioux and Chippewa warriors, where reporters stayed for days anticipating further engagements.

records.l: Sioux, Novel-10146
records.s: The Sioux occupied a strip along the Minnesota River and were hereditary enemies of the Chippewas. Divided between a government-favored farming party and an opposing Indian party, they had grievances over land, trader accounts, annuity deductions, and delayed payments, and communicated with Hole-in-the-Day. Before and during the 1862 outbreak, they attacked settlers, Company B, and fought at Fort Ridgely, New Ulm, Birch Coulie, and Wood Lake. Routed at Wood Lake, many at Camp Release were implicated in massacres, and the Sioux forfeited their Minnesota lands.

records.l: Chippewas, Novel-10146
records.s: are_commanded_by Hole-in-the-day [during the Shakopee engagement] A party of Chippewa warriors under Chief Hole-in-the-day surprised Sioux near Shakopee and opened fire, killing or wounding fifteen or twenty. Eight or ten Chippewas were killed during the engagement.

records.l: Atlantic cable, Novel-10146
records.s: The Atlantic cable was successfully laid in 1858, enabling messages between Great Britain and Queen Victoria and President Buchanan; it operated for about four weeks, ending with its last message on St. Paul's celebration.

records.l: celebration of the successful laying of the Atlantic cable, Novel-10146
records.s: takes_place_in St. Paul [on the first day of September 1858] St. Paul held an elaborate celebration on September 1, 1858, with a procession nearly two miles long, military units, floats, civic officials, secret societies, and thousands of spectators. Fireworks were postponed because of a storm, and the celebration coincided with the last message exchanged between England and America.

records.l: Queen Victoria, Novel-10146
records.s: Queen Victoria exchanged messages with President Buchanan after the Atlantic cable was completed. Her representative in St. Paul's 1858 procession was Miss Rosa Larpenteur.

records.l: United States, Novel-10146
records.s: United States is a place where many cities organized bucket fire departments early in the nineteenth century; hand engines became common about fifty years later, and Cincinnati introduced the first paid steam fire department. Later, after President Abraham Lincoln’s assassination, it was plunged into mourning with draped buildings and church memorial services.

records.l: St. Paul procession, Novel-10146
records.s: The St. Paul procession honoring the Atlantic cable, nearly two miles long and led by marshal-in-chief A.C. Jones, marched for three and one-half hours with diverse civic, military, religious, trade, and citizen participants to its destination.

records.l: Pioneer Hook and Ladder Company No. 1, Novel-10146
records.s: Pioneer Hook and Ladder Company No. 1 was a volunteer fire company organized under the city charter in November 1854, whose members had to respond promptly to fire alarms. It included foreman Isaac A. Banker, officers, and members Washington M. Stees and Charles H. Williams, later chief and assistant chief engineers. In 1856 its accounts went to St. Paul and it owned fire equipment; it participated in an 1859 parade.

records.l: Minnehaha Engine Company No. 2, Novel-10146
records.s: Minnehaha Engine Company No. 2, organized in winter 1857-1858, was a prosperous engine company with Grant and O'Connor among its officers. Its engine house near Third and Jackson streets served members as a lounging and reading room, and it participated in the 1859 parade.

records.l: Hope Engine Company No. 1, Novel-10146
records.s: Hope Engine Company No. 1, organized in 1857, petitioned for hose and included foreman Michael Leroy with assistants R.C. Wiley and Joseph S. Herey. It received a double-deck hand engine in 1858, moved from Franklin and Fourth streets to Third street, and disbanded over the first steamer’s engineer.

records.l: Pioneer Press company, Novel-10146
records.s: Pioneer Press, a newspaper, absorbed the Minnesotian in 1861 and united with the Pioneer in 1874. By 1908, Frank Moore had served it and its antecedents for fifty years, heading its composing room; it employed George H. Colgrave.

records.l: Atlantic cable enterprise, Novel-10146
records.s: succeeds_after_attempts four attempts [first in 1857, second in 1858, third in 1863, successful in 1865] The Atlantic cable enterprise required four attempts before success: in 1857, 1858, 1863, and 1865. The 1858 cable operated for about four weeks, while a new company laid a cable in 1866 that was in successful operation at the time described.

records.l: Cyrus W. Field, Novel-10146
records.s: Cyrus W. Field projected the Atlantic cable enterprise, received unanimous thanks from Congress, and declined a knighthood Great Britain would have offered.

records.l: railroad construction scheme, Novel-10146
records.s: collapses suddenly The railroad construction scheme promised state bonds to companies for graded railroad mileage and was expected to revive employment and commerce after the panic of 1857. It collapsed when the bonds could not be negotiated, the companies defaulted, and the state's credit was compromised.

records.l: railroad development in Minnesota, Novel-10146
records.s: The Five Million Loan amendment encouraged railroad development in Minnesota by offering $10,000 per mile for road graded and ready to iron. Nearly 250 miles were graded before the state foreclosed on the lines and later donated them to new organizations.

records.l: steamboat travel, Novel-10146
records.s: Steamboat travel, historically used on the upper Mississippi, was the primary route there: pleasant in summer, but difficult and costly eastward in winter, forcing merchants to stock goods from November through April.

records.l: telegraphic communication, Novel-10146
records.s: is_absent_from St. Paul [when the cable completion news arrived] St. Paul had no telegraphic communication when the Atlantic cable was completed, so news of the event arrived several days late. The city later celebrated after messages had been exchanged between Queen Victoria and President Buchanan.

records.l: Sons of Malta, Novel-10146
records.s: The Sons of Malta were a secret order organized in the early 1850s that expanded rapidly throughout the West. After receiving a charter from Pittsburgh in 1858, Pioneer editorial staff established a successful St. Paul lodge at Empire Hall, drawing merchants, lawyers, doctors, printers, and many local men. Its elaborate, secret initiations investigated candidates and included confessions, frightening ceremonies, and rubber-blanket bouncing. Its membership and reputation declined after member Rev. John Penman exposed its secret work in Harper's Weekly.

records.l: Minnesotian and Times, Novel-10146
records.s: The Minnesotian and Times was a consolidated newspaper, politically arranged from two rival Republican papers. Managed by Dr. Foster and Thomas M. Newson, it was marked by their uncordial relationship and ended when their partnership dissolved around the legislature’s adjournment.

records.l: St. Paul Press, Novel-10146
records.s: St. Paul Press, also called the St. Paul Daily Press, was founded in 1861 by W. R. Marshall and Thomas F. Slaughter using the Times office and material leased from Thomas M. Newson. Its competition led Dr. Foster to sell the Minnesotian plant, ending their rivalry. It employed foremen, moved in 1869, and united with Pioneer in 1874.

records.l: Daily North Star, Novel-10146
records.s: The Daily North Star was a short-lived Democratic newspaper established in St. Paul during the 1860 presidential campaign to support John C. Breckinridge. H. H. Young was brought to start it. It published regularly through the election, then collapsed when officeholders no longer contributed support.

records.l: state printer, Novel-10146
records.s: is_selected_by legislature [after the 1859 election] The office of state printer became the subject of a vigorous contest after the Republican victory in 1859. The Minnesotian and Times both sought the position, while Orville Brown of Faribault entered the race and nearly secured the legislative printing for that village. George W. Moore received the printing of the journals of the two legislative houses as part of the settlement of the former newspaper partnership.

records.l: Sons of Malta initiation, Novel-10146
records.s: is_exposed_in Harper’s Weekly [with numerous illustrations] The Sons of Malta's secret initiation involved hooded candidates being questioned about their conduct before the full lodge, despite believing they were in a private chamber. The ceremony included frightening sounds, public humiliation, and other physical ordeals, including bouncing candidates from a rubber blanket. Rev. John Penman's anger over his treatment led him to publish an illustrated exposure of the secret work.

records.l: The Great Sioux Outbreak in 1862, Novel-10146
records.s: The Great Sioux Outbreak in 1862 was Indian warfare in western Minnesota during the Civil War. Beginning without warning on August 18, it caused a Sioux massacre across the reservation, spread rapidly, killed people, destroyed property, and rendered 30,000 homeless within a week. After the Wood Lake battle, Gen. Pope declared the war over; troops remained despite calls to remove them.

records.l: United States government, Novel-10146
records.s: In 1862, during the Civil War, the United States government was heavily occupied and considered unprepared for the Sioux outbreak. It delayed Sioux annuity payments, though its officers promoted farming, supplied tools and seed, and built houses for some Sioux. After events at Sumter, St. Paul citizens pledged it earnest support, urging enlistment and aid for servicemen’s families.

records.l: Confederate States, Novel-10146
records.s: The Confederate States adopted "Dixie" as their national air after it became popular in New Orleans and throughout the South during the Civil War.

records.l: Ulysses S. Grant, Novel-10146
records.s: Ulysses S. Grant commanded Union forces at Pittsburg Landing, directing divisions despite an injured ankle, stopping a flight, and leading the second-day pursuit. His Fort Henry and Fort Donelson successes made superiors jealous. Afterward he became second to Henry W. Halleck, who succeeded him, and was reassigned to Memphis.

records.l: Don Carlos Buell, Novel-10146
records.s: Don Carlos Buell commanded the Army of the Cumberland and was criticized for taking nineteen days to move approximately eighty-five miles to the Tennessee River. His troops, including divisions under Nelson and Thomas, reinforced Grant during the battle; Grant did not believe Buell was guilty of the charges later made against him.

records.l: Little Crow, Novel-10146
records.s: Little Crow was born at Kaposia and influenced the 1858 sale of part of the Minnesota River reservation strip, drawing Sioux criticism. He became the acknowledged head of the war party and was described as chief instigator of the insurrection. After refusing surrender at Camp Release, he escaped, was killed by Lamson near Hutchinson, and his scalp was preserved by the Minnesota Historical Society.

records.l: Other Day, Novel-10146
records.s: Other Day, an educated Dakota Indian who adopted Christianity and civilized habits, guided sixty-two Minnesota River refugees through several places to safety. After arriving in St. Paul, he credited the Great Spirit for their escape and supported Gen. Sibley by fighting with the whites.

records.l: Ingersoll Hall, Novel-10146
records.s: Constructed in 1860 on Bridge Square, Ingersoll block was a city block whose third-floor hall drew audiences for several years. It hosted speakers Edward Everett, Ralph Waldo Emerson, John B. Gough, and Mrs. Scott Siddons; Company C used it for drills and enlistment meetings. In February 1861, a Young Men's Christian Association social and supper raised library funds for about 350 books.

records.l: Fort Ridgely, Novel-10146
records.s: Fort Ridgely was a lightly protected post besieged during the Great Sioux Outbreak in 1862 by an estimated 700 or 800 Sioux warriors. About 150 Fifth Regiment men, fifty Renville Rangers, and civilians defended it for more than a week until relief arrived with the advance of Sibley’s force.

records.l: New Ulm, Novel-10146
records.s: was_attacked_by Sioux [repeatedly, with burning and pillaging] New Ulm was attacked by Sioux forces that killed citizens and burned buildings. After a later attack, its defenders evacuated about 1,200 to 1,500 noncombatants to Mankato, and nearly 200 houses had been burned.

records.l: Mankato, Novel-10146
records.s: Mankato held the condemned Indians in a large jail before the authorized executions. Thirty-eight Dakota prisoners were executed there on December 26, 1862.

records.l: Birch Coulie, Novel-10146
records.s: Birch Coulie was the site of a camp established by Maj. Joseph R. Brown’s detachment about fifteen miles from Fort Ridgely. The camp’s attractive but exposed location left roughly 150 men vulnerable to a large Sioux attack.

records.l: Battle of Wood Lake, Novel-10146
records.s: Battle of Wood Lake, the Indian war's only real battle, occurred at Wood Lake on September 23. About 800 of Gen. Sibley's men fought roughly 800 Sioux; Col. Marshall's 400-man charge routed them, with four whites killed and forty or fifty wounded.

records.l: Wood Lake, Novel-10146
records.s: Wood Lake was the vicinity where foraging parties from the Third regiment were fired upon on the morning of September 23, 1862.

records.l: Birch Coulie battle, Novel-10146
records.s: The Birch Coulie battle began around 4 a.m. when 500 or 600 armed, mostly mounted Sioux fired on Maj. Joseph R. Brown’s roughly 150-man command. The defenders held out for two days until relief arrived, with about half killed or wounded.

records.l: Sioux massacre, Novel-10146
records.s: The Sioux massacre began on August 18 with attacks on settlers and spread throughout the reservation and isolated communities. The text reports that about 1,000 people were killed in less than a week, millions of dollars in property were destroyed, and 30,000 people were made homeless.

records.l: Fort Ridgely siege, Novel-10146
records.s: The Fort Ridgely siege lasted several days and included two attempted assaults by Sioux forces. Defenders improvised ammunition by opening spherical case shot, making cartridges, and cutting nail rods into projectiles until relief arrived.

records.l: New Ulm attacks, Novel-10146
records.s: The New Ulm attacks included an initial assault that killed citizens and burned homes, followed several days later by a larger encirclement and assault. Flandrau’s defenders drove the Sioux away, but lost ten men killed and about forty wounded before evacuating the town.

records.l: Camp Release, Novel-10146
records.s: Gen. Sibley's command reached Camp Release on September 26, where a large Indian camp surrendered after preliminary consultations. The captives held there were released.

records.l: Indian camp at Camp Release, Novel-10146
records.s: contains mixed bloods and white women and children [about 250 captives] The Indian camp at Camp Release contained many Indians who had participated in the massacres and held about 250 mixed bloods and white women and children. The entire camp surrendered after Gen. Sibley avoided a hostile demonstration that he believed might lead to the prisoners' annihilation.

records.l: mixed bloods and white women and children, Novel-10146
records.s: are_released_at Camp Release [after the entire camp surrendered] About 250 mixed bloods and white women and children were held by the Indian camp at Camp Release. They were released when the camp surrendered.

records.l: military tribunal, Novel-10146
records.s: convicts condemned Indians [321 defendants found guilty] Gen. Sibley formed a military tribunal to investigate and try Indians suspected of participating in the recent atrocities. After sittings from September 30 to November 5, it found 321 guilty, sentencing 303 to death and the remainder to imprisonment.

records.l: condemned Indians, Novel-10146
records.s: The condemned Indians were taken to Mankato and confined in a specially constructed jail; after executions were reduced to thirty-eight, the remaining prisoners stayed until spring and were transported to Davenport and the Missouri river.

records.l: execution of the thirty-eight Dakota prisoners, Novel-10146
records.s: occurs_at Mankato [on December 26, 1862] The thirty-eight Dakota prisoners were hanged at Mankato on December 26, 1862. Their bodies were placed together in a sandbar grave and were later taken away by students and others familiar with dissection.

records.l: transportation of military supplies, Novel-10146
records.s: uses wagon [because there were no railroads] Because there were no railroads, military supplies had to be transported by wagon. The authorities impressed teams into government service when volunteers were insufficient, sent Company K of the Eighth regiment to enforce the order, and provided escorts for supply trains.

records.l: Ladies Aid Society, Novel-10146
records.s: Ladies Aid Society in St. Paul organized to sew and provide supplies for wounded soldiers and destitute refugees, meeting at Ingersoll Hall; Stella Selby led it and M.O. Holyoke collected sanitary supplies.

records.l: Dakota lands in Minnesota, Novel-10146
records.s: Dakota lands in Minnesota, about 750,000 acres valued at $15,000,000, are forfeited to the government following the outbreak, along with a $68,000 annual annuity for fifty years.

records.l: St. Paul fire department, Novel-10146
records.s: The St. Paul Fire Department developed from volunteer companies organized in the 1850s, including Pioneer Hook and Ladder Company No. 1, Hope Engine Company No. 1, and Minnehaha Engine Company No. 2. It held its first annual parade in 1859. By March 1860 it had three fire engines, one fire truck, and one hundred men. After its first steamer arrived August 11, 1866, it expanded despite the city’s lack of waterworks in 1869, relying on cisterns and river water pumped through over two thousand feet of hose. At present it has 211 paid men, 15 steamers, four chemicals, eight hook and ladder companies, and 122 horses; chiefs include Wash M. Stees and Bartlett Presley.

records.l: firemen and fires of pioneer days, Novel-10146
records.s: is_a brief history The unit describes pioneer firemen responding to alarms with hand engines, hooks, ladders, and bucket brigades. Firemen worked the engine brakes, sometimes requiring spectators or people compelled by the police to relieve them, and many enlisted during the war.

records.l: old machine, Novel-10146
records.s: is_used_by old firemen [in the poem's recollection] The old machine is remembered in a poem by Gus Wiliams as a former fire apparatus with which firemen ran through flames and danger. The poem says that only a few of the old firemen remained, while their memories and spirits endured.

records.l: fire engines, Novel-10146
records.s: is_a firefighting equipment Early fire engines included wheeled tanks, hand engines, and engines equipped with pumps, air chambers, suction pipes, and leather hose. St. Paul received its first engine through John McCloud and Thompson Ritchie and later purchased two double-deck hand engines that arrived in August 1858.

records.l: R.C. Knox, Novel-10146
records.s: R.C. Knox first tried to organize a St. Paul fire brigade in fall 1851, raised subscription money for ladders, and was reputed to outlast a dozen ordinary men at fires.

records.l: John McCloud, Novel-10146
records.s: John McCloud, a hardware dealer and member of McCloud & Bro., jointly bought and brought the first fire engine introduced in the Northwest to St. Paul with Thompson Ritchie. He was an original member and the only surviving city resident of Pioneer Hook and Ladder Company No. 1's original roll.

records.l: first parade of the St. Paul fire department, Novel-10146
records.s: The first parade of the St. Paul fire department took place September 12, 1859, with 175 men from Pioneer Hook and Ladder, Hope Engine, Minnehaha Engine, and Rotary Independent companies participating.

records.l: first steamer, Novel-10146
records.s: The first steamer arrived in St. Paul on August 11, 1866, was initially housed by Hope Engine Company No. 1 with appointed staff, then transferred to St. Paul Hose Company No. 1 after disbandment.

records.l: Mrs. Bartlett Presley, Novel-10146
records.s: Mrs. Bartlett Presley supports the volunteer fire department as a guardian angel, attending fires during cold nights and severe storms to provide coffee and sandwiches, earning firemen’s lasting gratitude.

records.l: Michael E. Ames, Novel-10146
records.s: Michael E. Ames, a St. Paul legal fraternity member living in uppertown, escaped a fire that destroyed his sleeping apartments after asking firemen to wait.

records.l: St. Paul fire department annual parade of 1859, Novel-10146
records.s: The St. Paul fire department annual parade of 1859 was held on September 12 and included four companies. The 175 participants completed a line of march and were reviewed by the mayor and common council in front of the old city hall.

records.l: paid fire department, Novel-10146
records.s: replaces volunteer fire department [after the volunteer era] The paid fire department followed the volunteer period and expanded as St. Paul grew. At the time described, it had 211 paid men, 15 steamers, 4 chemicals, 8 hook and ladder companies, and 122 horses.

records.l: volunteer fire department, Novel-10146
records.s: The volunteer fire department was organized through companies such as Pioneer Hook and Ladder Company No. 1, Hope Engine Company No. 1, and Minnehaha Engine Company No. 2. Its members received exemptions from jury duty, poll tax, road work, and state military service for five years, and many prominent citizens served in its ranks.

records.l: firefighting equipment, Novel-10146
records.s: Firefighting equipment discussed in the unit includes marked buckets, ladders, hooks, hand engines, hose, cisterns, steamers, chemical apparatus, and horses. St. Paul initially had limited equipment, then acquired two double-deck hand engines in 1858 and additional apparatus as the city expanded.

records.l: hotel fires, Novel-10146
records.s: is_a list of hotels destroyed by fire [during St. Paul's early history] The unit lists hotels destroyed by fire during St. Paul’s early history, including the Daniels house, Sintominie hotel, Rice house, New England hotel, Winslow house, American house, International hotel, Cosmopolitan hotel, Central house, Emmert house, Greenman house, Mansion house, Park Place hotel, and Carpenter house.

records.l: Daniels house, Novel-10146
records.s: Daniels house was a hotel on Eagle street near Seven Corners, finished and furnished shortly before strong wind hindered firemen and it was destroyed in the 1852 Daniels house fire; furniture was partly saved.

records.l: Sintominie hotel, Novel-10146
records.s: Hotel at Sixth and John streets, constructed by C.W. Borup; Howard Ward and E.C. Rich prepared to open it before the Sintominie hotel fire totally destroyed it.

records.l: Rice house, Novel-10146
records.s: Rice house was a three-story hotel on Third street near Market, built by Henry M. Rice and commonly considered St. Paul’s first brick building. A principal hotel, it hosted Minnesota’s territorial legislature and the territory’s supreme court before burning to the ground in early winter 1856.

records.l: New England hotel, Novel-10146
records.s: New England hotel was a two-story log house in St. Paul, among its first hotels. Gov. and Mrs. Ramsey lived there in 1849, giving it recognition as the first gubernatorial mansion, before the March 16, 1860 fire destroyed it.

records.l: International hotel, Novel-10146
records.s: The International hotel, formerly the Fuller house, was a five-story brick building at Seventh and Jackson streets, built by A.G. Fuller in 1856 for about $110,000. Renamed in 1861 and once regarded as the best hotel in the West, it burned in the February 3, 1869 fire.

records.l: Cosmopolitan hotel, Novel-10146
records.s: The Cosmopolitan hotel, a European-plan hotel in a three-story brick building at Third and Franklin streets, was remodeled from a former banking house by Bechtner & Kottman, then burned while full of lodgers; many lost everything, and its remaining walls collapsed onto Dr. Schell’s building.

records.l: Emmert house, Novel-10146
records.s: The Emmert house was a hotel and later boarding house on Bench street near Wabasha, built in territorial times by Fred Emmert. No longer a hotel, it housed a family and boarders when fire destroyed it in winter 1868; firemen rescued two people sick with smallpox, and W.L. Wilson took them to safety.

records.l: Greenman house, Novel-10146
records.s: Greenman house was a three-story frame building at Fifth and St. Peter streets, built in the early 1870s. Mr. Greenman sold it to John Summers; while Summers owned it, the Greenman house fire destroyed it.

records.l: Mansion house, Novel-10146
records.s: The Mansion house was a three-story frame hotel built by Nicholas Pottgieser for $12,000 at Wabasha and Fifth streets, a popular resort where, in 1866, guest Hawkes accidentally killed his wife and was acquitted.

records.l: Park Place hotel, Novel-10146
records.s: Park Place hotel was a four-story frame family hotel at Summit avenue and St. Peter street, formerly fashionable but unoccupied when it burned to the ground on May 19, 1878. The suspected incendiary fire seriously injured four firemen, who recovered.

records.l: Carpenter house, Novel-10146
records.s: Carpenter house was a hotel at Summit avenue and Ramsey street, built by Warren Carpenter on a picturesque site overlooking the city to attract tourists. The panic of 1857 and Civil war thwarted plans; it later burned to the ground January 26, 1879.

records.l: 1852 Daniels house fire, Novel-10146
records.s: is_a hotel fire [the first hotel fire of any importance] The 1852 Daniels house fire was the first hotel fire of importance described in the unit. A strong wind prevented the small group of firemen from saving the newly finished building, though furniture was rescued.

records.l: March 16, 1860 St. Paul fire, Novel-10146
records.s: The March 16, 1860 St. Paul fire began in a small wooden building on Third street near Jackson, became the city’s most destructive fire to that time, burned thirty-four buildings including two hotels, and was stopped from crossing Robert street into lower town.

records.l: Winslow house fire, Novel-10146
records.s: The Winslow house fire occurred in the fall of 1862 and was caused by a defective stovepipe in the cupola. The four-story brick hotel was beyond control when firemen arrived, and only a few badly damaged pieces of furniture were saved.

records.l: Cosmopolitan hotel fire, Novel-10146
records.s: The Cosmopolitan hotel fire destroyed a hotel full of lodgers, many of whom lost all they owned. The walls remained standing afterward despite being declared dangerous, and a later collapse crushed Dr. Schell’s nearby frame building, though he survived with no serious injury.

records.l: Emmert house fire, Novel-10146
records.s: The Emmert house fire occurred during the winter of 1868. Two occupants suffering from smallpox were rescued by firemen but were left in the street until W.L. Wilson learned of their situation the next day and took them to safety.

records.l: February 3, 1869 International hotel fire, Novel-10146
records.s: The February 3, 1869 International hotel fire began in the basement, probably from a laundry lamp, on a cold, gale-driven night. Pete O’Brien helped more than two hundred guests escape; no lives were lost, but the hotel and four other buildings were destroyed.

records.l: May 1870 Concert Hall fire, Novel-10146
records.s: The May 1870 Concert Hall fire began beneath the sidewalk, where combustible materials were stored, and rapidly engulfed the building. Charles and August Mueller leaped from an upper-floor window and survived after months of suffering, while McClellan, who operated a dressmaking establishment there, was burned to death.

records.l: St. Paul Concert Hall, Novel-10146
records.s: St. Paul Concert Hall was a concert hall in a three-story building on Third street near Market, with six or seven stories on the river side and a large basement hall. Built by J.W. McClung in 1857, it held about 400 or 500 people. Its basement location made it somewhat inaccessible and limited demand, yet it hosted speeches and musical gatherings. It was destroyed in the May 1870 Concert Hall fire.

records.l: Athenaeum, Novel-10146
records.s: The Athenaeum, built in 1859 by the German Reading Society, was for several years St. Paul's only amusement hall with a stage and drop curtain. It hosted Peter and Caroline Richings, dramatic performances, and a Sanitary Commission benefit; during the Sioux massacre, it sheltered maimed refugees.

records.l: firemen, Novel-10146
records.s: Firemen fought numerous St. Paul fires despite strong winds, bitter cold, limited equipment, and a lack of waterworks. They saved furniture at the Daniels house, rescued guests and smallpox patients, and at the International hotel were aided by the calm direction of Pete O’Brien.

records.l: hotel guests, Novel-10146
records.s: Hotel guests faced narrow escapes during several fires. At the American house they escaped in bitter cold while thieves stole their belongings, and at the International hotel more than two hundred guests fled in nightclothes without any lives being lost.

records.l: fire, Novel-10146
records.s: The unit describes fires caused or suspected to have been caused by strong winds, defective stovepipes, lamps, and possible incendiarism. Fires destroyed hotels and other buildings, threatened entire sections of St. Paul, and sometimes required rescues from severe cold, smoke, flames, or collapsing walls.

records.l: Irvine hall, Novel-10146
records.s: Irvine hall was an amusement hall in a three-story, three-cornered building on Third street at Seven Corners. Later called Melodeon hall, it hosted Dan Emmet's minstrel company in 1857–1858 and the Hutchinson family in summer 1858.

records.l: Dan Emmet, Novel-10146
records.s: Dan Emmet was a minstrel performer who organized the first traveling minstrel troupe in the United States in 1843. He later led a company at Irvine hall in 1857–1858 and wrote popular melodies, including "Dixie," while connected with Bryant's Minstrels.

records.l: Hutchinson family, Novel-10146
records.s: The Hutchinson family was a patriotic concert-giving family that generally sang its own music. It frequently visited St. Paul, and Hutchinson in McLeod county was named after it. During the Civil War, Gen. McClellan removed it from the Army of the Potomac for abolitionist songs. In 1902, John W. Hutchinson was identified as its last surviving member.

records.l: R.C. Munger, Novel-10146
records.s: R.C. Munger was Dan Emmet’s friend in St. Paul, encouraged and financed publication of “Dixie,” received an early printed copy, and saw it first sung in the West at Munger Bros.’ music store.

records.l: Dixie, Novel-10146
records.s: Dixie, an air written by Dan Emmet with Bryant's Minstrels in New York City, was first sung west at Munger Bros, spread through minstrel programs, became the Confederate States' national air, and Lincoln called it national property by capture.

records.l: Sanitary Commission, Novel-10146
records.s: receives_funds_from sanitary fair [several thousand dollars from St. Paul citizens] The sanitary commission received several thousand dollars from the successful 1864 sanitary fair in St. Paul. The fair was part of a broader practice of holding fairs in principal Northern cities to raise money for the commission.

records.l: Market Hall, Novel-10146
records.s: Market Hall, built in 1853 at Wabasha and Seventh streets, became one of St. Paul’s principal places of amusement, hosting the Hough Dramatic Company before serving the Wide Awakes as a drill hall in 1860.

records.l: William Henry Acker, Novel-10146
records.s: William Henry Acker, born in New York State in 1833, came to St. Paul in 1854 and became a respected military leader. He was captain of the Pioneer Guards, commanded the Wide-Awakes in 1860, and, at the war’s outbreak, served as Minnesota’s adjutant general and organized a company for the First Minnesota Regiment. Wounded at Bull Run, he became captain in the Seventeenth United States Regulars. He was killed leading his company at Pittsburg Landing; his funeral was at St. Paul’s Church, and Acker Post was named for him.

records.l: Mazurka hall, Novel-10146
records.s: Mazurka hall was the principal amusement hall of the city for a time. Built by the Elfelt brothers in 1850, it occupied the second story of their old frame building at Third and Exchange streets. It hosted swell entertainments in the early 1850s, including a ball where J.Q.A. Ward met and soon married Miss Pratt.

records.l: Mozart hall, Novel-10146
records.s: Mozart hall, the People’s theater, was an old frame building on the corner of Fourth and St., built by Charles N. Mackubin in 1860 at the Third Street end of the Metropolitan hotel site; it joined Masonic hall for a winter 1864 sanitary fair.

records.l: Masonic hall, Novel-10146
records.s: Masonic hall, an old frame building on the Fourth Street corner of the Metropolitan hotel site, was built by Charles N. Mackubin in summer 1860 and joined with Mozart hall for a large sanitary-fair entertainment in winter 1864.

records.l: sanitary fair, Novel-10146
records.s: benefits sanitary commission [held during the winter of 1864] A sanitary fair held in the winter of 1864 combined Mozart hall and Masonic hall for a large entertainment. Its proceeds helped the nearly depleted funds of the sanitary commission, and the event raised several thousand dollars.

records.l: Second Minnesota Infantry Regiment, Novel-10146
records.s: The Second Minnesota Infantry Regiment was a Union infantry regiment from Minnesota, organized in 1861 under Colonel H.P. Van Cleve and headquartered at Fort Snelling. It moved toward Washington, was redirected to Louisville, reported to W.T. Sherman, and joined George H. Thomas's First Division. In the Mill Springs campaign, it camped at Logan's Cross Roads, fought in the center under heavy fire, used bayonets, lost twelve killed and thirty-five wounded, received praise, and was presented a silk flag.

records.l: Adalina Patti, Novel-10146
records.s: Adalina Patti was a concert performer, about sixteen in 1857. That year, on her first appearance in St. Paul, she traveled with the Ole Bull Concert company by small steamboat through river towns and performed in the old capitol’s house of representatives hall.

records.l: old capitol, Novel-10146
records.s: contains house of representatives [the hall served as a concert venue] The old capitol provided the only available venue for Adalina Patti's 1857 concert. Two boys who had been using the house for smoking and playing cards accidentally caused a fire that nearly burned through its floor.

records.l: house of representatives, Novel-10146
records.s: The hall of the house of representatives hosted Adalina Patti's 1857 concert, Washington's Birthday exercises, a mass meeting supporting the government after the attack on Sumter, and the first Republican state convention after Minnesota entered the Union. The hall was also the scene of speeches, resolutions, and political nominations.

records.l: Sumter, Novel-10146
records.s: After Maj. Anderson was compelled to lower the Stars and Stripes on Sumter's walls, St. Paul citizens held a mass meeting to express indignation at the attempt of the Cotton States to disrupt the government. The meeting pledged support to the government, urged young men to enlist, and promised financial aid for dependents of those who served.

records.l: John S. Prince, Novel-10146
records.s: John S. Prince, mayor of St. Paul, presided over the mass meeting held after the events at Sumter. He was assisted by several prominent citizens serving as vice presidents.

records.l: John M. Gilman, Novel-10146
records.s: John M. Gilman was one of the principal speakers at the mass meeting held after the events at Sumter. Although he had been the Democratic candidate for Congress the previous fall, he expressed hearty sympathy with the meeting's support for the government and received strong approval.

records.l: Confederate forces, Novel-10146
records.s: Confederate forces were a military force commanded overall by Albert Sidney Johnston and also by P. G. T. Beauregard. They held Beech Grove, advanced near Logan's Cross Roads, and were driven off with about 600 casualties. They later attacked Grant's army, failed to destroy it or stop a counterattack, and retreated toward Corinth.

records.l: old opera house, Novel-10146
records.s: The old opera house on Wabasha Street, on the ground now occupied by the Grand block, was completed in winter 1866–67 and opened with local talent. Its boxes and some parquet seats were auctioned; Macfarland Dramatic Company became its first regular company. Seating about 1,000, it later drew large audiences for Frederick Douglass and other speakers.

records.l: Frederick Douglass, Novel-10146
records.s: addresses_audience_at old opera house [during a lecture with standing room only] Frederick Douglass addressed a large audience at the old opera house in St. Paul. During his lecture, two Republicans in an upper box applauded loudly while standing behind W.H. Shelley, causing the audience to think Shelley was supporting Douglass and had returned to the Republican fold; Shelley eventually left in disgust.

records.l: Capt. E.Y. Shelly, Novel-10146
records.s: Capt. E.Y. Shelly was a pioneer printer of Minnesota, born in Bucks county, Pa., in 1827 and trained in Philadelphia. After service in the Third United States dragoons during the Mexican War, he reached St. Paul in July 1849 as Minnesota’s first permanent printer. He worked for the Register, Pioneer, and Daily Democrat, served in Brackett’s battalion during the Civil War, was mustered out in 1865, and continued printing afterward.

records.l: George W. Benedict, Novel-10146
records.s: George W. Benedict, familiar to longtime residents, served as foreman of the St. Paul Press before becoming editor and publisher of the Sauk Rapids Sentinel.

records.l: Louis E. Fisher, Novel-10146
records.s: Louis E. Fisher was a printer, foreman of the Commercial Advertiser, and longtime editor of the Pioneer and Pioneer Press. A staunch Democrat, he ran unsuccessfully for governor of Minnesota and was described as a potential model governor.

records.l: George W. Armstrong, Novel-10146
records.s: George W. Armstrong, known as the Beau Brummel of early territorial printers for wearing kid gloves while making up forms at the Pioneer, was elected state treasurer on the Democratic ticket in 1857 and later entered real estate.

records.l: David Ramaley, Novel-10146
records.s: David Ramaley, a leading Northwest printer, spent nearly fifty years as printer, reporter, editor, publisher, and type founder, remaining active throughout his long trade career.

records.l: James M. Culver, Novel-10146
records.s: James M. Culver was a fastidious printer, St. Paul’s first delegate to the International Typographical Union, and remembered by Sons of Malta for resisting a ceremony’s canine portion.

records.l: William Jebb, Novel-10146
records.s: William Jebb, a ready, fluent, well-informed debater in the Pioneer composing room and former St. Paul Times reporter, left reporting after writing about stolen prized chickens and ending the report with a papal bull of excommunication.

records.l: O.G. Miller, Novel-10146
records.s: O.G. Miller was a well-known, musically inclined St. Paul printer who belonged to the Great Western band, sang tenor in churches, and was a 33d Degree Mason; after his death, Masonic hall held a midnight funeral service.

records.l: Andrew Jackson Morgan, Novel-10146
records.s: Andrew Jackson Morgan was a printer-politician brought to St. Paul by Col. D.A. Robertson, who made him foreman of the Democrat; he later edited it. He claimed to resemble Stephen A. Douglas and carried a silver dollar reportedly given by Andrew Jackson at his christening. He died in Ohio.

records.l: P. G. T. Beauregard, Novel-10146
records.s: P. G. T. Beauregard served with Albert Sidney Johnston as a Confederate commander at Pittsburg Landing. He reportedly said that before sundown he would water his horses in the Tennessee River or in hell, and later reported Confederate losses of 10,699.

records.l: Fort Donelson, Novel-10146
records.s: was_attacked_by Gen. Buckner [during the Civil War] Brackett's battalion was the only Minnesota force engaged at Fort Donelson during its attack and surrender in February 1862. Capt. E.Y. Shelly's unit performed exhausting service to prevent Gen. Buckner from receiving reinforcements, and the regiment later returned to defend the fort against attacks in August 1862 and February 1863.

records.l: Louisville, Novel-10146
records.s: presents silk flag presented to the Second Minnesota [through its mayor] Louisville became the Second Minnesota's destination after its planned movement to Washington was changed. The regiment later returned there, where Mayor J.M. Dolph presented it with a silk flag in recognition of its conduct at Mill Springs.

records.l: Pittsburg Landing, Novel-10146
records.s: Pittsburg Landing, on the Tennessee River, was the principal Union position and battlefield vicinity in the April 6–7 battle. Union troops and reinforcements arrived by steamer and used the landing and nearby river positions during the fighting. The First Minnesota battery arrived in late February 1862, fought there, and William Henry Acker was killed there.

records.l: Brackett's battalion, Novel-10146
records.s: Brackett's battalion was a military battalion of three Minnesota companies, mustered in September 1861. Initially assigned to Curtis horse and later the Fifth Iowa cavalry, it was the only Minnesota force engaged at Fort Donelson, then served in scouting, railroad protection, Tennessee campaigns, and Gen. Sully's Dakota campaign.

records.l: printing and typesetting, Novel-10146
records.s: Printing and typesetting was Capt. E.Y. Shelly’s profession before and after military service. Historically overlapping with theater, it joined technical and editorial work with politics, publishing, and civic service. Territorial offices and newspapers relied on mobile printers and notable compositors, but the iron printer diminished composing rooms’ former sociability and informal intellectual exchange.

records.l: territorial printers, Novel-10146
records.s: Territorial printers were a group of printers, reporters, editors, publishers, foremen, and type founders. Closely affiliated with editors, they worked and often slept in printing offices because hotels were scarce and economy mattered. Their composing rooms fostered debate, literary quotation, and sociability. The record lists many members, including Capt. E.Y. Shelly, and identifies a smaller set then known to survive.

records.l: James Mills, Novel-10146
records.s: James Mills came early to Minnesota, worked at the Pioneer office and its editorial department, then after the war returned to Pittsburgh as Pittsburgh Post editor-in-chief.

records.l: John P. Owens, Novel-10146
records.s: John P. Owens, a printer, first edited and published the Minnesotian with George W. Moore, then partnered with John O. Terry.

records.l: John O. Terry, Novel-10146
records.s: John O. Terry, St. Paul’s first hand pressman, partnered with John P. Owens to publish the Minnesotian, then long served as assistant postmaster and held trusted positions.

records.l: The decisive battle of Mill Springs, Novel-10146
records.s: The decisive battle of Mill Springs was a battle in Kentucky, part of the American Civil War and the first important Union victory in the Southwest after its outbreak. Led against Confederate commander Zollicoffer, with the Second Minnesota Infantry Regiment as a Union hero, it inflicted about 600 Confederate losses, cost 248 Union losses, captured twelve cannon, opened a route to East Tennessee, and forced Albert Sidney Johnston’s withdrawal.

records.l: William Tecumseh Sherman, Novel-10146
records.s: commanded Sherman's division [Union division during the battle] William Tecumseh Sherman commanded a Union division whose position saw some of the hardest fighting on the first day. He was wounded slightly twice, had a ball pass through his hat, and lost several horses, while his resistance was important to the Union defense.

records.l: George H. Thomas, Novel-10146
records.s: commands Second Minnesota Infantry Regiment [as commander of the First division] George H. Thomas commanded the First Division that included the Second Minnesota, the Eighteenth United States Infantry, and the Ninth and Thirty-fifth Ohio regiments. His troops began the Mill Springs campaign on January 1, 1862.

records.l: Mill Springs campaign, Novel-10146
records.s: is_led_by George H. Thomas The Mill Springs campaign began on January 1, 1862, under George H. Thomas. The troops marched through rain, sleet, and mud before camping near Logan's Cross Roads and engaging the Confederate forces at Beech Grove.

records.l: Logan's Cross Roads, Novel-10146
records.s: is_located_near Beech Grove [eight miles north] Logan's Cross Roads was the Union camp where George H. Thomas's troops assembled before the battle. It lay eight miles north of Zollicoffer's entrenched Confederate camp at Beech Grove.

records.l: Beech Grove, Novel-10146
records.s: is_a Confederate camp [intrenched rebel camp] Beech Grove was the site of Zollicoffer's entrenched Confederate camp, located eight miles south of Logan's Cross Roads. Confederate forces withdrew from the area after the battle.

records.l: Bailie Peyton, Novel-10146
records.s: Bailie Peyton, a Confederate lieutenant and son of a prominent Union man in Tennessee, refused to surrender at the decisive battle of Mill Springs, shot Lieutenant Stout, was immediately killed, and had his sword captured by Lieutenant Tuttle.

records.l: Zollicoffer, Novel-10146
records.s: Zollicoffer, a Nashville Confederate commander who had opposed Tennessee's secession, followed the state after it seceded, commanded forces at the decisive battle of Mill Springs, and was killed there when Colonel Fry shot him.

records.l: Colonel Fry, Novel-10146
records.s: kills Zollicoffer [according to his own account] Colonel Fry of the Fourth Kentucky reported that he killed Zollicoffer during the battle. He described shooting the Confederate general in the breast after Zollicoffer's companion fired at him.

records.l: Union victory at Mill Springs, Novel-10146
records.s: An important Union victory, it broke up the Confederate right flank, opened a route into East Tennessee, helped force Albert Sidney Johnston's troops from Bowling Green to Nashville, and caused rejoicing among loyal residents.

records.l: Albert Sidney Johnston, Novel-10146
records.s: was_killed_at The Great Battle of Pittsburg Landing [first day] Albert Sidney Johnston commanded the Confederate forces at Pittsburg Landing. He was killed during the first day's battle while attempting to induce a Confederate brigade to charge the enemy.

records.l: Kentucky, Novel-10146
records.s: Kentucky was the setting for the Mill Springs campaign and battle, which loyal Kentuckians viewed as a victory over rebel invaders from Tennessee, Mississippi, and Alabama. Kentucky troops, including Wolford's First Cavalry and the Fourth Kentucky Infantry, were among the first to confront the invaders.

records.l: The Great Battle of Pittsburg Landing, Novel-10146
records.s: The Great Battle of Pittsburg Landing, also called Shiloh, was a two-day Civil War battle at Pittsburg Landing on April 6–7, 1862. Confederate forces attacked the Union Army of the Tennessee; the Army of the Cumberland under Buell reinforced it. The First Minnesota battery fought advancing Confederate forces for hours, notably at the Hornet's Nest, helping keep Union lines from being forced toward the Tennessee River. After Buell arrived, it was held in reserve on April 7. Union forces ultimately drove the Confederates from the field amid heavy casualties on both sides.

records.l: Army of the Tennessee, Novel-10146
records.s: was_commanded_by Ulysses S. Grant [during the battle] The Army of the Tennessee, commanded by Ulysses S. Grant, was attacked at Pittsburg Landing before the arrival of much of Don Carlos Buell's army. It resisted the Confederate assault and, after receiving reinforcements, helped drive the enemy toward Corinth.

records.l: Army of the Cumberland, Novel-10146
records.s: was_commanded_by Don Carlos Buell [during the battle] The Army of the Cumberland, under Don Carlos Buell, was expected to join Grant's forces at Pittsburg Landing. The text states that critics believed Buell could have made the junction earlier and thereby reduced the Union loss of life.

records.l: Henry W. Halleck, Novel-10146
records.s: Henry W. Halleck suspended Grant, assumed command of Union forces at Pittsburg Landing after the battle, placed Grant second, built unused fortifications, and was then ordered to Washington.

records.l: Lew Wallace, Novel-10146
records.s: commanded Union division [arrived from Crump's Landing after nightfall] Lew Wallace brought 5,000 Union troops from Crump's Landing after nightfall on the first day. His division appeared on the Confederate left during the retreat and was strongly reinforced on the second day.

records.l: Tennessee River, Novel-10146
records.s: The Union forces were positioned near the Tennessee River at Pittsburg Landing. The Confederate plan was to reach the river after defeating Grant, but gunboat fire and Union resistance prevented that result.

records.l: Church of Shiloh, Novel-10146
records.s: is_a old log church [near the hardest fighting] The Church of Shiloh was an old log church about three miles from Pittsburg Landing. Some of the hardest fighting occurred in its vicinity, giving the battle its alternate name, the Battle of Shiloh.

records.l: Grant's command of the Army of the Tennessee, Novel-10146
records.s: Grant's command of the Army of the Tennessee was threatened before the battle when Halleck suspended him, but a restoration order arrived before Grant learned of the suspension. After the battle, Halleck placed Grant second in command until Grant later received command of the Department of West Tennessee.

records.l: Grant's military reputation, Novel-10146
records.s: was_subject_to allegations of drunkenness [during the battle controversy] Grant's military reputation was damaged by accusations that he was drunk, absent from the battlefield, and unprepared for the Confederate attack. The text rejects those claims by describing his active direction of the battle and noting that his army made a firm resistance.

records.l: Buell's delayed reinforcement, Novel-10146
records.s: was_attributed_to Don Carlos Buell [slow advance to the Tennessee River] Buell's delayed reinforcement was criticized as a possible cause of the Union army's terrible first-day losses. The text states that Buell was at Columbia on March 19 and required nineteen days to reach the Tennessee River, although his troops eventually reinforced Grant.

records.l: Union casualties at Shiloh, Novel-10146
records.s: numbered 13,047 [1,754 killed, 8,408 wounded, and 2,885 missing] The Union casualties in the two days of fighting were reported as 1,754 killed, 8,408 wounded, and 2,885 missing. The first day also saw approximately 2,200 men captured with Prentiss and about 6,000 inexperienced recruits flee toward the river.

records.l: Grant's alleged drunkenness, Novel-10146
records.s: was_alleged_during The Great Battle of Pittsburg Landing [charge described as false by the narrative] Grant's alleged drunkenness was one of several charges made against him after the battle. The text states that he was instead in the saddle from early morning until late at night, directing Union divisions despite severe pain from a sprained ankle.

records.l: First Minnesota battery, Novel-10146
records.s: The First Minnesota battery was a light artillery organization organized at Fort Snelling in fall 1861 under first captain Emil Munch. After receiving equipment in St. Louis, it joined Grant's army through Prentiss' division and was transferred there before Pittsburg Landing. The only Minnesota organization engaged in that battle, it helped hold the Hornet's Nest, drove off rebel batteries, suffered losses, and was commended. It later served in the Vicksburg and Atlanta campaigns and the March to the Sea.

records.l: Emil Munch, Novel-10146
records.s: Emil Munch was made the first captain of the First Minnesota battery when it was organized at Fort Snelling in the fall of 1861. During the Battle of Pittsburg Landing, his horse was shot in the head and he was wounded in the thigh, preventing him from continuing in the battle; Lieutenant Pfaender then took command.

records.l: assassination of Abraham Lincoln, Novel-10146
records.s: is_a assassination The assassination was announced over the wires on the morning of April 15, 1865, after Lincoln was shot by an assassin. It caused nationwide grief and condemnation and was remembered as an especially appalling event.

records.l: death of Abraham Lincoln, Novel-10146
records.s: President Lincoln’s death, caused by an assassin’s bullet shortly after Richmond’s fall and Lee’s surrender, ended his life and led to nationwide mourning and church commemoration.

records.l: House of Hope church, Novel-10146
records.s: House of Hope church on Walnut Street became a mourning-filled house of sorrow after Lincoln’s assassination, holding a crowded, solemn memorial service for Abraham Lincoln.

records.l: Frederick A. Noble, Novel-10146
records.s: Frederick A. Noble, pastor of House of Hope church, is portrayed as an eloquent, learned, fearless, forcible, and aggressive divine. During the Rebellion he supports the Union with stirring war addresses, admires Abraham Lincoln, and after Lincoln’s death delivers an emotional memorial sermon praising Lincoln and eulogizing Seward.

records.l: House of Hope congregation, Novel-10146
records.s: House of Hope congregation is an intensely patriotic group, with many members serving at the front; Lincoln’s death brings a household-like loss and widespread weeping at a memorial service.

records.l: Union cause, Novel-10146
records.s: The Union cause is believed by Frederick A. Noble to be just and destined for final triumph, sustaining his support for vigorous war prosecution.

records.l: assassination conspiracy, Novel-10146
records.s: An assassination conspiracy targets the president, vice president, and cabinet; conspirators kill Lincoln, while Secretary of State Seward survives.

records.l: John Wilkes Booth, Novel-10146
records.s: John Wilkes Booth fires the bullet that kills Abraham Lincoln at the Civil War's end; his act is remembered as a horrific crime.

records.l: Lincoln's assassination memorial sermon, Novel-10146
records.s: Frederick A. Noble’s House of Hope church sermon after the assassination recounts Lincoln’s early history and presidential achievements, condemns the killing, and eulogizes William H. Seward.

records.l: voyageur, Novel-10146
records.s: A solitary voyageur journeys north on the Mississippi River bearing peace and goodwill to red men, then returns to St. Paul more than eighty years later, aged, sees transformation and Okon dominance, and departs in anguish.

records.l: Robert A. Smith, Novel-10146
records.s: Robert A. Smith is portrayed allegorically as a young paleface foretold by a dusky maiden to become mighty chief of the great city. The later scene identifies him as St. Paul’s 1902 mayoral candidate, ruling with Okon support and dispensing offices.

records.l: dusky maiden, Novel-10146
records.s: An astrologer, the dusky maiden foretells Robert’s future, gives him an elixir promising lasting life and power over enemies, and counsels caution, withdrawal from danger, and favoring the Okons.

records.l: Okons, Novel-10146
records.s: The Okons, lineal descendants of sea kings from the bogs of Tipperary, aid Robert A. Smith when city requirements outgrow him, then in the later city they and their followers control every office within his gift.

records.l: followers of the Okons, Novel-10146
records.s: control offices [within the gift of Robert A. Smith] The followers of the Okons are to receive and retain offices through Robert’s patronage. In the later city, they possess every office within the paleface’s gift alongside the Okons.

records.l: great city, Novel-10146
records.s: has magnificent building [in its midst] The dusky maiden predicts that a great city will eventually be built on the ground Robert surveys. When the voyageur returns, it has become a populous and technologically advanced metropolis with enormous buildings and rapid transportation.

records.l: magnificent building, Novel-10146
records.s: houses Robert A. Smith [as high and mighty ruler] A magnificent building erected through the generosity of the people stands in the midst of the transformed city. Robert, supported by the Okons, rules from it.

records.l: offices, Novel-10146
records.s: The dusky maiden instructs Robert to arrange the offices within his gift so that the Okons and their followers remain securely established. In the later city, the Okons and their followers occupy every such office.

records.l: prophecy of the dusky maiden, Novel-10146
records.s: is_fulfilled_by Robert A. Smith [as ruler of the great city] The prophecy states that Robert will become the long-reigning chief of a great city, avoid firm political commitments, and depend on the Okons and their followers. The later events are presented as its fulfillment, including Robert’s mayoral campaign in 1902 and the Okons’ control of the offices.

records.l: city government and political patronage, Novel-10146
records.s: is_controlled_by Okons [with followers of the Okons] The city government is portrayed as centered on Robert, who preserves support by avoiding decisions that might alienate opposing parties and by relying on the working majority to resolve controversies. Political patronage keeps the Okons and their followers in all offices within his gift.

records.l: transformation of the city, Novel-10146
records.s: produces great city [over more than four score of years] When the voyageur returns after more than eighty years, the former wilderness has become a vast modern city. Cultivated fields, steamers, steam-powered and electrically powered transportation, gigantic buildings, and a large population replace the earlier frontier setting.

records.l: narrator, Novel-10146
records.s: The narrator, about twelve and living in a small northern Pennsylvania village, secretly attends a spelling match despite being deemed too young, spells “phthisic,” defeats four schools, and gains an established reputation as a champion speller.

records.l: small village, Novel-10146
records.s: A small northern Pennsylvania village, mountainous and sparsely settled, lacks railroad and telegraph; its residents’ prosperity and intellectual opportunities are limited before later improvements.

records.l: school districts, Novel-10146
records.s: School districts generally offered reading, writing, and arithmetic as principal studies for up to six months yearly when able; older children missed summer school to cultivate soil, and four districts joined a grand spelling contest.

records.l: our school, Novel-10146
records.s: participates_in spelling match [as one of four schools in the grand contest] The narrator's school participated in the grand spelling contest against three other schools. It was declared to have furnished the champion speller after the narrator correctly spelled "phthisic."

records.l: schoolmaster from the narrator's district, Novel-10146
records.s: A schoolmaster teaches the narrator’s district school and, at a spelling contest, notices the narrator apart, calls them one of its best spellers, pronounces words, expects “phthisic,” and confirms the correct spelling.

records.l: pupils and scholars, Novel-10146
records.s: are_ranked_by spelling ability [in the order of their reputation as spellers] The pupils and scholars from four schools lined up for the spelling contest according to their reputations as spellers. One after another, the older scholars were eliminated by simple words and then by "phthisic," leaving the narrator as the only contestant standing.

records.l: spelling match, Novel-10146
records.s: A Saturday-night spelling match at a country crossroads brings four schools together, including other districts, and ends with the narrator's school established as winner.

records.l: phthisic, Novel-10146
records.s: Phthisic is a difficult word absent from the spelling book, used to eliminate contestants; the narrator, familiar with it, correctly spells it to finish the match.

records.l: spelling championship, Novel-10146
records.s: is_won_by our school [among four districts] The spelling championship among the four districts went to the narrator's school because the narrator outlasted the other contestants. The narrator was thereafter recognized as the champion speller and was no longer placed last in the line.

records.l: Frank Moore, Novel-10146
records.s: Frank Moore, born in Tioga county, Pa., came to St. Paul and began work for the Minnesotian on April 17, 1858, at fifteen, doing errands, deliveries, and other printer’s-devil duties. He joined the Pioneer Press when it absorbed the Minnesotian in 1861, except for Civil war volunteer service, and continued after the 1874 merger. By sixty-five, he had led the composing room for about forty years and was noted for loyalty, devotion, and efficiency.

records.l: fiftieth anniversary of Frank Moore's connection with the paper, Novel-10146
records.s: is_celebrated_by informal dinner honoring Frank Moore [at Magee's] Frank Moore’s fiftieth anniversary of connection with the Pioneer Press was celebrated on April 17, 1908, with an informal dinner at Magee’s attended by a dozen old employees of the paper.

records.l: composing room, Novel-10146
records.s: is_led_by Frank Moore [for about forty years] Frank Moore served as superintendent of the Pioneer Press composing room for about forty years. He continued to fill the position efficiently at age sixty-five, as the newspaper grew from its early beginnings into a large modern operation.

records.l: Travels in Morocco
records.s: This document is a descriptive and travel account of Morocco, its neighboring Tunisian Sahara, and the Jereed, combining social observation, political history, geography, commerce, and personal narrative. It begins with Morocco’s Jewish communities, especially at Mogador and in the Atlas, describing changing treatment, customs, beliefs, marriage, and vulnerability, including Mogador’s later devastation. It then traces the Maroquine dynasties to the ruling Shereefs, whose descent from Ali and Fatima underpins their religious and political authority. Muley Suleiman and Muley Abd Errahman are central figures, alongside discussions of slavery, European relations, and British influence. The middle chapters survey Morocco as an empire of uncertain bounds and uneven imperial control. They describe its peoples, Berbers, Arabs, Moors, Jews, and Blacks, its Atlas Mountains, climate, products, mines, trade, horses, tribal regions, ports, coastal towns, imperial cities, oases, and caravan routes. Fez, Mequinez, Morocco, and Tafilett receive particular attention, while the text repeatedly emphasizes local tribal independence, uncertain population figures, neglected resources, and perceived urban decline. The Figheegh oasis cluster illustrates both productive irrigation and conflict over water. The narrative then shifts to events at Mogador, where disputes involving Jewish youths and Moors occur and the Governor states that the Sultan will resist anti-slavery appeals unless compelled by superior force. It moves to Tunisian territory, explaining the date-palm economy of El-Jereed before following Captain Balfour, Richard Reade, and Sidi Mohammed, Bey of the Camp, on an expedition toward Kairwan, Ghafsa, Toser, and Nefta. Their journey records the Bey’s camp and administration, justice and bastinado, saints, tribute collection, hunting, ruins, springs, oasis agriculture, date harvesting, waterworks, and harsh weather. Sheikh Tahid’s imprisonment, sale of his gardens, and release illustrate the Bey’s fiscal power. The travelers finally return to Tunis, and the narrator leaves Mogador on the Renshaw schooner, reaching England after a month of gales. An appendix recounts the French bombardment and capture of Mogador in August 1844, the flight of authorities and residents, the sacking and burning by wild tribes, the escape of European residents, and severe losses suffered by Jews and other inhabitants. Notes further distinguish Shereefs from Marabouts and summarize Barbary’s peoples, places, geography, and traditions.

records.l: Morocco, Travels in Morocco
records.s: Morocco is an independent Mussulman kingdom in North Africa, part of Barbary and ruled by the Shereefian dynasty, whose princes claim descent through Ali and Fatima. Also called El-Gharb, Mogrel-el-Aksa, and sometimes the Country of the Sultan Muley Abd Errahman, it is bounded by the Mediterranean and Straits of Gibraltar in the north, the Atlantic in the west, southern deserts and the Sahara in the south, and Algeria, the Atlas, and Tafilett in the east. Its history is presented through Saracen-founded monarchies, civil war after Yezeed’s death, later rule by Muley Suleiman and Muley Abd Errahman, and relations with European powers involving diplomacy, trade, piracy, slavery, and treaties. The country is a large central ridge, crossed northeast to southwest by the Atlas Mountains, with slopes toward the Atlantic and rivers toward the Sahara. Its climate and soil resemble Spain and Portugal: northern provinces are more like Spain, while southern ones have less rain and more desert heat. Although it has extremes of heat and cold and much desolate, uncultivated land, it is described as among Africa’s healthiest countries. Large rivers are numerous but not navigable far inland; northern rivers are short and full, and southern rivers are longer and often nearly dry. The coast has few, poorly protected ports. Agriculture centers on wheat and barley, with irrigated vegetables, fruits, forests of Argan and oak, cork, cedar, date-palm, and palmetto. Resources include silver, copper, sulphur, salt, amethyst, and materials used for fine leathers. Morocco is divided into Fez, central Morocco, Tafilett, and Sous, as well as natural regions and central districts.
