records.l: tribute of the Jereed, Travels in Morocco
records.s: The tribute is a yearly levy collected by a Sheikh, who gathers dates from the people and pays the Bey a fixed sum on arrival. At Toser it is assessed at two bunches for each date-tree; those unable to provide it face imprisonment and punishment. It includes 500 camel-loads of dates from Toser, Nefta, and surrounding districts, plus money and woollen goods, totaling 529 loads and an estimated £9,110, excluding smaller animal presents.

records.l: loted, Travels in Morocco
records.s: The loted is a deer-like animal about the size of a fallow deer, with a deer-like head whose eye sits farther up. The female lacks a goat-like beard and has long hair from head to chest and over the fore-legs. Sheikh Ali brought in a female and young one he had shot.

records.l: Sahara mirage, Travels in Morocco
records.s: Sahara mirage is the repeated appearance of water on salt-covered or sandy surfaces, causing travelers to see shores, bays, and islands before recognizing a salt plain with sand heaps, not a lake.

records.l: Ghabs, Travels in Morocco
records.s: Ghabs is a place with better-built towns, a water-filled river, fertile soil, and dates inferior to those of the Jereed; Santa Maria arrives safely after a lonely journey.

records.l: Sultan Kaed, Travels in Morocco
records.s: Sultan Kaed, a Hammama chief, became one of its greatest leaders, distinguished himself in fighting against the French before Constantina, and died at an extremely old age.

records.l: sale of Sheikh Tahib's gardens, Travels in Morocco
records.s: Sheikh Tahib's gardens were sold for 15,000 piastres; his wife added 1,000 piastres, and Sheikh Tahib was set at liberty.

records.l: date harvest, Travels in Morocco
records.s: The date harvest comes in considerable quantity but not great abundance, including esteemed Degalah; superior ripeness is attributed to only one day of rain in the Jereed during the past year.

records.l: Moorish feastdays, Travels in Morocco
records.s: include lascivious actions [performed by men and women as indispensable entertainment] On Moorish feastdays, masked men performed lascivious and indecent actions, sometimes dressing as women and dancing indecently. Such actions were described as an indispensable part of the entertainment.

records.l: death of Sultan Kaed, Travels in Morocco
records.s: is_a death Sultan Kaed, one of the greatest chiefs of the Hammama, died. He was extremely old, and the text remarks that people live to a good old age in the burning climate.

records.l: Moorish authorities, Travels in Morocco
records.s: Moorish authorities at Rabat held high duties and commerce monopolies, detained European residents during danger, then fled or failed to prevent the city's destruction.

records.l: Europeans of Mogador, Travels in Morocco
records.s: are_exposed_to Mogador sack and destruction [during the bombardment and sack] The British Consul, his wife, Mr. and Mrs. Robertson, and other Europeans were detained in Mogador during the bombardment. Several escaped through the violence of the sack, aided by Mr. Lucas and others, while some residents were left behind.

records.l: railways, Travels in Morocco
records.s: Railways are proposed for Tunis, alongside water ducts, to distribute water and transport it from Zazwan to the Jereed. The text notes French discussion of an Algiers–Blidah line and argues developed Tunisian resources could make railways profitable.

records.l: water supply, Travels in Morocco
records.s: originates_at Zazwan [the best and most delicious water in the Regency] The party found bad, salty water at Sheesheeah, brought from some distance. Ancient aqueducts and water-regulating structures were seen at Byrlafee and Gilma, and the text proposes using railway lines and ducts to carry good water from Zazwan to the dry deserts of the Jereed.

records.l: return march to Tunis, Travels in Morocco
records.s: has_destination Tunis The return march involved camps at Sheesheeah, Ghortabah, Ghafsa, Byrlafee, Sidi-Ben-Habeeba, Sidi-Mahammedeah, and Momakeeah before the party reached Tunis. The march was marked by abrupt changes from intense heat to freezing cold, difficult clay roads, strong winds, locusts, and the deaths or disappearance of many people and animals.

records.l: deaths from extreme weather, Travels in Morocco
records.s: On the march back to Tunis near Ghortabah, excessive heat killed two prisoners and one Turk. A sudden temperature fall then killed ten men, followed by eight burials, three missing men, and many dead camels and horses.

records.l: sea voyage from Mogador, Travels in Morocco
records.s: lasts one month [at sea and out of view of shore] After departing Mogador, the vessel soon lost sight of land and spent the next month at sea. The narrator remained in bed for twenty-five days, living on bread, water, and a little biscuit, while a horse and a young vulture died during the voyage; an aoudad survived and was later lodged in Regent’s Park.

records.l: gales at sea, Travels in Morocco
records.s: come_from north and north-east [successive gales of foul wind] The voyage encountered successive gales of foul wind from the north and northeast, with huge rising waves and foam. The schooner’s bows were repeatedly under water, and Captain Taylor sometimes rushed on deck to swear at the gale and sea.

records.l: Renshaw schooner, Travels in Morocco
records.s: The Renshaw schooner is a beautiful, fine-sailing, flat-bottomed shallow-draft vessel made for Barbary ports. After the narrator leaves the Governor at Mogador, it carries the narrator, a horse, young vulture, and an aoudad for Mr. Willshire and the Zoological Society through severe Atlantic weather.

records.l: French bombarding squadron, Travels in Morocco
records.s: French bombarding squadron comprising Gemappes, Suffren, Triton, Belle Poule, Asmodee, Pluton, and brigs; it silenced Mogador's batteries before French forces landed on the isle.

records.l: Warspite, Travels in Morocco
records.s: is_a English frigate The English frigate Warspite reached Mogador on 13 August. Its captain strongly remonstrated with the Moorish authorities but could not obtain permission for the British Consul, his wife, or other Europeans to leave.

records.l: wife of the British Consul, Travels in Morocco
records.s: is_detained_in Mogador [during the bombardment] The wife of the British Consul was refused permission to leave because Sidi Abdallah Deleero claimed that husband and wife were one. During the escape, she spoke Arabic to a marauding band and persuaded them not to kill her or her companions.

records.l: Mr. Robertson, Travels in Morocco
records.s: is_detained_in Mogador [during the bombardment] Mr. Robertson escaped with his wife and four children during the sack of Mogador. He narrowly avoided a sabre blow and reached the water-port after one of his daughters was threatened with a dagger for money.

records.l: Mrs. Robertson, Travels in Morocco
records.s: is_detained_in Mogador [during the bombardment] Mrs. Robertson escaped with her infant and another child but became separated from Mr. Robertson in the crowd. She later rejoined him at the water-port in a fainting condition.

records.l: Mr. Lucas, Travels in Morocco
records.s: Mr. Lucas, rescuer of detained Europeans, builds a raft, reaches the French brig Canard for help, returns by boat, and arranges fugitives’ transfer to the Warspite.

records.l: Moorish garrison, Travels in Morocco
records.s: defends isle of Mogador The Moorish garrison defended Mogador and the isle but was overcome by the French. About five hundred Moors were reported killed on the isle.

records.l: wild tribes, Travels in Morocco
records.s: Wild tribes entered Mogador after authorities fled, sacking and burning it while attacking inhabitants, especially Jews and Europeans, with murder, assault, robbery, and violence.

records.l: Jews of Mogador, Travels in Morocco
records.s: The Jews of Mogador, especially those in the Jewish quarter, were exposed to assault, robbery, stripping, and murder during the sack. Poor Jews were maltreated, and many were left to accompany the natives in misery.

records.l: isle of Mogador, Travels in Morocco
records.s: has_parts Mogador forts and batteries Nine hundred French troops landed on the isle of Mogador on 16 August. After a rough encounter with the garrison, they captured the isle and its forts.

records.l: Mogador forts and batteries, Travels in Morocco
records.s: The Mogador forts and batteries were subjected to the French squadron's fire and were eventually silenced. The Moorish defenders abandoned them after the death of their best gunner.

records.l: Mogador water-port, Travels in Morocco
records.s: The Mogador water-port served as the intended place of escape for the Consul's party and the Robertson family. Mr. Lucas reached it by boat after contacting the French fleet, and the fugitives were subsequently rescued from the area.

records.l: escape of the detained Europeans, Travels in Morocco
records.s: is_a escape [from the sack of Mogador] The detained Europeans escaped during the night through streets filled with fighting and plunder. The British Consul's party and the Robertson family endured attacks, while Mr. Lucas secured rescue by rafting to the French fleet.

records.l: commerce with Morocco, Travels in Morocco
records.s: has_part Tangier Commerce with Morocco included British and foreign imports of textiles, metals, dyes, foodstuffs, and manufactured goods in exchange for hides, wool, wax, almonds, fruit, grain, oil, and other produce. The unit gives commercial details for Tangier, Mogador, Rabat, and Mazagan and repeatedly attributes limited trade to high duties, monopolies, and restrictive fiscal laws.

records.l: Mogador commerce, Travels in Morocco
records.s: has_part Mogador exports Mogador exported valuable Moroccan products and imported mainly Manchester cotton goods and other manufactured articles for local and inland consumption. Its trade increased because of strong demand for olive oil, and the text states that more liberal government would greatly expand commerce.

records.l: Mogador exports, Travels in Morocco
records.s: Mogador's exports included olive oil, almonds, gums, wool, seeds, skins, ostrich feathers, and occasional maize, valued in 1855 for British and foreign ports.

records.l: Mogador imports, Travels in Morocco
records.s: Mogador imports comprised British and foreign goods, including Manchester cottons, foodstuffs, metals, textiles, and mirrors; in 1855 British imports totaled L136,496 7s. 6d., with goods consumed inland to Timbuctoo.

records.l: human sacrifice, Travels in Morocco
records.s: is_rejected_by Moors [throughout Barbary] The text rejects the report that a beautiful young girl was sacrificed before the Sultan of Morocco, calling it an unmitigated libel. It states that human sacrifice is repudiated by every class in Barbary and is unknown to the Moors.

records.l: Atlantic System, Travels in Morocco
records.s: is_a mountain system [covering the heights of the Maghreb and elevations of the Sahara] The Atlantic System is the name Monsieur Balbi gives to the extensive mountain system of the Maghreb and the elevations scattered through the Sahara. Its principal ridge is said to extend from near Cape Noun on the Atlantic to east of the Great Syrte in Tripoli, with its greatest heights in Morocco.

records.l: Musical Instruments
records.s: Al-Farabi's court performance produced emotional effects laughter, sadness, and rage (through changes of musical mode)
records.q: Scarcer had he commenced his performance in a certain musical mode when he set all his audience laughing aloud, notwithstanding the efforts of the courtiers to suppress so unbecoming an exhibition of mirth in the royal presence. In truth, even the caliph himself was compelled to burst out into a fit of laughter. Presently the performer changed to another mode, and the effect was that immediately all his hearers began to sigh, and soon tears of sadness replaced the previous tears of mirth. Again he played in another mode, which excited his audience to such a rage that they would have fought each other if he, seeing the danger, had not directly gone over to an appeasing mode. records.l: Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, I.
records.s: The narrator examines the limits of self-knowledge, recognizing that other people may perceive weaknesses in him that he cannot see. He reflects on his loneliness, desire for approbation and love, physical awkwardness, failed public influence, and tendency to seek consolations for wounded vanity. He concludes that self-partiality and egoism distort moral judgment, while attention to the world and sympathy with other people can correct self-occupation. Although he remains imperfect and dependent on the common lot, he has developed a stronger habit of listening to and taking interest in the experiences of others.

records.l: the narrator, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, I.
records.s: The narrator studies his own character while acknowledging that he is liable to be absurd or incompetent without knowing it. He describes himself as a bachelor who longs for approbation, sympathy, and love, but he increasingly turns his attention from his own importance toward the experiences of other people.

records.l: self-knowledge and self-ignorance, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, I.
records.s: The narrator believes he knows himself better than casual acquaintances do, yet recognizes that other people may know aspects of his powers and appearance that remain hidden from him. He learns through observing others that he is also capable of unconscious self-delusion and self-betrayal.

records.l: self-partiality and egoism, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, I.
records.s: The narrator discovers that both self-satisfaction and self-discontent can distort judgment. He rejects consolations that turn personal disappointment into spiritual superiority and tries to correct the egoism that makes his own benefit seem central to the world's justice.

records.l: the human race, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, I.
records.s: Human beings are liable to laugh, shriek, or curl the lip at folly in others while remaining unaware that the same folly resembles themselves. They share a common susceptibility to absurdity, self-delusion, and incompetence.

records.l: acquaintances, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, I.
records.s: Other people can perceive the narrator's weaknesses and physical awkwardness more readily than he can, and their reactions sometimes discourage his attempts to speak or be agreeable. They also confide their triumphs, grievances, theories, and private experiences to him, treating him as a sympathetic listener.

records.l: Delectable Mountain, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, I.
records.s: The narrator imagines Delectable Mountain as a standpoint from which he might see things with proportions less determined by self-partiality. It represents the impartial perspective he strives to reach.

records.l: the world, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, I.
records.s: The narrator regards the world as a mighty volume containing the struggling action of a myriad lives, each life being as dear to itself as his is to him. Attending to the world's varied matter can free him from narrow self-occupation.

records.l: autobiography, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, I.
records.s: The narrator holds that autobiography must be incomplete because of both necessary reticence and self-ignorance. He says that self-betrayal can partly compensate for what an autobiographer deliberately or unknowingly leaves out.

records.l: sympathy and interest in others, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, I.
records.s: The narrator tries to widen his personal sensitiveness into a beneficent sympathy by becoming interested in the experiences and fortunes of others. This habit grows stronger as he restrains his desire to redirect their confidences toward himself.

records.l: Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, My conversational reticences about myself turn into garrulousness on paper--as t
records.s: The speaker says that conversational reticence about personal matters becomes garrulousness through writing. The act of writing creates an illusion of a distant, approving audience, while a distinct critical auditor would inhibit the speaker. The speaker leaves judgment of the manuscripts to others but refuses to solicit an opinion from the friend during life, fearing a verdict that they are flat rather than subtle. The speaker connects this self-awareness to a loving laughter at the weaknesses of acquaintances, measured against an ideal self or God within.

records.l: the narrator, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, My conversational reticences about myself turn into garrulousness on paper--as t
records.s: The speaker is reticent about personal matters in conversation but becomes garrulous on paper. The speaker enjoys imagining approval, fears candid criticism, and acknowledges fellowship with acquaintances in their weaknesses.

records.l: writing and authorship, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, My conversational reticences about myself turn into garrulousness on paper--as t
records.s: The act of writing brings the speaker a vague and delightful illusion of an audience. It allows the speaker to write freely, including about personal matters, despite past experience.

records.l: the audience, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, My conversational reticences about myself turn into garrulousness on paper--as t
records.s: The imagined audience is hazy, distant, and multitudinous, making an approving chorus to the speaker's sentences and paragraphs. A distinct audience member would be critical and would inhibit the speaker.

records.l: the illusion of an audience, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, My conversational reticences about myself turn into garrulousness on paper--as t
records.s: The illusion is of a liberal, far-off, hazy assembly more numerous than the visionary One and nearer to the speaker's idiom than the Cherokees. The speaker keeps this illusion while leaving the manuscripts to judgment outside the imagination.

records.l: the manuscripts, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, My conversational reticences about myself turn into garrulousness on paper--as t
records.s: The speaker leaves the manuscripts to an external judgment but does not ask to hear that judgment during life. The speaker fears they may be judged flat and may be most usefully applied in lighting a domestic fire.

records.l: the narrator's published humorous romance, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, My conversational reticences about myself turn into garrulousness on paper--as t
records.s: The speaker refers to the one published work as having the same fault that may affect the manuscripts: flatness rather than a subtlety that would explain popular neglect.

records.l: the friend, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, My conversational reticences about myself turn into garrulousness on paper--as t
records.s: The speaker will not ask the friend, before the speaker has been buried decently, what the friend really thinks of the speaker's abilities. The friend might become exasperated by reading the manuscripts and could demonstrate that they are flat.

records.l: judgment of the manuscripts, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, My conversational reticences about myself turn into garrulousness on paper--as t
records.s: Judgment of the manuscripts is left outside the speaker's imagination. The speaker wishes the friend to use judgment only to insure against a posthumous mistake, not to deliver a candid verdict during the speaker's life.

records.l: the weaknesses of acquaintances, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, My conversational reticences about myself turn into garrulousness on paper--as t
records.s: The speaker intends to note the weaknesses of acquaintances while acknowledging fellowship with them. Such observations are presented as compatible with a loving laughter rather than merely with superiority.

records.l: acquaintances, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, My conversational reticences about myself turn into garrulousness on paper--as t
records.s: The acquaintances are people whose weaknesses the speaker may note. The speaker says that a sense of superiority may underlie barbarous laughter toward them.

records.l: loving laughter, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, My conversational reticences about myself turn into garrulousness on paper--as t
records.s: Loving laughter recognizes the superiority not of the laugher over others but of the ideal self. It holds up the mirror and the scourge to the speaker's pettiness as well as to the pettiness of neighbours.

records.l: the ideal self, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, My conversational reticences about myself turn into garrulousness on paper--as t
records.s: The ideal self is the only recognized superiority in loving laughter. It holds the mirror and the scourge against human pettiness.

records.l: God, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, My conversational reticences about myself turn into garrulousness on paper--as t
records.s: God is referred to as part of the 'God within,' associated with the ideal self that holds the mirror and the scourge for human pettiness.

records.l: Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, II.
records.s: The narrator argues that people should judge the present age with as much fairness and affection as the past, since every period contains both beauty and ugliness. He explains that his own attachment to the past comes chiefly from memories of his father and childhood, not from a belief that earlier societies were better. The narrator describes his father, a country parson who knew people of every social rank and was loved by his parishioners despite collecting tithes. He also recalls riding with his father through the English countryside and reflects on how the national landscape shaped his early imagination and continuing affection for England.

records.l: the narrator, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, II.
records.s: The narrator rejects the habit of scorning contemporaries while idealising the past, arguing that every age contains both poetic and prosaic elements. He attributes his affection for earlier times chiefly to his father's memories and his own childhood, and concludes that moral proportion requires attachment to what is near and admiration for what he knows best.

records.l: the narrator's father, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, II.
records.s: The narrator's father was a country parson who knew miners, weavers, field-labourers, farmers, aristocrats, and other parishioners through close daily contact. He was a Tory, collected his tithe carefully, composed or reused a limited supply of sermons, and was nevertheless beloved because he had no lasting feud with rich or poor. He taught that a clergyman should feel in himself a bit of every class.

records.l: contemporaries, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, II.
records.s: Contemporaries are often unfairly flouted by people who praise the ancients or an imagined past. The narrator insists that those doing the actual work of the world deserve affection and fairness, even though they have faults.

records.l: retrospective optimists, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, II.
records.s: Retrospective optimists treat distant ages, especially Greece and Italy, as more graceful and poetic than the present. The narrator argues that they overlook the vulgar and sordid elements that existed in those societies as well.

records.l: the present age, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, II.
records.s: The present age is described as containing both ugly modern developments and opportunities for useful work, theoretical insight, poetic innovation, and benevolent influence. The narrator resolves not to grumble at the age into which he was born.

records.l: the past, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, II.
records.s: The past is often imagined as majestic and graceful, but the narrator maintains that its beauty must be considered alongside its ugliness, ignorance, bores, detractors, and social limitations. He values it chiefly through personal memory and inherited experience rather than through an indiscriminate idealisation.

records.l: the narrator's childhood, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, II.
records.s: The narrator's childhood was shaped by his father's stories, his father's popularity among parishioners, and periods of care at different homesteads after his mother's death. He spent years accompanying his father on horseback through the surrounding parishes, where he formed lasting impressions of people and landscapes.

records.l: the narrator's father's time, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, II.
records.s: The narrator's father's time is presented as neither wholly prosaic nor wholly admirable, but as a period whose people and institutions can be understood through personal memory. It gave the narrator knowledge of varied social ranks and an enduring perspective on rural English life.

records.l: England, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, II.
records.s: England appears as a country whose villages, markets, hedgerows, and rural classes shaped the narrator's early understanding of human life. Even after travelling imaginatively or literally among distant landscapes, the narrator retains an affectionate connection to England.

records.l: the parishioners, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, II.
records.s: The parishioners grumbled about their obligations to the narrator's father, especially the tithe, but they still welcomed him and loved him. After the narrator's mother's death, they cared for the nine-year-old narrator at their homesteads.

records.l: the English rural population, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, II.
records.s: The English rural population of the narrator's father's time included miners, weavers, field-labourers, farmers, and people of other ranks whose motives and habits could be learned through daily fellowship. The narrator suggests that this population may have changed enough that his father would find the present rural population difficult to understand.

records.l: the English countryside, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, II.
records.s: The national landscape, especially the midland uplands, hedgerows, grassy roadsides, villages, and markets, provided a deep root of the narrator's national life and language. Its memory continues to give him affectionate joy and has mingled with his conservative prepossessions.

records.l: Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, That part of my father's prime to which he oftenest referred had fallen on the d
records.s: The narrator recalls his father's conservative view of England during the political reaction following the French Revolution and the rise of Napoleon. He contrasts his father's idealized England with the changing England of the present, while describing how railways, canals, and other labor reshape the countryside. The narrator admits that his affection for rural England is partly visionary but still values the ideals formed by childhood. He now identifies himself chiefly with London, though he retains his early attachment to home and familiar landscapes.

records.l: the narrator, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, That part of my father's prime to which he oftenest referred had fallen on the d
records.s: The narrator recalls learning from his father to revere Government and distrust rebels, reformers, and revolutionary doctrine. He describes his lasting affection for England's rural landscapes and childhood associations, while acknowledging that these attachments may be partly shaped by illusion. He now considers his consciousness chiefly metropolitan and identifies himself with the "Nation of London."

records.l: the narrator's father, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, That part of my father's prime to which he oftenest referred had fallen on the d
records.s: The narrator's father regarded revolutionary teachers as a mixture of fools and scoundrels and believed that national welfare depended on a strong Government maintaining order. He admired England's Church and Constitution, praised rulers from Mr Pitt to the Duke of Wellington before Catholic emancipation, and blamed national troubles less on administrators than on subjects who failed to be grateful and mind their own business.

records.l: England, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, That part of my father's prime to which he oftenest referred had fallen on the d
records.s: England is presented as a country that combines great stability with susceptibility to gradual change. The narrator regards it as lovable and historically continuous, yet marked by changing institutions, technology, labor, and political attitudes.

records.l: the Government, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, That part of my father's prime to which he oftenest referred had fallen on the d
records.s: Government was treated by the narrator's father as an object of awe and as the chief force required to maintain order. The narrator learned to place it in opposition to the morally charged idea of a rebel.

records.l: the old England, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, That part of my father's prime to which he oftenest referred had fallen on the d
records.s: The old England of the narrator's memory had saleable or privately presented boroughs, poorly supplied prisons, bloated charities, non-resident clergy, militia-balloting, and widespread ignorance of how later generations would judge it. It also included a living good old king and a rural society that the narrator found more romantically exciting than his own adventures.

records.l: the national life of England, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, That part of my father's prime to which he oftenest referred had fallen on the d
records.s: The national life of England is likened to scenery that avoids great convulsions while showing delicate effects from minor changes. It preserves a strong family likeness even as political, social, and technological developments alter its appearance.

records.l: the English countryside, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, That part of my father's prime to which he oftenest referred had fallen on the d
records.s: The English countryside consists of midland plains, woodlands, pastures, hedge-parted fields, commons, rivers, villages, cottages, barns, churches, and other familiar features. Because these features are readily altered yet retain signs of permanence, they create sympathy with human labor and encourage tender attachment to the past.

records.l: the industrial transformation of the landscape, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, That part of my father's prime to which he oftenest referred had fallen on the d
records.s: Industrial transformation appears in canals, railways, steam, navvies, cuttings, bridges, and changed levels through the hills. These works visibly insert new directions of human labor into the landscape without wholly erasing its familiar expression.

records.l: the narrator's childhood, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, That part of my father's prime to which he oftenest referred had fallen on the d
records.s: The narrator's childhood was a warm formative period in which his affections were "fledged" within a small domestic nest. He imagined crises involving swords and firearms, found his father's England exciting, and developed enduring loves for its rural scenery and inherited traditions.

records.l: London, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, That part of my father's prime to which he oftenest referred had fallen on the d
records.s: London is described as a busy, anxious metropolis, eager in thought and strife and also marked by indigestion or hunger. The narrator's bachelor's hearth is located there, and he says that his consciousness is chiefly metropolitan and that he belongs to the "Nation of London."

records.l: Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, III.
records.s: The unit concerns Merman's attempt to challenge Grampus's epoch-making work through a theory about the connection of symbolic monuments associated with the Magicodumbras and Zuzumotzis. After Merman publishes his book, Grampus writes a devastating review attacking Merman's learning and competence, and the controversy makes Merman notorious across Britain, America, Germany, and France. Julia Merman supports her husband's ideas and tries to protect him from further trouble. The unit presents this public humiliation as an example of the cruelty that can accompany worship of Truth.

records.l: Truth, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, III.
records.s: Truth is presented as a serene and beneficent goddess whose worshippers still commit cruelty in her name through personal sarcasm, ridicule, and controversial attacks.

records.l: Merman, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, III.
records.s: Merman is a versatile conveyancer and periodical writer who studies many moral, physical, linguistic, and historical questions. He eventually concentrates on the comparative history of ancient civilisations and develops a theory challenging Grampus, but his published work is publicly ridiculed and he becomes notorious as a supposedly shallow and incompetent scholar.

records.l: Julia Merman, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, III.
records.s: Julia Merman is Merman's supportive wife, described as a 'nice little woman' with discernment and wisdom. After Merman explains the importance of his new ideas, she avoids contradicting him and chiefly worries about increasing his troubles.

records.l: Grampus, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, III.
records.s: Grampus is the author of an influential work on ancient civilisations and the scholar whom Merman challenges. After learning of Merman's attack, he writes a crushing reply that exposes Merman's alleged ignorance and errors.

records.l: Magicodumbras, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, III.
records.s: The Magicodumbras are symbolic monuments or related historical subjects whose connection across widely scattered races becomes central to Merman's theory. Merman claims that Grampus is wrong about them, while public discussion treats lax views of them as a danger to sound inquiry.

records.l: Zuzumotzis, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, III.
records.s: The Zuzumotzis are associated with the Magicodumbras in Merman's theory about ancient civilisations. Merman believes he has found the correct clue concerning them, but his views become objects of ridicule after Grampus's attack.

records.l: the connection of symbolic monuments, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, III.
records.s: The possible connection of symbolic monuments common to widely scattered races gives Merman his breakthrough idea. He believes this connection will regenerate history, transform views of social origins, and correct Grampus's account.

records.l: the comparative history of the ancient civilisations, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, III.
records.s: Merman has studied the comparative history of the ancient civilisations for many years without allowing it to narrow his attention to other subjects. He later concentrates on it and produces the theory that brings him into conflict with Grampus.

records.l: the dispute between Grampus and Merman, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, III.
records.s: The dispute begins when Merman publishes a book attacking Grampus's account of the Magicodumbras and Zuzumotzis. It attracts attention in America, Germany, England, and France, but public interest focuses mainly on the personal ridicule directed at Merman rather than on the historical issues.

records.l: Grampus's epoch-making work, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, III.
records.s: Grampus's epoch-making work is widely praised as a revelation and is initially known to Merman through his study of ancient civilisations. Merman concludes that Grampus is wrong about the Magicodumbras and Zuzumotzis and writes a book intended to overturn his conclusions.

records.l: Merman's book, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, III.
records.s: Merman's book attacks Grampus's interpretation and presents Merman's theory about the Magicodumbras, Zuzumotzis, and ancient social origins. Grampus eventually reads it and responds with a crushing review, after which Merman's mistakes and alleged lack of scholarly competence become widely discussed.

records.l: the truth-worship controversy, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, III.
records.s: The truth-worship controversy is described as a form of public conflict in which victims suffer bruising, laceration, and lifelong maiming through sarcasm and slanderous ridicule rather than physical torture. Merman's treatment after challenging Grampus is offered as a prominent example.

records.l: the review attack on Merman, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, III.
records.s: The review attack on Merman is written by Grampus and identifies Merman without requiring a signature through its distinctive knowledge and epithets. It portrays Merman as lacking the necessary precision and learning, uses an elaborate comparison to a walrus-like sciolist, and makes him a subject of widespread amusement and notoriety.

records.l: Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Meanwhile, how did he like it?
records.s: Merman devotes months to defending his counter-theory against Grampus, producing a sixty-page rejoinder and gathering learning to support it. Grampus and his followers turn Merman, the Magicodumbras, and the Zuzumotzis into objects of public ridicule, while Merman becomes increasingly isolated and obsessed with answering his critics. His controversy damages his legal and editorial prospects, exhausts his household finances, and leaves Julia struggling to maintain the household. Merman eventually takes a post far below his earlier prospects, and although he later recognizes some of his former errors and sees his central idea accepted, he remains embittered and prematurely worn down.

records.l: Merman, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Meanwhile, how did he like it?
records.s: Merman becomes convinced that his counter-theory is fundamentally right and spends months studying German works and oriental languages to defend it against Grampus. He publishes a sixty-page rejoinder, but public ridicule, financial hardship, and social isolation follow; he eventually takes a post far below his earlier prospects and remains marked by bitterness and premature weariness.

records.l: Julia Merman, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Meanwhile, how did he like it?
records.s: Julia tries to preserve the charm of home and soothe Merman's excitement while managing the household's declining resources. She sells the best jewel among her wedding presents to pay the rent without telling Merman that the sacrifice resulted from his unsuccessful controversy, and she remains affectionate and resigned despite his increasing indifference.

records.l: Grampus, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Meanwhile, how did he like it?
records.s: Grampus's learning and authority make Merman feel that Grampus has used scholarship to conceal sophistical evasions. Grampus does not answer Merman's rejoinder, while his followers attack Merman's theory; Merman later claims that a new work by Grampus shifts ground in a way suggesting that Grampus is appropriating his ideas.

records.l: the dispute between Grampus and Merman, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Meanwhile, how did he like it?
records.s: The controversy begins with Merman's attempt to correct Grampus on matters involving the Magicodumbras and Zuzumotzis. Merman's rejoinder fails to provoke Grampus, but Grampus's followers expand the dispute into books, lectures, journalism, popular literature, and sermons, making Merman a byword for speculative error.

records.l: Merman's counter-theory, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Meanwhile, how did he like it?
records.s: Merman maintains that his counter-theory is fundamentally correct despite collateral mistakes. He argues that minute learning can obstruct clear judgment, especially concerning the Magicodumbras and Zuzumotzis, and that history and varied observation of people provide better preparation; he later sees the main idea behind his theory adopted and respected without acknowledgment of his role.

records.l: Magicodumbras, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Meanwhile, how did he like it?
records.s: The Magicodumbras are a central subject of Merman's disputed theory and of the controversy with Grampus. They become widely repeated as part of Merman's supposed absurdity, are treated by Grampus's followers as subsidiary to Grampus's system, and contribute nothing to Merman's financial support.

records.l: Zuzumotzis, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Meanwhile, how did he like it?
records.s: The Zuzumotzis are paired with the Magicodumbras as central elements in Merman's theory and in the ridicule directed at him. Their names become popularly associated with questionable or absurd ideas, while Merman's continuing fixation on them damages his professional reputation and income.

records.l: the rejoinder, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Meanwhile, how did he like it?
records.s: The rejoinder is a sixty-page work of concentrated argument in which Merman acknowledges his mistakes, restates his theory, and offers alternative interpretations of evidence cited by Grampus. It is eventually printed by a modest medium without requiring Merman to pay for insertion, but it receives no reply from Grampus and instead prompts further ridicule by Grampus's followers.

records.l: Merman's legal and editorial career, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Meanwhile, how did he like it?
records.s: Merman neglects rare clients and editorial opportunities while researching and writing about the controversy. His reputation as a sober thinker, safe writer, and sound lawyer is irretrievably damaged, his contributions become too dull to attract editors, and he is eventually forced into a post far beneath his earlier prospects.

records.l: Merman's household finances, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Meanwhile, how did he like it?
records.s: Merman's controversy produces no income and causes his small reserve capital to be nearly exhausted. Julia reduces household wants and sells a valuable wedding jewel to pay the rent, while Merman's eventual low-level post becomes necessary because the household is conspicuously poor.

records.l: Merman's bitterness and decline, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Meanwhile, how did he like it?
records.s: Merman's certainty in his own correctness grows under resistance, and the scorn of competent critics and ridicule from incompetent ones become a chronic source of resentment. He turns from a flexible, sociable man into a bore, loses friends and opportunities, and develops an aged, weakened mind; although he later speaks less about the controversy and recognizes some former errors, its bitter effects remain irrevocable.

records.l: Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, IV.
records.s: The narrator reflects on Lentulus, a respectable and benevolent man whose reserved manner suggests immense but undisclosed originality. Lentulus disparages celebrated poets and philosophers without possessing detailed knowledge of their work, believing that he could produce better poetry and correct the errors of all previous thinking. The narrator concludes that Lentulus's confidence is conceit: his apparent neutrality conceals expansive ignorance and self-estimation unsupported by achievement. Lentulus's lack of words prevents his ideas from causing much harm, and the narrator ends by treating his silence as a blessing.

records.l: Lentulus, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, IV.
records.s: Lentulus is presented as a well-positioned, polite, sociable, and benevolent man who appears unpretending but privately believes that poets, philosophers, and scientists have largely been mistaken. He claims to compose superior poetry as he goes along and to possess abundant reformative thoughts, though he knows little of particular poets or established systems and never develops his ideas clearly. His silence keeps his addled originalities and vague conclusions from doing much harm.

records.l: the narrator, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, IV.
records.s: The narrator initially interprets Lentulus's reserved judgments as possible evidence of unpublished poetry or a revolutionary philosophy. He investigates Lentulus through private conversation and gradually concludes that Lentulus is not a great poet, critic, or philosopher, but a good-natured man with enormous and unsupported confidence in his own thoughts.

records.l: vanity and arrogance, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, IV.
records.s: Conceit appears in Lentulus's contentedly ignorant confidence in his rambling thoughts and in his complacent estimate of his own intellectual powers. The narrator explains that conceit may remain hidden under silence or apparent neutrality, where it avoids the tests that might expose a person's lack of definiteness.

records.l: society, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, IV.
records.s: Society mistakes Lentulus for an agreeable, unopinionated man who can serve as an admiring listener or vote for others' friends. Lentulus believes that the confused condition of society reveals widespread errors in thinking, marriage, social arrangements, and moral schemes.

records.l: poets, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, IV.
records.s: Lentulus assents to praise of celebrated poets with visible reserve, as though he knows that they are merely versifiers. He knows little of particular poets but believes that poetry should use true ideas and that the world has no notion what poetry will become; the narrator concludes that Lentulus cannot eclipse or fundamentally revise the poets.

records.l: philosophers, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, IV.
records.s: Lentulus treats philosophers as mistaken and suggests that all thinking before his own has been an elaborate error. He names Plato, Robert Owen, and Dr Tuffle as equally wrong, despite lacking a developed knowledge of philosophical systems.

records.l: poetics, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, IV.
records.s: Lentulus implies that existing poetics is inadequate and that he could establish principles for a new kind of poetry. The narrator initially suspects that Lentulus possesses a revolutionary treatise on poetics, but learns that Lentulus has neither written such a work nor clearly formulated its principles.

records.l: philosophic thinking, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, IV.
records.s: Lentulus claims that philosophic thinking has been fundamentally mistaken until the beginning of his own reflections. His proposed insights range loosely over logic, miracles, marriage, electricity, motives, and causes, but remain unwritten or insufficiently organized.

records.l: human error, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, IV.
records.s: Lentulus regards human error as pervasive in poetry, philosophy, science, social institutions, and ordinary reasoning. He treats his unfamiliarity with established doctrines as evidence that he can correct the errors of previous thinkers, though the narrator sees his conclusions as blind denials and disjointed commonplaces.

records.l: heterodoxy, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, IV.
records.s: Lentulus regards heterodoxy as a power in itself and mistakes his lack of acquaintance with established doctrines for creative dissidence. His heterodox opinions remain mostly private because he lacks the words to turn them into a system or gather followers.

records.l: Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, V.
records.s: The unit contrasts ordinary, socially motivated insincerity with Hinze’s deliberate and habitual excessive deference. Hinze treats Felicia’s conventional observations as profound revelations, embarrassing her with reverent attention and elaborate compliments. He similarly venerates Tulpian and repeats the opinions of distinguished people, not for a clear personal advantage but from a formed habit and lack of independent judgments. The narrator concludes that Hinze is not exactly a hypocrite, but an ill-gifted conversationalist whose make-believe reverence lacks any deep motive or genuine admiration.

records.l: Hinze, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, V.
records.s: Hinze is an Alsatian whose family has been settled in England for more than one generation. He is superlatively deferential, habitually praising others’ wisdom, treating ordinary remarks as remarkable revelations, and citing the opinions of distinguished people. He is well off, has no evident ambition or specific gain in view, and lacks enough independent judgment to distinguish his flattering words from his thoughts.

records.l: Felicia, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, V.
records.s: Felicia is described as a clever, sensible, vivacious, and kindly disposed woman who helps her distinguished husband and makes her receptions agreeable. When first speaking with Hinze, she offers conventional observations on subjects including Italian travel, Ariosto, French politics, German music, art, and Shakespeare. Hinze’s reverent attention embarrasses and confuses her, causing her to stumble in her replies and resist being treated as an oracle.

records.l: excessive deference (Hinze's behavior), Impressions of Theophrastus Such, V.
records.s: Hinze’s excessive deference appears in his lowered voice, downcast eyes, careful handling of his hat, worshipful tones, and repeated compliments. He asks grand questions, recapitulates commonplace opinions as profound insights, and eagerly attends to the crotchets of Tulpian while appealing to others’ authority. The behavior is a habitual form of attitudinising rather than a calculated attempt to obtain patronage, and it has no contrasting sneering or backbiting side.

records.l: insincerity (social intercourse), Impressions of Theophrastus Such, V.
records.s: The unit presents a little unpremeditated insincerity as an unavoidable part of social intercourse, since people often speak to avoid offending, lack the exact words for their thoughts, or fill conversational gaps with familiar opinions. It argues that this common frailty should be treated leniently, while deliberate and studied forms of insincerity deserve impatience. Hinze’s behavior is more troubling because his deference is a persistent make-believe without a strong appetite, clear purpose, or genuine admiration to excuse it.

records.l: Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, VI.
records.s: The unit examines bad temper as a habitual disposition that is often excused even when it produces persistently offensive conduct. Touchwood is presented as a fundamentally good and capable man whose quarrelsome, capricious temper makes intimacy difficult and undermines the value of his apologies and kindnesses. The text argues that high character requires dependable principles and that uncontrolled temper can distort judgment, especially in public life and partisanship. It therefore doubts that Touchwood should enter Parliament and instead wishes that he would write the great book of which he is thought capable.

records.l: temper, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, VI.
records.s: Temper is described primarily as the proportion and mode in which qualities are mingled, but in common usage it often means an habitual state or general tendency. Bad temper is frequently treated as separate from character and excused as a mood, although it can produce rude, cruel, inconsistent, and unjust behaviour. A temper of this kind interrupts the formation of healthy mental habits by disturbing the harmony between perception, conviction, and impulse.

records.l: Touchwood, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, VI.
records.s: Touchwood is regarded as a good fellow, a steadfast friend, a defender of the oppressed, and an affectionate-hearted person, but his insolent, quarrelsome, haughty, neglectful, and antagonistic behaviour makes close intimacy insupportable. His bad temper causes him to contradict others, resist expectations, adopt opinions suddenly, and treat people harshly without provocation. He is thought capable of excellent public service or a great book, but the unit doubts whether his temper would allow him to maintain sound judgment and integrity in public life.

records.l: character, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, VI.
records.s: High character is said to require qualities that can be safely calculated on and that have become principles or laws habitually obeyed. Good feelings and good deeds do not compensate for repeated unjust judgments, rude behaviour, cruel words, or unreliable conduct. The unit doubts that a high order of character can coexist with a temper like Touchwood's.

records.l: bad-tempered man, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, VI.
records.s: A bad-tempered man may possess good feelings, perform good deeds, and have a fundamentally good disposition, but his behaviour remains ugly when temper repeatedly causes harm. He cannot make past injuries harmless through later excessive friendliness or promises of future gentleness. If he wants to compensate on a larger scale, he must prove himself a substantial benefit to contemporary and future generations through a beneficent discovery, stimulating work of genius, or powerful process.

records.l: public man, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, VI.
records.s: A public man with an uncontrolled temper is in danger of using facts and questions only to justify an attitude adopted impulsively rather than to gain rectifying knowledge. His honesty may be dragged captive by his temper, forcing him to defend insulting words or maintain consistency with opinions expressed in a contradictory mood. The unit therefore regards public life as especially hazardous for someone like Touchwood.

records.l: Parliament, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, VI.
records.s: The unit rejects the hope that Touchwood should be elected to Parliament and use his abilities to serve his country there. It argues that frequent speaking in Parliament would make it difficult for him to preserve integrity of opinion and avoid discreditable partisanship.

records.l: public life, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, VI.
records.s: Public life would expose Touchwood's capricious temper to consequences more serious than the inconsistencies it currently produces in private life. His words, once spoken in a bitter or contradictory mood, could create a public necessity to justify them through later opinions and acts.

records.l: partisanship, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, VI.
records.s: Partisanship may be determined by temper rather than knowledge when a person suddenly adheres to an opinion and then seeks evidence to justify the attitude he has assumed. In a public career, this temper-driven partisanship could compromise judgment, integrity, and consistency.

records.l: Touchwood's great book, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, VI.
records.s: Touchwood's great book is a comprehensive work that everyone believes he is capable of writing, although his great powers have so far been believed in rather than demonstrated. The text wishes that he would produce it and place his best self permanently on record, providing society with an unvarying service that would make his daily incalculableness easier to bear. It wonders whether his love of disappointing expectations has helped keep the book unwritten.

records.l: apology and amends, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, VI.
records.s: Touchwood's apologies and acts of amends are often excessive, artificial, and experienced as a penance for earlier offences rather than as spontaneous goodwill. Such kindnesses cannot restore the injured person's lost confidence or erase the discomfort caused by his previous behaviour. The utmost response available is to remember his better deeds, bear him no malice, and refuse to treat his amends as compensation.

records.l: Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, VII.
records.s: The unit concerns Spike, a cotton manufacturer and elector whose private interests gradually make him a representative of wider political needs. Although he is not inwardly attached to Progress as an abstraction, his long involvement in spinning and weaving has made him a devotee of it in practice. He supports the Reform Bill and the Repeal of the Corn Laws because expanded political representation and foreign markets benefit trade. His objections to legislation affecting his own trade become public-spirited because the same problems affect his trading neighbours.

records.l: Spike, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, VII.
records.s: Spike is a wealthy cotton manufacturer and elector who votes on the side of Progress, though he is not inwardly attached to that name. He prides himself on being a Liberal, supports the Reform Bill and the Repeal of the Corn Laws, and becomes a political element because his trade-related self-interest is shared by his neighbours. His private economic concerns are thereby transformed into a demand for general public benefit.

records.l: Progress, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, VII.
records.s: Progress is an abstraction with many specific names and forms of activity. Spike serves Progress through spinning and weaving and votes on its side, although he does not consciously identify himself with Progress under that name.

records.l: spinning and weaving, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, VII.
records.s: Spinning and weaving are presented as the chief manufacturing and wholesale form through which Spike has unconsciously served Progress from his early years.

records.l: cotton manufacture, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, VII.
records.s: Cotton manufacture enabled Spike to make his fortune and attain the chief object of his ambition. His understanding of the trade also made him recognize that an enlarged market for his business required the enlargement of his neighbours' markets.

records.l: Reform Bill, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, VII.
records.s: The Reform Bill gave Spike a strong political opinion. He believed that the large trading towns ought to send members, and portraits of the Reform heroes hung in his library.

records.l: Liberalism, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, VII.
records.s: Liberalism is represented through Spike's pride in being a Liberal. His support reflects his views on the Reform Bill and trade rather than a broad or deeply examined set of political principles.

records.l: Repeal of the Corn Laws, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, VII.
records.s: Spike was thoroughly convinced of the Repeal of the Corn Laws. He believed that foreign people from whom corn was taken might then be able to buy cotton goods they had previously gone without.

records.l: Corn Laws, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, VII.
records.s: The Corn Laws are connected with Spike's concern for foreign markets. Their repeal appeared to him capable of expanding the market for cotton goods.

records.l: legislation, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, VII.
records.s: Spike objects to items of legislation when they hamper his own trade. Because the same legislation hampers his neighbours' trade, his demand for change becomes a shared political demand rather than merely a selfish one.

records.l: Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, VIII.
records.s: The unit examines Mordax, an intellectually gifted and generally kind man whose vanity makes him deny error and respond cruelly to contradiction. Acer argues that true fairness and goodwill are shown by defending overlooked claims, while the narrator maintains that good qualities can coexist with serious defects in particular situations. The discussion contrasts intellect with moral nature, emphasizing that both can be uneven and that sympathy for those immediately affected should restrain grand justifications for cruelty. Mordax's arrogance is illustrated alongside Pummel's self-satisfied refusal to admit surprise or ignorance.

records.l: Mordax, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, VIII.
records.s: Mordax is ardent in intellectual work, public-spirited, affectionate, and skilled at expressing ingenious ideas and elevated feeling. He refuses to admit error or welcome ideas that are new to him, and when his ego is threatened by contradiction he can become unscrupulous, cruel, polemically rude, and self-justifying. His kindness toward a sick friend and his generosity in other relations are presented as compatible with this specific brutality, which arises when his arrogant egoism is inflamed.

records.l: Acer, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, VIII.
records.s: Acer questions the value of virtues that must continually be asserted against appearances. He argues that fairness and goodwill are tested by whether a person uses public influence tenderly toward obscure or disadvantaged people whose claims may otherwise be ignored.

records.l: Laniger, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, VIII.
records.s: Laniger is fiercely attacked by Mordax and, lacking a talent for repartee, comes to believe that Mordax is a wolf at heart. Laniger suffers from the attack while his friends fail to form a lively conception of his pain.

records.l: The Watch-Dog of Knowledge, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, VIII.
records.s: The Watch-Dog of Knowledge is the title of this unit, which considers the dangers of guarding inquiry through arrogant correction and cruel exclusion. The unit argues that the defense of truth should be restrained by fairness, kindness, and fellow-feeling toward contemporaries.

records.l: self-respect, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, VIII.
records.s: Mordax's self-respect is described as fiery and as demanding that only monarchs of thought should have an advantage over him. When threatened by correction or contradiction, it contributes to his refusal to admit error and to his cruelty.

records.l: moral tests, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, VIII.
records.s: Acer's moral tests focus on whether a public figure treats poorly placed or overlooked people tenderly and recognizes claims that others will not defend. The narrator replies that such tests may be as delusive as ignorant people's haphazard tests of intellect and learning.

records.l: intellect, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, VIII.
records.s: Intellect is not treated as a uniform, ready-made ability that guarantees competence in every department. A person may excel in one field and be inept in another, because intense application or a special facility in one medium can hinder performance elsewhere.

records.l: moral nature, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, VIII.
records.s: A person's moral nature is not to be judged by its weakest point any more than intellect is. Kindly and generous dispositions may coexist with unfair or cruel actions in situations that peculiarly inflame egoism.

records.l: vanity and arrogance, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, VIII.
records.s: Vanity and arrogance, though compatible with otherwise worthy character, become cruel and self-justifying when unchecked. They are portrayed as fierce inner beasts that must be restrained by wider reason.

records.l: sympathy and interest in others, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, VIII.
records.s: Sympathy and fellow-feeling should provide checks on actions by making people consider those immediately affected rather than relying only on distant, grand motives. The narrator argues that actions beneficial to future ages will usually also show beneficence and grace toward contemporaries.

records.l: truth and justice, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, VIII.
records.s: Truth and justice are invoked by Mordax as reasons for scourging incompetent or presumptuous intruders. The unit warns that such elevated motives can disguise cruelty and insists that fairness and kindness toward the person immediately concerned must be considered first.

records.l: polemical rudeness, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, VIII.
records.s: Mordax's conscience is active in some relationships but does not trouble him over his polemical rudeness and brutality. He can leave the care of a sick friend and immediately write a merciless rejoinder against someone who challenges his intellectual authority.

records.l: humility, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, VIII.
records.s: Humility is presented as an admission of error and a frank welcome of ideas not previously present in one's mind. Pummel lacks this quality, since he cannot acknowledge being newly informed, while self-satisfied people are especially eager to expose conceit in others.

records.l: Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, IX.
records.s: The unit concerns Mixtus, whose youthful religious, philanthropic, democratic, and intellectual commitments have been displaced and complicated by his marriage to Scintilla, increasing wealth, and integration into fashionable London society. Scintilla’s prettiness, liveliness, music, and worldly associations captivated Mixtus, while her indifference to religious and theoretical ideas made his former habits socially impractical. Mixtus has become a wealthy commercial man and lavish host, but he feels personally submerged and uncertain because his present identity conflicts with his earlier ideals. His kindness and intellectual interests remain, yet he alternates between defending money and affirming the superior value of mind, genius, religion, and social benevolence.

records.l: Mixtus, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, IX.
records.s: Mixtus becomes very wealthy through commercial activity, maintains a London mansion, and gains recognition chiefly as a genial and useful rich man. He retains substantial knowledge, kindness, religious memories, and intellectual interests, but his earlier convictions have been displaced by worldly success and he no longer knows how to understand himself as a whole.

records.l: Scintilla, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, IX.
records.s: Scintilla is a pretty, lively, musical woman who associates with wealthy Greek merchant families and artists. She regards religious, social, and philosophical seriousness as ridiculous or dull, yet she is not described as wicked; she wants the advantages of being a rich man’s wife and believes Mixtus’s bachelor habits can be laughed out of him.

records.l: Mr Apollos, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, IX.
records.s: Mr Apollos is an eloquent Congregational preacher who studied in Germany and held liberal, advanced views beyond the ordinary teaching of his sect. Mixtus attended his lectures for young men and once regarded his teaching as part of his religious and intellectual formation.

records.l: London, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, IX.
records.s: London is where Mixtus met Scintilla during a business sojourn and encountered a wealthy, brilliant social world in which money appeared to provide unusual dominance. He later establishes a mansion there and entertains half-aristocratic, professional, and artistic society.

records.l: wealth and money, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, IX.
records.s: Mixtus grows richer than he had imagined and comes to regard money as the chief means of obtaining what is best worth having. He also continues to affirm, when prompted, the supreme value of mind and genius, producing an unresolved alternation between material wealth and nonmaterial ideals.

records.l: commercial success, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, IX.
records.s: Mixtus’s ability in business and growing commercial success help draw him toward Scintilla and the London world of wealth. His commercial position ultimately becomes the main category by which others judge him, despite his knowledge and former aspirations.

records.l: religion, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, IX.
records.s: Mixtus once had strong religious principles and yearnings, attended Mr Apollos’s lectures, and worked among the poor. He has not wholly abandoned religion, but he feels bashful about his former faith and keeps it private because his current position and avowed objects seem incompatible with public acknowledgment.

records.l: Christianity, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, IX.
records.s: Mixtus once viewed the spread of Christianity as a great consequence of commercial intercourse with black, brown, and yellow populations. Later he prioritizes establishing commercial intercourse, allowing even a little war if it proves necessary as a pioneer of Christianity.

records.l: religious and social reform, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, IX.
records.s: As a young man, Mixtus expected to use his future wealth chiefly for religious and reforming purposes and held strongly democratic views concerning aristocratic and landed privilege. He retains benevolence and helps the needy, the clever, and the industrious, but his commercial responsibilities increasingly produce bitterness toward obstructive workers.

records.l: intellectual life and study, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, IX.
records.s: Mixtus once renounced personal ease for study, religious communion, and good works, and he continues to read and collect works on colonisation and the social conditions of foreign countries. He hopes to complete manuscripts and can discuss historical and geographical subjects, although fashionable acquaintances treat his expertise with suspicion.

records.l: social class and status, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, IX.
records.s: Mixtus is not considered well-born, but his wealth gives him access to half-aristocratic, professional, and artistic society. Even among these acquaintances, however, he is chiefly classified as a rich man rather than as an intellectual, religious figure, or authority in art.

records.l: Mixtus's divided identity, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, IX.
records.s: Mixtus’s earlier religious, philanthropic, democratic, and intellectual self remains in conflict with his wealthy commercial identity. In unreserved conversation he moves among what he was, what he is, and what others think he is, without reaching a stable point of view.

records.l: the marriage of Mixtus and Scintilla, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, IX.
records.s: Mixtus marries Scintilla after being captivated by her charm and by the worldly possibilities surrounding her. Their marriage joins his serious former interests to her indifference toward doctrine and theory, and it contributes to his submergence in a society unlike the one he once idealized.

records.l: Mixtus's earlier religious and philanthropic life, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, IX.
records.s: Before his marriage, Mixtus visited and exhorted the poor in the alleys of a great provincial town, attended Mr Apollos’s lectures, and associated with people distinguished by religious, philanthropic, or intellectual enthusiasm. He intended his prospective wealth to serve religious and reforming purposes rather than merely personal ease.

records.l: Mixtus's fashionable society, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, IX.
records.s: Mixtus’s fashionable society consists of half-aristocratic, professional, and artistic people whom he entertains with splendour. They value him as a wealthy, commercially successful, genial acquaintance, but generally disregard his opinions, doubt his artistic judgment, and know little of his earlier religious and intellectual life.

records.l: Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, X.
records.s: The unit argues that indiscriminate burlesque debases the moral currency by turning sacred, heroic, and pathetic subjects into objects of laughter. It distinguishes La Bruyere’s refined use of ridicule from the dull habit of forcing jokes onto every serious topic, warning that this damages education, art, and human sentiments. The unit predicts that Shakspere may increasingly be known through burlesques rather than his original plays and cites Sainte Beuve’s warning that civilisation can rapidly decline during crises. It concludes that a society habituated to mocking everything, like the Tirynthians, may become incapable of seriousness when serious action is required.

records.l: La Bruyere, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, X.
records.s: La Bruyere is quoted as saying that ridicule should be identified where it genuinely exists and drawn out gracefully in a way that pleases and instructs. His formulation is used to distinguish discriminating wit from the indiscriminate burlesquing of serious subjects.

records.l: wit and humour, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, X.
records.s: Wit and humour are described as capable of playing harmlessly or beneficially around egoism, absurdity, and vice. Their proper exercise depends on discrimination, varied sensibilities, sympathetic insight, and a just perception grounded in knowledge.

records.l: burlesque, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, X.
records.s: Burlesque is criticized for appropriating sacred, heroic, and pathetic themes and reducing noble forms to caricature. The unit warns that repeated exposure to such mockery can poison children’s primary associations with great works, people, and solemn events.

records.l: moral currency, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, X.
records.s: Moral currency names the value of inspiring facts and traditions in producing generous motives and elevating social life. It is debased when greedy buffoonery lowers the value of historic beauty, majesty, and pathos, leaving desecrated symbols unable to command ennobling emotions.

records.l: Shakspere, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, X.
records.s: Shakspere is said to be falsely reputed to be known by the English people in the present generation. The unit predicts that the next generation may know him chiefly through burlesques and that his plays may acquire a new life as pantomimes.

records.l: Sainte Beuve, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, X.
records.s: Sainte Beuve is cited as warning that civilisation can decline with extraordinary speed during periods of insurrectionary disturbance. He emphasizes that civilisation and life are learned and invented achievements, while savagery remains close at hand whenever people lose their footing.

records.l: civilisation, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, X.
records.s: Civilisation is presented as a learned and invented achievement rather than something identical with nature or innate in humanity. Its material structures are considered helpless without the spiritual protection provided by sentiments and ideal feelings, and it can lose centuries of results within weeks of crisis.

records.l: human sentiments, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, X.
records.s: Human sentiments are described as delicate elements of civilisation that are easily perishable. They provide the invisible moral force that supports compassion, trust, constancy, shame, and the elevation of social existence.

records.l: historic beauty, majesty, and pathos, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, X.
records.s: Historic beauty, majesty, and pathos are treated as sources of ennobling emotions and generous motives. The unit warns that indiscriminate burlesque can desecrate these qualities and reduce the spiritual nourishment they provide.

records.l: Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XI.
records.s: The unit examines Euphorion’s inconsistent attitude toward intellectual property: he recognizes ancient and well-known sources but treats many recent borrowings as belonging to everybody or nobody. It argues that knowingly presenting another person’s philosophical or scientific ideas as original is morally comparable to more obvious forms of plagiarism, even when it cannot be legally proved. The text also warns that accusations of plagiarism are easily mistaken because ideas may arise independently, memories fail, and people often assume that prominent or fluent individuals must be the originators. Aquila illustrates the conversational appropriation of other people’s information, while the discussion of original authorship emphasizes the misleading influence of reputation and public expectations.

records.l: Euphorion, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XI.
records.s: Euphorion opposes communistic principles regarding material property but accepts them readily regarding ideas. He credits ancient and earlier writers when defending their priority, yet may present recently borrowed ideas as his own by appealing to the universal, inherited, and diffusive nature of thought. His omissions may arise from faulty memory, reluctance to associate good material with an unfashionable source, or a belief that naming the source would weaken the material.

records.l: Aquila, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XI.
records.s: Aquila is an agreeable and amusing conversationalist who habitually appropriates information and formulations offered by other people. Although he has not read many epoch-making modern books, he gathers clever statements and allusions through conversation and gradually improves them without admitting mistakes or corrections. His fluency and appearance lead others to credit him with knowledge, as shown when he turns a correction about the product of nine thirteens into an apparently intentional continuation of his argument.

records.l: intellectual property, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XI.
records.s: The unit treats intellectual property as a form of spiritual or mental production whose ownership is often obscured by the shared inheritance of human thought. It acknowledges that ideas develop through collective preparation and transmission, but rejects using this truth to excuse the non-payment of identifiable intellectual debts. Public recognition tends to favor prominent names, while less fashionable or obscure sources may be used privately without acknowledgment.

records.l: original authorship, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XI.
records.s: Original authorship is presented as difficult to define because contemporary thinkers may arrive independently at similar ideas and because old ideas can reappear without any remembered label. The unit criticizes the assumption that a fluent, reputable person must have originated an unusual view, noting that public judgments about authorship are often based on hollow preconceptions. It also describes how people may sincerely believe that an excellent idea belongs especially to them because it fits their existing sense of their own wisdom.

records.l: plagiarism, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XI.
records.s: Plagiarism is distinguished between obvious frauds, such as copying a poem or falsely claiming an invention, and the quieter appropriation of philosophical or scientific ideas. The latter may have the same moral quality even when it escapes public shame or legal enforcement, but accusations require caution because coincidence, forgotten sources, and mistaken assumptions about what someone must have read can produce false conclusions. The unit maintains that borrowing another person’s idea, forgetting its source, and treating it as one’s own reveals weakness in mental grasp and rectitude.

records.l: acknowledgment of intellectual debts, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XI.
records.s: The unit argues that acknowledgment should extend to intellectual debts that are unlikely to be detected or enforced. It compares such recognition to traditional susceptibility concerning debts of honour and criticizes the failure to name fellow-workers whose ideas have been used.
