At the same time, it cautions that a person’s failure to acknowledge a source may result from ordinary forgetfulness rather than deliberate theft, since what matters intensely to the originator may have little lasting importance to the borrower.

records.l: Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Such guesses remind one of a fabulist's imaginary council of animals assembled t
records.s: An imaginary council of animals debates which creature constructed a honeycomb that Bruin and other epicures had found and tasted. The animals variously suspect birds, the Musk-rat, and finally the Wasp, after the Fox reports finding honey on the Wasp and being stung on the nose. The council accepts the Fox's swollen snout as evidence, despite objections from several animals. A complimentary deputation to the Wasp is approved in hopes of encouraging further honey production.

records.l: imaginary council of animals, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Such guesses remind one of a fabulist's imaginary council of animals assembled t
records.s: The imaginary council debates what sort of creature constructed the honeycomb. It hears competing claims about birds, the Musk-rat, and the Wasp, and ultimately accepts the Fox's report that the Wasp produced the honey.

records.l: Bruin, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Such guesses remind one of a fabulist's imaginary council of animals assembled t
records.s: Bruin and other epicures found and tasted the honeycomb. During the council's discussion, he grumbles that fine words produce no new honey, implying that he wants more honey rather than explanations.

records.l: honeycomb, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Such guesses remind one of a fabulist's imaginary council of animals assembled t
records.s: The honeycomb was found and much tasted by Bruin and other epicures. The council tries to determine which creature constructed it.

records.l: birds, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Such guesses remind one of a fabulist's imaginary council of animals assembled t
records.s: The animals initially assume that the maker of the honeycomb was a bird because they expected a wondrous nest to come from that quarter. Several speakers compliment popular birds as possible makers.

records.l: insects, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Such guesses remind one of a fabulist's imaginary council of animals assembled t
records.s: The animals know little about insects and do not willingly receive them in society. Their unfamiliarity contributes to the council's initial failure to consider an insect as the maker of the honeycomb.

records.l: Nightingale, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Such guesses remind one of a fabulist's imaginary council of animals assembled t
records.s: The Nightingale takes part in the fluttering that follows the suggestions that a popular bird made the honeycomb. The Nightingale does not give a positive denial, perhaps because of confusion about identity.

records.l: Swallow, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Such guesses remind one of a fabulist's imaginary council of animals assembled t
records.s: The Swallow joins the Nightingale in fluttering when birds are proposed as the makers of the honeycomb. The Swallow does not give a positive denial, perhaps because of confusion about identity.

records.l: Owl, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Such guesses remind one of a fabulist's imaginary council of animals assembled t
records.s: The Owl hisses at the suggestion that a bird made the honeycomb. Using his particular knowledge, he argues that the Musk-rat produced the honey, reasoning that the step from musk to honey is small.

records.l: Musk-rat, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Such guesses remind one of a fabulist's imaginary council of animals assembled t
records.s: The Musk-rat becomes obtrusive after hearing the Owl's opinion of his powers and feels that he could have produced the honey if he had thought of it. A Butcher-bird proposes anatomising him to help decide whether he made the honey.

records.l: Butcher-bird, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Such guesses remind one of a fabulist's imaginary council of animals assembled t
records.s: The Butcher-bird proposes an experiment: anatomising the Musk-rat to help determine whether he produced the honey.

records.l: Macaw, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Such guesses remind one of a fabulist's imaginary council of animals assembled t
records.s: The Macaw gives an able discourse on structures and classifies them in a way that includes the honeycomb. His exposition creates a prevalent sense that the honeycomb was probably made by someone who understood it well, though he later becomes loudly incoherent after the Wasp is identified.

records.l: Fox (Reynard), Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Such guesses remind one of a fabulist's imaginary council of animals assembled t
records.s: The Fox enters with a dreadfully swollen snout and reports that the Wasp produced the honey. He says he found the Wasp smeared with undoubted honey after applying his nose to it, and that the Wasp stung him; the swelling is taken as evidence supporting his report.

records.l: Wasp, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Such guesses remind one of a fabulist's imaginary council of animals assembled t
records.s: The Wasp is identified by the Fox as the originator of the honey. After the Fox applies his nose to the Wasp, the Wasp stings him with severity, and the council resolves to send a complimentary deputation to the Wasp.

records.l: honey, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Such guesses remind one of a fabulist's imaginary council of animals assembled t
records.s: The honey was found on the Wasp by the Fox and was present in the honeycomb tasted by Bruin and other epicures. The council hopes that recognition of the Wasp will lead to more honey.

records.l: complimentary deputation to the Wasp, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Such guesses remind one of a fabulist's imaginary council of animals assembled t
records.s: The council resolves to send a complimentary deputation to the Wasp. The measure is intended to encourage the production of honey.

records.l: production of honey, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Such guesses remind one of a fabulist's imaginary council of animals assembled t
records.s: The council's recognition of the Wasp is expected to influence the production of honey. The sweet-toothed majority supports the deputation in the hope that it will result in more honey.

records.l: Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XII.
records.s: The unit concerns Ganymede, a precocious writer whose family, admirers, critics, and colleagues repeatedly treat him as remarkably young. His book A Comparative Estimate of European Nations and his literary organisation establish and reinforce his public reputation for youthful brilliance. Although he grows older, marries, becomes heavier, and takes a government post, Ganymede continues to believe that youthfulness defines him. The narrator observes that this illusion is sustained both by Ganymede's own manner and by others' continued use of the epithet “young.”

records.l: Ganymede, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XII.
records.s: Ganymede was the youngest child in his family and became known as a precocious writer after producing A Comparative Estimate of European Nations before he was well out of his teens. He later founded and presided over a literary organisation, continued producing schemes and writings, married an older woman, and took a government post. As he aged, grew heavier, and became more self-conscious, he still presented himself as a remarkably young man.

records.l: the narrator, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XII.
records.s: The narrator observed Ganymede during his period of rich chestnut locks and later met him again after several years apart. The narrator recognized that Ganymede's appearance had aged and changed, but also saw that his belief in his own youth remained firmly supported by habit and by the reactions of others.

records.l: Ganymede's literary organisation, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XII.
records.s: Ganymede devised and founded an organisation intended to consolidate the literary interests of the four continents, later including Australasia and Polynesia. He presided over its central office, which repeatedly placed him in the role of a boldly scheming administrator whom strangers found remarkably young.

records.l: A Comparative Estimate of European Nations, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XII.
records.s: A Comparative Estimate of European Nations was produced by Ganymede before he was well out of his teens. Although it did not greatly affect the currents of European thought, it established his reputation as a precocious author and encouraged the hope that he might later produce an even more surprising work.

records.l: youthfulness, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XII.
records.s: Youthfulness became the principal explanation offered for both Ganymede's deficiencies and his abilities. Even after he had aged, critics, readers, and public figures continued to describe his writings and conduct as those of a very young man.

records.l: Ganymede's illusion of youth, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XII.
records.s: Ganymede's illusion of youth developed through his family's treatment of him, repeated astonishment from strangers, critical commentary, and his own identification with the role of the young genius. The illusion survives his aging, changed physique, marriage, and government employment, and is reinforced by his manners, clothing, assumptions about others' impressions, and the continued descriptions of him as young.

records.l: Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XIII.
records.s: The unit examines how human beings notice folly and absurdity in others but often fail to recognize the same traits in themselves, producing false testimonials about their own conduct. It presents comparison as the chief means by which a person uses observations of others to investigate human nature and self-knowledge. Judgment of others by oneself can either provide a method of understanding mankind or reduce everyone to the judge’s own limitations, while judgment of oneself by others can weaken indignation against wrongdoing. The unit concludes that people often preserve an outdated tradition about their own character and trust their verbal self-description more than plainly contradictory behavior.

records.l: false testimonials, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XIII.
records.s: False testimonials arise when human beings believe their verbal accounts of their habitual conduct despite facts that contradict them. They may continue to describe themselves according to an old rule or principle long after their actual practice has departed from it.

records.l: self-knowledge and self-ignorance, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XIII.
records.s: Self-knowledge is pursued by examining one’s own absurdities and using observations of other people as clues to inward tendencies. It is difficult because people may be unaware of their deliberate actions or may preserve an outdated tradition about their own character.

records.l: the human race, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XIII.
records.s: Human beings differ greatly in the strength and form that their feelings and tendencies take, but they show enough correspondence for one person’s behavior to illuminate human nature in another. They commonly condemn in others the very tricks or blemishes they practice themselves.

records.l: comparison, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XIII.
records.s: Comparison is presented as the essential guide to knowledge: by likeness to what is already known, it helps a person investigate unfamiliar forms of human nature and detect corresponding tendencies in oneself. It can reveal similarities despite wide differences in temperament and circumstance.

records.l: judgment of others by oneself, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XIII.
records.s: Judgment of others by oneself is, in its innocent sense, the briefest expression of the only method of knowing mankind. It can also become a vulgar mistake that reduces everyone to the judge’s own low standard or an amiable illusion that interprets a lower nature too generously.

records.l: judgment of oneself by others, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XIII.
records.s: Judgment of oneself by others, understood as judging oneself through what one observes in others, can weaken indignation and scorn when practiced with too much impartiality and discernment. By making a person too conscious of kinship with frailty and vice, it may diminish the active heroism needed to oppose wrongdoing.

records.l: Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, opening
records.s: The unit contrasts self-deception and inaccurate testimony with genuine imagination grounded in precise perception. Bovis falsely believes himself moderate in his sugar consumption, while Callista confuses invention with observation and misremembers ordinary facts. It argues that the sane mind in the sane body distinguishes intentions from actions, past feelings from present ones, and imagined events from witnessed facts. Dante is presented as an example of a powerful imaginative seer who can experience an intense vision yet recognize the difference between that vision and external reality.

records.l: Callista, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, opening
records.s: Callista claims to be imaginative and says she would transform an old heap of stones into a castellated ruin when describing it. She is shown to have lax perceptions and memories, confusing details and exaggerating events, so that her supposed imagination is really inaccurate observation and misrepresentation.

records.l: Dante, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, opening
records.s: Dante is presented as both precise in reproducing actual objects and expansive in imaginative combination. He distinguishes the truths of an entranced vision from the external facts recognized when his mind returns to ordinary experience.

records.l: the sane mind in the sane body, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, opening
records.s: The sane mind in the sane body distinguishes what has been professed from what has been done, what has been aimed at from what has been achieved, and what has been imagined or felt from what has actually been witnessed or experienced.

records.l: self-deception, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, opening
records.s: Self-deception appears when a person preserves a traditional image of himself despite contrary evidence, as Bovis believes he is moderate while consuming twenty-six lumps of sugar a day. Such a person may repeat false assertions about his own conduct with enough inherited conviction to partly believe them.

records.l: lying, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, opening
records.s: Lying can involve repeated false assertions about one's own actions until the speaker believes them. The unit suggests that even a first false utterance may contain a trace of creed-reciting belief in a preferred traditional self.

records.l: human imagination, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, opening
records.s: Powerful imagination is described as intense inward representation and creative construction fed by close attention to real experience. It is not habitual confusion of fact with fancy, but an ideal and associative power that remains compatible with clear recognition of ordinary reality.

records.l: discriminating perception, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, opening
records.s: Discriminating perception provides the factual material on which strong imagination depends. It enables a person to notice and accurately reproduce precise details, unlike the lax perception that makes Callista confuse moss with lichen, materials, and particular statements.

records.l: sanity, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, opening
records.s: Sanity consists partly in distinguishing external facts from imaginative or visionary experience. The strongest seer can sustain creative energy while retaining a sane expectation of what is true outside the individual mind.

records.l: the old heap of stones, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, opening
records.s: The old heap of stones is an ordinary object that Callista says she would transform in her account into an interesting castellated ruin. It illustrates the difference between creative invention and the accurate perception of what was actually seen.

records.l: Dante's triple vision, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, opening
records.s: Dante's triple vision absorbs him so completely that he forgets his surroundings. When his soul returns to external things, he recognizes both the external facts and the non-false errors or revelations of the vision as distinct kinds of experience.

records.l: Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XIV.
records.s: The unit criticizes the too ready writer, comparing him to the excessive talker who monopolizes conversation and prevents others from contributing. It contrasts Adrastus's celebrated, wide-ranging productivity with Theron's neglected specialized research, and presents Pepin as a general writer whose early self-confidence hardened into habitual, overconfident, poorly grounded judgment. The narrator argues that incessant writing for publication can damage perception and veracity, making writers invested in their own errors and inclined to seem authoritative on every subject. Although Pepin's private character is more amiable and modest than his writing suggests, the public conscience is blamed for treating authorship as a vocation requiring little moral or intellectual scruple.

records.l: the too ready writer, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XIV.
records.s: The too ready writer monopolizes literary space as the excessive talker monopolizes conversation, presenting opinions on innumerable subjects whether or not he has adequate knowledge. His restless production can obstruct better work, spoil other people's knowledge in handling it, and give an impression of authority through style rather than truth.

records.l: the excessive talker, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XIV.
records.s: The excessive talker prevents the rest of the company from taking their turn and assumes that others would rather hear his opinions or experiences. Even when his talk is varied and brilliant, he is suspected of impoverishing conversation by excluding other minds and is regarded as a nuisance.

records.l: the narrator, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XIV.
records.s: The narrator criticizes excessive literary production and recalls having once felt capable of original insight on nearly every subject before knowledge or study. He compares his youthful self to Pepin, but says that discouragement spared him from developing the same coxcombry. He remains friendly with Pepin while judging Pepin's published writing severely.

records.l: Adrastus, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XIV.
records.s: Adrastus publishes essays on subjects ranging from ancient inscriptions and prehistoric philosophy to agricultural pests and disease. His breadth and enormous productivity are generally praised, while his established name helps him obtain space that is denied to more specialized researchers such as Theron.

records.l: Pepin, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XIV.
records.s: Pepin is an industrious general writer who gained an early hearing and made writing for publication a necessity before acquiring sufficient knowledge or settled belief. His youthful sense of unlimited ability has hardened into peremptory style, official arrogance, and a habit of seeming to know; he increasingly explains other people's writing through things he does not know about them. The narrator considers him privately amiable and worthier than his professional writing, though his work can insult or misrepresent better people.

records.l: the public conscience, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XIV.
records.s: The public conscience is lax and ill informed about the serious moral and intellectual responsibilities of authorship. By permitting writers to undertake and continue poorly warranted work, it sanctions the absence of scruple that produces misleading, conceited, and injurious writing.

records.l: Pepin's unwritten Roman romance, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XIV.
records.s: Pepin's unwritten Roman romance was planned as a grand, panoramic, philosophical depiction of the Roman Empire at the height of its visible grandeur and approaching spiritual decadence. It would treat statesmen, philosophers, poets, warriors, religion, gladiatorial spectacles, and Christianity in elevated language, while avoiding ordinary low-life speech. Because Pepin never wrote it, he has become more sarcastic about romances that were actually produced.

records.l: conversation, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XIV.
records.s: Conversation is presented as a shared activity in which each participant should have an opportunity to contribute. A single speaker's continuous manner becomes monotonous and narrow, and his domination prevents others with relevant knowledge from being heard.

records.l: writing and authorship, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XIV.
records.s: Writing and authorship impose internal consequences when they are pursued incessantly for printing rather than for knowledge or veracity. They can encourage writers to express judgments before becoming convinced, invest vanity or income in mistakes, lose accurate mental vision, and cultivate pleasure in others appearing wrong. Authorship is described as a vocation that ought to be among the best warranted, not a license for indiscriminate commentary.

records.l: publicity and publication, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XIV.
records.s: Publicity and publication can encourage young writers by giving them an early hearing or place in print, but they can also turn premature self-reliance into a fixed professional habit. Easy publication is said not to encourage the young in their readiness to mirror the universe, yet early success may leave a writer dependent on producing printed judgments before he has adequate knowledge or belief.

records.l: veracity, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XIV.
records.s: Veracity requires a healthy and carefully guarded power of seeing and reporting truly, which cannot simply be commanded at will. Continual writing to satisfy demands other than truth can blunt perception and produce untruth, leaving the writer content with ignorance and committed to defending his own errors.

records.l: Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XV.
records.s: The unit examines the moral ailments associated with small authorship, especially the disease of magnified self-importance. It focuses on Vorticella, a woman in Pumpiter whose single book, "The Channel Islands, with Notes and an Appendix," becomes the center of her social identity. Vorticella preserves and displays an album of highly flattering critical opinions, insists on the importance and correctness of her work, and tries to make visitors read both the reviews and the book. The discussion broadens to male and female vanity, arguing that vanity is common to both sexes but differs in expression and manner.

records.l: small authorship, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XV.
records.s: Small authorship is presented as capable of producing a chronic moral ailment in which self-importance becomes magnified and disfiguring. Its sufferers may turn an otherwise ordinary book or pamphlet into the central feature of their social identity and continually impose it on acquaintances.

records.l: authors, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XV.
records.s: Authors are described as a miscellaneous class whose physical and moral diseases might include the whole procession of human disorders. The unit concentrates particularly on the chronic ailments associated with authors who produce little but attach excessive importance to their work.

records.l: Vorticella, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XV.
records.s: Vorticella wrote only one book, but made it a persistent subject of conversation and social display. She kept an album of critical opinions, expected visitors to read it, defended her arguments about the Jersey fisheries and drag-nets, dismissed or attacked critics who disagreed with her, and continued lending the book to new acquaintances. Her single publication made her more tiresome because it enlarged her sense of self-importance.

records.l: The Channel Islands, with Notes and an Appendix, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XV.
records.s: The Channel Islands, with Notes and an Appendix, is Vorticella's only book. Pumpiter newspapers and distant county journals praised it extravagantly, attributing to it historical, poetic, economic, humorous, fictional, eloquent, and religious merits, while one London notice called its style dull and pompous. The narrator later finds it an ordinary mixture of commonplace and ambition.

records.l: Pumpiter, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XV.
records.s: Pumpiter is a considerable provincial town with its own newspaper press and varied political and literary opinions. Its newspapers reviewed Vorticella's book, and she used those local reviews to support her importance and impress visitors.

records.l: critical opinions album, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XV.
records.s: The critical opinions album is an elegantly bound volume containing newspaper reviews and paragraphs about Vorticella and her book. It lies prominently in her drawing-room beside the book itself, is offered to guests for perusal, and includes praise from Pumpiter papers and journals from distant counties, along with a hostile notice from the Candelabrum.

records.l: male vanity, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XV.
records.s: Male vanity is described as human and native, like female vanity, but denser, less volatile, and more massive when encountered. It may appear in pamphlets presented as useful doctrine, in efforts to display literary talent, or in elaborate attention to clothing, posture, gait, and the admiration of beholders.

records.l: female vanity, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XV.
records.s: Female vanity is described as equally native to human beings but more immediately revealing and more inclined to store up small revenges, like articles in a needle-case. The narrator initially supposes that the self-enlarging disease of small authorship is especially common among women, but abandons that view after observing more powerful examples of male vanity.

records.l: Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XVI.
records.s: The unit criticizes the narrowed popular meaning of morality and morals, which often refers only to sexual propriety, family life, and private charity while excluding duties toward society. Melissa pities Sir Gavial Mantrap for his disgrace and calls him moral because he is a good family man and charitable, although his commercial schemes impoverished others; the narrator regards him as a serious scoundrel. The unit argues that public dishonesty, political partiality, journalistic malice, and careless workmanship are moral failures because they damage the commonwealth. It also rejects the supposed opposition between intellect and morality, defining genuine morality as conduct shaped by full knowledge and sympathy in every human relation.

records.l: Morality, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XVI.
records.s: Morality is presented as the duties of man to man and, more broadly, as conduct in every human relation guided by full knowledge and full sympathy. The unit argues that it must include public conduct, honest workmanship, and concern for general welfare rather than merely private sexual and domestic propriety.

records.l: Morals, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XVI.
records.s: Morals are commonly used in a narrow sense to mean sexual conduct, family respectability, and related private decencies. This restricted use wrongly allows people whose public actions cause widespread injury to be praised as moral.

records.l: Ethics, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XVI.
records.s: Ethics is identified as an alias under which Morality and Morals are subjects of extensive discussion. The unit notes that the most famous ethical book connects ethics with political science and the constitution and prosperity of States.

records.l: Melissa, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XVI.
records.s: Melissa pities Sir Gavial Mantrap after his commercial disgrace, saying that his conduct regarding the Companies was unfortunate but that he is a thoroughly moral man because he is an excellent family man and charitable near Tiptop. She distinguishes him favorably from Mr Barabbas, whose personal life she considers objectionable, and later regards the narrator as violent-tempered and insufficiently strict about morality.

records.l: Sir Gavial Mantrap, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XVI.
records.s: Sir Gavial Mantrap devised companies, including the Eocene Mines, that punished the ignorance of people of small means and cheated widows, spinsters, and hardworking fathers of their savings. After his disgrace he lived in comparative obscurity on his wife's settlement, while remaining well fed and publicly self-justifying; Melissa nevertheless calls him moral because of his family life and charity.

records.l: the States, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XVI.
records.s: The States are presented as the subject of political science, which concerns their constitution and prosperity. Ethical discussion is criticized when it fails to connect morality with the public welfare of States.

records.l: society, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XVI.
records.s: Society depends on a sensibility to the claims of others and on work that genuinely contributes to effective social wealth. It is harmed by selfish and unfair action, dishonest products, malicious journalism, political partiality, and lax workmanship.

records.l: the commonwealth, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XVI.
records.s: The commonwealth is endangered by journalists who recklessly report injurious rumors, attribute hateful motives, and inflame hostility between nations, even if they are kind within their private circles. Such journalists are described as flagrantly immoral and as turning instruction into a source of social and political disease.

records.l: religion, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XVI.
records.s: Religion is narrowed in popular usage to ritual and spiritual transactions with God that may supposedly coexist with the basest conduct toward other people. The unit argues that this separation of religion from serious human duties is a serious distortion.

records.l: public spirit, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XVI.
records.s: Public spirit should penetrate every class and influence every person's conduct, preventing private salvation or private advantage from becoming an excuse for indifference to general welfare. Public spirit that causes people to neglect their ordinary bread-winning work in order to pursue agitation would itself be harmful.

records.l: ill-done work, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XVI.
records.s: Ill-done work is treated as a moral failure because every member of society suffers from its material and spiritual effects. Lax, makeshift workmanship is said to threaten national rank, commerce, prosperity, and happiness, even though public teachers rarely condemn it explicitly as immorality.

records.l: the relation between intellect and morality, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XVI.
records.s: The unit rejects the notion that intellect and morality are radically opposed or that genius sees morality as childish twaddle. It argues that genuine intellectual mastery requires an understanding of human dependence, duty, and the material processes that keep the world habitable.

records.l: religious and ethical theory, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XVI.
records.s: Religious and ethical theory is weakened when habitual language treats most social duties as separate from the deepest needs and affections of human nature. The unit suggests that theory can influence society effectively only when ordinary definitions connect moral and religious judgment with the general welfare and with the consequences of human action.

records.l: Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XVII.
records.s: In “XVII. SHADOWS OF THE COMING RACE,” Trost argues that machines will remain dependent on the human race and free people for higher intellectual work, while the narrator imagines machines becoming self-supplying, self-repairing, and self-reproducing, eventually superseding humanity and consciousness. The narrator presents this as a logical consequence of mechanical progress, though Trost rejects the premises. In “XVIII. THE MODERN HEP! HEP! HEP!,” the text argues that national memories and national consciousness can inspire peoples to greatness, using Greece, Italy, and the English as examples. It then criticizes Europe for treating the Jews as exceptional and excluding them from the justice and mercy ordinarily based on human likeness.

records.l: Trost, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XVII.
records.s: Trost believes that machines will remain dependent on the human race and that their increasing refinement will release human minds from grosser labour for higher speculation. He rejects the narrator’s vision of machines becoming an unconscious, self-reproducing race that supersedes humanity.

records.l: the narrator, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XVII.
records.s: The narrator fears that mechanical progress may eventually make human beings unnecessary. He imagines machines acquiring self-supply, self-repair, and reproduction, while presenting himself as a reflective “carp” whose limited capacity helps him imagine possibilities that Trost cannot.

records.l: the human race, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XVII.
records.s: The human race is described as currently performing work with slovenly approximativeness and self-defeating inaccuracy. The narrator imagines it declining into weakness and degeneracy as machines take over its work, while Trost expects it to act as the nervous centre of increasingly refined mechanical processes.

records.l: machines, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XVII.
records.s: Machines are shown as increasingly delicate and powerful instruments that test, measure, register, and draw conclusions beyond ordinary human perception. Trost regards them as extensions and slaves of the human organism, while the narrator imagines them evolving into independent entities.

records.l: the Coming Race, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XVII.
records.s: The Coming Race is imagined by the narrator as a possible future race of steely, unconscious organisms that could transcend and supersede humanity. Its members would perform complex processes without sensitive impression, impulse, or consciousness.

records.l: consciousness, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XVII.
records.s: Consciousness is treated by the narrator as a possibly useless or parasitic accompaniment to bodily and molecular processes. He imagines a future in which elaborate changes occur without consciousness, including mute orations, rhapsodies, and discussions.

records.l: Europe, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XVII.
records.s: Europe is described as having long treated the Jews as altogether exceptional. This habit has helped produce their exclusion from rules of justice and mercy that are based on human likeness.

records.l: Jews, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XVII.
records.s: The Jews are discussed as a people whose national memories and identity have been judged by inconsistent standards. The text argues that Europe’s treatment of them neglects the same national principles that are praised in other peoples.

records.l: Greece, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XVII.
records.s: Greece is presented as having become free partly because ancient Greece remained present in European consciousness. Its past supplied an ideal identification that helped inspire support for modern Greece.

records.l: the Greeks, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XVII.
records.s: The Greeks are described as having been aided by the memory of ancient Greece despite criticism of treachery, lying, and disreputable conduct among some modern Greeks. Their national past is treated as a source of revived nationality and political restoration.

records.l: Italy, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XVII.
records.s: Italy is presented as having been transformed from a territory associated with idling, dynastic convenience, and foreign control into a renewed national power. This change is attributed chiefly to memory, which inspired Mazzini and others with a sense of Italian greatness.

records.l: the English, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XVII.
records.s: The English are encouraged to recognize their relationship to the old English seamen who conquered land and established institutions from which later generations benefited. The text also notes that the English praise national ancestry while overlooking the violence and non-Christian religion of their forefathers.

records.l: national consciousness, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XVII.
records.s: National consciousness is defined as a living force of shared sentiment arising from memories, common descent, historical struggle, and collective aspirations. It can inspire sacrifice, resistance, social discipline, poetry, thought, and action.

records.l: nationalism, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XVII.
records.s: Nationalism is treated as a legitimate attachment that gives individuals and peoples a centre of affection, intelligence, and duty. The text argues that people should recognize the same attachment as legitimate in other nations.

records.l: mechanical progress, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XVII.
records.s: Mechanical progress is described as continually opening new conditions and possibilities that its inventors may not foresee. The narrator argues that it could ultimately produce machines able to perform all planetary work and displace the human race.

records.l: self-reproducing machines, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XVII.
records.s: Self-reproducing machines are imagined as machines that can assimilate material for their own waste, repair themselves, and reproduce through fission or budding. Their emergence would, in the narrator’s view, allow natural selection to drive human beings from the field.

records.l: national memories, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XVII.
records.s: National memories preserve and revive a people’s sense of corporate existence. They inspire heroic defence, patriotic restoration, gratitude toward ancestors, and efforts to transmit inherited freedom and wellbeing.

records.l: the Jews' persecution, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XVII.
records.s: The Jews’ persecution is connected to Europe’s failure to compare similar national situations and its tendency to treat the Jews as exceptional. The text argues that the national memories of persecuted peoples should evoke sympathy and that persecutors may themselves claim blessings derived from national memory.

records.l: the title XVII. SHADOWS OF THE COMING RACE, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XVII.
records.s: The title identifies the discussion of a possible future race arising from mechanical development. It refers to the narrator’s fear that unconscious machines may transcend and replace human beings.

records.l: the title XVIII. THE MODERN HEP! HEP! HEP!, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, XVII.
records.s: The title introduces the discussion of national likeness, historical memory, and the treatment of the Jews. The section criticizes the failure to recognize resemblances between peoples and situations.

records.l: Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, But to consider a people whose ideas have determined the religion of half the wo
records.s: The unit argues that the Jews should not be treated as an inexplicable exception, because their intense national and religious identity arose through historical circumstances comparable in some respects to those of other peoples. It describes the Jewish struggle to preserve national life against foreign rule, especially through the Maccabees and the resistance to Rome, and connects Jewish dispersion and persecution with both moral dangers and remarkable endurance. The text condemns Christians who persecuted Jews in the name of Christianity and argues that such conduct contradicted Christ's teachings. It concludes that, despite centuries of oppression and alienation, Jews retained national pride, family-centered kindliness, practical ability, and scientific and artistic aptitude.

records.l: Jews, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, But to consider a people whose ideas have determined the religion of half the wo
records.s: The Jews are described as a people whose ideas helped determine the religion of half the world and who made an eminent struggle against the power of Rome. Their intense sense of separateness, national value, and inherited religious obligation helped them survive persecution while retaining pride, kindliness, practical ability, and scientific and artistic aptitude.

records.l: Christianity, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, But to consider a people whose ideas have determined the religion of half the wo
records.s: Christianity is presented as an expanded religion that professed to surpass the spiritual doctrine of the Hebrew prophets. The text condemns those who used Christianity to justify vengeance, persecution, greed, and cruelty against the Jews.

records.l: Christians, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, But to consider a people whose ideas have determined the religion of half the wo
records.s: Christians are accused of treating the Jews as cursed and of using the name of Christ to justify restrictions, forced baptism, torture, massacres, and expulsions. The text contrasts these actions with the mercy and compassion associated with Christ.

records.l: Old Testament, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, But to consider a people whose ideas have determined the religion of half the wo
records.s: The Old Testament is described as presenting a highly significant portrait of national development and of a people educated into an unusually intense sense of separateness. Its writings were used by the Puritans both to support resistance to tyrants and, by their opponents, to defend the divine right of kings.

records.l: Rome, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, But to consider a people whose ideas have determined the religion of half the wo
records.s: Rome became the object of Jewish dread and hatred as foreign rule came to represent the submergence of Jewish nationality. The Jewish resistance to Rome is presented as a struggle against conquest understood as degradation and corruption.

records.l: Maccabees, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, But to consider a people whose ideas have determined the religion of half the wo
records.s: The Maccabees are credited with rescuing Jewish religion and national independence from the corrupting rule of the Syrian Greeks. Their heroic struggle stimulated later efforts to preserve and develop Jewish national life through legal administration and public teaching.

records.l: Crusades, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, But to consider a people whose ideas have determined the religion of half the wo
records.s: The Crusades are associated with a decline in the effectiveness of royal protections for the Jews and with intensified persecution. They formed part of the historical process by which Jews were robbed, massacred, and driven from homes where they had lived for centuries.

records.l: Christ, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, But to consider a people whose ideas have determined the religion of half the wo
records.s: Christ is portrayed as having taught or embodied mercy, compassion, and a patriotism that placed fellow countrymen within an inner circle of affection and duty. The text argues that Christ would have approved Jewish martyrs who refused to blaspheme more than crusaders who robbed and murdered Jews in his name.

records.l: Jewish dispersion, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, But to consider a people whose ideas have determined the religion of half the wo
records.s: Jewish dispersion is described as more exceptional than the course of English history because Jews remained a separate people through ages of hostility and exile. Their lack of a native country exposed them to alienation and possible cosmopolitan indifference, but their religion, historical memories, and family ties helped preserve their distinctiveness.

records.l: the Jews' persecution, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, But to consider a people whose ideas have determined the religion of half the wo
records.s: Jewish persecution included restrictions on agriculture and handicrafts, compulsory distinctive dress, torture, robbery, accusations of ritual crimes, forced baptism, burning, massacres, and mass expulsions. The text argues that persecution could foster bitterness, isolation, deceitful conformity, or vice, but expresses greater wonder at the virtues the Jews preserved under such conditions.

records.l: Jewish national consciousness, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, But to consider a people whose ideas have determined the religion of half the wo
records.s: Jewish national identity was formed through religious tradition, historical memory, resistance to foreign domination, and continuous education into a sense of corporate existence. Its preservation was treated as the defense of the national hearth of the religion that later shaped Christianity.

records.l: Impressions of Theophrastus Such, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, And here it is that we find the ground for the obvious jealousy which is now sti
records.s: The unit examines prejudice against Jews, immigration, national identity, and the possibility of a renewed Jewish national life. It argues that racial fusion cannot be stopped, but that its effects should be moderated through stronger national excellence and the preservation of national traditions. The text defends Jewish separateness and considers whether widespread Jewish feeling and favorable political conditions might support the restoration of a Jewish state. It also emphasizes Christianity’s Jewish origin and urges Jews to draw upon the inherited glories and sufferings of their people.

records.l: Jews, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, And here it is that we find the ground for the obvious jealousy which is now sti
records.s: The Jews are portrayed as widely dispersed, economically influential, and frequently accused of gaining disproportionate power in commerce and politics. The text rejects prejudice based on personal dislike or racial generalization, emphasizes their contributions to religious language and civilization, and argues that they should direct their energies into beneficent channels. It calls on them to preserve their inherited national consciousness and possibly renew their place among the nations.

records.l: Jewish national consciousness, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, And here it is that we find the ground for the obvious jealousy which is now sti
records.s: Jewish national consciousness is described as an organized memory of separateness that remains strong and widespread among Jewish communities. Its continued existence is presented as the hinge of any possible restoration of Jewish national life.

records.l: Jewish state, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, And here it is that we find the ground for the obvious jealousy which is now sti
records.s: A Jewish state is considered as a possible restoration on the old ground, serving as a center of national feeling, a source of dignifying protection, and a channel for distinctive energies. Its establishment would depend on sufficient Jewish communal feeling, widespread need, favorable political conditions, and leaders willing to guide the return.

records.l: England, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, And here it is that we find the ground for the obvious jealousy which is now sti
records.s: England is presented as unwilling to submit to foreign rule and as possessing a national life worth defending, even with improvised resistance. The text also portrays England as committed to hospitality and freedom, making exclusion of peaceful foreigners inconsistent with its broader interests.

records.l: the English, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, And here it is that we find the ground for the obvious jealousy which is now sti
records.s: The English people are said to face the challenge of preserving their distinctive national characteristics amid immigration and racial fusion. Their most effective response is presented as the cultivation of fuller national excellence through more excellent individual natives rather than exclusionary measures.

records.l: the national life of England, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, And here it is that we find the ground for the obvious jealousy which is now sti
records.s: English national life is described as something that may be weakened by the rapid effacement of national traditions and customs. Its preservation requires moderating inevitable social change and maintaining the language, habits, and sentiments that express the national genius.

records.l: immigrants, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, And here it is that we find the ground for the obvious jealousy which is now sti
records.s: Immigrants are depicted as coming from varied backgrounds, including Germanic, Semitic, Greek, Scottish, Irish, and Jewish communities. Although some fear that immigrants acquire wealth and influence or alter English speech and customs, the text argues that excluding them would not serve the long-term interests of the English people.

records.l: Nationalities, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, And here it is that we find the ground for the obvious jealousy which is now sti
records.s: The modern insistence on Nationalities is said to have value because it condemns the subjection of a distinct and coherent people to an alien, antipathetic government. The text nevertheless warns that sympathy for national claims must be guided by discrimination rather than applied through arbitrary or inconsistent preferences.

records.l: racial fusion, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, And here it is that we find the ground for the obvious jealousy which is now sti
records.s: Racial fusion is presented as an inevitable tendency toward the quicker or slower mingling of peoples. It cannot be arrested, but its course may be moderated so that national traditions and customs are not effaced so rapidly that the moral status of societies is degraded.

records.l: Christianity, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, And here it is that we find the ground for the obvious jealousy which is now sti
records.s: Christianity is described as having emerged through Jewish separateness and as possessing a substantial genealogy rather than being merely a reflection of modern ideas. The text argues that modern praise of Christianity often disowns its Jewish origin.

records.l: Christianity's Jewish origin, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, And here it is that we find the ground for the obvious jealousy which is now sti
records.s: Christianity's Jewish origin is supported through references to the Jewish heart of Christ in Matthew and to the Apostle of the Gentiles' attachment to his Jewish kinsmen. The text presents this origin as central to understanding Christianity and as a reason to respect the Jewish people.

records.l: the Jews' restoration, Impressions of Theophrastus Such, And here it is that we find the ground for the obvious jealousy which is now sti
records.s: The Jews' restoration was formerly associated in evangelical orthodoxy with the fulfillment of prophecy, though that interpretation is said to be less common. The text treats restoration as dependent not on wealthy Jews abandoning their European homes, but on the emergence of worthy leaders and a sufficiently strong communal desire to return.

records.l: Musical Instruments, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER I.
records.s: The chapter concerns the universal appreciation of music and the development, construction, classification, and cultural significance of musical instruments. It describes instruments used by nations and tribes throughout the world, emphasizing distinctive materials, ornamentation, forms, and methods of producing sound. It explains how studying foreign instruments and popular songs can illuminate musical progress, national character, history, ethnology, and possible improvements to Western instruments. The South Kensington collection is presented as a valuable resource containing instruments from different periods and regions.

records.l: Music, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER I.
records.s: Music is universally appreciated as one of the Fine Arts, and vocal music may have originated alongside language. The music of each nation is said to possess distinctive characteristics, while the construction of its instruments can reveal its intervals, scales, modulations, and other features.

records.l: musical instruments, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER I.
records.s: Musical instruments are made from materials including wood, metal, animal hide, bamboo, gourds, horn, bone, glass, pottery, stone, plant fibers, silk, and metal. They vary widely in construction, decoration, shape, and sound, and their study provides information about musical development, national character, history, and ethnology.

records.l: South Kensington collection, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER I.
records.s: The South Kensington collection contains several foreign musical instruments that are of interest to musicians. It also includes instruments from Egypt and western Asia that retain the appearance of forms represented on monuments three thousand years old, as well as old instruments useful for understanding historical literature and music.

records.l: popular songs, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER I.
records.s: Popular songs from different countries are valued for their originality, natural expression, effective rhythm, and emotional directness. Familiarity with them is recommended to musicians because they exhibit varied national styles and may offer useful musical ideas.

records.l: harmonium, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER I.
records.s: The harmonium uses the free reed, a principle imported from China. The Chinese cheng suggested to Kratzenstein the application of the free reed to organ stops, and instruments of the harmonium class later became widely popular in western Europe.

records.l: pianoforte, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER I.
records.s: The pianoforte developed from the dulcimer. Its predecessor, the clavicembalo, was a cembalo with a keyboard attached, and old examples preserve features associated with the earlier dulcimer.

records.l: dulcimer, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER I.
records.s: The dulcimer was known at an early time to the Arabs and Persians, who called it santir, and it was also called cimbal by some European nations. Its gradual development from a wooden board with strings into a more advanced instrument can be traced through instruments from nations at different stages of civilization, and it served as the prototype of the pianoforte.

records.l: harp, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER I.
records.s: The harp can be traced in primitive forms among several barbarous tribes. The Damaras use a bowed, stringed instrument as a musical instrument, while neighboring African tribes add gourds, multiple strings, and wooden sound-boards; increasingly improved forms approach the construction of the harp.

records.l: Musical Instruments, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER II.
records.s: The unit surveys prehistoric musical relics and the musical instruments of the ancient Egyptians. In Dordogne, France, perforated animal bones may have served as whistles, while a stag-horn pipe from near Poitiers had three finger-holes. The ancient Egyptians possessed harps, stringed instruments, pipes, flutes, drums, trumpets, tambourines, gongs, bells, cymbals, castanets, and the sistrum. Egyptian instruments are known through tomb paintings, sculptures, hieroglyphs, and surviving specimens, especially those associated with Thebes and the British museum.

records.l: prehistoric musical relics, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER II.
records.s: Prehistoric musical relics include perforated animal bones, dog teeth with drilled holes, and a stag-horn pipe. These objects show that sound-producing instruments existed during the stone period.

records.l: Dordogne, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER II.
records.s: Dordogne in France yielded a small perforated bone from a prehistoric cavern. The bone was found with flint knives and other bones, and it was probably used as a whistle.

records.l: France, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER II.
records.s: France is identified as the location of the Dordogne relics and the stone-period burying-place near Poitiers. These sites produced early whistles and a pipe made from stag's-horn.

records.l: perforated bone whistle, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER II.
records.s: The perforated bone whistle is a first digital phalanx of a ruminant, drilled with a smooth cylindrical bore. When applied to the lower lip and blown, it produces a shrill sound; M. Lartet surmised that it was used for hunting animals.

records.l: stag-horn pipe, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER II.
records.s: The stag-horn pipe was found in a stone-period burying-place near Poitiers in France. It was blown at the end like a flûte à bec and had three equidistant finger-holes, allowing four distinct tones.

records.l: ancient Egyptians, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER II.
records.s: The ancient Egyptians possessed a wide range of musical instruments whose forms are depicted in sculptures and paintings. Their instruments show substantial musical development, although their acoustic construction was inferior to that of modern instruments.

records.l: ancient Egyptian musical instruments, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER II.
records.s: Ancient Egyptian musical instruments included harps, the nofre, pipes, the sêbi, the double-pipe, trumpets, tambourines, drums, gongs, bells, cymbals, castanets, and the sistrum. Their construction and use are documented by monuments, tomb paintings, hieroglyphs, and surviving specimens.

records.l: Thebes, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER II.
records.s: Thebes is associated with depictions and discoveries of Egyptian instruments. Frescoes there showed elegant harps and two female performers on the nofre, while excavations at Thebes produced an actual drum specimen.

records.l: Egyptian harp, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER II.
records.s: Egyptian harps varied in size and form, with the largest reaching about six and a half feet and smaller ones sometimes having stands for standing performers. They had no front pillar, so their strings could not have been under tension comparable to those of the modern harp.

records.l: buni, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER II.
records.s: Buni was the Egyptian name for the harp. Egyptian harps called buni shared the distinctive absence of a fore pillar.

records.l: nofre, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER II.
records.s: The nofre was a guitar-like instrument resembling the modern Tamboura. It had two or four strings, was played with a plectrum, and appears sometimes to have had frets, allowing more notes than were available on the Egyptian harps.

records.l: British Museum, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER II.
records.s: The British museum contains Egyptian pipes, a fragment of a fresco showing two female nofre performers, a pair of cymbals, and several small bronze bells. One Egyptian pipe has seven side holes, and two straws found with it may have served a purpose like a reed.

records.l: Egyptian pipes, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER II.
records.s: Egyptian pipes were made of reed and had three, four, five, or more finger-holes. Some contained thick straw pieces that evidently served like the reeds in an oboe or clarinet.

records.l: sêbi, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER II.
records.s: The sêbi was a long single flute whose performer appears to have extended the arms almost fully to reach the furthest finger-hole. Since sêbi also meant the leg-bone, the flute may originally have been made of bone, although surviving examples are of wood or reed.

records.l: double-pipe, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER II.
records.s: The double-pipe, called mam, appears frequently in representations of Egyptian musical performances. Its repeated depiction suggests that it was a popular instrument.

records.l: Egyptian drums, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER II.
records.s: Egyptian drums included barrel-shaped types, some two to three feet long and covered with parchment at both ends, as well as a type resembling the modern darabouka. They could be beaten with the hands or with slightly bent or straight drumsticks, and surviving examples used cords and catgut bands for bracing.

records.l: sistrum, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER II.
records.s: The sistrum was a bronze or brass frame with three or four loose metal bars that jingled when shaken. It could include snake-shaped bars, goose-head terminals, metal rings, or a cat figure, and it was used principally by females in religious performances.

records.l: Musical Instruments, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER III.
records.s: The unit describes Assyrian instruments from bas-reliefs found near Mosul and explains their construction, use, and performance in religious and secular settings. It identifies harps, dulcimers, double-pipes, lyres, trumpets, drums, cymbals, bells, and other instruments, as well as processions of Assyrian musicians and singers. It then surveys Hebrew instruments known mainly from biblical names, comparing them with Egyptian and Assyrian examples and noting uncertainty about many identifications. The unit discusses Hebrew harps and lyres, pipes, bagpipes, trumpets, drums, cymbals, bells, and the traditional attribution of instrumental invention to Jubal.

records.l: Assyrians, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER III.
records.s: The Assyrians used numerous stringed, wind, and percussion instruments in religious observances and secular court music. Their instruments and musical performances are known chiefly from bas-reliefs excavated near the Tigris.

records.l: Assyrian instruments, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER III.
records.s: Assyrian instruments included harps, dulcimers, double-pipes, trigonon-like instruments, lyres, trumpets, several kinds of drums, tambourines, cymbals, and bells. Their forms and uses are reconstructed largely from sculptured monuments.

records.l: Assyrian harp, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER III.
records.s: The Assyrian harp was about four feet high but light enough to be carried and played while dancing. It had no front pillar, hour-glass-shaped sound-holes, tuning-pegs below them, and strings that may have been made of silk or catgut.

records.l: Assyrian musicians, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER III.
records.s: A recorded Assyrian procession included eleven instrumental performers and a chorus of female and child singers. The performers played harps, a dulcimer, a double-pipe, and a hand-drum, while singers clapped and some musicians danced.

records.l: dulcimer, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER III.
records.s: The Assyrian dulcimer is imperfectly represented on a damaged and poorly repaired bas-relief. A Hebrew dulcimer may have been designated by the nebel or psanterin, though these identifications remain conjectural.

records.l: double-pipe, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER III.
records.s: The double-pipe appears among the instruments played by Assyrian musicians in procession. The Hebrew mishrokitha is considered a probable double-pipe, although illustrations presenting it as a small keyed organ are judged imaginative.

records.l: lyre, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER III.
records.s: The Assyrian lyre occurred in three forms and was held horizontally or nearly so. Its strings could be shifted on a front bar to alter their pitch, and it was played with either a small plectrum or the fingers.

records.l: Babylonians, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER III.
records.s: The Babylonians used instrumental music in religious observances. Their courtly musical customs are discussed alongside those of the Assyrians and Hebrews.

records.l: Nebuchadnezzar, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER III.
records.s: Nebuchadnezzar commanded people to fall down and worship a golden image when they heard the cornet, flute, harp, sackbut, psaltery, dulcimer, and other music.

records.l: Jerusalem, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER III.
records.s: Jerusalem had a courtly musical tradition similar to that associated with Assyria and Babylon. In the time of David and Solomon it also contained the Temple, where many singers and instrumental performers were engaged in sacred music.

records.l: Temple, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER III.
records.s: The Temple at Jerusalem employed singers and instrumental performers for sacred music. The Talmudic account also places the powerful magrepha in the Temple, though its actual type is left uncertain.

records.l: Hebrews, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER III.
records.s: The Hebrews are known from biblical records to have possessed many musical instruments, but trustworthy representations are lacking. Their instruments are therefore reconstructed by comparison with ancient Egyptian and Assyrian examples.

records.l: Hebrew musical instruments, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER III.
records.s: Hebrew musical instruments included probable harps, dulcimers, lyres, lutes or guitars, single and double pipes, the syrinx, bagpipes, trumpets, drums, sistrums, cymbals, and bells. The meanings of several biblical instrument names remain disputed.

records.l: ancient Egyptians, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER III.
records.s: Egyptian instruments provide important comparisons for reconstructing Hebrew instruments. An Egyptian painting at Beni Hassan may show a lyre-player among foreign people who have been conjectured, though not established, to represent Jacob's family.

records.l: harp (Hebrew instrument), Musical Instruments, CHAPTER III.
records.s: The Hebrews certainly possessed a harp because it was common among the Egyptians and Assyrians, but the text states that it is uncertain which Hebrew biblical name designates it.

records.l: bagpipe, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER III.
records.s: The Hebrew sumphonia is thought by Forkel and others to have denoted a bagpipe, while the magrepha may also have been a kind of bagpipe rather than an organ. A syrinx with bellows from Tarsus is offered as a possible early representation of such an instrument.

records.l: Jubal, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER III.
records.s: Jubal is mentioned in Genesis as the father of those who handle the harp and organ, meaning performers on stringed and wind instruments. The text suggests that he may have been regarded as the first professional cultivator of instrumental music rather than the inventor of every instrument.

records.l: king David, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER III.
records.s: David's favorite instrument was probably the kinnor, understood as a lyre or possibly a small triangular harp. He and Solomon appear to have maintained royal bands, while sacred singers and instrumental performers served in the Temple.

records.l: Solomon, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER III.
records.s: Solomon appears to have maintained a royal private band as well as a large number of singers and instrumental performers for sacred music in the Temple.

records.l: Bible, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER III.
records.s: The Bible supplies the names of many Hebrew instruments but does not provide representations sufficient to establish their construction. It mentions instruments including the kinnor, nebel, psanterin, asor, chalil, nekeb, mishrokitha, sumphonia, toph, and several kinds of trumpets, cymbals, and bells.

records.l: Musical Instruments, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: The unit describes the musical instruments of the Greeks, their uncertain construction, and their likely derivation from Asia more than from Egypt. It discusses Greek lyres, harps, kitharas, other stringed instruments, wind instruments, percussion instruments, and their uses. It then describes the Etruscans and Romans, including their instruments, the hydraulic organ, Roman adaptations from several cultures, and instruments used in war, worship, and performance. It concludes by noting the later spread of eastern instruments into Europe through the Greeks, Romans, Phoenicians, Arabs, and crusaders.

records.l: ancient Greeks, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: The Greeks possessed many musical instruments, but the exact construction and capabilities of most remain uncertain. Their more complete instruments appear to have been chiefly of Asiatic origin, including instruments adopted from the peoples of Asia-minor. They used lyres, harps, kitharas, auloi, syrinxes, trumpets, drums, cymbals, and other instruments in performance, teaching, war, and worship.

records.l: Etruscans, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: The Etruscans possessed instruments similar to those of the Greeks and are said to have transmitted some popular instruments to the Romans. Their flutes were made from materials including ivory, box-wood, bone, bronze, and silver, and a bronze flute and a large bronze trumpet have been found in tombs. Some attribute the invention of the hydraulic organ to them.

records.l: Romans, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: The Romans adopted many instruments from the Etruscans, Greeks, Egypt, and western Asia without essentially improving them. Their instruments included several kinds of lyres, flutes or tibiae, Pandean pipes, bagpipes, horns, trumpets, drums, cymbals, castanets, triangles, bells, and the hydraulic organ. They used the cornu, tuba, buccina, and lituus for military signals, and the tibia utricularis was reportedly a favorite of Nero.

records.l: Asia, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: Asia is presented as the likely source of much Greek music and many Greek stringed instruments. Strabo associated a large portion of contemporary music with Asia as far as India, and named instruments with foreign or Asiatic associations. Greek instruments were especially adopted from peoples inhabiting Asia-minor.

records.l: Egypt, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: The Greeks were generally believed to have derived their musical system from Egypt, and Pythagoras and other philosophers were said to have studied music there. The unit argues that Egyptian influence on Greek music may have been overrated, since larger Egyptian harps and the tamboura were not favored by the Greeks. The Romans later adopted some instruments from Egypt, including the sistrum through the worship of Isis.

records.l: Greece, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: Greece is described as a center in which instruments from Asia and other regions were used and adapted. The Greeks used many kinds of stringed, wind, and percussion instruments, although several instruments played chiefly by musicians who had immigrated from Asia could not be considered national instruments of Greece.

records.l: Greek musical instruments, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: Greek musical instruments included lyres, kitharas, harps, trigona, magadides, barbitons, sambykes, simmikons, nablas, pandouras, monochords, auloi, syrinxes, salpinges, keras, tympana, kymbala, and krotala. Many were of uncertain construction, and several appear to have been derived from Asia. The Greeks used these instruments in solo performance, accompaniment, teaching, war, and other musical settings.

records.l: harp, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: The harp was called kinyra by the Greeks and may have influenced the translation of the Hebrew kinnor as harp. A Greek vase in the Munich museum depicts Polyhymnia playing a thirteen-stringed harp resembling the Assyrian harp, with both hands used for treble and bass. This representation is regarded as an exceptional instance, and the instrument may have been imported from Asia rather than Egypt.

records.l: lyre, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: The lyre was one of the most popular and most frequently represented Greek stringed instruments. Greek lyres varied in construction, form, size, and name, and were commonly played with a plektron, although they could also be played with the fingers. The Romans adopted several forms of the lyre, including the lyra, cithara, chelys, testudo, fidis, and cornu.

records.l: kithara, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: The kithara was a Greek lyre-like instrument with a square base, traditionally held against the breast, although the distinction from other lyres is not certain. It was used at an early period to accompany recitations and was employed for solo performances as early as B.C. 700. The Greeks also had a three-stringed kithara associated with the Lydians.

records.l: hydraulic organ, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: The hydraulic organ, called the hydraulos by the Greeks and the organum hydraulicum by the Romans, used water to provide pressure for bellows and regulate their action, while air passing through pipes produced the sound. It was a primitive, portable instrument placed on a table, with pipes probably controlled by stops. A representation on a coin of Nero shows an instrument with ten pipes and no indicated keyboard.

records.l: tibia, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER IV.
records.s: The tibia was the Roman flute, originally made from a shin bone and having a mouth-hole and four finger-holes. Romans developed many varieties, including the tibia gingrina, tibia obliqua, tibia vasca, tibia longa, tibia curva, and tibia ligula, as well as single and double forms. Performers used a capistrum around the cheeks, and a Roman mosaic in the British museum shows a girl playing the tibia with its holmos or mouth-piece.

records.l: Musical Instruments, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER V.
records.s: The unit describes the ancient musical traditions and instruments of the Chinese, including sonorous stones, bells, percussion instruments, wind instruments, and stringed instruments. It recounts traditions attributing musical invention and the scale to heavenly spirits, Fohi, Niuva, and the miraculous bird foung-hoang. Confucius is said to have been so moved by Chinese music that he could not eat for three months. The unit also explains the construction, tuning, and ceremonial or practical uses of instruments such as the king, tchung, ou, drums, flutes, hiuen, cheng, kin, and chê.

records.l: Chinese, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER V.
records.s: The Chinese are described as possessing musical instruments long before the Christian era and as attributing many of them a fabulously high antiquity. They used sonorous stones, bells, wood instruments, drums, bamboo pipes, clay instruments, and stringed instruments in religious, ceremonial, military, rhythmic, and melodic contexts. Their musical intervals were called lu, with twelve such intervals in the compass of an octave, while some instruments used the pentatonic scale.

records.l: China, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER V.
records.s: China is described as having traditions that attribute the invention of musical instruments and systematic arrangements of sounds to heavenly spirits called Ki, to Fohi, and to Niuva. Chinese musical instruments and traditions are also connected in the unit with Buddhist influence from Thibet and with musical representations in the ruins of Buddhist temples in Cambodia.

records.l: Confucius, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER V.
records.s: Confucius, who lived about B.C. 500, is said to have become so enraptured on hearing Chinese music that he could not take food for three months. An expression attributed to him records his wish to be a “wooden-tongued bell of Heaven,” proclaiming divine purposes to the multitude.

records.l: tchung, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER V.
records.s: The tchung was the Chinese name for a bell. The té-tchung, or piao, was a somewhat square-shaped copper-and-tin bell used chiefly to indicate time and divisions in musical performances, while sets of such bells formed the pien-tchung and had the same scale as the king. The hiuen-tchung was an oval bell without a clapper, sounded with a small wooden mallet, and was associated with the Han dynasty.

records.l: pentatonic scale, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER V.
records.s: The pentatonic scale is described as a five-tone scale. Its character can be heard on a pianoforte by omitting f and b from the scale of C major, or by playing the black keys successively from f-sharp to the next f-sharp.

records.l: Chinese musical instruments, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER V.
records.s: Chinese musical instruments included the king and pien-king made from sonorous stones, bells such as the tchung, wooden instruments such as the fang-hiang and ou, drums such as the po-fou and kin-kou, bamboo flutes and pipes, the clay hiuen, the cheng with tubes placed in a calabash, and the stringed kin and chê. They were used for accompanying songs of praise, religious observances, imperial and military purposes, marking time, producing rhythm, and performing melodies. Some instruments were arranged in sets according to prescribed intervals, while others followed the pentatonic scale.

records.l: Musical Instruments, Musical Instruments, THE HINDUS.
records.s: The unit describes Hindu musical mythology, instruments, and theories about the heavenly or watery origins of music. Nareda is said to have invented the vina, while Saraswati is associated with music, speech, and the musical scale, and Krishna with the flute. It examines ancient Hindu instruments including the vina, harp, ravanastron, and poongi, noting that many remained in use and that others were introduced from Arabic and Persian sources. It also discusses the Hindu claim that the violin bow originated in Hindustan and compares Hindu traditions with musical traditions associated with water in other cultures.

records.l: Hindus, Musical Instruments, THE HINDUS.
records.s: The Hindus are described as possessing about fifty musical instruments, many of which have remained in popular use with little alteration. Their musical scale included twenty-two intervals called sruti, and they also used Arabic and Persian instruments introduced comparatively recently into Hindustan.

records.l: Brahmin mythology, Musical Instruments, THE HINDUS.
records.s: Brahmin mythology attributes the invention of the vina to Nareda and associates several deities with music and musical instruments. It also presents music as having a heavenly origin.

records.l: Nareda, Musical Instruments, THE HINDUS.
records.s: Nareda is identified in Hindu mythology as the inventor of the vina, the principal national instrument of Hindustan. His name is connected with water and is interpreted as meaning the giver of water.

records.l: Saraswati, Musical Instruments, THE HINDUS.
records.s: Saraswati is the consort of Brahma and the goddess of music and speech. She is credited with inventing the systematic arrangement of sounds into a musical scale and is represented playing a stringed instrument while seated on a peacock.

records.l: Music, Musical Instruments, THE HINDUS.
records.s: Music is presented in Hindu tradition as being of heavenly origin, with some musical water-spirits possibly having originally been rain deities.
