The text also suggests that the rhythm of waves and the murmur of running water may have inspired traditions about music and instruments originating from water.

records.l: Krishna, Musical Instruments, THE HINDUS.
records.s: Krishna, in his incarnation as Vishnu, is represented as a beautiful youth playing upon a flute. The Hindus construct a distinctive flute regarded as Krishna's favourite instrument.

records.l: flute, Musical Instruments, THE HINDUS.
records.s: The Hindus construct a peculiar kind of flute that they regard as the favourite instrument of Krishna.

records.l: water, Musical Instruments, THE HINDUS.
records.s: Water is associated with the origins of musical instruments in traditions from several regions. The text connects Nareda with water, describes instruments made from aquatic materials or bones, and suggests that the sounds of waves and running water may have encouraged these beliefs.

records.l: harp, Musical Instruments, THE HINDUS.
records.s: The Hindu harp, called chang, had become almost obsolete. Earlier drawings depict it with a triangular frame, making it closely resemble the Assyrian harp in construction, shape, and size.

records.l: Hindustan, Musical Instruments, THE HINDUS.
records.s: Hindustan is described as the home of the vina and as a possible place of origin for the fiddle-bow. Several instruments are said to have spread from Hindustan and Thibet eastward, with alterations, as far as Japan.

records.l: violin bow, Musical Instruments, THE HINDUS.
records.s: The Hindus claim to have invented the violin bow and associate its early use with the ravanastron. Sanskrit works dating from approximately 1500 to 2000 years ago are said to contain names for the bow, supporting the possibility that it originated in Hindustan.

records.l: Musical Instruments, Musical Instruments, THE PERSIANS AND ARABS.
records.s: The unit describes Persian and Arabian musical instruments, their development, and the transmission of instruments and musical practices from Persia through the Arabs and Spain into Europe. It discusses the Persian harp, lute, dulcimer, violin-type instruments, flutes, and oboes, as well as the Arabian system dividing the octave into seventeen one-third-tones. It also explains how the Arabs adopted Persian musical instruments after conquering Persia and how the Saracens and Moors introduced several of them into Europe. The unit concludes with the traditional story of Al-Farabi's court performance, in which changes of musical mode produced laughter, sadness, anger, and sleep.

records.l: Persians, Musical Instruments, THE PERSIANS AND ARABS.
records.s: The Persians possessed musical instruments and a musical culture that were more advanced than those of the Arabs when the Arabs conquered Persia. They used various forms of the chang, smaller musical intervals than semitones, and instruments including the lute, tamboura, kanoon, santir, rebab, kemangeh, nay, and surnay.

records.l: Arabs, Musical Instruments, THE PERSIANS AND ARABS.
records.s: The Arabs adopted Persian instruments and musical practices after conquering Persia, including the harp, lute, and kemangeh. Their theorists described a musical system dividing the octave into seventeen one-third-tones, and Arabian instruments were later carried into Spain and Europe.

records.l: Persia, Musical Instruments, THE PERSIANS AND ARABS.
records.s: Persia had a more advanced cultivation of music and superior musical instruments than the Arabs at the time of the Arab conquest in A.D. 641. Persian musical theory is presented as the basis for the system preserved in the earliest Arabian writings on musical theory.

records.l: Khosroo Purviz, Musical Instruments, THE PERSIANS AND ARABS.
records.s: Khosroo Purviz was the Persian monarch during whose lifetime the sculptures at Tackt-i-Bostan are said to have been executed. The sculptures depict musicians, including harpers, trumpet players, drummers, a flutist, a player of a pandean pipe, and a bagpipe player.

records.l: harp, Musical Instruments, THE PERSIANS AND ARABS.
records.s: The harp, called chang by the Persians and junk by the Arabs, was formerly a favorite Persian instrument but gradually fell into disuse. Persian harps appeared in sculptures and manuscripts, and an old Persian chang probably appears in a seventeenth-century representation of a Turkish woman playing the harp.

records.l: Arab conquest of Persia, Musical Instruments, THE PERSIANS AND ARABS.
records.s: The Arab conquest of Persia took place in A.D. 641. The Arabs found Persian musical cultivation and instruments superior to their own and soon adopted them.

records.l: octave division into seventeen one-third-tones, Musical Instruments, THE PERSIANS AND ARABS.
records.s: The octave division into seventeen one-third-tones formed part of the musical system described by the earliest preserved Arabian writers on musical theory. Frets on instruments such as the lute and tamboura were regulated to produce these intervals accurately.

records.l: lute, Musical Instruments, THE PERSIANS AND ARABS.
records.s: The lute was brought to Mekka through the Arab musician Nadr Ben el-Hares Ben Kelde, who learned Persian singing and lute performance at the court of Khosroo Purviz. Before the tenth century the Arabian lute had four strings or pairs of strings, and a fifth tone was added around the tenth century; its silk strings and frets were carefully constructed according to the seventeen-interval system.

records.l: Al-Farabi, Musical Instruments, THE PERSIANS AND ARABS.
records.s: Al-Farabi was one of the earliest known Arabian musical theorists and lived at the beginning of the tenth century. He did not mention the fiddle-bow, and his musical reputation was associated with Spain and Cordova.

records.l: Spain, Musical Instruments, THE PERSIANS AND ARABS.
records.s: Spain was a place where Al-Farabi acquired his proficiency and where schools of music flourished at Cordova toward the end of the ninth century. Musical instruments brought there by the Saracens and Moors were subsequently diffused toward northern Europe.

records.l: Saracens, Musical Instruments, THE PERSIANS AND ARABS.
records.s: The Saracens introduced eastern musical instruments into Spain. Through their presence, instruments such as the kuitra, el-oud, rebab, and nakkarah were gradually transmitted toward northern Europe.

records.l: Moors, Musical Instruments, THE PERSIANS AND ARABS.
records.s: The Moors introduced eastern musical instruments into Spain, from where those instruments were gradually diffused toward northern Europe. Their influence also contributed the Moorish dance, or morrice dance.

records.l: Europe, Musical Instruments, THE PERSIANS AND ARABS.
records.s: Europe received several musical instruments through Spain from the Saracens and Moors. These included the gittern or kuitra, lute or el-oud, rebec or rebab, naker or nakkarah, and other instruments adopted in northern Europe.

records.l: Al-Farabi's court performance, Musical Instruments, THE PERSIANS AND ARABS.
records.s: During Al-Farabi's court performance, he played the lute in successive musical modes that made the audience laugh, sigh and weep, become enraged, and finally fall into profound sleep. He then departed while the listeners slept; the story is compared with the account of Timotheus performing before Alexander the Great in Dryden's "Alexander's Feast."

records.l: Musical Instruments, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: The unit examines musical instruments made and used by American Indians, especially the Aztecs and Peruvians, before European influence. It describes pottery and bone pipes, flutes, whistles, and the Peruvian huayra-puhura, noting that some instruments reveal aspects of the musical systems of their makers, including use of the pentatonic scale. It also discusses trumpets and related instruments, including the juruparis of Indians near the Rio Haupés and the botuto used near the Orinoco. Religious, funerary, martial, and ceremonial purposes are attributed to several of these instruments.

records.l: American Indians, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: American Indians made and used a wide variety of musical instruments before European influence, including pipes, flutes, syrinxes, trumpets, and sound-producing vessels. Some instruments were used in religious ceremonies, warfare, funerals, dances, signaling, and entertainment.

records.l: Aztecs, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: The Aztecs made pottery whistles and pipes, including the pito, and used flutes in religious observances and solemn orations. Their instruments included a variety of pipes, some of which followed intervals conforming to the pentatonic scale.

records.l: Peruvians, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: The Peruvians made bone flutes, syrinxes called huayra-puhura, and other pipes. Their songs apparently used different orders of intervals for different kinds of tunes, and some instruments were arranged according to the pentatonic scale.

records.l: American musical instruments, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: Ancient American musical instruments provide evidence about the artistic development, social condition, and musical systems of the Indians who made them. The surviving examples include instruments of pottery, bone, cane, stone, wood, and other materials.

records.l: pipes and flutes, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: Pipes and flutes are among the most frequently preserved ancient instruments of the Aztecs and Peruvians because pottery and bone resist decay. They included whistles, small pipes, flageolet-like instruments, bone flutes, and syrinxes.

records.l: Mexican whistle, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: The Mexican whistle was a small baked-clay instrument, often shaped as a grotesque human, animal, bird, or flower. Some had a finger-hole that produced two tones, while others contained a loose clay ball that made a shrill, whirring sound when the whistle was blown; it most likely served mainly for signaling.

records.l: Aztec pito, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: The Aztec pito was a reddish-pottery pipe resembling a flageolet and equipped with four finger-holes. Specimens examined by the writer, ranging from about six to nine inches in length, had the same pitch and an order of intervals conforming to the pentatonic scale; the instrument was used in religious observances and appeared in Aztec religious symbolism.

records.l: pentatonic scale, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: The pentatonic scale characterized the intervals of the Aztec pito and the tones of a Peruvian huayra-puhura from a tomb at Arica. The text presents this arrangement as evidence that these instruments' intervals were deliberately organized.

records.l: Peruvian bone flute, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: A Peruvian bone flute found in an ancient tomb was made from a human bone and had four upper finger-holes, with the blowing end at one extremity. Two similar bone flutes from Truxillo are in the British Museum; one has five upper holes, and another has four upper holes and one underneath, with hardened paste or resin at the blowing end.

records.l: Peruvian syrinx, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: The Peruvian huayra-puhura was a syrinx made of cane or stone, sometimes ornamented with embroidery or designs. A British Museum specimen from a tomb at Arica has fourteen reed pipes in two rows, one open and one closed so that octaves are produced, while another stone specimen has eight pipes and lateral finger-holes that lower certain pitches by a semitone.

records.l: trumpets, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: Trumpets were used by American Indians for signaling in war, ceremonies, mourning, and funeral dances. Examples include conch trumpets, long wooden or bamboo instruments, the juruparis, the turé, the Mexican acocotl, and the clay botuto.

records.l: Orinoco, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: Near the Orinoco, Gumilla found a wooden trumpet nearly seven feet long. He also observed the botuto among Indian tribes near the river; this baked-clay trumpet was commonly three or four feet long, though some were enormous, and its deep sound was used in mourning and funeral dances.

records.l: juruparis, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER VI.
records.s: The juruparis was a venerated trumpet of Indians on the Rio Haupés, a tributary of the Rio Negro. Women were forbidden to see it under threat of death, and youths could not see it until completing initiatory fastings and scourgings; it was hidden in a stream and brought out at night during feasts, when it was blown outside houses.

records.l: Musical Instruments, Musical Instruments, ” [Illustration] As regards instruments of percussion, a kind of drum deserves s
records.s: The unit describes the Mexican teponaztli, a wooden drum with two vibrating tongues that produced two regulated pitches. It discusses its construction, carvings, gum-covered drumsticks, varied sizes, loudness, and surviving examples among relatively isolated Mexican Indians. It also mentions related percussion instruments in other parts of America, including skin-covered drums, the Peruvian huanca, chhilchiles, and the Mexican ajacaxtli rattle. The rattle was made from a gourd or pottery, with small pebbles enclosed inside and a wooden handle sometimes attached.

records.l: teponaztli, Musical Instruments, ” [Illustration] As regards instruments of percussion, a kind of drum deserves s
records.s: The teponaztli was generally made from a single block of very hard wood, hollowed to leave a thin sound-board with two vibrating tongues. The tongues produced two distinct sounds whose interval could be a third, fourth, fifth, sixth, or octave, and their pitch could be regulated by shaving the wood. The instrument was carved with fanciful designs, played with sticks covered in elastic ule, and ranged from small neck-carried drums to specimens over five feet long that could be heard three miles away.

records.l: rattle, Musical Instruments, ” [Illustration] As regards instruments of percussion, a kind of drum deserves s
records.s: The rattle was popular among Indians before the discovery of America. The Mexicans called it ajacaxtli; it was usually made from an oval or round gourd pierced with holes, fitted with a wooden handle, and filled with small pebbles, though rattles were also made of pottery.

records.l: Musical Instruments, Musical Instruments, [Illustration] The Tezcucans (or Acolhuans) belonged to the same race as the Azt
records.s: The Tezcucans, also called Acolhuans, belonged to the same race as the Aztecs but were described as surpassing them in knowledge and social refinement. Their monarch Nezahualcoyotl opposed human sacrifice and built a temple dedicated to “The unknown god, the cause of causes,” whose nine-story tower held musical instruments for summoning worshippers to prayer. Ixtlilxochitl reported that the temple contained a sonorous metal struck with a mallet, though it is unclear whether it was a gong or a bell. The unit also discusses Peruvian bells, Mexican horse bells called yotl, and sonorous stones used as musical instruments in South America.

records.l: Tezcucans, Musical Instruments, [Illustration] The Tezcucans (or Acolhuans) belonged to the same race as the Azt
records.s: The Tezcucans, or Acolhuans, belonged to the same race as the Aztecs. They were described as greatly surpassing the Aztecs in knowledge and social refinement.

records.l: Aztecs, Musical Instruments, [Illustration] The Tezcucans (or Acolhuans) belonged to the same race as the Azt
records.s: The Aztecs belonged to the same race as the Tezcucans, who were described as surpassing them in knowledge and social refinement. The Aztecs used yotl-bells and represented them in picture-writings as objects paid in tribute to their sovereigns.

records.l: Nezahualcoyotl, Musical Instruments, [Illustration] The Tezcucans (or Acolhuans) belonged to the same race as the Azt
records.s: Nezahualcoyotl was a wise monarch of the Tezcucans who abhorred human sacrifices. He erected a temple dedicated to “The unknown god, the cause of causes.”

records.l: temple of the unknown god, Musical Instruments, [Illustration] The Tezcucans (or Acolhuans) belonged to the same race as the Azt
records.s: The temple was erected by Nezahualcoyotl and dedicated to “The unknown god, the cause of causes.” It had a nine-story tower topped with various musical instruments used to summon worshippers to prayer.

records.l: sonorous metal, Musical Instruments, [Illustration] The Tezcucans (or Acolhuans) belonged to the same race as the Azt
records.s: A sonorous metal at the top of the temple’s tower was struck with a mallet. The record does not make clear whether it was a gong or a bell.

records.l: Ixtlilxochitl, Musical Instruments, [Illustration] The Tezcucans (or Acolhuans) belonged to the same race as the Azt
records.s: Ixtlilxochitl was a native of Mexico and of royal descent who lived in the beginning of the seventeenth century. He described the sonorous metal in a historical essay and may have been familiar with the musical practices of his countrymen.

records.l: Peruvians, Musical Instruments, [Illustration] The Tezcucans (or Acolhuans) belonged to the same race as the Azt
records.s: The Peruvians were known to have used bells, since a small copper specimen was found in an old Peruvian tomb. They called their bells chanrares, although it remains uncertain whether that term referred instead to horse bells.

records.l: Peruvian bell, Musical Instruments, [Illustration] The Tezcucans (or Acolhuans) belonged to the same race as the Azt
records.s: A small copper bell was found in one of the old Peruvian tombs. The specimen was deposited in the museum at Lima, and M. de Castelnau published a drawing of it.

records.l: horse bells, Musical Instruments, [Illustration] The Tezcucans (or Acolhuans) belonged to the same race as the Azt
records.s: Horse bells were certainly known to the Mexicans, although it is uncertain whether the Peruvian name chanrares designated them. The bells were nearly round and were compared with the Schellen attached to horses by Germans.

records.l: yotl-bells, Musical Instruments, [Illustration] The Tezcucans (or Acolhuans) belonged to the same race as the Azt
records.s: The Mexicans called their horse bells yotl. Yotl-bells were depicted in Aztec picture-writings among the objects paid as tribute to sovereigns, and a cluster of them was held in the British museum's collection of Mexican antiquities.

records.l: sonorous stones, Musical Instruments, [Illustration] The Tezcucans (or Acolhuans) belonged to the same race as the Azt
records.s: Sonorous stones were known in South America and were used for musical purposes in olden times. When struck by a hard substance, they could produce musical or metallic sounds.

records.l: musical instrument of green sonorous stone, Musical Instruments, [Illustration] The Tezcucans (or Acolhuans) belonged to the same race as the Azt
records.s: G. T. Vigne saw this instrument among Indian antiquities preserved in Cuzco, Peru. It was a flat-sided, pointed, arched green stone about a foot long, with a hole for suspension; when struck, it produced a singularly musical note.

records.l: Amazon-stone, Musical Instruments, [Illustration] The Tezcucans (or Acolhuans) belonged to the same race as the Azt
records.s: Humboldt described Amazon-stone as producing a metallic sound when struck by a hard substance. American Indians formerly cut it into thin, centrally perforated plates and suspended them by strings; the stone was not found exclusively near the Amazon.

records.l: Musical Instruments, Musical Instruments, ” As regards the ancient stringed instruments of the American Indians our inform
records.s: The unit describes the musical instruments, songs, ceremonies, and musical institutions of the American Indians, especially the Mexicans, Tezcucans, and Peruvians. It discusses the uncertain evidence for ancient stringed instruments, including the Peruvian tinya, and compares American instruments and scales with those of Asia and other regions. It also records the use of music in warfare, agriculture, religious observances, mourning, public celebrations, and Christian missions. The unit concludes that present-day Indian musical practices preserve some ancient instruments and traditions but have also been affected by oppression and foreign influence.

records.l: American Indians, Musical Instruments, ” As regards the ancient stringed instruments of the American Indians our inform
records.s: The American Indians are described as having possessed varied musical instruments, songs, dances, ceremonies, and musical institutions before European discovery. Their musical traditions are compared with those of peoples in Asia, Africa, and other regions, while their present-day musical accomplishments are said to be below the standard of their ancestors.

records.l: stringed instruments of the American Indians, Musical Instruments, ” As regards the ancient stringed instruments of the American Indians our inform
records.s: Information about the ancient stringed instruments of the American Indians is described as scanty. The Peruvian tinya is identified as a five- or seven-stringed instrument that may have resembled a guitar, but no specimens are said to survive in museums because of the fragility of their materials.

records.l: Mexicans, Musical Instruments, ” As regards the ancient stringed instruments of the American Indians our inform
records.s: The Mexicans possessed historical, war, love, secular, and sacred songs, as well as musical instruments used in temples and public celebrations. Boys were taught sacred chants by priests, and professional musicians served persons of high position.

records.l: Aztecs, Musical Instruments, ” As regards the ancient stringed instruments of the American Indians our inform
records.s: The Aztecs are described as having many claims to civilization and as rivaling their neighbors in splendid living and magnificent structures. Clavigero stated that they were entirely unacquainted with stringed instruments, but the text questions the correctness of that claim.

records.l: Tezcucans, Musical Instruments, ” As regards the ancient stringed instruments of the American Indians our inform
records.s: The Tezcucans are described as being more advanced than the Aztecs in the cultivation of the arts and sciences. Their best histories, poems, code of laws, and dialect were regarded as superior, and Tezcuco possessed the Council of music.

records.l: Montezuma, Musical Instruments, ” As regards the ancient stringed instruments of the American Indians our inform
records.s: Montezuma is described as maintaining a grand establishment. J. Ranking claimed that fiddle, flute, snail-shell, kettle-drum, and other instruments were played during his repasts, but the text considers this assertion unreliable because its source is not given.

records.l: Peruvians, Musical Instruments, ” As regards the ancient stringed instruments of the American Indians our inform
records.s: The Peruvians possessed the five- or seven-stringed tinya and used trumpeters and drummers in their carefully organized military divisions. They held musical celebrations after victories, performed music at festivals and funerals, composed agricultural songs and elegiac haravis, and employed haravecs as minstrel-composers.

records.l: musical performances, Musical Instruments, ” As regards the ancient stringed instruments of the American Indians our inform
records.s: Musical performances were considered indispensable at public celebrations among the Peruvians and were used in warfare, festivals, mourning, agricultural labor, religious observances, and Christian missionary work. They included songs, instrumental music, dancing, processions, and dramatic representations.

records.l: Peru, Musical Instruments, ” As regards the ancient stringed instruments of the American Indians our inform
records.s: In Peru, each army division had trumpeters called cqueppacamayo and drummers called huancarcamayo. The country had agricultural songs, haravis, minstrels called haravecs, and religious and Christian musical performances that continued in some form among Indian Christians.

records.l: Inca, Musical Instruments, ” As regards the ancient stringed instruments of the American Indians our inform
records.s: The Inca was honored in Peruvian agricultural hymns that celebrated his deeds and dynasty. After returning victorious from battle, the Inca went first to the temple of the Sun to offer thanksgiving, and songs were also performed at the obsequies of deceased monarchs.

records.l: Prescott, Musical Instruments, ” As regards the ancient stringed instruments of the American Indians our inform
records.s: Prescott is cited for describing the grandeur and ostentatious pageantry of the Aztecs and the superior cultural attainments attributed to the Tezcucans. He also described Peruvian royal funeral observances involving processions, banners, bards, minstrels, and songs commemorating the dead monarch.

records.l: Peruvian agricultural songs, Musical Instruments, ” As regards the ancient stringed instruments of the American Indians our inform
records.s: Peruvian agricultural songs were sung while the people cultivated the lands of the Inca. Their words glorified the Inca and his dynasty, and their rhythm regulated the laborers' work; the songs often included the word hailli, meaning "Triumph."

records.l: Council of music, Musical Instruments, ” As regards the ancient stringed instruments of the American Indians our inform
records.s: The Council of music was an institution founded in Tezcuco to promote music along with history, astronomy, and other arts and sciences. It functioned as an academy for general education and is presented as evidence of the remarkable intellectual attainments of the Mexican Indians.

records.l: Nezahualcoyotl, Musical Instruments, ” As regards the ancient stringed instruments of the American Indians our inform
records.s: Nezahualcoyotl is identified as the wise monarch who founded the Council of music in Tezcuco. The institution advanced music, other arts, and sciences rather than serving music alone.

records.l: Tezcuco, Musical Instruments, ” As regards the ancient stringed instruments of the American Indians our inform
records.s: Tezcuco is described as the place where Nezahualcoyotl founded the Council of music. The unit also mentions a great temple at Tezcuco containing a sonorous metal object that some inquirers believed to be a gong.

records.l: central America, Musical Instruments, ” As regards the ancient stringed instruments of the American Indians our inform
records.s: In central America, Dominican priests composed a sacred poem in the Guatemalian dialect recounting important biblical events and performed it with musical instruments. The music influenced a powerful cazique and helped spread the new doctrines among his subjects.

records.l: pentatonic scale, Musical Instruments, ” As regards the ancient stringed instruments of the American Indians our inform
records.s: The Mexican pipe and Peruvian syrinx were deliberately constructed to produce only the intervals of the pentatonic scale. The scale is also associated in the unit with Peruvian cachua, Scotch national dances, Chinese instruments, and various ancient Asian peoples.

records.l: North American Indians, Musical Instruments, ” As regards the ancient stringed instruments of the American Indians our inform
records.s: North American Indians who converted to Christianity after the emigration of the puritans to New England were praised for their musical talent. Their singing of John Elliot's translation of the psalms into Indian verse was described by witnesses as excellent and most ravishing.

records.l: Guatemala, Musical Instruments, ” As regards the ancient stringed instruments of the American Indians our inform
records.s: Guatemala is identified as a place where the African marimba, introduced by slaves, became rather popular among the natives. The text says that such adaptations can be distinguished from genuine old Indian inventions.

records.l: Musical Instruments, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: The unit examines musical instruments used by European nations during the Middle Ages, relying on representations in manuscripts, sculptures, and paintings. It discusses the lyre, cithara, psalterium, harp, rotta, Welsh crwth, and various fiddles, while noting uncertainty about the dates and accuracy of some depictions. The text describes the development and changing names of these instruments, their relationships to Asiatic forms, and their use by Anglo-Saxons, German and Celtic bards, Scandinavian skalds, and other performers. King David is repeatedly shown playing instruments such as the harp, rotta, and lyre in medieval manuscripts.

records.l: European nations, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: The earliest known European instruments were more similar in form and construction to Asiatic instruments than later European examples. Little material improvement in European instrument construction is perceptible over nearly a thousand years, although evidence from the first five or six centuries of the Christian era is scarce.

records.l: Middle Ages, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: Representations of musical instruments from the Middle Ages survive in manuscripts, sculptures, and paintings. These sources provide valuable evidence, but their dates and accuracy are sometimes uncertain.

records.l: musical instruments, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: Medieval musical instruments are studied through artistic representations, with sculptures considered more reliable than frescoes. Their names often changed over time, and older Latin writers frequently applied the same name to instruments differing in form, power, and compass.

records.l: lyre, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: The lyre appears in Christian monuments dating from the fourth century, including one depiction of Christ as Apollo touching it. It was used in popular pastimes in western Europe, and ninth-century Anglo-Saxon imagery shows a gleeman playing it with a plectrum.

records.l: Anglo-Saxons, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: The Anglo-Saxons accompanied vocal performances with a harp that was more or less triangular and represented a transition from the lyre to the harp. An Anglo-Saxon manuscript also depicts one gleeman playing the lyre and another playing a double-pipe.

records.l: cithara, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: Cithara was a name applied to several stringed instruments that varied greatly in form, sound power, and compass. A ninth-century cithara from the St. Blasius manuscript appears to improve on the triangular psalterium because it has a small sound-board at the top.

records.l: psalterium, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: Medieval writers used psalterium for simple triangular and square stringed instruments, even though the forms differed. A small psalterium with strings over a sound-board was apparently the prototype of the citole, and the fourteenth-century psalterium had the trapezium shape of the dulcimer.

records.l: harp, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: The harp was especially popular in central and northern Europe and was favored by German and Celtic bards and Scandinavian skalds. Medieval representations include a harp with twelve strings and two sound holes, while some early forms lacked the front pillar.

records.l: king David, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: King David is depicted playing the harp in an Anglo-Saxon manuscript from the beginning of the eleventh century. Other manuscripts show him playing the rotta, including representations from the seventh, eighth, and tenth centuries.

records.l: Welsh crwth, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: The Welsh crwth is described as a species of fiddle resembling the rotta, but with a central finger-board and only a few strings. A modern crwth is illustrated, while an earlier three-stringed form called Crwth Trithant is described as resembling a violin or, more properly, a rebeck.

records.l: fiddle, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER VII.
records.s: An Anglo-Saxon fiddle, or fithele, from an eleventh-century manuscript has a pear-shaped body and four strings, although no bridge is shown. Fiddle-bow use is recorded in Germany in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, and Peterborough cathedral contains a possibly twelfth-century depiction whose instrument resembles the modern violin.

records.l: Musical Instruments, Musical Instruments, [Illustration] [Illustration] CHAPTER VIII.
records.s: The unit explains the construction and historical use of several medieval instruments, including the organistrum, monochord, wind instruments, organs, and percussion instruments. It describes the monochord as chiefly a theoretical instrument and notes the diatonic musical scale used about a thousand years ago, with both b-flat and b-natural. The organ developed from early pneumatic and hydraulic forms with very few pipes and required many performers to operate. It also distinguishes the portable regal organ from another instrument called the regal, consisting of sonorous wooden slabs.

records.l: monochord, Musical Instruments, [Illustration] [Illustration] CHAPTER VIII.
records.s: The monochord had a single string stretched over two fixed bridges on an oblong box. Its string could be tightened or slackened with a turning screw, while a movable bridge regulated the marked intervals; it was chiefly used by theorists and was poorly suited to musical performance.

records.l: musical scale, Musical Instruments, [Illustration] [Illustration] CHAPTER VIII.
records.s: About a thousand years ago, the musical scale was diatonic except for the seventh interval, which was chromatic because both b-flat and b-natural belonged to the scale. The notation of the period showed its compass and order of intervals.

records.l: Middle Ages, Musical Instruments, [Illustration] [Illustration] CHAPTER VIII.
records.s: During the middle ages, wind instruments included flutes, syrinxes, trumpets, hunting horns, sackbuts, and early forms of the organ. Some instruments had quaint forms and rude construction, while medieval concerts also used the cumbrous organistrum and various percussion instruments.

records.l: organ, Musical Instruments, [Illustration] [Illustration] CHAPTER VIII.
records.s: The organ is described as the most important wind instrument and the king of all musical instruments. Early organs had about a dozen pipes, and the largest made about nine hundred years ago had only three octaves without chromatic intervals; later examples show progress in construction. The pedal is generally attributed to Bernhard, who lived in Venice about 1470, though earlier indications of its invention exist.

records.l: hydraulic organ, Musical Instruments, [Illustration] [Illustration] CHAPTER VIII.
records.s: The pneumatic organ was sculptured on an obelisk erected in Constantinople under Theodosius the Great toward the end of the fourth century. Men standing on its bellows pressed them to supply wind. By the beginning of the fourteenth century, it appears to have entirely supplanted the hydraulic organ.

records.l: regal, Musical Instruments, [Illustration] [Illustration] CHAPTER VIII.
records.s: The regal was a small portable organ, often tastefully shaped and embellished, with keys generally like those of an organ but smaller. Sculptured representations survive in Beverley Minster and Melrose Abbey, and a painting by Melozzo da Forli shows a regal with keys resembling the pistons of certain brass instruments. The name regal was also applied to a percussion instrument made of sonorous wooden slabs arranged like a harmonica.

records.l: Musical Instruments, Musical Instruments, [Illustration] CHAPTER IX.
records.s: The unit examines medieval orchestras and the instruments represented in sculptures, noting that artists may have used imagination but probably depicted instruments familiar to their contemporaries. It describes a twelve-performer group formerly at St. Georges de Boscherville, including viols, harps, an organistrum, a syrinx, stringed instruments, and bells, as well as a tumbler. It discusses several types of viol and their tuning, including the development of side strings later used in instruments such as the theorbo and archlute. It also examines the orchestras on the Portico della gloria at Santiago da Compostella and in the minstrels’ gallery of Exeter cathedral.

records.l: orchestras of the Middle Ages, Musical Instruments, [Illustration] CHAPTER IX.
records.s: They are represented on medieval monuments, though their sculptors may have relied partly on imagination. The instruments shown were probably ones admitted into contemporary orchestras and provide evidence about medieval instrumental music.

records.l: orchestra at St. Georges de Boscherville, Musical Instruments, [Illustration] CHAPTER IX.
records.s: It is a twelve-performer group, reportedly dating from the end of the eleventh century and now preserved in the museum of Rouen. It includes performers on viols, an organistrum, a syrinx, several stringed instruments, harps, and a tintinnabulum, with a tumbler standing on his head.

records.l: St. Georges de Boscherville, Musical Instruments, [Illustration] CHAPTER IX.
records.s: Its abbey formerly displayed the bas-relief containing the twelve-performer musical group. The relief was later removed to the museum of Rouen.

records.l: viol, Musical Instruments, [Illustration] CHAPTER IX.
records.s: It appears in the St. Georges de Boscherville group in two playing positions: one instrument is held between the knees like a violoncello, while another is held almost like a violin. The viols at Santiago da Compostella are also shown in related forms.

records.l: harp, Musical Instruments, [Illustration] CHAPTER IX.
records.s: Small harps appear in the St. Georges de Boscherville orchestra, including one played by a crowned musician. Another crowned musician plays a harp with a plectrum in the right hand and the fingers of the left hand.

records.l: viol family, Musical Instruments, [Illustration] CHAPTER IX.
records.s: Several kinds were used, differing in size, compass, number of strings, and tuning. One type had a string beside the finger-board, while other types placed all strings over it; side strings were later adopted on instruments including the lira di braccio and lute.

records.l: violin, Musical Instruments, [Illustration] CHAPTER IX.
records.s: Its modern manner of being held may have an older origin than expected, since one medieval viol is shown held almost precisely as the violin is held.

records.l: orchestra on the Portico della gloria, Musical Instruments, [Illustration] CHAPTER IX.
records.s: It consists of twenty-four seated, life-sized figures in high relief, each holding an instrument. The group includes an organistrum, small and triangular harps, salterios, and several forms of vihuela; the performers are tuning or preparing rather than actively playing.

records.l: Portico della gloria, Musical Instruments, [Illustration] CHAPTER IX.
records.s: It is the triple portal of the pilgrimage church at Santiago da Compostella. Its central arch contains the twenty-four musical elders, and an inscription on the lintel states that it was executed in 1188.

records.l: Santiago da Compostella, Musical Instruments, [Illustration] CHAPTER IX.
records.s: Its famous pilgrimage church contains the Portico della gloria, whose sculptures show instruments used in Spain around the twelfth century. A cast of the sculpture is held in the Kensington museum.

records.l: twenty-four elders, Musical Instruments, [Illustration] CHAPTER IX.
records.s: They are represented as seated figures around the central arch of the Portico della gloria, each with an instrument. Their instruments include organistrum, harps, salterios, and different forms of vihuela.

records.l: vihuela, Musical Instruments, [Illustration] CHAPTER IX.
records.s: The Spanish viol of the twelfth century is represented in several forms on the Portico della gloria. Some resemble the rebec and have three strings, while larger examples have broader bodies, incurved sides, and different sound-holes; no bows are shown.

records.l: minstrels’ gallery of Exeter cathedral, Musical Instruments, [Illustration] CHAPTER IX.
records.s: Its fourteenth-century front has twelve niches, each containing a winged figure or angel playing an instrument. The instruments identified include the cittern, bagpipe, clarion, rebec, psaltery, syrinx, sackbut, regals, gittern, shalm, timbrel, and cymbals.

records.l: Exeter cathedral, Musical Instruments, [Illustration] CHAPTER IX.
records.s: It contains the fourteenth-century minstrels’ gallery, whose sculptured front represents twelve angelic or winged instrumentalists. A cast of this sculpture is also held at South Kensington.

records.l: Musical Instruments, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER X.
records.s: The chapter surveys post-mediæval instruments, including the virginal, lute, theorbo, viols, recorder, bagpipe, bells, and carillons, describing their construction, use, tone, and historical development. It explains that older instruments often had distinctive and attractive tone qualities and ornamentation, even though modern instruments have been more highly perfected. The chapter discusses bell-ringing and carillon traditions in England and various European countries, including their mechanisms and musical possibilities. It concludes that the history of music helps explain the characteristics of musical instruments and the effects composers create with them.

records.l: virginal, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER X.
records.s: The virginal originated during the middle ages and became highly popular at a later period. A specimen from the time of Elizabeth was held at South Kensington.

records.l: lute, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER X.
records.s: The lute was once nearly as popular as the pianoforte. It developed from four pairs of catgut strings to instruments with many more strings, used frets made of tightly fastened catgut, and varied in size from treble-lutes to bass-lutes. Lutes were valued for their rich, mellow tone and elegant decoration, although they later fell into oblivion.

records.l: pianoforte, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER X.
records.s: The pianoforte was invented at the beginning of the eighteenth century and became highly popular. Its characteristics inspired composers to create effects that cannot be properly rendered on other instruments.

records.l: theorbo, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER X.
records.s: The theorbo was a double-necked lute that appears to have come into use during the sixteenth century. It had additional bass strings beside the finger-board that could not be shortened by the fingers; its largest forms were the archlute and chitarrone.

records.l: recorder, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER X.
records.s: The recorder was known in Shakespeare's time, as shown by the stage direction in Hamlet, but it later became scarce. An illustration of the instrument was copied from a London work of 1683.

records.l: bagpipe, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER X.
records.s: The bagpipe was a long-established favorite among Celtic races and was also admired by Slavonic nations. In Poland and the Ukraine it could be made from the whole skin of a goat, while the instrument was of high antiquity in Ireland and was represented in Irish sources.

records.l: bell, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER X.
records.s: The bell was especially popular in England, where bell-ringing had been a favored amusement for centuries. Bells were suspended in varied ways in different countries, including separate towers, timber frames, church gateways, and even oak trees.

records.l: England, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER X.
records.s: England had a long tradition of bell-ringing and peal-ringing. Paul Hentzner reported in 1598 that English people enjoyed loud noises and sometimes rang bells for hours, while Egelric of Croyland was recorded as having cast six bells around 960.

records.l: carillon, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER X.
records.s: The carillon consists of a set of differently sized and tuned bells and was especially popular in the Netherlands and Belgium, though it also appeared elsewhere in Europe. It could be operated by clockwork or by a performer using manual keys and pedals; its sound was intended to be heard from a distance, since rapid passages could become confused when heard nearby.

records.l: peal-ringing, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER X.
records.s: Peal-ringing was described as a pastime especially national to England. Peals commonly contained eight bells tuned to the diatonic scale, though sets of ten or twelve also occurred, and the bells were swung forcefully so that their mouths rose completely upward.

records.l: musical instruments, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER X.
records.s: Musical instruments had greatly improved in construction since the previous century, but this progress was thought by some to have reduced variety in tone color. Older instruments were often more distinctive in sound and more beautiful in appearance, and each instrument's characteristics made it especially suitable for particular musical effects.

records.l: history of music, Musical Instruments, CHAPTER X.
records.s: The history of music was presented as a means of explaining the development and characteristics of musical instruments. Studying the music of different nations was said to clarify features that would otherwise appear obscure.

records.l: Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: The document is a sequence of reflective essays and character sketches concerned with self-knowledge, vanity, morality, intellectual life, public conduct, national feeling, and prejudice. It opens with a narrator candidly examining his own loneliness, wounded vanity, failed influence, and difficulty in knowing himself, arguing that sympathy and attention to other people correct egoism. Writing, he says, encourages confessional garrulousness by imagining a distant approving audience. His memories of his father, a beloved country parson, and of childhood journeys through England explain his affection for the past and rural landscape, even while he recognizes that present England is changing and that London now claims him most strongly. A series of portraits then exposes particular moral and intellectual failures. Merman’s scholarly dispute with Grampus ruins his prospects, finances, and peace, showing the cruelty surrounding the worship of Truth. Lentulus embodies baseless self-confidence; Hinze empty deference; Touchwood destructive bad temper; Spike the way private commercial interests can become practical public politics; Mordax vanity and cruelty under contradiction; Mixtus the confusion of former ideals with wealth and fashionable life; Ganymede the enduring illusion of being “young”; Vorticella the self-importance of minor authorship; and Pepin and other prolific writers the dangers of writing faster than knowledge or judgment permit. The essays repeatedly distinguish real moral seriousness from appearances. They condemn universal burlesque, plagiarism and careless claims of originality, self-deception, inaccurate personal testimony, and a narrow morality that excuses public dishonesty so long as private family conduct seems respectable. Genuine morality requires knowledge and sympathy in every relation, including politics, commerce, journalism, and workmanship. The closing sections widen from individual character to society and history. Trost disputes the narrator’s speculation that self-supplying, self-repairing machines might supersede humanity. The discussion then turns to national memory, the treatment of Jews, and European exclusion. Rejecting the idea that Jews are an inexplicable exception, the text traces their endurance through foreign rule, dispersion, and persecution; condemns Christian persecution as contrary to Christ’s teachings; recognizes Jewish national pride and capacities; and considers whether preserved national feeling and favorable conditions could support renewed Jewish national life. Throughout, the document urges clearer perception, humility, sympathy, and resistance to vanity, cruelty, and inherited prejudice.

records.l: the narrator, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: The narrator is a bachelor and fellow human being who studies his own character with unusual tenacity of memory for his actions, sufferings, and private inward experience. Though he wants approbation, love, and social acceptance, and lacks acceptance and the love of the person he loves best, he recognizes his own vanity, cowardice about candid opinions, absurdity, and the shared weaknesses he detects in others. Reticent in conversation but garrulous in writing, he imagines an audience, distrusts judgments on manuscripts, and becomes a listener to others' confidences. His effort to attend to other lives develops into a habit of resisting self-partiality and judging neighbours fairly. As the youngest and only surviving child of his father and also his mother's child, he receives the past through childhood and his father's recollections. His father teaches reverence for Government and distrust of rebels, reformers, and revolutionary doctrine. He forms an early attachment to national rural landscape, while admitting that illusion may shape it. Yet he rejects contempt for contemporaries and idealization of earlier ages: every age has poetic and prosaic elements. Affectionate toward the present age, he is content to belong to it; although he loves remembered landscape, his consciousness becomes metropolitan and he identifies with London. His observations of others test this self-aware outlook. He first reads Lentulus's reserve as possible hidden poetry or revolutionary philosophy, then learns that it masks unsupported confidence rather than greatness. He knows and later re-encounters Ganymede, seeing outward age in him while recognizing that habit and others' reactions preserve Ganymede's belief in his own youth. Advanced in age himself, though resisting that description, the narrator remains observant, humane, self-questioning, and alert to the distance between appearance, self-belief, and reality.
records.t: The narrator is a bachelor and fellow human being who studies his own character with unusual tenacity of memory for his actions, sufferings, and private inward experience. Though he wants approbation, love, and social acceptance—and lacks acceptance and the love of the person he loves best—he recognizes his own vanity, cowardice about candid opinions, absurdity, and the shared weaknesses he detects in others. Reticent in conversation but garrulous in writing, he imagines an audience, distrusts judgments on manuscripts, and becomes a listener to others' confidences. His effort to attend to other lives develops into a habit of resisting self-partiality and judging neighbours fairly. As the youngest and only surviving child of his father and also his mother's child, he receives the past through childhood and his father's recollections. His father teaches reverence for Government and distrust of rebels, reformers, and revolutionary doctrine. He forms an early attachment to national rural landscape, while admitting that illusion may shape it. Yet he rejects contempt for contemporaries and idealization of earlier ages: every age has poetic and prosaic elements. Affectionate toward the present age, he is content to belong to it; although he loves remembered landscape, his consciousness becomes metropolitan and he identifies with London. His observations of others test this self-aware outlook. He first reads Lentulus's reserve as possible hidden poetry or revolutionary philosophy, then learns that it masks unsupported confidence rather than greatness. He knows and later re-encounters Ganymede, seeing outward age in him while recognizing that habit and others' reactions preserve Ganymede's belief in his own youth. Advanced in age himself, though resisting that description, the narrator remains observant, humane, self-questioning, and alert to the distance between appearance, self-belief, and reality.

records.l: self-knowledge and self-ignorance, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Self-knowledge is an incomplete natural history of one’s inward self, limited by self-ignorance and possible self-betrayal. It begins with recognizing that others may see hidden powers, appearance, delusion, and betrayal; it unfolds through examining one’s absurdities and others’ tendencies, despite unawareness and outdated self-traditions.

records.l: self-partiality and egoism, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Self-partiality and egoism distort judgment through self-satisfaction or discontent, foster spiritual pride through egoistic consolation, and are corrected by rejecting personal benefit as central to justice.

records.l: the human race, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: The human race is presented as a conscious organismic species whose members differ in mental climate, solar energy, and the scale of their feelings and tendencies, yet can recognize one another through shared possibilities. It produces ideas and combinations as a sum total, but is marked by absurdity, self-delusion, incompetence, and condemning in others what it practices itself. Currently working with slovenly approximativeness and self-defeating inaccuracy, it may decline into weakness and degeneracy as machines take over, or become the nervous centre of increasingly refined mechanical processes.

records.l: acquaintances, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: The acquaintances perceive the narrator’s powers, appearance, weaknesses, and awkwardness more readily than he does, sometimes discouraging him. They confide triumphs, grievances, theories, and private experiences in him as a sympathetic listener. As he reflects on their weaknesses, his reticence becomes written garrulousness and may involve superior, barbarous laughter.

records.l: Delectable Mountain, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: is_a desired standpoint [for seeing things with reduced self-partiality] The narrator imagines Delectable Mountain as a standpoint from which he might see things with proportions less determined by self-partiality. It represents the impartial perspective he strives to reach.

records.l: the world, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: contains a myriad of struggling lives [each life dear to itself] The narrator regards the world as a mighty volume containing the struggling action of a myriad lives, each life being as dear to itself as his is to him. Attending to the world's varied matter can free him from narrow self-occupation.

records.l: the narrator's published humorous romance, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: A humorous, unique published romance, it fails through flatness and insufficient subtlety, despite being tasted in Cherokee translation; the speaker’s reticence about self becomes garrulousness on paper.

records.l: autobiography, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: is necessarily incomplete [because of reticence and self-ignorance] The narrator holds that autobiography must be incomplete because of both necessary reticence and self-ignorance. He says that self-betrayal can partly compensate for what an autobiographer deliberately or unknowingly leaves out.

records.l: sympathy and interest in others, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Sympathy and interest in others overcome self-occupation by widening personal sensitivity. The narrator develops beneficent fellow-feeling by attending to others’ experiences rather than redirecting confidences to himself, then argues that sympathy should restrain harmful conduct by prioritizing grace toward those immediately affected alongside future good.

records.l: writing and authorship, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Writing and authorship are a creative act that give the speaker a delightful illusion of an audience and turn personal reticence into freedom on paper. Yet, when pursued incessantly for publication rather than knowledge or veracity, they bring harmful internal consequences: premature judgment, vanity or income tied to error, dulled vision, and pleasure in others’ mistakes. Authorship therefore requires scruple.

records.l: the audience, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: The imagined audience is a hazy, far-off, multitudinous assemblage, nearer in idiom than the Cherokees and more numerous than the One. Its imagined approval turns the speaker's reticence into garrulous writing; a distinct member would inhibit it.

records.l: the illusion of an audience, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: An illusion of a liberal, far-off, hazy assembly, numerous and idiom-near, is kept as manuscripts face judgment outside imagination, but is fatalized when a distinct auditor or foreground physiognomy emerges.

records.l: authors, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Authors are a miscellaneous class afflicted by physical and moral disorders, especially chronic ailments in those who produce little yet overvalue their work, and accept pleasing punishment for the One.

records.l: the manuscripts, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: The manuscripts are left to judgment outside the speaker’s imagination; feared as flat and lacking subtilty, they unfold from reticent self-expression into paper garrulousness and may end as fuel for a domestic fire.

records.l: the friend, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: A friend reads and judges the speaker’s manuscripts, perhaps exasperated, to protect against posthumous error; before burial, the speaker avoids asking the friend’s true opinion, fearing proof that the work is flat.

records.l: judgment of the manuscripts, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: is_outside the speaker's imagination Judgment of the manuscripts is left outside the speaker's imagination. The speaker wishes the friend to use judgment only to insure against a posthumous mistake, not to deliver a candid verdict during the speaker's life.

records.l: the weaknesses of acquaintances, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: are_subject_to loving laughter [along with the speaker's own pettiness] The speaker intends to note the weaknesses of acquaintances while acknowledging fellowship with them. Such observations are presented as compatible with a loving laughter rather than merely with superiority.

records.l: loving laughter, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: recognises_superiority_in the ideal self [as the only recognised superiority] Loving laughter recognizes the superiority not of the laugher over others but of the ideal self. It holds up the mirror and the scourge to the speaker's pettiness as well as to the pettiness of neighbours.

records.l: the ideal self, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: is the God within [as understood in loving laughter] The ideal self is the only recognized superiority in loving laughter. It holds the mirror and the scourge against human pettiness.

records.l: God, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: God is the God within, part of the ideal self; it holds mirror and scourge confronting our own and our neighbours’ pettiness, emerging in written garrulousness from conversational reticence.

records.l: the narrator's father, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: The narrator’s father was an English country parson, a Tory, and a small-scale pluralist, born about the same time as Scott and Wordsworth. Raised in close contact with aristocracy and experienced among miners, weavers, labourers, farmers, and other parishioners, he believed clergy should share something of every class. He carefully collected tithe and relied on a recurring year’s supply of sermons, yet remained beloved because he kept no lasting quarrel with rich or poor. He revered Government, Church, and Constitution, regarded rebels and revolutionary teachers as evil or foolish, and held that national welfare required strong rule, order, gratitude, and obedient subjects.

records.l: contemporaries, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Contemporaries are often unfairly flouted by people who praise the ancients or an imagined past. The narrator insists that those doing the actual work of the world deserve affection and fairness, even though they have faults.

records.l: retrospective optimists, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Retrospective optimists idealize the past, scorn contemporaries, and praise ancients; the narrator says they ignore vulgar, sordid elements in Greece and Italy.

records.l: the present age, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: The present age mixes ugly modern things with lost ancient beauty, yet offers work, insight, poetry, and benevolence, prompting its narrator to accept rather than grumble.

records.l: the past, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: The past mixes beauty with ugliness and social limitations; rather than idealizing it as majestic, the narrator values it through personal memory and inheritance.

records.l: the narrator's childhood, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: The narrator's childhood is a warm, formative period rooted in family affection, his father's sermons, stories, popularity, and England. After his mother's death, he lives among parishioners at different homesteads, preferring their variety to the Hall. Riding his pony beside his father through surrounding parishes, he absorbs people and landscapes, imagines crises with swords and firearms, and develops lasting loves of rural scenery and inherited traditions.

records.l: the narrator's father's time, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: The narrator’s father’s youth, recalled personally, reveals varied social ranks and rural English life as a period neither wholly prosaic nor admirable, giving the narrator enduring perspective.

records.l: London, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: London is a busy, anxious metropolitan environment of thought, strife, hunger, and responsive political, social, and literary weather-signs. It frames the narrator's bachelor hearth and sense of belonging to the Nation of London, with a Square garden sycamore. It also begins Mixtus's meeting with Scintilla and grows into the site of his mansion and wealthy, mixed social entertainments.

records.l: England, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: England is the narrator’s Motherland, a country rooted in native landscape, national life, language, the English Church, and Constitution. Its countryside, woodlands, pastures, fields, rivers, villages, markets, hedgerows, and midland plains, formed the narrator’s early understanding of human life and remains affectionately significant. England is marked by stability, historical continuity, and a conservative spirit, while also changing gradually in institutions, technology, labor, and political attitudes without great convulsions. Its central shared principle is refusal of foreign rule, with national life defended even through improvised resistance. At the same time, hospitality and freedom are presented as world-wide blessings, making exclusion of peaceful foreigners inconsistent with its interests.
records.t: England is the narrator’s Motherland, a country rooted in native landscape, national life, language, the English Church, and Constitution. Its countryside—woodlands, pastures, fields, rivers, villages, markets, hedgerows, and midland plains—formed the narrator’s early understanding of human life and remains affectionately significant. England is marked by stability, historical continuity, and a conservative spirit, while also changing gradually in institutions, technology, labor, and political attitudes without great convulsions. Its central shared principle is refusal of foreign rule, with national life defended even through improvised resistance. At the same time, hospitality and freedom are presented as world-wide blessings, making exclusion of peaceful foreigners inconsistent with its interests.

records.l: Greece, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: is_a modern nation [whose independence is attributed to the presence of ancient Greece in European consciousness] Greece is presented as having become free partly because ancient Greece remained present in European consciousness. Its past supplied an ideal identification that helped inspire support for modern Greece.

records.l: Italy, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: has_been_unified through national memory [under the influence of Mazzini and Dante's example] Italy is presented as having been transformed from a territory associated with idling, dynastic convenience, and foreign control into a renewed national power. This change is attributed chiefly to memory, which inspired Mazzini and others with a sense of Italian greatness.

records.l: the parishioners, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: The parishioners, including miners, weavers, field-labourers, and farmers, grumble while paying tithes and obligations to the narrator's father, yet welcome and love him; after the narrator's mother's death, they care for the nine-year-old narrator at their homesteads.

records.l: the English rural population, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: is mixed [in the present day] The English rural population of the narrator's father's time included miners, weavers, field-labourers, farmers, and people of other ranks whose motives and habits could be learned through daily fellowship. The narrator suggests that this population may have changed enough that his father would find the present rural population difficult to understand.

records.l: the English countryside, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: The English countryside is a national landscape of midland uplands and plains, woodlands, pastures, hedgerows, roadsides, rivers, villages, markets, cottages, barns, and churches. Readily altered by human labour yet marked by permanence and railway-driven world-wide change, it roots national life and language, inspires affectionate joy and sympathy with labour, and fosters tender attachment to the past and conservative prepossessions.

records.l: the Government, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Government, revered by the narrator’s father as the chief force for maintaining order, is opposed in the narrator’s learning to the morally charged idea of a rebel.

records.l: the old England, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Old England is a remembered rural society, romantically exciting to the narrator, with a living good old king. Before parliamentary reform, it has saleable or privately presented boroughs, waterless prisons mixing felons and maniacs, bloated charities, non-resident jovial clergy, militia-balloting, and ignorance of later judgment.

records.l: the national life of England, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: England’s national life is a distinctive tradition-rooted continuity, likened to scenery: it avoids great convulsions yet responds delicately to political, social, and technological change. Though it retains a family likeness, rapid loss of traditions, customs, language, habits, and sentiments may weaken it; preservation requires moderating inevitable change.

records.l: the industrial transformation of the landscape, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: is_a sign of world-wide change [visible in the countryside] Industrial transformation appears in canals, railways, steam, navvies, cuttings, bridges, and changed levels through the hills. These works visibly insert new directions of human labor into the landscape without wholly erasing its familiar expression.

records.l: Truth, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Truth, a serene beneficent goddess, receives worship amid controversy as worshippers commit cruelty through sarcasm, ridicule, and attacks.

records.l: Merman, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Merman is a lawyer, conveyancer, writer, and editor whose early promise and budding practice fail to advance. Married to Julia with two children, he supports himself partly through miscellaneous periodical writing while pursuing moral, physical, linguistic, and historical studies. For many years he investigates ancient civilisations and proposes a connection among symbolic monuments of widely scattered races. Convinced that Grampus is wrong about Magicodumbras and Zuzumotzis, he writes a book attacking Grampus's interpretation. A review answers with epigrams and ridicule, making Merman widely notorious; the learned know him more through the attack than by reading him. He remains civil but firm in controversy, studies German print and Pali intensely, and publishes a condensed sixty-page rejoinder, admitting mistakes while defending his central theory. The dispute damages his former reputation as a sober thinker, safe writer, and sound lawyer, and causes him to neglect his legal and editorial career. Under want he accepts a post far beneath earlier prospects. In later life he is conspicuously poor, becomes a bore through repeating his arguments, and grows bitter toward the world after public and opponents' treatment.

records.l: Julia Merman, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Julia Merman is Merman’s supportive wife, affectionate and heroic amid domestic hardship. Guided by his ideas, she avoids disagreement and tries not to increase his troubles. As his controversy leaves the household with declining resources and he grows indifferent, she preserves the home’s charm, reduces wants, manages finances, and secretly sells her best wedding jewel to pay rent.

records.l: Grampus, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Grampus is an eminent, world-famous Cetacean scholar and author of an influential work on ancient civilisations. Challenged by Merman, he publishes a crushing review defending sound inquiry and exposing alleged ignorance and errors. His authority deters rebuttal; he later leaves Merman unanswered while followers continue his research, arguments, and attacks, amid Merman's claim that Grampus shifts ground and appropriates ideas.

records.l: Magicodumbras, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: The Magicodumbras are symbolic monuments or related historical subjects linking widely scattered races in Merman’s disputed theory. Merman rejects Grampus’s account, while public discussion warns that lax views threaten sound inquiry. Repeated as supposed absurdity, they are treated as subsidiary to Grampus’s system and bring Merman no financial support.

records.l: Zuzumotzis, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: The Zuzumotzis are subsidiary elements in Grampus's system and, paired with the Magicodumbras, central to Merman's theory about ancient civilisations. Merman claims a correct clue, but Grampus's attack turns the theory into ridicule; the names become associated with absurd ideas, harming Merman's reputation and income.

records.l: the connection of symbolic monuments, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: concerns Magicodumbras [and Zuzumotzis] The possible connection of symbolic monuments common to widely scattered races gives Merman his breakthrough idea. He believes this connection will regenerate history, transform views of social origins, and correct Grampus's account.

records.l: the comparative history of the ancient civilisations, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: is_an_interest_of Merman [longstanding] Merman has studied the comparative history of the ancient civilisations for many years without allowing it to narrow his attention to other subjects. He later concentrates on it and produces the theory that brings him into conflict with Grampus.

records.l: the dispute between Grampus and Merman, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: The dispute begins when Merman publishes a book correcting and attacking Grampus’s account of the Magicodumbras and Zuzumotzis. Though it gains attention in America, Germany, England, France, and Paris, Merman’s rejoinder does not provoke Grampus. Grampus’s followers spread ridicule through publications, lectures, journalism, popular literature, and sermons, damaging Merman’s legal and editorial career and contributing to his bitterness and decline.

records.l: Grampus's epoch-making work, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: is_a book [widely acclaimed as a revelation] Grampus's epoch-making work is widely praised as a revelation and is initially known to Merman through his study of ancient civilisations. Merman concludes that Grampus is wrong about the Magicodumbras and Zuzumotzis and writes a book intended to overturn his conclusions.

records.l: Merman's book, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Merman's book attacks Grampus's interpretation and presents a theory about the Magicodumbras, Zuzumotzis, and ancient social origins; Grampus's crushing review makes its mistakes widely discussed.

records.l: the truth-worship controversy, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: The truth-worship controversy is a publicly sanctioned conflict in which sarcasm and slanderous ridicule inflict cruel, lasting harm; Merman's treatment after challenging Grampus exemplifies its progression from challenge to maiming.

records.l: the review attack on Merman, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: The review attack on Merman appears in the leading Review three weeks after Grampus read the book. Written recognizably by Grampus, it pillories Merman’s alleged incompetence, portraying him as imprecise and unlearned and making him widely amusing and notorious.

records.l: Merman's counter-theory, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Merman's counter-theory concerns Magicodumbras and Zuzumotzis. Merman defends its fundamental correctness despite collateral mistakes, rejects minute learning as an obstacle to judgment, favors history and varied observation, and later sees its main idea adopted without credit.

records.l: the rejoinder, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: The rejoinder is a sixty-page work of concentrated argument in which Merman acknowledges his mistakes, restates his theory, and offers alternative interpretations of evidence cited by Grampus. It is eventually printed by a modest medium without requiring Merman to pay for insertion, but it receives no reply from Grampus and instead prompts further ridicule by Grampus's followers.

records.l: Merman's legal and editorial career, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: is irretrievably damaged [by the controversy] Merman neglects rare clients and editorial opportunities while researching and writing about the controversy. His reputation as a sober thinker, safe writer, and sound lawyer is irretrievably damaged, his contributions become too dull to attract editors, and he is eventually forced into a post far beneath his earlier prospects.

records.l: Merman's household finances, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Merman's household finances are strained by his unprofitable controversy; capital is nearly exhausted, Julia cuts wants and sells a wedding jewel for rent, and Merman's low-level post becomes necessary.

records.l: Merman's bitterness and decline, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Merman's bitterness and decline is a chronic, irrevocable deterioration caused by prolonged disappointment and resistance. His certainty and resentment grow amid criticism and ridicule; he becomes inflexible, loses friends and opportunities, and suffers mental weakening. Though he later speaks less and admits errors, the damage endures.

records.l: Lentulus, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Lentulus is a man remembered as fair in society: well-looking, polite, acceptable, sociable at clubs and dinners, and supported by a business in which he does nothing. Benevolent and free from envy, hatred, and malice, he nevertheless has vast, ignorant confidence in his own rambling originality. He dismisses poets, philosophers, and scientific thought as mistaken, knows little of particular poets or doctrines, and defines poetry as artificial language expressing unreal sentiments. He claims to compose superior poetry spontaneously, considers writing on philosophic thinking, and expects his views on electricity to offend the scientific world. Yet he never clearly develops these reformative ideas; his silence leaves his vague, addled conclusions harmless.

records.l: vanity and arrogance, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Vanity and arrogance are complacent self-estimate unwarranted by performance, sometimes hidden by silence or apparent neutrality that avoids testing. Though compatible with worthy character, unchecked conceit becomes cruel and self-justifying; wider reason must restrain these fierce inner beasts.

records.l: society, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: misjudges Lentulus [as an unopinionated, useful social listener] Society mistakes Lentulus for an agreeable, unopinionated man who can serve as an admiring listener or vote for others' friends. Lentulus believes that the confused condition of society reveals widespread errors in thinking, marriage, social arrangements, and moral schemes.

records.l: poets, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: are_admired_by narrator [with grateful admiration across all ages] Lentulus assents to praise of celebrated poets with visible reserve, as though he knows that they are merely versifiers. He knows little of particular poets but believes that poetry should use true ideas and that the world has no notion what poetry will become; the narrator concludes that Lentulus cannot eclipse or fundamentally revise the poets.

records.l: philosophers, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Lentulus treats philosophers as mistaken and suggests that all thinking before his own has been an elaborate error. He names Plato, Robert Owen, and Dr Tuffle as equally wrong, despite lacking a developed knowledge of philosophical systems.

records.l: poetics, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Lentulus implies that existing poetics is inadequate and that he could establish principles for a new kind of poetry. The narrator initially suspects that Lentulus possesses a revolutionary treatise on poetics, but learns that Lentulus has neither written such a work nor clearly formulated its principles.

records.l: philosophic thinking, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Lentulus claims that philosophic thinking has been fundamentally mistaken until the beginning of his own reflections. His proposed insights range loosely over logic, miracles, marriage, electricity, motives, and causes, but remain unwritten or insufficiently organized.

records.l: human error, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: is_subject_to Lentulus [through his mistaken confidence in private insights] Lentulus regards human error as pervasive in poetry, philosophy, science, social institutions, and ordinary reasoning. He treats his unfamiliarity with established doctrines as evidence that he can correct the errors of previous thinkers, though the narrator sees his conclusions as blind denials and disjointed commonplaces.

records.l: heterodoxy, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
