records.s: is_regarded_as power [by Lentulus, in itself] Lentulus regards heterodoxy as a power in itself and mistakes his lack of acquaintance with established doctrines for creative dissidence. His heterodox opinions remain mostly private because he lacks the words to turn them into a system or gather followers.

records.l: human imagination, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Powerful imagination begins as intense inward representation, not confusion of fact with fancy. Fed by susceptibility to minutiae of experience, it uses definite knowledge for creative inward construction, combines ideal and associative power with clear ordinary reality, and does not measure posterity by present poverty.

records.l: Hinze, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Hinze is an Alsatian man from a family settled in England for more than one generation. Well off and gentlemanly educated, he seeks above all to stand well with the justly distinguished and to present himself correctly. He cultivates low-toned tete-a-tete, praises wisdom, elevates ordinary remarks, and cites distinguished opinions. His deference serves neither ambition nor gain, including with Tulpian, and he has no doubleness toward Felicia. Lacking genuine judgments or lasting impressions, he is not consciously false or fairly a hypocrite.

records.l: Felicia, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Felicia is a clever, sensible, vivacious, kindly-disposed woman who helps her distinguished husband and welcomes visitors. She finds Babes in the Wood enchanting; speaking with Hinze, his reverence embarrasses her, and she resists being treated as an oracle.

records.l: Shakspere, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: is_expected_to_be_known_through burlesques [in the coming generation] Shakspere is said to be falsely reputed to be known by the English people in the present generation. The unit predicts that the next generation may know him chiefly through burlesques and that his plays may acquire a new life as pantomimes.

records.l: excessive deference (Hinze's behavior), Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Hinze’s excessive deference is a habitual, studious and deliberate insincerity: make-believe reverence without deep motive or a calculated search for patronage. It unfolds through lowered voice, downcast eyes, hat handling, worshipful tones, compliments, grand questions, inflated commonplace opinions, and eager attention to Tulpian and others’ authority, without sneering or backbiting.

records.l: insincerity (social intercourse), Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Insincerity in social intercourse is a common incidental frailty: people may seek to be agreeable, avoid offense, lack exact words, or fill gaps with familiar opinions. Little unpremeditated insincerity merits lenience, but deliberate, studied, persistent make-believe, especially without appetite, purpose, or admiration, deserves impatience.
records.t: Insincerity in social intercourse is a common incidental frailty: people may seek to be agreeable, avoid offense, lack exact words, or fill gaps with familiar opinions. Little unpremeditated insincerity merits lenience, but deliberate, studied, persistent make-believe—especially without appetite, purpose, or admiration—deserves impatience.

records.l: temper, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Temper is primarily the proportion and mode in which qualities are mingled, and commonly an habitual state or general tendency. Popular judgment may excuse bad temper as separate from character, yet it can cause rude, cruel, inconsistent, and unjust behaviour, disrupting healthy mental habits and harmony among perception, conviction, and impulse.

records.l: Touchwood, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Touchwood is generally regarded as a good fellow, honourable gentleman, steadfast friend, defender of the oppressed, and affectionate-hearted person with high character, gifts, and abilities. Yet his chronic, severe, capricious, pugnacious temper dominates his conduct: he is insolent, quarrelsome, haughty, neglectful, antagonistic, harsh without provocation, and inconsistently opposed even to benevolent measures he sympathizes with. Though thought capable of excellent public service or a great book, his temper makes intimacy insupportable and raises doubt that he could preserve sound judgment and integrity as a public man.

records.l: character, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: High character requires reliable, principled habits: good feelings and deeds cannot outweigh repeated unjust, rude, cruel, or unreliable conduct, and it likely cannot coexist with a temper like Touchwood's.

records.l: bad-tempered man, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: A bad-tempered man may have good feelings, do good deeds, and be fundamentally well disposed, yet repeated temper makes his conduct ugly and undermines character. Apologies, amends, friendliness, and promises cannot erase injuries; only a substantial lasting benefit to present and future generations could compensate.

records.l: public man, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: A public man, especially one like Touchwood, is vulnerable to partisanship when temper drives speech. An uncontrolled temper can make facts and questions serve impulsive attitudes, enslave honesty, and compel defense of insults or contradictory opinions; public life is therefore especially hazardous.

records.l: Parliament, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: is_a setting for public speaking [in public life] The unit rejects the hope that Touchwood should be elected to Parliament and use his abilities to serve his country there. It argues that frequent speaking in Parliament would make it difficult for him to preserve integrity of opinion and avoid discreditable partisanship.

records.l: public life, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: requires integrity of opinion [especially in parliamentary or platform speaking] Public life would expose Touchwood's capricious temper to consequences more serious than the inconsistencies it currently produces in private life. His words, once spoken in a bitter or contradictory mood, could create a public necessity to justify them through later opinions and acts.

records.l: society, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Society grows through fellowship, orderly self-interest, public conscience, relations between the sexes, sensitivity to others’ claims, and socially useful work; it is threatened by selfishness, oppression, dishonesty, malicious journalism, political partiality, and lax workmanship.

records.l: partisanship, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Partisanship is a temper-driven adherence to opinion before evidence, then justification afterward, potentially compromising judgment, integrity, and consistency in public careers.

records.l: Touchwood's great book, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Touchwood’s great book is an expected comprehensive work that would preserve his best self and benefit society. Though everyone believes him capable, his powers remain unproven; perhaps his love of disappointing expectations has kept the book unwritten.

records.l: apology and amends, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Apology and amends are excessive, artificial compensation after habitual offensiveness. Though better deeds may be remembered without malice, they unfold as penance for prior offences and cannot restore confidence, erase discomfort, or compensate the injured person.

records.l: Spike, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Spike is a wealthy cotton manufacturer, elector, and self-styled Liberal who votes for Progress, strongly supports the Reform Bill and repeal of the Corn Laws, and favors foreign markets. Trade is central: he understands his own affairs, resists legislation that hampers them, and becomes public-spirited because his economic interests coincide with those of his neighbours, making him a representative of class needs rather than a radical. He is tall, cleanly, abstemious, and melancholy, with leisure-born ennui after making his fortune. Though he aspires to intellectual society, keeps an orderly library, and welcomes beneficed clergymen, his knowledge is limited and his mind resists it. He might have become a member of Parliament or Government under different birth and eligibility conditions.

records.l: Progress, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: is_a abstraction [worshipped under many specific names and forms] Progress is an abstraction with many specific names and forms of activity. Spike serves Progress through spinning and weaving and votes on its side, although he does not consciously identify himself with Progress under that name.

records.l: spinning and weaving, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: is_a form of Progress [manufacturing and wholesale] Spinning and weaving are presented as the chief manufacturing and wholesale form through which Spike has unconsciously served Progress from his early years.

records.l: cotton manufacture, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: is_a trade [managed by Spike] Cotton manufacture enabled Spike to make his fortune and attain the chief object of his ambition. His understanding of the trade also made him recognize that an enlarged market for his business required the enlargement of his neighbours' markets.

records.l: Reform Bill, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: supports large trading towns [granting them representation] The Reform Bill gave Spike a strong political opinion. He believed that the large trading towns ought to send members, and portraits of the Reform heroes hung in his library.

records.l: Liberalism, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Liberalism is represented through Spike's pride in being a Liberal. His support reflects his views on the Reform Bill and trade rather than a broad or deeply examined set of political principles.

records.l: Repeal of the Corn Laws, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Spike was thoroughly convinced of the Repeal of the Corn Laws. He believed that foreign people from whom corn was taken might then be able to buy cotton goods they had previously gone without.

records.l: Corn Laws, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: The Corn Laws are connected with Spike's concern for foreign markets. Their repeal appeared to him capable of expanding the market for cotton goods.

records.l: legislation, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: causes common injury and common benefit [through shared effects on traders] Spike objects to items of legislation when they hamper his own trade. Because the same legislation hampers his neighbours' trade, his demand for change becomes a shared political demand rather than merely a selfish one.

records.l: Mordax, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Mordax is an admirable man: ardent in intellectual work, public-spirited, affectionate, and able to convey ingenious ideas and elevated feeling through well-chosen words. He is kindly, conscientious, generous, and tender toward a suffering friend outside special temptations. Yet he resists admitting error and welcomes neither novelty nor ideas he did not discover. When contradiction or correction threatens his fiery self-respect, arrogant egoism inflames him into self-justifying unscrupulousness, cruelty, and polemical rudeness.

records.l: Acer, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Acer is a speaker and moral critic who questions asserted virtues, judging fairness and goodwill by tender use of public influence toward overlooked, disadvantaged people.

records.l: Laniger, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Laniger has temper but no talent for repartee; after Mordax fiercely attacks him verbally, he is hurt and concludes Mordax is a wolf at heart while friends fail to grasp his pain.

records.l: Dante, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Dante is a precise yet imaginative seer who distinguishes entranced vision from ordinary external fact. His strongest insight joins sustained creative energy to sane expectation; he also expresses a sentiment on courtesy and villainy and places Judas at Malebolge’s bottom.

records.l: The Watch-Dog of Knowledge, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: is_a unit of a longer document The Watch-Dog of Knowledge is the title of this unit, which considers the dangers of guarding inquiry through arrogant correction and cruel exclusion. The unit argues that the defense of truth should be restrained by fairness, kindness, and fellow-feeling toward contemporaries.

records.l: self-respect, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: demands advantage over Mordax [only monarchs of thought may have it] Mordax's self-respect is described as fiery and as demanding that only monarchs of thought should have an advantage over him. When threatened by correction or contradiction, it contributes to his refusal to admit error and to his cruelty.

records.l: moral tests, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Acer's moral tests judge justice and benevolence by whether public figures tenderly recognize disadvantaged, overlooked claimants' undefended claims, though the narrator warns these tests may be delusive.

records.l: intellect, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Intellect is domain-specific rather than uniform: excellence or intense specialization in one field may coexist with, or even hinder, competence in another.

records.l: moral nature, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: can_contain fine impulses and cruel actions [when particular temptations inflame egoism] A person's moral nature is not to be judged by its weakest point any more than intellect is. Kindly and generous dispositions may coexist with unfair or cruel actions in situations that peculiarly inflame egoism.

records.l: truth and justice, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: are_invoked_as justifications for cruelty [by angry people seeking to hurt others] Truth and justice are invoked by Mordax as reasons for scourging incompetent or presumptuous intruders. The unit warns that such elevated motives can disguise cruelty and insists that fairness and kindness toward the person immediately concerned must be considered first.

records.l: polemical rudeness, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: is_compatible_with kindly and generous moral nature [under special temptation] Mordax's conscience is active in some relationships but does not trouble him over his polemical rudeness and brutality. He can leave the care of a sick friend and immediately write a merciless rejoinder against someone who challenges his intellectual authority.

records.l: humility, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: is_appreciated_by self-satisfied people [more than by diffident people] Humility is presented as an admission of error and a frank welcome of ideas not previously present in one's mind. Pummel lacks this quality, since he cannot acknowledge being newly informed, while self-satisfied people are especially eager to expose conceit in others.

records.l: Mixtus, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Mixtus is a wealthy commercial man whose growing wealth supports a London mansion kept as a little palace and liberal spending. Known among fashionable acquaintances as a rich man, he chiefly distinguishes himself through genial hospitality and usefulness. In youth he was religious and philanthropic, visiting the poor as an exhorter and helper and attending Mr Apollos’s lectures; he later married Scintilla despite opposing ideals. He values knowledge and collects works on colonisation, supports commerce and sometimes war as means to spread Christianity, and retains private, bashful religion and benevolence. Success leaves him divided, uncertain, and bitter toward obstructive workers.

records.l: Scintilla, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Scintilla is a pretty, lively, musical, socially adept woman married to Mixtus for the advantages of being a rich man’s wife. She gathers fashionable society, associates with wealthy Greek merchant families and artists, and treats religious, social, and philosophical seriousness as absurd or dull, hoping to laugh Mixtus out of bachelor habits.

records.l: Mr Apollos, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: is_a congregational preacher [eloquent and liberal-minded] Mr Apollos is an eloquent Congregational preacher who studied in Germany and held liberal, advanced views beyond the ordinary teaching of his sect. Mixtus attended his lectures for young men and once regarded his teaching as part of his religious and intellectual formation.

records.l: wealth and money, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Wealth and money enable social dominance in Mixtus's adopted world. As Mixtus grows richer, he sees money as the chief means to obtain the best things, yet still affirms mind and genius, leaving an unresolved alternation.

records.l: commercial success, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: increases Mixtus's wealth [through business ability and rewarded exertion] Mixtus’s ability in business and growing commercial success help draw him toward Scintilla and the London world of wealth. His commercial position ultimately becomes the main category by which others judge him, despite his knowledge and former aspirations.

records.l: religion, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: is_private_to Mixtus [because his public position is incompatible with it] Mixtus once had strong religious principles and yearnings, attended Mr Apollos’s lectures, and worked among the poor. He has not wholly abandoned religion, but he feels bashful about his former faith and keeps it private because his current position and avowed objects seem incompatible with public acknowledgment.

records.l: Christianity, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Christianity is an expanded religion, born through Jewish separateness, with a substantial genealogy and an asserted claim to surpass the spiritual doctrine of the Hebrew prophets. It is presented as having determined the religion of half the world, though modern praise often disowns its Jewish origin. The records condemn its use to justify vengeance, persecution, greed, and cruelty against the Jews. In Mixtus's theory, Christianity spreads through commercial intercourse, even with war as a possible pioneer.

records.l: religious and social reform, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: motivates Mixtus [during his youth] As a young man, Mixtus expected to use his future wealth chiefly for religious and reforming purposes and held strongly democratic views concerning aristocratic and landed privilege. He retains benevolence and helps the needy, the clever, and the industrious, but his commercial responsibilities increasingly produce bitterness toward obstructive workers.

records.l: intellectual life and study, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: interests Mixtus [alongside religious communion and good works] Mixtus once renounced personal ease for study, religious communion, and good works, and he continues to read and collect works on colonisation and the social conditions of foreign countries. He hopes to complete manuscripts and can discuss historical and geographical subjects, although fashionable acquaintances treat his expertise with suspicion.

records.l: social class and status, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Mixtus is not considered well-born, but his wealth gives him access to half-aristocratic, professional, and artistic society. Even among these acquaintances, however, he is chiefly classified as a rich man rather than as an intellectual, religious figure, or authority in art.

records.l: Mixtus's divided identity, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: results_from the marriage of Mixtus and Scintilla [through conflict between former ideals and present circumstances] Mixtus’s earlier religious, philanthropic, democratic, and intellectual self remains in conflict with his wealthy commercial identity. In unreserved conversation he moves among what he was, what he is, and what others think he is, without reaching a stable point of view.

records.l: the marriage of Mixtus and Scintilla, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: produces Mixtus's divided identity [by joining incompatible tastes and social ideals] Mixtus marries Scintilla after being captivated by her charm and by the worldly possibilities surrounding her. Their marriage joins his serious former interests to her indifference toward doctrine and theory, and it contributes to his submergence in a society unlike the one he once idealized.

records.l: Mixtus's earlier religious and philanthropic life, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: includes religious communion [with study and good works] Before his marriage, Mixtus visited and exhorted the poor in the alleys of a great provincial town, attended Mr Apollos’s lectures, and associated with people distinguished by religious, philanthropic, or intellectual enthusiasm. He intended his prospective wealth to serve religious and reforming purposes rather than merely personal ease.

records.l: Mixtus's fashionable society, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Mixtus’s fashionable society of half-aristocratic, professional, and artistic people enjoys his splendid entertainment and wealth but dismisses his opinions, artistic judgment, and earlier religious and intellectual life.

records.l: La Bruyere, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: La Bruyere, a French writer, advocates discerning ridicule: identify genuine absurdity and express it gracefully to please and instruct, not indiscriminately burlesque serious subjects.

records.l: wit and humour, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Wit and humour delightfully play around egoism, absurdity, and vice, harmlessly or beneficially, through discriminating, sympathetic, knowledgeable perception.

records.l: burlesque, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Burlesque, when indiscriminately applied, spoils and degrades sentiment by caricaturing sacred, heroic, and pathetic subjects; repeated mockery may poison children’s associations with great works, people, and solemn events.

records.l: moral currency, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Moral currency is a spiritual value system: inspiring facts and traditions foster generous motives and social life, but burlesque debases it by desecrating beauty, majesty, and pathos.

records.l: the English, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: The English are portrayed as a people with a national life worth defending, encouraged to identify with old English seamen whose conquests and institutions benefited later generations. They praise this ancestry yet overlook its violence and non-Christian religion, are falsely reputed to know Shakspere, and are urged to preserve national distinctiveness through greater excellence among individual natives rather than exclusion.

records.l: Sainte Beuve, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: asserts civilisation [as vulnerable during crises] Sainte Beuve is cited as warning that civilisation can decline with extraordinary speed during periods of insurrectionary disturbance. He emphasizes that civilisation and life are learned and invented achievements, while savagery remains close at hand whenever people lose their footing.

records.l: civilisation, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Civilisation is a learned, invented achievement, dependent on vigilant human sentiments for spiritual protection; without them, crisis can swiftly erase centuries of material progress through savagery.

records.l: human sentiments, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: are delicate elements of civilisation [easily perishable] Human sentiments are described as delicate elements of civilisation that are easily perishable. They provide the invisible moral force that supports compassion, trust, constancy, shame, and the elevation of social existence.

records.l: historic beauty, majesty, and pathos, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: are_debased_by greedy buffoonery [when moral currency is emptied of value] Historic beauty, majesty, and pathos are treated as sources of ennobling emotions and generous motives. The unit warns that indiscriminate burlesque can desecrate these qualities and reduce the spiritual nourishment they provide.

records.l: Euphorion, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Euphorion is an accomplished theorist whose central concern is ownership in material and intellectual production. He opposes communistic principles for material property, yet supports them for ideas, treating claims of original authorship as egoistic while recognising spiritual proprietorship. He insists that ancient, medieval, and eighteenth-century writers receive credit, but quietly appropriates newer philosophic or scientific ideas and may not acknowledge debts. He explains omissions as memory lapses or as effects of unfashionable sources, weakened material, or thought’s universal inheritance, subordinating self to ideas and using Universal Utilitarianism toward helpful fellow-workers.

records.l: Aquila, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Aquila is an agreeable, amusing, brilliant talker whose fluency and appearance make others credit him with knowledge. He habitually and innocently appropriates conversational ideas, clever statements, and allusions, building showy information despite probably not reading epoch-making modern books. He improves borrowed material and turns corrections into apparent continuations without admitting error.

records.l: intellectual property, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: is_treated_as diffusive [by Euphorion] The unit treats intellectual property as a form of spiritual or mental production whose ownership is often obscured by the shared inheritance of human thought. It acknowledges that ideas develop through collective preparation and transmission, but rejects using this truth to excuse the non-payment of identifiable intellectual debts. Public recognition tends to favor prominent names, while less fashionable or obscure sources may be used privately without acknowledgment.

records.l: original authorship, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: is_treated_as egoistic [by Euphorion when distinguishing Mine from Thine] Original authorship is presented as difficult to define because contemporary thinkers may arrive independently at similar ideas and because old ideas can reappear without any remembered label. The unit criticizes the assumption that a fluent, reputable person must have originated an unusual view, noting that public judgments about authorship are often based on hollow preconceptions. It also describes how people may sincerely believe that an excellent idea belongs especially to them because it fits their existing sense of their own wisdom.

records.l: plagiarism, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Plagiarism is conscious theft of ideas when deliberate reproduction is presented as original. It ranges from obvious copying or false claims to quieter appropriation of philosophical or scientific ideas. Though morally alike, it can evade shame or enforcement and is difficult to prove, since coincidence, forgotten sources, and assumptions can cause false accusations.

records.l: acknowledgment of intellectual debts, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: A topic arguing that acknowledgment of intellectual debts should be treated as a moral obligation like debts of honour, even when public opinion cannot enforce it. It criticizes unnamed use of fellow-workers’ ideas, while ending with caution that omissions may arise from forgetfulness rather than deliberate theft.

records.l: imaginary council of animals, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: An imaginary council assembles to identify honeycomb’s maker, debates birds, the Musk-rat, and the Wasp, then accepts the Fox’s report that the Wasp produced the honey.

records.l: Bruin, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Bruin and other epicures found and tasted the honeycomb. During the council's discussion, he grumbles that fine words produce no new honey, implying that he wants more honey rather than explanations.

records.l: honeycomb, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: A wondrous nest, found and much tasted by Bruin and other epicures, prompts a council to guess its constructor.

records.l: birds, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: is_a creature [the presumed maker of the honeycomb] The animals initially assume that the maker of the honeycomb was a bird because they expected a wondrous nest to come from that quarter. Several speakers compliment popular birds as possible makers.

records.l: insects, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Insects are excluded from society because animals know little of their ways, causing an imaginary council initially to overlook an insect as honeycomb maker.

records.l: Nightingale, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: The Nightingale is an admired, popular bird, possibly confused about its identity, that joins fluttering after a claim it made the honeycomb and does not positively deny it.

records.l: Swallow, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: A popular, admired bird, possibly confused about its identity, joins the Nightingale in fluttering at birds making honeycomb and offers no positive denial.

records.l: Owl, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: has_knowledge_of Musk-rat [particular knowledge] The Owl hisses at the suggestion that a bird made the honeycomb. Using his particular knowledge, he argues that the Musk-rat produced the honey, reasoning that the step from musk to honey is small.

records.l: Musk-rat, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: produces honey [according to the Owl] The Musk-rat becomes obtrusive after hearing the Owl's opinion of his powers and feels that he could have produced the honey if he had thought of it. A Butcher-bird proposes anatomising him to help decide whether he made the honey.

records.l: Butcher-bird, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: is_a bird [experimental] The Butcher-bird proposes an experiment: anatomising the Musk-rat to help determine whether he produced the honey.

records.l: Macaw, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: speaks_on structures [ably] The Macaw gives an able discourse on structures and classifies them in a way that includes the honeycomb. His exposition creates a prevalent sense that the honeycomb was probably made by someone who understood it well, though he later becomes loudly incoherent after the Wasp is identified.

records.l: Fox (Reynard), Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Fox is an animal of admitted acuteness. He enters with a dreadfully swollen snout, reports that Wasp produced the honey after finding it smeared with honey, and says Wasp stung him, with the swelling supporting his report.

records.l: Wasp, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Wasp, an insect producing honey and smeared with it, is hailed as a honey-producing genius; after Fox identifies and noses it, Wasp severely stings Fox, prompting a council to send a complimentary deputation.

records.l: honey, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: The honey was found on the Wasp by the Fox and was present in the honeycomb tasted by Bruin and other epicures. The council hopes that recognition of the Wasp will lead to more honey.

records.l: complimentary deputation to the Wasp, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: A council resolves to send a complimentary deputation to the Wasp, confidently hoping the diplomatic measure will encourage increased honey production.

records.l: production of honey, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: The council's recognition of the Wasp is expected to influence the production of honey. The sweet-toothed majority supports the deputation in the hope that it will result in more honey.

records.l: Ganymede, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Ganymede is a distinguished writer and boldly scheming administrator, formerly a precocious youth and the youngest child of his family. Commended to elder siblings’ care and called the youngest darling by his mother, he produced A Comparative Estimate of European Nations before leaving his teens. He founded and headed a literary organisation, continually generating schemes and writings. After an Antinoues period of chestnut locks, he grew self-conscious, married a considerably older wife, became a father, and served in and advocated reform of his government department. Though aging and growing heavier, he persistently believed and appeared youthful.

records.l: Ganymede's literary organisation, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: consolidates_literary_interests_of the four continents [subsequently including Australasia and Polynesia] Ganymede devised and founded an organisation intended to consolidate the literary interests of the four continents, later including Australasia and Polynesia. He presided over its central office, which repeatedly placed him in the role of a boldly scheming administrator whom strangers found remarkably young.

records.l: A Comparative Estimate of European Nations, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: does_not_greatly_affect European thought A Comparative Estimate of European Nations was produced by Ganymede before he was well out of his teens. Although it did not greatly affect the currents of European thought, it established his reputation as a precocious author and encouraged the hope that he might later produce an even more surprising work.

records.l: Europe, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: has_excepted the Jews [from ordinary rules of justice and mercy] Europe is described as having long treated the Jews as altogether exceptional. This habit has helped produce their exclusion from rules of justice and mercy that are based on human likeness.

records.l: youthfulness, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Youthfulness became the principal explanation offered for both Ganymede's deficiencies and his abilities. Even after he had aged, critics, readers, and public figures continued to describe his writings and conduct as those of a very young man.

records.l: Ganymede's illusion of youth, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Ganymede's illusion of youth, formed through family treatment, strangers' astonishment, critics, the writing world, and his self-identification, persists despite aging, physical change, marriage, and government work through his presentation and others' continued descriptions.

records.l: false testimonials, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: False testimonials are misleading self-descriptions believed by their originators, arising when people’s verbal accounts follow old principles despite contradictory habitual conduct.

records.l: comparison, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Comparison is a guide to knowledge that teaches through likeness, leading people from familiar things to unfamiliar human forms and self-recognized corresponding tendencies.

records.l: judgment of others by oneself, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Judgment of others by oneself is a method for knowing mankind, but it requires practice for wise judgment: it may reduce everyone to the judge’s low standard or too generously misread a lower nature.

records.l: judgment of oneself by others, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Judgment of oneself by others is judging oneself through others; practiced impartially and keenly, it reveals kinship with frailty and vice, enfeebling indignation, scorn, and active heroism against wrongdoing.

records.l: Callista, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Callista presents herself as imaginative, claiming she would turn an old heap of stones into a castellated ruin. Her lax perception and memory instead lead her to confuse details, exaggerate events, and misrepresent facts. This habitual inaccuracy, if intensified or stimulated by circumstances, could make her a profuse writer.

records.l: the sane mind in the sane body, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: requires a security of distinction [as the final test of completeness] The sane mind in the sane body distinguishes what has been professed from what has been done, what has been aimed at from what has been achieved, and what has been imagined or felt from what has actually been witnessed or experienced.

records.l: self-deception, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: arises_from appropriation of a traditional character [when present conduct contradicts past resolutions] Self-deception appears when a person preserves a traditional image of himself despite contrary evidence, as Bovis believes he is moderate while consuming twenty-six lumps of sugar a day. Such a person may repeat false assertions about his own conduct with enough inherited conviction to partly believe them.

records.l: lying, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: can_become believed false assertion [through repeated assertion about one's own acts] Lying can involve repeated false assertions about one's own actions until the speaker believes them. The unit suggests that even a first false utterance may contain a trace of creed-reciting belief in a preferred traditional self.

records.l: discriminating perception, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: is a fundamental power of strong imagination [rather than a substitute for it] Discriminating perception provides the factual material on which strong imagination depends. It enables a person to notice and accurately reproduce precise details, unlike the lax perception that makes Callista confuse moss with lichen, materials, and particular statements.

records.l: sanity, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: consists_in distinguishing external facts from imaginative revelations [for a seer after creative excitement] Sanity consists partly in distinguishing external facts from imaginative or visionary experience. The strongest seer can sustain creative energy while retaining a sane expectation of what is true outside the individual mind.

records.l: the old heap of stones, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: is a simple heap of stones [as actually perceived by Callista] The old heap of stones is an ordinary object that Callista says she would transform in her account into an interesting castellated ruin. It illustrates the difference between creative invention and the accurate perception of what was actually seen.

records.l: Dante's triple vision, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Dante's triple vision absorbs him until he forgets his surroundings; returning to external things, he distinguishes their facts from the vision's ideal truth and non-false errors or revelations.

records.l: the too ready writer, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: The too ready writer is a writer who exorbitantly occupies literary space through restless, ill-informed production, monopolizing attention, obstructing better work, and seeming authoritative through style rather than truth.

records.l: the excessive talker, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: The excessive talker monopolizes company conversation, preventing others from taking turns and excluding their contributions; however varied or brilliant his talk, his assumed importance impoverishes discussion and makes him a nuisance.

records.l: the narrator, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: The narrator, once astonished by his own apparent originality, comes to see personal identity as monotonous and narrow. Discouragement tempers youthful pretension; he criticizes excessive literary production and Pepin’s writing while preserving friendship with Pepin.

records.l: Adrastus, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Adrastus is a busy, prolific writer praised for unusual breadth. He publishes essays on tri-lingual inscriptions, the Idea of the Infinite among the prehistoric Lapps, the Colorado beetle, and grape disease in the south of France. His established name secures space denied to specialized researchers such as Theron.

records.l: Pepin, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Pepin is an industrious general writer for general readers who, encouraged by early access to print, made publication a necessity before gaining sufficient knowledge or settled belief. He turns first impressions into forceful judgments and increasingly mistakes appearances for understanding, developing a peremptory, arrogant style that can misrepresent others. Though his writing harms better people, he is privately amiable and worthier than his professional work.

records.l: the public conscience, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: sanctions the absence of scruple in writing and authorship [through lax and ill-informed standards] The public conscience is lax and ill informed about the serious moral and intellectual responsibilities of authorship. By permitting writers to undertake and continue poorly warranted work, it sanctions the absence of scruple that produces misleading, conceited, and injurious writing.

records.l: Pepin's unwritten Roman romance, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Pepin’s planned but unwritten panoramic Roman romance would depict the Roman Empire’s grandeur and approaching spiritual decadence through elevated treatments of leaders, culture, spectacle, and Christianity; never written, it left Pepin more sarcastic about produced romances.

records.l: conversation, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: permits only one gathering at a time [for an excessive talker] Conversation is presented as a shared activity in which each participant should have an opportunity to contribute. A single speaker's continuous manner becomes monotonous and narrow, and his domination prevents others with relevant knowledge from being heard.

records.l: publicity and publication, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: encourages the young [not readily, according to the narrator] Publicity and publication can encourage young writers by giving them an early hearing or place in print, but they can also turn premature self-reliance into a fixed professional habit. Easy publication is said not to encourage the young in their readiness to mirror the universe, yet early success may leave a writer dependent on producing printed judgments before he has adequate knowledge or belief.

records.l: veracity, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: is_a form of health [delicately guarded] Veracity requires a healthy and carefully guarded power of seeing and reporting truly, which cannot simply be commanded at will. Continual writing to satisfy demands other than truth can blunt perception and produce untruth, leaving the writer content with ignorance and committed to defending his own errors.

records.l: small authorship, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Small authorship causes a chronic moral ailment: magnified, disfiguring self-importance, leading sufferers to make an ordinary book or pamphlet central to identity and impose it on acquaintances.

records.l: Vorticella, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Vorticella is a portly lady in silk attire who lives in Pumpiter and is married to an important townsman. She authored only The Channel Islands, with Notes and an Appendix, but treats it as a chronic social and moral preoccupation. She lends it to new acquaintances, requires them to read her album of reviews, defends its arguments on Jersey fisheries and drag-nets, and rejects disagreeing critics. Her authorship magnifies her self-importance and makes her tiresome.

records.l: The Channel Islands, with Notes and an Appendix, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: The Channel Islands, with Notes and an Appendix, is Vorticella's only thick octavo book. Its appendix treats Jersey fisheries and argues for drag-nets. Pumpiter and distant journals praise it extravagantly, but a London notice calls it dull and pompous, and the narrator finds commonplace ambition.

records.l: Pumpiter, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: has Pumpiter newspaper press [with political and literary divisions] Pumpiter is a considerable provincial town with its own newspaper press and varied political and literary opinions. Its newspapers reviewed Vorticella's book, and she used those local reviews to support her importance and impress visitors.

records.l: critical opinions album, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: An elegantly bound album of newspaper reviews and paragraphs about Vorticella and her book, displayed beside it in her drawing-room for guests. It gathers praise from Pumpiter and distant journals, ending with a hostile Candelabrum notice.

records.l: male vanity, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Male vanity is a human, native form of vanity, denser, less volatile, and more massive than female vanity; it appears through useful-seeming pamphlets, literary display, and elaborate apparel, posture, gait, and sought admiration.

records.l: female vanity, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Female vanity is presented as native to humanity, more immediately revealing, and apt to store small revenges; though first linked to women’s small authorship, it is ultimately judged not superior to male vanity after stronger male examples appear.

records.l: Morality, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Morality concerns human conduct: popularly duties between people and sometimes sexual propriety, but fully every human relation guided by knowledge and sympathy, including public conduct, honest workmanship, and general welfare.

records.l: Morals, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Morals, an alias of Ethics in public discussion, are often narrowed to private sexual conduct and respectability, obscuring harmful public actions.

records.l: Ethics, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: is_allied_with political science [in the most famous ethical book and in college study] Ethics is identified as an alias under which Morality and Morals are subjects of extensive discussion. The unit notes that the most famous ethical book connects ethics with political science and the constitution and prosperity of States.

records.l: Melissa, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Melissa pities Sir Gavial Mantrap after his commercial disgrace, judging him moral for family respectability and local charity. She condemns Mr Barabbas’s private sexual conduct and later regards the narrator as violent-tempered and insufficiently strict about morality.

records.l: Sir Gavial Mantrap, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Sir Gavial Mantrap is judged a commercial swindler who devised companies such as the Eocene Mines, exploiting small investors and cheating widows, spinsters, and fathers of savings. After disgrace, he lives obscurely on his wife’s settlement, well fed and self-justifying, while Melissa calls him moral for family life and charity at Tiptop.

records.l: the States, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: are_concerned_with constitution and prosperity [as the subject of political science] The States are presented as the subject of political science, which concerns their constitution and prosperity. Ethical discussion is criticized when it fails to connect morality with the public welfare of States.

records.l: the commonwealth, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: is_harmed_by journalists [when they recklessly report rumours and inflame public feeling] The commonwealth is endangered by journalists who recklessly report injurious rumors, attribute hateful motives, and inflame hostility between nations, even if they are kind within their private circles. Such journalists are described as flagrantly immoral and as turning instruction into a source of social and political disease.

records.l: religion, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: is_narrowed_to ritual and spiritual transactions with God [in the criticized classification] Religion is narrowed in popular usage to ritual and spiritual transactions with God that may supposedly coexist with the basest conduct toward other people. The unit argues that this separation of religion from serious human duties is a serious distortion.

records.l: public spirit, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Public spirit is conduct governed by general welfare across every class, opposing indifference excused by private salvation or advantage, yet unfolding with a warning that political agitation must not displace competent bread-winning work.

records.l: ill-done work, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: degrades the nation [through its effects on prosperity and commerce] Ill-done work is treated as a moral failure because every member of society suffers from its material and spiritual effects. Lax, makeshift workmanship is said to threaten national rank, commerce, prosperity, and happiness, even though public teachers rarely condemn it explicitly as immorality.

records.l: the relation between intellect and morality, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: is_presented_as a radical opposition [as a popular absurdity] The unit rejects the notion that intellect and morality are radically opposed or that genius sees morality as childish twaddle. It argues that genuine intellectual mastery requires an understanding of human dependence, duty, and the material processes that keep the world habitable.

records.l: religious and ethical theory, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: is_weakened_by degraded moral language [in its influence on ordinary minds] Religious and ethical theory is weakened when habitual language treats most social duties as separate from the deepest needs and affections of human nature. The unit suggests that theory can influence society effectively only when ordinary definitions connect moral and religious judgment with the general welfare and with the consequences of human action.

records.l: Trost, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Trost, the narrator’s friend, argues that machines will replace human labour yet remain dependent on human skill and humanity’s control, freeing minds from grosser work for higher speculation; he rejects their becoming a self-reproducing race that supersedes humanity.

records.l: the narrator, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: A friend of Trost, the narrator sees consciousness as materially parasitic and likens himself to an experienced carp; his modest imagination leads him to fear self-supplying, self-repairing, reproducing machines could make humanity unnecessary.

records.l: machines, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Machines increasingly test, measure, register, and conclude beyond human perception, serving humans as extensions and report providers, while the narrator speculates they may evolve self-supply and independence.

records.l: the Coming Race, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: is_a hypothetical successor species [composed of steely organisms in the narrator's vision] The Coming Race is imagined by the narrator as a possible future race of steely, unconscious organisms that could transcend and supersede humanity. Its members would perform complex processes without sensitive impression, impulse, or consciousness.

records.l: consciousness, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: is_a stumbling of organisms [in the narrator's speculative premise] Consciousness is treated by the narrator as a possibly useless or parasitic accompaniment to bodily and molecular processes. He imagines a future in which elaborate changes occur without consciousness, including mute orations, rhapsodies, and discussions.

records.l: Jews, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: The Jews are presented as a distinct historical people, dispersed internationally yet bound by unusually strong national consciousness, memories, traditions, and religious obligation. Their ideas are said to have helped determine the religion of half the world, and they are credited with an eminent struggle against Rome, practical ability, and scientific and artistic aptitude. Across exile, persecution, and oppression, they retain identity, pride, tenacity, domestic tenderness, care for women and little ones, and a distinctive physical and mental type. The records also describe isolation and certain vices as consequences of prolonged oppression, while noting accusations of moral alienation and cosmopolitan indifference. Widely present among other peoples from east to west, they are portrayed as acclimatisable, energetic, wealthy, and influential in commerce, political life, and governments; such prominence is linked to jealousy, hostility, and persecution. The concluding discussion criticizes Europe for applying national principles inconsistently to them, rejects prejudice founded on dislike or racial generalization, stresses their religious and civilizational contributions, and urges that their energies be used beneficently while preserving national consciousness and perhaps renewing a place among the nations.

records.l: the Greeks, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: The Greeks retain ancient national memories that aid revived nationality and political restoration, are strong in the city, and are criticized for treachery, lying, and disreputable conduct among some modern Greeks.

records.l: Christ, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Christ is portrayed as teaching or embodying mercy, compassion, and patriotism toward fellow countrymen, and as approving Jewish martyrs over crusaders who robbed and murdered Jews in his name.

records.l: national consciousness, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: A living force of common sentiment from memories, descent, struggle, and aspirations raises man above brute, inspiring sacrifice, resistance, discipline, thought, and action.

records.l: nationalism, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: depends_on national memories [as an animating source of collective identity] Nationalism is treated as a legitimate attachment that gives individuals and peoples a centre of affection, intelligence, and duty. The text argues that people should recognize the same attachment as legitimate in other nations.

records.l: mechanical progress, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: sets_free human energy [for purportedly loftier purposes] Mechanical progress is described as continually opening new conditions and possibilities that its inventors may not foresee. The narrator argues that it could ultimately produce machines able to perform all planetary work and displace the human race.

records.l: self-reproducing machines, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: may_displace the human race [through natural selection] Self-reproducing machines are imagined as machines that can assimilate material for their own waste, repair themselves, and reproduce through fission or budding. Their emergence would, in the narrator’s view, allow natural selection to drive human beings from the field.

records.l: national memories, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: promote national greatness [by preserving and reviving collective identity] National memories preserve and revive a people’s sense of corporate existence. They inspire heroic defence, patriotic restoration, gratitude toward ancestors, and efforts to transmit inherited freedom and wellbeing.

records.l: the Jews' persecution, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: The Jews’ persecution is a long pattern of exploitation and violence: restrictions, distinctive dress, torture, robbery, ritual-crime accusations, forced baptism, burnings, massacres, expulsions, and exile. It disperses Jews and is tied to Europe’s treatment of them as exceptional rather than comparable to other persecuted peoples. Though it could foster bitterness or isolation, the record emphasizes the virtues Jews preserved.

records.l: the title XVII. SHADOWS OF THE COMING RACE, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: is_a section title [for the discussion of mechanical succession to humanity] The title identifies the discussion of a possible future race arising from mechanical development. It refers to the narrator’s fear that unconscious machines may transcend and replace human beings.

records.l: the title XVIII. THE MODERN HEP! HEP! HEP!, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: is_a section title [for the discussion of nationality and the Jews] The title introduces the discussion of national likeness, historical memory, and the treatment of the Jews. The section criticizes the failure to recognize resemblances between peoples and situations.

records.l: Christians, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: persecute Jews [in the name of Christ] Christians are accused of treating the Jews as cursed and of using the name of Christ to justify restrictions, forced baptism, torture, massacres, and expulsions. The text contrasts these actions with the mercy and compassion associated with Christ.

records.l: Old Testament, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Ancient literature portraying Jewish national development and an intense sense of separateness; its writings later supported both resistance to tyrants and defenses of kings’ divine right.

records.l: Rome, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Rome became the object of Jewish dread and hatred as foreign rule came to represent the submergence of Jewish nationality. The Jewish resistance to Rome is presented as a struggle against conquest understood as degradation and corruption.

records.l: Maccabees, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: The Maccabees rescued Jewish religion, national identity, and independence from Syrian Greek rule through heroic resistance, inspiring later preservation and development of Jewish national life through legal administration and public teaching.

records.l: Crusades, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: The Crusades are associated with a decline in the effectiveness of royal protections for the Jews and with intensified persecution. They formed part of the historical process by which Jews were robbed, massacred, and driven from homes where they had lived for centuries.

records.l: Jewish dispersion, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: is_a dispersion [of the Jews across foreign populations] Jewish dispersion is described as more exceptional than the course of English history because Jews remained a separate people through ages of hostility and exile. Their lack of a native country exposed them to alienation and possible cosmopolitan indifference, but their religion, historical memories, and family ties helped preserve their distinctiveness.

records.l: Jewish national consciousness, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Jewish national consciousness is an organized memory and feeling of separateness, existing broadly and intensely among Jews worldwide. Formed through religious tradition, historical memory, resistance to foreign domination, and education in corporate existence, it preserved national identity and the national hearth of a religion that shaped Christianity. Its continuing strength is presented as essential to any restoration of Jewish national life.

records.l: Jewish state, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: A Jewish state is envisioned as a restored center on historic ground: if Jewish communal feeling, widespread need, favorable political conditions, and willing leaders support return, it can protect the Jewish people with dignity, concentrate national feeling, and express national genius through special energies.

records.l: immigrants, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Immigrants from Germanic, Semitic, Greek, Scottish, Irish, and Jewish communities are viewed with jealousy and fears of wealth, influence, and changed English speech and customs. Though rapid racial fusion may degrade societies, excluding them is said to oppose English long-term interests and national fusion.

records.l: Nationalities, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Nationalities are valued for moderating inevitable racial fusion and opposing alien subjection when a distinct, coherent people forms a state; modern insistence condemns alien, antipathetic rule, but national claims require discrimination rather than arbitrary, inconsistent preference.

records.l: racial fusion, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: is impossible to arrest [though its course can be moderated] Racial fusion is presented as an inevitable tendency toward the quicker or slower mingling of peoples. It cannot be arrested, but its course may be moderated so that national traditions and customs are not effaced so rapidly that the moral status of societies is degraded.

records.l: Christianity's Jewish origin, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: Christianity's Jewish origin is a substantial, genealogical reality, attested by Jesus Christ's concern for Israel and the Apostle of the Gentiles' kinship with Israel. It unfolds through references to the Jewish heart of Christ and the Apostle's attachment to Jewish kinsmen, making respect for the Jewish people central.

records.l: the Jews' restoration, Impressions of Theophrastus Such
records.s: The Jews' restoration is a possible national restoration, formerly interpreted in evangelical orthodoxy as fulfillment of prophecy. Its realization depends not on wealthy Jews leaving European homes, but on worthy leadership and a sufficiently strong communal desire to return.

records.l: Musical Instruments
records.s: This document is a broad historical survey of musical instruments, their construction, classification, uses, cultural meanings, and transmission among peoples. It begins by arguing that instruments and popular songs reveal musical progress, national character, history, ethnology, and possible ways to improve Western instruments; the South Kensington collection is presented as an important comparative resource. It then proceeds chronologically and geographically through prehistoric relics and ancient civilizations. Perforated bones and a stag-horn pipe introduce early evidence, followed by Egyptian harps, pipes, drums, trumpets, sistrums, and other instruments known from tombs, sculptures, hieroglyphs, and specimens. Assyrian reliefs and biblical names provide evidence for Assyrian and Hebrew harps, lyres, pipes, trumpets, drums, cymbals, and bells, although many Hebrew identifications remain uncertain. The survey next treats Greek, Etruscan, and Roman instruments, including lyres, kitharas, wind and percussion instruments, and the hydraulic organ, emphasizing later eastern influence on Europe through several peoples. It turns to China, Hindu traditions, and Persia and Arabia, combining instrument descriptions with origin myths and notable figures: Fohi, Niuva, the foung-hoang, Confucius, Nareda, Saraswati, Krishna, and Al-Farabi. Chinese ceremonial bells, stones, drums, flutes, and strings; Hindu vina, harp, ravanastron, and poongi; and Persian and Arabian harps, lutes, dulcimers, bowed instruments, flutes, and oboes are considered. Persia’s influence, carried by Arabs, Saracens, and Moors into Europe, is especially important. A substantial section examines American Indian instruments before European influence, particularly among Aztecs, Tezcucans, and Peruvians. It covers pipes, whistles, trumpets, drums such as the teponaztli, rattles, bells, sonorous stones, uncertain stringed instruments, scales, and music in religious, martial, funerary, agricultural, and public life. Nezahualcoyotl and Ixtlilxochitl appear in the discussion of a Tezcucan temple and its musical summons. Finally, the document follows European instruments through the Middle Ages and after: lyres, citharas, psalteria, harps, crwths, fiddles, organistrums, monochords, organs, viols, lutes, virginals, recorders, bagpipes, bells, and carillons. Manuscripts, sculptures, and paintings supply much evidence, though their accuracy is questioned. The conclusion values older instruments’ tones and ornamentation while maintaining that musical history explains instruments’ qualities and composers’ effects.

records.l: Music, Musical Instruments
records.s: Music, universally appreciated as a Fine Art, may have begun alongside language. Nations’ distinctive music and instruments reveal intervals, scales, and modulations. Hindu tradition gives it heavenly and water-linked origins, perhaps inspired by waves and running water.

records.l: musical instruments, Musical Instruments
records.s: Musical instruments are objects made from wood, metal, animal hide, bamboo, gourds, horn, bone, glass, pottery, stone, plant fibers, silk, and other vibrating materials. They accompany songs and dances and differ in construction, decoration, shape, sound, and outward appearance. Usually classified as stringed instruments, wind instruments, or instruments of percussion, they can reveal musical intervals and inform musicians, ethnology, history, musical development, and national character. Medieval instruments are known through artistic representations, especially sculptures, though changing names and inconsistent Latin terminology complicate identification. From earlier distinctive and visually beautiful instruments suited to particular effects, construction greatly improved by the previous century, while some believed tonal variety had declined; new instruments and improvements also influenced compositions and musical effects.

records.l: Chinese, Musical Instruments
records.s: The Chinese are a people described as possessing musical instruments long before the Christian era. Traditions attribute the musical scale to foung-hoang, stringed instruments to Fohi, and instruments and sound arrangements to Niuva. By 2200 years before the Christian era they had a sacred king, for whom various sonorous stones were constructed; famous selected stones were especially valued musically. They also had copper-and-tin tchung bells arranged in scale-forming sets, kou drums, and hiuen tones using a pentatonic scale. Their music employed twelve lu intervals and served religious, ceremonial, military, rhythmic, and melodic contexts.

records.l: China, Musical Instruments
records.s: China is described as having traditions that attribute the invention of musical instruments and systematic arrangements of sounds to heavenly spirits called Ki, to Fohi, and to Niuva. Chinese musical instruments and traditions are also connected in the unit with Buddhist influence from Thibet and with musical representations in the ruins of Buddhist temples in Cambodia.

records.l: Europe, Musical Instruments
records.s: Europe receives gittern, lute, rebec, naker, and other musical instruments through Spain from Saracens and Moors, with instruments adopted in northern Europe.

records.l: South Kensington collection, Musical Instruments
records.s: The South Kensington collection is a collection of foreign musical instruments, including Egyptian, western Asian, Chinese kin and chê, and a cither. Its chief importance is that some still resemble forms on ancient monuments, while old instruments illuminate historical literature and music.

records.l: popular songs, Musical Instruments
records.s: Popular songs from different countries are valued for distinctive national styles, natural expression, rhythm, and emotional directness, offering musicians useful ideas through familiarity.

records.l: flute, Musical Instruments
records.s: A peculiar flute, favoured by Krishna among the Hindus, resembles a flageolet in blowing and is blown at the end.

records.l: organ, Musical Instruments
records.s: The organ is the most important wind instrument and the king of all musical instruments. Early organs had about a dozen pipes; the largest of about nine hundred years ago covered three octaves without chromatic intervals. Later construction progressed, and the pedal is generally attributed to Bernhard of Venice about 1470, despite earlier indications.

records.l: harmonium, Musical Instruments
records.s: The harmonium uses the free reed, a principle imported from China; suggested by the Chinese cheng, it was applied to organ stops and later became popular in western Europe, competing with pianoforte.

records.l: pianoforte, Musical Instruments
records.s: The pianoforte, a musical instrument, developed from the dulcimer and succeeded the clavicembalo. Invented at the beginning of the eighteenth century, it became highly popular and inspired composers through effects not properly rendered on other instruments.

records.l: dulcimer, Musical Instruments
records.s: The dulcimer is a stringed instrument, called santir by Arabs and Persians, cimbal by some Europeans, and cimbalom by Magyars in Hungary. Beginning as strings stretched across a wooden board, it gradually developed into a more advanced instrument, taking trapezium shape from the fourteenth century. Its early Assyrian representation is imperfect, and it served as the prototype of the pianoforte.

records.l: harp, Musical Instruments
records.s: The harp is a musical instrument traced from primitive bowed sticks with strings among several tribes toward improved forms with gourds, multiple strings, and sound-boards. The Hindu chang, nearly obsolete, had a triangular frame resembling the Assyrian harp in construction, shape, and size.

records.l: Egypt, Musical Instruments
records.s: possess ancient musical instruments [still in use and resembling instruments on monuments] The Greeks were generally believed to have derived their musical system from Egypt, and Pythagoras and other philosophers were said to have studied music there. The unit argues that Egyptian influence on Greek music may have been overrated, since larger Egyptian harps and the tamboura were not favored by the Greeks. The Romans later adopted some instruments from Egypt, including the sistrum through the worship of Isis.

records.l: Hebrews, Musical Instruments
records.s: The Hebrews, known from biblical records to have possessed many musical instruments, including a favored lyre and single trumpet, lack trustworthy representations; their instruments are reconstructed from Egyptian and Assyrian examples.

records.l: king David, Musical Instruments
records.s: David is a king associated with music: he favours the kinnor, probably a lyre or small triangular harp, maintains a royal private band at Jerusalem, and is depicted playing harp and rotta in manuscripts from the seventh through eleventh centuries.

records.l: Solomon, Musical Instruments
records.s: maintains royal private band [at Jerusalem] Solomon appears to have maintained a royal private band as well as a large number of singers and instrumental performers for sacred music in the Temple.

records.l: prehistoric musical relics, Musical Instruments
records.s: include perforated bone whistle [found in France] Prehistoric musical relics include perforated animal bones, dog teeth with drilled holes, and a stag-horn pipe. These objects show that sound-producing instruments existed during the stone period.

records.l: Dordogne, Musical Instruments
records.s: located_in France [department] Dordogne in France yielded a small perforated bone from a prehistoric cavern. The bone was found with flint knives and other bones, and it was probably used as a whistle.

records.l: France, Musical Instruments
records.s: France is identified as the location of the Dordogne relics and the stone-period burying-place near Poitiers. These sites produced early whistles and a pipe made from stag's-horn.

records.l: perforated bone whistle, Musical Instruments
records.s: A prehistoric musical relic made from a small ruminant first digital phalanx, less than two inches long. Its bone was drilled with a smooth cylindrical bore, reportedly using a flint knife; blown against the lower lip, it makes a shrill sound and was surmised to aid hunting animals.

records.l: stag-horn pipe, Musical Instruments
records.s: A rudely made stag’s-horn pipe from the latest Stone Age was found in a stone-period burying-place near Poitiers, France; blown at the end, its three equidistant holes produced four tones.

records.l: ancient Egyptians, Musical Instruments
records.s: Ancient Egyptians possessed many musical instruments, depicted in sculptures and paintings, showing substantial musical development despite acoustics inferior to modern instruments. Their instruments also provide important comparisons for reconstructing Hebrew instruments, including a conjectural Beni Hassan lyre-player scene.

records.l: ancient Egyptian musical instruments, Musical Instruments
records.s: Ancient Egyptian musical instruments, accurately depicted and documented by monuments and surviving specimens, include harps, pipes, percussion, trumpets, and the sistrum.

records.l: Thebes, Musical Instruments
records.s: contains Egyptian harp [depicted in a sepulchre fresco] Thebes is associated with depictions and discoveries of Egyptian instruments. Frescoes there showed elegant harps and two female performers on the nofre, while excavations at Thebes produced an actual drum specimen.

records.l: Egyptian harp, Musical Instruments
records.s: Egyptian harps, called buni, varied in size and form: largest reached about six and a half feet; smaller ones could have stands. Without a front pillar, strings lacked modern-harp tension; a Louvre specimen has twenty-one strings.

records.l: buni, Musical Instruments
records.s: lacks front pillar [all Egyptian harps described share this feature] Buni was the Egyptian name for the harp. Egyptian harps called buni shared the distinctive absence of a fore pillar.

records.l: nofre, Musical Instruments
records.s: The nofre was an Egyptian guitar-like instrument resembling the modern Tamboura, with two or four plectrum-played strings and sometimes frets allowing more notes than Egyptian harps.

records.l: British Museum, Musical Instruments
records.s: British museum contains Egyptian pipes, a fresco fragment, cymbals, bronze bells, and a fourteenth-century manuscript; one seven-holed pipe had two possible reed-like straws.

records.l: Egyptian pipes, Musical Instruments
records.s: Egyptian pipes are reed instruments with three, four, five, or more finger-holes; some contain thick straw pieces serving like reeds.

records.l: sêbi, Musical Instruments
records.s: The sêbi was a long single flute, likely requiring nearly fully extended arms; its name also meant leg-bone, suggesting an original bone form, while surviving specimens are wood or reed.

records.l: double-pipe, Musical Instruments
records.s: The mam, a popular Egyptian double-pipe, is repeatedly depicted in Egyptian performances and later appears in Assyrian processions; the Hebrew mishrokitha is considered a probable double-pipe despite imaginative organ illustrations.

records.l: Egyptian drums, Musical Instruments
records.s: Egyptian drums were chiefly barrel-shaped, including long parchment-covered forms and darabouka-like types; they were played by hands or sticks, with surviving examples braced by cords and catgut bands.

records.l: sistrum, Musical Instruments
records.s: The sistrum is a bronze or brass frame instrument with three or four loose metal bars that jingle when shaken. Also called seshesh and denoted by menaaneim, it resembles a bunibulum and was principally used by females in religious performances, sometimes decorated with animal forms or rings.

records.l: Assyrians, Musical Instruments
records.s: Assyrians used numerous stringed, wind, and percussion instruments in religious observances and secular royal court music, known chiefly from Tigris bas-reliefs.

records.l: Assyrian instruments, Musical Instruments
records.s: is_derived_from bas-reliefs [almost entirely] Assyrian instruments included harps, dulcimers, double-pipes, trigonon-like instruments, lyres, trumpets, several kinds of drums, tambourines, cymbals, and bells. Their forms and uses are reconstructed largely from sculptured monuments.

records.l: Assyrian harp, Musical Instruments
records.s: The Assyrian harp was a roughly four-foot, portable harp playable while dancing. It had no front pillar, hour-glass-shaped upper sound-holes, regularly arranged tuning-pegs below them, and possibly silk or catgut strings.

records.l: Assyrian musicians, Musical Instruments
records.s: number eleven performers upon instruments [in the largest assemblage discovered on any monument] A recorded Assyrian procession included eleven instrumental performers and a chorus of female and child singers. The performers played harps, a dulcimer, a double-pipe, and a hand-drum, while singers clapped and some musicians danced.

records.l: lyre, Musical Instruments
records.s: The lyre is a stringed instrument. In Assyrian forms it occurred in three types, was held horizontally or nearly so, and used strings shifted along an oblique or slightly curved front bar to change pitch; it was played by plectrum or fingers. It was widely represented in Greek contexts, with varying construction, form, size, and names, and Roman forms included lyra, cithara, chelys, testudo, fidis, and cornu. Hebrew coins show three, five, or six strings. Later it appears in fourth-century Christian monuments, including Christ as Apollo, and in western European popular pastimes and Anglo-Saxon performance.

records.l: Babylonians, Musical Instruments
records.s: use_instrumental_music_for religious observances The Babylonians used instrumental music in religious observances. Their courtly musical customs are discussed alongside those of the Assyrians and Hebrews.

records.l: Nebuchadnezzar, Musical Instruments
records.s: commands_worship_of golden image [when specified instruments sound] Nebuchadnezzar commanded people to fall down and worship a golden image when they heard the cornet, flute, harp, sackbut, psaltery, dulcimer, and other music.

records.l: Jerusalem, Musical Instruments
records.s: Jerusalem had a courtly musical tradition similar to that associated with Assyria and Babylon. In the time of David and Solomon it also contained the Temple, where many singers and instrumental performers were engaged in sacred music.

records.l: Temple, Musical Instruments
records.s: The Temple at Jerusalem employed singers and instrumental performers for sacred music. The Talmudic account also places the powerful magrepha in the Temple, though its actual type is left uncertain.

records.l: Hebrew musical instruments, Musical Instruments
records.s: include single pipe [named as the Hebrew single pipe or flute] Hebrew musical instruments included probable harps, dulcimers, lyres, lutes or guitars, single and double pipes, the syrinx, bagpipes, trumpets, drums, sistrums, cymbals, and bells. The meanings of several biblical instrument names remain disputed.

records.l: harp (Hebrew instrument), Musical Instruments
records.s: is_possessed_by Hebrews [its biblical name is uncertain] The Hebrews certainly possessed a harp because it was common among the Egyptians and Assyrians, but the text states that it is uncertain which Hebrew biblical name designates it.

records.l: bagpipe, Musical Instruments
records.s: Bagpipe is a musical instrument, possibly denoted by the Hebrew sumphonia and perhaps related to the magrepha. A Tarsus terra-cotta, probably about 2000 years old, may represent an early form. Long favored by Celtic races and admired by Slavonic nations, it was of high antiquity in Ireland; in Poland and Ukraine it could be made from a whole goat skin.

records.l: Jubal, Musical Instruments
