records.s: Jubal is mentioned in Genesis as the father of those who handle harp and organ, and may be regarded as the first professional cultivator of instrumental music rather than inventor of every instrument.

records.l: Bible, Musical Instruments
records.s: mentions kinnor [as the oldest stringed instrument and invention of Jubal] The Bible supplies the names of many Hebrew instruments but does not provide representations sufficient to establish their construction. It mentions instruments including the kinnor, nebel, psanterin, asor, chalil, nekeb, mishrokitha, sumphonia, toph, and several kinds of trumpets, cymbals, and bells.

records.l: ancient Greeks, Musical Instruments
records.s: Ancient Greeks possessed many musical instruments, though most constructions and capabilities remain uncertain. Their system was generally believed derived from Egypt, while more complete instruments chiefly came from Asia and Asia Minor. They favored the lyre, used kithara, aulos, syrinx, and monochord in performance and teaching, and reserved salpinx and keras for war.

records.l: Etruscans, Musical Instruments
records.s: The Etruscans excel early in the arts, possess Greek-like instruments, and may invent the hydraulic organ; they use flutes and trumpets of varied materials and are said to transmit popular instruments to the Romans.

records.l: Romans, Musical Instruments
records.s: Romans derived or adopted many musical instruments from Etruscans, Greeks, Egypt, and western Asia, without essentially improving them. Their favorite stringed instrument was the lyre; their range included lyres, flutes, pipes, bagpipes, percussion, horns, trumpets, and hydraulic organ. They used cornu and tuba for war signals, while Nero favored tibia utricularis.

records.l: Asia, Musical Instruments
records.s: Asia is presented as the likely source of much Greek music and many Greek stringed instruments. Strabo associated a large portion of contemporary music with Asia as far as India, and named instruments with foreign or Asiatic associations. Greek instruments were especially adopted from peoples inhabiting Asia-minor.

records.l: Greece, Musical Instruments
records.s: Greece is described as a center in which instruments from Asia and other regions were used and adapted. The Greeks used many kinds of stringed, wind, and percussion instruments, although several instruments played chiefly by musicians who had immigrated from Asia could not be considered national instruments of Greece.

records.l: Spain, Musical Instruments
records.s: introduced instruments [by Saracens and Moors] Spain was a place where Al-Farabi acquired his proficiency and where schools of music flourished at Cordova toward the end of the ninth century. Musical instruments brought there by the Saracens and Moors were subsequently diffused toward northern Europe.

records.l: England, Musical Instruments
records.s: has_regal_representations regal [in old ecclesiastical edifices] England had a long tradition of bell-ringing and peal-ringing. Paul Hentzner reported in 1598 that English people enjoyed loud noises and sometimes rang bells for hours, while Egelric of Croyland was recorded as having cast six bells around 960.

records.l: Greek musical instruments, Musical Instruments
records.s: Greek musical instruments included lyres, kitharas, harps, trigona, magadides, barbitons, sambykes, simmikons, nablas, pandouras, monochords, auloi, syrinxes, salpinges, keras, tympana, kymbala, and krotala. Many were of uncertain construction, and several appear to have been derived from Asia. The Greeks used these instruments in solo performance, accompaniment, teaching, war, and other musical settings.

records.l: harp, Musical Instruments
records.s: A thirteen-stringed harp resembling an Assyrian harp was called kinyra by the Greeks; a Greek vase shows it played with both hands for treble and bass, possibly imported from Asia and influencing kinnor’s translation.

records.l: kithara, Musical Instruments
records.s: The kithara is a Greek lyre-like instrument with a square base, held against the breast; its distinction from other lyres is uncertain. It accompanied recitations early, then served solo performances by B.C. 700; a three-stringed Lydian form existed.

records.l: hydraulic organ, Musical Instruments
records.s: The hydraulic organ, or hydraulos/organum hydraulicum, was a primitive portable air-powered organ. Water provided pressure for its bellows and regulated them, but air through pipes made the sound. Placed on a table, it likely used stops and may have had ten pipes without a keyboard. It was later supplanted by the pneumatic organ by the early fourteenth century.

records.l: tibia, Musical Instruments
records.s: The tibia was a Roman flute, originally made from a shin bone with a mouth-hole and four finger-holes. Romans developed many varieties, including single and double forms; performers used a capistrum, and a mosaic shows a girl playing one with a holmos.

records.l: Confucius, Musical Instruments
records.s: Confucius lived about 500 B.C.; hearing Chinese music so enraptured him that he could not eat for three months, and he wished to proclaim divine purposes to the multitude.

records.l: sonorous stones, Musical Instruments
records.s: Sonorous stones are rhythmical instruments and musical material known in South America in olden times; when struck by a hard substance, they produce musical or metallic sounds.

records.l: tchung, Musical Instruments
records.s: The tchung is the Chinese name for a bell. Its forms include the square copper-and-tin té-tchung or piao for marking time and musical divisions, sets called pien-tchung, and the clapperless oval hiuen-tchung, struck with a wooden mallet and popular in the Han dynasty.

records.l: pentatonic scale, Musical Instruments
records.s: The pentatonic scale is a five-tone scale, heard on a pianoforte by omitting f and b from C major or playing successive black keys from f-sharp. It is presented as a deliberately organized interval system in Aztec, Mexican, and Peruvian instruments, including the pito, huayra-puhura, pipe, and syrinx. It is also associated with Peruvian cachua, Scotch national dances, Chinese instruments, and ancient Asian peoples.

records.l: Chinese musical instruments, Musical Instruments
records.s: Chinese musical instruments included the king and pien-king made from sonorous stones, bells such as the tchung, wooden instruments such as the fang-hiang and ou, drums such as the po-fou and kin-kou, bamboo flutes and pipes, the clay hiuen, the cheng with tubes placed in a calabash, and the stringed kin and chê. They were used for accompanying songs of praise, religious observances, imperial and military purposes, marking time, producing rhythm, and performing melodies. Some instruments were arranged in sets according to prescribed intervals, while others followed the pentatonic scale.

records.l: Hindus, Musical Instruments
records.s: Hindus are described through their music: they possess about fifty instruments, many long unchanged, including ancient vina, a Krishna-favoured flute, Arabic and Persian instruments, violin, and chorus. Their scale divides the octave into twenty-two sruti intervals; instruments span older traditions and comparatively recent introductions.

records.l: Brahmin mythology, Musical Instruments
records.s: Brahmin mythology attributes the invention of the vina to Nareda and associates several deities with music and musical instruments. It also presents music as having a heavenly origin.

records.l: Nareda, Musical Instruments
records.s: In Hindu mythology, Nareda is a god, inventor of the vina, whose name is interpreted as giver of water.

records.l: Saraswati, Musical Instruments
records.s: Saraswati is a goddess of music and speech and consort of Brahma, associated with Minerva. Credited with inventing the musical scale, she is represented playing a stringed instrument while seated on a peacock.

records.l: Krishna, Musical Instruments
records.s: Krishna, in incarnation as Vishnu, is represented as a beautiful youth playing a flute, the distinctive favourite instrument constructed by Hindus.

records.l: water, Musical Instruments
records.s: is_associated_with stringed instrument [in widespread origin traditions] Water is associated with the origins of musical instruments in traditions from several regions. The text connects Nareda with water, describes instruments made from aquatic materials or bones, and suggests that the sounds of waves and running water may have encouraged these beliefs.

records.l: Hindustan, Musical Instruments
records.s: Hindustan is described as home of the principal national vina and a possible origin of the fiddle-bow, from which instruments spread eastward, altered, toward Japan.

records.l: violin bow, Musical Instruments
records.s: The violin bow is claimed by Hindus to have been invented in Hindustan, possibly for the ravanastron, with Sanskrit names dating 1500–2000 years ago; some historians instead claim England or Wales.

records.l: Persians, Musical Instruments
records.s: Persians had instruments resembling Assyrians’ and Hebrews’ before the Christian era, and later possessed an advanced musical culture with chang forms, small intervals, and diverse instruments before Arab conquest.

records.l: Arabs, Musical Instruments
records.s: Arabs adopted Persian instruments and musical practices after conquering Persia, developed theorized seventeen one-third-tone octaves, then carried instruments into Spain and Europe.

records.l: Persia, Musical Instruments
records.s: Persia had a more advanced cultivation of music and superior musical instruments than the Arabs at the time of the Arab conquest in A.D. 641. Persian musical theory is presented as the basis for the system preserved in the earliest Arabian writings on musical theory.

records.l: Khosroo Purviz, Musical Instruments
records.s: is_associated_with Tackt-i-Bostan [sculptures said to have been executed during his lifetime] Khosroo Purviz was the Persian monarch during whose lifetime the sculptures at Tackt-i-Bostan are said to have been executed. The sculptures depict musicians, including harpers, trumpet players, drummers, a flutist, a player of a pandean pipe, and a bagpipe player.

records.l: harp, Musical Instruments
records.s: The harp, called chang by Persians and junk by Arabs, was formerly favored in Persia, appearing in sculptures and manuscripts, but gradually fell into disuse; an old Persian chang may appear in a seventeenth-century representation.

records.l: Arab conquest of Persia, Musical Instruments
records.s: occurred_in Persia [A.D. 641] The Arab conquest of Persia took place in A.D. 641. The Arabs found Persian musical cultivation and instruments superior to their own and soon adopted them.

records.l: octave division into seventeen one-third-tones, Musical Instruments
records.s: A musical system used by Arabs: earliest preserved Arabian theory described an octave divided into seventeen one-third-tones, with lute and tamboura frets regulated for accurate intervals.

records.l: lute, Musical Instruments
records.s: The lute is a stringed musical instrument, called el-oud in Arabic. It was brought to Mekka by Nadr Ben el-Hares Ben Kelde after he learned Persian singing and lute performance at Khosroo Purviz’s court. Before the tenth century, the Arabian lute had four paired strings; around the tenth century a fifth tone was added, with silk strings and frets regulated by seventeen one-third-tones. It later used catgut strings and movable catgut frets, six-line notation, and sizes from treble-lute to bass-lute. It developed to twelve pairs of strings in the seventeenth-century English lute, was prized for mellow tone and decoration, then fell into oblivion.

records.l: Al-Farabi, Musical Instruments
records.s: Al-Farabi, an early tenth-century Arabian musical theorist, did not mention the fiddle-bow; his musical reputation was associated with Spain and Cordova.

records.l: Saracens, Musical Instruments
records.s: introduced_instruments_into Spain [including eastern instruments later diffused into northern Europe] The Saracens introduced eastern musical instruments into Spain. Through their presence, instruments such as the kuitra, el-oud, rebab, and nakkarah were gradually transmitted toward northern Europe.

records.l: Moors, Musical Instruments
records.s: introduced_instruments_into Spain [including eastern instruments later diffused into northern Europe] The Moors introduced eastern musical instruments into Spain, from where those instruments were gradually diffused toward northern Europe. Their influence also contributed the Moorish dance, or morrice dance.

records.l: Al-Farabi's court performance, Musical Instruments
records.s: Al-Farabi’s court performance in Bagdad unfolds as he plays lute in successive musical modes, moving the audience through laughter, sadness, rage, and finally profound sleep, after which he departs while the listeners remain asleep.

records.l: American Indians, Musical Instruments
records.s: American Indians possessed and made varied musical instruments before European contact, including pipes, flutes, syrinxes, trumpets, and sound-producing vessels. Their music accompanied ceremonies, warfare, funerals, dances, signaling, and entertainment. They also had songs, dances, ceremonies, and musical institutions; their present-day accomplishments are described as below those of their ancestors.

records.l: Aztecs, Musical Instruments
records.s: The Aztecs are a group sharing a race with the Tezcucans and described as having many claims to civilization, splendid living, and magnificent structures. Their preserved musical instruments include pipes, flutes, huehuetl, pottery whistles, pito, and yotl-bells. They used flutes in religious observances and solemn orations, made pipes with pentatonic intervals, and depicted tribute bells in picture-writings. They were said to lack stringed instruments, though that claim is questioned.

records.l: Peruvians, Musical Instruments
records.s: The Peruvians are described through their music and musical roles. They made bone flutes, syrinxes called huayra-puhura, other pipes, and bells possibly called chanrares; they also possessed the five- or seven-stringed tinya. Their songs used different interval orders, with indications of a pentatonic scale. Music accompanied organized military trumpeters and drummers, victory celebrations, festivals, funerals, agricultural songs, and elegiac haravis, composed by haravecs.

records.l: American musical instruments, Musical Instruments
records.s: Ancient American musical instruments, genuine contrivances of American Indians before European influence, reveal their makers’ artistic development, social condition, and musical systems through surviving pottery, bone, cane, stone, wood, and other instruments, including those used to summon worshippers to prayer.

records.l: pipes and flutes, Musical Instruments
records.s: Pipes and flutes, often preserved because pottery and bone resist decay, included whistles, small pipes, flageolet-like instruments, bone flutes, and syrinxes.

records.l: Mexican whistle, Musical Instruments
records.s: The Mexican whistle is a small baked-clay instrument, often shaped as a grotesque human figure, bird, beast, or flower. Some have a top finger-hole producing two tones; others contain a loose clay ball whose vibration creates a shrill, whirring sound when blown. It most likely served mainly for signaling.

records.l: Aztec pito, Musical Instruments
records.s: The Aztec pito is a reddish-pottery pipe, called pito by the Mexican Spaniards, resembling a flageolet and fitted with four finger-holes. Examined specimens varied from six to nine inches yet shared one pitch and a pentatonic interval order; it was used in religious observances and appeared in Aztec religious symbolism.

records.l: Peruvian bone flute, Musical Instruments
records.s: A Peruvian flute found in an ancient tomb was made from a human bone, with four finger-holes on its upper surface and a blowing end at one extremity. Similar bone flutes from Truxillo in the British Museum differ in hole arrangements and blowing-end material.

records.l: Peruvian syrinx, Musical Instruments
records.s: The Peruvian huayra-puhura is a syrinx made of cane or stone, sometimes ornamented. A tomb specimen from Arica in the British Museum has fourteen reed pipes in two rows, open and closed to produce octaves. Another greenish-stone specimen, procured by Paroissien from a Peruvian tomb, has eight pipes and lateral finger-holes that lower pitches by a semitone. Its intervals were purposely arranged to produce a pentatonic scale.

records.l: trumpets, Musical Instruments
records.s: are_used_for signals in war [among Indians at the time of the discovery of America] Trumpets were used by American Indians for signaling in war, ceremonies, mourning, and funeral dances. Examples include conch trumpets, long wooden or bamboo instruments, the juruparis, the turé, the Mexican acocotl, and the clay botuto.

records.l: Orinoco, Musical Instruments
records.s: has Indian tribes [in its vicinity] Near the Orinoco, Gumilla found a wooden trumpet nearly seven feet long. He also observed the botuto among Indian tribes near the river; this baked-clay trumpet was commonly three or four feet long, though some were enormous, and its deep sound was used in mourning and funeral dances.

records.l: juruparis, Musical Instruments
records.s: Juruparis is a mysterious, greatly venerated trumpet of Indians on the Rio Haupés. Made from slips forming the inner tube of Paxiaba palm and usually four to five feet long, it is hidden in a forest stream, revealed at night for feasts, and blown outside houses. Women and uninitiated youths are forbidden to see it. Specimens are at Kew gardens.

records.l: teponaztli, Musical Instruments
records.s: The teponaztli is a drum, generally made from a single block of very hard wood, hollowed into a somewhat oblong-square body with a thin sound-board and two vibrating wooden tongues. Beaten with two drumsticks covered at the ends with ule, its tongues produce two distinct sounds; shaving the wood regulates pitch. Their interval may be a third, fourth, fifth, sixth, or octave and conforms to a diatonic series excepting the seventh. It is often carved with fanciful designs and ranges from small strap-carried forms to Mexican specimens over five feet long, audible for three miles. Some are preserved by Indians in Mexico.

records.l: Mexicans, Musical Instruments
records.s: calls teponaztli The Mexicans possessed historical, war, love, secular, and sacred songs, as well as musical instruments used in temples and public celebrations. Boys were taught sacred chants by priests, and professional musicians served persons of high position.

records.l: rattle, Musical Instruments
records.s: A rattle is an instrument of percussion, popular among Indians before the discovery of America. Usually made from an oval or round hollowed gourd with holes, a wooden handle, and little pebbles inside, it was also made of pottery; Mexicans called it ajacaxtli.

records.l: Tezcucans, Musical Instruments
records.s: The Tezcucans, or Acolhuans, were of the same race as the Aztecs but were described as greatly surpassing them in knowledge, social refinement, and the arts and sciences. Their histories, poems, laws, and dialect were regarded as superior, and Tezcuco possessed the Council of music.

records.l: Nezahualcoyotl, Musical Instruments
records.s: Nezahualcoyotl is a wise monarch of the Tezcucans. He abhors human sacrifices, erects a large temple to “The unknown god, the cause of causes,” and founds the Council of music at Tezcuco, which advances music, other arts, and sciences.

records.l: temple of the unknown god, Musical Instruments
records.s: A large temple erected by Nezahualcoyotl and dedicated to the unknown god, “the cause of causes,” rises with a nine-story tower whose top-mounted musical instruments summon worshippers to prayer.

records.l: sonorous metal, Musical Instruments
records.s: is_a musical instrument [struck with a mallet] The Tezcucans (or Acolhuans) belonged to the same race as the Azt] A sonorous metal at the top of the temple’s tower was struck with a mallet. The record does not make clear whether it was a gong or a bell.

records.l: Ixtlilxochitl, Musical Instruments
records.s: Ixtlilxochitl, a Mexican of royal descent living in the early seventeenth century, wrote a historical essay describing sonorous metal and may have known his countrymen’s musical practices.

records.l: Peruvian bell, Musical Instruments
records.s: A small copper bell was found in an old Peruvian tomb, then deposited in the museum at Lima, where M. de Castelnau published a drawing of it.

records.l: horse bells, Musical Instruments
records.s: is_known_to Mexicans [certainly] The Tezcucans (or Acolhuans) belonged to the same race as the Azt] Horse bells were certainly known to the Mexicans, although it is uncertain whether the Peruvian name chanrares designated them. The bells were nearly round and were compared with the Schellen attached to horses by Germans.

records.l: yotl-bells, Musical Instruments
records.s: Yotl-bells are nearly round horse bells called yotl by the Mexicans. Depicted in Aztec picture-writings as tribute paid to sovereigns, they are represented by a cluster held in the British Museum’s Mexican antiquities collection.

records.l: musical instrument of green sonorous stone, Musical Instruments
records.s: A musical instrument made of green sonorous stone, preserved among Indian antiquities in Cuzco. About a foot long and an inch and a half wide, it is flat-sided, pointed, and arched, with a back hole for string suspension; when suspended and struck, it produces a singularly musical note.

records.l: Amazon-stone, Musical Instruments
records.s: Amazon-stone, named after the Amazon by early European visitors to America, makes a metallic sound when struck. Though not found only near the Amazon, American Indians formerly cut it into thin, centrally perforated plates and suspended them by strings.

records.l: stringed instruments of the American Indians, Musical Instruments
records.s: is_a musical instruments [ancient] Information about the ancient stringed instruments of the American Indians is described as scanty. The Peruvian tinya is identified as a five- or seven-stringed instrument that may have resembled a guitar, but no specimens are said to survive in museums because of the fragility of their materials.

records.l: Montezuma, Musical Instruments
records.s: Montezuma is described as maintaining a grand establishment. J. Ranking claimed that fiddle, flute, snail-shell, kettle-drum, and other instruments were played during his repasts, but the text considers this assertion unreliable because its source is not given.

records.l: fiddle, Musical Instruments
records.s: has_sound_holes two sound-holes [in a Peterborough cathedral representation] An Anglo-Saxon fiddle, or fithele, from an eleventh-century manuscript has a pear-shaped body and four strings, although no bridge is shown. Fiddle-bow use is recorded in Germany in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, and Peterborough cathedral contains a possibly twelfth-century depiction whose instrument resembles the modern violin.

records.l: musical performances, Musical Instruments
records.s: is_a principal part of public celebrations [with dancing] Musical performances were considered indispensable at public celebrations among the Peruvians and were used in warfare, festivals, mourning, agricultural labor, religious observances, and Christian missionary work. They included songs, instrumental music, dancing, processions, and dramatic representations.

records.l: Peru, Musical Instruments
records.s: Peru organizes its army carefully, with division trumpeters and drummers, and sustains agricultural songs, minstrels, and religious and Christian musical performances among Indian Christians.

records.l: Inca, Musical Instruments
records.s: visits temple of the Sun [after returning victorious from battle] The Inca was honored in Peruvian agricultural hymns that celebrated his deeds and dynasty. After returning victorious from battle, the Inca went first to the temple of the Sun to offer thanksgiving, and songs were also performed at the obsequies of deceased monarchs.

records.l: Prescott, Musical Instruments
records.s: Prescott is cited for describing the grandeur and ostentatious pageantry of the Aztecs and the superior cultural attainments attributed to the Tezcucans. He also described Peruvian royal funeral observances involving processions, banners, bards, minstrels, and songs commemorating the dead monarch.

records.l: Peruvian agricultural songs, Musical Instruments
records.s: Peruvian agricultural songs are hymns sung while cultivating the lands of the Inca; they glorify the Inca and his dynasty, use rhythm to regulate laborers’ work, and often include hailli, meaning “Triumph.”

records.l: Council of music, Musical Instruments
records.s: The Council of music was an academy for general education founded at Tezcuco, promoting music alongside history, astronomy, and other arts and sciences; it is presented as evidence of remarkable intellectual attainments.

records.l: Tezcuco, Musical Instruments
records.s: contains Council of music [founded by Nezahualcoyotl] Tezcuco is described as the place where Nezahualcoyotl founded the Council of music. The unit also mentions a great temple at Tezcuco containing a sonorous metal object that some inquirers believed to be a gong.

records.l: central America, Musical Instruments
records.s: In central America, Dominican priests composed a sacred poem in the Guatemalian dialect recounting important biblical events and performed it with musical instruments. The music influenced a powerful cazique and helped spread the new doctrines among his subjects.

records.l: North American Indians, Musical Instruments
records.s: possess musical instruments [genuine old Indian contrivances, including rattles, drums, flutes, and whistles] North American Indians who converted to Christianity after the emigration of the puritans to New England were praised for their musical talent. Their singing of John Elliot's translation of the psalms into Indian verse was described by witnesses as excellent and most ravishing.

records.l: Guatemala, Musical Instruments
records.s: has African marimba [introduced through African slaves and popular among natives] Guatemala is identified as a place where the African marimba, introduced by slaves, became rather popular among the natives. The text says that such adaptations can be distinguished from genuine old Indian inventions.

records.l: European nations, Musical Instruments
records.s: European instruments initially resembled Asiatic instruments, then showed little material construction improvement for nearly a thousand years, amid scarce evidence from the first five or six Christian-era centuries.

records.l: Middle Ages, Musical Instruments
records.s: The Middle Ages are documented through manuscripts, sculptures, and paintings that preserve uncertain but valuable evidence of musical instruments. Wind instruments ranged from flutes and trumpets to early organs, alongside quaintly made instruments, organistrums, and percussion in medieval concerts.

records.l: Anglo-Saxons, Musical Instruments
records.s: use harp [to accompany vocal performances] The Anglo-Saxons accompanied vocal performances with a harp that was more or less triangular and represented a transition from the lyre to the harp. An Anglo-Saxon manuscript also depicts one gleeman playing the lyre and another playing a double-pipe.

records.l: cithara, Musical Instruments
records.s: Cithara is a name for several stringed instruments varying greatly in form, sound power, and compass; a ninth-century St. Blasius example has a small top sound-board and appears to improve on the triangular psalterium.

records.l: psalterium, Musical Instruments
records.s: Psalterium denotes medieval triangular or square stringed instruments; a small sound-board form apparently prototyped the citole, while by the fourteenth century it became trapezium-shaped like a dulcimer.

records.l: harp, Musical Instruments
records.s: The harp is a more or less triangular stringed instrument among the Anglo-Saxons. Especially popular in central and northern Europe, it was favored by German and Celtic bards and Scandinavian skalds. Medieval forms include twelve strings and two sound holes, though some early forms lacked a front pillar. Small harps appear in the St. Georges de Boscherville orchestra, played by crowned musicians with fingers or a plectrum.

records.l: violin, Musical Instruments
records.s: The violin is occasionally played pizzicato and held like a viol; a medieval viol may show its modern holding manner’s older origin.

records.l: Welsh crwth, Musical Instruments
records.s: The Welsh crwth is a fiddle resembling the rotta, distinguished by a central finger-board and few strings. It is shown in a modern form, then traced to the three-stringed Crwth Trithant, resembling a violin or rebeck.

records.l: monochord, Musical Instruments
records.s: Monochord is a stringed instrument with one string on fixed bridges over an oblong box; a turning screw adjusts tension and a movable bridge marks scale intervals, serving chiefly theorists rather than performance.

records.l: musical scale, Musical Instruments
records.s: The musical scale was diatonic about a thousand years ago, except for a chromatic seventh interval because it included both b-flat and b-natural; period notation showed its compass and interval order.

records.l: regal, Musical Instruments
records.s: The regal was a small, often embellished portable organ with smaller organ-like keys. It appears in sculptured representations at Beverley Minster and Melrose Abbey, and in a painting with piston-like keys. The name also denoted a percussion instrument of sonorous wooden slabs arranged like a harmonica.

records.l: orchestras of the Middle Ages, Musical Instruments
records.s: Medieval orchestras are represented by sculptors on monuments; although partly imaginative, the depicted instruments probably reflect contemporary orchestras and evidence medieval instrumental music.

records.l: orchestra at St. Georges de Boscherville, Musical Instruments
records.s: A twelve-performer orchestra bas-relief, formerly ornamenting the abbey at St. Georges de Boscherville, features mostly crowned musicians, varied instruments, and a head-standing tumbler; reportedly late eleventh century, it was removed to and is preserved in the museum of Rouen.

records.l: St. Georges de Boscherville, Musical Instruments
records.s: CHAPTER IX.] Its abbey formerly displayed the bas-relief containing the twelve-performer musical group. The relief was later removed to the museum of Rouen.

records.l: viol, Musical Instruments
records.s: The viol is a bowed string instrument, most commonly with five strings, shown in sculptures held between the knees or almost like a violin.

records.l: viol family, Musical Instruments
records.s: has several kinds [differing in size and compass of sound] CHAPTER IX.] Several kinds were used, differing in size, compass, number of strings, and tuning. One type had a string beside the finger-board, while other types placed all strings over it; side strings were later adopted on instruments including the lira di braccio and lute.

records.l: orchestra on the Portico della gloria, Musical Instruments
records.s: The orchestra on the Portico della gloria is a group of twenty-four life-sized seated elders in high relief, dated 1188, each holding instruments including organistrum, harps, salterios, and vihuelas, shown tuning or preparing rather than playing.

records.l: Portico della gloria, Musical Instruments
records.s: is_located_at Santiago da Compostella [in Spain] CHAPTER IX.] It is the triple portal of the pilgrimage church at Santiago da Compostella. Its central arch contains the twenty-four musical elders, and an inscription on the lintel states that it was executed in 1188.

records.l: Santiago da Compostella, Musical Instruments
records.s: CHAPTER IX.] Its famous pilgrimage church contains the Portico della gloria, whose sculptures show instruments used in Spain around the twelfth century. A cast of the sculpture is held in the Kensington museum.

records.l: twenty-four elders, Musical Instruments
records.s: Twenty-four elders are seen by St. John in the Apocalypse, then depicted seated around Portico della gloria’s central arch, each with an instrument.

records.l: vihuela, Musical Instruments
records.s: A Spanish viol of the twelfth century, represented on the Portico della gloria in several forms: smaller three-string examples resemble rebec, while larger ones have broader bodies and different sound-holes; no bows appear.

records.l: minstrels’ gallery of Exeter cathedral, Musical Instruments
records.s: A fourteenth-century gallery at Exeter cathedral, its front unfolds across twelve niches, each holding a winged figure or angel playing instruments from cittern and bagpipe to timbrel and cymbals.

records.l: Exeter cathedral, Musical Instruments
records.s: CHAPTER IX.] It contains the fourteenth-century minstrels’ gallery, whose sculptured front represents twelve angelic or winged instrumentalists. A cast of this sculpture is also held at South Kensington.

records.l: virginal, Musical Instruments
records.s: A musical instrument originating in the middle ages, later highly popular; a specimen from Elizabeth's time was held at South Kensington.

records.l: theorbo, Musical Instruments
records.s: The theorbo was a double-necked lute that appears to have come into use during the sixteenth century. It had additional bass strings beside the finger-board that could not be shortened by the fingers; its largest forms were the archlute and chitarrone.

records.l: recorder, Musical Instruments
records.s: The recorder, an old musical instrument mentioned in Hamlet, was known in Shakespeare’s time, illustrated in 1683, and later became scarce.

records.l: bell, Musical Instruments
records.s: Bell is a musical instrument especially popular in England for centuries, suspended in towers, frames, gateways, and oak trees.

records.l: carillon, Musical Instruments
records.s: A carillon is a musical instrument made of differently sized, tuned bells, popular in the Netherlands and Belgium and found in Germany and Italy. It may have thirty-seven bells, hand keys and pedals spanning over three octaves, and is played, often by a church organist, or operated by clockwork. Its distant sound is its central purpose.

records.l: peal-ringing, Musical Instruments
records.s: Peal-ringing is a pastime especially national to England, using usually eight diatonically tuned bells, sometimes ten or twelve, swung forcefully mouth-upward.

records.l: history of music, Musical Instruments
records.s: elucidates musical instruments [by reference to the music of different nations] The history of music was presented as a means of explaining the development and characteristics of musical instruments. Studying the music of different nations was said to clarify features that would otherwise appear obscure.

records.s: colossal statue of Chaacmol is a representation identified by competing interpretations
records.q: Dr. Jesus Sanchez, Professor of Archaeology in the National Museum of Mexico, ignoring altogether the circumstances accompanying the discovery of the statue, has published in the _Anales del Museo Nacional_, a long dissertation--full of erudition, certainly--to prove that the statue discovered by me at Chichen-Itza, was a representation of the _God of the natural production of the earth_, and that the name given by me was altogether arbitrary; and, also, because an article has appeared in the _North American Review_ for October, 1880, signed by Mr. Charnay, in which the author, after re-producing Mr. Sanchez's writing, pronounces _ex cathedra_ and _de perse_, but without assigning any reason for his opinion, that the statue is the effigy of the _god of wine_--the Mexican Bacchus--without telling us which of them, for there were two.

records.s: The unit describes Yucatan’s flat limestone terrain, underground water system, climate, vegetation, agriculture, and natural resources. It discusses the caves and senotes that characterize the peninsula, the absence of surface rivers and lakes, and the causes proposed for its freedom from earthquakes. It also describes Uxmal, Mayapan, Kaba, and other ancient ruins, as well as the continuing conflict between the Santa Cruz Indians and the Yucatecans. The unit explains that hennequen has become the principal commercial crop of the white-controlled territory, contributing to shortages of maize.

records.l: Yucatan, Vestiges of the Mayas, or, Facts tending to prove that Communications and Intimate Relations must have existed, in very remote times, between the inhabitants of Mayab and those of Asia and Africa, Vestiges of the Mayas
records.s: Yucatan is a low, mostly flat limestone peninsula between the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean Sea. It contains extensive caves, senotes, underground currents, tropical forests, coastal mangrove sloughs, and fertile but predominantly stony land.

records.l: Uxmal, Vestiges of the Mayas, or, Facts tending to prove that Communications and Intimate Relations must have existed, in very remote times, between the inhabitants of Mayab and those of Asia and Africa, Vestiges of the Mayas
records.s: Uxmal is a ruined city near a low range of hills containing possible marble quarries and red iron oxide. Its monuments have sculptured marble ornaments, artificial water reservoirs, and a building called the Governor's house, beneath which the text suggests a cave may exist.

records.l: Santa Cruz Indians, Vestiges of the Mayas, or, Facts tending to prove that Communications and Intimate Relations must have existed, in very remote times, between the inhabitants of Mayab and those of Asia and Africa, Vestiges of the Mayas
records.s: The Santa Cruz Indians control about two-thirds of the peninsula, including its richest and most fertile territories. They export mahogany and other woods through agents at Belize and have waged war against the Yucatecans since 1847.

records.l: Maya civilization, Vestiges of the Mayas, or, Facts tending to prove that Communications and Intimate Relations must have existed, in very remote times, between the inhabitants of Mayab and those of Asia and Africa, Vestiges of the Mayas
records.s: The text associates ancient cities, monuments, artificial mounds, reservoirs, and Katun columns with the earlier inhabitants of Yucatan. It states that isolated Katun columns were erected at least 6,000 years ago, according to the account.

records.l: Yucatecans, Vestiges of the Mayas, or, Facts tending to prove that Communications and Intimate Relations must have existed, in very remote times, between the inhabitants of Mayab and those of Asia and Africa, Vestiges of the Mayas
records.s: The Yucatecans control about one-third of the peninsula and have been confined largely to stony land. Their principal source of wealth is hennequen, while shortages of maize have led merchants to import it from New York.

records.l: Spaniards, Vestiges of the Mayas, or, Facts tending to prove that Communications and Intimate Relations must have existed, in very remote times, between the inhabitants of Mayab and those of Asia and Africa, Vestiges of the Mayas
records.s: The white inhabitants control the less fertile one-third of Yucatan and are largely restricted to cultivating hennequen. They import ocher, marble flooring, maize, and sugar because local production is insufficient or mineral resources remain unexploited.

records.l: Indians, Vestiges of the Mayas, or, Facts tending to prove that Communications and Intimate Relations must have existed, in very remote times, between the inhabitants of Mayab and those of Asia and Africa, Vestiges of the Mayas
records.s: Indians serve as local sources of information about caves, senotes, and ruins, although some reports are presented as traditional stories. Indians of Santa Cruz cut and export valuable woods, while Indians from Chemax reportedly know of water sheets near Kaba.

records.l: Yucatan War, Vestiges of the Mayas, or, Facts tending to prove that Communications and Intimate Relations must have existed, in very remote times, between the inhabitants of Mayab and those of Asia and Africa, Vestiges of the Mayas
records.s: The conflict described as beginning in 1847 is a war in which the Santa Cruz Indians wage war to the knife against the Yucatecans. It prevents foreigners from safely visiting the ruins of Kaba and leaves the Santa Cruz Indians in possession of most of the peninsula.

records.l: earthquakes, Vestiges of the Mayas, or, Facts tending to prove that Communications and Intimate Relations must have existed, in very remote times, between the inhabitants of Mayab and those of Asia and Africa, Vestiges of the Mayas
records.s: Earthquakes frequently convulse Mexico, Guatemala, Cuba, and other West India Islands, but Yucatan is described as entirely free from them. The text attributes this immunity, in the author's opinion, to the peninsula's many caves and senotes, which allegedly vent underground gases.

records.l: epidemics, Vestiges of the Mayas, or, Facts tending to prove that Communications and Intimate Relations must have existed, in very remote times, between the inhabitants of Mayab and those of Asia and Africa, Vestiges of the Mayas
records.s: Epidemics of yellow fever, smallpox, and other diseases occur in Yucatan, generally after the rainy season and especially after excessive rains. Poor drainage, stagnant water, overcrowding, and decomposing matter are identified as contributing causes.

records.l: yellow fever, Vestiges of the Mayas, or, Facts tending to prove that Communications and Intimate Relations must have existed, in very remote times, between the inhabitants of Mayab and those of Asia and Africa, Vestiges of the Mayas
records.s: Yellow fever is endemic in Yucatan, generally in a mild form. During epidemic outbreaks, including the one mentioned in the unit, both natives and unacclimated foreigners can die from it.

records.l: senotes, Vestiges of the Mayas, or, Facts tending to prove that Communications and Intimate Relations must have existed, in very remote times, between the inhabitants of Mayab and those of Asia and Africa, Vestiges of the Mayas
records.s: Senotes are immense circular holes, usually containing water, with diameters of about 50 to 500 feet and perpendicular walls 50 to 150 feet deep. Some have currents, some are dry, and some contain thermal mineral water with sulphurous odor and vapor; local stories attribute unusual properties to their waters.

records.l: caves of Yucatan, Vestiges of the Mayas, or, Facts tending to prove that Communications and Intimate Relations must have existed, in very remote times, between the inhabitants of Mayab and those of Asia and Africa, Vestiges of the Mayas
records.s: The caves of Yucatan are numerous, extensive, and generally unexplored. They contain stalactites, stalagmites, springs, streams, shrimps, and fishes, and are presented as possible outlets for gases beneath the peninsula.

records.l: subterranean water, Vestiges of the Mayas, or, Facts tending to prove that Communications and Intimate Relations must have existed, in very remote times, between the inhabitants of Mayab and those of Asia and Africa, Vestiges of the Mayas
records.s: Subterranean water supplies the caves, senotes, and rare surface aguadas of Yucatan. Since the peninsula has no surface rivers and almost no lakes, plants, animals, and inhabitants depend heavily on underground water and seasonal rain.

records.l: Yucatan climate, Vestiges of the Mayas, or, Facts tending to prove that Communications and Intimate Relations must have existed, in very remote times, between the inhabitants of Mayab and those of Asia and Africa, Vestiges of the Mayas
records.s: Yucatan has a mild, comparatively healthy tropical climate with moisture-laden air and an average temperature of about 80 degrees Fahrenheit. Temperatures may reach 96 degrees in July and August and rarely fall below 65 degrees in December, while rainy-season moisture and poor drainage contribute to disease.

records.l: stony soil, Vestiges of the Mayas, or, Facts tending to prove that Communications and Intimate Relations must have existed, in very remote times, between the inhabitants of Mayab and those of Asia and Africa, Vestiges of the Mayas
records.s: The stony soil of Yucatan consists mainly of limestone with only a few inches of arable loam formed from stone detritus and decomposed vegetation. Despite its thinness, it can be highly fertile, and it supports large trees as well as the hennequen plant.

records.l: maize, Vestiges of the Mayas, or, Facts tending to prove that Communications and Intimate Relations must have existed, in very remote times, between the inhabitants of Mayab and those of Asia and Africa, Vestiges of the Mayas
records.s: Maize is the staple food of all classes in Yucatan. Its cultivation has declined as landowners convert fields to hennequen, producing a shortage that led to imports from New York at advanced prices.

records.l: hennequen plant, Vestiges of the Mayas, or, Facts tending to prove that Communications and Intimate Relations must have existed, in very remote times, between the inhabitants of Mayab and those of Asia and Africa, Vestiges of the Mayas
records.s: The hennequen plant, identified as agave sisalensis, grows well on Yucatan's stony soil and requires little water or care. White landowners increasingly plant it for commerce instead of maize because its fiber is in strong demand.

records.l: hennequen fiber, Vestiges of the Mayas, or, Facts tending to prove that Communications and Intimate Relations must have existed, in very remote times, between the inhabitants of Mayab and those of Asia and Africa, Vestiges of the Mayas
records.s: Hennequen fiber is obtained from the hennequen plant and used to manufacture cordage. Its demand in the United States and Europe makes it Yucatan's principal export and its main source of wealth.

records.s: The unit concerns Yucatan, its Indigenous and mixed population, and the remains of Maya civilization. It describes the Mayas’ cities, monuments, writing, sciences, language, and funerary practices, while recounting the Spanish arrival in 1517 and the need for further study of American archaeology. Mrs. Le Plongeon and Augustus Le Plongeon investigate monuments at Chichen-Itza and elsewhere, identifying Chaacmol’s tomb, statue, and funeral chamber. The text also appeals to the Mexican government for permission to recover ancient books hidden in monumental buildings.

records.l: Yucatan, Vestiges of the Mayas, or, Facts tending to prove that Communications and Intimate Relations must have existed, in very remote times, between the inhabitants of Mayab and those of Asia and Africa, The population of the country, about 250,000 souls all told, are mostly Indians
records.s: Yucatan is described as having a population of about 250,000, mostly Indians and people of mixed blood. Its forests contain numerous ruined cities and monuments, and its inhabitants still speak a complex language.

records.l: Mayas, Vestiges of the Mayas, or, Facts tending to prove that Communications and Intimate Relations must have existed, in very remote times, between the inhabitants of Mayab and those of Asia and Africa, The population of the country, about 250,000 souls all told, are mostly Indians
records.s: The Mayas are presented as a highly civilized people who built cities, roads, causeways, and monuments, and developed writing, mathematics, astronomy, sculpture, painting, and grammar. Their funerary practices included cremation, statues representing the dead, and beliefs concerning reincarnation.

records.l: Mayapan, Vestiges of the Mayas, or, Facts tending to prove that Communications and Intimate Relations must have existed, in very remote times, between the inhabitants of Mayab and those of Asia and Africa, The population of the country, about 250,000 souls all told, are mostly Indians
records.s: Mayapan is identified as the site where a gnomon was found by the author, providing evidence of Maya knowledge of mathematical and astronomical sciences.

records.s: The Mexican government is asked to grant permission for the author to recover ancient books from buildings where they are hidden. The text also states that the government transported the head of Chaacmol’s colossal statue to Mexico without the author’s consent or compensation.

records.l: American archaeology, Vestiges of the Mayas, or, Facts tending to prove that Communications and Intimate Relations must have existed, in very remote times, between the inhabitants of Mayab and those of Asia and Africa, The population of the country, about 250,000 souls all told, are mostly Indians
records.s: American archaeology is defended against European scientists who dismiss it because they believe no relationship existed between American and Old World civilizations. The author argues that the ruins of Yucatan and Central America had not yet been thoroughly or scientifically explored.

records.s: The Spanish are said to have been surprised by the stone monuments, cities, roads, boats, and civilized inhabitants they encountered in Yucatan. Their arrival brought them into contact with a people dressed in white cotton and possessing polite manners.

records.s: The Spanish conquest is included among the wars, invasions, and social and religious convulsions that damaged the surviving remains of earlier civilizations. Historians of the Conquest recorded the Spanish reaction to the monuments and inhabitants of Yucatan.

records.s: Uxmal is cited for its architectural monuments, bas-reliefs, and mural paintings. Mrs. Le Plongeon is said to have given a correct description of its monuments in letters to the New York World.

records.s: Chichen-Itza contains the funeral chamber of Chaacmol, monumental buildings, mural paintings, inscriptions, and statues of dead personages. Its monuments are studied through photography, surveys, plans, and analysis of their ornaments and designs.

records.s: The monuments of Yucatan include large ruined cities, stone buildings, bas-reliefs, statues, and mural paintings that reveal the achievements and customs of their builders. The text argues that they require systematic and patient archaeological study.

records.s: Mrs. Le Plongeon worked with the author after arriving at Progresso in 1873. She contributed descriptions of the monuments of Uxmal, Ake, and Mayapan and helped investigate Maya remains.

records.s: He worked with Mrs. Le Plongeon to photograph, survey, and study Maya monuments after arriving at Progresso in 1873. He excavated at Chichen-Itza and reported discoveries concerning Chaacmol’s tomb and statue.

records.l: Chaacmol, Vestiges of the Mayas, or, Facts tending to prove that Communications and Intimate Relations must have existed, in very remote times, between the inhabitants of Mayab and those of Asia and Africa, The population of the country, about 250,000 souls all told, are mostly Indians
records.s: Chaacmol is identified as a warrior whose shield bore round green spots and whose totem was the spotted tiger. His tomb contained urns with remains interpreted as his brains, heart, and viscera, along with jade ornaments and other objects.

records.l: Chaacmol's funeral chamber, Vestiges of the Mayas, or, Facts tending to prove that Communications and Intimate Relations must have existed, in very remote times, between the inhabitants of Mayab and those of Asia and Africa, The population of the country, about 250,000 souls all told, are mostly Indians
records.s: Chaacmol’s funeral chamber is located on the eastern wall of the gymnasium at Chichen-Itza. Its mural paintings depict Chaacmol in battle, his corpse prepared for cremation, and funerary scenes involving the extraction and preservation of the heart and other organs.

records.l: colossal statue of Chaacmol, Vestiges of the Mayas, or, Facts tending to prove that Communications and Intimate Relations must have existed, in very remote times, between the inhabitants of Mayab and those of Asia and Africa, The population of the country, about 250,000 souls all told, are mostly Indians
records.s: The head of the colossal statue of Chaacmol was found near the urns in his burial monument. It was taken to the National Museum of Mexico aboard the gunboat Libertad without the author’s consent or compensation.
