records.s: The wood-cutters are neighborhood representatives who supply passing steamboats with wood. Ranging from men of sterling integrity to floating drinkers and card players, they settle personal quarrels under early boatmen's law through supervised unarmed contests.

records.l: the Red Stone, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: is_a steamboat The Red Stone is connected with the wreck in which Don Carlo was left senseless after an explosion. Suza Fairfield is later identified as the young woman who pulled Don Carlo from the river after the accident.

records.l: steamboats, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: carry twenty-four cords of wood [at one landing, after improvements] Steamboats drive the wood trade on the Ohio and Mississippi rivers, with some taking on twenty-four cords of wood at one landing. Their calls for wood after dark cause woodmen to rush from their cabins with torches, giving Shirt-Tail Bend its name. The Red Stone later explodes while landing on the Kentucky shore, killing and injuring many people.

records.l: the Carlo wood yard, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: The Carlo wood yard, jointly owned and equally operated by Don Carlo and Dan Carlo, sees a large wood sale; Dan leaves for headquarters, and Don remains to confront them.

records.l: Shirt-Tail Bend, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: Shirt-Tail Bend is a Mississippi River locality, named for woodmen who ran out in shirt-tails to supply steamboats at night. Initially settled by wood-cutters, it has wood yards, Sundown Hill cabin, and no schoolhouse, church, or post-office. It is associated with Don Carlo, S. S. Simon, and Brindle Bill. After Don Carlo's victory, planters arrive, Simon becomes prominent, and small towns develop.

records.l: headquarters, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: Headquarters is an old abandoned cabin at the edge of a small cane-brake, distant from the river. Used by Brindle Bill and others for gambling, drinking, cards, and a scheme against Dan, it holds the jug, admits Don Carlo through the chimney, and is later burned by Simon’s wife.

records.l: the wood business, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: is_a principal source of revenue [in Shirt-Tail Bend] The wood business is the principal source of revenue at Shirt-Tail Bend, and large quantities of cord or steam wood are sold to passing steamboats. Don and Dan Carlo operate as equal partners, but Don pays the expenses while Dan takes half the proceeds and spends them. The business brings thousands of dollars into the Bend without initially producing broader improvements.

records.l: the gambling scheme against Dan Carlo, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: is_a scheme to swindle Dan Carlo [planned at headquarters] S. S. Simon, Sundown Hill, and Brindle Bill are described as banding together at headquarters to swindle Dan Carlo after a large sale of wood. Simon's wife warns that Dan's money will go that night. Don interrupts the scheme by entering the cabin and raking the money from the table.

records.l: the fight between Don Carlo and Brindle Bill, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: is_a physical contest [settled according to the early boatmen's law] Brindle Bill starts the fight after claiming the gambling money and saying that Don Carlo has insulted him. Brindle Bill is stronger, but Don is more active and fights with true pluck. The fight ends when Simon's wife sets fire to headquarters, and Don retains the money.

records.l: the fire at headquarters, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: is_caused_by Simon's wife [to end the fight and force the men outside] Simon's wife starts the fire by applying a firebrand to the cane pile against the west end of headquarters. A strong west breeze carries the flames over the cabin roof, forcing the men outside. The fire ends the fight between Don Carlo and Brindle Bill.

records.l: Red Stone explosion, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: The Red Stone explosion, a steamboat disaster, leaves Don Carlo severely stunned and injured, then leads to his rescue from the wreck while returning home.

records.l: Don Carlo's money, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: is_taken_from the gambling scheme against Dan Carlo [Don Carlo raked it from the table] Don Carlo's money is taken from the gambling table after he enters headquarters through the chimney. Brindle Bill claims it, but Don's fight with him and the fire at headquarters end the dispute. Don Carlo is said to have been justly entitled to the money.

records.l: the half-way castle, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: The half-way castle is an early brick house on the southern bank of the Ohio River, about halfway between Louisville and Cincinnati. Don Carlo is left there in a severely stunned but nonfatal condition after the Red Stone accident.

records.l: Tom Fairfield, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: Tom Fairfield was a Virginia descendant who ran away from home at twelve and settled near Boone Station in Kentucky. Able to read and write, he was restless, industrious but inconsistent, and tried writing, planting, boatman’s work, and preaching. He was popular at wedding parties, raced his fleet horse for corn whisky, married Susan Lasco, and fathered Rose Simon Fairfield and two other daughters. Through his wife he received gourds and built a cabin on land under the Henderson claim, but his family experienced poverty. After his wife’s attack of the jerks, he abandoned church meetings; after her death and the loss of his claim, whisky increasingly dominated his life. He was presumed frozen and buried under snow.

records.l: Rose Fairfield, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: Rose Fairfield, also called Rose Simon Fairfield, is Tom Fairfield and Susan Lasco’s daughter. During separation from her family, she cares for baby Suza in a cold cabin, is rescued with Roxie and Suza, and becomes Mrs. Evaline Estep’s foster daughter before Estep adopts her after her parents die. Identified through a breast-pin and marriage certificate, she inherits the Lasco estate, then dies childless and intestate of yellow fever returning from New Orleans.

records.l: Suza Fairfield, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: Suza Fairfield, the youngest Fairfield sister, begins as a shivering baby in an unheated cabin and is taken in, raised, and educated by Aunt Katy Demitt until she can leave as a free woman. At eleven, an orphan, she bravely escapes Tom Ditamus after he abducts her, returning through the woods to Port William. She becomes Port William’s belle, attracts suitors but stays with Aunt Katy, meets and rescues Don Carlo from the Red Stone wreck, and is reportedly engaged to him.

records.l: Aunt Katy Demitt, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: Aunt Katy Demitt is a nearest neighbor and first benefactress of the Fairfield sisters, an economical, industrious woman in Port William. After learning of the children’s plight, she orders Joe and Dick to bring them from the cabin, shelters them, claims eleven-year-old Suza in the settlers’ council, and becomes Suza’s foster mother. She supports their household by knitting stockings, keeps private savings and a will, and later reveals that Demitt relations sought Suza’s removal. She confirms that she has bequeathed her possessions to Suza.

records.l: the early settlers, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: The early settlers in Kentucky endured repeated Indian attacks and violent conflict, remained devotedly religious as preachers improved backwoods society, and nearby settlers gathered to decide care for orphaned sisters.

records.l: the Indians, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: call Kentucky [“The dark and bloody ground”] The Indians used Kentucky as a hunting ground before white settlement and fought among themselves and with white men there. Some Indian bands attacked cabins, killed women and children, and captured or tortured white men. Their conflicts helped give Kentucky the name “the dark and bloody ground.”

records.l: white men, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: are_in_conflict_with the Indians [in a war of extermination in Kentucky] White men in Kentucky fought the Indians in a prolonged and sometimes exterminating conflict. When captured by Indians, they might be taken to towns in Ohio and burned at the stake or tortured to death.

records.l: Virginia, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: admits Kentucky [into the Union] Virginia was Tom Fairfield’s birthplace and the place from which he ran away as a boy. Tom hoped to return there and claim an inheritance, although he said Virginia law gave the land estate to the eldest son.

records.l: Kentucky, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: Kentucky, a new-born State admitted into the Union in 1792, lies between the Cumberland Mountains and the Ohio river, with fertile, black, undulating, wooded land. Once called “the dark and bloody ground,” it endured Indian incursions until 1795. During war, it sought peace and remained in the Union, but was invaded on both sides as Cliff Carlo joined Southern armies.

records.l: Port William, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: Port William is the first settlement and a village at the mouth of the Kentucky River, where it meets the Ohio, on Ohio River bottom land. Its landing draws keel boats, boatmen, idle citizens, and whisky sellers, sustaining a corn-whisky trade through groceries and saloons. It is where Rose Simon and her sisters are separated, where Aunt Katy and Suza Fairfield live, and where Suza returns and later rides with Don Carlo.

records.l: Kentucky River, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: guides Suza Fairfield's escape [toward Port William] Suza Fairfield follows the Kentucky River during her escape because she knows it will lead her to Port William. When the road diverges, she travels through woods and underbrush along the river until she can rejoin the road.

records.l: the Indian-white conflict in Kentucky, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: The Indian-white conflict in Kentucky continued after the American Revolutionary War and was described as a war of extermination. Indians attacked isolated cabins and captured white men, while white settlers responded with intense hatred and vengeance. The conflict ended before Tom Fairfield reached manhood.

records.l: the jerks, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: is_a spasmodic religious phenomenon [chiefly affecting females during church services] The jerks were a spasmodic religious phenomenon that occurred during church services, especially among women. Tom Fairfield’s wife suffered an attack in a meeting of the New Lights, throwing her head and body violently until her combs flew and her hair cracked like a wagon whip. Tom was frightened and never attended a meeting again.

records.l: poverty, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: affects Tom Fairfield [after the failed land claim and missed crop] Poverty confronted Tom Fairfield and his family after he returned from a long boat trip too late to raise a crop and then endured a cold winter. Tom and his wife sat sadly by the dying fire, hoping that future inheritances might improve their condition. After Tom’s wife died and his land claim failed, poverty left the three daughters without adequate food, fuel, or protection.

records.l: Tom Fairfield's alcoholism, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: contributes_to Tom Fairfield's death [through intoxication and exposure] Tom Fairfield became too fond of whisky after repeatedly winning bottles in Kentucky wedding races and associating with dissipated boatmen. At Port William he was drinking late at night when Dave Deminish threw him out after he heaved at a glass of spoiled beer. His drinking contributed to the belief that he became intoxicated, froze, and died in the snow.

records.l: Tom Fairfield's death, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: After Tom Fairfield was expelled from Dave Deminish’s shop, a severe snowstorm began during the night. He failed to return to his cabin, and the settlers concluded that he had frozen to death under the snow, although his body is not shown being found in this unit.

records.l: the snowstorm, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: has_depth twenty-four inches [of snow] The snowstorm began in the middle of the night after Tom Fairfield left the whisky shop. By morning, twenty-four inches of snow covered the ground, trapping the Fairfield sisters in their cold cabin and making their rescue difficult.

records.l: the Fairfield sisters' rescue, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: is_cared_for_by Aunt Katy [after Roxie seeks help] Roxie Fairfield walked through the deep snow to Aunt Katy’s house to seek help for herself, Rose, and Suza. Aunt Katy directed Joe and Dick to bring them back on a wood slide, with Suza wrapped in a blanket in her rocking trough. The children were warmed and later placed with Aunt Katy, Aunt Fillis Foster, and Mrs. Evaline Estep.

records.l: the cabin, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: Tom Fairfield built the cabin for his family on land whose Henderson claim Virginia later set aside. During Tom’s absence, Roxie, Rose, and Suza endured freezing conditions with scant wood and food until Roxie sought help and they were rescued.

records.l: John A. Lasco, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: John A. Lasco, an English passenger on the Brandywine and Susan Lasco’s older brother, searches America for her for three years. Badly injured in the Brandywine’s burning, he briefly survives, dictates bequests to Susan, her descendants, and his caregiver, then dies.

records.l: Chicago, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: Chicago is a city named for wild onion, called Chikago by Indians. For a quarter of a century it has fewer than one hundred inhabitants. After Daymon moves there, works as a day laborer, and accepts fifteen acres for a debt, its unparalleled growth lets him sell land and become wealthy. Roxie lives among its moneyed aristocracy, where the pleasure party forms and Simon returns before his death. During the war, loyal Chicago is where Roxie discusses the Simon estate with Governor Morock.

records.l: Brandywine, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: Brandywine, a heavily freighted steamboat carrying many passengers, grounds on a deep sand bar and burns late at night, destroying it.

records.l: family estate (the Lasco family estate), Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: The Lasco family estate had been held in abeyance because family papers were lost. After the papers are recovered, John A. Lasco sells the property and deposits twenty thousand dollars in a western bank for Susan Lasco and her descendants.

records.l: Lasco family papers, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: are_hidden_by Alonzo Phelps [before he left the country] The Lasco family papers are recovered after a condemned man, Alonzo Phelps, confesses where he concealed them. John A. Lasco carries papers identifying the bank holding the inheritance, and the papers are entrusted to the woman caring for him to dry and deliver to a respectable lawyer in Memphis.

records.l: John A. Lasco's bequest, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: has_value twenty thousand dollars [deposited in a western bank] John A. Lasco's bequest gives twenty thousand dollars deposited in a western bank to Susan Lasco and her descendants. He also leaves the one hundred ten dollars in his pocket to the woman of the cabin who cared for him.

records.l: Susan Lasco's breast-pin, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: is_inscribed_with Presented to Susan Lasco by her brother, John A. Lasco, 1751 Susan Lasco's breast-pin bears the inscription, "Presented to Susan Lasco by her brother, John A. Lasco, 1751." Rose Simon produces it as evidence of her connection to John A. Lasco.

records.l: Tom Fairfield and Susan Lasco marriage certificate, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: certifies_marriage_of Tom Fairfield and Susan Lasco The marriage certificate of Tom Fairfield and Susan Lasco had been kept for years in Rose Simon's box of family keepsakes. Rose produces it along with the breast-pin when claiming the Lasco inheritance.

records.l: burning of the Brandywine, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: During the burning of the Brandywine, the pilot directs the vessel toward the wrong shore, where it grounds on a deep sand bar and burns to the water's edge. Many passengers drown, while others escape on pieces of the wreck.

records.l: Lasco inheritance fraud, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: The Lasco inheritance fraud is carried out by Brindle Bill, S. S. Simon, and Sundown Hill: they forge an inheritance claim, falsely identify Rose Simon Fairfield as the sole surviving child, recover twenty thousand dollars from the Lasco estate, then threaten to find her sisters for further payments.

records.l: yellow fever, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: causes_death_of Rose Simon Fairfield [after her attack in New Orleans] Rose Simon Fairfield is attacked by yellow fever while traveling in New Orleans to select furniture for her new house. She dies on the way home and is buried in Louisiana.

records.l: Tom Ditamus, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: Tom Ditamus, a lazy, cowardly man with a wife, two dirty children, and an ox-drawn covered wagon, agrees to transport Suza Fairfield for ten dollars and captures her for the Demitt relations. Suza escapes while his family sleeps, and he continues traveling after discovering she is gone.

records.l: Demitt relations, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: The Demitt relations plot to obtain Aunt Katy's money, believing Suza Fairfield may inherit; they hire Tom Ditamus to take Suza to the Cumberland Mountains and isolate her.

records.l: Aunt Katy's money, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: Aunt Katy's money is the subject of speculation among the Demitt relations. Aunt Katy shows Suza Fairfield five hundred dollars in gold and silver that she has saved through her own work and economy.

records.l: Aunt Katy's will, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: Aunt Katy's will is witnessed by old Ballard and old Father Tearful. It bequeaths all of Aunt Katy's earthly possessions to Suza Fairfield.

records.l: Suza Fairfield's capture, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: Tom Ditamus captures Suza Fairfield in a foggy morning near his camp, threatening her with a gag and placing her in his covered wagon. He takes her south with his wife and children toward the backwoods of the Cumberland Mountains.

records.l: Suza Fairfield's escape, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: Suza Fairfield escapes at night after persuading Tom Ditamus that she hates Aunt Katy and would go anywhere to leave her. She follows the Kentucky River, crosses White's Creek at a ford, rejoins the road, and reaches Aunt Katy's house in Port William by dawn.

records.l: Don Carlo's rescue, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: A brave young woman rushes into the water and drags Don Carlo's lifeless body to shore after the Red Stone wreck. At the camp meeting, Don learns that the rescuer is Suza Fairfield.

records.l: camp meeting, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: is_a protracted religious meeting [held in the woods near water] A camp meeting is held near Port William, with preaching, prayer meetings, love feasts, and visitors camping in the woods. Don Carlo attends it hoping to meet the young woman who saved him and there sees Suza Fairfield.

records.l: Don Carlo and Suza Fairfield's courtship, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: leads_to marriage [as reported by neighborhood talk] Don Carlo is immediately attracted to Suza Fairfield at the camp meeting and learns that she is his rescuer. They ride side by side toward Port William, and the neighborhood says that they are engaged to be married.

records.l: The Second Generation, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: is_a later generation of characters [scene title] The Second Generation begins after the characters from the preceding part have died or passed from the stage of life. It follows descendants including Young Simon and Cæsar Simon as they confront inheritance, poverty, gambling, and the consequences of family history.

records.l: Young Simon, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: Young Simon, the only son of S. S. Simon by a second wife, is a wealthy cotton planter who inherits four thousand acres of plantations, more than six hundred slaves, and an estate worth more than a million dollars. His mother is dead, and he has poor health and little family knowledge. In the last stage of consumption, he travels toward New Orleans and the West Indies for relief, learns Roxie Daymon’s family mystery, becomes engaged to her, returns to Chicago, dictates a will in her favor, and dies shortly afterward.

records.l: Cæsar Simon, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: Cæsar Simon, son of S. S. Simon’s brother and raised by two penniless sisters, grows up imaginative, mischievous, and unwilling to work. He leaves Tennessee, becomes a gambler, and learns he is heir to S. S. Simon’s estate. Knowing family circumstances involving Roxie Daymon and Simon, he helps Simon pursue the inheritance dispute, hires Gov. Morock to challenge the will after Simon’s death, and goes to Kentucky for Cliff Carlo’s help. He then leaves for Missouri, joins Price’s army as private number 77, and proves brave and penetrating-minded despite a selfish disposition. Severely wounded at Wilson’s Creek, he is saved by Steve Brindle and a Cherokee Indian. His recurring fear of 77 and his failure to acknowledge Steve in prosperity trouble him. At Helena he recognizes Steve among federal soldiers, falls in battle during the retreat, and becomes the last male link of the Simon family.

records.l: Cole Conway, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: Cæsar Simon, alias Cole Conway in Paducah, partners with Steve Sharp in gambling; after they lose their money, he tells Steve Brindle his true name and family history.

records.l: Steve Brindle, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: Steve Brindle, also called Steve Sharp, describes himself as a come-by-chance, the son of Brindle Bill and Nancy Wade, whose parents were unmarried; his mother was a sister of Sundown Hill. A private in General Pearce’s Arkansas army and a federal soldier, he recognizes Cole Conway as Cæsar Simon and becomes his old comrade. After sharing money and family history, Steve saves Cæsar’s life at Wilson’s Creek with a Cherokee Indian’s help. Cæsar later denies him amid wealth and power; Steve is reported wounded after Elkhorn, with a card alleging Cæsar deserted.

records.l: Steve Sharp, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: Steve Sharp is Cole Conway's gambling partner in Paducah, Kentucky. He later identifies himself as Steve Brindle and exchanges family histories with Conway.

records.l: Roxie Daymon, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: Roxie Daymon, also called Roxie Fairfield, is a near relative of the Simon family and part of its hidden history. During the first year of the war, she lives in Chicago, is reputed rich despite receiving no Simon-estate dividends, and remains loyal to the federal government. She consults Governor Morock about contesting the Simon will and seeking plantation cotton. Later, married to a young mechanic, she lives happily in a cottage and reads The Workman's Saturday Night to forget the past; her possible survival or descendants torment S. S. Simon.

records.l: Western States, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: The Western States undergo rapid settlement and progress during the decade from 1840 to 1850. The iron horse and magnetic telegraph are successfully put into operation across them.

records.l: West and Southwest, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: The history of the West and Southwest during the first half of the nineteenth century is described as full of romance and truth stranger than fiction. The region experiences the rise of a moneyed aristocracy and the rapid expansion of cotton cultivation and slavery.

records.l: the Confederate States of America, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: The Confederate States of America provide no promised pay or assistance to General Price’s initial Missouri army, which nevertheless takes the field using weapons and supplies gathered from citizens and captured from Federal forces.

records.l: Paducah, Kentucky, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: Paducah, Kentucky, is where Cæsar Simon, using the name Cole Conway, joins Steve Sharp in gambling. After they lose their last money, the two sleep in an old straw shed outside the village.

records.l: the decade from 1840 to 1850, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: The decade from 1840 to 1850 is described as one of the most important periods in the settlement and progress of the Western States. During it, the iron horse and magnetic telegraph begin successful operation across the region.

records.l: the settlement and progress of the Western States, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: is_a historical development [especially significant from 1840 to 1850] The settlement and progress of the Western States accelerate during the decade from 1840 to 1850. New transportation and communication technologies contribute to this transformation.

records.l: cotton cultivation, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: is_concentrated_in Southern States [during the first half of the nineteenth century] Cotton cultivation in the Southern States expands to gigantic proportions during the first half of the nineteenth century. Young Simon becomes a cotton planter through his inheritance.

records.l: slavery, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: Slavery is central to the plantation economy described in the unit. Young Simon inherits more than six hundred slaves, and S. S. Simon's demand for labor leads him to have them summoned before daylight.

records.l: the iron horse, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: is_put_into_operation_in Western States [during the decade from 1840 to 1850] The iron horse is identified as one of the great motive powers of modern civilization. It is successfully put into operation across the Western States during the decade from 1840 to 1850.

records.l: the magnetic telegraph, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: is_put_into_operation_in Western States [during the decade from 1840 to 1850] The magnetic telegraph is identified with the iron horse as a major force in modern civilization. It is successfully put into operation across the Western States during the decade from 1840 to 1850.

records.l: the Simon estate, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: The Simon estate, inherited by Young Simon from S. S. Simon, includes four thousand-acre plantations and more than six hundred slaves and is described as one of Arkansas’s largest. Valued at more than a million dollars, or more than a million and a quarter, it passes after Young Simon’s death to Roxie Daymon. Cousin Cæsar contests the inheritance with others involved, and the plantations and residence are later devastated by fire.

records.l: the Simon plantations, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: S. S. Simon's four one-thousand-acre plantations organize enslaved labor by an early bell before daylight; President Lincoln's proclamation of freedom abolishes the enslaved people's monetary value, transforming what the plantations contain.

records.l: the slaves on S. S. Simon's plantations, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: The slaves on S. S. Simon's plantations number more than six hundred. They are required to be ready to resume work as soon as they can see each morning.

records.l: the dream of the steam carriage, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: concerns the steam carriage [dreamed by Cole Conway] In his dream, Cæsar Simon sees a steam carriage, finds gold and a rule containing directions, and travels south with Steve Brindle. The dream includes a speed gauge, a boiler, and a pump-like handle that seems to draw water from the dry road; Brindle interprets it as a sign of Cæsar's inheritance.

records.l: the steam carriage, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: An imagined light, four-wheeled road vehicle carries six passengers in its passenger box, follows the golden rule, and has a pilot, rear engineer and fireman, brass boiler, and phosphorus-and-tinder heat source.

records.l: death, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: ends life [as part of the human passage from cradle to grave] Death is presented as a gradual succession in which old people pass away and new people take their places. S. S. Simon dies from swamp fever, and Young Simon follows him after a short life marked by poor health.

records.l: Roxie Daymon (daughter), Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: Roxie Daymon, only daughter of Roxie Fairfield, is raised and educated among Chicago’s moneyed aristocracy and reaches womanhood. After losing every property case, she becomes destitute. Traveling with a pleasure party to New Orleans, she becomes engaged to young Simon and, after his death, inherits his whole estate under his will.

records.l: Governor Morock, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: Governor Morock is a lawyer associated with the Simon will, operating from the law office at No. 77 Strait street and described as fashionable in Chicago. He exploits Roxie Daymon’s destitution by offering, for fifty dollars, to arrange a legal loophole or “shadow” marriage. He writes young Simon’s will for ten dollars, then takes one thousand dollars in advance from Cousin Cæsar to challenge it, seeking further fees. During the war, he promises money and testimony may break the will and tries to obtain cotton through a federal officer, but gains nothing despite spending nearly all of Cæsar’s money. He ultimately retires, or is retired, from law and survives by cheaply selling his bad reputation for dirty work.

records.l: Cliff Carlo, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: Cliff Carlo, oldest son and representative man of the Carlo family descended from Don Carlo and Suza Fairfield, is a prosperous Kentucky farmer and subscriber to THE ROUGH DIAMOND. During the Simon estate dispute, he consults Cousin Cæsar but stays noncommittal because Roxie Daymon is a near relative, writes Governor Morock, then joins the Southern armies and survives the war unharmed.

records.l: the pleasure party, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: A Chicago pleasure party of young people, including Roxie Daymon and young Simon, agrees to pay Roxie’s expenses, travels by steamer to New Orleans, then returns to Chicago.

records.l: the Simon will, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: The Simon will bequeaths Young Simon’s entire estate to Roxie Daymon, dictated to Governor Morock. After Simon’s death, cousin Cæsar contests it through Morock, alleging Simon lacked capacity; Morock proposes using money to arrange testimony about Simon’s mental faculties.

records.l: the inheritance dispute, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: concerns Young Simon’s estate [over the validity of Young Simon's will] The inheritance dispute begins when cousin Cæsar objects to Roxie Daymon receiving young Simon’s entire estate. Gov. Morock advises Cæsar to challenge the will and accepts one thousand dollars in advance to undertake the case.

records.l: the pleasure trip to New Orleans, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: A group of young Chicago people arranges an October pleasure trip to New Orleans on the Roman Eagle, where Roxie meets Simon and a mystery about her family arises.

records.l: Roxie Daymon and Young Simon’s engagement, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: Roxie Daymon and young Simon become engaged after the trip and are expected to marry the following spring in Chicago. Simon continues to think of Roxie despite seeing many beautiful women during his travels.

records.l: Roxie Daymon and Young Simon’s proposed marriage, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: The proposed marriage is set for the spring of 1861 in Chicago. It is postponed when Simon returns seriously ill and can no longer stand alone.

records.l: Young Simon’s death, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: Young Simon dies in a Chicago hotel as cousin Cæsar keeps vigil overnight; his remains are prepared and transferred to Arkansas for burial beside his father.

records.l: poverty and destitution, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: affects Roxie Daymon (daughter) [after the loss of her fortune] Roxie Daymon is told that she has lost everything and is hopelessly destitute and penniless. She replies that her mother was once a poor, penniless girl and that she can endure poverty as well.

records.l: Roxie Daymon’s family history, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: Roxie says that her mother was Roxie Fairfield, an orphan girl raised in Kentucky. Aunt Patsy Perkins told her that her mother had two sisters, Rose and Suza, whom she called poor trash; cousin Cæsar later learns that Roxie is connected to heirs of a twenty-thousand-dollar claim with twenty years of interest against Simon’s estate.

records.l: General Sterling Price, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: General Sterling Price is a military commander in the war. In Missouri, he leads an improvised Southern army that marches, fights Federals, captures supplies and weapons, advances to Lexington, and retreats south. At Helena, he commands infantry, captures the center fort, shelters men from gunboat shelling, and orders their retreat.

records.l: the late civil war between the States of the American Union, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: The late civil war between the States of the American Union, a civil war arising from two civilizations under one government, deeply affects the characters through service, divided loyalties, deaths, wounds, opportunism, and property destruction. It continues nearly two years after Helena, then ends when depleted, weary Southern soldiers lay down their arms.

records.l: War Between the States, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: is_a the late civil war between the States of the American Union The War Between the States begins after the firing on Fort Sumter and the opposing calls to arms in the North and South. It draws Cousin Cæsar, Cliff Carlo, and many others into military service and destroys the Simon plantations.

records.l: Missouri, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: Missouri is a state invaded by federal troops in 1861, becoming the principal theater of General Sterling Price’s first-year campaign as his army marches and fights across it.

records.l: Springfield, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: Springfield is the usual name given to the battle of Oak Hill, where Federal troops under General Lyon fought Confederate forces under Generals McCulloch, Price, and Pearce. Cousin Cæsar is wounded there after General Lyon is killed and the Federals retreat.

records.l: the federal government, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: The federal government calls for five hundred thousand men through Congress, sends forces into Missouri after Fort Sumter, then during the first year will not interfere with loyal men's slaves.

records.l: the Union, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: is_opposed_by the Confederate States of America [in the war] The Union loses the border slave States when they withdraw and join the South, except for Kentucky, which remains inactive in the hope of peace. The war then brings Federal military operations into Missouri and other contested regions.

records.l: the federal army, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: The federal army invades Missouri under General Lyon, fights Price’s forces at Springfield and Wilson’s Creek, retreats after Lyon’s death, and occupies fortified Lexington before its capture. Later, it fortifies Helena with about four thousand men, three forts, and a gunboat.

records.l: Price’s army, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: Price’s army is an unpaid, poorly equipped volunteer force of varied people, initially unarmed; about eight thousand bayonet-guns cross the Mississippi after surviving irregular provisions, capturing Federal equipment, and fighting across Missouri.

records.l: the southern armies, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: The southern armies, weary, war-worn, and sadly deficient in numbers at the end of the war, faced fortified Helena; nearly two years after the battle, they laid down their arms and ended the war.

records.l: the battle of Wilson’s Creek, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: The battle of Wilson’s Creek, also called Oak Hill or Springfield, occurs at Springfield on August 10, 1861; Lyon is killed leading a charge, Federals retreat, and Cæsar is wounded.

records.l: the first year of the war in Missouri, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: is_unparalleled_in the history of war on this continent [except for an earlier Kentucky Indian or border war] The first year of the war in Missouri is portrayed as an unusually harsh campaign in which Price’s army marches more than eight hundred miles, often lacks food and equipment, and fights frequent engagements. Despite these hardships, the army remains cheerful and is said never to lose a battle on Missouri soil during that year.

records.l: the 77 superstition, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: The 77 superstition troubles Cousin Cæsar after he is assigned the number 77 and later receives a card bearing the same number. He interprets Steve Brindle’s message that Cæsar Simon had deserted as possibly meaning that Steve had 'fallen off' and wanted Cæsar to follow him.

records.l: three forts at Helena, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: The three forts at Helena were defended by the federals. General Price carried the center fort, while Marmaduke and Fagan failed to carry the northern and southern forts.

records.l: General Holmes, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: General Holmes commands Price's infantry division in a July 4, 1863 attack on fortified Helena with about 4,900 men, but repeated efforts fail to capture remaining federal positions.

records.l: General Price's division of infantry, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: has_strength about fourteen hundred men General Price's division of infantry numbered about 1,400 men under General Holmes's command. It was assigned to attack the center fort.

records.l: Fagan's brigade of Arkansas infantry, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: has_strength fifteen hundred men Fagan's brigade of Arkansas infantry numbered about 1,500 men. It was assigned to attack the southern fort but failed.

records.l: Marmaduke's division of Arkansas and Missouri cavalry, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: has_strength about two thousand Marmaduke's division of Arkansas and Missouri cavalry numbered about 2,000 men. It was assigned to attack the northern fort but failed.

records.l: the attack on Helena, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: A military attack on fortified Helena by four thousand nine hundred men began at daylight on July 4, 1863; Price succeeded, but Marmaduke and Fagan failed, ending in retreat with heavy losses.

records.l: Price's men, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: suffers_loss heavy loss [during the retreat] Price's men captured the center position and sheltered themselves as best they could while the gunboat shelled the captured fort. They later retreated under orders with heavy loss.

records.l: the battle, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: The battle took place at Helena on the holiday of American Independence. General Price carried one position, but the other positions held, and the retreat was made under deadly enemy fire.

records.l: the retreat of Price's men, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: The retreat of Price's men was ordered after General Holmes failed to carry the other positions. It was accomplished with heavy loss.

records.l: the Simon family, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: The Simon family lost its last male-line link when Cæsar Simon fell. After the war, the Simon plantations and the last foot of Simon land were lost through sales.

records.l: the proclamation of freedom, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: Issued by President Lincoln, it abolished slaves’ monetary value on Simon plantations, knocking dollars and cents out of flesh and blood.

records.l: President Lincoln, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: President Lincoln issued the proclamation of freedom.

records.l: the Simon land, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life
records.s: is_sold_at the sheriff's sale [to pay judgments, just and unjust] The last foot of the Simon land was sold at sheriff's sale to pay judgments described as just and unjust.

records.l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882

records.l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, SOAKING PITS FOR STEEL INGOTS.
records.s: John Gjers describes the soaking pit process for rolling steel ingots using their own initial heat, without a fuel-fired heating furnace. The process places freshly stripped ingots in individually covered, preheated brick-lined pits for 20–30 minutes, allowing internal heat to become more evenly distributed. At the Darlington Steel and Iron Company's Works, about 125 tons per shift were bloomed by this method, and double-head rails were rolled directly from treated ingots with satisfactory quality. The process is intended to reduce fuel use, labor, furnace maintenance, oxidation, and loss of steel yield.

records.l: John Gjers, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, SOAKING PITS FOR STEEL INGOTS.
records.s: John Gjers introduced and describes a process for rolling steel ingots with their own initial heat by using soaking pits instead of a heating furnace. He introduced the method at the Darlington Steel and Iron Company's Works in early June and reports successful blooming and direct rolling of double-head rails.

records.l: Darlington Steel and Iron Company's Works, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, SOAKING PITS FOR STEEL INGOTS.
records.s: The Darlington Steel and Iron Company's Works began using the soaking pit process in early June. The works were blooming about 125 tons of steel per shift, or approximately 300 ingots every twelve hours, and had successfully rolled a considerable number of double-head rails directly from treated ingots.

records.l: soaking pit process, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, SOAKING PITS FOR STEEL INGOTS.
records.s: The soaking pit process transfers freshly stripped steel ingots into preheated, covered pits, where they stand for about 20–30 minutes while their heat becomes nearly uniform. It is intended to permit rolling with the ingot's initial heat, eliminate the need for a fuel-fired heating furnace, reduce oxidation, and improve steel yield.

records.l: soaking pits, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, SOAKING PITS FOR STEEL INGOTS.
records.s: Soaking pits are upright, slightly oversized pits built in brickwork below floor level and lined with firebrick. Each pit is covered after an ingot is placed inside; the hot brickwork retains and equalizes heat, while gas released by the ingot fills the pit and excludes atmospheric air.

records.l: steel ingot, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, SOAKING PITS FOR STEEL INGOTS.
records.s: A steel ingot contains apparent and latent heat in excess of that required for rolling. After being stripped, it is placed in a heated soaking pit, where its internal heat is redistributed and its surface becomes hot enough for rolling without a conventional reheating operation.

records.l: rolling of steel ingots, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, SOAKING PITS FOR STEEL INGOTS.
records.s: Rolling of steel ingots can be performed after the ingots have soaked for approximately 20–30 minutes. The treated ingots can be sent directly to the rolls, and the text reports satisfactory double-head rails produced by this method.

records.l: heating furnace, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, SOAKING PITS FOR STEEL INGOTS.
records.s: The heating furnace is the previously universal means of reheating steel ingots before rolling. The soaking pit process is presented as a way to dispense with such furnaces, the fuel they consume, their gas generators, their maintenance, and losses caused by oxidation or overheating.

records.l: blooming mill, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, SOAKING PITS FOR STEEL INGOTS.
records.s: The blooming mill receives ingots removed from the soaking pits and swung to its live rollers by a crane. The machinery at Darlington was not adapted for rolling off in one heat, although it successfully bloomed the treated ingots and directly rolled some double-head rails.

records.l: ingot crane, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, SOAKING PITS FOR STEEL INGOTS.
records.s: The ingot crane places stripped ingots into the soaking pits and later removes them and swings them to the blooming mill. The recommended arrangement uses a crane capable of commanding both the pits and the mill's live rollers; with such a crane, four men and a boy could pass the full make through the pits.

records.l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, TEMPERING BY COMPRESSION.
records.s: L. Clemandot devised a method called tempering by compression for treating metals, especially steel. The process heats metal to a cherry red, compresses it strongly, and maintains pressure until it cools completely. The resulting metal is exceedingly hard, has contracted molecularly, and has a fine grain that resembles polished nickel. Compressed steel also acquires coercitive force and retains magnetism, with no loss observed after three months.

records.l: L. Clemandot, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, TEMPERING BY COMPRESSION.
records.s: L. Clemandot devised a method of treating metals, especially steel, called tempering by compression.

records.l: tempering by compression, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, TEMPERING BY COMPRESSION.
records.s: Tempering by compression consists of heating metal to a cherry red, compressing it strongly, and maintaining the pressure until the metal is completely cooled. The process produces effects resembling tempering, including great hardness, molecular contraction, and fine grain.

records.l: metals, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, TEMPERING BY COMPRESSION.
records.s: Metals can be treated by heating them to a cherry red and compressing them until they cool. Compression modifies their molecular state, and hydraulic pressure has a greater effect than hammering or hardening.

records.l: fluid steel, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, TEMPERING BY COMPRESSION.
records.s: Steel treated by compression becomes exceedingly hard and develops molecular contraction and a fine grain. Compressed steel also acquires coercitive force and retains its magnetism, with no loss observed after three months.

records.l: compression, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, TEMPERING BY COMPRESSION.
records.s: Compression is applied strongly to heated metal and maintained until the metal is completely cooled. Its effect is described as greater than that of hammering and hardening, especially when those operations are performed on nearly cold metal.

records.l: pressure, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, TEMPERING BY COMPRESSION.
records.s: Pressure is maintained during cooling in tempering by compression. The operation can be measured and graduated, allowing tempering at a specified pressure, and hydraulic pressure is said to have a particularly strong effect.

records.l: tempering, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, TEMPERING BY COMPRESSION.
records.s: Tempering and tempering by compression produce similar results. Their phenomena may involve molecular approximation and amorphism, producing homogeneity through the absence of crystallization.

records.l: coercitive force, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, TEMPERING BY COMPRESSION.
records.s: Compressed steel acquires coercitive force, which enables it to absorb magnetism. Its relationship to the durability of compressed steel is identified as requiring study.

records.l: magnetism, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, TEMPERING BY COMPRESSION.
records.s: Compressed steel acquires magnetism-absorbing properties through coercitive force. Experiments had shown no loss of magnetism after three months.

records.l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ECONOMICAL STEAM POWER.
records.s: In “Economical Steam Power,” William Barnet Le Van explains that economical steam power depends on the coordinated arrangement of engines, boilers, and transmission accessories. He compares single and subdivided power systems, engine forms, condensing and non-condensing engines, and different engine classes according to their first cost, operating hours, fuel, water, repairs, and depreciation. Using a flouring mill in Philadelphia as an example, he shows that replacing two engines with one first-class automatic engine greatly reduced coal and feed-water consumption and saved $4,954 over 300 operating days.

records.l: Economical Steam Power, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ECONOMICAL STEAM POWER.
records.s: Economical steam power requires a judicious arrangement of engines, boilers, and transmission accessories. William Barnet Le Van emphasizes that the most economical choice depends on the plant's circumstances, operating schedule, fuel and water costs, and required power.

records.l: William Barnet Le Van, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ECONOMICAL STEAM POWER.
records.s: William Barnet Le Van argues that steam-power users often fail to consider how the costs and operating conditions of engines, boilers, and accessories affect economy. He illustrates his argument with calculations comparing two engines with one first-class automatic engine.

records.l: steam power, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ECONOMICAL STEAM POWER.
records.s: Steam power can be made more economical through careful plant planning and by selecting equipment suited to the particular situation. Dividing power among several engines can reduce shafting and transmission costs and limit the effects of stoppages.

records.l: engine, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ECONOMICAL STEAM POWER.
records.s: An engine should be selected by considering its first cost, fuel consumption, operating hours, lubrication, repairs, depreciation, and boiler requirements. Le Van states that engines driving manufactories generally cannot be too high a class because fuel savings usually outweigh the interest on their additional first cost.

records.l: boiler, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ECONOMICAL STEAM POWER.
records.s: Boilers are one of the principal components whose first cost and interest charges must be considered. A non-condensing engine operated at high steam pressure may require a stronger boiler, potentially offsetting the additional cost of a condensing engine.

records.l: horizontal engine, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ECONOMICAL STEAM POWER.
records.s: The horizontal engine is described as the best form in most cases where machinery must be driven, particularly for large powers. It is said to be more durable and less expensive than a beam engine, capable of higher speed, and less demanding in engine-house and foundation costs.

records.l: condensing engine, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ECONOMICAL STEAM POWER.
records.s: A well-constructed condensing engine is generally economically preferable when sufficient condensing water is available at moderate cost. Its greater economy is said to justify the additional purchase cost except in very small-power cases or where exhaust steam from a non-condensing engine can be used for heating or drying.

records.l: automatic engine, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ECONOMICAL STEAM POWER.
records.s: An automatic engine costs more than a plain slide-valve engine but can reduce fuel, lubrication, repair, depreciation, and boiler-power costs. In the cited flouring mill example, one first-class automatic engine replaced two engines and reduced the stated annual coal and water costs from $11,503 to $6,560.

records.l: mill, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ECONOMICAL STEAM POWER.
records.s: A mill's economical power arrangement depends on its required total power and the relationship among its engines, boilers, transmission equipment, and operating conditions. Dividing power among several engines can allow one department to stop while the others continue operating.

records.l: flouring mill in Philadelphia, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ECONOMICAL STEAM POWER.
records.s: The flouring mill in Philadelphia operated two engines rated at seventy indicated horsepower each for an average of twenty-four hours per day on 300 days per year. After replacement by one automatic engine developing 142 horsepower, the stated coal and water costs fell from $11,503 to $6,560, producing a reported annual saving of $4,954.

records.l: Philadelphia, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ECONOMICAL STEAM POWER.
records.s: Philadelphia is identified as the location of the flouring mill example and as a city where water was charged at three dollars per horsepower per annum. First-class engines were charged the same water rate as inferior engines despite their lower water consumption.

records.l: coal, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ECONOMICAL STEAM POWER.
records.s: Coal is a major operating cost in steam power, and its price and the engine's hourly consumption determine whether a more expensive engine is economical. In the example, coal consumption fell from five and one-half pounds to three pounds per hour per horsepower, reducing the stated 300-day cost from $11,088 to $6,134.

records.l: feed water, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ECONOMICAL STEAM POWER.
records.s: Feed water consumption is used as a measure of engine economy. The two original engines required 40,320,000 pounds annually, while the replacement engine required 30,672,000 pounds, a reported saving of 9,648,000 pounds, or 31.4 percent.

records.l: replacement of the two engines, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ECONOMICAL STEAM POWER.
records.s: The replacement of the two engines with one first-class automatic engine produced the same stated work with lower coal and feed-water consumption. The reported total cost of coal and water decreased by $4,954 over 300 days.

records.l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RIVER IMPROVEMENTS NEAR ST.
records.s: River improvements near St. Louis on the Mississippi River are progressing satisfactorily through jetty construction, mattress placement, bank revetment, and related work. At Twin Hollow, Carroll's Island, and Beard's Island, engineers are addressing sand bars and protecting or concentrating the river channel. About 1,200 men, thirty barges and scows, two steam launches, and the stern-wheel steamer A. A. Humphreys are employed. The work has cost about $200,000, and an appropriation of approximately $600,000 for the ensuing year offers prospects for a clear channel.

records.l: river improvements near St. Louis, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RIVER IMPROVEMENTS NEAR ST.
records.s: The improvements are progressing satisfactorily. They employ jetty construction, mattresses, hurdles, willow interweaving, and stone revetments to improve the river channel.

records.l: Mississippi River, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RIVER IMPROVEMENTS NEAR ST.
records.s: The Mississippi River near St. Louis is being improved to concentrate its stream, prevent widening, and provide a clear channel.

records.l: St. Louis, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RIVER IMPROVEMENTS NEAR ST.
records.s: St. Louis is the location near which the Mississippi River improvements are being carried out. Twin Hollow lies thirteen miles from St. Louis.

records.l: jetty system, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RIVER IMPROVEMENTS NEAR ST.
records.s: The jetty system is described as effective, with lines of mattresses accumulating sand deposits from the river surface to nearly sixteen feet high.

records.l: mattresses, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RIVER IMPROVEMENTS NEAR ST.
records.s: Mattresses have accumulated sand deposits near the surface of the river to nearly sixteen feet in height. At Carroll's Island, mattresses 125 feet wide have been placed, and 4,000 feet have been begun at Beard's Island.

records.l: Twin Hollow, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RIVER IMPROVEMENTS NEAR ST.
records.s: Twin Hollow is thirteen miles from St. Louis and six miles from Horse-Tail Bar. Engineering forces are working there on a sand bar extending across the widest portion of the river.

records.l: sand bar (at Twin Hollow), Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RIVER IMPROVEMENTS NEAR ST.
records.s: The sand bar at Twin Hollow extends over the widest portion of the river. Hurdles are built from the shore to concentrate the stream on the obstruction, while willows interwoven between piles protect the river from widening.

records.l: Carroll's Island, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RIVER IMPROVEMENTS NEAR ST.
records.s: At Carroll's Island, 125-foot-wide mattresses have been placed and the banks have been revetted with stone from ordinary low water to a 16-foot stage. There is plenty of water over the bar, with a minimum reported depth of twelve feet.

records.l: Beard's Island, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RIVER IMPROVEMENTS NEAR ST.
records.s: Beard's Island is also being improved and has the largest force of men engaged at any one place. Four thousand feet of mattresses have been begun there, with work expected to continue until floating ice suspends operations.

records.l: men employed on the improvements, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RIVER IMPROVEMENTS NEAR ST.
records.s: About 1,200 men are employed on the improvements. They are working across the different river sections, including Beard's Island.

records.l: W. F. Fries, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RIVER IMPROVEMENTS NEAR ST.
records.s: W. F. Fries is the resident engineer directing the different sections of the improvements.

records.l: E. M. Currie, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RIVER IMPROVEMENTS NEAR ST.
records.s: E. M. Currie is the superintending engineer directing the different sections of the improvements.

records.l: appropriation for the ensuing year, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RIVER IMPROVEMENTS NEAR ST.
records.s: The appropriation for the ensuing year approximates $600,000. It follows about $200,000 in actual money already expended on the improvements.

records.l: clear channel, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RIVER IMPROVEMENTS NEAR ST.
records.s: The prospect of a clear channel is described as gratifying to those interested in the river, in light of the ongoing improvements and the appropriation for the ensuing year.

records.l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, BUNTE'S BURETTE FOR THE ANALYSIS OF FURNACE GASES. .. _Mode of Measuring the Gases and Absorption_.
records.s: Dr. Buente's burette is presented as a simpler and more easily operated apparatus for analyzing blast-furnace gases than the various Orsat apparatus. The procedure describes filling the burette, measuring gas volumes, and absorbing carbonic acid, oxygen, and oxide of carbon with specified liquids. Combustion in a heated tube, using atmospheric air and a palladium wire, permits quantitative analysis of hydrogen and oxide of carbon. Changes in gas volume after absorption or combustion are used to calculate the proportions of the gases.

records.l: Bunte's burette, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, BUNTE'S BURETTE FOR THE ANALYSIS OF FURNACE GASES. .. _Mode of Measuring the Gases and Absorption_.
records.s: Bunte's burette is used for the analysis of furnace gases and is described as simpler to use than the apparatus of Orsat. It permits rapid absorption of oxide of carbon and measures gas composition from volume contractions after absorption or combustion.

records.l: Dr. Buente, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, BUNTE'S BURETTE FOR THE ANALYSIS OF FURNACE GASES. .. _Mode of Measuring the Gases and Absorption_.
records.s: Dr. Buente devised the burette used for analyzing blast-furnace gases.

records.l: blast-furnace gases, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, BUNTE'S BURETTE FOR THE ANALYSIS OF FURNACE GASES. .. _Mode of Measuring the Gases and Absorption_.
records.s: Blast-furnace gases are analyzed with the burette by measuring their initial volume and determining the contractions caused by absorption and combustion.

records.l: gas analysis, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, BUNTE'S BURETTE FOR THE ANALYSIS OF FURNACE GASES. .. _Mode of Measuring the Gases and Absorption_.
records.s: Gas analysis with the apparatus involves filling the burette, restoring the gas to its original pressure, and measuring volume changes after chemical absorption or combustion.

records.l: absorbing liquid, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, BUNTE'S BURETTE FOR THE ANALYSIS OF FURNACE GASES. .. _Mode of Measuring the Gases and Absorption_.
records.s: The absorbing liquid for oxide of carbon is prepared from saturated copper chloride in hydrochloric acid with a small quantity of dissolved tin chloride and spirals of red copper. Caustic potassa or pyrogallate of potassa is used for other absorptions, and the liquids can be replaced or washed out before measurement.

records.l: caustic potassa, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, BUNTE'S BURETTE FOR THE ANALYSIS OF FURNACE GASES. .. _Mode of Measuring the Gases and Absorption_.
records.s: Caustic potassa is sucked into the burette to absorb carbonic acid. It is also used with pyrogallic acid and potash to determine oxygen, and it is allowed to enter after combustion when analyzing oxide of carbon.

records.l: pyrogallate of potassa, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, BUNTE'S BURETTE FOR THE ANALYSIS OF FURNACE GASES. .. _Mode of Measuring the Gases and Absorption_.
records.s: Pyrogallate of potassa is used to absorb oxygen after carbonic acid has been removed with caustic potassa. It must be completely removed from the burette before the acid copper chloride solution is introduced.

records.l: oxide of carbon, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, BUNTE'S BURETTE FOR THE ANALYSIS OF FURNACE GASES. .. _Mode of Measuring the Gases and Absorption_.
records.s: The burette permits rapid absorption of oxide of carbon, although part of the absorbing liquid must be replaced three or four times for the last fractions. Oxide of carbon can also be quantitatively analyzed by combustion, with the total contraction from combustion and absorption multiplied by two-thirds giving its volume.

records.l: carbonic acid, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, BUNTE'S BURETTE FOR THE ANALYSIS OF FURNACE GASES. .. _Mode of Measuring the Gases and Absorption_.
records.s: Carbonic acid is absorbed by caustic potassa, and the resulting diminution in gas volume gives its volume in a combustion smoke analysis. Combustion of oxide of carbon produces an equal volume of carbonic acid.

records.l: oxygen, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, BUNTE'S BURETTE FOR THE ANALYSIS OF FURNACE GASES. .. _Mode of Measuring the Gases and Absorption_.
records.s: Oxygen is determined after carbonic acid has been absorbed by allowing an aqueous solution of pyrogallic acid and potash to enter the burette. Its presence darkens the liquid, and agitation continues until no further absorption occurs.

records.l: hydrogen, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, BUNTE'S BURETTE FOR THE ANALYSIS OF FURNACE GASES. .. _Mode of Measuring the Gases and Absorption_.
records.s: Hydrogen is analyzed by combustion with atmospheric air in the heated combustion tube. The contraction caused by burning it, multiplied by two-thirds, gives the original volume of hydrogen burned.

records.l: water, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, BUNTE'S BURETTE FOR THE ANALYSIS OF FURNACE GASES. .. _Mode of Measuring the Gases and Absorption_.
records.s: Water fills the burette and funnel, drives gas into or out of the apparatus, and establishes the pressure needed for measurement. It is also used to wash absorbing liquids from the burette, except that dilute hydrochloric acid is used when an acid copper chloride solution is employed.

records.l: combustion tube, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, BUNTE'S BURETTE FOR THE ANALYSIS OF FURNACE GASES. .. _Mode of Measuring the Gases and Absorption_.
records.s: The combustion tube is heated to redness by a Bunsen burner or alcohol lamp. A mixture of gas and atmospheric air passes through it in the presence of a palladium wire, causing combustion.

records.l: combustion of gas, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, BUNTE'S BURETTE FOR THE ANALYSIS OF FURNACE GASES. .. _Mode of Measuring the Gases and Absorption_.
records.s: Combustion of gas is carried out by mixing the burette gas with atmospheric air and passing the mixture through the heated combustion tube. After cooling and restoring the original pressure, the contraction is measured to calculate hydrogen or oxide of carbon.

records.l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE "UNIVERSAL" GAS ENGINE.
records.s: The Universal gas engine was invented by J. A. Ewins and H. Newman and made by T. B. Barker of Birmingham. It is a simple, single-acting gas engine made in sizes from one-eighth to one horse-power, with larger sizes being developed. Its main new feature is a rotary ignition valve that uses radial slots to pass flame into the cylinder and ignite the gas-air charge. The engines were reported to work successfully and to have low operating costs.

records.l: Universal gas engine, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE "UNIVERSAL" GAS ENGINE.
records.s: The Universal gas engine is a simple, single-acting engine invented by J. A. Ewins and H. Newman and made by T. B. Barker. It was constructed in sizes from one-eighth horse-power to one horse-power, with larger sizes being made, and was reported to work successfully at low gas cost.

records.l: gas engine design, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE "UNIVERSAL" GAS ENGINE.
records.s: The design draws an explosive mixture of gas and air into the cylinder and ignites it once per revolution without compressing the charge. It uses valve and ignition mechanisms that can be duplicated at the front end to make the engine double-acting, while an eccentric keeps the exhaust valve open during the return stroke.

records.l: rotary ignition, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE "UNIVERSAL" GAS ENGINE.
records.s: The rotary ignition consists of a ratchet plate or flat disk with small radial slots that successively align with a slot at the end of the cylinder. When aligned, flame from the igniting gas jet passes through the openings and ignites the charge; the mechanism has a very small range of motion and is described as requiring no lubrication or attention.

records.l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] GAS FURNACE FOR BAKING REFRACTORY PRODUCTS.
records.s: The gas furnace for baking refractory products is a smaller annular furnace designed for small establishments, with a baking chamber set into the ground and covered by movable refractory-clay slabs. Gas enters through channels, pipes, and vertical conduits before emerging through tuyeres into the baking chamber. A smoking furnace supplies hot gases for preliminary heating, with adjustable cold-air intake allowing its output temperature to vary from about 30 to 50 degrees upward. The smoking apparatus heated by gas avoids the cinders, dust, and difficult gradual heating associated with ordinary smoking systems.

records.l: gas furnace for baking refractory products, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] GAS FURNACE FOR BAKING REFRACTORY PRODUCTS.
records.s: The gas furnace for baking refractory products has a baking chamber only one and a half meters high and covered by removable refractory-clay slabs rather than a vault. A small car on a movable track removes each slab from an emptied compartment and places it over a newly filled compartment. Gas passes through channel G, pipe a, vertical conduits b, and tuyeres into the chamber.

records.l: refractory products, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] GAS FURNACE FOR BAKING REFRACTORY PRODUCTS.
records.s: Refractory products are baked in the furnace's chamber. The chamber is gradually heated, and the products are not exposed to cinders or dust from the heating process.

records.l: smoking furnace, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] GAS FURNACE FOR BAKING REFRACTORY PRODUCTS.
records.s: The smoking furnace, S, provides gas-heated preliminary heating or smoking. Air enters through apertures in its cover, combustion produces very hot gases, and these gases pass through tube e and vertical conduits b' into the smoking chamber. Adjustable registers admit cold, dry air to vary the temperature of the gases released through tube e.

records.l: smoking apparatus heated by gas, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] GAS FURNACE FOR BAKING REFRACTORY PRODUCTS.
records.s: The smoking apparatus heated by gas eliminates the cinders and dust associated with the ordinary system and makes gradual heating of objects to be baked easier. At the beginning, cold air lowers the smoke-gas temperature to 30 or 50 degrees; the air entrances are then gradually closed to increase the temperature as desired.

records.l: gas, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] GAS FURNACE FOR BAKING REFRACTORY PRODUCTS.
records.s: Gas enters the furnace through channel G, pipe a, and vertical conduits before being discharged through tuyeres into the baking chamber. In the smoking furnace, gas passes through tube t, where it is mixed with air and burned, producing hot gases that are directed into the smoking chamber.

records.l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE EFFICIENCY OF FANS.
records.s: The unit explains the work required to move air and the factors affecting the efficiency of fans. It describes how blade shape, speed, area, and casing influence air motion, power consumption, noise, and pressure. It presents a calculation estimating the power and air delivery of a fan, while noting that such efficiency is not achieved in practice. Mr. Buckle's recommended fan proportions for pressures of 3 to 6 ounces per square inch are also given.

records.l: efficiency of fans, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE EFFICIENCY OF FANS.
records.s: The efficiency of fans depends more on their proportions than on blade shapes, provided that easy curves and no sharp angles are used. Blade and case designs influence noise and modify efficiency, especially at high speeds, but recorded experiments are few and much ignorance remains about true efficiency.

records.l: fan, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE EFFICIENCY OF FANS.
records.s: A fan puts the weight of air in motion, overcoming inertia and frictional resistances. Air enters at the center and escapes at the circumference, with its motion changed through a right angle; gradually curved blades reduce violent deflection and noise. The fan's power requirement depends on blade area, air pressure, and the velocity of the center of effort, while its casing should widen as an arithmetical spiral toward the discharge opening.

records.l: atmospheric air, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE EFFICIENCY OF FANS.
records.s: Air possesses weight, with approximately 13.141 cubic feet weighing one pound at a pressure of 14.7 pounds per square inch and a temperature of 62 degrees. In a fan, air is accelerated outward by centrifugal force and tends to move tangentially to the blade path rather than directly radially. The pressure against the blades corresponds to the weight of a column of air whose height is determined by the air's velocity.

records.l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, MACHINE FOR COMPRESSING COAL REFUSE INTO FUEL.
records.s: The unit concerns the utilization of coal refuse to manufacture agglomerated artificial fuel for railways, steamboats, industry, and domestic heating. It describes the preparation of coal refuse, including sifting, washing, partial drying, mixing with coal dust and pitch, crushing, steaming, and conversion into a plastic paste. It also describes Bilan's machine, which compresses the paste into spherical conglomerates using four coordinated moulding wheels. The machine can produce about 40 tons of globular artificial fuel per day.

records.l: coal refuse, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, MACHINE FOR COMPRESSING COAL REFUSE INTO FUEL.
records.s: Coal refuse is sifted to separate dust from coal grains, with the nut size removed and sold separately. The grains are washed by size, partially drained or dried, then mixed with coal dust and eight to ten percent broken coal pitch before being crushed and formed into fuel.

records.l: artificial fuel, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, MACHINE FOR COMPRESSING COAL REFUSE INTO FUEL.
records.s: Artificial fuel made from coal refuse is an agglomerated fuel used on railways and steamboats, in industry, and for domestic heating. Bilan's machine produces it in spherical or globular form.

records.l: agglomerating machine, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, MACHINE FOR COMPRESSING COAL REFUSE INTO FUEL.
records.s: An agglomerating machine should be simple, accessible for cleaning, and designed to permit worn parts to be changed with minimal interruption. It should apply powerful, progressive compression over as much of the conglomerate's surface as possible and remove the product from the mould without relying on fouling pistons or springs.

records.l: manufacture of artificial fuel from coal refuse, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, MACHINE FOR COMPRESSING COAL REFUSE INTO FUEL.
records.s: The manufacture involves sifting and classifying the refuse, washing and partly drying the coal grains, mixing them with coal dust and pitch, crushing the mixture, converting it into a plastic paste with superheated steam, and distributing it into moulds for compression.

records.l: plastic paste, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, MACHINE FOR COMPRESSING COAL REFUSE INTO FUEL.
records.s: The coal mixture becomes a plastic paste in a pug-mill when superheated steam is admitted. The paste is then led into an agitator to remove steam and distribute the material into the moulds of the compressing machine.

records.l: spherical conglomerates, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, MACHINE FOR COMPRESSING COAL REFUSE INTO FUEL.
