records.s: Spherical conglomerates are formed when four vertical moulding wheels, each carrying quarter-sphere cavities, meet and enclose the paste. After further rotation separates the wheels, the finished balls drop out.

records.l: Bilan, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, MACHINE FOR COMPRESSING COAL REFUSE INTO FUEL.
records.s: Bilan is associated with the machine shown for manufacturing spherical conglomerates intended for domestic purposes.

records.l: Bilan's machine, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, MACHINE FOR COMPRESSING COAL REFUSE INTO FUEL.
records.s: Bilan's machine has a cast-iron frame supporting four vertical moulding wheels arranged at right angles, along with a hopper, vertical helices, shafts, screws, gears, and beveled pinions. The wheels progressively compress the paste from four quarters, and their mould-carrying segments can be removed and replaced when worn. The machine produces about 40 tons of globular artificial fuel per day.

records.l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, HANK SIZING AND WRINGING MACHINE.
records.s: The unit describes a hank sizing and wringing machine made by Heywood & Spencer of Radcliffe, near Manchester. The machine uses geared hooks to twist hanks, hold them briefly while excess size is wiped off, and then reverse the twist before removal. It can be used for sizing and fancy dyeing, with running performed on one side while finishing is performed on the other. The makers claim production rates of about 36 10-pound bundles per hour at finishing and 45 bundles in 2-pound wringers at running.

records.l: Hank sizing and wringing machine, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, HANK SIZING AND WRINGING MACHINE.
records.s: The hank sizing and wringing machine consists of two vats with driving gear between them and hooks whose spacing can be adjusted to the length or size of the hanks. It twists hanks, holds them briefly for excess size to be wiped off, reverses the twist, and removes them by hand or with a lifting lattice.

records.l: Heywood & Spencer, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, HANK SIZING AND WRINGING MACHINE.
records.s: Heywood & Spencer, of Radcliffe, near Manchester, made the hank sizing machine described. The makers claim that a double machine can finish about 36 10-pound bundles per hour or run about 45 bundles in 2-pound wringers.

records.l: hank, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, HANK SIZING AND WRINGING MACHINE.
records.s: The hank is lifted from a vat and placed on the machine's hooks. It is twisted two, two and a half, three, or more times, held while excess size is wiped off, then untwisted and removed for transport to the drying stove.

records.l: sizing, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, HANK SIZING AND WRINGING MACHINE.
records.s: Sizing uses a customary double operation consisting of running followed by finishing. The machine can perform running on one side while finishing occurs on the other, and it can also run on both sides if required.

records.l: wringing, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, HANK SIZING AND WRINGING MACHINE.
records.s: Wringing hanks by hand is described as severe labor that limits production and can make even colors difficult to obtain in dyeing. The machine is intended to carry out this heavy work more quickly and reliably.

records.l: running, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, HANK SIZING AND WRINGING MACHINE.
records.s: Running is the first operation in sizing and can be carried on one side while finishing occurs on the other, or on both sides. The makers claim a production rate of about 45 bundles in 2-pound wringers.

records.l: finishing, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, HANK SIZING AND WRINGING MACHINE.
records.s: Finishing is the second operation in sizing and can be performed simultaneously with running on the opposite side. The makers claim a production rate of about 36 10-pound bundles per hour at finishing.

records.l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] IMPROVED COKE BREAKER.
records.s: The improved coke breaker used by the South Metropolitan Gas Company consists of a single drum with cutting edges that breaks coke against a fixed grid. Its capacity can be changed by adding or removing cast rings, while the grid distance controls the fineness of the broken coke. The machine requires little power, produces relatively little waste, and can separate the output into larger coke, clean breeze, and dust. At full capacity, it can break about 8 tons per hour, and broken coke generally sells for 2s. to 2s. 6d. more per ton than large coke.

records.l: improved coke breaker, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] IMPROVED COKE BREAKER.
records.s: The improved coke breaker uses a single revolving drum with cutting edges to break coke against a fixed grid, without toothed gearing. Its capacity is adjusted by varying the number of cast rings, and the fineness of the product is controlled by changing the grid's distance from the drum. It can be made in different sizes, including hand-powered versions, and the full-size machine can break about 8 tons of coke per hour.

records.l: South Metropolitan Gas Company, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] IMPROVED COKE BREAKER.
records.s: The South Metropolitan Gas Company uses the improved coke breaker. A full-size machine at its Old Kent Road works was driven by a one horse power Otto gas-engine and broke two tons of coke in half an hour during a trial.

records.l: coke, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] IMPROVED COKE BREAKER.
records.s: Coke is broken by the improved coke breaker and screened into larger coke, clean breeze, and dust. The dust is used at the works to mix with lime in the purifiers. Broken coke generally fetches 2s. to 2s. 6d. more per ton than large coke, while the machine produces only a small quantity of waste.

records.l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] IMPROVEMENT IN PRINTING MACHINERY.
records.s: The improvement in printing machinery is the design of Alfred Godfrey of Clapton. It uses a vibrating rack, A, and a pinion, a1, supported by a radial arm, a2, mounted on the shaft, a3, which supports the driving wheel, a4. The arrangement is intended to transmit easy, uniform, and silent motion to the rack and table through the vibrating movement of the arm, pinion, and rack.

records.l: improvement in printing machinery, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] IMPROVEMENT IN PRINTING MACHINERY.
records.s: It employs a vibrating rack, A, and a pinion, a1, supported by a radial arm, a2, mounted on the shaft, a3. The arrangement transmits an easy, uniform, and silent motion to the rack and table.

records.l: Alfred Godfrey, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] IMPROVEMENT IN PRINTING MACHINERY.
records.s: Alfred Godfrey, of Clapton, designed the improvement in printing machinery.

records.l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] A CHARACTERISTIC MINING "RUSH.
records.s: The unit describes a mining rush in Southern New Mexico, centered on the newly active Perche district near Lake Valley and Hillsboro. Jack Shedd made the first great strike in the Perche district on August 15, finding surface blocks of exceptionally rich silver ore. The discovery drew about 2,000 prospectors and led to more than 1,000 claims, while properties such as the Solitaire and Bullion attracted investors and development. The Perche district appeared likely to become a major mining center despite uncertainty about some discoveries.

records.l: mining rush, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] A CHARACTERISTIC MINING "RUSH.
records.s: The mining rush spread through the Perche district after reports of rich silver discoveries, drawing about 2,000 people and producing more than 1,000 located prospects. The excitement was compared with the speculative enthusiasm of mining-stock buyers in New York.

records.l: Southern New Mexico, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] A CHARACTERISTIC MINING "RUSH.
records.s: Southern New Mexico is presented as a prospective mining center because of the activity around Lake Valley, the Black Range, and especially the Perche district.

records.l: Lake Valley, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] A CHARACTERISTIC MINING "RUSH.
records.s: Lake Valley had previously been considered likely to become the central mining camp of the region. News of discoveries in the Perche district caused workers and prospectors to leave Lake Valley and head there.

records.l: Perche district, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] A CHARACTERISTIC MINING "RUSH.
records.s: The Perche district lies on the eastern flanks of the Mimbres Mountains, about twenty-five miles northwest of Lake Valley and ten miles west of Hillsboro. Rich discoveries, including the Solitaire and Bullion, brought intense excitement and made the district's future appear assured.

records.l: prospectors, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] A CHARACTERISTIC MINING "RUSH.
records.s: Prospectors rapidly entered the Perche district after the first discoveries, arriving on foot, on mules, and with minimal supplies. Within a month, roughly 2,000 prospectors and other people were there, and more than 1,000 prospects had been located.

records.l: Mimbres Mountains, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] A CHARACTERISTIC MINING "RUSH.
records.s: The Mimbres Mountains are part of the Rocky Mountain range and run generally north and south, parallel to the Rio Grande and about forty miles west of it. The Perche district is located on their eastern flanks.

records.l: Black Range, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] A CHARACTERISTIC MINING "RUSH.
records.s: The northern half of the Mimbres Mountains is known as the Black Range. It experienced mining excitement about a year and a half earlier, and the reopening of the Ivanhoe was expected to stimulate the region.

records.l: Hillsboro, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] A CHARACTERISTIC MINING "RUSH.
records.s: Hillsboro is a promising mining town about ten miles east of the Perche district, with some mills and approximately 300 people. Three forks of the Perche River unite there.

records.l: Jack Shedd, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] A CHARACTERISTIC MINING "RUSH.
records.s: Jack Shedd, who had discovered the Robinson mine in Colorado, was prospecting near the south branch of the north fork of the Perche River on August 15 when he made the district's first great strike. He found surface pieces and large blocks of exceptionally rich silver ore, and his location, the Solitaire, later attracted the interest of ex-Governor Tabor and Mr. Wurtzbach.

records.l: first great strike in the Perche district, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] A CHARACTERISTIC MINING "RUSH.
records.s: The first great strike in the Perche district consisted of surface float found on a heavily timbered ridge by Jack Shedd. It included a 150-pound lump of ore worth an average of $11 per pound and an 87-pound block of horn silver containing specimens nearly 75 percent silver.

records.l: Solitaire, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] A CHARACTERISTIC MINING "RUSH.
records.s: The Solitaire was Jack Shedd's location and showed what appeared to be a contact vein with porphyry and limestone walls, in places forming a thirty-foot-wide ledge. Its quartz vein carried sulphides and visible horn silver, with reported average assays of $350 to $500, but a later claim that it was only a blind lead lacked confirmation.

records.l: ex-Governor Tabor, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] A CHARACTERISTIC MINING "RUSH.
records.s: Ex-Governor Tabor was reported to have bought the Solitaire from Jack Shedd for $100,000 on August 25, but that report was described as untrue. His representative had examined the properties, and the Governor had apparently bonded the mine while viewing it favorably.

records.l: silver ore, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] A CHARACTERISTIC MINING "RUSH.
records.s: Silver ore discovered in the Perche district included native silver, silver sulphides, horn silver, and quartz carrying sulphides. The reported discoveries ranged from exceptionally rich surface specimens to ore in the Bullion and other developing properties.

records.l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE SOY BEAN.
records.s: The unit concerns the Soy bean and its nutritional qualities and uses. The British Medical Journal reports that Prof. E. Kinch describes it as more like animal food than any other known vegetable production because it is rich in fat and albuminoids. It is widely used as food in China and Japan, has been cultivated with fair success in Italy and France, and provides foods and useful fodder from its straw.

records.l: Soy bean, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE SOY BEAN.
records.s: The Soy bean is described as being singularly rich in fat and albuminoids, and as approaching more nearly to animal food than any other known vegetable production. It is largely used as food in China and Japan; efforts to acclimatize it in Europe have achieved fair success in Italy and France. Many foods are made from it, and its straw is useful fodder.

records.l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON A NEW ARC ELECTRIC LAMP. .. _Electrical Arrangement_.
records.s: W.H. Preece describes a new arc electric lamp and the system invented by M. Abdank. The system separates the regulator from the lamp, allowing the lamp to be installed in inaccessible locations while the regulator remains accessible. A balance using two solenoids controls a break that makes minute adjustments to the carbon electrodes as carbon is consumed, maintaining a steady electric arc. An automatic cut-off protects series-connected lamps by replacing a failed lamp with an equivalent resistance.

records.l: W.H. Preece, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON A NEW ARC ELECTRIC LAMP. .. _Electrical Arrangement_.
records.s: W.H. Preece presented the new arc electric lamp to the Section and revised the paper describing it. He reported that the lamp operated with constant steadiness.

records.l: new arc electric lamp, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON A NEW ARC ELECTRIC LAMP. .. _Electrical Arrangement_.
records.s: The new arc electric lamp has a fixed negative carbon and a movable positive carbon. Its regulation is separated from the lamp, allowing the lamp to be fixed in an inaccessible place.

records.l: arc electric lighting, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON A NEW ARC ELECTRIC LAMP. .. _Electrical Arrangement_.
records.s: Arc electric lighting is affected by the consumption of its carbon electrodes, which can cause flickering and irregularity. The described system aims to make the light steady through automatic, very small adjustments.

records.l: M. Abdank, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON A NEW ARC ELECTRIC LAMP. .. _Electrical Arrangement_.
records.s: M. Abdank invented the system described by W.H. Preece. His system separates the regulator from the lamp and uses automatic regulation.

records.l: Abdank lamp system, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON A NEW ARC ELECTRIC LAMP. .. _Electrical Arrangement_.
records.s: The Abdank lamp system uses an external regulator consisting of a balance and a cut-off. It regulates the carbon gap in short successive steps and includes an automatic cut-off for accidents when several lamps are connected in series.

records.l: regulator, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON A NEW ARC ELECTRIC LAMP. .. _Electrical Arrangement_.
records.s: The regulator is separated from the lamp and may be placed where it can be inspected and manipulated easily. It uses a balance and a cut-off to compensate for carbon consumption and maintain the required electrical resistance.

records.l: carbon electrodes, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON A NEW ARC ELECTRIC LAMP. .. _Electrical Arrangement_.
records.s: The bottom or negative carbon is fixed, while the top or positive carbon moves vertically. The positive carbon is lifted when current energizes an electromagnet, and the regulator later allows the carbons to approach by about 0.01 to 0.02 millimeter at a time.

records.l: electromagnet, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON A NEW ARC ELECTRIC LAMP. .. _Electrical Arrangement_.
records.s: An electromagnet lifts the rod carrying the positive carbon when current passes through its coil. Another electromagnet controls the break that releases the rack and permits the carbons to approach.

records.l: lamp balance, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON A NEW ARC ELECTRIC LAMP. .. _Electrical Arrangement_.
records.s: The lamp balance consists of two solenoids: one carrying the main current and one carrying a shunt current. Changes in current alter their opposing magnetic effects, causing an iron rod to break or restore contact and thereby control the lamp's adjustment.

records.l: automatic cut-off, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON A NEW ARC ELECTRIC LAMP. .. _Electrical Arrangement_.
records.s: The automatic cut-off is used when several lamps are connected in series. If a lamp fails or a carbon breaks, it connects the circuit through a resistance equivalent to the lamp, allowing the other lamps to continue operating and enabling rapid relighting when contact is restored.

records.l: dynamo machine, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON A NEW ARC ELECTRIC LAMP. .. _Electrical Arrangement_.
records.s: The dynamo machine supplies the current to the series-connected lamps. Its positive lead passes through the balance and the lamps before returning to its negative pole.

records.l: series-connected lamps, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON A NEW ARC ELECTRIC LAMP. .. _Electrical Arrangement_.
records.s: Series-connected lamps receive current successively from the dynamo machine, with the current returning from each lamp to the balance and then proceeding to the next. The automatic cut-off allows a failed lamp to be bypassed by a resistance.

records.l: electric arc, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON A NEW ARC ELECTRIC LAMP. .. _Electrical Arrangement_.
records.s: The electric arc forms when the electromagnet lifts the positive carbon away from the negative carbon. It continues to burn steadily while the current remains constant, with the regulator compensating for increased resistance as the arc changes.

records.l: carbon consumption, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON A NEW ARC ELECTRIC LAMP. .. _Electrical Arrangement_.
records.s: Carbon consumption changes the distance and resistance between the electrodes. The regulator compensates by allowing the carbon support to fall in continual, nearly invisible increments.

records.l: flickering and irregularity of light, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON A NEW ARC ELECTRIC LAMP. .. _Electrical Arrangement_.
records.s: Flickering and irregularity of light are attributed to variations in the consumption of the carbons. The Abdank system is intended to prevent these effects through small and rapid regulatory movements that do not affect the main current.

records.l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, APPARATUS FOR OBTAINING PURE WATER FOR PHOTOGRAPHIC USE.
records.s: The unit concerns methods and apparatus for obtaining clean or distilled water for photographic use. It explains that rain-water collected after roofs have been washed can provide clean soft water, and describes an automatic shunt for diverting the initial dirty flow. It also discusses glass and metal distillation apparatus for preparing highly pure water, especially for nitrate baths and emulsions. The text details photographic problems caused by chlorides, lime, calcium oxalate, and other impurities in water.

records.l: apparatus for obtaining pure water for photographic use, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, APPARATUS FOR OBTAINING PURE WATER FOR PHOTOGRAPHIC USE.
records.s: The apparatus includes an automatic shunt for diverting rain-water until a roof has been washed, as well as glass and metal stills for distillation. The text recommends distilled water for nitrate baths and emulsion preparation.

records.l: water, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, APPARATUS FOR OBTAINING PURE WATER FOR PHOTOGRAPHIC USE.
records.s: Naturally occurring water contains dissolved inorganic and organic impurities and gases. Impurities in water can shorten the effectiveness of iron and pyrogallic developers, produce calcium oxalate veils on negatives, and affect silver prints and carbon printing.

records.l: rain-water, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, APPARATUS FOR OBTAINING PURE WATER FOR PHOTOGRAPHIC USE.
records.s: Rain-water collected in a secluded district after previous rain can be exceptionally pure, containing little more than traces of carbonic acid and other atmospheric gases. In towns, especially when it flows over dirty roofs, it can become contaminated, but clean rain-water collected after the roofs are washed is valuable for photographic work.

records.l: distilled water, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, APPARATUS FOR OBTAINING PURE WATER FOR PHOTOGRAPHIC USE.
records.s: Distilled water is recommended for preparing the nitrate bath and should always be used in preparing emulsion. It can be produced in a glass apparatus or in a metal still with a tin condensing worm, provided the apparatus is kept clean.

records.l: soft water, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, APPARATUS FOR OBTAINING PURE WATER FOR PHOTOGRAPHIC USE.
records.s: Clean soft water is useful for photographic processes because developers remain effective longer and carbon printing can be carried out more rapidly or at a lower temperature. Soft water collected from dirty roofs, however, may contain substantial carbonaceous and organic contamination.

records.l: automatic shunt for diverting rainwater, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, APPARATUS FOR OBTAINING PURE WATER FOR PHOTOGRAPHIC USE.
records.s: The automatic shunt prevents water from entering a cistern until the roof has been thoroughly washed. Its operation depends on a valve, lever, weight, and vessel with a small hole that restores the apparatus after rain ceases; careful adjustment of these parts is required.

records.l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, [Illustration] BLACK PHOSPHORUS.
records.s: P. Thenard examines black, or dark gray, phosphorus and challenges the view that it is always ordinary phosphorus mixed with traces of a metallic phosphide. A specimen became white when melted and stayed white after sudden cooling, but turned black again when allowed to become superfused and then contacted with white or black phosphorus. When part of the specimen was dissolved in carbon disulphide, only a trace of very pale yellow matter remained undissolved, appearing to be amorphous phosphorus.

records.l: BLACK PHOSPHORUS, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, [Illustration] BLACK PHOSPHORUS.
records.s: Black phosphorus is described as possibly not always being a mixture of ordinary phosphorus and traces of a metallic phosphide. A dark gray specimen became white when melted and remained white after sudden cooling, but became black again after superfusion when brought into contact with white or black phosphorus. Most of the specimen dissolved in carbon disulphide, leaving only a trace of very pale yellow matter that seemed to be amorphous phosphorus.

records.l: P. THENARD, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, [Illustration] BLACK PHOSPHORUS.
records.s: P. Thenard challenges the customary explanation of black phosphorus as a mixture of ordinary phosphorus with traces of a metallic phosphide. He submitted a specimen of black or dark gray phosphorus to the Academy and reported its changes under melting, cooling, superfusion, and contact with other forms of phosphorus.

records.l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, COMPOSITION OF STEEP WATER.
records.s: The unit describes the composition of water in which malt has been steeped, according to M. C. Leeuw. It contains 0.56 percent organic matter and 0.52 percent mineral matter, for a total of 1.08 percent dry matter, including 0.033 percent nitrogen. Its mineral matter includes potash, phosphoric acid, lime, soda, magnesia, sulphuric acid, traces of oxide of iron, and no chlorine or silica.

records.l: steep water, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, COMPOSITION OF STEEP WATER.
records.s: Steep water is water in which malt has been steeped. According to M. C. Leeuw, it contains 1.08 percent total dry matter, consisting of 0.56 percent organic matter and 0.52 percent mineral matter, and contains 0.033 percent nitrogen.

records.l: composition of steep water, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, COMPOSITION OF STEEP WATER.
records.s: The composition of steep water includes 0.193 percent potash, 0.031 percent phosphoric acid, 0.012 percent lime, 0.047 percent soda, 0.016 percent magnesia, and 0.007 percent sulphuric acid. Oxide of iron is present in traces, while chlorine and silica are absent.

records.l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, 212 " SCHREIBER'S APPARATUS FOR REVIVIFYING BONE-BLACK. .. _The Animal Black Furnace_.
records.s: Schreiber's apparatus revivifies bone-black by washing it with water and acid in a rotary washer, then drying, reheating, and cooling it for reuse. The apparatus includes filters, wells, a washer, an elevator, an automatic drying system, and a continuous furnace. The animal black furnace uses undulating cast-iron retorts heated by a coke fire, followed by cooling pipes that deliver the treated black ready for bagging. An apparatus of the described dimensions can revivify 120 hectoliters of bone-black in twenty-four hours using 360 to 400 kilogrammes of coke.

records.l: Schreiber's apparatus for revivifying bone-black, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, 212 " SCHREIBER'S APPARATUS FOR REVIVIFYING BONE-BLACK. .. _The Animal Black Furnace_.
records.s: Schreiber's apparatus transfers used bone-black from wells to a rotary washer, then uses a steam filter, elevator, drier, furnace retorts, and cooling pipes to process it continuously. Its elevator and gearing operate automatically after the gearing lever is engaged.

records.l: bone-black, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, 212 " SCHREIBER'S APPARATUS FOR REVIVIFYING BONE-BLACK. .. _The Animal Black Furnace_.
records.s: Bone-black loses its decolorizing properties when its pores become filled with absorbed salts and insoluble compounds from sugar refining. In the apparatus, it is washed, elevated while wet, dried, revivified in heated retorts, cooled, and discharged ready to be bagged and reused.

records.l: revivification of bone-black, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, 212 " SCHREIBER'S APPARATUS FOR REVIVIFYING BONE-BLACK. .. _The Animal Black Furnace_.
records.s: Revivification frees bone-black from absorbed salts and insoluble compounds so that it can be used again. The text describes fermentation and washing as methods, noting a tendency to abandon fermentation in favor of washing with water and acid in a rotary washer.

records.l: rotary washer, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, 212 " SCHREIBER'S APPARATUS FOR REVIVIFYING BONE-BLACK. .. _The Animal Black Furnace_.
records.s: The rotary washer receives bone-black directly from the wells and discharges it near a steam filter beneath the floor. The steam filter directs the wet black toward an elevator, which carries it to the drier.

records.l: automatic drying system, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, 212 " SCHREIBER'S APPARATUS FOR REVIVIFYING BONE-BLACK. .. _The Animal Black Furnace_.
records.s: The automatic drying system is located at the upper part of the furnace and was devised to dry bone-black as it exits the washer. It consists of two undulating pipes with openings for steam to escape, while waste heat and combustion products pass through the space between them before leaving through the chimney.

records.l: animal black furnace, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, 212 " SCHREIBER'S APPARATUS FOR REVIVIFYING BONE-BLACK. .. _The Animal Black Furnace_.
records.s: The animal black furnace has a masonry casing, a coke-fired chamber, and two rows of undulating cast-iron retorts enclosed in refractory clay blocks. Bone-black passes from the hopper through the drier, retorts, and cooling pipes; the cooling pipes end in rotary cylinders that regulate its discharge into a rail car. The furnace can revivify 120 hectoliters of bone-black in twenty-four hours with 360 to 400 kilogrammes of coke.

records.l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] SOAP AND ITS MANUFACTURE, FROM A CONSUMER'S POINT OF VIEW.
records.s: The article explains to consumers how to make pure, neutral potash soap and contrasts it with soda soap. It gives directions for mixing caustic potash lye with tallow, grease, or oil, and describes how the mixture becomes soap after standing warm for a week. It recommends cotton seed oil for manufacturers and laundry soap, warns that products sold as crystal, ball, or rock potash are actually caustic soda, and discusses the possible benefits of fleece scouring for sheep owners.

records.l: soap, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] SOAP AND ITS MANUFACTURE, FROM A CONSUMER'S POINT OF VIEW.
records.s: The article presents practical instructions for consumers to make pure and unadulterated soap. It explains that soap made with tallow or grease can be nearly as hard as soda soap, while soap made with oil can be remelted with water to produce a bright, harder, and stiffer product.

records.l: consumers, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] SOAP AND ITS MANUFACTURE, FROM A CONSUMER'S POINT OF VIEW.
records.s: Consumers are shown how to make neutral potash soap for household and laundry use. The article cautions them to distinguish genuine caustic potash from products falsely sold as potash.

records.l: potash soap, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] SOAP AND ITS MANUFACTURE, FROM A CONSUMER'S POINT OF VIEW.
records.s: Potash soap is described as superior to soda soap, especially for washing wool or woolen fabrics. When made with pure caustic potash, it can be neutral and suitable for wool washing, household use, and laundry purposes.

records.l: soda soap, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] SOAP AND ITS MANUFACTURE, FROM A CONSUMER'S POINT OF VIEW.
records.s: Soda soap is compared unfavorably with potash soap, particularly for washing wool or woolen fabrics. The article states that potash soap is superior to soda soap even when the soda soap is pure and well made.

records.l: caustic potassa, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] SOAP AND ITS MANUFACTURE, FROM A CONSUMER'S POINT OF VIEW.
records.s: Pure caustic potash is used to make neutral potash soap. Twenty pounds are dissolved in two gallons of water, cooled to about 90 F, and mixed with eighty pounds of melted tallow, grease, or oil; the article warns that it melts and deteriorates quickly when exposed to air.

records.l: caustic soda, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] SOAP AND ITS MANUFACTURE, FROM A CONSUMER'S POINT OF VIEW.
records.s: Caustic soda is described as a different substance from caustic potash, although the two look alike. Products called crystal potash, ball potash, or rock potash are said to contain caustic soda, often adulterated, rather than potash.

records.l: hard soap, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] SOAP AND ITS MANUFACTURE, FROM A CONSUMER'S POINT OF VIEW.
records.s: The method for making pure neutral potash soap is said to be almost identical to the method for making hard soap with pure powdered caustic soda. Potash soap made with tallow can become nearly as hard as soda soap.

records.l: wool and woolen fabrics, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] SOAP AND ITS MANUFACTURE, FROM A CONSUMER'S POINT OF VIEW.
records.s: Potash soap is recommended for washing wool and woolen fabrics because it is considered superior to soda soap for this purpose. The article says it can be used to wash wool and the cloth made from it.

records.l: tallow or grease, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] SOAP AND ITS MANUFACTURE, FROM A CONSUMER'S POINT OF VIEW.
records.s: Tallow or grease should be free from salt before being used to make potash soap. Eighty pounds are melted, cooled to about 130 F, and mixed with caustic potash lye; the article identifies these materials as economical and readily available to farmers and householders.

records.l: cotton seed oil, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] SOAP AND ITS MANUFACTURE, FROM A CONSUMER'S POINT OF VIEW.
records.s: Cotton seed oil is recommended for manufacturers or for making laundry soap. The article says it produces a magnificent soap that lathers very freely.

records.l: fleece scouring, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ] SOAP AND ITS MANUFACTURE, FROM A CONSUMER'S POINT OF VIEW.
records.s: Fleece scouring involves washing wool while it is still growing on the sheep with potash soap made from waste tallow available on sheep farms. The article says it could benefit sheep owners by improving the condition of their wool and cleaning the sheep's skin.

records.l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, COTTON SEED OIL.
records.s: S.S. Bradford reports on using cotton seed oil in place of olive oil for lead plaster and several pharmacopoeial liniments. He found that cotton seed oil produced lead plaster of equally good quality when one and one-half pints of boiling water were used instead of one-half pint. It performed well in Linimentum Ammoniae, Linimentum Camphorae, and Linimentum Chloroformi, but was unsuitable for Linimentum Calcis. Bradford also observed that cotton seed oil turned reddish when mixed with liquor plumbi subacetatis, providing a way to detect small amounts of it in olive oil.

records.l: S.S. Bradford, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, COTTON SEED OIL.
records.s: S.S. Bradford had manufactured lead plaster for six years and investigated whether cotton seed oil could replace olive oil. He also tested cotton seed oil in several pharmacopoeial liniments and reported its effects.

records.l: cotton seed oil, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, COTTON SEED OIL.
records.s: Cotton seed oil can be used to make lead plaster of equally good quality as plaster made with olive oil when one and one-half pints of boiling water are added. It makes a better-consistency Linimentum Ammoniae, is superior to olive oil for dissolving camphor in Linimentum Camphorae, and performs well in Linimentum Chloroformi, but it is unsuitable for Linimentum Calcis because it does not readily saponify and separates quickly. When mixed with liquor plumbi subacetatis, it turns reddish after twelve to twenty-four hours, a change detectable in mixtures containing five percent or less cotton seed oil.

records.l: lead plaster, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, COTTON SEED OIL.
records.s: Lead plaster made with cotton seed oil was found by S.S. Bradford to be equally as good as that made with olive oil when the U. S. P. process was modified by using one and one-half pints of boiling water instead of one-half pint.

records.l: olive oil, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, COTTON SEED OIL.
records.s: Olive oil was the oil traditionally used by S.S. Bradford for lead plaster and was compared with cotton seed oil in several liniments. When pure olive oil is mixed with liquor plumbi subacetatis, it does not undergo the reddish color change observed with cotton seed oil.

records.l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE FOOD AND ENERGY OF MAN.
records.s: Prof. de Chaumont’s lecture explains how food is used to build and repair the human body, produce energy, and generate animal heat. It classifies food into nitrogenous substances, fats, starches and sugars, salts, water, and air, emphasizing the need for adequate quantities and variety. The lecture also discusses alcohol, tea, coffee, tobacco, and oatmeal gruel in relation to fatigue and useful work. It concludes by addressing scurvy outbreaks among seamen and urging varied provisions, including potatoes and lime-juice, aboard ships.

records.l: Prof. de Chaumont, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE FOOD AND ENERGY OF MAN.
records.s: Prof. de Chaumont delivered a lecture at the Sanitary Congress at Newcastle-on-Tyne on September 28, 1882. He discussed the uses and classes of food, the energy of the body, alcohol, fatigue, tobacco, and scurvy among seamen.

records.l: man, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE FOOD AND ENERGY OF MAN.
records.s: Man is described as probably naturally frugivorous, like the monkeys, though he began eating animal food many ages ago. His digestive apparatus appears adapted to food capable of yielding nutriment, and his system can accommodate itself to changes in diet.

records.l: food, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE FOOD AND ENERGY OF MAN.
records.s: Food is defined as any substance taken into the body and used to build or repair tissues, provide energy and animal heat, or control or assist those functions. The definition includes water and air, although they are not ordinarily recognized as food.

records.l: human nutrition, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE FOOD AND ENERGY OF MAN.
records.s: Human nutrition is best maintained by a due admixture and variety of the four classes of aliment discussed in the lecture. Water and salts are also required, and monotony of diet can seriously affect health, digestion, and assimilation.

records.l: energy of the body, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE FOOD AND ENERGY OF MAN.
records.s: The energy of the body is derived from food, particularly from its non-nitrogenous parts. Heat is described as a form of convertible energy that can perform useful or productive work.

records.l: organic substances, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE FOOD AND ENERGY OF MAN.
records.s: Organic substances are divided into nitrogen-containing substances and substances that do not contain nitrogen. The latter include fats, starches, and sugars.

records.l: nitrogenous substances, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE FOOD AND ENERGY OF MAN.
records.s: Nitrogenous substances are needed to build up tissues in the young and repair and renew them in adults. They include animal albumin, fibrin, myosin or synronin, casein, blood substances, and vegetable glutin and legumin; they also contribute to bodily energy when broken down and oxidized.

records.l: non-nitrogenous food, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE FOOD AND ENERGY OF MAN.
records.s: Non-nitrogenous food includes fats, starches, and sugars. Modern experiments are said to show that these substances, rather than the nitrogenous part of food, provide most of the body's energy.

records.l: fats, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE FOOD AND ENERGY OF MAN.
records.s: Fats are non-nitrogenous constituents that contribute energy. Examples recommended in a varied diet include butter, lard, suet, and oil.

records.l: starches and sugars, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE FOOD AND ENERGY OF MAN.
records.s: Starches and sugars are non-nitrogenous food constituents that provide energy. Examples include starch from wheat, potatoes, rice, and peas, as well as cane-sugar and milk-sugar.

records.l: human body, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE FOOD AND ENERGY OF MAN.
records.s: The human body is compared to a machine or engine that requires fuel in proportion to the work performed and the speed at which it is done. Its tissues and fluids, except fat, contain nitrogen, and its processes follow universal physical laws.

records.l: alcohol, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE FOOD AND ENERGY OF MAN.
records.s: Alcohol may be a comfort and blessing when properly used but becomes a bane and curse in excess. Experiments at Netley indicated that beyond an amount represented by about one and a half to two pints of beer, it provided no convertible energy; it could give a temporary stimulus followed by depression and was generally not given before or during work.

records.l: scurvy, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE FOOD AND ENERGY OF MAN.
records.s: Scurvy is presented as a serious maritime health problem associated with inadequate or monotonous provisions. Its prevention may require varied food, proper supplies of lime-juice, and substantial provisions of fresh and dried potatoes.

records.l: scientific experiments on food and energy, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE FOOD AND ENERGY OF MAN.
records.s: Scientific experiments and the work of Joule, Lyon Playfair, Clausius, Tyndall, Helmholtz, and others established that heat is a mode of motion and convertible energy. Experiments by Dr. Parkes at the laboratory at Netley showed that alcohol beyond a limited amount did not provide convertible energy.

records.l: scurvy outbreaks, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE FOOD AND ENERGY OF MAN.
records.s: Scurvy outbreaks had increased again, reaching ninety-nine in 1881, after a serious falling off since 1873. Mr. Thomas Gray attributed this possibly to neglect of varied food scales, and the lecture also suggests neglect of regulations concerning lime-juice.

records.l: lecture on food and energy, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE FOOD AND ENERGY OF MAN.
records.s: The lecture on food and energy explains the classification and uses of food, the relation between nutrition and bodily work, and the importance of variety in diet. It also considers alcohol and other restoratives, tobacco, scurvy among seamen, and the need for shipowners or the legislature to protect maritime health.

records.l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RATTLESNAKE POISON.
records.s: Henry H. Croft discusses whether rattlesnake poison is an alkaloid and reports tests of its reaction with iodine. Mr. Pedler had reported that platinic chloride destroys or neutralizes snake poison, probably by forming an insoluble double platinic chloride. Croft observed a dense light-brown precipitate when iodine solution was added to poison from a rattlesnake, and he describes iodine in potassium iodide as a favored Texas remedy for rattlesnake bites. He questions the usefulness of potassium permanganate after poison has been absorbed and reports finding ammonium urate in the snake's bladder.

records.l: Henry H. Croft, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RATTLESNAKE POISON.
records.s: Henry H. Croft reports experiments and observations on rattlesnake poison in Texas. He tested poison from a rattlesnake with iodine solution, considered possible chemical explanations for remedies, and questioned the therapeutic value of potassium permanganate after absorption.

records.l: Mr. Pedler, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RATTLESNAKE POISON.
records.s: Mr. Pedler reported that snake poison is destroyed or neutralized by platinic chloride, probably through formation of an insoluble double platinic chloride. He also referred to potassium permanganate but allowed that it would probably be ineffective after the poison had been absorbed.

records.l: Texas, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RATTLESNAKE POISON.
records.s: Texas is described as a place where rattlesnakes are very common and people camping out are exposed to their bites. Croft conducted his observations there, at Hermanitas Ranch, far from chemical laboratories.

records.l: rattlesnake poison, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RATTLESNAKE POISON.
records.s: Rattlesnake poison was suggested to be an alkaloid-like substance. Poison taken from a fully charged rattlesnake gland produced a dense light-brown, apparently amorphous precipitate when iodine solution was added.

records.l: rattlesnake, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RATTLESNAKE POISON.
records.s: Croft killed a moderately sized rattlesnake identified as Crotalus horridus that had not bitten anything. Its poison gland was fully charged with white, opaque poison, and its bladder contained a considerable quantity of light-brown amorphous ammonium urate.

records.l: rattlesnake bites, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RATTLESNAKE POISON.
records.s: Croft says iodine in potassium iodide is a favored remedy for rattlesnake bites in Texas. He reports having observed the mixture's efficacy in two cases, one involving a buck and the other a dog.

records.l: iodine, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RATTLESNAKE POISON.
records.s: Iodine was proposed as a possible antidotal agent because it formed a precipitate with rattlesnake poison, as it does with many alkaloids. Croft observed a dense light-brown precipitate immediately after adding iodine solution to the poison.

records.l: potassium iodide, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RATTLESNAKE POISON.
records.s: A strong solution of iodine in potassium iodide is described as a popular Texas remedy for rattlesnake bites. Potassium iodide can also be combined with ferric chloride to make an extemporaneous solution for testing alkaloids and perhaps snake poison.

records.l: iodine solution, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RATTLESNAKE POISON.
records.s: Iodine solution was applied in reported cases of rattlesnake bites and was tested directly on rattlesnake poison. It immediately produced a dense light-brown precipitate with no crystalline structure visible under the microscope.

records.l: platinic chloride, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RATTLESNAKE POISON.
records.s: Platinic chloride was reported by Mr. Pedler to destroy or neutralize snake poison. Croft attributes this action probably to formation of an insoluble double platinic chloride, as occurs with almost all alkaloids.

records.l: alkaloids, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, RATTLESNAKE POISON.
records.s: The poisonous principle in snakes was described by a French chemist as possibly belonging to the alkaloids. Croft compared the reaction of rattlesnake poison with iodine to the precipitates produced by most alkaloids and mentions a ferric chloride and potassium iodide mixture as a convenient alkaloid test.

records.l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE CHINESE SIGN MANUAL.
records.s: The unit describes the use of finger and palm impressions as signatures in China, especially in courts, the army, and certain domestic transactions. Chinese courts require criminals to validate confessions with a thumb-print, while digital signatures are also used to prevent personation and repudiation. The text discusses observations by Henry Faulds and W. J. Herschel concerning skin-furrows, heredity, government registration, medical jurisprudence, and ethnology. It concludes that Chinese and European finger rugae differ, but their variation is too great for reliable ethnic or hereditary classification.

records.l: The Chinese Sign Manual, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE CHINESE SIGN MANUAL.
records.s: The Chinese Sign Manual concerns the use of finger, thumb, and palm impressions as signatures in China. It describes their application in courts, the army, and transactions involving the sale or divorce of persons.

records.l: Henry Faulds, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE CHINESE SIGN MANUAL.
records.s: Henry Faulds solicits information from China about skin-furrows on the hand. His observations on Japanese finger-tips are described as having an ethnic bearing and relating to heredity.

records.l: W. J. Herschel, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE CHINESE SIGN MANUAL.
records.s: W. J. Herschel solicits information about skin-furrows on the hand. After twenty years in charge of registration offices in India, he employed finger marks as sign manuals to prevent personation and repudiation.

records.l: China, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE CHINESE SIGN MANUAL.
records.s: China uses digital impressions as sign manuals in courts, the army, and certain domestic transactions. The text states that the practice may have become common after the Han period.

records.l: India, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE CHINESE SIGN MANUAL.
records.s: India is where W. J. Herschel employed finger marks in registration offices for twenty years to prevent personation and repudiation.

records.l: skin-furrows on the hand, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE CHINESE SIGN MANUAL.
records.s: Skin-furrows on the hand are the subject on which Henry Faulds and W. J. Herschel solicit information. The unit treats them as relevant to sign manuals, medical jurisprudence, and ethnology.

records.l: medical jurisprudence, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE CHINESE SIGN MANUAL.
records.s: Medical jurisprudence is identified as one field to which the study of skin-furrows may have a bearing. The unit particularly connects digital signatures with the legal validation of confessions.

records.l: ethnology, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE CHINESE SIGN MANUAL.
records.s: Ethnology is identified as another field potentially affected by the study of skin-furrows. The text concludes that finger rugae do not provide a reliable basis for distinguishing populations.

records.l: heredity, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE CHINESE SIGN MANUAL.
records.s: Heredity is connected with Henry Faulds's observations on the finger-tips of the Japanese. The unit concludes that finger striae are not a basis for studying heredity.

records.l: fingerprint identification, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE CHINESE SIGN MANUAL.
records.s: Fingerprint identification is represented by the use of finger, thumb, and palm impressions as sign manuals. The text considers such marks difficult to forge or repudiate because the finger rugae remain substantially unchanged from the cradle to the grave.

records.l: Chinese courts, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE CHINESE SIGN MANUAL.
records.s: Chinese courts require criminals to sign confessions by impressing the whorls of their thumb-tips. Women use the right thumb and men the left, and a confession is not legally valid without the prisoner's thumb-print.

records.l: the army, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE CHINESE SIGN MANUAL.
records.s: The army sometimes requires digital signatures to prevent personation. The general in command at Wenchow enforces the practice among his troops, and descriptions of persons note the relative numbers of volutes and coniferous finger-tips.

records.l: criminals, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE CHINESE SIGN MANUAL.
records.s: Criminals in Chinese courts must attest their confessions with thumb-prints before they can legally be executed. A contumacious culprit may be tortured until he performs this required act.

records.l: confession, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE CHINESE SIGN MANUAL.
records.s: A confession is required for the legal execution of a criminal in the Chinese courts. It must be attested by the prisoner's thumb-print to be valid.

records.l: personation and repudiation, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE CHINESE SIGN MANUAL.
records.s: Personation and repudiation are the acts that finger marks are used to prevent in Indian registration offices and in military applications. The text also describes digital signatures as difficult to forge or repudiate.

records.l: Chinese people, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE CHINESE SIGN MANUAL.
records.s: The Chinese people's finger rugae are said to differ from those of Europeans. However, the text finds too little uniformity among them for the rugae to serve as a basis for ethnic distinction or heredity.

records.l: Europeans, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE CHINESE SIGN MANUAL.
records.s: Europeans are used as a comparison group for Chinese finger rugae. The text states that Chinese and European rugae differ, but that the observed variation does not support reliable ethnic classification.

records.l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, LUCIDITY.
records.s: Matthew Arnold argued that lucidity was the great need of England and an indispensable condition for serious intellectual and spiritual construction. He contrasted the French national tendency toward lucidity with the English national tendency toward seriousness, while warning that both qualities could be accompanied by serious defects. He identified Voltaire as the chief agent of France's eighteenth-century movement toward lucidity and compared him with Luther. Arnold criticized the Salvation Army and the Oxford movement associated with Dr. Pusey for building on assumptions that lucidity would have exposed as no longer valid, and he endorsed schools and universities as the best means of cultivating lucidity.

records.l: Matthew Arnold, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, LUCIDITY.
records.s: Matthew Arnold said that the word he wished to leave in his audience's memories was lucidity. He identified lucidity as England's great want and argued that schools and universities could help cultivate it.

records.l: lucidity, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, LUCIDITY.
records.s: Lucidity is the perception that notions long current lack truth and validity, are no longer possible, and can no longer serve. Arnold presents it as inevitable and indispensable, and as the condition of all serious construction for the future.

records.l: France, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, LUCIDITY.
records.s: France is described as having a national turn for lucidity. Its eighteenth-century movement toward lucidity was associated particularly with Voltaire, although France's lucidity was accompanied by faults such as a want of seriousness and reverence.

records.l: England, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, LUCIDITY.
records.s: England is described as having a national turn for seriousness rather than lucidity. Its thinkers often drew back from free inquiry when it conflicted with established beliefs and conventions, and Arnold said that England had not yet founded the reign of lucidity.

records.l: French people, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, LUCIDITY.
records.s: The French people are described as having a national turn for lucidity. They are also said to display, alongside lucidity, a want of seriousness and reverence.

records.l: English people, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, LUCIDITY.
records.s: The English people are described as naturally serious and as possessing reverence, respect, and love for the past. Arnold suggested that lucidity, when it came among them, might be joined to these qualities without the dangers seen elsewhere.

records.l: seriousness, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, LUCIDITY.
records.s: Seriousness is presented as a valuable and indispensable quality of England, even though it may be accompanied by false ideas, prejudice, and other disagreeable defects. Arnold contrasts it with the French tendency toward lucidity.

records.l: Voltaire, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, LUCIDITY.
records.s: Voltaire is identified as the principal agent of France's eighteenth-century travail for lucidity. Although Arnold says that Voltaire harmed France through his lack of seriousness and reverence, he credits Voltaire's lucidity with doing good and compares him to the Luther of the eighteenth-century cultivated classes.

records.l: Luther, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, LUCIDITY.
records.s: Luther is admired for working for conduct, which Arnold says was more than working merely for intelligence. Like Voltaire, Luther opposed the object of his antipathy with conviction, energy, genius, and masterly power, carrying his world with him.

records.l: Salvation Army, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, LUCIDITY.
records.s: The Salvation Army is presented as a movement displaying numbers, funds, energy, devotedness, excitement, and conversions, but a total absence of lucidity. Arnold says that a little lucidity would make the movement impossible because it assumes a basis that is no longer possible or receivable.

records.l: Dr. Pusey, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, LUCIDITY.
records.s: Dr. Pusey is described as having recently ended a long, devoted, laborious, influential, pure, and pathetic life. The movement associated with his earlier name is said to have produced people worthy of respect, admiration, and love, but also to have rested on assumptions that lucidity would have exposed as unsound.

records.l: schools and universities, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, LUCIDITY.
records.s: Schools and universities are presented as the best agency for generating lucidity, especially through serious and disinterested studies connected with one another and continued into adult life. Arnold says that this process may be slow but is sure.

records.l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON SOME APPARATUS THAT PERMIT OF ENTERING FLAMES.
records.s: The unit describes apparatus and experiments designed to protect people entering flames, focusing on Humphry Davy's wire-gauze discovery and Chevalier Aldini's protective suit. Aldini's demonstrations included handling hot iron, walking over fires, breathing amid flames, and entering burning passages while shielded by metallic gauze and asbestos cloth. Hot-house and furnace experiments involving Joseph Banks, Charles Blagden, Dr. Solander, and others showed that people could withstand very high dry temperatures, partly because perspiration cools the body. The account also considers human respiration in flames and proposes that Egyptian mystery fire-walking may have used a concealed fire beneath a grate.

records.l: apparatus for entering flames, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON SOME APPARATUS THAT PERMIT OF ENTERING FLAMES.
records.s: The apparatus was designed to let a person enter flames without being burned. It consisted mainly of metallic-gauze armor, including a helmet, cuirass, skirt, boots, and a shield, combined with coarse alum-soaked clothing and asbestos coverings for the head, hands, and feet.

records.l: Humphry Davy, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON SOME APPARATUS THAT PERMIT OF ENTERING FLAMES.
records.s: Humphry Davy observed that very fine wire gauze cooled a flame so that it could not pass through the meshes. He attributed the effect to the metal's conductivity and radiating power and used it in constructing a miners' lamp.

records.l: Chevalier Aldini, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON SOME APPARATUS THAT PERMIT OF ENTERING FLAMES.
records.s: Chevalier Aldini applied Davy's wire-gauze discovery to an envelope intended to allow a person to enter flames. He traveled through Europe giving free demonstrations of the apparatus, including demonstrations before a committee of the Academic des Sciences in Paris.

records.l: metallic gauze, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON SOME APPARATUS THAT PERMIT OF ENTERING FLAMES.
records.s: Metallic gauze cooled flames enough to prevent them from traversing its meshes. In Aldini's apparatus it formed the protective armor, double-gauze boots, and a shield, and it was also used to cover a basket carrying a child.

records.l: asbestos cloth, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON SOME APPARATUS THAT PERMIT OF ENTERING FLAMES.
records.s: Asbestos cloth covered the wearer's head, hands, and feet beneath or within the metallic-gauze apparatus. A single layer was used for the bonnet and stockings, while double layers formed the gloves, and a child carried into flames wore an asbestos bonnet.

records.l: Aldini's demonstrations, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON SOME APPARATUS THAT PERMIT OF ENTERING FLAMES.
records.s: Aldini's demonstrations began with holding a finger wrapped in asbestos and double wire gauze in a candle or alcohol flame. Assistants also handled red-hot iron, carried firebrands over burning fagots, and entered intense flames while wearing the protective apparatus.

records.l: Paris, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON SOME APPARATUS THAT PERMIT OF ENTERING FLAMES.
records.s: In Paris, an exhibition was held before a committee from the Academic des Sciences. Two burning straw fences formed a passage through which six men wearing Aldini suits walked, while one carried an eight-year-old child in a wire-gauze-covered basket.

records.l: Aldini's six experimenters, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON SOME APPARATUS THAT PERMIT OF ENTERING FLAMES.
records.s: Six men wearing Aldini suits entered the passage between two blazing straw fences and walked slowly backward and forward while the fire was fed from outside. One of them carried an eight-year-old child who wore only an asbestos bonnet.

records.l: fire-walking demonstrations, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON SOME APPARATUS THAT PERMIT OF ENTERING FLAMES.
records.s: In some demonstrations, experimenters holding firebrands walked for five minutes over a large grating beneath which fagots were burning. Aldini's six experimenters also walked through a narrow passage between blazing fences, and one man later entered a clear fire whose flames rose eighteen feet while carrying a child.

records.l: hot-house experiments, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON SOME APPARATUS THAT PERMIT OF ENTERING FLAMES.
records.s: Joseph Banks, Charles Blagden, and Dr. Solander remained for ten minutes in a hot-house at 211 degrees Fahrenheit while their bodies stayed near normal temperature. Blagden later endured eight minutes in a hot-house reaching 262 degrees Fahrenheit, while eggs placed nearby were baked hard in twenty minutes.

records.l: human resistance to heat, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON SOME APPARATUS THAT PERMIT OF ENTERING FLAMES.
records.s: The unit attributes human resistance to high temperatures partly to reduced carbonic-acid exhalation and reduced internal combustion as external heat rises. It also emphasizes that dry, moving air is more tolerable than humid air because evaporation of perspiration cools the body, while contact with hot liquids or solids is especially dangerous.

records.l: human respiration in flames, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON SOME APPARATUS THAT PERMIT OF ENTERING FLAMES.
records.s: The experiments are presented as evidence that a person can breathe in the midst of flames. This ability is attributed not only to cooling as air passes through wire gauze but also to the human organs' considerable resistance to heat.

records.l: Egyptian mysteries, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, ON SOME APPARATUS THAT PERMIT OF ENTERING FLAMES.
records.s: The unit considers whether initiation rites connected with the Egyptian mysteries may have involved crossing a burning chamber over an incandescent grate. It suggests that the account in the Abbe Terrason's "Sethos" may be better explained by a fire in a ditch beneath a grate, which would prevent flames from reaching the person crossing it.

records.l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE BUILDING STONE SUPPLY.
records.s: The unit describes the development and distribution of the building stone supply in the United States, including granite, sandstone or freestone, limestone, marble, slate, and other stones. It explains that early settlers mainly used wood and imported brick and stone, but American quarrying expanded during the nineteenth century. Major quarrying centers and uses are identified, including construction, paving, monuments, lime production, roofing, and sidewalks. The account names notable buildings, quarries, and regions associated with these materials.

records.l: building stone supply, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE BUILDING STONE SUPPLY.
records.s: The building stone supply developed slowly in the United States because early settlers relied mainly on wood and imported brick and stone. The unit traces the growth of domestic quarrying and describes the principal American sources and uses of granite, freestone, limestone, marble, slate, and other stones.

records.l: stone, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE BUILDING STONE SUPPLY.
records.s: Stone was used only slightly as a building material in the early history of the country. Loose stone was readily gathered for foundations, while more substantial building stone was initially imported by Dutch and English settlers.

records.l: Boston, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE BUILDING STONE SUPPLY.
records.s: Boston used imported brick, tile, slate, and stone in its early buildings. King's Chapel in Boston was identified as the first recorded building constructed from American stone.

records.l: King's Chapel, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE BUILDING STONE SUPPLY.
records.s: King's Chapel in Boston was erected in 1752 and is recorded as the first building made from American stone. Its stone was granite brought from Braintree, Massachusetts.

records.l: granite, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE BUILDING STONE SUPPLY.
records.s: Granite is particularly abundant in New England and occurs in lesser quantities elsewhere in the country. It was used for major buildings, monuments, paving, and breakwaters, and could be quarried into blocks of almost any size and shape.

records.l: New England, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE BUILDING STONE SUPPLY.
records.s: New England contains especially abundant granite and also has sandstone, marble, and slate sources. Granite from the region became an important building material, while much of its marble was described as inferior to that of Vermont and Berkshire, Massachusetts.

records.l: Quincy granite, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE BUILDING STONE SUPPLY.
records.s: Quincy granite was used in the old Merchants' Exchange and Astor House in New York, the Custom House in New Orleans, and many other buildings along the Atlantic coast. It weighs about 165 pounds per cubic foot and was shipped to distant markets.

records.l: Quincy quarries, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE BUILDING STONE SUPPLY.
records.s: The Quincy quarries were the first granite quarries in the country to be extensively developed, with work beginning early in the nineteenth century. The first railroad in the country, a three-mile horse railroad built in 1827, was constructed from these quarries to the Neponset River.

records.l: Quincy, Mass., Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE BUILDING STONE SUPPLY.
records.s: Quincy, Massachusetts, became an important center of granite production early in the nineteenth century. Its granite was transported to distant markets, including New Orleans, and was used in numerous prominent buildings.

records.l: New York, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE BUILDING STONE SUPPLY.
records.s: New York used Quincy granite in the old Merchants' Exchange and Astor House, and its old City Hall and Custom House were among the early marble buildings. New York also obtained granite from Staten Island and sandstone from Portland and other quarrying regions.

records.l: freestone, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE BUILDING STONE SUPPLY.
records.s: Freestone, or sandstone, came into use earlier than granite, although its American use was still relatively late. It was used for buildings, paving, curbing, sidewalks, and furnace hearth-stones.

records.l: Portland quarries, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE BUILDING STONE SUPPLY.
records.s: The Portland quarries, opposite Middletown on the Connecticut River, were worked before the Revolution and shipped sandstone to many distant parts of the country. Their stone was also associated with the fossil bird footprints discovered there in 1802.

records.l: Portland stone, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE BUILDING STONE SUPPLY.
records.s: Portland stone supplied most of the brownstone fronts in New York City, although some buildings used thin layers of it over brick walls. It was widely distributed from the Portland quarries.

records.l: limestone, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE BUILDING STONE SUPPLY.
records.s: Limestone was used for building where granite or sandstone was not readily available, and hammer-dressed limestone could resemble granite. It was also widely used for roads and sidewalks and was burned into lime, although the quality of lime varied by region.

records.l: marble, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE BUILDING STONE SUPPLY.
records.s: Marble was abundant in the United States and appeared in many colors and varieties. It was used for statuary, gravestones, ornamental features, and increasingly for building exteriors, with important sources in Vermont and a belt extending through the eastern and southern states.

records.l: Girard College, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE BUILDING STONE SUPPLY.
records.s: Girard College was among the earliest marble buildings mentioned in the unit. Its pillars came from Berkshire, Massachusetts, which ranked next after Vermont in marble reputation.

records.l: Rutland, Vt., Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE BUILDING STONE SUPPLY.
records.s: Rutland, Vermont, was identified as the source of American marble fully as fine as famous Carrara marble. The surrounding belt yielded the largest variety and choicest specimens, including the only quality described as fit for statuary.

records.l: slate, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, THE BUILDING STONE SUPPLY.
records.s: Slate was used in colonial times for gravestones and to some extent for roofing and school purposes, though most supplies then came from Wales. American quarrying expanded during the nineteenth century, particularly in Pennsylvania, Maine, Vermont, New York, Maryland, and Michigan.

records.l: Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, AN INDUSTRIAL REVOLUTION.
records.s: The Census reports that the number of farms in the United States nearly doubled within twenty years, despite slower population growth. The increase resulted from the division of great estates, the creation of farms in newly settled regions, and growing markets supplied by cities and towns. Farm growth was substantial in older Northern States and especially rapid in several Southern States and the Northwest. The expansion of farm ownership and occupancy is described as an industrial revolution that may produce important political changes.

records.l: Industrial Revolution, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, AN INDUSTRIAL REVOLUTION.
records.s: The division and multiplication of farms in several Southern States, together with broader changes in agricultural organization, are described as an industrial revolution.

records.l: Census, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, AN INDUSTRIAL REVOLUTION.
records.s: The Census gives account of a near doubling in the number of farms within twenty years and provides state-level comparisons of farm growth.

records.l: farms, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, AN INDUSTRIAL REVOLUTION.
records.s: The number of farms has virtually doubled within twenty years. Growth occurred through the division of great estates, the creation of farms in newly settled regions, and increased demand from cities and towns.

records.l: farm owners or occupants, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, AN INDUSTRIAL REVOLUTION.
records.s: There were 205,000 more farm owners or managers in New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Indiana, and Illinois than a decade earlier. Farm owners or occupants are described as standing on a different footing from wage laborers.

records.l: great estates, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, AN INDUSTRIAL REVOLUTION.
records.s: The division of great estates contributed substantially to the increase in the number of farms.

records.l: population of the country, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, AN INDUSTRIAL REVOLUTION.
records.s: The population of the country did not increase in the same proportion as the number of farms.

records.l: United States, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, AN INDUSTRIAL REVOLUTION.
records.s: The country experienced a major increase in the number of farms, with especially rapid growth in newer western and several Southern regions.

records.l: cities and towns, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, AN INDUSTRIAL REVOLUTION.
records.s: The growth of cities and towns created markets for larger supplies of products that could be advantageously grown on moderate-sized farms.

records.l: agriculture, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, AN INDUSTRIAL REVOLUTION.
records.s: Agriculture changed through the multiplication and division of farms. Southern agriculture generally continued to favor large farms and the employment of many hands where land remained abundant.

records.l: division of estates, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, AN INDUSTRIAL REVOLUTION.
records.s: The division of estates was a major cause of the increase in farms, especially in several older Southern States.

records.l: Northern States, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, AN INDUSTRIAL REVOLUTION.
records.s: The number of farms increased even in the older Northern States, though less than in the far West and South. Growth became greater in Northern States farther west toward the Mississippi River.

records.l: Southern States, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, AN INDUSTRIAL REVOLUTION.
records.s: Several Southern States experienced very large increases in farms. In some regions the growth resulted mainly from new settlements, while in several older Southern States it reflected the division of estates.

records.l: New York, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, AN INDUSTRIAL REVOLUTION.
records.s: New York gained 25,000 farms, or 11.5 percent, since 1870.

records.l: New Jersey, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, AN INDUSTRIAL REVOLUTION.
records.s: New Jersey's number of farms increased 12.2 percent.

records.l: Pennsylvania, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, AN INDUSTRIAL REVOLUTION.
records.s: Pennsylvania's number of farms increased 22.7 percent.

records.l: Ohio, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, AN INDUSTRIAL REVOLUTION.
records.s: Ohio's number of farms increased 26.1 percent in ten years.

records.l: Indiana, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, AN INDUSTRIAL REVOLUTION.
records.s: Indiana's number of farms increased 20.3 percent in ten years.

records.l: Illinois, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, AN INDUSTRIAL REVOLUTION.
records.s: Illinois's number of farms increased 26.1 percent in ten years.

records.l: Michigan, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, AN INDUSTRIAL REVOLUTION.
records.s: Michigan experienced an increase of more than 55 percent in the number of farms, as new railroads opened regions to settlement.

records.l: Wisconsin, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882, AN INDUSTRIAL REVOLUTION.
records.s: Wisconsin had about the same increase in railroad mileage as Michigan but reported only a 28 percent increase in farms.
