Separate male and female plants bear catkins or flowers, then drupaceous fruit and seeds with embryos; germination produces fleshy cotyledons and leaves in threes.

records.l: Conifers, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
records.s: Conifers include the Maidenhair tree, which is closely allied to the Yew despite being destitute of resin. Their affinities with higher Cryptogams are illustrated by features such as the corpuscles in their seeds and the Maidenhair tree's peculiar venation.

records.l: Broadlands, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
records.s: contains Maidenhair tree [in the gardens; about 40 feet high] The illustrated Maidenhair tree is growing at Broadlands, Hants. It is about 40 feet high, has a trunk 7 feet in girth at 3 feet from the ground, and has branches spreading 45 feet.

records.l: The Woods of America collection, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
records.s: The Woods of America is a collection of American woods prepared by the American Museum of Natural History for exhibition. It contains 394 logs representing all but 26 varieties of trees indigenous to the United States, with accompanying foliage, fruits, flowers, commercial products, water-color drawings, scientific diagrams, and a herbarium. Prepared on the third floor of the Arsenal in Central Park, it is expected to be the country’s only complete collection of its kind, with no comparable royal-museum collection known in England, France, or Germany. It supports education, landscape gardening, and forest-tree conservation.

records.l: American Museum of Natural History, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
records.s: American Museum of Natural History, supervised by Prof. Bickmore, prepares The Woods of America collection in the Arsenal’s third floor, receiving United States specimens for scientific, educational, architectural, gardening, and forestry use.

records.l: Prof. Bickmore, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
records.s: Prof. Bickmore, superintendent of the American Museum of Natural History, promotes neglected American woods’ commercial value through exhibitions and directs a log-seasoning method that prevents splitting by boring beside the heart.

records.l: logs, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
records.s: The logs are six-foot specimens selected for quality, arriving green and protected at the museum. They are seasoned, diagrammed, and cut through the center to display bark, sapwood, heartwood, growth rings, and grain.

records.l: tree varieties represented in the collection, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
records.s: has_representatives_from United States [every State or Territory] THE WOODS OF AMERICA.] The collection represents all but 26 of the indigenous tree varieties of the United States, with the remaining specimens expected before winter. Notable specimens include persimmon, honey locust, yucca, Douglas spruce, nut pine, white ash, sycamore, and California redwood.

records.l: seasoning of wood, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
records.s: causes checking [when wood splits in radiating lines] THE WOODS OF AMERICA.] Seasoning is required to dry the green logs before exhibition, but it can cause checking or season cracking as the wood splits in radiating lines. The sapwood seasons more quickly than the heartwood, and the splitting can ruin a specimen, as happened to the persimmon log; boring a hole alongside the heart is being tried as a preventive measure.

records.l: Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The Child's Health Primer introduces primary-school pupils to physiology and hygiene, especially the effects of alcohol, other narcotics, and tobacco on the human body. This unit explains joints, bones, the spine, ribs, and care of the body, including posture and footwear. It teaches children that tobacco is harmful during growth, with special warnings about cigarettes and chewing tobacco. The unit concludes with review questions about the lessons.

records.l: Child's Health Primer For Primary Classes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The Child's Health Primer is a simple, practical introduction to physiology and hygiene for pupils in the ordinary third reader grade. It develops only the physiological facts needed to explain the effects of alcohol, tobacco, opium, and other truths of hygiene.

records.l: Primary Schools, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Primary Schools are identified as the schools for whose children this work was prepared. The book is intended to help teach pupils in these schools about health and the effects of alcoholics and other narcotics.

records.l: physiology and hygiene, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Physiology and hygiene are taught together in connection with facts about the human body and the preservation of health. The unit presents basic information about bones, joints, muscles, nerves, organs, food, strength, and the effects of harmful substances.

records.l: health, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Health is connected with the proper care of the body and with avoiding substances that weaken it. The unit advises upright posture, properly fitting shoes, and avoiding tobacco.

records.l: alcohol, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Alcohol is presented as a popular poison whose effects on the human body, life, and character pupils should learn about in time. The book includes chapters on what alcohol is, beer, distilling, and alcohol.

records.l: other narcotics, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Other narcotics are included among the substances whose effects on the human system pupils are to study. Opium is specifically listed as one of the subjects treated in the book.

records.l: tobacco, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Tobacco is described as harmful to men and especially harmful to boys while they are growing. It can stunt growth, hurt the mind, weaken the body, and prevent bones from growing as well as they otherwise would.

records.l: opium, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Opium is named as one of the substances whose effects are addressed by the book. The text lists a separate chapter on opium but gives no further details about it in this unit.

records.l: children, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Children's bones contain more gristle than the bones of older people, so they bend easily. Children are told to sit and stand erect, avoid twisting their limbs, and protect their growing bodies from tobacco.

records.l: boy, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: A boy who uses tobacco while growing is said to make every part of his body less strong than it otherwise would be. A boy who smokes cannot become as large and fine-looking a man as he would have become without smoking.

records.l: body, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The human body is described as having about two hundred bones joined together in useful ways. It is also said to be built during childhood and later repaired as it wears out.

records.l: joints, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Joints connect the bones and allow the body to bend and move. Hinge-joints occur in the elbows, knees, fingers, and toes, while ball-and-socket joints occur in the shoulders and hips; a soft fluid keeps them moist and moving easily.

records.l: bones, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Bones form the body's framework and include long bones, short bones, ribs, shoulder-blades, collar-bones, and the bones of the spine. They contain lime and gristle; children's bones have more gristle, while old people's bones contain more lime and therefore break more easily.

records.l: spine, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The spine is made of twenty-four small bones with elastic cushions of gristle between them. These cushions help absorb jolts, but leaning over work can press them out of shape and cause a person to become round-shouldered or hump-backed.

records.l: tobacco use by youth, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Tobacco use by youth is described as a great danger because the body and mind are still developing. A youth from seven to fourteen who begins to smoke or chew will not have as fine a body and mind at twenty-one as if tobacco had never been used.

records.l: cigarettes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Cigarettes are small but are described as very poisonous. The text warns that smoking them can harm growing boys and girls.

records.l: chewing tobacco, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Chewing tobacco is described as an even worse and more filthy habit than smoking. The frequent spitting it causes is disgusting to others and harms the chewer's health.

records.l: Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER II. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The unit explains that muscles move the joints by tightening and relaxing, much like stretched rubber straps move a door. Muscles are attached to bones by strong cords called tendons, and different body parts have stronger muscles according to the work they do. Exercise and active work strengthen muscles, while idleness weakens them. Alcohol can change part of the muscles into fat, reducing their strength, so drinking beer does not make a person stronger.

records.l: muscles, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER II. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Muscles move the joints by contracting and then returning to their original shape, and tendons fasten them to bones. Muscles become strong through use, while idleness weakens them. Alcohol may change part of the muscles to fat, taking away some of their strength.

records.l: joints, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER II. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Joints are moved by two or more muscles that work together, with one muscle shortening while another stretches. Muscles are fastened to the bones around the joints by tendons.

records.l: exercise, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER II. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Exercise and active work help muscles grow strong. Running, coasting, games of ball, and other brisk play and work strengthen muscles, while idle habits make them weak.

records.l: alcohol, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER II. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Alcohol often changes part of the muscles into fat and thereby reduces their strength. Beer contains alcohol, so drinking beer may make a person fleshy without making the person stronger.

records.l: Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER III. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The unit explains how the brain, spinal cord, nerves, and muscles communicate to control movement, breathing, feeling, and other body functions. It describes how nerves carry messages to the brain and how the brain sends orders back to muscles, including when a finger touches a hot stove. It teaches that the brain and nerves need sleep, rest, and good care. It warns that alcohol, liquor, and tobacco injure or deaden the brain and nerves and can make people careless, unhealthy, or poorer scholars.

records.l: brain, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER III. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The brain is the part of the body that thinks and is kept safe in a strong box made of bone. It receives messages from the nerves and sends orders to the muscles; one part also keeps breathing and other automatic work going. The thinking part needs quiet sleep and good care.

records.l: nerves, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER III. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Nerves are little white cords or threads connecting the brain with the rest of the body, with many branching from the spinal cord. They carry messages, allow the body to feel pain and pleasure, and become tired from doing one thing too long. Alcohol and tobacco injure or deaden them.

records.l: spinal cord, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER III. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The spinal cord is a large cord that lies safely in a bony case made by the spine. Many nerves branch off from it.

records.l: muscles, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER III. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Muscles move when the brain sends them messages. Some muscles move quietly and steadily without conscious thought, including the muscles that move the chest during breathing.

records.l: body, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER III. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The body is a busy workshop in which many kinds of work continue day and night. Its organs keep working during sleep, and it should be kept pure, strong, and in good order.

records.l: alcohol, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER III. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Alcohol is described as a poison rather than food that makes a person strong. It injures the brain and nerves, prevents messages from being sent properly, and can make people careless. Even a little can make the head ache and hurt the brain and nerves.

records.l: liquor, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER III. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Liquor can slowly poison the body when it is drunk frequently, even if the person is not a drunkard. People who drink liquor may be less able to bear sickness and less likely to get well.

records.l: tobacco, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER III. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Tobacco deadens or puts the nerves to sleep, so a person may fail to feel cold or tired without actually being helped. A boy who smokes or chews tobacco may not remember lessons as well and is usually not as polite or good as he otherwise would be.

records.l: messages, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER III. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Messages travel along separate nerve threads so they do not become mixed or confused. When a finger touches a hot stove, a message tells the brain that the finger will burn, and the brain sends a message to the muscles to contract, bend the joint, and pull the finger away.

records.l: Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, _] CHAPTER IV. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: This unit explains how fruit juices change when their sugar turns into alcohol and a gas. It describes how grapes are pressed into grape-juice, which can become wine, and how apple-juice can become cider. It teaches that alcohol is a poisonous liquid that can harm the body and mind and may lead a person to become a drunkard. It also warns that wine and cider are unsafe drinks because they contain alcohol.

records.l: alcohol, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, _] CHAPTER IV. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Alcohol is a thin liquid and a poison formed when the sugar in fruit-juice changes. It remains mixed with the water, harms the body and mind, and can make a person want more alcohol.

records.l: grape-juice, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, _] CHAPTER IV. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Grape-juice is squeezed from ripe grapes and left in a warm place. Its sugar changes into alcohol and a gas, so the juice is no longer suitable for making jelly and becomes wine.

records.l: sugar, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, _] CHAPTER IV. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Sugar is found in ripe fruit-juices. When grape-juice or apple-juice is left standing, its sugar changes into alcohol and bubbles of gas.

records.l: grapes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, _] CHAPTER IV. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Ripe grapes contain water, sugar, and a grape flavor. They may be squeezed to obtain their juice, which can change into wine.

records.l: wine, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, _] CHAPTER IV. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Wine is changed grape-juice containing water, alcohol, and grape flavor. It can also be made from currants, elderberries, and other fruits, and its alcohol may lead some drinkers to become drunkards.

records.l: cider, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, _] CHAPTER IV. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Cider is made from apples. Its sugar begins changing into alcohol and gas soon after the apple-juice is pressed out, and cider can make its drinkers ill-tempered and cross.

records.l: drunkards, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, _] CHAPTER IV. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: A drunkard is a person who continues taking more and more drinks that contain alcohol. Wine has made many drunkards.

records.l: alcoholic fermentation of fruit juice, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, _] CHAPTER IV. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Alcoholic fermentation of fruit juice occurs when the sugar in grape-juice or apple-juice changes into alcohol and bubbles of gas. The alcohol remains in the juice while the gas rises and goes into the air.

records.l: Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, notes
records.s: The unit is a footnote about a gas. It states that this gas is called car bon'ic acid gas. No other information is provided.

records.l: car bon'ic acid gas, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, notes
records.s: Car bon'ic acid gas is identified as the name of the gas mentioned in the footnote.

records.l: Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, ] CHAPTER V. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The unit explains how the brewer makes beer from barley by sprouting the grain so its starch changes into sugar, then adding water and yeast. The yeast helps change the sugar into gas and alcohol, and hops may give the beer a bitter taste. It teaches that barley could be good food, but beer contains alcohol, which is described as a poison. Two boys are compared: one drinks alcoholic beverages and the other abstains, and the abstaining boy is presented as more likely to succeed and be trusted.

records.l: beer, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, ] CHAPTER V. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Beer is made from barley after its starch has been changed into sugar and yeast has helped change the sugar into gas and alcohol. Hops may be added to give beer a bitter taste, but beer is not good food because it contains alcohol.

records.l: alcohol, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, ] CHAPTER V. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Alcohol is produced when yeast helps change sugar into gas and alcohol. The unit calls alcohol a poison and says that people should not drink beer because it contains alcohol.

records.l: grains, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, ] CHAPTER V. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Grain contains starch instead of sugar. When grain is kept moist and warm and begins to sprout, its starch starts to turn into sugar.

records.l: starch, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, ] CHAPTER V. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Starch is found in all kinds of grain. During sprouting, starch changes into sugar, and the brewer uses this change to make beer from barley.

records.l: sugar, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, ] CHAPTER V. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Sugar is formed from the starch in grain when the grain begins to sprout. The brewer preserves the sugar and adds yeast to help change it into gas and alcohol.

records.l: sprouting grain, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, ] CHAPTER V. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Sprouting grain is kept warm and moist so that its starch can turn into sugar. The brewer stops the sprouting before the sugar is used to feed the growing root and stem.

records.l: barley, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, ] CHAPTER V. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Barley is a kind of grain used by the brewer to make beer. It can also be ground into barley-cakes or pearl barley, which would be good food.

records.l: brewer, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, ] CHAPTER V. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The brewer sprouts barley in a warm, moist place and stops the process at the right time to save the sugar. He soaks the malt in water, adds yeast, sometimes adds hops, and watches for bubbles showing that sugar is going and alcohol is coming.

records.l: malt, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, ] CHAPTER V. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Malt is sprouted grain. The brewer soaks malt in water and adds yeast to begin the work of changing its sugar into gas and alcohol.

records.l: boy who drinks alcoholic beverages, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, ] CHAPTER V. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The boy who drinks wine, cider, and beer poisons his body and mind with alcohol. He becomes different from the boy who abstains and is presented as less likely to be selected for good work or trusted with an engine or a bank.

records.l: boy who abstains from alcoholic beverages, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, ] CHAPTER V. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The boy who abstains from alcoholic beverages never allows wine, cider, or beer to pass his lips. He does not poison his body and mind with alcohol and is presented as more likely to have a good chance in life.

records.l: alcohol poisoning, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, ] CHAPTER V. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Alcohol poisoning is described as poisoning the body and mind with alcohol. The boy who drinks wine, cider, and beer is said to suffer this poisoning, while the boy who abstains does not.

records.l: alcoholic fermentation of fruit juice, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, ] CHAPTER V. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The unit describes yeast helping to change sugar into gas and alcohol. The brewer knows the work is progressing by watching for bubbles of gas, which show that sugar is going and alcohol is coming.

records.l: Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, notes
records.s: This unit consists of Footnote B. The footnote names carbonic acid gas. No further information is provided.

records.l: car bon'ic acid gas, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, notes
records.s: Carbonic acid gas is named in Footnote B. No further information about it is provided in this unit.

records.l: Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, ] CHAPTER VI. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The unit explains distilling by showing how boiling water becomes steam and then returns to water when cooled. It teaches that alcohol turns to vapor more easily than water turns to steam, so alcohol can be collected first from liquids containing it, though repeated distillation is needed to make it pure. Brandy, rum, whiskey, and gin are distilled from wine, cider, and liquors made from corn, rye, or barley. The unit warns that distilled liquor contains much alcohol, while people who drink large amounts of weaker beverages may also become drunkards.

records.l: distilling, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, ] CHAPTER VI. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Distilling is the process of turning a liquid into vapor by boiling it and then turning the vapor back into liquid. Water can be distilled, and liquids containing alcohol can be distilled to make the alcohol stronger.

records.l: water, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, ] CHAPTER VI. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: When water boils, it turns into steam. When steam touches a cold plate or tin cover, it turns back into drops of water.

records.l: steam, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, ] CHAPTER VI. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Steam is water turned into vapor by boiling. It changes back into drops of water when it touches something cold.

records.l: vapor, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, ] CHAPTER VI. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Vapor is the term used instead of steam when discussing the boiling of alcohol. Alcohol vapor is collected first because alcohol requires less heat to vaporize than water requires to turn into steam.

records.l: alcohol, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, ] CHAPTER VI. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Alcohol turns to vapor with less heat than water turns to steam. It is collected first from liquids containing it, but it is mixed with water and must be distilled many times to become pure. Each distillation makes it stronger by increasing the proportion of alcohol.

records.l: liquor, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, ] CHAPTER VI. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Liquor can contain alcohol and can be made from corn, rye, or barley. Distilled liquor is nearly one-half alcohol, and a glass of strong liquor can injure a person more quickly than a glass of weaker liquor.

records.l: wine, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, ] CHAPTER VI. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Wine contains relatively little alcohol compared with distilled liquor. Brandy and other distilled liquors can be made from wine, and a person who drinks large amounts of wine may become a drunkard.

records.l: cider, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, ] CHAPTER VI. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Cider contains relatively little alcohol compared with distilled liquor. Distilled liquor can be made from cider, but drinking large amounts of cider can provide a great deal of alcohol and may lead to drunkenness.

records.l: beer, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, ] CHAPTER VI. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Beer contains relatively little alcohol compared with distilled liquor. A beer-drinker may consume a great deal of alcohol by drinking much more of the weaker beverage and may become a drunkard.

records.l: Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER VII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The unit explains that alcohol looks like water but burns with a blue, smokeless flame that gives much heat. Alcohol preserves dead bodies, as shown by a tree-toad that remains unchanged after years in a bottle of alcohol. Beer, wine, and cider contain a little alcohol, while brandy, rum, whiskey, and gin are nearly one half alcohol. Alcohol can create a growing desire for alcoholic drinks, leading some drinkers to become drunkards.

records.l: alcohol, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER VII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Alcohol looks like water but burns when a lighted match is held near it. Its blue flame gives much heat but little light and makes no smoke or soot. Alcohol preserves dead bodies from decaying and is contained in various drinks.

records.l: water, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER VII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Water looks like alcohol but will not burn. A dead tree-toad would have soon decayed if it had been put into water.

records.l: tree-toad (in the bottle of alcohol), Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER VII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The tree-toad was put into a bottle of alcohol years ago and is still there looking as it did on the first day. The alcohol has kept it from decaying.

records.l: beer, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER VII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Beer contains a little alcohol.

records.l: wine, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER VII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Wine contains a little alcohol. Wine-jelly and wine-sauce can teach a person to like the taste of alcohol.

records.l: cider, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER VII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Cider contains a little alcohol. Drinking cider can be a step toward drinking stronger liquors.

records.l: brandy, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER VII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Brandy is nearly one half alcohol. Drinking brandy is presented as a possible later stage after drinking weaker alcoholic drinks.

records.l: rum, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER VII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Rum is nearly one half alcohol. Drinking rum is presented as a possible later stage after drinking weaker alcoholic drinks.

records.l: whiskey, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER VII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Whiskey is nearly one half alcohol. Drinking whiskey is presented as a possible later stage after drinking weaker alcoholic drinks.

records.l: alcoholic drinks, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER VII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Alcoholic drinks can become more desirable to a person as the person drinks more. People who habitually take them may care more for them than for anything else, even while knowing that the drinks are ruining them.

records.l: drinker, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER VII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: A drinker may be deceived into thinking that taking more alcohol will be good for him. The more he takes, the more he often wants, and he may progress from cider, wine, or beer to whiskey, brandy, or rum.

records.l: appetite for alcohol, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER VII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: An appetite for alcohol may sometimes be formed in childhood. It can strongly beg for the poison, especially after a person learns to like the taste of alcohol.

records.l: drunkards, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER VII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Drunkards are made when people progress from drinking cider, wine, or beer to drinking whiskey, brandy, or rum.

records.l: Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER VIII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: A farmer replaced corn, wheat, and potatoes with tobacco, whose leaves were dried, pressed into cakes, rolled into cigars, or ground into snuff. Tobacco contains nicotine, a strong poison, and working with it can make people pale and sickly. Boys often become sick when they first try smoking, but may continue until they get used to it. Smoking does not usually kill a man immediately because he does not swallow all the nicotine, but taking small amounts of poison repeatedly is unsafe and not truly helpful.

records.l: farmer, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER VIII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The farmer changed his crops from corn, wheat, and potatoes to tobacco. He dried the tobacco leaves and had them made into cakes, cigars, and snuff.

records.l: tobacco, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER VIII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Tobacco grows tall and produces broad, green leaves. Its leaves can be pressed into cakes, rolled into cigars, or ground into snuff, and working with it can make people pale and sickly.

records.l: nicotine, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER VIII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Nicotine is a strong poison found in tobacco. One drop is enough to kill a dog, and the amount in one cigar could kill two men if taken pure.

records.l: poison, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER VIII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The text describes nicotine as a poison. A person may take in small amounts of it through smoking, but repeated exposure is not safe or truly helpful.

records.l: boy, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER VIII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Boys who first try smoking are almost always made sick. They may continue because they think smoking is manly, eventually becoming used to it.

records.l: snuff mill, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER VIII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The snuff mill stood beside a stream in a pleasant place with trees, fresh air, and open windows. Despite its surroundings, the tobacco smell was so strong that a visitor repeatedly went outside for pure air, and the worker said the smell had made him sick at first.

records.l: smoking and tobacco use, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER VIII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Smoking and other tobacco use expose people to nicotine. Smoking a cigar does not usually kill a man immediately because he does not swallow the nicotine, but tobacco use provides no real help and can be unsafe.

records.l: first-use sickness, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER VIII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: First-use sickness is the body's warning that tobacco is dangerous and poisonous. It tries to stop a boy before greater harm is done, but the sickness may disappear as the body becomes used to the tobacco.

records.l: taking nicotine or poison repeatedly, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER VIII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Taking small amounts of nicotine or poison day after day cannot be considered safe. The text says that repeated exposure is not really helpful to anyone.

records.l: Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER IX. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The unit explains that narcotics are substances that can put the nerves to sleep, naming alcohol, tobacco, and opium. It says that opium is a poison made from poppy juice and used in medicines. Soothing-syrup containing opium may quiet babies by injuring their tender nerves and poisoning their bodies. Children are warned never to give soothing-syrup to babies instead of caring for them patiently.

records.l: narcotics, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER IX. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: A narcotic is a substance that has the power to put the nerves to sleep. Alcohol, tobacco, and opium are called narcotics.

records.l: opium, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER IX. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Opium is a narcotic poison made from the juice of poppies. It is used in medicines and may be put into soothing-syrups.

records.l: soothing-syrup, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER IX. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Soothing-syrup may be given to babies to keep them from crying, but it does so by injuring their tender nerves and poisoning their little bodies. It is described as a dangerous enemy rather than a true comfort.

records.l: baby, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER IX. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: A baby may be given soothing-syrup to quiet it, but the opium in the syrup can injure its tender nerves and poison its body. The text says that babies should receive patient and kind care instead.

records.l: Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER X. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: This unit explains that organs are body parts with special work, focusing especially on the teeth, stomach, and organs in the chest and abdomen. It describes how the teeth cut and grind food, while the stomach and gastric juice change food into a fluid that can nourish every part of the body. It also gives instructions for caring for the teeth and stomach and explains how alcohol and tobacco harm digestion, the mouth, and other people. Doctors learned about the stomach by observing food placed into a soldier's stomach through an opening left by a wound.

records.l: organs, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER X. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: An organ is a part of the body that has some special work to do. The eye is the organ of sight, and the stomach takes care of the food people eat.

records.l: stomach, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER X. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The stomach is a strong bag with muscular walls and a lining that prepares gastric juice. Its muscles squeeze, roll, and mix food until it becomes a thin, grayish fluid. The stomach needs rest and warmth to work well, and alcohol can injure it, cause sores, and sometimes lead to death.

records.l: tooth, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER X. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The front teeth cut food, and the back teeth grind it. They should be protected from cracking nuts or biting thread, cleaned carefully, and brushed before breakfast and at night.

records.l: enamel, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER X. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Enamel is a hard, smooth covering over the bone of a tooth. If it is broken, the tooth soon decays and aches, and a dentist cannot cover it with new enamel.

records.l: chest, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER X. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The chest is the upper room of the bony case formed by the spine, ribs, shoulder-blades, and collar-bones. It contains the heart and lungs.

records.l: abdomen, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER X. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The abdomen is the lower room of the bony case. It contains the stomach, liver, and some other organs.

records.l: heart, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER X. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The heart is one of the useful organs located in the chest.

records.l: lungs, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER X. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The lungs are useful organs located in the chest.

records.l: gastric juice, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER X. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Gastric juice is prepared by the lining of the stomach and is kept ready for use. It mixes with food and helps change it into a thin, grayish fluid. Alcohol injures the gastric juice so that it cannot mix properly with food.

records.l: food, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER X. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Food is cut and ground by the teeth, then mixed with gastric juice and changed in the stomach. Afterward, it is sent through the body to feed the bones, muscles, nerves, brain, skin, finger nails, hair, and eyes. Children need food to grow, while grown people need it to mend parts that wear out.

records.l: gastric digestion, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER X. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Gastric digestion changes eaten food into a form that can be carried through the body and used to feed its parts. It depends on the teeth doing their work, the stomach being warm and rested, and the gastric juice mixing with the food.

records.l: body, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER X. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The body receives prepared food for its bones, muscles, nerves, brain, skin, finger nails, hair, and eyes. Every part needs food to grow or to be mended when it wears out.

records.l: children, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER X. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Children need food each day to make larger bones, muscles, and skin as their bodies grow. They are advised to let the stomach rest instead of eating constantly.

records.l: alcohol, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER X. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Alcohol in wine, cider, brandy, and other drinks is carried away quickly but harms the stomach while it remains there. It injures the gastric juice, may cause sores in the stomach when used repeatedly, and can sometimes cause the drinker to die.

records.l: tobacco, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER X. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Tobacco makes the mouth dry, causes extra saliva to flow, discolors the teeth, makes bad sores in the mouth, and often causes throat disease. Tobacco smoke and its strong smell can make the air unpleasant and unfit to breathe.

records.l: saliva, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER X. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Saliva helps prepare food in the mouth before it enters the stomach. Tobacco mixes with saliva, and when the tobacco juice is spit out, saliva needed for preparing food is also lost.

records.l: mouth, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER X. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The mouth contains saliva that helps prepare food before it reaches the stomach. Tobacco can make the mouth dry, discolor the teeth, and cause bad sores.

records.l: Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, notes
records.s: The unit concerns food and the organs involved in preparing it. It states that the liver partly prepares food. Some other organs also help prepare the food.

records.l: food, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, notes
records.s: Food is partly prepared by the liver and some other organs.

records.l: liver, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, notes
records.s: The liver partly prepares food.

records.l: Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, ] CHAPTER XI. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The chapter explains what the body needs from food to grow, remain strong, and stay well. It describes the importance of pure water, lime for bones, and salt in the diet. It identifies flesh-making foods for muscles and fat-making foods for warmth and comfort. It also explains how sugar and starch make fat and warns that candy may contain harmful substances and cannot provide complete nourishment.

records.l: body, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, ] CHAPTER XI. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The body is made partly of water and needs pure water, food for its bones and muscles, salt, and fat for warmth and comfort. It receives water from drinks and from foods such as fruits, vegetables, beefsteak, and bread.

records.l: food, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, ] CHAPTER XI. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Food supplies the body with water, lime, salt, flesh-making substances, and fat-making substances. Much of it comes from the earth through grains, grass, vegetables, and the animals that eat them.

records.l: water, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, ] CHAPTER XI. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Water is needed for the body and is used in preparing food. It may come from clouds, cisterns, springs, or wells, but water standing in lead pipes or coming from a well near a drain or stable may make people sick.

records.l: lime, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, ] CHAPTER XI. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Lime is needed by the bones. Grass and grains take lime from the earth, and people get it from milk, bread, oat-meal porridge, and other foods.

records.l: milk, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, ] CHAPTER XI. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Milk supplies lime for the bones and also helps make muscle and fat. The text calls milk the best kind of food because it provides muscle, fat, and bones with what they need.

records.l: salt, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, ] CHAPTER XI. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: People and animals need salt mixed with their food. Cows, sheep, wild cattle, and buffaloes seek salt, and people get a little salt even when they do not add it to food.

records.l: flesh-making foods, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, ] CHAPTER XI. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Flesh-making foods are needed by the muscles. They include milk, wheat, corn, oats, meat, and eggs.

records.l: fat-making foods, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, ] CHAPTER XI. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Fat-making foods provide the fat needed to keep the body warm and comfortable. They include sugar, starch, cream, rice, butter, and fat meat.

records.l: fat, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, ] CHAPTER XI. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Fat forms cushions and wrappings in parts of the body and helps keep it warm and comfortable. Fat from alcohol is described as badly made and in the wrong place, while good fat comes from suitable foods.

records.l: sugar, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, ] CHAPTER XI. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Sugar is a fat-making food, but a person would starve if fed only on sugar. The starch in unripe fruit and other foods must change into sugar before it can mix with the blood and help feed the body.

records.l: candy, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, ] CHAPTER XI. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Candy may provide more sugar than is good for children, and it is sometimes poisonous. Pure sugar candy dissolves completely in water, while candy containing white earth leaves it at the bottom because candy-makers may use the cheaper substance in place of sugar.

records.l: Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The unit explains how dinner is prepared, chewed, swallowed, digested, and carried through the body. Cooking makes meat, vegetables, and bread easier for the mouth and stomach to work on, while ripe fruit does not need fire-cooking. Saliva changes starch into sugar, and the stomach mixes the food with gastric juice before it enters the intestines and blood. The blood carries nourishment throughout the body to make and mend bones, muscles, skin, hair, eyes, and brain.

records.l: dinner, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Dinner may include roast beef, potatoes, tomatoes, squash, bread, butter, salt, water, peaches, bananas, oranges, and grapes. After digestion, it can help make and mend the different parts of the body.

records.l: food, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Food is cooked, chewed, swallowed, worked over in the stomach, and prepared for passage into the blood. The blood carries its nourishment to every part of the body.

records.l: cooking, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Cooking prepares meat, vegetables, and bread to be easily worked upon by the mouth and stomach. Food that is well cooked is said to be worth twice as much as food that is poorly cooked.

records.l: saliva, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Saliva moistens and mixes food in the mouth. It changes starch into sugar, which must happen before the food can be taken into the blood.

records.l: starch, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Starch in food needs to be changed into sugar before it can be taken into the blood. Saliva changes starch into sugar during chewing.

records.l: sugar, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Sugar is produced when saliva changes starch in food. A piece of dry cracker tastes sweet after it has been chewed because its starch is being changed into sugar.

records.l: chewing, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Chewing allows saliva to mix with food and change its starch into sugar. Food should be chewed slowly and well; otherwise, the stomach has extra work.

records.l: swallowing, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Swallowing sends food safely into the passage leading to the stomach when the trap-door at the top of the windpipe shuts. Speaking while food is in the mouth may allow food to enter the windpipe and cause choking.

records.l: stomach, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The stomach works swallowed food over and mixes it with gastric juice until it becomes a gray fluid. It then sends the prepared food toward the intestines; hurriedly swallowed food may give the stomach extra work and cause aching.

records.l: blood, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The blood takes prepared food from the intestines and carries it to the heart. The heart pumps it with the blood through the lungs and throughout the body, where it provides material for making and mending body parts.

records.l: body, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The body receives food through the blood to make bone, muscle, skin, hair, eyes, and brain. Food can also help mend broken parts, such as a broken bone.

records.l: digestion and nutrition, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The unit describes digestion and nutrition as the preparation of food by cooking, chewing, saliva, the stomach, and the intestines, followed by its transport in the blood. This process supplies the body with material to make and repair its parts.

records.l: Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XIII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The chapter explains that people should eat good, simple food, exercise in the open air, and breathe pure air to grow and keep strong. It teaches that alcohol, including beer and cider containing alcohol, does not give real strength and may make people feel strong only temporarily. A captain found that sailors worked better and felt stronger without rum when they were given plentiful food and hot coffee. The chapter concludes that strength of mind is the best kind of strength and that alcohol and tobacco weaken clear thinking.

records.l: strength, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XIII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Strength is gained by eating good, simple food, exercising in the open air, and taking pure air into the lungs. Alcohol does not give real strength, and the feeling of strength it produces lasts only a little while.

records.l: food, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XIII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Food supplies the blood with materials to carry to every part of the body. Meat, milk, eggs, wheat, corn, and oats are named as foods for muscles, while sugar, starch, fat, cream, and oil are named for fat and heat.

records.l: alcohol, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XIII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Alcohol cannot make good muscles, bone, nerve, or brain, so it cannot give real strength. It puts the nerves to sleep, may make people imagine they can do more than they really can, and later leaves them feeling weaker.

records.l: rum, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XIII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Rum is distilled from molasses and contains about one half alcohol. Sailors were once given rum every day and were given twice as much during great storms, but a captain found that it did not make them stronger.

records.l: body, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XIII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The body grows strong through open-air exercise, pure air, and good, simple food. A strong, healthy body with well-trained hands is described as a valuable possession.

records.l: mind, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XIII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The mind, or brain strength, is described as the very best kind of strength. Alcohol makes the head ache and deadens the nerves, preventing the brain from thinking well.

records.l: muscles, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XIII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Muscles grow through plenty of exercise and are supported by food carried to them by the blood. Alcohol cannot make good muscles.

records.l: people, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XIII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: People used to think that alcohol made them strong. Some people also say that beer gives strength, but the chapter explains that the food part of the grain has mostly been turned into alcohol.

records.l: captain, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XIII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: A captain watched sailors drinking rum and saw that they became no stronger and later felt weaker. He then took a ship to sea without rum, provided plentiful food, and gave the sailors hot coffee during storms.

records.l: sailors, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XIII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Sailors were once given rum every day and extra rum during great storms. After crossing the ocean without rum but with good food and hot coffee, they said they had worked better and felt stronger.

records.l: ship, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XIII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Ships were once expected to carry a great deal of rum for sailors. One captain took a ship to sea without rum and found that the sailors worked better and felt stronger.

records.l: exercise, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XIII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Exercise in the open air helps make the muscles grow and contributes to gaining strength. Pure air taken into the lungs also helps purify the blood.

records.l: alcohol and strength, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XIII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Alcohol and strength are presented as opposites: alcohol cannot build muscles, bone, nerve, or brain and therefore cannot give real strength. It may only create a temporary false feeling of strength by dulling the nerves.

records.l: strength of body, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XIII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Strength of body can be measured by pulling a weight over a pulley and marking how high it is raised. It can be gained through exercise in the open air, pure air, and good, simple food.

records.l: Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XIV. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The unit explains that the heart is a strong muscular organ in the chest that pumps blood through arteries and veins. The blood carries food from the stomach to every part of the body and must be especially pure for the brain. Exercise in fresh air strengthens the heart and warms the body, while alcohol can poison the blood, affect the brain, and harm the heart. The review questions concern the heart, blood circulation, exercise, food, alcohol, and related organs and tissues.

records.l: heart, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XIV. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The heart is in the chest and is made of very thick, strong muscle. It pumps blood through arteries and receives it back through veins. Exercise helps it work well, while alcohol can make it beat too fast, tire it, and become fatty.

records.l: muscles, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XIV. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Muscle makes up the heart and enables it to pump blood. Alcohol can harm muscles, and a fatty heart cannot work as well as a muscular heart.

records.l: blood, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XIV. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Blood carries food from the stomach to every part of the body and leaves each part what it needs. It must be good and pure for the brain, but alcohol or tobacco can poison it.

records.l: artery, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XIV. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Arteries are tubes through which the heart pumps blood. They have thousands of little branches that extend throughout the body.

records.l: veins, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XIV. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Veins are tubes that bring blood back to the heart. Some of the smaller veins can be seen in the wrist.

records.l: body, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XIV. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The body receives food carried by the blood to every part. Exercise in fresh air warms the body better than a fire could do.

records.l: pulse, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XIV. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The pulse is the steady beating felt when a finger presses on an artery in the wrist. It tells how fast the heart is pumping and the blood is flowing, and a doctor feels it when someone is sick.

records.l: food, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XIV. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The stomach prepares food, after which the blood takes it up and carries it throughout the body. Good food helps make good blood.

records.l: brain, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XIV. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The brain needs a great deal of very pure, good blood to remain strong. Alcohol in the blood goes partly to the brain, affects the nerves, and can make a man lose control over his actions.

records.l: alcohol, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XIV. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Alcohol can poison the blood and affect the brain and nerves. It can also make the heart beat too fast, tire it, and cause it to become fatty.

records.l: exercise, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XIV. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Good exercise in the fresh air makes the heart work well and warms the body better than a fire could do. During running, the heart beats faster and gets an instant of rest between beats.

records.l: Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XV. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: This chapter explains how the lungs help purify the blood by taking in fresh air and sending out impure air. It describes the need for the lungs to have room to expand and for people to keep rooms well ventilated. It teaches that breathing through the nose helps keep dust and impurities from reaching the lungs. It also asks readers to apply what they have learned about alcohol’s effects on muscles and nerves to the lungs.

records.l: lungs, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XV. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The lungs are beside the heart in the chest and help change impure, bluish blood into pure, red blood. Their air-cells expand to take in air and contract to send it out. They need fresh air and plenty of room, and they work steadily by night and day.

records.l: blood, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XV. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The blood carries food throughout the body and gathers worn-out matter. After collecting impurities, it becomes dull and bluish in the veins. The lungs prepare it to return to the heart pure and red.

records.l: heart, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XV. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The heart receives blood that has been purified by the lungs and pumps it through the body. The heart is near the lungs.

records.l: body, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XV. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The body depends on pure blood to remain well and strong. When the lungs cannot take in enough air to purify the blood, the whole body suffers and life may be shortened.

records.l: fresh air, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XV. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Fresh air enables the lungs to do their work, while the waste matter breathed out by the lungs poisons the air. Close rooms can make a person dull and sleepy or cause a headache, while fresh air can make the person feel better.

records.l: alcohol, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XV. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The chapter asks whether alcohol helps the lungs and directs the reader to apply what has already been learned about alcohol’s effects on muscles and nerves. The review asks why alcohol is not good for the lungs.

records.l: breathing, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XV. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Breathing continues by night and day, with a short pause between breaths that gives the lungs rest. It is better to breathe through the nose than through the mouth because hairs inside the nose catch dust and other impurities.

records.l: Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVI. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The chapter explains how the skin of the body removes waste matter through perspiration tubes and pores. It describes the care needed to keep the skin, clothing, and bed-clothes clean and well aired. It also reviews the work of the stomach, blood, heart, lungs, and skin in keeping the body healthy. These processes continue day and night without conscious thought because nerves send messages to the muscles.

records.l: body, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVI. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The body is covered with skin and lined with a more delicate kind of skin. It is kept healthy as the stomach, blood, heart, lungs, and skin perform their work of preparing food, carrying materials, using fresh air, and removing waste matter.

records.l: skin, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVI. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The skin covers the body, contains many nerves, and carries away waste matter and water through tiny perspiration tubes. It should be washed with soap and water so its pores do not become clogged and it can remain fresh and healthy.

records.l: worn-out matter, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVI. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Waste matter is carried away from the body through the skin, as well as in other ways. It passes through the perspiration tubes and should be washed off the skin because it can clog the pores.

records.l: perspiration, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVI. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Perspiration consists of little drops of water that come through tiny holes in the skin called pores. It carries waste matter and water out of the body and is produced continually in both winter and summer.

records.l: stomach, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVI. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The stomach prepares food for the blood to take.

records.l: blood, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVI. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The blood is pumped out of the heart to carry food to every part of the body and to take away worn-out matter. The lungs use fresh air to make the dark, impure blood bright and pure again.

records.l: heart, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVI. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The heart pumps the blood out so that it can carry food throughout the body and take away worn-out matter.

records.l: lungs, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVI. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The lungs use fresh air in making the dark, impure blood bright and pure again.

records.l: work of the body, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVI. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The work of the body includes the stomach preparing food, the blood carrying food and removing worn-out matter, the lungs using fresh air to purify the blood, and the skin carrying away waste matter. This work continues day and night without conscious thought because nerves send messages to the muscles.

records.l: Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The unit explains the five senses, with special attention to sight and hearing. It describes how the eyes, pupils, nerves of sight, ears, and nerve of hearing work, and teaches care of the eyes and ears. Stories about boys who looked at the sun, a boy who made himself cross-eyed, and the boy's father illustrate the dangers of injuring these organs. It also explains that alcohol can weaken the work of all the senses.

records.l: the five senses, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The five senses are sight, touch, taste, smell, and hearing. They are ways of learning about things around a person.

records.l: sight, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Sight is one of the five senses and depends on the eyes and the nerve of sight. Its delicate nerves can be harmed by too much or too little light.

records.l: hearing, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Hearing is one of the five senses and depends on the ears and the nerve of hearing. It can be harmed by putting hard or sharp objects into the ears.

records.l: the eyes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The eyes take pictures of things and send accounts of what is seen to the brain. They need protection from very bright light, insufficient light, and careless actions.

records.l: the pupil, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The pupil is a round, black opening in the middle of the eye, with a muscle around it. The muscle makes it smaller in bright light and larger in darkness.

records.l: the nerve of sight, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The nerve of sight is in a little, round room behind the pupil and carries accounts of what is seen to the brain. It is delicate and can be seriously harmed by bright light or trying to see in the dark.

records.l: the light, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The light should be sufficient for reading and studying but should not be faced directly when it is very bright. While writing, it should come from the left side so that the hand's shadow does not fall on the work.

records.l: the ears, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The visible ears are pieces of gristle curved to catch sounds and pass them to the true ears deeper in the head. They should be washed with a soft towel and should not have hard or sharp objects put into them.

records.l: the nerve of hearing, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The nerve of hearing is deeper in the head and sends an account of each sound to the brain. It is in less danger than the nerve of sight, but it can be injured when a pin breaks the ear's drum.

records.l: the boys who looked at the sun, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The boys foolishly tried to see which could look straight at the sun the longest. Their eyes and brains were greatly harmed, and the boy who looked longest died as a result.

records.l: the boy who made himself cross-eyed, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The boy tried to imitate a schoolmate who was cross-eyed by turning his own eyes. He could not turn them back properly, and doctors were never able to set them quite right despite painful treatment.

records.l: the boy's father, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The boy's father laid his ear against a door crack to feel the wind blow into it when he was young. He afterward suffered severe earache and often had earache throughout his life.

records.l: alcohol, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Alcohol can confuse the nerves and weaken the work of touching, tasting, seeing, smelling, and hearing. A person who habitually uses alcoholic drinks may have trembling hands, thick speech, difficulty walking straight, or may think he sees things that are not present.

records.l: care of the eyes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVII. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Care of the eyes requires avoiding direct bright light, having enough light for reading, and positioning light on the left while writing. The eyes should not be strained by looking at the sun, reading in twilight, or imitating crossed eyes.

records.l: Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVIII. / WHAT MAKES US WARM? .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The unit explains that body heat is produced by work inside the body, carried by the blood, and lost through the skin and breath. Exercise increases blood flow and warmth, while clothing helps retain existing heat rather than producing it. Alcohol creates a temporary feeling of warmth by bringing hot blood to the skin, but it increases heat loss and dulls awareness of cold. Accounts of Arctic explorers and the Greely party show that alcohol and tobacco did not help people endure severe cold, hunger, and freezing.

records.l: heat and cold, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVIII. / WHAT MAKES US WARM? .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Heat is produced by work inside the body and is carried throughout it by the blood. Cold causes heat to be lost, especially when cool air carries it away from the skin.

records.l: body heat, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVIII. / WHAT MAKES US WARM? .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Body heat comes from work that is constantly taking place inside the body. It is carried by the blood and continually passes off through the skin and in the breath.

records.l: clothing, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVIII. / WHAT MAKES US WARM? .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Clothing keeps existing body heat from escaping and helps prevent cold air from reaching the skin. Woolen under-garments, thick boots, and stockings are recommended for cold weather.

records.l: children, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVIII. / WHAT MAKES US WARM? .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: A child is warm inside even when the fingers are cold. Children generally feel warmer than old people because their hearts beat faster, usually eighty to ninety times a minute.

records.l: blood, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVIII. / WHAT MAKES US WARM? .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The blood is warmed by work inside the body and carries heat to every part of it. Faster blood flow brings more heat and makes a person feel warmer.

records.l: body, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVIII. / WHAT MAKES US WARM? .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The body produces heat through its internal work but loses heat through the skin and breath. When the skin is chilled, perspiration tubes may close and prevent waste matter from leaving properly.

records.l: alcohol, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVIII. / WHAT MAKES US WARM? .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Alcohol brings hot blood to the tiny tubes near the skin, creating a temporary feeling of warmth. It actually increases heat loss, dulls the nerves, and can make a person freeze more quickly.

records.l: Arctic explorers, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVIII. / WHAT MAKES US WARM? .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Arctic explorers report that alcohol does not keep them warm. They travel through icy regions, sometimes use dog sledges and Esquimau huts, and may drink oil and eat walrus meat.

records.l: Greely party, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVIII. / WHAT MAKES US WARM? .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The Greely party consisted of twenty-six men who were rescued from the Arctic seas after months of starving and freezing. Nineteen died, seven were found alive, and one of those seven died soon afterward.

records.l: tobacco, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVIII. / WHAT MAKES US WARM? .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Tobacco did not help the men of the Greely party during their hardship. It probably weakened their stomachs and made it harder for them to use poor food effectively.

records.l: Arctic expedition ordeal, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVIII. / WHAT MAKES US WARM? .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The Greely party's ordeal involved months of hunger and extreme cold in the Arctic seas. Most of the men died, while those who survived generally had not used tobacco or had used it only seldom.

records.l: cold exposure and freezing, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XVIII. / WHAT MAKES US WARM? .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Cold exposure causes the body to lose heat and can lead to freezing and death. Alcohol may make freezing happen more quickly because it increases heat loss and prevents a person from recognizing the danger.

records.l: Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XIX. / COST OF ALCOHOL. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The unit explains that spending money on alcohol or liquor is wasteful because it brings harm rather than useful benefits. It describes how beer, wine, and whiskey can quickly consume a dollar, and says that avoiding liquor could reduce sickness, poverty, crime, and the need for policemen and prisons. It also explains that buying tobacco burns up money while harming the smoker. The unit states that six hundred million dollars are spent on tobacco in the country each year.

records.l: alcohol, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XIX. / COST OF ALCOHOL. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Alcohol costs a great deal of money. Money spent on alcohol is described as wasted, or worse than wasted, because it does no good and only causes harm.

records.l: money, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XIX. / COST OF ALCOHOL. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Money can be saved or spent in good and pleasant ways, but spending it on liquor or tobacco wastes it. A dollar spent on two mugs of beer a day is wasted in ten days.

records.l: wasting money, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XIX. / COST OF ALCOHOL. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Wasted money is money spent on something that does no good but only causes harm. Money spent on liquor or tobacco is presented as wasted or worse than wasted.

records.l: cost of alcohol, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XIX. / COST OF ALCOHOL. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The cost of alcohol can quickly use up a dollar: two mugs of beer a day consume a dollar in ten days, while wine or whiskey use it sooner because they cost more.

records.l: tobacco, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XIX. / COST OF ALCOHOL. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Tobacco is compared to a dollar bill that is burned up, because buying and smoking it quickly wastes money. Smoking tobacco also hurts the person who uses it.

records.l: cost of tobacco, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XIX. / COST OF ALCOHOL. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: The yearly cost of tobacco in the country is six hundred million dollars. This money is described as burned up, wasted, and worse than wasted.

records.l: liquor, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XIX. / COST OF ALCOHOL. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Liquor includes beer, wine, and whiskey in the unit's examples of wasteful spending. If no liquor were drunk, men, women, and children would be better and happier, and fewer policemen, jails, and prisons would be needed.

records.l: six hundred million dollars, Child's Health Primer for Primary Classes, CHAPTER XIX. / COST OF ALCOHOL. .. REVIEW QUESTIONS.
records.s: Six hundred million dollars are spent in this country every year for tobacco. The unit describes this amount as money burned up, wasted, and worse than wasted.
