records.l: Gallegher and Other Stories, Gallegher and Other Stories, The older man stepped quickly across the floor, but before he reached the middle
records.s: Ellen returns while her father and Latimer are discussing a test involving Latimer's past love. She admits that she arranged the test as a joke, but recoils from Latimer and asks her father to make him leave. Latimer passionately defends his character, explaining that overcoming his love for the other woman made him honest and worthy of Ellen. Ellen still tells him to go to the other woman, so Latimer leaves and resolves to continue without returning to her.

records.l: Ellen, Gallegher and Other Stories, The older man stepped quickly across the floor, but before he reached the middle
records.s: Ellen enters with her head lowered after listening to the discussion. She says she conducted the test as a joke because she wanted to frighten Latimer and laugh at his response, but she becomes exhausted and distressed. She draws close to her father, asks him to make Latimer leave, and later tells him to go to the other woman.

records.l: Latimer, Gallegher and Other Stories, The older man stepped quickly across the floor, but before he reached the middle
records.s: Latimer pleads with Ellen to believe that he loves only her and argues that the test based on hypothetical conditions is unjust and meaningless. He says that he overcame his love for another woman when it became impossible and that this struggle made him honest, clean, and worthy of Ellen. When Ellen tells him to go to the other woman, he leaves and turns resolutely away from the north, where she is located.

records.l: Ellen's father, Gallegher and Other Stories, The older man stepped quickly across the floor, but before he reached the middle
records.s: Ellen's father receives her with pity and concern and listens as Latimer explains his past and his feelings. He becomes convinced that Latimer has spoken honorably and says he would have been proud if a son had spoken as Latimer did. He urges Ellen to understand Latimer and watches him leave with sympathy and concern.

records.l: the other woman, Gallegher and Other Stories, The older man stepped quickly across the floor, but before he reached the middle
records.s: The other woman is the person whom Latimer previously loved but renounced when their love became a crime or became impossible. Latimer says that both of them put their love away and that her silence may have involved suffering.

records.l: the test by hypothetical conditions, Gallegher and Other Stories, The older man stepped quickly across the floor, but before he reached the middle
records.s: The test by hypothetical conditions is the trick Ellen used to discover what Latimer would say about his past love. Latimer calls it a silly, needless, and horrible mistake that confuses and stultifies them by treating what is not real or possible as significant.

records.l: love between Latimer and the other woman, Gallegher and Other Stories, The older man stepped quickly across the floor, but before he reached the middle
records.s: Latimer says that he loves Ellen more than all the world and that his love for her is certain without needing words to prove it. He also describes a former love that he and the other woman suppressed and sacrificed, claiming that overcoming it helped make him honest and worthy.

records.l: Gallegher and Other Stories, Gallegher and Other Stories, THE TRAILER FOR ROOM NO.
records.s: Snipes, a homeless boy who works as a trailer for Alf Wolfe's green-goods gang, encounters an old farmer searching for his son, Abraham. Believing Abraham has gone to buy counterfeit money, Snipes tries to protect him, but the farmer rushes into room No. 8 and confronts Wolfe before discovering that Abraham is actually in New York to buy a ring. The farmer and Abraham reunite at Grand Central Depot, and the farmer invites Snipes to live on the family farm, but Snipes chooses to remain in New York and return to watching for Wolfe's signal.

records.l: Snipes, Gallegher and Other Stories, THE TRAILER FOR ROOM NO.
records.s: Snipes is a young homeless boy who works as a trailer for Alf Wolfe's green-goods men, earning a quarter for each victim he shadows. He sympathizes with the old farmer, tells him he will protect Abraham, helps him reach Grand Central Depot, and is invited to live on the farm, but chooses to remain in New York.

records.l: Alf Wolfe, Gallegher and Other Stories, THE TRAILER FOR ROOM NO.
records.s: Alf Wolfe is the chief of the green-goods men operating from room No. 8. When the old farmer confronts him, Wolfe overpowers him but does not injure him or turn him over to the police, instead sending him away.

records.l: the old farmer, Gallegher and Other Stories, THE TRAILER FOR ROOM NO.
records.s: The old farmer comes to New York looking for Abraham, whom he believes has been lured into buying counterfeit money by Perceval, Alf Wolfe's business name. He confronts Wolfe, is escorted out by Snipes, reunites with Abraham at Grand Central Depot, and invites Snipes to return with them to the farm.

records.l: Abraham, Gallegher and Other Stories, THE TRAILER FOR ROOM NO.
records.s: Abraham is the old farmer's son, whom his father believes has gone to room No. 8 with $200 to buy counterfeit money. He is actually in New York to buy a ring after receiving permission to marry Kate without first saving $2,000.

records.l: the green-goods men, Gallegher and Other Stories, THE TRAILER FOR ROOM NO.
records.s: The green-goods men send circulars offering counterfeit money and arrange meetings where suspected customers can be watched and robbed. Alf Wolfe leads the group connected with room No. 8, and Snipes works for them as a trailer.

records.l: Case's tenement, Gallegher and Other Stories, THE TRAILER FOR ROOM NO.
records.s: Case's tenement contains room No. 8, which is rented by the green-goods men. Its residents have learned to leave visiting countrymen to the men operating from that room.

records.l: room No. 8, Gallegher and Other Stories, THE TRAILER FOR ROOM NO.
records.s: Room No. 8 is the rented headquarters where Alf Wolfe and the green-goods men meet prospective customers. The old farmer enters it looking for Abraham and confronts Wolfe, but Abraham is not there.

records.l: New York, Gallegher and Other Stories, THE TRAILER FOR ROOM NO.
records.s: New York is portrayed as a crowded, harsh city associated with crime, poverty, and the green-goods operation. Snipes knows the city well but rejects the farmer's offer to leave it for the country.

records.l: Grand Central station, Gallegher and Other Stories, THE TRAILER FOR ROOM NO.
records.s: Grand Central Depot is where Snipes takes the exhausted old farmer and where the farmer unexpectedly finds Abraham. The farmer and Abraham reunite there before preparing to return home.

records.l: green goods, Gallegher and Other Stories, THE TRAILER FOR ROOM NO.
records.s: Green goods is the technical term for counterfeit bills. The green-goods men offer countrymen large amounts of it in exchange for smaller amounts of legitimate money, claiming that the only victim is the Government.

records.l: counterfeit money, Gallegher and Other Stories, THE TRAILER FOR ROOM NO.
records.s: Counterfeit money is what the green-goods men claim to sell to their customers. The old farmer mistakenly believes Abraham has come to New York to spend $200 on $2,000 worth of counterfeit money.

records.l: the trailer's work, Gallegher and Other Stories, THE TRAILER FOR ROOM NO.
records.s: The trailer's work is to shadow a prospective customer from the first meeting with the green-goods men to a later meeting and report any suspicious behavior. Snipes is skilled at remaining unnoticed, following people through crowds, and alerting Wolfe if a customer appears to be a detective.

records.l: Abraham's trip to New York, Gallegher and Other Stories, THE TRAILER FOR ROOM NO.
records.s: Abraham travels to New York with the $200 he saved, but not to buy counterfeit money. After the Deacon permits him to marry Kate without requiring $2,000, he comes on the first train to buy a ring.

records.l: Gallegher and Other Stories, Gallegher and Other Stories, "THERE WERE NINETY AND NINE" Young Harringford, or the "Goodwood Plunger," as he was perhaps better known at that time, had come to Monte Carlo in a very different spirit and in a very different state of mind from any in which he had ever visited the place before.
records.s: Young Harringford, also known as Cecil and the “Goodwood Plunger,” comes to Monte Carlo intending to kill himself after losing his fortune, estranging his family, and suffering severe mental and physical distress. He recalls how his gambling began with his successful backing of Siren in the Goodwood Cup, followed by greater winnings, mounting debts, and disgrace. His final gamble on the Grand Prix fails when Frou Frou defeats the English horse, leaving him convinced that suicide is his only escape. At the Casino, he destroys his father’s conciliatory letter and waits for the lights to go out so he can carry out his plan.

records.s: Young Harringford, whose name is Cecil, comes to Monte Carlo alone and disinherited after losing his fortune through gambling. Once celebrated as the “Goodwood Plunger,” he now intends to kill himself and tears up his father’s letter instead of returning home.

records.l: Harringford's father, Gallegher and Other Stories, "THERE WERE NINETY AND NINE" Young Harringford, or the "Goodwood Plunger," as he was perhaps better known at that time, had come to Monte Carlo in a very different spirit and in a very different state of mind from any in which he had ever visited the place before.
records.s: Harringford’s father had rejected him for bringing the family name into disgrace through gambling, but later recognized his own error and invited Cecil to return home. He writes that Cecil is dearer to him than his other sons and that he cannot be at rest unless Cecil comes back.

records.l: the girl from Surrey, Gallegher and Other Stories, "THERE WERE NINETY AND NINE" Young Harringford, or the "Goodwood Plunger," as he was perhaps better known at that time, had come to Monte Carlo in a very different spirit and in a very different state of mind from any in which he had ever visited the place before.
records.s: The girl from Surrey lives near Harringford’s family and has been an important object of his affection. Harringford watched her lighted window when she was ill, longs to meet her again, and learns from his father that she has asked about him without regard for what others might think.

records.s: Monte Carlo is the place Harringford chooses for his planned death because it is unlike his home and because he remembers a young Russian who killed himself there after losing at the tables. He travels there from Paris and waits outside the Casino late at night.

records.s: Harringford stands beside a pillar of the Casino, watching the lights above the green tables and waiting for them to be extinguished. He plans to act after the Casino closes, regarding the place as a fitting setting for his death.

records.s: Surrey is the home of Harringford’s family and the setting of the neighboring estate where the girl lives. Harringford remembers its fields, trout springs, park, and terraces, and longs to return there despite believing that he has lost the right to do so.

records.s: The Grand Prix is Harringford’s final gambling coup, on which he stakes his hopes of restoring his fortune, reconciling with his father, and seeing the girl again. The English horse fails to win, as Frou Frou passes the goal, and Harringford returns to Paris in despair.

records.l: gambling and debt, Gallegher and Other Stories, "THERE WERE NINETY AND NINE" Young Harringford, or the "Goodwood Plunger," as he was perhaps better known at that time, had come to Monte Carlo in a very different spirit and in a very different state of mind from any in which he had ever visited the place before.
records.s: Harringford begins gambling after coming into his money and secretly backs Siren with enormous sums, winning a fortune at the Goodwood Cup. His later losses bring visits to lenders, borrowing, threats of executions, and debts he cannot repay, culminating in the failed Grand Prix wager.

records.l: Harringford's mental and physical distress, Gallegher and Other Stories, "THERE WERE NINETY AND NINE" Young Harringford, or the "Goodwood Plunger," as he was perhaps better known at that time, had come to Monte Carlo in a very different spirit and in a very different state of mind from any in which he had ever visited the place before.
records.s: Harringford suffers a numb feeling and sharp pain in his head, trembling nerves, twitching, loss of appetite, shivering, insomnia, and fear that his mind is failing. He repeatedly tests whether his speech and thoughts are sensible and believes that only death can stop the pain, doubts, and terror.

records.l: Harringford's planned suicide, Gallegher and Other Stories, "THERE WERE NINETY AND NINE" Young Harringford, or the "Goodwood Plunger," as he was perhaps better known at that time, had come to Monte Carlo in a very different spirit and in a very different state of mind from any in which he had ever visited the place before.
records.s: Harringford decides that he will kill himself at Monte Carlo if his final gambling coup fails. He believes suicide will bring rest and peace, feels that others would understand if they experienced his suffering, and waits for the Casino lights to go out before acting.

records.l: Harringford's father's letter, Gallegher and Other Stories, "THERE WERE NINETY AND NINE" Young Harringford, or the "Goodwood Plunger," as he was perhaps better known at that time, had come to Monte Carlo in a very different spirit and in a very different state of mind from any in which he had ever visited the place before.
records.s: Harringford’s father’s letter urges him to come home and forgive the past, invoking the story of the Prodigal Son and promising him peace and welcome. It says that Cecil is the first-born, dearer to him than the other ninety-nine, and that the girl from Surrey still asks about him; Harringford reads it for the last time and tears it into pieces.

records.s: The Goodwood Plunger is approached at Monte Carlo by a short, plainly dressed French woman who asks him to speak with her husband, Louis. Louis has won a large amount gambling but refuses to stop, risking the money needed to buy the rest of Carbut's bakery store. The woman believes Louis will listen to the Goodwood Plunger, whom she considers fortunate, rich, and experienced. The Goodwood Plunger initially misunderstands her request but finally agrees to find Louis and speak with him.

records.s: The Goodwood Plunger is approached by a distressed French woman who asks him to persuade Louis to stop gambling. He is initially disoriented and misunderstands her, but eventually understands that Louis has won money and is risking it, and asks her to point Louis out.

records.s: The woman is French, short, plainly dressed, and newly married to Louis. She explains that Louis has won a substantial amount at gambling but will not stop, and she begs the Goodwood Plunger to warn him because their future depends on the money.

records.s: Louis is the woman's husband, an apprentice to old Carbut the baker and a part-owner of the bakery store. Though he is not usually a gambler, he has become excited after winning money at the tables and continues to risk it, hoping to buy another third of the store.

records.s: Monte Carlo is the setting where the woman and Louis have come during their marriage tour. The woman says they should not be there because the gambling tables are not for people like them, and they are due to return to Paris the next day.

records.s: Carbut's bakery store is partly owned by Louis, who is an apprentice there and owns a third of it. Old Carbut may sell Louis the entire store for 20,000 francs and retire, but Louis's continued gambling threatens the couple's ability to acquire the remaining share.

records.l: gambling, Gallegher and Other Stories, As he turned, a woman came forward from out the lighted hall, hovered uncertainl
records.s: Gambling at the tables has caused Louis to become excited and reckless despite his usual lack of interest in gambling. He has won a large amount but continues risking it instead of stopping, and the woman asks the Goodwood Plunger to persuade him to quit.

records.l: money, Gallegher and Other Stories, As he turned, a woman came forward from out the lighted hall, hovered uncertainl
records.s: The money Louis has won represents many months or years of hard work and saving for the couple. They need it to secure the rest of Carbut's bakery store, but Louis risks losing it by continuing to gamble.

records.s: Cecil Harringford intervenes when a Frenchman continues gambling at Monte Carlo despite his wife's concern, and he helps them protect their winnings. After the Frenchman wins more than 20,000 francs at roulette, Cecil puts the money in the woman's care and sends the couple by train to Paris. At the station, the couple thank Cecil for making them happy, which reminds him of his father's letter and strengthens his desire to return home. Cecil tells Walters that they are going home to England, and he falls asleep peacefully, speaking of happiness for the rest of their lives.

records.s: Cecil Harringford stops the Frenchman from continuing to gamble and divides the winnings so that the Frenchman, his wife, and Cecil can place separate bets. He takes the money from the table, puts it into the woman's skirt, sends the couple to Paris, and then decides to return to England with Walters.

records.s: The Frenchman repeatedly bets his winnings on red and becomes increasingly excited when he wins. After Cecil prevents him from risking everything in one final coup, he leaves for Paris with his wife, becomes grateful and humble, and promises never to return to Monte Carlo.

records.s: The woman asks Cecil to stop her husband because he is risking money that could relieve their debt and support their home. She receives the winnings, travels with her husband to Paris, and thanks Cecil for helping them establish a happier life.

records.s: Walters is found by Cecil reading or writing a letter to Cecil's father. He helps pack Cecil's things, is relieved when Cecil decides to leave, and watches over him as he falls asleep speaking about going home.

records.s: Monte Carlo is the place where the Frenchman has been gambling and where Cecil has seen people arrive rich and leave as paupers. Cecil insists that the Frenchman and his wife leave it that night.

records.s: Paris is the couple's destination after Cecil sends them away from Monte Carlo. They are expected to arrive there by morning and return to their home and shop.

records.s: Casino gambling is shown as dangerous because the Frenchman nearly risks all of the couple's money even after winning a large sum. Cecil intervenes because he has seen gamblers become paupers.

records.s: The roulette game produces successive wins for the Frenchman on red before the ball settles on seven, which is red, odd, and below eighteen. Cecil uses the result to secure a larger combined win and then prevents another wager.

records.s: The money is repeatedly placed on red, won, divided into three possible stakes, and finally gathered by Cecil and placed in the woman's care. It is packed into a heavy bag and taken with the couple to the train.

records.s: The woman says that the Frenchman has won half of the 20,000 francs, and Cecil later tells him that he has won more than 20,000 francs. The winnings are used to secure the couple's future rather than being risked again.

records.s: Cecil hurries the couple onto the train to Paris and purchases their tickets. Before the guard locks the compartment, he tells them they are alone and cannot leave until they return home.

records.s: The departure for Paris follows the couple's successful roulette wagers and Cecil's decision to remove them from Monte Carlo. The woman and her husband leave gratefully while Cecil remains alone on the platform.

records.s: Cecil decides to take the first available train and return to England with Walters. He describes this homecoming as a return to England, Harringford, and his father.

records.s: The Frenchman tells Cecil that he has made the couple happy for the rest of their lives, and the train's wheels echo those words after their departure. Cecil connects the phrase with his father's letter and later repeats it while falling asleep.

records.l: Gallegher and Other Stories, Gallegher and Other Stories, THE CYNICAL MISS CATHERWAIGHT Miss Catherwaight's collection of orders and decorations and medals was her chief offence in the eyes of those of her dear friends who thought her clever but cynical.
records.s: Miss Catherwaight, known for her cynical wit, collects medals and decorations that their recipients have pawned or sold, calling them dishonored honors. She finds a tarnished silver heart medal inscribed as a gift from Henry Burgoyne to Lewis L. Lockwood and goes to Lockwood's law office to learn its history. Mr. Latimer explains that Henry Burgoyne, now Judge Burgoyne, and Lewis Lockwood were devoted boyhood friends who later quarrelled over a woman and have remained estranged. Miss Catherwaight learns that the medal was stolen from Lockwood during a burglary and decides she cannot keep or exhibit it.

records.l: Miss Catherwaight, Gallegher and Other Stories, THE CYNICAL MISS CATHERWAIGHT Miss Catherwaight's collection of orders and decorations and medals was her chief offence in the eyes of those of her dear friends who thought her clever but cynical.
records.s: Miss Catherwaight is a clever young woman whom some friends consider cynical because of her collection and her unpleasant remarks about society. She collects dishonored medals, visits pawnshops on the Bowery and Park Row, and seeks to learn the stories behind the objects she buys. After finding the silver heart medal connected with Lewis Lyman Lockwood, she visits his office, feels ashamed of her intrusion, and decides she cannot keep or tell its story.

records.l: Miss Catherwaight's collection of dishonored honors, Gallegher and Other Stories, THE CYNICAL MISS CATHERWAIGHT Miss Catherwaight's collection of orders and decorations and medals was her chief offence in the eyes of those of her dear friends who thought her clever but cynical.
records.s: Miss Catherwaight's collection contains more than a hundred medals and decorations purchased during travels with her father. Each was awarded for public service, virtue, bravery, statesmanship, or artistic genius and was later pawned or sold by its recipient. She calls the collection dishonored honors, the Orders of the Knights of the Almighty Dollar, pledges to patriotism and the pawnshops, and honors at second-hand.

records.l: Lewis Lyman Lockwood, Gallegher and Other Stories, THE CYNICAL MISS CATHERWAIGHT Miss Catherwaight's collection of orders and decorations and medals was her chief offence in the eyes of those of her dear friends who thought her clever but cynical.
records.s: Lewis Lyman Lockwood is a lawyer whose office Miss Catherwaight visits after finding a medal bearing his name. Mr. Latimer says the medal had been in Lockwood's safe when he lived on Thirty-fifth Street and was taken by burglars. Lockwood had been devoted friends with Henry Burgoyne, but they quarrelled over a woman and have remained apart.

records.l: Judge Burgoyne, Gallegher and Other Stories, THE CYNICAL MISS CATHERWAIGHT Miss Catherwaight's collection of orders and decorations and medals was her chief offence in the eyes of those of her dear friends who thought her clever but cynical.
records.s: Judge Burgoyne is identified by Mr. Latimer as Henry Burgoyne, the former boyhood friend of Lewis Lockwood. He and Lockwood attended school together, roomed together at the State college, practised law together, and shared a love of shooting. He later became estranged from Lockwood after both men fell in love with the same woman.

records.l: Mr. Latimer, Gallegher and Other Stories, THE CYNICAL MISS CATHERWAIGHT Miss Catherwaight's collection of orders and decorations and medals was her chief offence in the eyes of those of her dear friends who thought her clever but cynical.
records.s: Mr. Latimer is the junior partner in Lewis Lockwood's law office and a dancing acquaintance of Miss Catherwaight. He tells her that the silver medal belonged to Lockwood, had been stolen in a burglary, and commemorated Lockwood's boyhood friendship with Henry Burgoyne. He also recounts the friends' shared history and their later quarrel.

records.l: Henry Burgoyne and Lewis L. Lockwood's boyhood friendship, Gallegher and Other Stories, THE CYNICAL MISS CATHERWAIGHT Miss Catherwaight's collection of orders and decorations and medals was her chief offence in the eyes of those of her dear friends who thought her clever but cynical.
records.s: Henry Burgoyne and Lewis L. Lockwood were close friends from their school days in Westchester County. They roomed together at the State college, began practising law together, shared their spare time and hunting trips, and were described as closer than brothers. Their friendship ended after both fell in love with the same woman and each believed the other had acted disloyally.

records.l: medals and decorations, Gallegher and Other Stories, THE CYNICAL MISS CATHERWAIGHT Miss Catherwaight's collection of orders and decorations and medals was her chief offence in the eyes of those of her dear friends who thought her clever but cynical.
records.s: The medals and decorations in Miss Catherwaight's collection were originally rewards for bravery, statesmanship, artistic genius, or other high virtues. Many were later pawned or sold, including French crosses of the Legion of Honor, English war medals, a Victoria Cross, and a congressional gold medal. Miss Catherwaight values them especially when their histories are discreditable.

records.l: silver heart medal from Henry Burgoyne to Lewis L. Lockwood, Gallegher and Other Stories, THE CYNICAL MISS CATHERWAIGHT Miss Catherwaight's collection of orders and decorations and medals was her chief offence in the eyes of those of her dear friends who thought her clever but cynical.
records.s: The silver heart medal is a cheap, tarnished object engraved with clasped hands and the words "From Henry Burgoyne to his beloved friend Lewis L. Lockwood" and "Through prosperity and adversity." Miss Catherwaight buys it from a Bowery pawnbroker, then learns from Mr. Latimer that it had been stolen from Lockwood's safe during a burglary. She decides she cannot keep or exhibit it after learning the painful story attached to it.

records.l: New York, Gallegher and Other Stories, THE CYNICAL MISS CATHERWAIGHT Miss Catherwaight's collection of orders and decorations and medals was her chief offence in the eyes of those of her dear friends who thought her clever but cynical.
records.s: New York is where Miss Catherwaight's father and daughter later live together and entertain at dinners after Mrs. Catherwaight's death. The city contains the pawnshops and loan offices where Miss Catherwaight searches for medals, as well as Lewis Lockwood's law office on Broadway and the former Lockwood residence on Thirty-fifth Street.

records.l: the Bowery, Gallegher and Other Stories, THE CYNICAL MISS CATHERWAIGHT Miss Catherwaight's collection of orders and decorations and medals was her chief offence in the eyes of those of her dear friends who thought her clever but cynical.
records.s: The Bowery is where Miss Catherwaight finds the silver heart medal in a pawnbroker's window among razors, pistols, and family Bibles. She is well known to the pawnshops and loan offices there, whose proprietors save medals for her and try to learn or invent their histories.

records.l: the collection of dishonored honors, Gallegher and Other Stories, THE CYNICAL MISS CATHERWAIGHT Miss Catherwaight's collection of orders and decorations and medals was her chief offence in the eyes of those of her dear friends who thought her clever but cynical.
records.s: The collection of dishonored honors is Miss Catherwaight's unusual hobby and consists of awards whose recipients have parted with them. She displays the objects to dinner guests and explains the circumstances of their sale or pawning, treating the contrast between public honor and private dishonor as the collection's chief interest. The silver heart medal prompts her to question whether every object should be treated as a collectible.

records.s: Miss Catherwaight learns that Lewis L. Lockwood and Henry Burgoyne were once close friends whose friendship was damaged by a misunderstanding involving her mother. After Lockwood visits to thank her for returning his medal, she urges him to reconcile with Burgoyne and let him keep the medal. Lockwood visits Burgoyne that night, and he and Burgoyne decide to take a shooting trip to Maryland. Mr. Latimer reports Lockwood's renewed happiness and agrees to manage matters at the office while they are away.

records.l: Miss Catherwaight, Gallegher and Other Stories, "} They had been sitting there some time, he with his hands folded on the evenin
records.s: Miss Catherwaight learns that Lockwood and Burgoyne separated because of a misunderstanding involving her mother. She urges Lockwood to keep the medal and reconcile with Burgoyne, believing that she can help undo the harm caused unwittingly by her mother.

records.l: Lewis Lyman Lockwood, Gallegher and Other Stories, "} They had been sitting there some time, he with his hands folded on the evenin
records.s: Lewis L. Lockwood visits Miss Catherwaight to thank her for returning his medal. He explains that he once misunderstood her mother's kindness and that pride prolonged the resulting separation from Burgoyne. After speaking with Burgoyne, he returns looking younger and happier and announces that they will go shooting in Maryland.

records.l: Judge Burgoyne, Gallegher and Other Stories, "} They had been sitting there some time, he with his hands folded on the evenin
records.s: Henry Burgoyne was formerly Lockwood's close friend and is now a judge and lawyer. Lockwood visits him to determine whether their long separation can end, and the two plan to go shooting together in Maryland.

records.l: Mr. Latimer, Gallegher and Other Stories, "} They had been sitting there some time, he with his hands folded on the evenin
records.s: Mr. Latimer accompanies Lockwood when Lockwood visits Miss Catherwaight and later waits at home for Lockwood's return. He explains that Lockwood has repeatedly prepared his gun for hunting but never gone, and he agrees to look after matters at the office while Lockwood and Burgoyne travel.

records.s: Miss Catherwaight's mother was once kind to Lockwood, whose misunderstanding of that kindness contributed to the rupture between Lockwood and Burgoyne. Miss Catherwaight believes her mother was unaware of the trouble she had caused.

records.s: The medal belonged to Lockwood and had been stolen and pawned before Miss Catherwaight found it in an old curiosity shop and returned it. Lockwood initially considers it a reminder of the past, but keeps it after Miss Catherwaight urges him to do so.

records.s: The misunderstanding arose from Lockwood's misinterpretation of Miss Catherwaight's mother's kindness and was prolonged by the pride of both Lockwood and Burgoyne. It caused them to stop meeting and cease knowing each other.

records.l: Henry Burgoyne and Lewis L. Lockwood's boyhood friendship, Gallegher and Other Stories, "} They had been sitting there some time, he with his hands folded on the evenin
records.s: Lockwood and Burgoyne were once very close friends who shared a strong sense of loyalty and enjoyed shooting together. Their friendship survives beneath the long separation, and Miss Catherwaight's intervention helps lead them toward reconciliation.

records.s: After Lockwood visits Burgoyne, the two decide to go on a shooting trip together. The trip is expected to last a few weeks.

records.s: Maryland is the destination of Lockwood and Burgoyne's planned shooting trip, which they intend to take for a few weeks.

records.l: Gallegher and Other Stories, Gallegher and Other Stories, " VAN BIBBER AND THE SWAN-BOATS It was very hot in the Park, and young Van Bibber, who has a good heart and a great deal more money than good-hearted people generally get, was cross and somnolent.
records.s: Van Bibber, waiting in the Park for his groom, hears three little girls from the East Side wishing they could ride the swan-boats. He pays for them to take a ride and enjoys showing them the fishes, birds, and supposedly wild parts of the lake. Afterward, the Girl He Knew and her brother tease him about the outing, but the Girl He Knew responds kindly. Van Bibber buys the girls enough tickets for a week of rides, and they return home delighted.

records.l: Van Bibber, Gallegher and Other Stories, " VAN BIBBER AND THE SWAN-BOATS It was very hot in the Park, and young Van Bibber, who has a good heart and a great deal more money than good-hearted people generally get, was cross and somnolent.
records.s: Van Bibber is hot, cross, and waiting for his groom when he notices three little girls admiring the swan-boats. He offers to pay for their ride, joins them despite his embarrassment, and points out the sights around the lake. After meeting the Girl He Knew and her brother, he buys the girls long strings of tickets for additional rides.

records.l: the three little girls from the East Side, Gallegher and Other Stories, " VAN BIBBER AND THE SWAN-BOATS It was very hot in the Park, and young Van Bibber, who has a good heart and a great deal more money than good-hearted people generally get, was cross and somnolent.
records.s: The three little girls from the East Side watch the swan-boats and discuss the sights that might be visible from the lake, including fishes, ducks, snakes, bears, and other wild animals. They cannot afford a ride until Van Bibber offers to take them. They enjoy the trip greatly, receive tickets for a week of rides, and return to their tenement sunburned and delighted.

records.l: the Girl He Knew, Gallegher and Other Stories, " VAN BIBBER AND THE SWAN-BOATS It was very hot in the Park, and young Van Bibber, who has a good heart and a great deal more money than good-hearted people generally get, was cross and somnolent.
records.s: The Girl He Knew encounters Van Bibber at the dock after his ride with the three little girls. She smiles at him with kindness and understanding, then invites him to join her and her brother at the stables after he has cared for the girls.

records.s: The brother meets Van Bibber at the lake after the swan-boat ride. He jokes about Van Bibber's trip and introduces the girls as Van Bibber's young lady friends from Hester Street, then teases the girls about smuggling laces and tipping the smoking-room steward.

records.s: The Park is very hot, and Van Bibber waits there for his groom before moving to a shaded bench near the lake. Its paths, bushes, artificial lake, and nearby stables provide the setting for the outing.

records.s: The lake is an artificial body of water with an island, rocks, shallow edges, bushes, and narrow straits. Fishes swim among the rocks, while sparrows and robins bathe in the shallows; the girls imagine that wild animals might live on the island.

records.l: the swan-boats, Gallegher and Other Stories, " VAN BIBBER AND THE SWAN-BOATS It was very hot in the Park, and young Van Bibber, who has a good heart and a great deal more money than good-hearted people generally get, was cross and somnolent.
records.s: The swan-boats are Lohengrin swans with paddle-wheel attachments that circle the lake beneath a parti-awning. Van Bibber initially considers them idiotic, but later rides one with the girls and buys them tickets for further trips.

records.l: the swan-boat ride, Gallegher and Other Stories, " VAN BIBBER AND THE SWAN-BOATS It was very hot in the Park, and young Van Bibber, who has a good heart and a great deal more money than good-hearted people generally get, was cross and somnolent.
records.s: The swan-boat ride is shady and pleasant, with the boat careening slightly as it turns. Van Bibber is embarrassed while other people can see him, but he relaxes in the narrow straits and helps the girls appreciate the sights.

records.l: riding the swan-boats, Gallegher and Other Stories, " VAN BIBBER AND THE SWAN-BOATS It was very hot in the Park, and young Van Bibber, who has a good heart and a great deal more money than good-hearted people generally get, was cross and somnolent.
records.s: Riding the swan-boats gives the three little girls great pleasure, and Van Bibber finds that they seem to enjoy it more than he has enjoyed expensive trips by yacht or steamship. Afterward, the girls use the tickets Van Bibber gives them until they are sunburned.

records.l: Van Bibber's generosity, Gallegher and Other Stories, " VAN BIBBER AND THE SWAN-BOATS It was very hot in the Park, and young Van Bibber, who has a good heart and a great deal more money than good-hearted people generally get, was cross and somnolent.
records.s: Van Bibber's generosity leads him to pay for the three little girls' swan-boat ride when they cannot afford it. He later buys each girl a long string of tickets so they can continue riding for a week.

records.s: Van Bibber attends a prizefight in Jersey City with young Travers and two reporters, then walks through New York at dawn and encounters a burglar escaping from a great house. He overpowers the burglar, who says he has just escaped prison and wants money to join his wife and daughter in the West. Instead of surrendering him, Van Bibber buys him a ticket to Helena, Montana, escorts him to the train, and gives him money. Later, Van Bibber reads that the burglar is Abe Hubbard, alias Jimmie the Gent, who has broken jail, and concludes that he has helped him escape the country.

records.s: Van Bibber encounters a burglar at dawn after seeing a man's head emerge from a door in the wall of a great house. He tackles the man, takes his revolver, and escorts him to Grand Central station instead of surrendering him. Van Bibber buys him a ticket to Helena, Montana, gives him money, and later reads that he has helped the escaped Abe Hubbard, alias Jimmie the Gent, leave the city.

records.l: reporter, Gallegher and Other Stories, VAN BIBBER'S BURGLAR There had been a dance up town, but as Van Bibber could not find Her there, he accepted young Travers's suggestion to go over to Jersey City and see a "go" between "Dutchy" Mack and a <DW52> person professionally known as the Black Diamond.
records.s: A reporter accompanying Van Bibber argues that city life offers no truly mysterious adventures and that its dramas usually arise from crime, poverty, or drink. He recounts a story Dickens told James Payn about a ragged man receiving a bouquet from a beautifully dressed woman at a ball. Another reporter holds the watch during the prizefight.

records.l: burglar, Gallegher and Other Stories, VAN BIBBER'S BURGLAR There had been a dance up town, but as Van Bibber could not find Her there, he accepted young Travers's suggestion to go over to Jersey City and see a "go" between "Dutchy" Mack and a <DW52> person professionally known as the Black Diamond.
records.s: The burglar emerges from the wall beside a great house carrying two bags of stolen property and a revolver. Van Bibber overpowers him, and the burglar says he has just escaped prison after serving seven years and refuses to return alive. He claims he stole to obtain money to join his wife and daughter in the West, and Van Bibber helps him travel to Helena, Montana.

records.s: A newspaper identifies the burglar Van Bibber helped as Abe Hubbard, an escaped burglar who has been traced to New York.

records.s: The newspaper identifies Abe Hubbard by the alias Jimmie the Gent and reports that he has broken jail.

records.s: Van Bibber returns to New York after the Jersey City fight and walks through its nearly deserted streets at dawn. The city is presented by the reporter as exciting but generally brutal, commonplace, and governed by recurring patterns of crime and poverty. Van Bibber helps the burglar leave New York by train.

records.s: Van Bibber brings the burglar to Grand Central station and asks where he wants to go. The burglar answers Helena, Montana, and Van Bibber buys him a ticket there.

records.s: Helena, Montana, is the destination the burglar gives when Van Bibber asks where he should send him. Van Bibber buys the burglar a train ticket to Helena, Montana.

records.s: The burglary is discovered when Van Bibber sees a man carrying two bags filled with projecting articles near the great house. He assumes the man has robbed the house and makes him leave the bags inside the kitchen door, where a servant can find them.

records.s: A newspaper reports that Abe Hubbard, alias Jimmie the Gent, has broken jail in New Jersey and has been traced to New York. It says detectives expect to recapture him but fear that friends may help him get out West.

records.s: The burglar says he has served his time in prison and describes returning there as returning to a grave. He claims he spent seven years imprisoned and fears another sentence of twenty years.

records.s: The burglar carries a revolver during the attempted escape. It goes off once during his struggle with Van Bibber, who kicks it from his hand and keeps it as a threat while escorting him to the station.

records.s: Two bags containing articles of different sizes lie at the burglar's feet. Van Bibber tells him to place the bags inside the kitchen door, where the servant will see them before the milkman does.

records.s: Van Bibber buys the burglar a ticket to Helena, Montana. He warns that the ticket can be sold downtown for half its value, and the burglar says he already knows that.

records.s: Van Bibber wants to prove the reporter wrong about the absence of unusual adventures in city life. His encounter with the burglar becomes the extraordinary incident he has been seeking, though he later wonders whether he acted correctly.

records.l: honest living, Gallegher and Other Stories, VAN BIBBER'S BURGLAR There had been a dance up town, but as Van Bibber could not find Her there, he accepted young Travers's suggestion to go over to Jersey City and see a "go" between "Dutchy" Mack and a <DW52> person professionally known as the Black Diamond.
records.s: The burglar says he intended to live honestly after joining his wife and daughter in the West. Van Bibber doubts whether the burglar truly means to live honestly but nevertheless gives him money and helps him leave.

records.l: Gallegher and Other Stories, Gallegher and Other Stories, " VAN BIBBER AS BEST MAN Young Van Bibber came up to town in June from Newport to see his lawyer about the preparation of some papers that needed his signature.
records.s: Cortlandt Van Bibber discovers that young Standish and Miss Cambridge have eloped and are searching for a clergyman and witnesses to marry them. He deceives young Standish's older brother by claiming that the couple has gone to Chicago, then arranges a public wedding with suitable guests, flowers, music, and a church ceremony. The couple is married at the Little Church Around the Corner and leaves for the Fall River boat. Van Bibber later worries that his lie has sent the older brother racing around Chicago in extreme heat.

records.l: Van Bibber, Gallegher and Other Stories, " VAN BIBBER AS BEST MAN Young Van Bibber came up to town in June from Newport to see his lawyer about the preparation of some papers that needed his signature.
records.s: Cortlandt Van Bibber recognizes young Standish and learns that he and Miss Cambridge have eloped without a clergyman or witnesses. He sends young Standish's older brother away by falsely saying that the couple has gone to Chicago, then arranges their wedding at the Little Church Around the Corner with invited guests, flowers, music, and other formalities. He acts as best man and afterward regrets sending the brother to Chicago rather than Jersey City.

records.l: young Standish, Gallegher and Other Stories, " VAN BIBBER AS BEST MAN Young Van Bibber came up to town in June from Newport to see his lawyer about the preparation of some papers that needed his signature.
records.s: Young Standish, also called Ted, has eloped with Miss Cambridge and is trying to find a clergyman to marry them before they return to Boston. When his older brother arrives, Van Bibber deceives the brother to protect the couple. Young Standish is married to Miss Cambridge in a public ceremony arranged by Van Bibber.

records.l: Miss Cambridge, Gallegher and Other Stories, " VAN BIBBER AS BEST MAN Young Van Bibber came up to town in June from Newport to see his lawyer about the preparation of some papers that needed his signature.
records.s: Miss Cambridge has eloped with young Standish but is frightened because they lack a clergyman, witnesses, and a parish registry. She agrees to rely on Van Bibber, who arranges a formal wedding for them. She weeps during the journey to the church but is smiling and happy when she walks up the aisle.

records.l: Little Church Around the Corner, Gallegher and Other Stories, " VAN BIBBER AS BEST MAN Young Van Bibber came up to town in June from Newport to see his lawyer about the preparation of some papers that needed his signature.
records.s: The Little Church Around the Corner is where Van Bibber arranges for young Standish and Miss Cambridge to be married. He secures the rector's cooperation, has the church opened at three o'clock, and arranges for music and the church bell.

records.l: the wedding, Gallegher and Other Stories, " VAN BIBBER AS BEST MAN Young Van Bibber came up to town in June from Newport to see his lawyer about the preparation of some papers that needed his signature.
records.s: The wedding is organized by Van Bibber to give the elopement publicity and avoid talk or scandal. It includes invited women and club men, flowers, music, a church bell, rice, and an old shoe, and is intended to appear as an orthodox and fashionable wedding in the newspapers.

records.l: the elopement, Gallegher and Other Stories, " VAN BIBBER AS BEST MAN Young Van Bibber came up to town in June from Newport to see his lawyer about the preparation of some papers that needed his signature.
records.s: The elopement concerns young Standish and Miss Cambridge, who leave without the approval or presence of their families and initially lack a clergyman and witnesses. Van Bibber protects them from discovery and converts the hurried plan into a formal wedding.

records.l: marriage ceremony, Gallegher and Other Stories, " VAN BIBBER AS BEST MAN Young Van Bibber came up to town in June from Newport to see his lawyer about the preparation of some papers that needed his signature.
records.s: The marriage ceremony takes place at the Little Church Around the Corner with an assistant organist, witnesses, and guests arranged by Van Bibber. Young Standish and Miss Cambridge are married there and then leave for the Fall River boat.

records.l: Dandy Dick
records.s: This document is the three-act play Dandy Dick. It centers on Augustin Jedd, Dean of St. Marvells, whose efforts to preserve dignity, fund the restoration of the Minister Spire, and control his household are undone by racing, betting, disguises, and misunderstandings. His daughters, Salome and Sheba Jedd, want to attend a masked ball with Gerald Tarver and Nugent Darbey, but their expensive dresses expose the family’s lack of ready money. The Dean has committed £1,000 to the Restoration Fund and must retrench. His widowed sister, Georgiana Tidman, formerly the racehorse owner George Tidd, arrives and proves a disruptive force, co-owning the racehorse Dandy Dick with Sir Tristram Mardon and secretly planning to bet on him. Georgiana agrees to stake Salome’s and Sheba’s money on Dandy Dick. At the Deanery, the Dean’s public offer brings seven wealthy donors to promise £1,000 each, making his own obligation urgent. When the Swan Inn burns, Dandy Dick is rescued and hidden in the Deanery stables. Georgiana persuades the reluctant Dean to bet £50 on the horse for the Restoration Fund. Edward Blore, sent to place the wager, secretly puts strychnine in Dandy Dick’s bolus in an attempt to keep him from racing, while mistakenly betting the Dean’s money on Bonny Betsy. Meanwhile, the girls return from the cancelled ball with Tarver and Darbey, who have arrived disguised as shabby Cavaliers. The confusion culminates when the Dean is arrested after being found administering medicine to Dandy Dick. At the police station, Hannah Topping recognizes him as her former master and tries to help him, but Noah Topping repeatedly mistakes events and adds charges against him. In the final return to the Deanery, the Dean is rescued and the various secrets emerge. Salome and Sheba have won fifty pounds at the races and accepted Tarver and Darbey; Georgiana has won £1,500 on the Handicap. The strychnine is traced to Blore, whose confession clears the Dean of poisoning the horse, though it reveals the Dean’s own concealed betting. Noah’s final accusation also collapses. Georgiana concludes that the Dean’s deceptions have damaged his authority, but offers help for the Spire through George Tidd. The play ends with the household accepting friendly laughter at the Dean’s folly.

records.l: Salome, Dandy Dick
records.s: Salome Jedd is Dr. Jedd’s about twenty-three-year-old daughter, sister to Sheba, niece to Georgiana Tidman, and the Dean’s child. An inexperienced young lady and a clergyman’s wife in training, she shares Sheba’s “wickedness and rebellion,” debts, and desire for independence. At first attracted to Gerald Tarver, she secretly plans a costly French Revolution costume and a visit to Durnstone’s masked ball despite the family’s need to retrench. With Sheba, she seeks Georgiana’s help to win money on Dandy Dick, joins plans to leave the Deanery, and assists the distressed Major Tarver. After the ball is cancelled, she returns angry over the wet journey and wasted expense, confronts Darbey and Tarver, then helps them escape. In the end, she accepts Major Tarver, is exposed as having attended the ball and incurred part of the £40 19s bill, confronts the Dean’s deception, and resolves with Sheba to begin life afresh after their marriage proposals.

records.l: Sheba, Dandy Dick
records.s: Sheba Jedd is a seventeen-year-old young lady, daughter of Augustin Jedd, niece of Georgiana Tidman, sister of Salome Jedd, and a clergyman’s wife in training. She is engaged to Mr. Darbey and attracted to Nugent Darbey. With Salome, she has little money, owes forty pounds, nineteen shillings, and shares a spirit of wickedness and rebellion. Distressed by the cost of a flower-girl costume, she plans to attend a masked ball with Darbey, seeks money from Dr. Jedd, and initially resents Georgiana’s arrival before quickly liking her. The sisters accept Georgiana’s betting plan to win money through Dandy Dick, secretly leave the Deanery, and attend the Durnstone ball in scandalous costumes. Though the ball is cancelled, they win fifty pounds at the Races but face the costume bill. Sheba helps protect Darbey, accepts his proposal after hesitation, and finally confronts the Dean over his deception and intended marriage.

records.l: Dr. Jedd, Dandy Dick
records.s: Dr. Jedd, also called Augustin and the Dean of St. Marvells, is a widowed father of Salome and Sheba, brother of Georgiana Tidman, and resident master of the Deanery. He is institutionally aligned with the Bishop of St. Marvells and concerned with the Minister Spire’s restoration. Though he has unpaid bills and no spare cash for his daughters’ dresses, he conditionally pledges one thousand pounds to the Restoration Fund if seven others match it. When seven wealthy donors do so, his obligation becomes pressing. Georgiana comes to live at the Deanery, embarrassing the dignified Dean through her racing language, manners, and association with Dandy Dick. He fears both her influence and the approaching races. After the Swan Inn burns, Georgiana seeks to house Dandy Dick at the Deanery; the Dean objects but cannot prevent Dandy Dick and Sir Tristram from staying. Financial pressure over the Spire leads him to let Georgiana place a fifty-pound bet on Dandy Dick through his long-serving butler, Edward Blore. Believing he is humanely treating a suffering horse’s chills, Dr. Jedd prepares and administers a veterinary bolus to Dandy Dick. It is taken as an attempt to give the horse an unfair advantage, and Blore identifies him as the supposed villain. Arrested in the Deanery stables for trespassing, handcuffed, and taken to the lock-up, he is also associated with accusations over Dandy Dick’s treatment and the Swan Inn fire. His disappearance alarms others; his family influence seems lost and his cherished dignity crushed. In the cell, Hannah recognizes and briefly frees him, but he refuses escape from conscience and concern for dignity. Noah recaptures him. Once identified as the Dean rather than an unknown intruder, he mildly accepts Noah’s error, withdraws any charge against the person found on his premises, and invites Noah and Hannah to dinner.

records.l: Major Tarver, Dandy Dick
records.s: Major Tarver is a middle-aged Army officer and gentleman in the Hussars, an invalid with an unstable liver whose excitement alternates with depression. At the Deanery, he helps arrange the evening and the girls’ costumes, plans to attend the ball as Charles the First, and loves Salome Jedd passionately. After dinner he suffers indigestion, loses the music for his intended song, and leaves when the Swan Inn fire is controlled. Later, shabby and miserable in his Cavalier costume, he carries a carriage umbrella, says the Military were summoned to St. Marvells, and begs Salome to smile on him again. Finally, weak and supported by Mr. Darbey, he claims rejection will ruin his health and is accepted by Salome.

records.l: Mr. Darbey, Dandy Dick
records.s: Mr. Darbey, Nugent Darbey, is a young, pompous Hussar lieutenant, officer, gentleman, and violin player, though also classified as a civilian in the military-civilian distinction. He loves and is attracted to Sheba Jedd. He first visits the Deanery with Gerald Tarver, helps arrange the girls’ attendance at a ball, and plans to appear as Charles the Martyr. He patronizes and quarrels with the Dean, plays violin with Sheba accompanying, resents Major Tarver’s singing, and later returns for his violin. In shabby Cavalier dress, he says the ball was cancelled and guards the ruined Swan Inn with Tarver. Finally, he brings Major Tarver to Salome and Sheba, then proposes to Sheba; after reflection, she accepts.

records.l: Blore, Dandy Dick
records.s: Blore is the venerable-looking butler and servant of Augustin, the Dean, working in the Deanery household. He is acquainted with Hannah Topping and gambles on horse races, both for himself and on commission for the kitchen. Hoping Bonny Betsy will win, he stakes his savings and then the Restoration Fund money on that horse. After taking the Dean’s fifty pounds to bet on Dandy Dick, he secretly puts strychnine in Dandy Dick’s bolus. He later visits Hannah at the police station, worried about the case’s effect on the Dean and Dandy Dick. Blore finally confesses his betting and poisoning; the Dean retains him in service in return for silence.

records.l: Georgiana, Dandy Dick
records.s: Georgiana Tidman, Mrs. Tidman, is the widowed younger sister of Augustin Jedd, the Dean, aunt of Salome and Sheba, and resident guest at the Deanery. A high-spirited but self-described feeble woman with a keen sense of right and wrong, she is devoted to horse racing, gambling on races, and her half-share in Dandy Dick. After her husband's death she continued his career as a horse-breeder and gentleman jockey under the racing name George Tidd, wearing crimson and black diamonds; she ultimately lost her horses and property. At the Deanery she arrives in masculine racing dress, declares her ownership interest in Dandy Dick, plans to bet every penny on him, and persuades others to stake money on the horse despite promising not to own one while among the Canons and Bishop. She serves tea while studying betting, rushes to save horses during the Swan Inn fire, shelters Dandy Dick in the Deanery stables, and worries over his singed tail during the storm. She presses the Dean to wager on Dandy Dick to aid the Spire, organizes food and champagne for the horse, and protects Salome and Sheba. She accompanies Sir Tristram in seeking the missing Dean, helps rally race-course associates to rescue him from the Hill, and wins fifteen hundred pounds on the Handicap. She becomes engaged to Sir Tristram and helps reveal Blore's strychnine in the bolus. At the end, she rebukes the Dean for deception and lost dignity, while offering George Tidd's thousand-pound loan for the Spire if he accepts being laughed at as a Sporting Dean.

records.l: the Deanery, Dandy Dick
records.s: The Deanery of St. Marvells is the residence of Dr. Jedd, the Dean, and home to Salome and Sheba. It includes a morning-room with a piano, stables, an old nursery available for lodging, and a kitchen, and it employs Deanery servants. It begins as the site of visits by Gerald Tarver and Nugent Darbey for ball plans and the expected arrival of Georgiana Tidman. Georgiana arrives as Augustin’s widowed sister, reunites with Augustin and Sir Tristram, and imagines remaining through the autumn meeting. The Deanery then hosts dinner and an evening gathering of tea, violin playing, and news of the Restoration Fund. After the Swan Inn fire, its stables shelter Dandy Dick, while the old nursery houses Sir Tristram. Smoking, the horse, gambling, and Georgiana’s conduct disrupt the Dean’s formerly respectable peace. Later, the household responds to an arrest and expected visit, the Dean is brought home and calls for comfort, the masked-ball attendance of his daughters is exposed, and Noah traces an unknown man there. The kitchen is offered to Noah and Hannah for lodging and dinner.

records.l: St. Marvells, Dandy Dick
records.s: St. Marvells is a locality with little serious crime, a police station, and a small class of expected offenders; it returns a Conservative. Augustin Jedd is Dean, and Noah becomes Head Constable after arriving with Hannah. On the eve of races there, Georgiana arrives at the Deanery, troubling Augustin.

records.l: Durnstone, Dandy Dick
records.s: Durnstone is a place containing the Athenaeum and the destination police station. It hosts a Fancy Dress Masked Ball, with Gerald Tarver and Nugent Darbey stationed there, and Georgiana Tidman stays at the Wheatsheaf. Later Noah plans to take a prisoner and the Dean there, where the Bench sits and the Dean’s case can be reported.

records.l: Durnstone Athenaeum, Dandy Dick
records.s: The Durnstone Athenaeum is where Salome and Sheba arrived expecting the ball, only to find a notice on the front door announcing its cancellation.

records.l: Fancy Dress Masked Ball at Durnstone, Dandy Dick
records.s: The Fancy Dress Masked Ball at Durnstone, promoted by the Officers of the Hussars, is planned for one night, with Salome and Sheba intending to attend secretly with Gerald Tarver and Nugent Darbey. Although a notice says it is cancelled after the Military are summoned to St. Marvells, it ultimately takes place; Salome and Sheba attend in French Revolution lady and flower-girl costumes.

records.l: St. Marvells Spring Meeting, Dandy Dick
records.s: The races at St. Marvells are scheduled for the following day and are a source of anxiety for Augustin because of Georgiana's racing interests. Georgiana and Sir Tristram discuss Dandy Dick's chances in connection with them. The Races are attended by Georgiana, Salome, and Sheba, with Georgiana winning fifteen hundred pounds over the Handicap and the girls winning fifty pounds. Dandy Dick wins, while Bonny Betsy loses.

records.l: Durnstone Handicap, Dandy Dick
records.s: The Durnstone Handicap is a horse race scheduled for the following day. Dandy Dick, ridden by Tom Gallawood at nine stone two, and Bonny Betsy are contenders. Georgiana believes Dandy Dick has backed himself and worries cold water may have hurt his chances, though his singed tail reduces his carried weight. Despite ten-to-one odds against Dandy Dick, he is seen as strong, while Blore favors Bonny Betsy.

records.l: the Restoration Fund, Dandy Dick
records.s: The Restoration Fund supports Minster Spire restoration. In the second act, it benefits from the Dean’s public thousand-pound offer, prompting seven wealthy donors to give matching sums; the Dean also directs a wager expected to add five hundred pounds toward the Spire.

records.l: the Minister Spire, Dandy Dick
records.s: The Minster Spire, somewhat out of repair, faces crumbling unless restoration begins immediately. The Dean, its principal creditor, offers a thousand-pound loan for preservation or repair, while Georgiana proposes using Dandy Dick’s race winnings to help fund the work.

records.l: the scandalous costumes, Dandy Dick
records.s: Dresses made in London from patterns as a French Revolution gown and flower-girl outfit arrive as cast-off clothing, cost forty pounds nineteen shillings, and are raffled for local charities.

records.l: the account for the fancy dresses, Dandy Dick
records.s: The account for the fancy dresses is a cash bill from Lewis Isaacs, Costumier to the Queen, for costumes hired for the masked ball at Durnstone. It totals forty pounds, nineteen shillings, including fifteen guineas for Salome’s gown, ten guineas for Sheba’s costume, trimmings, extras, and mislaid brown-paper patterns. Salome and Sheba owe the bill without Augustin’s knowledge and possess only fifteen shillings and threepence, so they seek Georgiana’s help to win money. The Dean, himself unable to settle his bills, later discovers the account and demands that the girls explain it; they promise to pay with their winnings.

records.l: retrenchment, Dandy Dick
records.s: is_a household policy [advocated by Dr. Jedd] Dr. Jedd says that the family's spending on clothes and other bills must be stopped and summarizes the solution as 'Retrench and Rejoice.' He hopes Georgiana Tidman will help impose the precepts of retrenchment.

records.l: the family finances, Dandy Dick
records.s: are_limited considerably under five hundred pounds [immediately commandable by Dr. Jedd] The family finances are strained by £156, 18 shillings and 3 pence in existing bills and by the costly dresses. Dr. Jedd says that he can immediately command considerably under £500, while he has pledged £1,000 to the Minister Spire restoration fund if seven other donors match it.

records.l: Sir Tristram, Dandy Dick
records.s: Sir Tristram is a bachelor, former Oxford associate and friend of Augustin Jedd, and a horseman/racing enthusiast. He stays at the Swan Inn with his horse, is a guest at the Deanery, habitually smokes a pipe, and co-owns the racehorse Dandy Dick, holding one half. Visiting Augustin, he eagerly discusses Dandy Dick's prospects in the Durnstone Handicap and learns that Georgiana, formerly George Tidd, owns the other half; they agree the horse is fit and likely to win. After Dandy Dick is rescued from the Swan Inn with a singed tail after cold water has been thrown over him, Sir Tristram and Georgiana arrange to move him to the Deanery stables. During a storm at the Deanery, Sir Tristram shares Georgiana's concern for the horse and hides with her to watch suspicious movement in the garden. He confronts Darbey and Tarver, questions Hatcham about the person who set fire to the inn, accompanies Georgiana to the police-station, dictates a description of the missing Dean, and helps plan and carry out the Dean's release and rescue. Learning that a bolus contained strychnine, he denounces the Dean. He proposes to Georgiana and is accepted. Finally, he helps show that the person secured in the stable is not the Dean and tells the Dean that there is no harm in laughter.

records.l: the Swan Inn, Dandy Dick
records.s: The Swan Inn is a place destroyed by fire. In the evening it catches fire; its horses are cleared out and Dandy Dick is rescued, with Georgiana proposing the Deanery stables. It is then reduced to guarded ruins.

records.l: Dandy Dick, Dandy Dick
records.s: Dandy Dick is a sporting racehorse owned jointly by Sir Tristram Mardon and Georgiana Tidman. Wearing black-and-white colors with a pink cap and ridden by Tom Gallawood, he is entered in the Durnstone Handicap, also called Dandy Dick’s handicap. Sir Tristram considers him fit and properly weighted, while Georgiana, confident from knowing him thoroughly, buys a half share and bets on him. After a fire at the Swan Inn, where he had been stabled, he is rescued safe but cold and with a singed, later reported lost, tail. He is sheltered in the Deanery stables, feeds steadily, and is treated cautiously for a possible chill while remaining a favored contender, ahead of Bonny Betsy according to the Dean. His prospects are endangered when Blore secretly adds strychnine to his bolus; reports then reveal that he was being nobbled and had been dosed, though the chemist’s analysis is pending. Despite these dangers, Dandy Dick runs and wins the Races in a common canter, after the Dean has instructed Blore to back him for the Restoration Fund.

records.l: Bonny Betsy, Dandy Dick
records.s: A horse handicap-race entrant loses the Races, finishing behind Dandy Dick with the policeman, after Blore plans to remove Dandy Dick but mistakenly wagers on her.

records.l: horse racing, Dandy Dick
records.s: is_a sport Horse racing has been a major part of Georgiana's past and remains an interest she cannot abandon. She says that she cannot live without horseflesh and continues to understand racing form, colors, stables, and betting despite promising Augustin that she would not own anything on four legs.

records.l: betting on Dandy Dick, Dandy Dick
records.s: is_intended_to_win the thousand-pound wager [Georgiana Tidman's stated ambition] Georgiana decides to bet every penny she has on Dandy Dick after judging that he is fit to win. She then agrees to let Salome and Sheba stake their limited money on him in hopes of covering their debt.

records.l: the thousand-pound wager, Dandy Dick
records.s: Georgiana Tidman proposes a thousand-sovereign wager tied to becoming richer by the next night and to her position in the Deanery. Alongside this, a race wager using the Dean’s fifty pounds was meant to back Dandy Dick for the Restoration Fund, but Blore placed it on Bonny Betsy.

records.l: Hatcham, Dandy Dick
records.s: Hatcham is a groom and stable man. He watches Dandy Dick overnight, carries Dandy’s dose, and reports that the villain who burned the Swan Inn was caught administering it and taken by constable to the lock-up.

records.l: the Military, Dandy Dick
records.s: is_summoned_to St. Marvells The Military were summoned to St. Marvells, preventing the ball from taking place. Darbey and Tarver say they were responding to the call of duty.

records.l: the dinner, Dandy Dick
records.s: is_a dinner [hot and served with ale] The dinner at the Deanery is called a success, although the mutton is overdone, the potatoes rattle, the custards are a first attempt, and the chimney appears to need sweeping. The guests are mostly silent, and the women jokingly describe it as a frightfully jolly dinner.

records.l: the fire at the Swan Inn, Dandy Dick
records.s: The Swan Inn fire, a bright red conflagration, interrupts music at the Deanery. It singes Dandy Dick's tail, prompts his rescue and Georgiana's sheltering him there. Hatcham suspects arson, says the Dean set it, and reports a villain caught and taken to the lock-up.

records.l: the Restoration Fund offer, Dandy Dick
records.s: The Dean’s thousand-pound Restoration Fund offer attracts seven wealthy matching donors for the Minster Spire, then obliges him to pay his own contribution, causing distress.

records.l: Noah Topping, Dandy Dick
records.s: Noah Topping is the rural, ill-fittingly dressed Head Constable of St. Marvells, married to Hannah and running the police station strictly and rigidly. Jealous of Hannah’s male friends, he threatens them and reacts strongly when he finds the Dean with her, locking the Dean in a cell and inventing charges including alienating Hannah’s affections and embezzling his meal. He holds an unknown man in custody, believes this lawful, and plans to take a prisoner to Durnstone after dinner, with a stop to see racing. He first suggests the missing Dean committed suicide, then produces and escorts the handcuffed Dean. Later, dishevelled, he says a lover escaped custody, wrongly identifies the Dean as that man, and is corrected before accepting an invitation to dinner with Hannah.

records.l: the military summons to St. Marvells, Dandy Dick
records.s: A military summons to St. Marvells sends the Military away, intended to watch the fire at the Swan; the ball is cancelled; Salome and Sheba enter.

records.l: gambling on horse races, Dandy Dick
records.s: takes_place_at St. Marvells [including Tattersall's Ring] Gambling on horse races becomes a possible solution to the Dean's financial problems when Georgiana urges him to stake fifty pounds on Dandy Dick. Blore reveals that he has previously gambled at races and accepts the Dean's money to place the wager.

records.l: the restoration of the Spire, Dandy Dick
records.s: The restoration of the Spire urgently needs about a thousand pounds to prevent collapse; lacking funds, Georgiana proposes a Dandy Dick wager to finance immediate work.

records.l: the Restoration Fund money, Dandy Dick
records.s: is_intended_for the Restoration Fund [fifty pounds] The Restoration Fund money consists of the fifty pounds the Dean gave Blore to wager on Dandy Dick. Blore instead placed it on Bonny Betsy, which lost.

records.l: the Bolus, Dandy Dick
records.s: The Bolus is a simple veterinary remedy for chills, carried in a basin by Hatcham and administered by the Dean to Dandy. Presented as a remedy, it was intended by the Dean to affect the race outcome. Blore secretly introduced a foreign element, and analysis found sixteen grains of strychnine.

records.l: strychnine, Dandy Dick
records.s: Strychnine, a poison and chief ingredient of a sixteen-grain bolus, was added by Blore to get Dandy Dick out of the race.

records.l: Augustin Jedd, Dandy Dick
records.s: Augustin Jedd is the Dean and Georgiana’s brother. He secretly directs Blore to back Dandy Dick with fifty pounds from the Restoration Fund, then deceives Sir Tristram and his daughters about his absence and the race wager. Detained by police for playing the three-card trick, he is rescued by Georgiana and Sir Tristram after being forcibly taken home from the Hill. He is horrified to discover that a bolus contained strychnine. Noah Topping also alleges that he is Hannah’s unknown lover and holds him in lawful custody before he is rescued, though Hatcham disputes that the man in the stable was the Dean.

records.l: the police station, Dandy Dick
records.s: The police station is an auxiliary country station in St. Marvells, partly a kitchen and containing official documents, implements, and a prisoner’s cell. Hannah cooks and admits visitors, Noah works as constable, and Georgiana and Sir Tristram report the Dean’s disappearance. The Dean is held there before transfer to Durnstone.

records.l: the arrest of the Dean, Dandy Dick
records.s: The arrest of the Dean follows his being caught administering a dose to Dandy and found trespassing in the Deanery stables. He is taken by cart to the lock-up, held overnight at St. Marvells under the usual rule, then brought from his cell in handcuffs and taken toward Durnstone.

records.l: the notice cancelling the ball, Dandy Dick
records.s: The notice cancelling the ball is posted on the front door of the Durnstone Athenaeum and reads, "Ball knocked on the head--Vivat Regina."

records.l: Hannah Topping, Dandy Dick
records.s: Hannah Topping, also called Hannah Evans and Mrs. Topping, is a young, skilled cook who formerly served the Dean at the Deanery and is Noah’s wife. At St. Marvells police station, where she cooks, she finds her former master imprisoned. Using the Dean’s whistle and plans involving old Nick, a cart, handcuffs, and a duplicate key, she tries to free and feed him, but Noah discovers the effort and the Dean is returned to his cell. She later admits Georgiana and Sir Tristram, continues arranging escape, and seeks forgiveness and reconciliation with the Dean for Noah.

records.l: the prisoner's cell, Dandy Dick
records.s: is_a strong-box [the local name for the cell] The prisoner's cell, called the Strong-box in St. Marvells, is entered through a massive door with a wicket and iron grating. Hannah unlocks it with a duplicate key to release the Dean, and Noah later locks the Dean inside again.

records.l: the arrested man, Dandy Dick
records.s: is_accused_of the alleged trespassing and attempted larceny [at the Deanery stables] The arrested man is described in the official book as a person found trespassing in the Deanery stables who refuses to give his name or any account of himself. He is the Dean, though Noah initially does not recognize him.

records.l: the journey to Durnstone, Dandy Dick
records.s: uses the cart [driven by Noah Topping] Noah intends to drive the Dean to Durnstone after dinner, using old Nick and passing the edge of the hill to get a glimpse of the racing. Hannah plans for the Dean to escape from the moving cart in Pear Tree Lane, but the plan is not carried out in this unit.

records.l: crime, Dandy Dick
records.s: Hannah says that crime levels everyone and believes the Dean's first offence merits giving him another start in life. The Dean insists that he is legally innocent, though he admits to a temporary moral aberration.

records.l: the alleged trespassing and attempted larceny, Dandy Dick
records.s: In the third act, the Dean is found trespassing in the Deanery stables, with an alleged intent connected to petty or attempted larceny, though no attempted larceny is proved. Hannah warns of a more serious charge, and Noah additionally accuses the Dean of alienating his wife's affections.

records.l: old Nick, Dandy Dick
records.s: Old Nick is a former Durnstone Fire Brigade horse. Noah plans to use him to take a cart quickly toward Durnstone, despite Hannah calling him vicious; his brigade service makes him answer a familiar double whistle. Later Hannah expects him to help bring the Dean back, but Noah leaves him at home.

records.l: Kitty, Dandy Dick
records.s: is_in Noah's cart Kitty is put in Noah's cart while Old Nick is left at home. Hannah realizes that this substitution prevents the Dean's planned escape.

records.l: Noah's cart, Dandy Dick
records.s: Noah's cart is a vehicle for taking the Dean, Augustin Jedd, to Durnstone, drawn by Old Nick on the journey. It contains Kitty and stands outside the police-station. Hannah's plan has the Dean jump clear and use a whistle while Old Nick runs on, but Noah leaves Old Nick at home.

records.l: the handcuffs, Dandy Dick
records.s: are_unlocked_by the duplicate key [after Noah is left behind] Noah selects and examines a pair of handcuffs before preparing to take the prisoner to Durnstone. Hannah gives the Dean a small key that will unlock them once he is free from Noah.

records.l: the duplicate key, Dandy Dick
records.s: unlocks the handcuffs [after the arrested man gets free from Noah] Hannah produces a duplicate key to the Strong-box and uses it to unlock the cell door. She later gives the Dean a small key intended to unlock his handcuffs during the planned escape.

records.l: the Dean's whistle, Dandy Dick
records.s: The Dean’s whistle, possessed by Augustin Jedd, is Hannah’s whistle. In the third act, Hannah gives it to the Dean and instructs him to blow in Pear Tree Lane and after leaving the cart. Its double-whistle signal summons old Nick to help return him safely to the Deanery.

records.l: the joint, Dandy Dick
records.s: is_favored_by Noah Topping [as a meal] The joint is Hannah's cooked meal and Noah's favorite dish. The Dean eats it after escaping from the cell, and Noah treats his eating of it as the embezzling of his midday meal.

records.l: the Dean's dignity, Dandy Dick
records.s: is_valued_by the Dean [as a priceless possession of middle age] The Dean calls his dignity a priceless possession of man's middle age. He refuses to notify the Deanery because appearing in the police records and returning publicly would seriously impair it.

records.l: Hannah's cooking, Dandy Dick
records.s: is_skillful highly [praised by the Dean] Hannah's cooking is presented as a source of comfort and leverage. The Dean recognizes her culinary skill, eats the joint she prepares, and admits that if every mouthful could carry him back an hour he would finish it.

records.l: the attempted escape plan, Dandy Dick
records.s: Hannah proposes that the Dean and Noah ride in a cart, signal at Pear Tree Lane, escape, and free the arrested man with a duplicate key after Noah and old Nick depart. The Dean rejects it, and Noah’s return prevents any attempt.

records.l: the charge of alienating Hannah's affections, Dandy Dick
records.s: is_held_against the Dean [by Noah Topping] Noah threatens to add a charge of alienating Hannah's affections to the charges already standing against the Dean. He makes the threat after finding the Dean being served Hannah's cooking.

records.l: the Dean's disappearance, Dandy Dick
records.s: is_reported_in the missing-person report Georgiana and Sir Tristram report that Augustin Jedd disappeared after retiring to rest and could not be found in the morning. The disappearance is complicated by the discovery that he is being held in the police-station cell.

records.l: the Dean's alleged suicide, Dandy Dick
records.s: is_a theory [Noah's theory] Noah theorizes that the missing Dean's disappearance is an ordinary case of suicide. Georgiana and Sir Tristram reject the idea, and the Dean is subsequently found alive in the cell.

records.l: the Dean's treatment of Dandy Dick, Dandy Dick
records.s: is_a simple remedy for chills [administered to a suffering beast] The Dean says he was administering a simple remedy for chills to a suffering beast. Georgiana says the analysis has not yet returned from the chemist, so the treatment's nature is not yet established.

records.l: the analysis, Dandy Dick
records.s: identifies strychnine [as sixteen grains in the bolus] The analysis of the bolus is brought to the Deanery by the chemist. It reports that the bolus contains sixteen grains of strychnine, prompting Sir Tristram and Georgiana to denounce the Dean before Blore confesses.

records.l: the Dean's deception, Dandy Dick
records.s: The Dean's deception includes hiding his absence and his involvement in the race wager from his family. Salome and Sheba discover that he has stooped to deception, while he also learns that they concealed their attendance at the masked ball and their gambling winnings.

records.l: the proposed marriages, Dandy Dick
