records.s: Major Tarver proposes to Salome and Mr. Darbey proposes to Sheba; both proposals are accepted. Sir Tristram also proposes to Georgiana, and she agrees to marry him.

records.l: Deception, Dandy Dick
records.s: is_a horse [called Deception] Deception is described by the Dean as having frosted the genial summer of the Deanery with the winter of Deceit. Georgiana says that once a person begins to use deception, it takes control and becomes difficult to stop.

records.l: the horse called Deception, Dandy Dick
records.s: is_a horse [named Deception] Georgiana compares Deception to a horse that takes the bit between its teeth once it is driven with the whip. She says that the Dean has been riding this horse hardest.

records.l: laughter at the Dean's expense, Dandy Dick
records.s: Laughter at the Dean's expense is proposed for a Sporting Dean; Sir Tristram permits it as harmless, while Georgiana limits it to friendly mockery of folly, not virtue, before Noah Topping rushes in dishevelled.

records.l: Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: This document is a collection of short stories centered on New York, Philadelphia, and Monte Carlo characters whose crises are resolved through courage, compassion, reconciliation, or impulsive generosity. It opens with office-boy Gallegher identifying fugitive Stephen S. Hade at Torresdale. He helps Michael E. Dwyer and Detective Hefflefinger seize Hade during an illegal prizefight, then risks arrest and pursuit to bring Dwyer’s report to the Philadelphia Press before deadline; the managing editor restores Gallegher’s position. Young Van Bibber next breaks his engagement, realizes his love for his fiancée, finds her in Central Park, and is understood to become engaged again. Rags Raegen, hiding after striking Pike McGonegal, finds abandoned baby Margaret, struggles to keep her alive, and finally surrenders at the Twenty-first Precinct so she can receive care; months later, he values her affection despite awaiting trial. In “The Other Woman,” the bishop tests Young Latimer’s suitability for Ellen by probing an earlier love. Ellen’s joking intervention turns painful, and Latimer leaves when she rejects his explanation that his past suffering made him worthy. Snipes, a homeless trailer for Alf Wolfe’s gang, helps bring an old farmer and Abraham together, but declines an offer of farm life to remain in New York. The ruined Goodwood Plunger, Cecil Harringford, arrives at Monte Carlo intending suicide, but helping a French couple preserve gambling winnings for a bakery changes him; he decides to return to England. Miss Catherwaight’s investigation of a pawned medal reunites Lewis Lockwood and Judge Burgoyne, former friends divided by a misunderstanding involving her mother. Several Van Bibber stories close the collection: he pays for East Side girls to ride swan-boats, sends an escaped burglar toward his family despite later learning his identity, and ingeniously arranges the eloping Standish and Miss Cambridge’s proper public wedding while misleading Standish’s older brother.

records.l: Rags Raegen, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Rags Raegen, also called Ragsey or Rags, is a young tough, ice-cart driver, and exceptional underwater swimmer tied to East River and Cherry Street thieves and bullies. Burdened by criminal bonds and a record dating to age ten, he is their hero but eventually shakes the gang's control. After a fight in which he shoots Pike McGonegal, he is pursued by police and accused of murder, though he claims self-defence. He escapes by seeming to drown in the East River and hides in Case's tenement, where he finds the sick, starving baby Margaret. Protecting, feeding, cooling, and comforting her changes him: despite considering flight after learning McGonegal has died, he cannot abandon her. He carries Margaret to the station-house for food and medical attention and voluntarily surrenders. Confined in the Tombs as the case awaits its outcome, he receives daily visits from the baby and later says he does not regret surrendering or leaving the gang, even when he expected to hang.

records.l: Miss Catherwaight, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Miss Catherwaight is a clever young woman, considered cynical by some friends for her collection of dishonored medals and her remarks about society. Once seen as cold and self-possessed, she travels widely with Mr. Catherwaight and regularly visits pawnshops and loan offices to buy decorations and uncover their histories. Her interest in a silver heart medal leads her to Lewis Lyman Lockwood. Ashamed of intruding into its story, she learns that Lockwood and Burgoyne were separated by a misunderstanding involving her mother. She urges Lockwood to keep the medal and reconcile with Burgoyne, hoping to repair harm her mother caused unwittingly.

records.l: Van Bibber, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Van Bibber is a twenty-five-year-old New Yorker: a wealthy, popular yet unspoiled young club man, respectable in society, fond of adventure, and possessed of a good heart. Though experienced as a best man or usher, he is not practised at lying. His emotional story begins when he breaks off his engagement and tells himself he should remain a bachelor. Remembering the three months with his fiancée, he realizes she was the source of his happiness, returns with the ring to their secluded place in Central Park, and rushes to her when he finds her there. On a hot day in the Park, initially cross and sleepy, he pays for three East Side girls to ride the swan-boats, accompanies them, shows them the sights, and buys them more tickets. After confronting and disarming a burglar, he chooses not to surrender him; instead he sends him west to Helena with a ticket and money, later learning the man was the escaped Abe Hubbard, alias Jimmie the Gent. Finally, as Cortlandt Van Bibber, he protects young Standish's elopement with Miss Cambridge through a false claim, organizes their formal wedding, and serves as best man, though he regrets where he sent Standish's brother.

records.l: Gallegher, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Gallegher is a young office-boy at the Press, living alone with his mother in a little house in the extreme northern part of Philadelphia. Short, broad, solid, muscular, and perpetually smiling, he has bright black eyes, street-trained knowledge, and an unusually developed talent for detection. His chief interest is crime: he knows criminals’ aliases, methods, imprisonment, whereabouts, and transgressions, and knows the officers of the twenty-second police district by name. He recognizes Stephen S. Hade from a possibly artificial finger, follows him from Kensington railroad station to Torresdale and the Eagle Inn, telegraphs Detective Hefflefinger, and brings the discovery to Michael E. Dwyer. He joins Dwyer and Hefflefinger, directs their cab, plans an escape route, enters Keppler’s barn, watches from a haymow, and helps identify and secure Hade. When Dwyer’s notebook must reach the Press, Gallegher takes it, deceives the gate officers, flees by cab, and drives through the night toward Philadelphia. Delayed, wet, exhausted, and nearly unable to stand, he reaches the Press with Dwyer’s copy, reports Hade’s capture and Dwyer’s arrest, and proudly says he beat the town.

records.l: the Press, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: The Press is a newspaper in Philadelphia. It employs Gallegher as an office-boy, but its managing editor discharges him for repeated truancy; Dwyer plans to seek his reinstatement after Gallegher discovers Hade. Late at night, its editors and compositors prepare the paper and await news of a fight and Hade’s arrest. The sporting editor sends a message, Dwyer acts as the Press’s representative, and payment depends on no other paper learning of the arrest. Gallegher races to deliver Dwyer’s notebook but is stopped seven blocks from the office.

records.l: Philadelphia, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Philadelphia is the city where Gallegher lives and works, with detailed knowledge of its police districts, criminals, and transportation. It lies about four miles south of the raid, glows faint yellow in the sky, is near Torresdale and the Eagle Inn, and is reached by Gallegher while delivering a report.

records.l: Richard F. Burrbank, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Richard F. Burrbank is a prominent, very wealthy New York railroad lawyer and railroad-stock owner, considered for many high offices, whose record ends with his being found dead from two pistol wounds above his heart.

records.l: the Burrbank murder, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: The Burrbank murder is an internationally reported investigation into Richard F. Burrbank’s killing, safe opening and $200,000 theft, with his secretary Stephen S. Hade suspected and missing.

records.l: Hade, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Hade, Richard F. Burrbank’s secretary, is suspected of Burrbank’s murder and the safe burglary on circumstantial evidence. After Burrbank’s death, he disappears, hiding near Torresdale as Mr. Carleton and using the alias Arlie Lane. Missing the right trigger finger shot off in childhood, he attends a fight in disguise, fearing Keppler and the risk of staying away. During a police raid, Hefflefinger seizes him; Hade offers money and part of his fortune for release, but is identified as the murderer, arrested, and captured.

records.l: the Champion of the United States, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: opposes the Would-be Champion [in the big fight] The Champion of the United States is scheduled to take part in a major fight near Philadelphia.

records.l: the Would-be Champion, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: The Would-be Champion is scheduled to fight the Champion of the United States near Philadelphia.

records.l: the Heenan-Sayers fight, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: The Heenan-Sayers fight is a heavily publicized contest between the Champion of the United States and the Would-be Champion, scheduled near Philadelphia in the Eagle Inn barn with $250 tickets. Editors await confirmation, initially doubting it occurred, until Gallegher brings the report. Correspondents urgently describe the fight and Hade’s final capture; afterward, the correspondents are arrested, and Captain Scott cites the fight as evidence that they broke the peace.

records.l: Detective Hefflefinger, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Detective Hefflefinger is a detective on Inspector Byrnes’s staff and in Byrnes’s detective force, carrying a badge and warrant. He comes to Philadelphia seeking a burglar, but the burglar has escaped. After Gallegher reports that Hade is near Torresdale, Hefflefinger agrees to arrest Hade quietly under a burglary pretext. He enters a barn, watches Hade during a fight, captures and handcuffs him in a police raid, rejects his bribe, and plans to take him to the station and then New York.

records.l: Inspector Byrnes, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Inspector Byrnes supervises the detective staff to which Detective Hefflefinger belongs.

records.l: New York, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: New York is a crowded, harsh place linked by trains and marked by the Bowery, Broadway, Thirty-fifth Street, pawnshops, loan offices, drug-store and cigar-store post-offices, vice, crime, poverty, and green-goods operations. Its scattered private post-offices are said to make vice and crime easy. It is repeatedly a destination and setting for danger: Richard F. Burrbank is murdered there, Hade is to be taken there after a planned arrest, and secrecy depends on newspapers there learning nothing. Snipes knows the city but refuses to exchange it for the country. After Mrs. Catherwaight's death, Miss Catherwaight's father and daughter live and entertain there while she searches for medals. At dawn, Van Bibber returns from Jersey City through nearly deserted streets; a reporter calls the city exciting yet brutal and commonplace, shaped by recurring crime and poverty. Van Bibber then helps a burglar leave by train.

records.l: Kensington railroad station, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: is_in Philadelphia [near Gallegher's home] Kensington railroad station is near Gallegher's home and has trains running toward the suburbs and New York. Gallegher sees the suspected Hade there, follows him, and boards the train to Torresdale.

records.l: Torresdale, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Torresdale is a station outside Philadelphia on the Pennsylvania Railroad, near the old Eagle Inn. It matters as the site where suspected Hade gets off, Gallegher arranges Detective Hefflefinger’s meeting, and plans are made to take Hade away on the one o’clock train. A cab reaches Torresdale; nearby, at Keppler’s barn, Hade is arrested after a fight.

records.l: the old Eagle Inn, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: is_a old roadside hostelry [known as a headquarters for pothunters and a battle-ground of cock-fights] The Eagle Inn is an old roadside hostelry near Torresdale known as a gathering place for pothunters and cock-fights. The suspected Hade, using the name Mr. Carleton, is staying there, and the big fight is scheduled in its barn.

records.l: Mr. Carleton, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Mr. Carleton is the assumed name of a well-dressed, gloved man staying at the Eagle Inn for his health; he acts nervously when asked about a fight, and Gallegher believes he is Stephen S. Hade.

records.l: Michael E. Dwyer, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Michael E. Dwyer is the sporting editor of the Press. After hearing Gallegher’s important report, he plans and joins a quiet trip to Torresdale with Gallegher and Detective Hefflefinger to secure Hade’s secret arrest, protect the story from competing papers, offer and share a $500 reward, and recommend Gallegher’s reinstatement.

records.l: the police, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: The police raid Keppler’s barn during a fight, break down doors, and trigger panic. They hem in and arrest newspaper correspondents and others, guard the gate, use patrol-wagons for prisoners, and permit Hefflefinger through after he shows a badge. After Gallegher escapes, an officer fires shots; city officers later stop his cab for unlit lamps and let it continue.

records.l: the $5,000 reward, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: The $5,000 reward is offered for Hade’s capture and delivery to the police. Dwyer says it will belong to Gallegher if Hade is caught, then offers Hefflefinger part of it for a secret arrest that keeps other newspapers uninformed.

records.l: the stolen fortune, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: The stolen fortune is $200,000 in bonds, stocks, and money, placed in Burrbank's safe the night before the murder and then taken.

records.l: Hade's arrest, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Hade's arrest is a secretly planned capture intended to avoid publicity from other newspapers. Gallegher and Michael E. Dwyer arrange for Detective Hefflefinger to seize the suspected Hade near the Eagle Inn after the fight and take him to New York on the one o'clock train. During a police raid, Hefflefinger uses his badge and a false burglary explanation to remove Hade from the barn. Editors waiting for confirmation are told by Gallegher that Hade was captured.

records.l: the Burrbank murder investigation, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: The investigation has produced a worldwide search for Stephen S. Hade, whose description was circulated by telegraph and cable. People suspected of being Hade have been arrested in various places, but Gallegher's discovery near Torresdale offers a possible breakthrough.

records.l: Mr. Dwyer, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Mr. Dwyer is a Press representative and newspaper correspondent serving as sporting editor. During a raid, he writes in Dwyer’s notebook, identifies himself to Hefflefinger, and offers $500 for Hade’s secret arrest as the supposed burglar. He enters Keppler’s barn, remains near Hade during the fight, and signals or identifies him. After Captain Scott orders the correspondents arrested, Dwyer resists, entrusts Gallegher with his notebook and report, and is arrested; Gallegher delivers Dwyer’s prepared copy to the Press.

records.l: the sporting crowd, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: is_composed_of sporting men [including club-men, brokers, politicians, comedians, amateur boxers, and others] The sporting crowd consists of sporting men, club-men, brokers, politicians, a comedian and his manager, amateur boxers, and others from cities around the country. Its members bet heavily, crowd around the ring, react violently to the fight, and panic when the police raid begins.

records.l: the fighters, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: are two prizefighters [physical combatants in the fight] The fighters enter the ring after the crowd has gathered and begin a brutal, closely contested bout. One fighter loses favor as the fight continues, while the other gains the advantage through repeated severe blows.

records.l: the barn (Keppler's barn), Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Keppler’s barn is a large building containing stalls, haymows, a ring, and a crowd gathered for an illegal fight. Gallegher and Hefflefinger enter through a window, and the police later raid it during the bout.

records.l: McGovern's cab, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: McGovern's cab, kept at Bachman's livery stable and associated with Luke McGovern, carries the sporting editor and Gallegher through a cold, snowy journey to Torresdale. It waits near the lower gate with its lamps out for a rapid departure. Later Gallegher finds it at the furthermost gate, frees it, and drives toward Philadelphia, where cabmen stop it and question him.

records.l: Gallegher's horse, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: pulls McGovern's cab [while driven by Gallegher] Gallegher's horse is chilled after standing in the cold but eagerly pulls the cab through the night. It carries him recklessly toward Philadelphia until the cabmen seize its head near the Press office.

records.l: the train, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: departs_for New York [at 1.20] The train passing the Torresdale station at 1.20 is intended to carry Hade secretly toward New York after his arrest. Hefflefinger plans to take that train with him.

records.l: the burglary, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: The burglary is the supposed offense used to conceal Hade’s true arrest. Hefflefinger tells the police that Hade is the burglar “Arlie” Lane, alias Carleton, and says he has papers authorizing the arrest.

records.l: the fight, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: is_a prizefighting [a secret bare-fist contest] The fight is held in Keppler’s barn before a carefully selected sporting crowd. It is a prolonged and exceptionally brutal contest, interrupted when the police break into the barn.

records.l: the police raid, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: The police raid targets a fight at the barn. It begins when barn doors are forced open, causing panic that scatters spectators; Hefflefinger seizes Hade and leaves. As the raid settles down, officers hold and arrest newspaper correspondents, amid disorder that lets Gallegher attempt to carry away the report.

records.l: the $500 payment, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: The $500 payment is the amount Dwyer promises Hefflefinger from the $5,000 reward for secretly arresting Hade. Hefflefinger expects to receive it after carrying out the plan.

records.l: the boxing ring, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: is_a square fighting enclosure [covered with sawdust and bounded by a heavy rope] The boxing ring is a square enclosure formed by wooden posts and heavy rope, with sawdust covering its floor. The two fighters battle inside it while the crowd presses around the ropes.

records.l: prizefighting, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Prizefighting draws the crowd to Keppler’s barn despite the storm and the threat of police interference. The illegal bout provides the setting in which Hade is located and arrested.

records.l: Captain Scott, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Captain Scott, a captain in charge of a raid, has newspaper correspondents arrested, declares they are under arrest, orders them taken to the station-house, and refuses release because they were under bonds to keep the peace and had fought again.

records.l: newspaper correspondents, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Newspaper correspondents, representing principal papers, are under peace bonds yet involved in a fight during a raid; as it settles, they demand to send reports, and Captain Scott arrests them for a station-house hearing.

records.l: police patrol-wagons, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: transport arrests of the newspaper men [to the station-house] Three police patrol-wagons move through the yard carrying unwilling prisoners packed together without protection from the sleet and rain. One patrol-wagon pursues Gallegher after he escapes, but he believes it is likely to become stuck in the mud.

records.l: arrests of the newspaper men, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Captain Scott orders the newspaper men taken into custody and sent to the station-house for a magistrate's hearing. The arrests threaten to delay their reports beyond the deadline for the next day's paper.

records.l: the Press office, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: The Press office is Gallegher's destination for delivering Dwyer's report. It is only seven blocks away when the cabmen stop him, and Gallegher insists that its staff will prove his story and pay for the cab's trip.

records.l: Dwyer's notebook, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Dwyer’s notebook contains his written account of the fight, including Gallegher’s work and Hade’s final capture. While the raid settles, Dwyer writes in it; Gallegher takes it from Dwyer’s coat, carries it toward the Press office, then hands over its damp, limp-covered copy.

records.l: the newspaper report of the fight, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: The newspaper report of the fight is the material Gallegher is trying to deliver before the printing forms are locked. Its timely arrival would allow the paper to beat the town and the country.

records.l: the patrol-wagon pursuit, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: pursues Gallegher's ride to the Press office [after Gallegher escapes the raid site] The patrol-wagon pursuit begins after Gallegher escapes from the raided house in McGovern's cab. Its gong and red and green lanterns follow him through the darkness, but the wagon falls behind as he drives toward Philadelphia.

records.l: managing editor, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: The managing editor of the Press uses a speaking-tube to tell the night editor there is no news, then orders printing to begin. When Gallegher arrives, he handles Dwyer’s copy, tends to the wet boy, and says he will not be dismissed.

records.l: night editor, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: The Press’s night editor, in the composing-room, repeatedly presses for news, urges printing rather than delay, and ends disappointed when Gallegher arrives.

records.l: city editor, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: A city editor in local and reportorial rooms seeks news, then helps a cab-driver support Gallegher into the composing-room and orders brandy.

records.l: Mr. Dwyer's copy, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: is_in notebook Gallegher delivers Mr. Dwyer's copy to the managing editor. The managing editor passes it to the foreman, who tears out its leaves and distributes them to the compositors.

records.l: news, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: The managing editor repeatedly answers that there is no news, and the city editor asks for an update. News finally arrives with Gallegher, who brings word of Mr. Dwyer's arrest and Hade's capture.

records.l: story, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: The editors hesitate to delay the paper for a purely hypothetical story. The night editor argues that if there were a story to print, Mr. Dwyer would have delivered it sooner.

records.l: printing the paper, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: is_delayed past the scheduled time [by the uncertainty about the story] The Press begins printing after the managing editor agrees that the paper cannot wait any longer. The foreman starts giving orders, but the arrival of Mr. Dwyer's copy allows the compositors to set the new material.

records.l: Van Bibber's fiancée, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Van Bibber's fiancée is a young, lovely, cultured woman, knowledgeable about the Louvre, painters, and cathedrals. After accepting a breakup and returning her engagement ring, she goes to their secluded box-bush dell, tearful, kisses a sprig of box, and is approached by Van Bibber.

records.l: the engagement and breakup, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: An engagement lasting three months of continual companionship ends when Van Bibber tries to make it appear his fiancée chose the separation. Regretting the breakup, he seeks her in a secluded dell; they reconcile and are seen driving home together.

records.l: the Avenue, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: is_a city avenue [through which Young Van Bibber walks northward] The Avenue is where Van Bibber walks north after leaving his fiancée. As he passes its streets, carriages and familiar club acquaintances prompt him to reflect on his former social life and on what he has lost.

records.l: Central Park, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Central Park is a place with a secluded box-bush dell, a lake, paths, bushes, an artificial lake, and nearby stables. Van Bibber enters it grieving a breakup and crosses the turf toward the secluded place where he and his fiancée met. Later, in hot weather, he waits for his groom and moves to a shaded bench near the lake.

records.l: the secluded box-bush dell, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: A secluded, pretty Central Park spot, marked by a circle of box and a green bench beneath a box bush, is Van Bibber and his fiancée’s favorite meeting place. He arrives intending to bury the engagement ring, but finds her beneath the bush breaking off a sprig.

records.l: Abraham's trip to New York, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Abraham travels to New York on the first train with the $200 he saved. After the Deacon permits him to marry Kate without requiring $2,000, he goes to buy a ring, not counterfeit money.

records.l: marriage, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Marriage is briefly rejected by Young Van Bibber after his fiancée pales on him after three months; he concludes he is not meant for it and imagines bachelorhood, but a reunion with her suggests that conclusion may not hold.

records.l: the engagement, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: The engagement has lasted three months of close companionship before Van Bibber ends it. After he finds his fiancée in their old meeting place, they are observed returning together in her brougham and are described as engaged.

records.l: Margaret, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Margaret is a female baby left in a tenement room while her parents are imprisoned on Blackwell's Island. She lies in bedding, needs milk, and is weakened by heat, inadequate food, and lack of care; deep blue rings surround her closed eyes, and her breathing becomes dangerously irregular. At first she uncertainly recognizes Rags Raegen, then greets him with smiles, coos, affection, and trust. Raegen gives her water and softened bread, watches over her through the night, and carries her to the station-house when she becomes ill after two days without food. A char-woman gives her milk and arranges medical care. After the Society rejects her family as caretakers, Raegen cares for her. Later, she visits him in the Tombs, reaches for him, and kisses him through the bars.

records.l: Pike McGonegal, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Pike McGonegal, a darling and hero of the Thirty-third Street tenements, is reported murdered by Ragsey Raegen. Raegen says McGonegal drew a pistol and was struck in self-defense; a cop supports the pistol claim.

records.l: police, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Police pursue Rags Raegen after he strikes McGonegal and falls. They block the East River, search Case's tenement and its roofs with a revolver, question one another, and fail to find him beneath bedding. As Rags considers escape, police watch ferries, railway depots, and a river boat to intercept departing criminals.

records.l: Case's tenement, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Case's tenement is a dark, mostly empty, largely untenanted building with few chances to move between rooms. While fleeing, Rags enters and eventually hides in a nearly bare room, where he encounters Margaret. It contains room No. 8, rented by green-goods men who receive visiting countrymen.

records.l: the rooftops, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: are_unfamiliar_to Rags Raegen [in Thirty-third Street] The rooftops are unfamiliar territory for Rags, unlike the roofs in his own neighborhood. Police pursue him across them, and Italians watching from nearby windows point him out to an officer, forcing him to retreat into the building.

records.l: the tenement building's interior, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: The building's dark, narrow interior has stairways, a roof ladder, and a small room with bedding, scant food, and whiskey. It offers little shelter: Rags runs upstairs, falls over a bucket, retreats from the roof, and hides from police in a room.

records.l: Rags's escape and hiding, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Rags’s escape and hiding unfolds during a police pursuit in Case’s tenement. He drops from a rooftop through a wooden trap, hides beneath bedding in a dark room, and remains still while police inspect it. Though he considers boatmen to Astoria or the Jersey shore, changing his name, and working elsewhere, Margaret’s condition keeps him concealed overnight as he cares for her.

records.l: Rags's pursuit by police, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: leads_to the rooftops [after the river escape route is blocked] Rags is pursued because the police saw him strike McGonegal and saw McGonegal fall. They close in on him from the stairs and roof, while another officer watches from the street, but Rags avoids capture.

records.l: Rags's fight with McGonegal, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Rags's fight with McGonegal was a street assault witnessed by police: Rags struck McGonegal, causing him to fall. It led to police pursuit and a criminal charge. Rags says he acted in self-defense, citing witnesses who saw McGonegal pull a pistol, and expects a short sentence.

records.l: the police pursuit of Raegen, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: The police pursuit of Raegen lasts two days. Police chase Rags through a building and over roofs, search rooms with revolvers, and leave believing him hidden under bedding. Detectives later find Raegen at the station-house, where he gives himself up after giving them a chase.

records.l: bedding, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: conceals Rags Raegen [during the police search] Rags dives beneath a pile of tossed-up bedding and presses himself against the wall to avoid detection. After the police leave, he gathers the bedding over himself again while listening, and later uses it as a place to sit while holding Margaret.

records.l: the ward detectives, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Ward detectives pursue Ragsey Raegen on suspicion, investigate with McGonegal's friends Wade and Heffner, and watch a tenement from across the street, causing Rags to remain inside while they are nearby.

records.l: the Twenty-first Precinct station-house, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: contains the reading-room The Twenty-first Precinct station-house receives Raegen when he brings in the sick and starving baby. Its sergeant, reserve squad, char-woman, and detectives become involved in caring for the baby and identifying Raegen.

records.l: the sun, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: The sun rises hissing from the East River as a broad, red disc of heat, sweeping the city with a man-of-war search-light glare; its light enters open windows and dangerously heats baby's bedding.

records.l: heat, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: causes Ragsey Raegen [with sleeplessness and whiskey contributing] The heat makes Rags ache and causes his eyes to smart, while Margaret gasps, weakens, and develops dark rings around her eyes. Rags cools her with water and fans her, but the heat contributes to his exhaustion and stupor.

records.l: milk, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: is_used_for Margaret [as desired nourishment] Rags believes milk is the food babies need and plans to obtain some from a passing milk-cart. Because he cannot get outside safely, he gives Margaret moistened ham and bread instead.

records.l: murder of Pike McGonegal, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: is_reported_by evening newspapers [as a full account] A newsboy announces a full account of the murder of Pike McGonegal by Ragsey Raegen. The announcement terrifies Rags, though he maintains that the killing was self-defense.

records.l: McGonegal's shooting, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: is_claimed_as self-defence [by Ragsey Raegen] Rags says he struck McGonegal after McGonegal pulled a gun on him. He maintains that he acted in self-defense, while the newspaper describes McGonegal's death as murder.

records.l: Rags's criminal record, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: is_kept_in Police Court [on Police Court blotters] Rags knows that his life history has been recorded in Police Court blotters since he was ten years old. He believes his record, his enemies, and his limited friends make secret and immediate flight his safest option.

records.l: the surly old sergeant, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: The surly old sergeant of the Twenty-first Precinct station-house, believing he has humor, answers Raegen facetiously, rejects using the station-house as dispensary or foundling hospital, then summons reserves and the char-woman after threats.

records.l: the char-woman, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: The char-woman, caretaker at the Twenty-first Precinct station-house, responds when an ill baby is brought downstairs. Taking the baby in her arms, she says heat and poor care caused its condition, orders milk, a surgeon, and ice, and insists it will not die.

records.l: the gang, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Raegen later says that he has shaken the gang.

records.l: the Society, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: has_decided the baby's family is unfit to care for the baby Raegen says that the Society has decided that the baby's family is not fit to take care of her.

records.l: the Tombs, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Raegen says that he sat in the Tombs expecting to hang while the case against him was going badly. The baby was brought to visit him there every day.

records.l: Raegen's surrender, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: is_a voluntary surrender [to the police] Raegen's surrender occurs when he brings the baby to the station-house and gives himself up. He insists that nobody captured him.

records.l: the case against Raegen, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: is_serious capital case [Raegen expects to hang] Raegen says that the case was once going dead against him and that he expected to hang in the Tombs. He refers to a cop swearing to McGonegal's drawing the pistol.

records.l: the baby's illness and starvation, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: is_caused_by inadequate care The baby becomes ill from the heat and has not eaten for two days, leaving her half-starved. The char-woman gives her milk, orders ice to be prepared, and summons the surgeon; she says the baby will not die.

records.l: Latimer, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Latimer is a young man, known well to the bishop and a frequent visitor to his study, who loves Ellen deeply and seeks to marry her. He presents himself as professionally established, self-respecting, and personally disinclined to dissipation, denying wild oats, anonymous letters, or any damaging past account. Yet he has loved another woman in a former forbidden relationship and remains separated from her. When the bishop raises a thirty-day hypothetical, Latimer refuses to answer, protests that its conditions are impossible, and says the other woman is neither dead nor available to a man like him, perhaps being married. He insists that he now prefers and loves Ellen above all else, believing God sent her as a reward. In pleading with Ellen, he says he overcame the earlier love by refusing to yield to it, and that the struggle made him honest, clean, and worthy of her. When Ellen tells him to go to the other woman, he leaves, turning away from the north where she is located toward rooms in the south.

records.l: Ellen, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Ellen is the bishop’s only daughter, a woman loved by young Latimer, whom she loves and intends to marry if her father agrees. Her father sees her future happiness as his responsibility and fears she would suffer if Latimer loved another woman again. Ellen initially teases Latimer for seeming afraid before he speaks to the bishop. After secretly testing him as a joke meant to frighten him, she enters distressed and exhausted, asks her father to send Latimer away, and tells Latimer to go to the other woman.

records.l: Ellen's father, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Ellen’s father is a bishop and priest, young for his high office, and Ellen’s sole surviving parent, guardian, and caregiver. Concerned about her future after she leaves his household, he knows Latimer’s family and likes young Latimer. When Latimer proposes marriage, he listens closely but tests whether Latimer’s past, especially another woman, could endanger Ellen’s happiness; Latimer’s refusal to answer a hypothetical convinces him that it reveals a true feeling. Later, after hearing Latimer explain his past and feelings, he pities Ellen, judges Latimer honorable, says he would have been proud to hear such words from a son, urges Ellen to understand him, and watches Latimer depart with sympathy and concern.

records.l: the bishop's study, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: The bishop's study is a richly furnished room with hundreds of books, pictures, etchings, plaster casts, dark red curtains, an open fire, ferns, and blue-and-white plaques. There, the bishop and young Latimer hold an extended conversation about Ellen's future.

records.l: the marriage proposal, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Young Latimer proposes marriage to Ellen through her father, telling the bishop that Ellen has agreed if her father does not oppose. He says he loves her and believes he can make her happy.

records.l: Latimer and Ellen's love, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: is_mutual love Young Latimer says that Ellen has become essential to his happiness and that a day without seeing her is wasted and discontented. He says that he loves her so deeply that making her happy is his chief desire. Ellen has told him that she loves him.

records.l: Latimer's past, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Latimer's past is examined for hidden dangers to Ellen. Young Latimer says he lived as other young men did but avoided dissipation as vulgar, and denies wild oats, an ugly story, an unreturned consequence, or any woman who could expose him by letter or accusation.

records.l: Latimer's future with Ellen, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Latimer envisions a long, quiet future with Ellen, including marriage and honorable ambition. He imagines using his position and resources to provide her comfort, pleasure, and charitable opportunities. The bishop agrees her material security would be assured, but worries that Latimer may not shield her from past consequences.

records.l: the test by hypothetical conditions, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: A test based on hypothetical conditions asks young Latimer to imagine thirty days before death with no moral or legal consequences, then choose between Ellen and another woman. The bishop treats Latimer’s refusal as an answer. Ellen used the trick to learn what he would say about his past love. Latimer condemns it as impossible, unjust, needless, and horrible, saying it confuses them by treating the unreal and impossible as significant.

records.l: the other woman, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: The other woman is alive and possibly married. Latimer loved her in the past, but they renounced their love when it became a crime or impossible, and she may have suffered silently. He suggests he might love her again if the obstacle between them ended.

records.l: love between Latimer and the other woman, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: This is Latimer’s past love for another woman, suppressed and sacrificed by both. Though he says overcoming it made him honest and worthy and insists he loves Ellen certainly above all else, the bishop raises that changed circumstances could revive the love after Latimer marries Ellen. Latimer calls the woman beyond the love of a man like himself, making it a forbidden or impossible temptation.

records.l: marriage, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: is_possible_between Latimer [with Ellen as his wife] The bishop warns that marriage to Ellen could occur before the obstacle separating Latimer from the other woman ended, making any later trouble difficult to remedy. Latimer suggests that the other woman may already be a married woman.

records.l: Snipes, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Snipes is a very young, homeless, imperfectly trained but skilled trailer for the green-goods men, paid a quarter per shadowed victim. Unnoticeable in crowds, patient, and able to follow men through changing streets, he resists compulsory reform. He aids and sympathizes with an old farmer, protects Abraham, reaches Grand Central Depot, and declines farm life to remain in New York.

records.l: Alf Wolfe, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Alf Wolfe, using the name Perceval, leads green-goods men from rented room No. 8; when confronted by an old farmer, he overpowers but releases him.

records.l: the old farmer, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: A strict-living father from a simple country family, he hosts city children at his farm, seeks Abraham in New York over counterfeit money, confronts Wolfe, reunites with Abraham, and invites Snipes home.

records.l: Abraham, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Abraham, the old farmer’s son, saves $200 for marriage, becomes engaged to Kate with the old Deacon’s consent, and goes to New York to buy a ring despite his father’s counterfeit-money suspicion.

records.l: the green-goods men, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Green-goods men rent room No. 8, circulate counterfeit-money offers, then arrange meetings to watch and rob suspected customers; Alf Wolfe leads, with Snipes trailing.

records.l: room No. 8, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Room No. 8 is the rented headquarters where Alf Wolfe and the green-goods men meet prospective customers. The old farmer enters it looking for Abraham and confronts Wolfe, but Abraham is not there.

records.l: the Bowery, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: contains pawnshops and loan offices The Bowery is where Miss Catherwaight finds the silver heart medal in a pawnbroker's window among razors, pistols, and family Bibles. She is well known to the pawnshops and loan offices there, whose proprietors save medals for her and try to learn or invent their histories.

records.l: Grand Central station, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Grand Central station, also called Grand Central Depot, is a railway station where tickets are sold. Van Bibber brings a burglar there and buys him a ticket for Helena, Montana. It is also where Snipes takes an exhausted old farmer, who unexpectedly reunites with Abraham before they prepare to return home.

records.l: green goods, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: is_a technical name for counterfeit bills Green goods is the technical term for counterfeit bills. The green-goods men offer countrymen large amounts of it in exchange for smaller amounts of legitimate money, claiming that the only victim is the Government.

records.l: counterfeit money, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: is_offered_for $500 [$5,000 worth offered] Counterfeit money is what the green-goods men claim to sell to their customers. The old farmer mistakenly believes Abraham has come to New York to spend $200 on $2,000 worth of counterfeit money.

records.l: the trailer's work, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: The trailer's work is to shadow a prospective customer from the first meeting with the green-goods men to a later meeting and report any suspicious behavior. Snipes is skilled at remaining unnoticed, following people through crowds, and alerting Wolfe if a customer appears to be a detective.

records.l: Young Harringford (Cecil, the Goodwood Plunger), Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Young Harringford, Cecil, is a young man known publicly as the Goodwood Plunger or The Plunger. Eldest son of the Harringford family, he is estranged from and effectively disinherited by his father after gambling losses, debts, and disgrace, though they still love one another. Loved by the girl from Surrey and attended by the longtime servant Walters, Cecil reaches Monte Carlo in worsening mental and physical distress. Having lost his fortune and unable to cover his debts, he seeks a final second chance through the Grand Prix and the English horse; if it fails, he plans suicide in Monte Carlo, away from home. There he is regarded as fortunate and rich by a distressed woman, who asks him to stop her husband Louis from gambling. Cecil learns Louis has won money but is risking it, intervenes, divides the winnings for separate bets, takes the money from the table, and places it in the woman's skirt. He sends the couple to Paris, abandons his suicidal course, and plans to return to England by the first available train with Walters.

records.l: Harringford's father, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Harringford's father rejects Young Harringford after gambling disgraces the family name, but later recognizes his error. Through Walters, he invites Cecil home, offering reconciliation and declaring him dearer than his other sons. He depends on Cecil to continue the family line and hopes his return will make him happy.

records.l: the girl from Surrey, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: A girl from Surrey living near the Harringford family estate is an important object of Young Harringford’s affection. During her illness, he watches her lighted window and longs to meet her again. She openly asks after him despite social judgment, showing concern as he comes to Monte Carlo in a changed state of mind.

records.l: Walters, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Walters, Cecil Harringford's longstanding, deeply devoted servant, is found handling a letter to Cecil's father, helps pack for Cecil's departure, feels relieved by the decision to leave, and watches over Cecil as he falls asleep longing for home.

records.l: Monte Carlo, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Monte Carlo is a place containing a Casino and gambling at its tables. Harringford comes from Paris intending to die there, choosing it because it differs from home and because he recalls a young Russian who killed himself after losing at the tables; he waits outside the Casino late at night. During a marriage tour, a woman and Louis are there, though she says gambling tables are not for people like them and they must return to Paris next day. A Frenchman gambles there until Cecil urges him and his wife to leave that night, having seen arrivals rich depart paupers.

records.l: Casino at Monte Carlo, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Casino at Monte Carlo is a place with green gambling tables and lights. Young Harringford, the “Goodwood Plunger,” stands by a pillar, watching the lights and waiting for closing. In a changed state of mind, he intends to die there after the lights are extinguished, considering the Casino a fitting setting.

records.l: Surrey, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Surrey is the home of Harringford’s family and the setting of the neighboring estate where the girl lives. Harringford remembers its fields, trout springs, park, and terraces, and longs to return there despite believing that he has lost the right to do so.

records.l: Paris, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Paris is the couple's destination after Cecil sends them away from Monte Carlo. They are expected to arrive there by morning and return to their home and shop.

records.l: Grand Prix, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: is_the_setting_for Siren's race [the final gambling coup] The Grand Prix is Harringford’s final gambling coup, on which he stakes his hopes of restoring his fortune, reconciling with his father, and seeing the girl again. The English horse fails to win, as Frou Frou passes the goal, and Harringford returns to Paris in despair.

records.l: gambling and debt, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: causes Harringford's mental and physical distress [through financial loss, disgrace, and isolation] Harringford begins gambling after coming into his money and secretly backs Siren with enormous sums, winning a fortune at the Goodwood Cup. His later losses bring visits to lenders, borrowing, threats of executions, and debts he cannot repay, culminating in the failed Grand Prix wager.

records.l: Harringford's mental and physical distress, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: includes fear of mental collapse [recurring and increasingly terrifying] Harringford suffers a numb feeling and sharp pain in his head, trembling nerves, twitching, loss of appetite, shivering, insomnia, and fear that his mind is failing. He repeatedly tests whether his speech and thoughts are sensible and believes that only death can stop the pain, doubts, and terror.

records.l: Harringford's planned suicide, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: is_intended_to_end Harringford's mental and physical distress [as an escape from pain, fear, and inability to rest] Harringford decides that he will kill himself at Monte Carlo if his final gambling coup fails. He believes suicide will bring rest and peace, feels that others would understand if they experienced his suffering, and waits for the Casino lights to go out before acting.

records.l: Harringford's father's letter, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Harringford’s father writes to Young Harringford, offering peace, forgiveness, and a welcome home. Invoking the Prodigal Son, he says Cecil, his first-born, is dearer than the other ninety-nine and that the girl from Surrey still asks about him. In Monte Carlo, Harringford reads the letter for the last time and tears it up.

records.l: woman (the Goodwood Plunger's interlocutor), Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: A pretty, rather short, plainly dressed French bourgeois woman is newly married to Louis and has no friends in Monte Carlo. Though she has dowry money for part of Carbut's bakery store, Louis's roulette winnings are crucial to paying their debt and creating the independent little shop she wants. She begs the Goodwood Plunger, Cecil, to stop Louis from gambling further. After receiving the winnings, she and Louis go to Paris, own a shop, and she gratefully credits Cecil with helping secure their happier future.

records.l: Louis, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Louis is a handsome young Frenchman, husband, apprentice to old Carbut in baking, and owner of a third of Carbut's bakery store. Though not usually a gambler, he plays dominoes at cafes and, at Monte Carlo, wins money at roulette, including 20,000 francs. Excited by repeated bets on red, he risks his winnings hoping to buy another third of the store. Cecil stops his final all-in gamble; Louis leaves for Paris with his wife, grateful, humble, and resolved never to return to Monte Carlo.

records.l: Carbut's bakery store, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Carbut's bakery store is a bakery partly owned by apprentice Louis, who holds a third. Old Carbut offers the remainder for 20,000 francs so he can retire, but Louis's gambling jeopardizes the couple's purchase.

records.l: gambling, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: takes_place_at Monte Carlo [at the tables] Gambling at the tables has caused Louis to become excited and reckless despite his usual lack of interest in gambling. He has won a large amount but continues risking it instead of stopping, and the woman asks the Goodwood Plunger to persuade him to quit.

records.l: money, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Money, saved by a woman with Louis through months or years of hard work, includes a dowry that paid for part of Carbut's bakery store. Louis wins money needed to buy the rest, but risks losing it by continuing to gamble.

records.l: casino gambling, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: includes roulette game Casino gambling is shown as dangerous because the Frenchman nearly risks all of the couple's money even after winning a large sum. Cecil intervenes because he has seen gamblers become paupers.

records.l: roulette game, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: The roulette game limits each person to 6,000 francs and uses red as an outcome. It unfolds with successive Frenchman wins on red, ending when seven brings Cecil a larger combined win before another wager is stopped.

records.l: money, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: is_a gold coin [in rolls] The money is repeatedly placed on red, won, divided into three possible stakes, and finally gathered by Cecil and placed in the woman's care. It is packed into a heavy bag and taken with the couple to the train.

records.l: 20,000 francs, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: is_won_by Frenchman (the woman's husband) [at roulette] The woman says that the Frenchman has won half of the 20,000 francs, and Cecil later tells him that he has won more than 20,000 francs. The winnings are used to secure the couple's future rather than being risked again.

records.l: train to Paris, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Train to Paris departs Monte Carlo at midnight; Cecil boards a couple, buys tickets, and warns they are alone in a locked compartment until home.

records.l: departure for Paris, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: A departure for Paris follows successful roulette wagers and Cecil's decision to remove a Frenchman and his wife from Monte Carlo; they leave gratefully while Cecil remains alone on the platform.

records.l: homecoming to England, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: is_planned_by Cecil Harringford Cecil decides to take the first available train and return to England with Walters. He describes this homecoming as a return to England, Harringford, and his father.

records.l: happiness for the rest of their lives, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: A promise that a couple will be happy for the rest of their lives is voiced by the Frenchman, echoed by train wheels, linked by Cecil to his father’s letter, and repeated as he sleeps.

records.l: Miss Catherwaight's collection of dishonored honors, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Miss Catherwaight’s collection of dishonored honors is a collection of more than a hundred medals and decorations bought during travels with her father. Its items, including Legion of Honor crosses, English war medals, a Victoria Cross, and named gold and silver medals, had been awarded for service, virtue, bravery, statesmanship, or artistic genius, then pawned or sold by their recipients. She calls them second-hand honors and pledges to patriotism and pawnshops.

records.l: Lewis Lyman Lockwood, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Lewis Lyman Lockwood is an old, unmarried lawyer whose named medal is found and returned through Miss Catherwaight. The medal had been kept in his safe on Thirty-fifth Street before burglars robbed his home. Lockwood had been devoted friends with Henry Burgoyne from boyhood, but they quarrelled over a woman whom both loved; Lockwood also misunderstood the kindness of Miss Catherwaight’s mother, and pride sustained the separation. He lives with and serves as guardian to Mr. Latimer, whom he adopts in a manner. After Miss Catherwaight returns the medal, Lockwood thanks her, speaks with Burgoyne, and returns happier, announcing that the two will go shooting in Maryland.

records.l: Judge Burgoyne, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Judge Burgoyne, identified as Henry Burgoyne, is a judge and lawyer and the former boyhood friend of Lewis Lockwood. They attended school, roomed at State college, practiced law, and shared shooting, but became estranged after both loved the same woman. Later, Lockwood visits Burgoyne to see whether their long separation can end, and they plan a shooting trip in Maryland.

records.l: Mr. Latimer, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Mr. Latimer, a young man, is Lewis L. Lockwood’s junior law-office partner, adopted charge, and ward, as well as a dancing acquaintance of Miss Catherwaight. He tells her that Lockwood’s stolen silver medal marked Lockwood’s boyhood friendship with Henry Burgoyne, recounting the friends’ history and later quarrel. He accompanies Lockwood to visit Miss Catherwaight, waits for Lockwood’s return, notes Lockwood’s unused hunting preparations, and agrees to manage the office while Lockwood and Burgoyne travel.

records.l: the woman loved by Lockwood and Burgoyne, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Miss Catherwaight's mother, married to Mr. Catherwaight, was kind to Lewis L. Lockwood before her marriage; his misunderstanding of that kindness unwittingly caused trouble between Lockwood and Burgoyne.

records.l: Henry Burgoyne and Lewis L. Lockwood's boyhood friendship, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Henry Burgoyne and Lewis L. Lockwood's boyhood friendship begins at school in Westchester County, deepens as they room together at State college, and continues when they practise law as a firm in Tuckahoe. They share leisure, hunting, shooting, and loyalty, and are described as closer than brothers. The old, deeply valued bond ends when both love the same woman and each believes the other disloyal. Despite a long separation, the friendship survives, and Miss Catherwaight's intervention moves them toward reconciliation.

records.l: medals and decorations, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Medals and decorations are awarded for public service and high virtues such as bravery, statesmanship, and artistic genius. After recipients pawn or sell them, they enter Miss Catherwaight’s collection, including French crosses, English war medals, a Victoria Cross, and a congressional gold medal; she especially values discreditable histories.

records.l: silver heart medal from Henry Burgoyne to Lewis L. Lockwood, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: A cheap, tarnished silver heart medal, engraved with clasped hands and inscribed “From Henry Burgoyne to his beloved friend Lewis L. Lockwood” and “Through prosperity and adversity,” belongs to Lewis L. Lockwood as a keepsake. Stolen from his safe during a burglary, it is pawned and appears in the Bowery, where Miss Catherwaight buys or finds it in an old curiosity shop. After Mr. Latimer tells her its painful history, she refuses to keep or exhibit it and returns it to Lockwood. Though he first sees it as a reminder of the past, he keeps it at her urging.

records.l: Maryland, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: is_the_destination_of Lockwood and Burgoyne's shooting trip [for a few weeks] Maryland is the destination of Lockwood and Burgoyne's planned shooting trip, which they intend to take for a few weeks.

records.l: the collection of dishonored honors, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: The collection of dishonored honors is Miss Catherwaight's unusual hobby and consists of awards whose recipients have parted with them. She displays the objects to dinner guests and explains the circumstances of their sale or pawning, treating the contrast between public honor and private dishonor as the collection's chief interest. The silver heart medal prompts her to question whether every object should be treated as a collectible.

records.l: misunderstanding between Lockwood and Burgoyne, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: A long estrangement between Lewis L. Lockwood and Henry Burgoyne began when Lockwood misread Miss Catherwaight's mother's kindness and endured because both men's pride prevented reconciliation.

records.l: Lockwood and Burgoyne's shooting trip, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Lockwood visits Burgoyne, and they decide to take a shooting trip together to Maryland, planned to last a few weeks.

records.l: the three little girls from the East Side, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: The three little girls from the East Side live on Hester Street with their mother and carry a lunch basket on an outing. In the Park, they watch the swan-boats and imagine lake sights. Unable to afford a ride, they are taken by Van Bibber, enjoy it, receive week-long tickets, and return to their tenement sunburned and delighted.

records.l: the Girl He Knew, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: The Girl He Knew is a young lady known to Van Bibber who wears a riding-habit. On a hot day in the Park, she meets him at the dock after his ride with three little girls, smiles kindly, and invites him to join her and her brother at the stables.

records.l: the brother (the Girl He Knew's brother), Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: is_a brother [of the Girl He Knew] The brother meets Van Bibber at the lake after the swan-boat ride. He jokes about Van Bibber's trip and introduces the girls as Van Bibber's young lady friends from Hester Street, then teases the girls about smuggling laces and tipping the smoking-room steward.

records.l: the lake, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: The lake is an artificial body of water in the Park, with a middle island, rocks, shallow edges, bushes, and narrow straits. Fish swim among its rocks, sparrows and robins bathe in its shallows, and girls imagine wild animals on the island.

records.l: the swan-boats, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: The swan-boats are Lohengrin swans with paddle-wheel attachments that circle the lake beneath a parti-awning. Though Van Bibber first considers them idiotic, he later rides one with the girls and buys tickets for further trips.

records.l: the swan-boat ride, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: provides views of fishes and ducks [according to Eddie Case] The swan-boat ride is shady and pleasant, with the boat careening slightly as it turns. Van Bibber is embarrassed while other people can see him, but he relaxes in the narrow straits and helps the girls appreciate the sights.

records.l: riding the swan-boats, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Riding the swan-boats gives the three little girls great pleasure, and Van Bibber finds that they seem to enjoy it more than he has enjoyed expensive trips by yacht or steamship. Afterward, the girls use the tickets Van Bibber gives them until they are sunburned.

records.l: Van Bibber's generosity, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: benefits the three little girls from the East Side [by providing tickets] Van Bibber's generosity leads him to pay for the three little girls' swan-boat ride when they cannot afford it. He later buys each girl a long string of tickets so they can continue riding for a week.

records.l: reporter, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: A gentleman of the press experienced throughout New York at all hours, he regards city reporters’ work as commonplace and repetitive, with dramas rooted in crime, poverty, or drink rather than mystery. While accompanying Van Bibber to a Jersey City prizefight, he argues this view, recounts a Dickens story, and another reporter keeps time.

records.l: burglar, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: The burglar is a recently released prisoner who has served seven years in prison. Escaping with a revolver and bags of stolen goods, he is overpowered by Van Bibber after emerging beside a great house. He refuses to return to prison alive and says he stole money to reach his wife, living in the West under another name, and his daughter, who does not know him. Van Bibber sends him to Helena, Montana, where he seeks an honest living with them.

records.l: Abe Hubbard, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Abe Hubbard, also known as Jimmie the Gent, is an escaped burglar traced to New York. A newspaper identifies him as the burglar whom Van Bibber helped after Van Bibber went to Jersey City to see a fight.

records.l: Jimmie the Gent, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: has_alias Abe Hubbard The newspaper identifies Abe Hubbard by the alias Jimmie the Gent and reports that he has broken jail.

records.l: Helena, Montana, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Helena, Montana, is the destination the burglar gives when Van Bibber asks where he should send him. Van Bibber buys the burglar a train ticket to Helena, Montana.

records.l: the burglary of the great house, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: is_committed_by burglar The burglary is discovered when Van Bibber sees a man carrying two bags filled with projecting articles near the great house. He assumes the man has robbed the house and makes him leave the bags inside the kitchen door, where a servant can find them.

records.l: Abe Hubbard's jail break, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Abe Hubbard, alias Jimmie the Gent, breaks jail in New Jersey and is traced to New York. A newspaper says detectives expect to recapture him, but fear his friends may help him escape out West.

records.l: prison, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: is_described_as grave [by the burglar] The burglar says he has served his time in prison and describes returning there as returning to a grave. He claims he spent seven years imprisoned and fears another sentence of twenty years.

records.l: revolver, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: The burglar carries a revolver during the attempted escape. It goes off once during his struggle with Van Bibber, who kicks it from his hand and keeps it as a threat while escorting him to the station.

records.l: stolen bags, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Two bags containing articles of different sizes lie at the burglar's feet. Van Bibber tells him to place the bags inside the kitchen door, where the servant will see them before the milkman does.

records.l: train ticket, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: destination Helena, Montana Van Bibber buys the burglar a ticket to Helena, Montana. He warns that the ticket can be sold downtown for half its value, and the burglar says he already knows that.

records.l: adventure, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Van Bibber wants to prove the reporter wrong about the absence of unusual adventures in city life. His encounter with the burglar becomes the extraordinary incident he has been seeking, though he later wonders whether he acted correctly.

records.l: honest living, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: The burglar says he intended to live honestly after joining his wife and daughter in the West. Van Bibber doubts whether the burglar truly means to live honestly but nevertheless gives him money and helps him leave.

records.l: young Standish, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Young Standish, or Ted, is the younger son of the Standish family and brother of elder Standish. He elopes with Miss Cambridge and seeks a clergyman to marry them before returning to Boston. When his older brother arrives, Van Bibber deceives him to protect the couple and arranges their public marriage.

records.l: Miss Cambridge, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: Miss Cambridge is a very young, very pretty lady who elopes with young Standish. Frightened because they lack a clergyman, witnesses, and parish registry, she relies on Van Bibber to arrange a formal wedding. Though she weeps on the journey, she smiles happily as she walks up the aisle.

records.l: Little Church Around the Corner, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: The Little Church Around the Corner is a church with an old rector and assistant organist. It hosts the marriage ceremony of young Standish and Miss Cambridge at three o’clock after Van Bibber secures the rector, opening, music, and bell arrangements.

records.l: the wedding, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: The wedding of Miss Cambridge and young Standish, called Ted, is properly and publicly arranged by Cortlandt Van Bibber at Little Church Around the Corner. To give their elopement publicity and prevent scandal, Van Bibber stages an orthodox, fashionable ceremony with prominent club-men witnesses, invited women, flowers, organ music, bell, rice, and an old shoe.

records.l: the elopement, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: The elopement concerns young Standish and Miss Cambridge, who leave without family approval or presence. With no clergyman or witnesses, Van Bibber protects them from discovery and, as best man, turns their hurried plan into a formal wedding.

records.l: marriage ceremony, Gallegher and Other Stories
records.s: takes_place_at Little Church Around the Corner [public and witnessed] The marriage ceremony takes place at the Little Church Around the Corner with an assistant organist, witnesses, and guests arranged by Van Bibber. Young Standish and Miss Cambridge are married there and then leave for the Fall River boat.
