records.s: Germany received translations, reviews, and imitations of Sterne’s letters, sermons, novels, and spurious writings. German criticism often accepted questionable works as genuine or treated them sympathetically, thereby contributing to a distinctive German image of Yorick.

records.l: Hamburg, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Naturally Sterne’s letters found readers in Germany, the Yorick-Eliza correspond
records.s: Hamburg was the site of several 1775 editions of the Yorick-Eliza letters and related collections. These editions were probably translated by Bode and were reviewed favorably, with Bode’s version preferred over another translation.

records.l: “Letters from Yorick to Eliza”, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Naturally Sterne’s letters found readers in Germany, the Yorick-Eliza correspond
records.s: The English edition of “Letters from Yorick to Eliza” was reviewed in German journals and translated in Hamburg in 1775. German reviewers discussed its tenderness, moral character, and authenticity, while Bode’s translation received particular praise.

records.l: Yorick-Eliza correspondence, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Naturally Sterne’s letters found readers in Germany, the Yorick-Eliza correspond
records.s: The Yorick-Eliza correspondence was especially successful with German readers. Reviewers generally regarded the relationship as extraordinarily tender but Platonic, although some questioned whether the letters were original or genuine.

records.l: Sermons of Mr. Yorick, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Naturally Sterne’s letters found readers in Germany, the Yorick-Eliza correspond
records.s: Sterne’s sermons were translated and reviewed in Germany but were less popular than his novels. A Leipzig translation appeared in 1770, and later commentary praised the sermons while sometimes attaching inaccurate information about Sterne and the English church to them.

records.l: “Sermons to Asses”, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Naturally Sterne’s letters found readers in Germany, the Yorick-Eliza correspond
records.s: “Sermons to Asses” was mistakenly associated with Sterne in some German publications and translations. The work was actually written by Rev. James Murray and directed against the established church, taxation, and coercive power.

records.l: Sentimental Journey, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Naturally Sterne’s letters found readers in Germany, the Yorick-Eliza correspond
records.s: The Sentimental Journey was treated by German critics as superior to the spurious or doubtful works attributed to Sterne. Yorick’s Meditations was placed below the Sentimental Journey and below Tristram Shandy, though above many artificial works then popular.

records.l: Tristram Shandy, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Naturally Sterne’s letters found readers in Germany, the Yorick-Eliza correspond
records.s: Tristram Shandy served as a standard against which German critics compared Sterne’s genuine and purported works. Yorick’s Meditations was judged inferior to it, and the Koran was evaluated in relation to Yorick’s other writings.

records.l: Koran, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Naturally Sterne’s letters found readers in Germany, the Yorick-Eliza correspond
records.s: The Koran was a purportedly posthumous work that English critics considered manifestly spurious, but it received considerably greater recognition in Germany. German translations appeared in 1771 and 1778, and several German reviewers accepted or warmly praised it despite acknowledging, in some cases, doubts about its authorship.

records.l: Platonic affection, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Naturally Sterne’s letters found readers in Germany, the Yorick-Eliza correspond
records.s: Platonic affection was the interpretation German reviewers applied to the tenderness of the Yorick-Eliza relationship. They argued that virtue and rectitude were preserved despite the correspondence’s emotional warmth.

records.l: authenticity of Sterne’s letters, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Naturally Sterne’s letters found readers in Germany, the Yorick-Eliza correspond
records.s: The authenticity of Sterne’s letters was repeatedly debated in Germany. Some reviewers accepted the Yorick-Eliza letters as genuine, while others suspected that particular letters or collections were fabricated, including letters later identified by a confessedly spurious 1780 collection as imitations.

records.l: “Sermons to Asses” authorship controversy, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Naturally Sterne’s letters found readers in Germany, the Yorick-Eliza correspond
records.s: The “Sermons to Asses” authorship controversy arose because German translations and criticism attributed the work to Sterne. The unit states that Rev. James Murray was its actual author and suggests that the German attribution resulted from ignorance, imitation, or a one-sided understanding of Sterne.

records.l: Laurence Sterne in Germany, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Sterne’s unacknowledged borrowings, his high-handed and extensive appropriation
records.s: The unit examines Laurence Sterne’s extensive unacknowledged borrowings and the largely moderate German response to them. George Ferriar’s investigations became known in Germany chiefly through Friedrich Nicolai’s 1795 summary, which defended Sterne’s creative adaptation, while Gotthold Ephraim Lessing had apparently noticed similar borrowings but remained silent. The unit also traces English imitations of Sterne, especially works modeled on the Sentimental Journey, and their German translations or adaptations. These included imitations attributed to Samuel Paterson, Schink, and others, as well as works presented as continuations or companions to Yorick’s travels.

records.l: Laurence Sterne, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Sterne’s unacknowledged borrowings, his high-handed and extensive appropriation
records.s: Laurence Sterne was criticized for extensive, unacknowledged appropriation of material from other writers, especially Burton’s Anatomy of Melancholy. Friedrich Nicolai nevertheless argued that Sterne’s additions, alterations, personal tone, Empfindsamkeit, and Laune made him more than a brainless copyist and that investigating his sources did not depreciate him.

records.l: Sterne’s unacknowledged borrowings, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Sterne’s unacknowledged borrowings, his high-handed and extensive appropriation
records.s: Sterne’s unacknowledged borrowings were noted in Germany as a result of George Ferriar’s investigations in England, but they did not seriously damage Sterne’s standing among his admirers. The subject remained an unavoidable element of English discussions of Sterne and his place in literature.

records.l: George Ferriar, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Sterne’s unacknowledged borrowings, his high-handed and extensive appropriation
records.s: George Ferriar investigated Sterne’s borrowings and presented passages from Burton’s Anatomy of Melancholy as evidence of Sterne’s theft. Friedrich Nicolai gave his findings a favorable and measured presentation in Germany, while Lichtenberg attacked Sterne more spitefully in connection with Ferriar’s essay.

records.l: Germany, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Sterne’s unacknowledged borrowings, his high-handed and extensive appropriation
records.s: Germany learned about Ferriar’s investigations mainly through Friedrich Nicolai’s résumé in the Berlinische Monatsschrift in 1795, since Ferriar’s book and the original Manchester society papers apparently were not reprinted or translated. German readers also encountered numerous English imitations of Sterne, particularly works modeled on the Sentimental Journey.

records.l: England, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Sterne’s unacknowledged borrowings, his high-handed and extensive appropriation
records.s: England was the setting for Ferriar’s investigations and for continuing debate over Sterne’s borrowings. It also produced numerous imitations, continuations, explanations, and protests connected with Sterne, several of which later reached Germany.

records.l: Gotthold Ephraim Lessing, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Sterne’s unacknowledged borrowings, his high-handed and extensive appropriation
records.s: Gotthold Ephraim Lessing possessed a copy of Burton’s Anatomy of Melancholy containing marks beside several passages that Ferriar later cited as evidence of Sterne’s theft. Although Lessing evidently recognized the borrowings, he remained silent about them.

records.l: Nicolai, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Sterne’s unacknowledged borrowings, his high-handed and extensive appropriation
records.s: Friedrich Nicolai summarized Ferriar’s findings in the February 1795 issue of the Berlinische Monatsschrift. He defended Sterne as a refined, ingenious, and humorous author whose creative additions and distinctive qualities justified his reputation, and he maintained that source investigations should explain rather than depreciate him.

records.l: Yorick, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Sterne’s unacknowledged borrowings, his high-handed and extensive appropriation
records.s: Yorick served as the central figure and stylistic model for many German translations and imitations of the Sentimental Journey. Works were published as journeys in Yorick’s manner, as continuations of his travels, or as productions associated with his supposed son, while one later title presented itself as a fifth volume of Yorick’s Empfindsame Reisen.

records.l: Tristram Shandy, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Sterne’s unacknowledged borrowings, his high-handed and extensive appropriation
records.s: Tristram Shandy was identified by Friedrich Nicolai as evidence of Sterne’s rich creative adaptation of borrowed material. Nicolai argued that the creator of Tristram Shandy compensated for a lack of learning through observation, thought, feeling, and original treatment.

records.l: Sentimental Journey, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Sterne’s unacknowledged borrowings, his high-handed and extensive appropriation
records.s: The Sentimental Journey was the principal Sterne work imitated in the English productions that reached Germany. German versions and adaptations included Empfindsame Reisen durch einen Theil der Niederlande, Die neue empfindsame Reise in Yoriks Geschmack, and Schink’s Empfindsame Reisen durch Italien, die Schweiz und Frankreich.

records.l: English imitations of Sterne, Laurence Sterne in Germany, Sterne’s unacknowledged borrowings, his high-handed and extensive appropriation
records.s: English imitations of Sterne reached Germany and were often grouped indiscriminately with the broader mass of Yorick production and influence. They included Samuel Paterson’s Another Traveller, Peter Pennyless, continuations of the Sentimental Journey, A Sentimental Journey intended as a sequel, and Fragments in the manner of Sterne, which were translated, adapted, or reprinted in German.

records.l: Laurence Sterne in Germany, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ] CHAPTER V STERNE’S INFLUENCE IN GERMANY Thus in manifold ways Sterne was introduced into German life and letters.
records.s: The unit describes Sterne’s broad influence in Germany, where he was regarded as a humane guide, emotional mentor, and model for conduct as well as literature. Johann Georg Jacobi’s “Lorenzodosen,” horn snuff-boxes associated with Yorick and Franciscan Lorenzo, became a popular sentimental fad and inspired proposed orders and rituals. Sterne’s influence also shaped German attitudes toward animals, travel writing, humor, whimsy, and literary imitation. Wieland absorbed Sterne’s style and motifs in several works while remaining an independent thinker who later criticized slavish imitation of Sterne.

records.l: Laurence Sterne, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ] CHAPTER V STERNE’S INFLUENCE IN GERMANY Thus in manifold ways Sterne was introduced into German life and letters.
records.s: Sterne was introduced into German life and letters as a figure of benignant humanity, sympathy, emotional expression, and practical moral guidance. His influence appeared in conduct, sentimental customs, travel writing, humor, and numerous German literary imitations, although the unit distinguishes independent engagement from slavish imitation.

records.l: Sterne’s influence in Germany, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ] CHAPTER V STERNE’S INFLUENCE IN GERMANY Thus in manifold ways Sterne was introduced into German life and letters.
records.s: Sterne’s influence in Germany extended beyond literature into social conduct and sentimental rituals, including the Lorenzodosen and proposed orders devoted to gentleness and reconciliation. It also encouraged more personal and humorous travel narratives, sympathy toward animals, and imitation of Sterne’s whimsical style.

records.l: Germany, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ] CHAPTER V STERNE’S INFLUENCE IN GERMANY Thus in manifold ways Sterne was introduced into German life and letters.
records.s: Germany accorded Sterne the honors and influence of a foreign cultural figure, treating him as a prophet, mentor, and authority on emotional and humane conduct. His works and associated customs spread through Germany and even reached Denmark and Livonia.

records.l: Yorick, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ] CHAPTER V STERNE’S INFLUENCE IN GERMANY Thus in manifold ways Sterne was introduced into German life and letters.
records.s: Yorick was judged in Germany to be a preceptor whose teachings could modify human relationships and conduct. His treatment of Franciscan Lorenzo, his sympathy for animals, and his sentimental and whimsical manner inspired customs, literary imitations, and discussions of travel and emotional expression.

records.l: Lorenzodosen, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ] CHAPTER V STERNE’S INFLUENCE IN GERMANY Thus in manifold ways Sterne was introduced into German life and letters.
records.s: Lorenzodosen were horn snuff-boxes bearing “Pater Lorenzo” on the outside and “Yorick” within, created to commemorate the emotional response to Sterne’s story of Franciscan Lorenzo. They became a widespread fad, were manufactured and sold commercially, and were associated with an oath to practice gentleness and restrain anger.

records.l: Jacobi, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ] CHAPTER V STERNE’S INFLUENCE IN GERMANY Thus in manifold ways Sterne was introduced into German life and letters.
records.s: Johann Georg Jacobi introduced the Lorenzodosen after reading Sterne’s account of Franciscan Lorenzo with his brother and several ladies. He explained the custom in an open letter to Gleim, promoted its spread among friends, and later noted that merchants had turned it into a commercial speculation.

records.l: Sentimental Journey, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ] CHAPTER V STERNE’S INFLUENCE IN GERMANY Thus in manifold ways Sterne was introduced into German life and letters.
records.s: The Sentimental Journey supplied the story of the poor Franciscan whose snuff-box inspired Jacobi and his companions to create the Lorenzodosen. Its account of Yorick’s sympathy also provided a model for German discussions of humane conduct and animal feeling.

records.l: Lorenzo, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ] CHAPTER V STERNE’S INFLUENCE IN GERMANY Thus in manifold ways Sterne was introduced into German life and letters.
records.s: Franciscan Lorenzo was honored by Jacobi and his companions as a model of gentleness, contentment, invincible patience, and forgiveness. They believed he deserved canonization more than the saints of the calendar and associated his memory with the Lorenzodosen.

records.l: Christoph Martin Wieland, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ] CHAPTER V STERNE’S INFLUENCE IN GERMANY Thus in manifold ways Sterne was introduced into German life and letters.
records.s: Wieland was one of Sterne’s most ardent admirers and intelligent interpreters, and Sterne’s style and motifs appear in several of Wieland’s works from 1768 to 1774. Wieland later continued to call Sterne the author from whom he would last part, while protesting against foolish and unsuccessful imitation of Sterne.

records.l: Johann Wolfgang Goethe, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ] CHAPTER V STERNE’S INFLUENCE IN GERMANY Thus in manifold ways Sterne was introduced into German life and letters.
records.s: Goethe is mentioned as the friend of Fritz Jacobi and as an author who later acknowledged an impulse from Yorick in his account of travel in the “Campagne in Frankreich.” The unit also notes that Goethe satirized Leuchsenring in “Pater Brey.”

records.l: Tristram Shandy, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ] CHAPTER V STERNE’S INFLUENCE IN GERMANY Thus in manifold ways Sterne was introduced into German life and letters.
records.s: Tristram Shandy contributed characters and motifs to German sentimental and eccentric culture, including Uncle Toby and Corporal Trim in the imagined cemetery at Marienwerder. Its Shandean style of narration was adopted in German novels dealing with middle-class domestic life, and Wieland later discussed a failed novel written in its style.

records.l: Laurence Sterne in Germany, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [37] Herder’s early acquaintance with Sterne has been already treated.
records.s: The unit examines Laurence Sterne’s continuing influence on German writers, especially Johann Wolfgang Goethe, while also discussing Johann Gottfried Herder and Gotthold Ephraim Lessing. It traces Goethe’s early exposure to Sterne in Strassburg, his later references to Sterne, possible parallels between their works, and Goethe’s explicit statements of indebtedness. It also investigates Goethe’s use of material from The Koran in Wilhelm Meister’s Journeyman Years and considers whether this constituted literary plagiarism. The unit concludes that Goethe’s relationship to Sterne involved admiration and cultural assimilation more than easily demonstrable direct imitation.

records.l: Johann Gottfried Herder, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [37] Herder’s early acquaintance with Sterne has been already treated.
records.s: Johann Gottfried Herder continued to admire Laurence Sterne after his early acquaintance with him. Soon after arriving in Paris, he praised Sterne’s characterization of the French people to Hartknoch, and his fifth “Wäldchen” refers to Sterne.

records.l: Laurence Sterne, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [37] Herder’s early acquaintance with Sterne has been already treated.
records.s: Laurence Sterne is presented as an important influence on eighteenth-century German writers, particularly through his humor, sentiment, tolerance, and attacks on pedantry and philistinism. Johann Wolfgang Goethe repeatedly expressed admiration for Sterne and returned to reading his works late in life.

records.l: Johann Wolfgang Goethe, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [37] Herder’s early acquaintance with Sterne has been already treated.
records.s: Johann Wolfgang Goethe first seems to have read Laurence Sterne’s works in Strassburg under Johann Gottfried Herder’s guidance. He later recommended Sterne to Jung-Stilling, read the story of poor Le Fevre aloud to the Darmstadt circle, referred to Sterne in letters and conversations, and acknowledged being infinitely indebted to Shakespeare, Sterne, and Goldsmith. Goethe also used or reproduced material associated with Sterne and The Koran in Wilhelm Meister’s Journeyman Years.

records.l: Johann Peter Eckermann, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [37] Herder’s early acquaintance with Sterne has been already treated.
records.s: Johann Peter Eckermann recorded several of Johann Wolfgang Goethe’s statements about Laurence Sterne. Goethe compared Eckermann to a second Shandy, while Eckermann discussed Sterne’s descriptions and ideas in conversation with Goethe.

records.l: Yorick, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [37] Herder’s early acquaintance with Sterne has been already treated.
records.s: Yorick is treated as a central vehicle for Laurence Sterne’s influence on German literature. Johann Wolfgang Goethe said that Yorick helped prepare the sentimental ground on which The Sorrows of Young Werther was built, and he later called Yorick Sterne a uniquely liberating and beautiful spirit.

records.l: Tristram Shandy, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [37] Herder’s early acquaintance with Sterne has been already treated.
records.s: Tristram Shandy was read aloud by Johann Wolfgang Goethe to the Darmstadt circle less than a year after his departure from Strassburg, specifically through the story of poor Le Fevre. Goethe also invoked Walter Shandy’s failure to attend to a squeaking door-hinge when comparing Johann Peter Eckermann to a second Shandy.

records.l: Sentimental Journey, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [37] Herder’s early acquaintance with Sterne has been already treated.
records.s: A Sentimental Journey Through France and Italy influenced the way travel writing was associated with the feelings and opinions of the traveler. Johann Wolfgang Goethe stated that he later tried to keep his own travel accounts objective, rather than follow the sentimental approach he attributed to Sterne.

records.l: The Sorrows of Young Werther, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [37] Herder’s early acquaintance with Sterne has been already treated.
records.s: The Sorrows of Young Werther contains no direct influence from Laurence Sterne that the unit can demonstrate, but it reflects a mental and emotional condition to which Sterne contributed. Johann Wolfgang Goethe later said that Yorick helped prepare the sentimental groundwork on which Werther was built.

records.l: Wilhelm Meister’s Journeyman Years, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [37] Herder’s early acquaintance with Sterne has been already treated.
records.s: Wilhelm Meister’s Journeyman Years included appendices containing miscellaneous sayings and reflections, among them material taken from The Koran and comments on Laurence Sterne. The material was added when the publisher found that the final two volumes were too thin, and it was later reprinted among Goethe’s posthumous works.

records.l: Koran, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [37] Herder’s early acquaintance with Sterne has been already treated.
records.s: The Koran was identified as the source of twenty sayings and reflections printed in the appendix to Wilhelm Meister’s Journeyman Years. It was also considered a possible source for the story of the Graf von Gleichen, which may have contributed to Johann Wolfgang Goethe’s Stella.

records.l: German literature, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [37] Herder’s early acquaintance with Sterne has been already treated.
records.s: German literature increasingly possessed native worth that may have overshadowed Laurence Sterne’s influence on writers such as Johann Gottfried Herder and Gotthold Ephraim Lessing. The unit nevertheless presents Sterne as a force in extending literary conventions and shaping German sentimental culture.

records.l: Empfindsamkeit, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [37] Herder’s early acquaintance with Sterne has been already treated.
records.s: Sentimentalism provided the emotional and intellectual ground on which The Sorrows of Young Werther was built. Johann Wolfgang Goethe associated Laurence Sterne and Yorick with the preparation of this ground, while distinguishing Sterne’s whim and sentiment from Goethe’s own treatment.

records.l: Goethe’s indebtedness to Sterne, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [37] Herder’s early acquaintance with Sterne has been already treated.
records.s: Goethe’s indebtedness to Sterne is expressed directly in his statement that he was infinitely indebted to Shakespeare, Sterne, and Goldsmith. He also described Sterne’s influence as formative at the chief point of his development and praised Sterne’s irony, broad outlook, gentleness toward opposition, and equanimity.

records.l: Sterne’s influence in Germany, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [37] Herder’s early acquaintance with Sterne has been already treated.
records.s: The unit emphasizes that literary influence between Laurence Sterne and Johann Wolfgang Goethe is difficult to measure because Goethe assimilated the spirit of predecessors and contemporaries. It identifies clear admiration and several possible connections, but finds few instances of demonstrable direct imitation.

records.l: literary plagiarism, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [37] Herder’s early acquaintance with Sterne has been already treated.
records.s: The question of literary plagiarism arises from Goethe’s publication of sayings in Wilhelm Meister’s Journeyman Years that were later identified as translations from The Koran, Laurence Sterne’s best-known forgery. Alfred Hédouin located the sources, while Robert Springer incorrectly stated that the material had only appeared after Goethe’s death; the unit establishes that it had been published during Goethe’s lifetime.

records.l: Strassburg, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [37] Herder’s early acquaintance with Sterne has been already treated.
records.s: Strassburg was where Johann Wolfgang Goethe seems first to have read Laurence Sterne’s works under Johann Gottfried Herder’s guidance. Letters from Goethe’s Strassburg period also suggest that Sterne remained highly esteemed by Herder.

records.l: Laurence Sterne in Germany, Laurence Sterne in Germany, In certain other manifestations, relatively subordinate, the German literature o
records.s: The German literature of the latter part of the eighteenth century and the beginning of the nineteenth was influenced by Laurence Sterne’s example in form, style, and ideas. Sterne’s narrative discontinuity, typographical eccentricities, direct appeals to readers, hobby-horse theory, traveler classifications, and emphasis on insignificant details were adopted or imitated in Germany. Yorick’s traveler classification and the hobby-horse became recurring conversational, literary, and fictional references. Jacob Minor argued that Sterne sharpened observation of self-deception and helped influence Wieland, Goethe, and Tieck in exposing false ideals and life-lies.

records.l: German literature of the latter part of the eighteenth century and the beginning of the nineteenth, Laurence Sterne in Germany, In certain other manifestations, relatively subordinate, the German literature o
records.s: It developed secondary manifestations of Laurence Sterne’s influence, including discontinuous narration, unrelated episodes, typographical eccentricity, direct conversation with the reader, and the adoption of Sternean ideas. German writers also used the hobby-horse, Yorick’s traveler classifications, and the theory that insignificant details determine great events.

records.l: Laurence Sterne, Laurence Sterne in Germany, In certain other manifestations, relatively subordinate, the German literature o
records.s: His example influenced German literature in narrative structure, typography, direct reader address, and the treatment of sentiment and humor. His hobby-horse theory, traveler classifications, emphasis on trifles, and worn-out-coin simile gained currency in Germany.

records.l: Yorick, Laurence Sterne in Germany, In certain other manifestations, relatively subordinate, the German literature o
records.s: His mock-scientific classification of travelers became a conversational and epistolary commonplace in Germany. His use of the term “hobby-horse” was playfully recalled by German writers, and his blank pages and other formal vagaries were associated with later eccentric books.

records.l: hobby-horse theory, Laurence Sterne in Germany, In certain other manifestations, relatively subordinate, the German literature o
records.s: It was warmly received in Germany and became a permanent figure, often with reminders of Yorick’s use of the term. The Revelation of St. John in “Sebaldus Nothanker” and Schottenius’s fifty-seven sermons are presented as hobby-horses, while Lessing also used the term.

records.l: Gotthold Ephraim Lessing, Laurence Sterne in Germany, In certain other manifestations, relatively subordinate, the German literature o
records.s: He referred to Yorick’s traveler classification in letters to Mendelssohn. In 1780 he described one traveler as inquisitive and another as emigrating, apologizing for adding to Yorick’s list; in 1768 he used “Steckenpferd” in a letter to Mendelssohn.

records.l: Walter Shandy, Laurence Sterne in Germany, In certain other manifestations, relatively subordinate, the German literature o
records.s: One of his favorite contentions was that great events depend fortuitously upon insignificant details. His philosophy that trifles determine existence was adopted in German fiction, including Wezel’s “Tobias Knaut” and “Die Grosse Begebenheit aus kleinen Ursachen.”

records.l: fortuitous dependence of great events upon insignificant details, Laurence Sterne in Germany, In certain other manifestations, relatively subordinate, the German literature o
records.s: It became a principle for developing events or character in German fiction. The idea is described as unquestionable in Wezel’s “Tobias Knaut” and as being appropriated wholesale in “Die Grosse Begebenheit aus kleinen Ursachen.”

records.l: Jacob Minor, Laurence Sterne in Germany, In certain other manifestations, relatively subordinate, the German literature o
records.s: In an article in Euphorion, he argued that Sterne helped sharpen observation of self-deception in small matters and of the human soul’s deceiving impulses. He held that Sterne inspired Wieland and Goethe to combat false ideals and life-lies, and that Tieck was schooled in Sterne for portraying conscious or unconscious life-lies.

records.l: Germany, Laurence Sterne in Germany, In certain other manifestations, relatively subordinate, the German literature o
records.s: It adopted and circulated numerous elements associated with Laurence Sterne, including discontinuous literary forms, typographical eccentricities, direct reader address, the hobby-horse theory, traveler classifications, and the idea that trifles determine major events. German writers and correspondence repeatedly alluded to Sterne and Yorick.

records.l: Laurence Sterne in Germany, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ] CHAPTER VI IMITATORS OF STERNE Among the disciples of Sterne in Germany whose literary imitation may be regarded as typical of their master’s influence, Johann Georg Jacobi is perhaps the best known.
records.s: This unit examines German imitators of Laurence Sterne, especially Johann Georg Jacobi and Johann Gottlieb Schummel, and their use of Sterne’s sentimental and whimsical techniques. Jacobi’s Winterreise and Sommerreise imitate A Sentimental Journey Through France and Italy but emphasize sentimentalism, instruction, animals, and humane religious figures more than Sterne’s whimsicality or descriptions of place. Schummel’s Empfindsame Reisen durch Deutschland is presented as a particularly extensive imitation, borrowing forms, motifs, narrative devices, characters, and expressions from both A Sentimental Journey Through France and Italy and Tristram Shandy. The discussion also considers contemporary responses to these works and the role of translations in spreading Sterne’s influence in Germany.

records.l: Jacobi, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ] CHAPTER VI IMITATORS OF STERNE Among the disciples of Sterne in Germany whose literary imitation may be regarded as typical of their master’s influence, Johann Georg Jacobi is perhaps the best known.
records.s: Johann Georg Jacobi is identified as one of the best-known German disciples of Sterne. His Winterreise and Sommerreise imitate Sterne’s sentimental travel writing, though Jacobi adds more exuberant fancy, mythological figures, serious instruction, sympathy for animals, and humane religious characters while largely avoiding Sterne’s whimsical side.

records.l: Laurence Sterne, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ] CHAPTER VI IMITATORS OF STERNE Among the disciples of Sterne in Germany whose literary imitation may be regarded as typical of their master’s influence, Johann Georg Jacobi is perhaps the best known.
records.s: Laurence Sterne is presented as the major English model for German sentimental writers. His works supplied imitators with sentimental episodes, travel structures, digressions, lists, pseudo-scientific analysis, abrupt interruptions, sympathy for animals and erring women, and distinctive expressions and narrative devices.

records.l: Yorick, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ] CHAPTER VI IMITATORS OF STERNE Among the disciples of Sterne in Germany whose literary imitation may be regarded as typical of their master’s influence, Johann Georg Jacobi is perhaps the best known.
records.s: Yorick serves as the central model for the German imitations discussed in the unit. Jacobi was reportedly called Uncle Toby in Gleim’s circle because of his enthusiasm for Sterne, while Schummel explicitly declares that he will follow Yorick’s footprints without claiming to equal him.

records.l: Schummel, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ] CHAPTER VI IMITATORS OF STERNE Among the disciples of Sterne in Germany whose literary imitation may be regarded as typical of their master’s influence, Johann Georg Jacobi is perhaps the best known.
records.s: Johann Gottlieb Schummel wrote Empfindsame Reisen while still a young man, apparently drawing his inspiration directly from reading Sterne. His narrative imitates the forms, incidents, sentimental relationships, digressions, interruptions, typographical devices, and expressions of Sterne’s works, although its central events are generally independent of the English models.

records.l: Winterreise, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ] CHAPTER VI IMITATORS OF STERNE Among the disciples of Sterne in Germany whose literary imitation may be regarded as typical of their master’s influence, Johann Georg Jacobi is perhaps the best known.
records.s: Winterreise was published in Düsseldorf in June 1769. It alternates prose and verse in a manner associated externally with Chapelle, but also uses short unnumbered chapters and sentimental travel episodes reminiscent of A Sentimental Journey Through France and Italy; it emphasizes fancy, sentiment, moral instruction, animal sympathy, and humane religious encounters.

records.l: Empfindsame Reisen durch Deutschland, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ] CHAPTER VI IMITATORS OF STERNE Among the disciples of Sterne in Germany whose literary imitation may be regarded as typical of their master’s influence, Johann Georg Jacobi is perhaps the best known.
records.s: Empfindsame Reisen durch Deutschland by Johann Gottlieb Schummel is described as one of the most typical and best-known acknowledged imitations of Yorick. Published in three volumes between Easter 1771 and spring 1772, it draws more constantly on A Sentimental Journey Through France and Italy than on Tristram Shandy, while also adapting many features of both works.

records.l: Tristram Shandy, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ] CHAPTER VI IMITATORS OF STERNE Among the disciples of Sterne in Germany whose literary imitation may be regarded as typical of their master’s influence, Johann Georg Jacobi is perhaps the best known.
records.s: Tristram Shandy is one of the two principal Sterne works used by Schummel as a source. Schummel adapts its treatment of parents, its eccentric narrative structure, its interruptions and digressions, its delayed dedication, and other Shandean devices.

records.l: Sentimental Journey, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ] CHAPTER VI IMITATORS OF STERNE Among the disciples of Sterne in Germany whose literary imitation may be regarded as typical of their master’s influence, Johann Georg Jacobi is perhaps the best known.
records.s: A Sentimental Journey Through France and Italy is the primary model for the sentimental travel writing examined here. Jacobi and Schummel borrow from its structure, characters, episodes, expressions, sympathy for people and animals, criticism of superficial travel writing, and techniques of sentimental and whimsical narration.

records.l: Germany, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ] CHAPTER VI IMITATORS OF STERNE Among the disciples of Sterne in Germany whose literary imitation may be regarded as typical of their master’s influence, Johann Georg Jacobi is perhaps the best known.
records.s: Germany is the principal setting in which Sterne’s influence is traced. German writers, translators, critics, and readers responded to Sterne’s works, producing sentimental travel narratives and debating the value and originality of these imitations.

records.l: imitators of Sterne, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ] CHAPTER VI IMITATORS OF STERNE Among the disciples of Sterne in Germany whose literary imitation may be regarded as typical of their master’s influence, Johann Georg Jacobi is perhaps the best known.
records.s: The imitators of Sterne discussed in this unit include Johann Georg Jacobi and Johann Gottlieb Schummel. They reproduce Sterne’s sentimental travel patterns and formal devices but often alter them through German settings, moral instruction, professional concerns, heightened emotionality, or reduced attention to whimsy.

records.l: Empfindsamkeit, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ] CHAPTER VI IMITATORS OF STERNE Among the disciples of Sterne in Germany whose literary imitation may be regarded as typical of their master’s influence, Johann Georg Jacobi is perhaps the best known.
records.s: Sentimentalism is represented through emotional sympathy, tears, humane treatment of animals, compassion for erring women, tender religious encounters, and concern with the moral relations among people. The unit treats Schummel’s work as an important document of sentimentalism and Jacobi’s writing as an intensified, more serious form of Sternean sentiment.

records.l: Sterne imitation in German literature, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ] CHAPTER VI IMITATORS OF STERNE Among the disciples of Sterne in Germany whose literary imitation may be regarded as typical of their master’s influence, Johann Georg Jacobi is perhaps the best known.
records.s: Imitation of Sterne in Germany involved borrowing not only plots but also narrative forms, section headings, digressions, lists, interruptions, typographical marks, character relationships, expressions, and sentimental motifs. The unit shows that such imitation could be direct and extensive while still producing works with independent events, German settings, and distinctive moral or pedagogical emphases.

records.l: Laurence Sterne in Germany, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ” The second volume is even more incoherent in narration, and contains less genu
records.s: The unit examines Schummel’s imitation of Laurence Sterne and Yorick in the second volume of his work, contrasting its sentimental episodes, digressions, typographical devices, and other Shandean features with their often awkward execution. It explains that the third volume largely abandons Sterne’s influence, incorporates several independent narratives, and concludes with Schummel’s unusually severe criticism of his own three-volume work. The unit also records Goethe’s harsh review of the second volume and the more varied reactions of contemporary German periodicals.

records.l: Schummel, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ” The second volume is even more incoherent in narration, and contains less genu
records.s: Schummel imitates Sterne in the second volume through sentimental episodes, digressions, typographical experiments, mock-scientific descriptions, coined words, and borrowings from Yorickian scenes. In the third volume he largely abandons Sterne’s stylistic manner, incorporates narratives and dramatic pieces of different kinds, and openly condemns many weaknesses of his own work.

records.l: Laurence Sterne, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ” The second volume is even more incoherent in narration, and contains less genu
records.s: Sterne’s treatment of sentiment, whimsy, humane feeling, mock science, digression, and typographical experimentation provides the principal model that Schummel attempts to follow. The unit presents Schummel’s imitation as frequently unsuccessful, while acknowledging his appreciation of Sterne’s methods.

records.l: Yorick, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ” The second volume is even more incoherent in narration, and contains less genu
records.s: Yorick serves as the central model for Schummel’s sentimental and whimsical narrator. Schummel imitates Yorick’s scene with the Monk in the episode with the house-dog, borrows the nettle-plucking at a grave, and echoes other features associated with Yorick’s sensibility.

records.l: Johann Wolfgang Goethe, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ” The second volume is even more incoherent in narration, and contains less genu
records.s: Goethe reviews the second volume in the Frankfurter Gelehrte Anzeigen on March 3, 1772. He calls the book a thistle found on Yorick’s grave, portrays Schummel as a childish imitator who calculates how to laugh and weep, and censures the book as beneath criticism.

records.l: Tristram Shandy, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ” The second volume is even more incoherent in narration, and contains less genu
records.s: Tristram Shandy is one of the two novels Schummel attempts to imitate. Schummel’s concluding self-criticism rejects his treatment of the narrator’s attitude toward his parents and admits that the ninety-page autobiography intended to be Tristram-like is ill conceived, incoherent, and poorly told.

records.l: the second volume, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ” The second volume is even more incoherent in narration, and contains less genu
records.s: The second volume is described as more incoherent in narration and less genuinely eventful than the first, with numerous ill-considered attempts at whimsy. It contains sentimental stories, direct and indirect borrowings from Sterne, digressions, unusual typography, mock-scientific passages, and anticipations of critical censure.

records.l: the third volume, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ” The second volume is even more incoherent in narration, and contains less genu
records.s: The third volume bears little relation to Sterne apart from its title and is divided into several loosely connected parts, including the stories of Caroline and Rosenfeld, a ballad, a play, and the preacher’s diary. It later returns to sentimental adventures, including vicarious begging for a maimed soldier-beggar and a blank page concerning a child-murderess, before ending in extended commentary on Schummel’s own work.

records.l: Die Grosse Begebenheit aus kleinen Ursachen, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ” The second volume is even more incoherent in narration, and contains less genu
records.s: Schummel’s three-volume work begins as an imitation of Sterne’s two novels but develops an increasingly contradictory relationship to that model. Its third volume contains Schummel’s admission that the imitation has few or none of the original’s beauties and many faults of its own.

records.l: the third volume’s concluding self-criticism, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ” The second volume is even more incoherent in narration, and contains less genu
records.s: The third volume’s concluding self-criticism is presented as an unusually candid condemnation of Schummel’s own extensive work. Schummel acknowledges imitation, bad taste, indelicacy, failed attempts at whimsical mannerisms, and the inadequacy of his effort to characterize the German people as Sterne characterized the English and French.

records.l: Goethe’s review of the second volume, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ” The second volume is even more incoherent in narration, and contains less genu
records.s: Goethe’s review of the second volume characterizes Schummel as someone who has taken Yorick’s weapons but lacks Yorick’s inward feeling. It contrasts Yorick’s spontaneous laughter and tears with Schummel’s self-conscious effort to calculate how he should appear to readers.

records.l: Sterne’s peculiar genius, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ” The second volume is even more incoherent in narration, and contains less genu
records.s: Sterne’s peculiar genius is associated with combining humane and pathetic feeling with whimsy, digression, emotional spontaneity, and unconventional form. Schummel recognizes and imitates these features but is repeatedly shown as unable to reproduce their effectiveness.

records.l: Shandean narration and stylistic devices, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ” The second volume is even more incoherent in narration, and contains less genu
records.s: Shandean narration and stylistic devices in the second volume include backward jumps in the narrative, numerous digressions, promised chapters on extraordinary subjects, black page margins, an upside-down line, irregular printing, dashes and exclamation points, mathematical calculations, mock-scientific descriptions, and coined words. The unit generally treats Schummel’s use of these devices as weak, awkward, or witless imitations.

records.l: Empfindsamkeit, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ” The second volume is even more incoherent in narration, and contains less genu
records.s: Sentimentalism dominates the story of the rescued baker’s wife and appears in Schummel’s treatment of the house-dog, the graveyard, the maimed soldier-beggar, and the child-murderess. The unit describes these episodes as sometimes excessive or abortive, although Schummel’s concern with humane feeling remains one of the more persistent elements of the work.

records.l: Schummel’s self-criticism, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ” The second volume is even more incoherent in narration, and contains less genu
records.s: Schummel’s self-criticism identifies his work as a flawed imitation of Sterne, with few or no beauties of the original and many faults of its own. He condemns much of the work as ill conceived, incoherent, poorly told, beneath criticism, excessively imitative, indelicate, and painfully unsuccessful, while retaining approval of the preacher’s speeches and a few other sections.

records.l: Laurence Sterne in Germany, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [19] After Schummel’s remarkable self-chastisement, one could hardly expect to f
records.s: The unit traces Sterne’s influence on German writers and works, especially Schummel, Johann Christian Bock, Göschen, and H. J. C. Hedemann. Schummel gradually abandoned sentimental imitation, while Bock’s Die Tagereise and related volumes directly adapted motifs and attitudes from Sterne and Jacobi. Göschen’s Reise von Johann combined Yorick-like travel, whimsy, and sentiment with German descriptive and informational tendencies. Hedemann’s Empfindsame Reise von Oldenburg nach Bremen used Sterne-like narrative self-consciousness and whimsy chiefly to satirize earlier sentimental travelers and sentimentalism.

records.l: Schummel, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [19] After Schummel’s remarkable self-chastisement, one could hardly expect to f
records.s: Schummel wrote the fourth part of Christian Opitz’s novel Die Gleichheit der menschlichen Herzen, possibly during or before the composition of the third volume of his own work. His Uebersetzer-Bibliothek contained passages in which Sterne was visible, including a reference to Slawkenberg’s book on noses, but his later Fritzen’s Reise nach Dessau and Reise durch Schlesien were largely free of Sterne-like whim and sentiment. In Reise durch Schlesien, he explicitly contrasted his former sentimental extravagance with his later, more worldly attitude.

records.l: Laurence Sterne, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [19] After Schummel’s remarkable self-chastisement, one could hardly expect to f
records.s: Sterne’s influence appears throughout the unit in German adaptations of his sentimental and Shandean styles. His works supplied motifs including the Sentimental Journey, Yorick’s encounters with the Chevalier de St. Louis, Maria of Moulines, the fille de chambre, the dead ass, the horn snuff-box, and the hobby-horse manner. Later writers increasingly imitated or parodied his whimsy and narrative self-consciousness while often losing his delicacy and subtlety.

records.l: Johann Christian Bock, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [19] After Schummel’s remarkable self-chastisement, one could hardly expect to f
records.s: Johann Christian Bock published Die Tagereise in 1770, later reissued as Die Geschichte eines empfundenen Tages, and wrote several anonymous sentimental travel volumes in the early 1770s. His work drew directly and indirectly through Jacobi on Sterne, adapting episodes involving a soldier-beggar, a peasant girl, a dead dog, a lady’s companion, and other sentimental encounters. Critics called Die Tagereise an unsuccessful and tiresome imitation, though it also contained original German patriotism, praise of Gellert, and moral and religious observations.

records.l: Die Tagereise, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [19] After Schummel’s remarkable self-chastisement, one could hardly expect to f
records.s: Die Tagereise, published by Johann Christian Bock in 1770 and reissued in 1775 as Die Geschichte eines empfundenen Tages, presents a journey in prose varied by verse. It is inspired partly by Sterne and partly through Jacobi, especially by the Sentimental Journey, and adapts several episodes and attitudes associated with Yorick. Contemporary critics generally regarded it as an unsuccessful, insufficient, or tiresome imitation, despite elements of genuine originality.

records.l: Jacobi, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [19] After Schummel’s remarkable self-chastisement, one could hardly expect to f
records.s: Jacobi influenced Johann Christian Bock’s Die Tagereise alongside Sterne. Bock’s work resembles Jacobi’s Winterreise in its outward form, particularly in the use of verse within a prose travel narrative. Bock’s later anonymous sentimental travel books also appeared in the context of Jacobi’s success.

records.l: Yorick, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [19] After Schummel’s remarkable self-chastisement, one could hardly expect to f
records.s: Yorick served German sentimental travelers as a model and a challenge to imitate his sympathetic behavior. Bock explicitly took Yorick and Jacobi with him on his journey and adapted Yorick’s encounters, reflections, humane sentiments, and self-questioning. Later writers used the figure of Yorick both as an ideal of sentiment and as an object of parody, and Matthias Claudius was called Germany’s Yorick by some contemporaries.

records.l: Tristram Shandy, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [19] After Schummel’s remarkable self-chastisement, one could hardly expect to f
records.s: Tristram Shandy supplied a Shandean model distinct from the sentimental manner of the Sentimental Journey. August von Kotzebue’s tale Die Geschichte meines Vaters used a grandfather modeled on Sterne’s hobby-horse idea, a servant resembling another Shandean original, irrelevant conversations, and long catalogues. Göschen’s Reise von Johann was also described as containing more Shandean suggestiveness in one episode, though its primary travel model was Yorick.

records.l: Göschen, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [19] After Schummel’s remarkable self-chastisement, one could hardly expect to f
records.s: Göschen wrote Reise von Johann, in which a master and servant travel through southern Germany in a relationship compared with Yorick and La Fleur or Captain Shandy and Corporal Trim. The book uses forced buoyancy, intentional inconsequence, narrative whimsy, sentimental episodes, accidental found papers, and occasional suggestiveness, but is burdened by German tendencies toward description and information. Ebeling incorrectly classed it as an imitation of von Thümmel; Schiller and Goethe discussed it in connection with the Xenien, but the proposed use of it was never carried out.

records.l: Reise von Johann, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [19] After Schummel’s remarkable self-chastisement, one could hardly expect to f
records.s: Reise von Johann depicts Johann and his master traveling through southern Germany. It imitates Yorick-like travel and includes adventures with maids, found papers, a death-bed scene, a village funeral, a whimsical Furth Catechismus, and a disturbing story found among a ragged woman’s papers. The work was associated with von Thümmel by Ebeling without sufficient reason and was considered by Schiller and Goethe as a possible subject for the Xenien, though no such use followed.

records.l: Empfindsame Reise von Oldenburg nach Bremen, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [19] After Schummel’s remarkable self-chastisement, one could hardly expect to f
records.s: Empfindsame Reise von Oldenburg nach Bremen was written by a Hanoverian army officer and is not a conventional sentimental journey filled with tearful sympathy toward people and animals. Nevertheless, it adopts Sterne-like whimsy, self-conscious discussion of writing, mock promises, formal self-examination, and satire of sentimental travel conventions. Its closing story, Das Ständchen, is told without much whim or satire but includes a Sternian double entendre.

records.l: H. J. C. Hedemann, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [19] After Schummel’s remarkable self-chastisement, one could hardly expect to f
records.s: H. J. C. Hedemann, a Hanoverian army officer, wrote Empfindsame Reise von Oldenburg nach Bremen. Although Ebeling emphatically denied that the book was inspired by Sterne, the unit identifies substantial Sterne-like features in its whimsical form and satirical treatment of earlier sentimental travelers. Hedemann’s narrator deliberately parodies sentimental hesitation, self-examination, conventional charity, falling in love, and the need to fill a travel book with anecdotes.

records.l: sentimental journeying, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [19] After Schummel’s remarkable self-chastisement, one could hardly expect to f
records.s: The sentimental journey became a widely imitated German literary form associated with Yorick, Jacobi, Bock, Schummel, and later writers. Its conventions included emotional encounters, sympathy for the poor and animals, self-questioning over trivial actions, and the search for sentimental scenes. By the late eighteenth century, writers such as Hedemann were treating the form satirically, and a contemporary review defined it as a forced mixture of familiar names, wit, and weak humor.

records.l: Empfindsamkeit, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [19] After Schummel’s remarkable self-chastisement, one could hardly expect to f
records.s: Sentimentalism initially encouraged German writers to imitate Yorick’s emotional sympathy and sentimental encounters. Schummel later rejected his own earlier sentimental extravagance, while Bock continued to use sentimental motifs in a more conventional way and Hedemann mocked the genre’s formulas. The unit presents later sentimental writing as increasingly stripped of Sterne’s delicacy and redirected toward whimsy, parody, morality, or information.

records.l: Sterne’s influence in Germany, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [19] After Schummel’s remarkable self-chastisement, one could hardly expect to f
records.s: Sterne’s influence on German literature appears in direct borrowing of episodes, motifs, character types, narrative techniques, and the sentimental journey format. Schummel, Bock, Kotzebue, Göschen, and Hedemann variously adapted the Sentimental Journey, Tristram Shandy, Yorick’s behavior, hobby-horsical characterization, catalogues, digressions, and self-conscious narration. The influence changed over time from earnest sentimental imitation to more self-aware, whimsical, or satirical treatments, often with German writers losing Sterne’s subtlety.

records.l: Laurence Sterne in Germany, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [54] Another work in which sentimentalism has dwindled away to a grinning shade,
records.s: The unit surveys German works influenced by Sterne, ranging from sentimental and comic adaptations to more direct imitations of Yorick’s Sentimental Journey. It discusses works by Andreas Geo. Fr. von Rabenau, Johann Moritz Schwager, Blankenburg, and others, while emphasizing E. A. A. von Göchhausen’s M . . . R . . . as an unusually sustained and self-conscious imitation. Göchhausen’s book imitates Sterne through digressions, readerly interruptions, typographical jokes, sentimental episodes, and borrowings from the Lorenzo episode, while gradually developing more independent material. The literary journals recognized the imitation, criticized its dependence on Sterne, and nevertheless praised aspects of the work.

records.l: Empfindsamkeit, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [54] Another work in which sentimentalism has dwindled away to a grinning shade,
records.s: Sentimentalism is described as having dwindled into a grinning shade in some later works, where only an irresponsible, light-hearted attitude remains connected with its great progenitor. In Göchhausen’s M . . . R . . ., sentiment is present but moderate, including sympathy for animals, poor travelers, and servants.

records.l: Laurence Sterne, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [54] Another work in which sentimentalism has dwindled away to a grinning shade,
records.s: Sterne serves as the central model for numerous German works discussed in the unit. His techniques are identified in digression, whimsical narrative machinery, direct conversation with readers, typographical eccentricity, sentimental episodes, and self-conscious imitation.

records.l: Shandy, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [54] Another work in which sentimentalism has dwindled away to a grinning shade,
records.s: The work is referred to through its abbreviated title, Shandy, as a source that some authors claimed not to have read before composing their own books. The Leben und Schicksale des Martin Dickius is said to imitate Sterne in places, and its digression on noses is treated as suspicious.

records.l: Yorick, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [54] Another work in which sentimentalism has dwindled away to a grinning shade,
records.s: Yorick is the principal model for Göchhausen’s journey and for many other imitations discussed in the unit. Göchhausen repeatedly invokes Yorick, defends his own borrowings from him, imitates the Lorenzo episode, uses a servant corresponding to La Fleur, and titles one section Yorick.

records.l: Jacobi, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [54] Another work in which sentimentalism has dwindled away to a grinning shade,
records.s: Jacobi is associated with the sentimental fashion and with the arbor mentioned in connection with Die Geschichte meiner Reise nach Pirmont. Göchhausen receives a Lorenzodose from J . . . and refers to Jacobi’s accompanying words; the traveler’s insistence that Pumper ride inside the coach may derive from Jacobi’s failure to be equally democratic.

records.l: E. A. A. von Göchhausen, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [54] Another work in which sentimentalism has dwindled away to a grinning shade,
records.s: E. A. A. von Göchhausen wrote M . . . R . . ., published at Eisenach in 1772 and later issued in several editions. He openly and repeatedly engages with his dependence on Sterne, while gradually moving from imitation toward his own satire of critics and philosophers and a Utopian fantasy of life on the moon.

records.l: M . . . R . . ., Laurence Sterne in Germany, [54] Another work in which sentimentalism has dwindled away to a grinning shade,
records.s: M . . . R . . . is an unusually well-received work inspired by Sterne and was judged worthy of several later editions. It imitates the Sentimental Journey in its brief titled chapters, sentimental incidents, digressions, reader interruptions, eccentric typography, and self-conscious defenses against accusations of theft, but its dependence on Sterne diminishes as it progresses.

records.l: Sentimental Journey, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [54] Another work in which sentimentalism has dwindled away to a grinning shade,
records.s: The Sentimental Journey awakens the narrator’s desire to travel when he reads it while sitting on a sofa. It supplies the model for the book’s title, structure, Yorick-like manner, Lorenzo episode, treatment of servants and travelers, and many of Göchhausen’s sentimental and comic devices.

records.l: Lorenzodosen, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [54] Another work in which sentimentalism has dwindled away to a grinning shade,
records.s: The Lorenzodose is a snuff-box sent to the author by J . . . on June 29th. It repeatedly restores the author’s sentimental focus, bears the letters of the word Yorick on its lid, and is linked to the author’s reflections on his conduct toward the postman.

records.l: Pumper, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [54] Another work in which sentimentalism has dwindled away to a grinning shade,
records.s: Pumper is Göchhausen’s servant and a man of feeling who grieves when horses crush dewdrops. He kills and then tenderly buries a marmot after being rebuked, is repeatedly involved in jokes about chapter organization, and is allowed to ride inside the coach with his master.

records.l: Lorenzo episode, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [54] Another work in which sentimentalism has dwindled away to a grinning shade,
records.s: The Lorenzo episode provides the direct model for Göchhausen’s scene involving the postman, postage money, the author’s capricious behavior, and subsequent self-reproach. It also informs the treatment of poor wandering monks and the recurring importance of the Lorenzodose.

records.l: critics, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [54] Another work in which sentimentalism has dwindled away to a grinning shade,
records.s: Critics are repeatedly addressed, mocked, and anticipated in M . . . R . . .. They object to devices such as the portmanteau, the use of a servant like La Fleur, and the borrowing of incidents from Yorick, while Göchhausen turns their objections into material for comic self-defense.

records.l: Sterne imitation in German literature, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [54] Another work in which sentimentalism has dwindled away to a grinning shade,
records.s: Sterne imitation is presented as widespread among the miscellaneous works discussed, though its quality and intensity vary. In M . . . R . . ., it is strongest at the beginning and includes formal structure, sentimental motifs, digression, readerly dialogue, narrative self-consciousness, and typographical play; reviewers condemned the dependence while praising parts of the book.

records.l: Laurence Sterne in Germany, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [69] Probably the best known novel which adopts in considerable measure the styl
records.s: The unit examines Johann Karl Wezel’s Tobias Knaut as a major German adaptation of the style of Tristram Shandy, combining the influence of Laurence Sterne and Henry Fielding with satire of Empfindsamkeit. It identifies numerous structural, typographical, narrative, and thematic parallels between Tobias Knaut and Sterne’s works, while emphasizing that Wezel’s episodes are more extraneous and that his satire sometimes opposes German sentimentalism. The unit also discusses Wegener’s Raritäten as a vulgar and pernicious imitation of Sterne, surveys scattered references to Sterne and Yorick in German literature, and assesses the limited or indirect Sternean qualities of writers including Adolph von Knigge, Moritz August von Thümmel, Theodor Gottlieb von Hippel, and Jean Paul. It concludes by noting that detailed studies of Thümmel, Hippel, and Jean Paul in relation to Sterne were intended as a continuation of the essay.

records.l: Tristram Shandy, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [69] Probably the best known novel which adopts in considerable measure the styl
records.s: Tristram Shandy serves as the principal model for many features of Tobias Knaut, including beginning the story ab ovo, episodical and digressive construction, conversations with the reader, typographical eccentricities, mock-pedantic learning, and theories about how trivial events shape later life. Wezel quotes it at length despite claiming that he had not read it when Tobias Knaut was begun.

records.l: Laurence Sterne, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [69] Probably the best known novel which adopts in considerable measure the styl
records.s: Laurence Sterne is presented as the dominant English influence on several German writers and as the source of numerous narrative, typographical, sentimental, and comic devices imitated by Wezel and Wegener. The unit also argues that German responses to Sterne ranged from admiration and productive adaptation to vulgar imitation and moral condemnation.

records.l: Tobias Knaut, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [69] Probably the best known novel which adopts in considerable measure the styl
records.s: Tobias Knaut, or Lebensgeschichte Tobias Knauts des Weisen sonst Stammler genannt, aus Familiennachrichten gesammelt, is described as probably the best-known German novel adopting the style of Tristram Shandy. It imitates Sterne in its digressions, readerly addresses, blank pages, mock scholarship, interrupted fragments, typographical play, and treatment of accidental events, while also satirizing Empfindsamkeit and the cult of originality.

records.l: Wezel, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [69] Probably the best known novel which adopts in considerable measure the styl
records.s: Johann Karl Wezel is credited with wit, narrative ability, knowledge of human nature, and a conscious plan in Tobias Knaut, but contemporary reviewers criticized his imitation of Sterne as obscuring his originality. His novel combines Sternean technique with satire directed against sentimentalism, exaggerated originality, and the German form of Sterne worship.

records.l: Henry Fielding, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [69] Probably the best known novel which adopts in considerable measure the styl
records.s: Henry Fielding’s influence is said to operate in Tobias Knaut alongside that of Sterne. The adventure involving Tobias and two maidens while he bathes is described as distinctly suggestive of Fielding.

records.l: Empfindsamkeit, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [69] Probably the best known novel which adopts in considerable measure the styl
records.s: Empfindsamkeit is treated as a target of Tobias Knaut’s satire. Wezel’s opposition to sentimentalism is presented as an important tendency that later became a guiding principle of Wilhelmine Arend.

records.l: Christoph Martin Wieland, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [69] Probably the best known novel which adopts in considerable measure the styl
records.s: Christoph Martin Wieland reviewed Tobias Knaut in his Merkur and, like Kurz, regarded Sterne’s influence as baneful. His Merkur also contains later references to Sterne and Yorick and condemns Wegener’s vulgar imitation.

records.l: Yorick, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [69] Probably the best known novel which adopts in considerable measure the styl
records.s: Yorick functions as a major model for characters, episodes, sentiments, and literary poses discussed in the unit. Selmann combines traits of Yorick and Walter Shandy, while German writers repeatedly invoke Yorick’s travels, Sensorium, sentimental responses, and encounters.

records.l: Walter Shandy, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [69] Probably the best known novel which adopts in considerable measure the styl
records.s: Walter Shandy is represented through theories about the dependence of great events on trifles and the importance of Christian names. Tobias Knaut echoes these ideas in stories involving a volume of Tacitus, Tobias’s hat, and the later citation of Walter Shandy’s theory in Adolph von Knigge’s Der Roman meines Lebens.

records.l: Selmann, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [69] Probably the best known novel which adopts in considerable measure the styl
records.s: Selmann is a compound of Yorick and the elder Shandy, with satiric exaggeration directed at the thirst for originals and overwrought sentimentalism. He is generous and sensitive to human pain, but also devotes himself to Shandean speculation about trivial relationships and repeatedly pursues supposedly sentimental or original experiences that prove to be jokes or deceptions.

records.l: Wegener’s Raritäten, ein hinterlassenes Werk des Küsters von Rummelsberg, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [69] Probably the best known novel which adopts in considerable measure the styl
records.s: Wegener’s Raritäten is presented as an example of the pernicious influence of Sterne, consisting of abrupt, conversational, affectedly merry prose and verse that reproduce Sterne’s ribaldry without his charm and grace. Its author explicitly describes trying to absorb Sterne’s spirit, while the work’s success is cited as evidence of perverted German literary taste.

records.l: Knigge, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [69] Probably the best known novel which adopts in considerable measure the styl
records.s: Adolph von Knigge is only remotely connected with Sterne. His Reise nach Braunschweig resembles Fielding and Smollett more than Sterne, although it includes conversation with the reader and perhaps a Sternean hobby-horse motif; his novels Peter Claus and Der Roman meines Lebens are not Sterne imitations, though both mention Sterne or quote ideas from him.

records.l: Moritz August von Thümmel, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [69] Probably the best known novel which adopts in considerable measure the styl
records.s: Moritz August von Thümmel adopted Sterne’s general idea of sentimental journeying in Reise in die mittäglichen Provinzen von Frankreich, while largely removing Sterne’s capriciousness and whimsicality. He also followed Sterne in bringing sensuous experience close to the border of the sensual.

records.l: Reise in die mittäglichen Provinzen von Frankreich, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [69] Probably the best known novel which adopts in considerable measure the styl
records.s: Reise in die mittäglichen Provinzen von Frankreich is characterized as an adaptation of Sterne’s general idea of sentimental travel. Its treatment is less capricious and whimsical than Sterne’s, but it retains a tendency to approach sensuality.

records.l: Sentimental Journey, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [69] Probably the best known novel which adopts in considerable measure the styl
records.s: The Sentimental Journey is used to date German enthusiasm for Sterne and German knowledge of Shandy. Heinse’s allusions to Sterne reportedly cease after August 23, 1771, which the unit connects with the publication and declining personal hold of The Sentimental Journey.

records.l: Theodor Gottlieb von Hippel, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [69] Probably the best known novel which adopts in considerable measure the styl
records.s: Theodor Gottlieb von Hippel wrote Lebensläufe nach aufsteigender Linie and Kreuz und Querzüge des Ritters A. bis Z., which are described as purely Shandean products. Their Sterne-derived humor struggles with pedagogical seriousness, and a detailed study of Hippel in relation to Sterne and Jean Paul is proposed.

records.l: Lebensläufe nach aufsteigender Linie, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [69] Probably the best known novel which adopts in considerable measure the styl
records.s: Lebensläufe nach aufsteigender Linie is identified as a Shandean work by Theodor Gottlieb von Hippel. Its humor is unmistakably imitated from Sterne but competes unsuccessfully with pedagogical seriousness.

records.l: Kreuz und Querzüge des Ritters A. bis Z., Laurence Sterne in Germany, [69] Probably the best known novel which adopts in considerable measure the styl
records.s: Kreuz und Querzüge des Ritters A. bis Z. is identified as another Shandean product by Theodor Gottlieb von Hippel. Like Lebensläufe nach aufsteigender Linie, it combines Sterne-derived humor with pedagogical seriousness.

records.l: Jean Paul, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [69] Probably the best known novel which adopts in considerable measure the styl
records.s: Jean Paul is described as undoubtedly indebted to Sterne for part of his literary equipment. His works demonstrate both his engagement with Sterne’s writings and the effect of that engagement on his own writing.

records.l: Sterne imitation in German literature, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [69] Probably the best known novel which adopts in considerable measure the styl
records.s: Sterne imitation in German literature appears in novels, travel narratives, poems, collections of anecdotes, typographical experiments, and casual literary allusions. The unit distinguishes strong imitations such as Tobias Knaut and Wegener’s Raritäten from remote connections, incidental references, and works that merely share an interest in personal travel or readerly address.

records.l: sentimental journeying, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [69] Probably the best known novel which adopts in considerable measure the styl
records.s: Sentimental travel is associated with Sterne’s influence on German literature, especially in Moritz August von Thümmel’s Reise in die mittäglichen Provinzen von Frankreich. Thümmel adopts the general idea while reducing the capricious and whimsical qualities of Sterne’s journey.

records.l: eighteenth-century German literary taste, Laurence Sterne in Germany, [69] Probably the best known novel which adopts in considerable measure the styl
records.s: Eighteenth-century German literary taste is criticized for rewarding vulgar and sexually explicit imitations of Sterne. The success of Wegener’s Raritäten is treated as evidence that public taste had become perverted, while other writers and reviewers condemned such imitation as pernicious.

records.l: Laurence Sterne in Germany, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ] CHAPTER VII OPPOSITION TO STERNE AND HIS TYPE OF SENTIMENTALISM Sterne’s influence in Germany lived its own life, and gradually and imperceptibly died out of letters, as an actuating principle.
records.s: Sterne’s influence in Germany gradually faded as an active literary principle, though Sterne himself remained a recognized prophet and leader. Opposition focused mainly on the unsuccessful adaptations of Yorick’s style and sentimentalism by German imitators, while critics such as Lessing, Goethe, and Herder continued to value Sterne. Georg Christopher Lichtenberg was the chief opponent of the sentimental tendency, attacking both Sterne’s personal character and the literary methods of Sterne’s disciples. Lichtenberg’s satires targeted sentimental journeying, eccentricity, lack of originality, and other tendencies associated with the Sentimentalists and Kraftgenies.

records.l: Laurence Sterne, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ] CHAPTER VII OPPOSITION TO STERNE AND HIS TYPE OF SENTIMENTALISM Sterne’s influence in Germany lived its own life, and gradually and imperceptibly died out of letters, as an actuating principle.
records.s: Sterne remained widely recognized in Germany as a prophet, uplifter, and leader, despite some criticism during the height of his popularity. Critics disagreed about his moral character: defenders praised his human heart and sympathies, while Georg Christopher Lichtenberg portrayed him as a manipulative writer whose personal selfishness contradicted the greatness of feeling in his novels.

records.l: Sterne’s influence in Germany, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ] CHAPTER VII OPPOSITION TO STERNE AND HIS TYPE OF SENTIMENTALISM Sterne’s influence in Germany lived its own life, and gradually and imperceptibly died out of letters, as an actuating principle.
records.s: Sterne’s influence in Germany developed independently and gradually died out as an actuating principle in literature. Its decline was accompanied by criticism of imitators who misunderstood or inadequately adapted Yorick’s ways of thinking and writing.

records.l: Empfindsamkeit, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ] CHAPTER VII OPPOSITION TO STERNE AND HIS TYPE OF SENTIMENTALISM Sterne’s influence in Germany lived its own life, and gradually and imperceptibly died out of letters, as an actuating principle.
records.s: Sentimentalism was criticized for encouraging artificial emotional display, eccentricity, and literary imitation. Lichtenberg attacked the sentimental tendencies of his age, including sentimental journeying and the practices associated with the Sentimentalists and Kraftgenies.

records.l: opposition to Sterne and his type of sentimentalism, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ] CHAPTER VII OPPOSITION TO STERNE AND HIS TYPE OF SENTIMENTALISM Sterne’s influence in Germany lived its own life, and gradually and imperceptibly died out of letters, as an actuating principle.
records.s: Opposition was directed chiefly against the misunderstanding and adaptation of Sterne’s methods rather than against Sterne himself. Some critics compared Sterne unfavorably with Addison, but defenders and major critics such as Lessing, Goethe, and Herder continued to express appreciation for him.

records.l: imitators of Sterne, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ] CHAPTER VII OPPOSITION TO STERNE AND HIS TYPE OF SENTIMENTALISM Sterne’s influence in Germany lived its own life, and gradually and imperceptibly died out of letters, as an actuating principle.
records.s: German imitators of Sterne were condemned for their incapacities, lack of originality, and unsuccessful reproduction of Yorick’s manner. Lichtenberg repeatedly ridiculed their efforts and satirized their eccentricities and sentimental journeying.

records.l: Christoph Martin Wieland, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ] CHAPTER VII OPPOSITION TO STERNE AND HIS TYPE OF SENTIMENTALISM Sterne’s influence in Germany lived its own life, and gradually and imperceptibly died out of letters, as an actuating principle.
records.s: Christoph Martin Wieland was criticized in 1772 for imitating Yorick in Diogenes. The review treated Wieland’s works as likely to outlast Sterne’s, but another reviewer called this compliment dubious and insulting, especially because of Wieland’s personal esteem for Sterne.

records.l: Georg Christoph Lichtenberg, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ] CHAPTER VII OPPOSITION TO STERNE AND HIS TYPE OF SENTIMENTALISM Sterne’s influence in Germany lived its own life, and gradually and imperceptibly died out of letters, as an actuating principle.
records.s: Georg Christopher Lichtenberg was presented as the chief opponent of the sentimental tendency and of Sterne’s disciples. He condemned Sterne’s alleged selfishness and artificial manipulation of emotion, questioned the sincerity of Sterne’s noble feelings, and satirized sentimental writers, eccentric literary fashions, and the lack of originality among German authors.

records.l: Gotthold Ephraim Lessing, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ] CHAPTER VII OPPOSITION TO STERNE AND HIS TYPE OF SENTIMENTALISM Sterne’s influence in Germany lived its own life, and gradually and imperceptibly died out of letters, as an actuating principle.
records.s: Gotthold Ephraim Lessing was identified as one of the clear-minded critics who unequivocally recognized Sterne’s importance. The text does not report any later withdrawal of his appreciation.

records.l: Johann Wolfgang Goethe, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ] CHAPTER VII OPPOSITION TO STERNE AND HIS TYPE OF SENTIMENTALISM Sterne’s influence in Germany lived its own life, and gradually and imperceptibly died out of letters, as an actuating principle.
records.s: Johann Wolfgang Goethe was identified as a clear-minded critic who expressed unequivocal appreciation for Sterne. His significant later words about Sterne came from the last years of his life, when the new century viewed the earlier literary fashion with almost incredulous amusement.

records.l: Johann Gottfried Herder, Laurence Sterne in Germany, ] CHAPTER VII OPPOSITION TO STERNE AND HIS TYPE OF SENTIMENTALISM Sterne’s influence in Germany lived its own life, and gradually and imperceptibly died out of letters, as an actuating principle.
records.s: Johann Gottfried Herder was identified as one of the far-seeing, clear-minded critics who recognized Sterne as a significant figure. The text does not report any later withdrawal of his appreciation.
