records.l: The 'Patriotes' of '37, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {1} CHAPTER I CANADIANS, OLD AND NEW The conquest of Canada by British arms in the Seven Years' War gave rise to a situation in the colony which was fraught with tragic possibilities.
records.s: The British conquest of Canada in the Seven Years' War placed French inhabitants under British rule, but the two communities generally lived together peacefully. French Canadians largely remained loyal to Great Britain during the American Revolution and the American invasion of Canada in 1775, encouraged by the policies of Murray and Carleton and the Quebec Act. They also fought alongside English Canadians during the War of 1812–1814, including Major de Salaberry's victory at Chateauguay. The later Rebellion in Canada was the only significant armed conflict between the two groups, with fighting at St Denis, St Charles, and St Eustache.

records.l: Canada, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {1} CHAPTER I CANADIANS, OLD AND NEW The conquest of Canada by British arms in the Seven Years' War gave rise to a situation in the colony which was fraught with tragic possibilities.
records.s: Canada came under British rule after the conquest in the Seven Years' War. French and English Canadians generally lived together in peace for a hundred and fifty years, apart from the Rebellion in Canada.

records.l: French Canadians, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {1} CHAPTER I CANADIANS, OLD AND NEW The conquest of Canada by British arms in the Seven Years' War gave rise to a situation in the colony which was fraught with tragic possibilities.
records.s: The French inhabitants were placed under the rule of a people with a different language, religion, laws, temperament, and political outlook. Most remained in Canada after the conquest and generally lived peacefully with English Canadians.

records.l: English population in Canada, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {1} CHAPTER I CANADIANS, OLD AND NEW The conquest of Canada by British arms in the Seven Years' War gave rise to a situation in the colony which was fraught with tragic possibilities.
records.s: English Canadians generally lived peacefully with French Canadians after the conquest. During the War of 1812–1814, they fought alongside French-Canadian militiamen, but during the Rebellion in Canada the two groups were arrayed against each other.

records.l: Canadians, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {1} CHAPTER I CANADIANS, OLD AND NEW The conquest of Canada by British arms in the Seven Years' War gave rise to a situation in the colony which was fraught with tragic possibilities.
records.s: Canadians, whether English or French, have reason to view the record of relations between the two communities with satisfaction. The text describes a hundred and fifty years of general peace and amity, interrupted by only one limited and brief outbreak resembling civil war.

records.l: British rule, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {1} CHAPTER I CANADIANS, OLD AND NEW The conquest of Canada by British arms in the Seven Years' War gave rise to a situation in the colony which was fraught with tragic possibilities.
records.s: British rule in Canada began after the conquest in the Seven Years' War. The text examines how French Canadians generally remained loyal to the British crown under that rule, despite the later Rebellion in Canada.

records.l: Seven Years' War, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {1} CHAPTER I CANADIANS, OLD AND NEW The conquest of Canada by British arms in the Seven Years' War gave rise to a situation in the colony which was fraught with tragic possibilities.
records.s: The Seven Years' War ended with the conquest of Canada by British arms. This conquest placed the French inhabitants under British rule.

records.l: conquest of Canada, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {1} CHAPTER I CANADIANS, OLD AND NEW The conquest of Canada by British arms in the Seven Years' War gave rise to a situation in the colony which was fraught with tragic possibilities.
records.s: The conquest of Canada created the possibility of prolonged conflict between French inhabitants and the British conquerors. Instead, most French inhabitants stayed, and relations between French and English Canadians were generally peaceful.

records.l: Sir Guy Carleton, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {1} CHAPTER I CANADIANS, OLD AND NEW The conquest of Canada by British arms in the Seven Years' War gave rise to a situation in the colony which was fraught with tragic possibilities.
records.s: Carleton was one of the successive governors whose conciliatory policy helped win the loyalty of French Canadians. When American forces invaded Canada in 1775, a much larger number of habitants enlisted under Carleton than joined the invaders.

records.l: Quebec Act of 1774, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {1} CHAPTER I CANADIANS, OLD AND NEW The conquest of Canada by British arms in the Seven Years' War gave rise to a situation in the colony which was fraught with tragic possibilities.
records.s: The Quebec Act, passed in the year before the American invasion of Canada in 1775, granted concessions that helped produce French-Canadian loyalty to Great Britain.

records.l: American Revolution, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {1} CHAPTER I CANADIANS, OLD AND NEW The conquest of Canada by British arms in the Seven Years' War gave rise to a situation in the colony which was fraught with tragic possibilities.
records.s: During the American Revolution, efforts were made to persuade French Canadians to join the American cause. Most French Canadians resisted those appeals and remained at least passively loyal to Great Britain.

records.l: Continental Congress, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {1} CHAPTER I CANADIANS, OLD AND NEW The conquest of Canada by British arms in the Seven Years' War gave rise to a situation in the colony which was fraught with tragic possibilities.
records.s: The Continental Congress sought to induce the French Canadians to join hands with the American revolutionaries. Its emissaries Franklin, Chase, and Carroll made eloquent appeals, but the mass of the people resisted them.

records.l: American invasion of Canada (1775), The 'Patriotes' of '37, {1} CHAPTER I CANADIANS, OLD AND NEW The conquest of Canada by British arms in the Seven Years' War gave rise to a situation in the colony which was fraught with tragic possibilities.
records.s: During the American invasion of Canada in 1775, Arnold and Montgomery invaded the colony. Most habitants remained at least passively loyal, while a few hundred may have joined the invaders and a much larger number enlisted under Carleton.

records.l: Quebec, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {1} CHAPTER I CANADIANS, OLD AND NEW The conquest of Canada by British arms in the Seven Years' War gave rise to a situation in the colony which was fraught with tragic possibilities.
records.s: Quebec was besieged by Arnold during the American invasion of Canada in 1775. Canadian officers including Dupre, Dambourges, Dumas, and Marcoux helped Carleton drive back the invading Americans.

records.l: Catholic clergy, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {1} CHAPTER I CANADIANS, OLD AND NEW The conquest of Canada by British arms in the Seven Years' War gave rise to a situation in the colony which was fraught with tragic possibilities.
records.s: The clergy remained firmly loyal to Great Britain in 1775 and used their influence in its favor. Haldimand later claimed that they had changed their opinions, but the text attributes his impression to dissatisfaction with his high-handed rule and notes that Mgr Briand was devoted to Great Britain.

records.l: French Revolution, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {1} CHAPTER I CANADIANS, OLD AND NEW The conquest of Canada by British arms in the Seven Years' War gave rise to a situation in the colony which was fraught with tragic possibilities.
records.s: The French Revolution widened the separation between France and Canada. Its anti-clerical and republican tendencies had little in common with Canada, which was described as a child of the ancien regime.

records.l: France, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {1} CHAPTER I CANADIANS, OLD AND NEW The conquest of Canada by British arms in the Seven Years' War gave rise to a situation in the colony which was fraught with tragic possibilities.
records.s: The French Revolution profoundly altered French Canadians' attitude toward France. The movement created a gap between France and Canada that, according to the text, had not been bridged.

records.l: War of 1812, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {1} CHAPTER I CANADIANS, OLD AND NEW The conquest of Canada by British arms in the Seven Years' War gave rise to a situation in the colony which was fraught with tragic possibilities.
records.s: During the War of 1812–1814, Canada was repeatedly invaded by American armies. French-Canadian militiamen under French-Canadian officers fought alongside English-speaking Canadians, and French-Canadian forces helped win the engagement at Chateauguay.

records.l: United States, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {1} CHAPTER I CANADIANS, OLD AND NEW The conquest of Canada by British arms in the Seven Years' War gave rise to a situation in the colony which was fraught with tragic possibilities.
records.s: The United States invaded Canada during the War of 1812–1814. Its earlier revolutionary forces also invaded Canada in 1775, but French Canadians generally resisted joining them.

records.l: French-Canadian militiamen, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {1} CHAPTER I CANADIANS, OLD AND NEW The conquest of Canada by British arms in the Seven Years' War gave rise to a situation in the colony which was fraught with tragic possibilities.
records.s: French-Canadian militiamen fought under French-Canadian officers alongside their English-speaking fellow-countrymen during the War of 1812–1814. At Chateauguay, Major de Salaberry and his French-Canadian soldiers won the day for British arms.

records.l: Major de Salaberry, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {1} CHAPTER I CANADIANS, OLD AND NEW The conquest of Canada by British arms in the Seven Years' War gave rise to a situation in the colony which was fraught with tragic possibilities.
records.s: Major de Salaberry led French-Canadian soldiers at Chateauguay during the War of 1812–1814. Their heroic prowess won the engagement for British arms.

records.l: Battle of Chateauguay, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {1} CHAPTER I CANADIANS, OLD AND NEW The conquest of Canada by British arms in the Seven Years' War gave rise to a situation in the colony which was fraught with tragic possibilities.
records.s: The engagement at Chateauguay was fought in the French province of Lower Canada during the War of 1812–1814. Major de Salaberry and his French-Canadian soldiers won the day for British arms.

records.l: Lower Canada, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {1} CHAPTER I CANADIANS, OLD AND NEW The conquest of Canada by British arms in the Seven Years' War gave rise to a situation in the colony which was fraught with tragic possibilities.
records.s: Lower Canada was the French province where the engagement at Chateauguay was fought. It was also the setting for the later fighting between French-Canadian rebels and British forces at St Denis, St Charles, and St Eustache.

records.l: rebellion of 1837, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {1} CHAPTER I CANADIANS, OLD AND NEW The conquest of Canada by British arms in the Seven Years' War gave rise to a situation in the colony which was fraught with tragic possibilities.
records.s: The Rebellion in Canada was the only occasion described as resembling civil war between French and English Canadians during a hundred and fifty years of British rule. French-Canadian veterans and English-Canadian veterans fought on opposing sides, including engagements at St Denis, St Charles, and St Eustache.

records.l: The 'Patriotes' of '37, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {7} CHAPTER II THE RIGHTS OF THE DEFEATED The British did not treat the French inhabitants of Canada as a conquered people; not as other countries won by conquest have been treated by their victorious invaders.
records.s: The British granted the French inhabitants of Canada property, civil, religious, and political protections after the conquest, including French civil law and equal political rights in Upper Canada and Lower Canada. These concessions helped preserve French Canadian loyalty to the British crown while strengthening French national identity and demands for wider liberties. In the first Parliament of Lower Canada, French-speaking members secured the use of the French language alongside English in the Assembly's proceedings and publications. Early debates remained generally civil, although racial bitterness emerged later during the regime of Sir James Craig.

records.l: British, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {7} CHAPTER II THE RIGHTS OF THE DEFEATED The British did not treat the French inhabitants of Canada as a conquered people; not as other countries won by conquest have been treated by their victorious invaders.
records.s: The British protected the property and civil rights of the French inhabitants of Canada rather than treating them as a conquered people. They also granted religious and political concessions that helped maintain French Canadian loyalty.

records.l: French Canadians, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {7} CHAPTER II THE RIGHTS OF THE DEFEATED The British did not treat the French inhabitants of Canada as a conquered people; not as other countries won by conquest have been treated by their victorious invaders.
records.s: The French inhabitants of Canada received guarantees of property, civil rights, and free religious exercise. They remained loyal to the British crown during the wars of 1775 and 1812, while becoming more jealous of their national identity and pressing for wider liberties.

records.l: Canada, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {7} CHAPTER II THE RIGHTS OF THE DEFEATED The British did not treat the French inhabitants of Canada as a conquered people; not as other countries won by conquest have been treated by their victorious invaders.
records.s: Canada received constitutional arrangements that preserved French civil law, recognized Catholic religious obligations, and divided the territory into Upper Canada and Lower Canada in 1791. French and English were subsequently used in the political proceedings of Lower Canada.

records.l: Capitulation of Montreal, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {7} CHAPTER II THE RIGHTS OF THE DEFEATED The British did not treat the French inhabitants of Canada as a conquered people; not as other countries won by conquest have been treated by their victorious invaders.
records.s: The Capitulation of Montreal in 1760 assured the Canadians of their property and civil rights and guaranteed them the free exercise of their religion.

records.l: Quebec Act of 1774, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {7} CHAPTER II THE RIGHTS OF THE DEFEATED The British did not treat the French inhabitants of Canada as a conquered people; not as other countries won by conquest have been treated by their victorious invaders.
records.s: The Quebec Act of 1774 granted the French civil law almost complete exclusion of the English common law. It also virtually established the Church of the vanquished through legal enforcement of Catholics' obligation to pay tithes.

records.l: French civil law, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {7} CHAPTER II THE RIGHTS OF THE DEFEATED The British did not treat the French inhabitants of Canada as a conquered people; not as other countries won by conquest have been treated by their victorious invaders.
records.s: The Quebec Act of 1774 restored the French civil law in Canada, making it the dominant legal system over the English common law.

records.l: French-Canadian Church, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {7} CHAPTER II THE RIGHTS OF THE DEFEATED The British did not treat the French inhabitants of Canada as a conquered people; not as other countries won by conquest have been treated by their victorious invaders.
records.s: The Roman Catholic Church was virtually established in Canada through the Quebec Act of 1774, which legally enforced the obligation of Catholics to pay tithes.

records.l: British government, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {7} CHAPTER II THE RIGHTS OF THE DEFEATED The British did not treat the French inhabitants of Canada as a conquered people; not as other countries won by conquest have been treated by their victorious invaders.
records.s: The British government pursued a conciliatory policy toward the French inhabitants of Canada. It made no objection to the use of French in the law-courts and its concessions helped keep French Canadians loyal to the British crown.

records.l: British crown, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {7} CHAPTER II THE RIGHTS OF THE DEFEATED The British did not treat the French inhabitants of Canada as a conquered people; not as other countries won by conquest have been treated by their victorious invaders.
records.s: The British crown retained the loyalty of the clergy, the seigneurs, and the great body of French Canadians through conciliatory measures during the wars of 1775 and 1812.

records.l: Upper Canada, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {7} CHAPTER II THE RIGHTS OF THE DEFEATED The British did not treat the French inhabitants of Canada as a conquered people; not as other countries won by conquest have been treated by their victorious invaders.
records.s: Upper Canada was created in 1791 as one of two provinces, predominantly English in population. It received political rights equal to those of Lower Canada.

records.l: Lower Canada, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {7} CHAPTER II THE RIGHTS OF THE DEFEATED The British did not treat the French inhabitants of Canada as a conquered people; not as other countries won by conquest have been treated by their victorious invaders.
records.s: Lower Canada was created in 1791 as the predominantly French province alongside Upper Canada. Its first Parliament met in 1792, and its Assembly recognized French alongside English in its proceedings and publications.

records.l: Act of 1791, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {7} CHAPTER II THE RIGHTS OF THE DEFEATED The British did not treat the French inhabitants of Canada as a conquered people; not as other countries won by conquest have been treated by their victorious invaders.
records.s: The Act of 1791 divided Canada into Upper Canada and Lower Canada and granted the two provinces precisely equal political rights. It created representative Assemblies in which Canadian Catholics could sit despite their exclusion from the House of Commons at Westminster.

records.l: Canadian representative Assemblies, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {7} CHAPTER II THE RIGHTS OF THE DEFEATED The British did not treat the French inhabitants of Canada as a conquered people; not as other countries won by conquest have been treated by their victorious invaders.
records.s: The Canadian representative Assemblies created by the Act of 1791 allowed Catholics of Canada to sit as members. This gave them privileges denied to their co-religionists in Great Britain.

records.l: legislature of Lower Canada, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {7} CHAPTER II THE RIGHTS OF THE DEFEATED The British did not treat the French inhabitants of Canada as a conquered people; not as other countries won by conquest have been treated by their victorious invaders.
records.s: The first Parliament of Lower Canada was called in 1792. Its opening raised the question of the status and use of the French language in the Assembly.

records.l: Assembly of Lower Canada, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {7} CHAPTER II THE RIGHTS OF THE DEFEATED The British did not treat the French inhabitants of Canada as a conquered people; not as other countries won by conquest have been treated by their victorious invaders.
records.s: The Assembly of Lower Canada had thirty-four French-Canadian members and sixteen English members, with the English members owing their election to French-Canadian voters. It elected Jean Antoine Panet as speaker and placed French on a level with English in its records and publications, making French the language of debate for practical purposes.

records.l: French language, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {7} CHAPTER II THE RIGHTS OF THE DEFEATED The British did not treat the French inhabitants of Canada as a conquered people; not as other countries won by conquest have been treated by their victorious invaders.
records.s: The French language was used in the Assembly of Lower Canada and was placed on a level with English in its records and official publications. By 1800, most members debated in French because only one or two English members ventured to speak English.

records.l: English language, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {7} CHAPTER II THE RIGHTS OF THE DEFEATED The British did not treat the French inhabitants of Canada as a conquered people; not as other countries won by conquest have been treated by their victorious invaders.
records.s: The English language was defended by English members as the language of the sovereign and the empire. Despite this position, it did not become the dominant language of debate in the early Assembly of Lower Canada.

records.l: official recognition of French, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {7} CHAPTER II THE RIGHTS OF THE DEFEATED The British did not treat the French inhabitants of Canada as a conquered people; not as other countries won by conquest have been treated by their victorious invaders.
records.s: French-Canadian members pressed for official recognition of French on a parity with English. The outcome placed French on a level with English in the Assembly's records and publications.

records.l: French political majority in Lower Canada, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {7} CHAPTER II THE RIGHTS OF THE DEFEATED The British did not treat the French inhabitants of Canada as a conquered people; not as other countries won by conquest have been treated by their victorious invaders.
records.s: The French political majority in Lower Canada consisted of thirty-four members compared with sixteen English members in the first Assembly. It elected Jean Antoine Panet as speaker and secured the use of French in Assembly proceedings.

records.l: English members of the Assembly, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {7} CHAPTER II THE RIGHTS OF THE DEFEATED The British did not treat the French inhabitants of Canada as a conquered people; not as other countries won by conquest have been treated by their victorious invaders.
records.s: The English members of the Assembly opposed the election of Jean Antoine Panet and argued that dealings with the king's representative should occur in English. They also argued that exclusive official use of English would assimilate the French Canadians and make them more loyal.

records.l: French-Canadian nationalism, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {7} CHAPTER II THE RIGHTS OF THE DEFEATED The British did not treat the French inhabitants of Canada as a conquered people; not as other countries won by conquest have been treated by their victorious invaders.
records.s: The concessions granted by the British strengthened the position of the French race in Canada and made Canadians more jealous of their national identity. This contributed to demands for still wider liberties.

records.l: racial bitterness in Lower Canada, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {7} CHAPTER II THE RIGHTS OF THE DEFEATED The British did not treat the French inhabitants of Canada as a conquered people; not as other countries won by conquest have been treated by their victorious invaders.
records.s: Racial bitterness had not characterized the earliest Assembly debates, which retained decorum and social intercourse. It began later, during the regime of Sir James Craig.

records.l: The 'Patriotes' of '37, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {13} CHAPTER III 'THE REIGN OF TERROR' During the session of 1805 the Assembly was confronted with the apparently innocent problem of building prisons.
records.s: A dispute over how to fund prisons in 1805 intensified racial conflict between the agrarian French Canadians and commercially oriented English Canadians in Lower Canada. The French response included founding Le Canadien in 1806 to defend their language, institutions, laws, and political position. After Sir James Craig became governor in 1807, he dismissed militia officers associated with the paper, suppressed Le Canadien, and arrested its printer and proprietors, including Pierre Bedard. Craig’s policy failed to suppress opposition and worsened relations between the two groups, while Sir George Prevost later pursued conciliation and restored Bedard to public office.

records.l: racial bitterness in Lower Canada, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {13} CHAPTER III 'THE REIGN OF TERROR' During the session of 1805 the Assembly was confronted with the apparently innocent problem of building prisons.
records.s: Racial conflict intensified during the 1805 debate over whether to fund prisons through a land tax or customs duties. The dispute led English Canadians to oppose French-Canadian domination and contributed to worsening relations between the two groups under Sir James Craig.

records.l: French Canadians, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {13} CHAPTER III 'THE REIGN OF TERROR' During the session of 1805 the Assembly was confronted with the apparently innocent problem of building prisons.
records.s: The French Canadians, whose interests were mainly agrarian, opposed a direct land tax and secured the adoption of extra customs duties. They established Le Canadien in 1806 to present their majority viewpoint in the House of Assembly and defend their language, institutions, and laws.

records.l: English population in Canada, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {13} CHAPTER III 'THE REIGN OF TERROR' During the session of 1805 the Assembly was confronted with the apparently innocent problem of building prisons.
records.s: The English Canadians, whose interests were generally commercial, advocated a direct tax on land and opposed the French proposal for additional customs duties. Their minority accused the French Canadians of imposing the burden of taxation and demanded an end to French-Canadian domination.

records.l: Pierre Bedard, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {13} CHAPTER III 'THE REIGN OF TERROR' During the session of 1805 the Assembly was confronted with the apparently innocent problem of building prisons.
records.s: Pierre Bedard was a member of the House of Assembly and a prominent figure on the staff of Le Canadien. Sir James Craig dismissed him from the militia and later arrested him when Le Canadien was suppressed; Bedard refused release without a trial and was eventually ejected from prison at bayonet point. Sir George Prevost later restored him to militia rank and made him a judge.

records.l: Sir James Craig, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {13} CHAPTER III 'THE REIGN OF TERROR' During the session of 1805 the Assembly was confronted with the apparently innocent problem of building prisons.
records.s: Sir James Craig became governor of Canada in 1807 and was suspicious of the loyalty of the French Canadians. He dismissed militia officers linked to Le Canadien, suppressed the newspaper in 1810, and arrested its printer and three proprietors. His policy failed to suppress opposition and embittered relations between the two races, and he later reportedly acknowledged that he had been deceived.

records.l: Canada, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {13} CHAPTER III 'THE REIGN OF TERROR' During the session of 1805 the Assembly was confronted with the apparently innocent problem of building prisons.
records.s: Canada was governed by Sir James Craig during a period when Napoleon was at the height of his power and British authorities feared enemy agents might be active there. Craig’s successor, Sir George Prevost, adopted a conciliatory policy toward the French Canadians.

records.l: Le Canadien suppression and arrests, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {13} CHAPTER III 'THE REIGN OF TERROR' During the session of 1805 the Assembly was confronted with the apparently innocent problem of building prisons.
records.s: In May 1810 Sir James Craig suppressed Le Canadien and arrested its printer and three proprietors: Taschereau, Blanchet, and Pierre Bedard. The stated pretext was the publication of notes about the conflict between the governor and the House of Assembly in Jamaica, but the deeper cause was Craig’s opposition to the newspaper’s policy.

records.l: War of 1812, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {13} CHAPTER III 'THE REIGN OF TERROR' During the session of 1805 the Assembly was confronted with the apparently innocent problem of building prisons.
records.s: When the War of 1812 broke out, Lower Canada showed less disloyalty than Upper Canada. The reduction of bitterness under Sir George Prevost’s conciliatory policy preceded this result.

records.l: Sir George Prevost, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {13} CHAPTER III 'THE REIGN OF TERROR' During the session of 1805 the Assembly was confronted with the apparently innocent problem of building prisons.
records.s: Sir George Prevost succeeded Sir James Craig and completely reversed Craig’s policy by seeking to conciliate the French Canadians. He restored Pierre Bedard to his militia rank and made him a judge, helping reduce racial bitterness.

records.l: Lower Canada, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {13} CHAPTER III 'THE REIGN OF TERROR' During the session of 1805 the Assembly was confronted with the apparently innocent problem of building prisons.
records.s: Lower Canada was the setting for the dispute over prison funding, the rise of Le Canadien, and Sir James Craig’s repression of French-Canadian political opposition. After Sir George Prevost adopted a conciliatory policy, Lower Canada showed less disloyalty during the War of 1812 than Upper Canada.

records.l: Reign of Terror, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {13} CHAPTER III 'THE REIGN OF TERROR' During the session of 1805 the Assembly was confronted with the apparently innocent problem of building prisons.
records.s: The 'Reign of Terror' refers to the period after Sir James Craig’s arrival in Canada when his government acted against French-Canadian opposition and Le Canadien. It included the dismissal of militia officers, the suppression of the newspaper, and the arrest of its printer and proprietors.

records.l: The 'Patriotes' of '37, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {21} CHAPTER IV THE RISE OF PAPINEAU In the year 1812 a young man took his seat in the House of Assembly for Lower Canada who was destined to play a conspicuous part in the history of the province during the next quarter of a century.
records.s: Louis Joseph Papineau entered the House of Assembly for Lower Canada in 1812 and became its speaker in 1815, guiding the Patriote party for much of the next twenty-two years. French Canadians sought greater constitutional power, especially control over revenue and the Executive, which were dominated by the Legislative Council and the Bureaucrats or Chateau Clique. Papineau opposed successive attempts to limit French-Canadian influence, including the Union Bill of 1822, and became embroiled in a bitter conflict with Lord Dalhousie. Financial disputes continued despite British efforts at compromise, and Papineau's uncompromising leadership contributed to a prolonged political deadlock.

records.l: Papineau, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {21} CHAPTER IV THE RISE OF PAPINEAU In the year 1812 a young man took his seat in the House of Assembly for Lower Canada who was destined to play a conspicuous part in the history of the province during the next quarter of a century.
records.s: Louis Joseph Papineau entered the House of Assembly for Lower Canada in 1812 at age twenty-six and was elected speaker three years later. He guided the Patriote party from the speaker's chair, opposed the government during the budget struggles, helped defeat the Union Bill of 1822, and later attacked Lord Dalhousie. The text portrays him as eloquent and influential but also unbending and lacking a spirit of compromise.

records.l: Assembly of Lower Canada, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {21} CHAPTER IV THE RISE OF PAPINEAU In the year 1812 a young man took his seat in the House of Assembly for Lower Canada who was destined to play a conspicuous part in the history of the province during the next quarter of a century.
records.s: The House of Assembly was elected by the people of Lower Canada but lacked control over the Executive and could have its measures rejected by the Legislative Council. It gradually sought control over the province's revenues and repeatedly refused to vote a permanent civil list, producing a long deadlock with the government.

records.l: Lower Canada, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {21} CHAPTER IV THE RISE OF PAPINEAU In the year 1812 a young man took his seat in the House of Assembly for Lower Canada who was destined to play a conspicuous part in the history of the province during the next quarter of a century.
records.s: Lower Canada was governed through institutions in which the governor, Executive Council, and Legislative Council were not responsible to the elected Assembly. Its political life was marked by conflict between French Canadians and the English-dominated governing class over constitutional power, finances, and appointments.

records.l: Patriote party, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {21} CHAPTER IV THE RISE OF PAPINEAU In the year 1812 a young man took his seat in the House of Assembly for Lower Canada who was destined to play a conspicuous part in the history of the province during the next quarter of a century.
records.s: The Patriote party represented the position of the French-Canadian majority in the Assembly and opposed the power of the Bureaucrats or Chateau Clique. Under Papineau's guidance, it resisted permanent financial settlements that would limit the Assembly's control and demanded reforms in the administration of Lower Canada.

records.l: British constitution, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {21} CHAPTER IV THE RISE OF PAPINEAU In the year 1812 a young man took his seat in the House of Assembly for Lower Canada who was destined to play a conspicuous part in the history of the province during the next quarter of a century.
records.s: French-Canadian members of the Assembly studied the law and customs of the British constitution and concluded that they lacked the powers enjoyed by the House of Commons in England. Papineau initially expressed admiration for the constitution and the blessings of British rule, but later opposed the colonial government more strongly.

records.l: Legislative Council, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {21} CHAPTER IV THE RISE OF PAPINEAU In the year 1812 a young man took his seat in the House of Assembly for Lower Canada who was destined to play a conspicuous part in the history of the province during the next quarter of a century.
records.s: The Legislative Council repeatedly rejected measures passed by the House of Assembly and blocked budgets during the dispute over the civil list. Its members were mainly of English birth, and many office-holders sat in it, leaving it under the influence of the executive government.

records.l: Bureaucrats, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {21} CHAPTER IV THE RISE OF PAPINEAU In the year 1812 a young man took his seat in the House of Assembly for Lower Canada who was destined to play a conspicuous part in the history of the province during the next quarter of a century.
records.s: The Bureaucrats were the local oligarchy that controlled the government of Lower Canada through the governor, Executive Council, and Legislative Council. They were generally of English birth and could often disregard the majority in the House of Assembly.

records.l: Chateau Clique, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {21} CHAPTER IV THE RISE OF PAPINEAU In the year 1812 a young man took his seat in the House of Assembly for Lower Canada who was destined to play a conspicuous part in the history of the province during the next quarter of a century.
records.s: The Chateau Clique was another name for the Bureaucrats, the English-dominated group that held the reins of government in Lower Canada. Conflict between it and the Patriotes intensified as the Assembly challenged executive control and financial practices.

records.l: House of Commons, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {21} CHAPTER IV THE RISE OF PAPINEAU In the year 1812 a young man took his seat in the House of Assembly for Lower Canada who was destined to play a conspicuous part in the history of the province during the next quarter of a century.
records.s: The House of Commons in England exercised control over the purse and could pressure the Executive by threatening to withhold supplies. A Union Bill concerning Upper and Lower Canada was introduced there in 1822, but Papineau and John Neilson helped secure its defeat.

records.l: British government, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {21} CHAPTER IV THE RISE OF PAPINEAU In the year 1812 a young man took his seat in the House of Assembly for Lower Canada who was destined to play a conspicuous part in the history of the province during the next quarter of a century.
records.s: The Imperial government appointed the governor and Executive Council through the Colonial Office and initially supplied funds needed to cover Lower Canada's deficit. In 1818 it accepted the Assembly's offer to vote most provincial revenue, and in 1830 Lord Goderich proposed another financial compromise involving a permanent civil list.

records.l: civil list, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {21} CHAPTER IV THE RISE OF PAPINEAU In the year 1812 a young man took his seat in the House of Assembly for Lower Canada who was destined to play a conspicuous part in the history of the province during the next quarter of a century.
records.s: The civil list was the permanent funding proposed for the salaries and civil expenses of the government. The Assembly insisted on voting it annually rather than for the sovereign's lifetime, while Lord Goderich later offered control of provincial revenue in exchange for a civil list of L19,000 voted for the lifetime of the king.

records.l: responsible government, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {21} CHAPTER IV THE RISE OF PAPINEAU In the year 1812 a young man took his seat in the House of Assembly for Lower Canada who was destined to play a conspicuous part in the history of the province during the next quarter of a century.
records.s: Responsible government was not yet established because the governor and Executive Council were responsible to the Colonial Office rather than to the Assembly. Sherbrooke's recommendation that the speaker sit on the Executive Council, and Mondelet's appointment to it, were described as steps toward responsible government.

records.l: Union Bill of 1822, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {21} CHAPTER IV THE RISE OF PAPINEAU In the year 1812 a young man took his seat in the House of Assembly for Lower Canada who was destined to play a conspicuous part in the history of the province during the next quarter of a century.
records.s: The Union Bill of 1822 proposed to unite Upper and Lower Canada in terms that French Canadians believed would extinguish the Lower-Canadian Assembly and subordinate the French to the English element. Louis Joseph Papineau and John Neilson went to London to oppose it and succeeded in having it shelved.

records.l: John Neilson, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {21} CHAPTER IV THE RISE OF PAPINEAU In the year 1812 a young man took his seat in the House of Assembly for Lower Canada who was destined to play a conspicuous part in the history of the province during the next quarter of a century.
records.s: John Neilson, the Scottish editor of the Quebec Gazette, accompanied Louis Joseph Papineau to London in 1822 to oppose the Union Bill. He helped secure its defeat and later joined Augustin Cuvillier and Denis B. Viger in a 1827 deputation that sought redress of grievances and Lord Dalhousie's removal.

records.l: Lord Dalhousie, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {21} CHAPTER IV THE RISE OF PAPINEAU In the year 1812 a young man took his seat in the House of Assembly for Lower Canada who was destined to play a conspicuous part in the history of the province during the next quarter of a century.
records.s: Lord Dalhousie became governor of Canada in 1819 and was described as liberal and friendly toward relations between the two races. Papineau attacked him over financial irregularities and Caldwell's defalcations, after which Dalhousie refused to recognize Papineau as speaker and dissolved the Assembly. A later deputation obtained Dalhousie's recall.

records.l: Lord Goderich, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {21} CHAPTER IV THE RISE OF PAPINEAU In the year 1812 a young man took his seat in the House of Assembly for Lower Canada who was destined to play a conspicuous part in the history of the province during the next quarter of a century.
records.s: Lord Goderich, at the Colonial Office in 1830, instructed Lord Aylmer to offer the Assembly control of nearly the entire provincial revenue in exchange for a permanent civil list of L19,000 for the lifetime of the king. Papineau and his friends defeated the proposal in 1831.

records.l: Lord Aylmer, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {21} CHAPTER IV THE RISE OF PAPINEAU In the year 1812 a young man took his seat in the House of Assembly for Lower Canada who was destined to play a conspicuous part in the history of the province during the next quarter of a century.
records.s: Lord Aylmer became governor of Canada in 1830 and was instructed to implement Lord Goderich's proposed financial compromise. The text describes him as disposed to be friendly, but Papineau's attitude toward him helped drive him toward the Chateau Clique.

records.l: financial quarrel, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {21} CHAPTER IV THE RISE OF PAPINEAU In the year 1812 a young man took his seat in the House of Assembly for Lower Canada who was destined to play a conspicuous part in the history of the province during the next quarter of a century.
records.s: The financial quarrel concerned whether the House of Assembly or the Executive should control provincial revenue and government expenditures. The Assembly refused to vote a permanent civil list, the Legislative Council rejected its budgets, and the resulting deadlock continued for many years.

records.l: control of the purse, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {21} CHAPTER IV THE RISE OF PAPINEAU In the year 1812 a young man took his seat in the House of Assembly for Lower Canada who was destined to play a conspicuous part in the history of the province during the next quarter of a century.
records.s: Control of the purse was the Assembly's potential means of forcing the Executive to obey it by withholding supplies. Lower Canada's Assembly initially lacked this power because provincial expenditures exceeded revenue and the Imperial exchequer covered the deficit, but later British proposals sought to give it broader control.

records.l: French Canadians, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {21} CHAPTER IV THE RISE OF PAPINEAU In the year 1812 a young man took his seat in the House of Assembly for Lower Canada who was destined to play a conspicuous part in the history of the province during the next quarter of a century.
records.s: French Canadians formed the majority in the House of Assembly and sought protection for their laws, religion, privileges, and national existence. They opposed the Union Bill of 1822 and resented the English-dominated administration, financial abuses, favoritism, and repeated obstruction by the Legislative Council.

records.l: English population in Canada, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {21} CHAPTER IV THE RISE OF PAPINEAU In the year 1812 a young man took his seat in the House of Assembly for Lower Canada who was destined to play a conspicuous part in the history of the province during the next quarter of a century.
records.s: The English population in Canada supplied most of the members of the two councils and dominated the governing class described as the Bureaucrats or Chateau Clique. French Canadians believed that the English element was being favored in government appointments and that the Union Bill of 1822 threatened to subordinate them to it.

records.l: The 'Patriotes' of '37, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {33} CHAPTER V THE NINETY-TWO RESOLUTIONS After 1830 signs began to multiply that the racial feud in Lower Canada was growing in intensity.
records.s: The racial and political conflict in Lower Canada intensified after 1830, with violence in Montreal, attacks on Lord Aylmer, and increasingly coercive conduct by Papineau in the Assembly of Lower Canada. Papineau moved from criticism of the 1791 constitution toward admiration for the United States and advocacy of an elective Legislative Council. The Ninety-Two Resolutions, passed in 1834 by a large majority, identified genuine abuses but also used revolutionary language, demanded Lord Aylmer's impeachment, and offered no clear plan for responsible government. Their passage divided the Patriote party, as John Neilson and other moderates broke with Papineau, while several prominent future Canadian leaders remained among his supporters.

records.l: Lower Canada, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {33} CHAPTER V THE NINETY-TWO RESOLUTIONS After 1830 signs began to multiply that the racial feud in Lower Canada was growing in intensity.
records.s: Lower Canada experienced increasing racial and political conflict after 1830. Its government and institutions were criticized for abuses involving the Legislative Council, public offices, wild lands, finances, and elections.

records.l: racial bitterness in Lower Canada, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {33} CHAPTER V THE NINETY-TWO RESOLUTIONS After 1830 signs began to multiply that the racial feud in Lower Canada was growing in intensity.
records.s: The racial feud in Lower Canada grew more intense after 1830. It contributed to the Montreal riot of 1832 and shaped the largely racial political struggle before 1837.

records.l: Montreal, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {33} CHAPTER V THE NINETY-TWO RESOLUTIONS After 1830 signs began to multiply that the racial feud in Lower Canada was growing in intensity.
records.s: Montreal was the scene of a by-election riot in 1832 in which troops fired on rioters, killing three and wounding two French Canadians. The county of Montreal was also criticized because the governor had failed to issue a writ for the election of a representative.

records.l: Lord Aylmer, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {33} CHAPTER V THE NINETY-TWO RESOLUTIONS After 1830 signs began to multiply that the racial feud in Lower Canada was growing in intensity.
records.s: Lord Aylmer was blamed by the Patriote press for the deaths in the Montreal riot and was accused by Papineau of slaughtering victims. The Ninety-Two Resolutions demanded his removal and impeachment, while the Patriotes also accused him of deliberately bringing cholera-infected immigrants into the province.

records.l: French Canadians, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {33} CHAPTER V THE NINETY-TWO RESOLUTIONS After 1830 signs began to multiply that the racial feud in Lower Canada was growing in intensity.
records.s: French Canadians were the victims killed and wounded when troops fired during the 1832 Montreal riot. Some French Canadians supported Papineau, while others, including moderates who became known as Chouayens, rejected his extreme course.

records.l: Papineau, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {33} CHAPTER V THE NINETY-TWO RESOLUTIONS After 1830 signs began to multiply that the racial feud in Lower Canada was growing in intensity.
records.s: Papineau became increasingly violent and domineering in the Assembly of Lower Canada, using his majority to expel or imprison opponents and threatening Quesnel with the loss of his seat. By 1832 he had rejected the constitution of 1791, admired the United States constitution, and made an elective Legislative Council the central demand of his party. He inspired the Ninety-Two Resolutions, though their revolutionary language and demand for Lord Aylmer's impeachment weakened their case before the British government.

records.l: Assembly of Lower Canada, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {33} CHAPTER V THE NINETY-TWO RESOLUTIONS After 1830 signs began to multiply that the racial feud in Lower Canada was growing in intensity.
records.s: The Assembly of Lower Canada was dominated for many purposes by Papineau's supporters. Papineau used its majority to expel members and imprison an opponent, but his proposal to refuse supply was defeated in 1833; in 1834 the Assembly passed the Ninety-Two Resolutions by fifty-six votes to twenty-four.

records.l: United States, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {33} CHAPTER V THE NINETY-TWO RESOLUTIONS After 1830 signs began to multiply that the racial feud in Lower Canada was growing in intensity.
records.s: Papineau increasingly looked toward the United States after losing faith in the British government's willingness to redress grievances. He admired the American constitution and the broad application of the elective principle, while the Ninety-Two Resolutions invoked the growth and example of the United States in language that suggested a threat of rebellion.

records.l: elective Legislative Council, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {33} CHAPTER V THE NINETY-TWO RESOLUTIONS After 1830 signs began to multiply that the racial feud in Lower Canada was growing in intensity.
records.s: The elective Legislative Council movement became the chief policy of the Patriote party under Papineau. It sought to remove the existing Legislative Council's buffering role between the governor's Executive Council and the Assembly.

records.l: Legislative Council, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {33} CHAPTER V THE NINETY-TWO RESOLUTIONS After 1830 signs began to multiply that the racial feud in Lower Canada was growing in intensity.
records.s: The Legislative Council of Lower Canada was described as nominated, reactionary, and subservient to the Executive Council. Papineau and his allies sought to make it elective, and the Ninety-Two Resolutions treated this as their principal constitutional reform.

records.l: Executive Council, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {33} CHAPTER V THE NINETY-TWO RESOLUTIONS After 1830 signs began to multiply that the racial feud in Lower Canada was growing in intensity.
records.s: The Executive Council stood behind the Legislative Council as part of the existing governmental structure. The Ninety-Two Resolutions criticized the Legislative Council's subservience to the Executive Council and vaguely referred to the Executive Council's vicious composition and irresponsibility.

records.l: John Neilson, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {33} CHAPTER V THE NINETY-TWO RESOLUTIONS After 1830 signs began to multiply that the racial feud in Lower Canada was growing in intensity.
records.s: John Neilson, once a strong supporter of Papineau, became alienated from him under Lord Aylmer. He opposed the expulsion of Mondelet, resisted the abolition of the Legislative Council, rebuked Papineau during the debate on judicial independence, and voted against the Ninety-Two Resolutions.

records.l: Patriote party, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {33} CHAPTER V THE NINETY-TWO RESOLUTIONS After 1830 signs began to multiply that the racial feud in Lower Canada was growing in intensity.
records.s: The Patriote party became increasingly associated with Papineau's revolutionary and republican views, although it included both French- and English-speaking supporters. Its extreme wing adopted the Ninety-Two Resolutions, while Neilson, Cuvillier, Quesnel, Stuart, Bedard, and Parent later broke away from Papineau's leadership.

records.l: Ninety-Two Resolutions, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {33} CHAPTER V THE NINETY-TWO RESOLUTIONS After 1830 signs began to multiply that the racial feud in Lower Canada was growing in intensity.
records.s: The Ninety-Two Resolutions were introduced in 1834 by Elzear Bedard and were reputedly drafted by A. N. Morin under Papineau's inspiration. They identified numerous genuine abuses but also attacked the colonial constitution, invoked the American Revolution, demanded Lord Aylmer's impeachment, and failed to propose a clear system of responsible government. They passed by fifty-six votes to twenty-four and caused significant divisions within the Patriote party.

records.l: British government, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {33} CHAPTER V THE NINETY-TWO RESOLUTIONS After 1830 signs began to multiply that the racial feud in Lower Canada was growing in intensity.
records.s: The British government was asked through the Ninety-Two Resolutions to address abuses in Lower Canada's administration. The Resolutions' tactless criticism of the constitution, republican claims, reference to the American Revolution, and demand for Lord Aylmer's impeachment were unlikely to receive favorable consideration.

records.l: responsible government, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {33} CHAPTER V THE NINETY-TWO RESOLUTIONS After 1830 signs began to multiply that the racial feud in Lower Canada was growing in intensity.
records.s: The Ninety-Two Resolutions did not clearly advocate responsible government. Papineau and his allies did not appear to understand the eventual solution of a provincial cabinet drawn from and responsible to the legislature, although Papineau unwittingly helped hasten its arrival.

records.l: The 'Patriotes' of '37, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {44} CHAPTER VI THE ROYAL COMMISSION A general election followed soon after the passing of the Ninety-Two Resolutions and revealed the strength of Papineau's position in the country.
records.s: After the Ninety-Two Resolutions, Papineau and the Patriote party gained overwhelming control of the Assembly of Lower Canada, while Britain delayed responding to the colony's grievances. The British government recalled Lord Aylmer and appointed Lord Gosford as governor and chief royal commissioner, with Sir Charles Grey and Sir George Gipps, to investigate and settle the dispute. Gosford pursued conciliation with French Canadians, but Sir Francis Bond Head's publication of his instructions exposed Britain's opposition to major constitutional changes and undermined Gosford's policy. Papineau's followers then restricted supplies, producing a severe supply crisis, while the royal commissioners' reports rejected responsible government and an elective Legislative Council.

records.l: Papineau, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {44} CHAPTER VI THE ROYAL COMMISSION A general election followed soon after the passing of the Ninety-Two Resolutions and revealed the strength of Papineau's position in the country.
records.s: Papineau's position was strengthened by the election, and he was supported by seventy members as speaker of the Assembly. He attacked Lord Aylmer, rejected confidence that Britain would redress Canadian grievances, opposed granting a permanent civil list, and did not yet advocate civil war.

records.l: Patriote party, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {44} CHAPTER VI THE ROYAL COMMISSION A general election followed soon after the passing of the Ninety-Two Resolutions and revealed the strength of Papineau's position in the country.
records.s: The Patriote party won the general election after the Ninety-Two Resolutions. Members who had opposed the Resolutions, including Neilson, Cuvillier, Quesnel, and Stuart, were defeated.

records.l: Ninety-Two Resolutions, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {44} CHAPTER VI THE ROYAL COMMISSION A general election followed soon after the passing of the Ninety-Two Resolutions and revealed the strength of Papineau's position in the country.
records.s: The Ninety-Two Resolutions were forwarded to Westminster through the Assembly's agent in London and through Lord Aylmer. They led the British House of Commons to appoint a special committee to investigate the grievances they described.

records.l: Assembly of Lower Canada, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {44} CHAPTER VI THE ROYAL COMMISSION A general election followed soon after the passing of the Ninety-Two Resolutions and revealed the strength of Papineau's position in the country.
records.s: The Assembly showed strong support for Papineau and adopted an increasingly confrontational position toward the executive government. In 1836 it refused to grant more than six months' supply and threatened to withhold further supplies unless the Patriote demands were met.

records.l: Lord Aylmer, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {44} CHAPTER VI THE ROYAL COMMISSION A general election followed soon after the passing of the Ninety-Two Resolutions and revealed the strength of Papineau's position in the country.
records.s: Lord Aylmer was recalled to make way for the appointment of a governor who could also serve as chief royal commissioner. The British authorities expressly relieved him from censure, while recognizing that his relations with the Assembly made him unlikely to help resolve the dispute.

records.l: Colonial Office, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {44} CHAPTER VI THE ROYAL COMMISSION A general election followed soon after the passing of the Ninety-Two Resolutions and revealed the strength of Papineau's position in the country.
records.s: The Colonial Office delayed action amid political instability in Britain before deciding to send a royal commission to Canada. Its policy under Lord Glenelg was to conciliate the Canadian Patriotes without making real constitutional concessions.

records.l: British government, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {44} CHAPTER VI THE ROYAL COMMISSION A general election followed soon after the passing of the Ninety-Two Resolutions and revealed the strength of Papineau's position in the country.
records.s: The British government sent a royal commission to investigate the disputes in Canada and appointed Lord Gosford as governor and chief royal commissioner. It did not contemplate major constitutional changes, especially an elective Legislative Council.

records.l: Lord Gosford, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {44} CHAPTER VI THE ROYAL COMMISSION A general election followed soon after the passing of the Ninety-Two Resolutions and revealed the strength of Papineau's position in the country.
records.s: Lord Gosford became governor of Canada and chief royal commissioner despite having no previous experience in public life or civil government. He pursued conciliation through social and official gestures, promised redress of grievances, and proposed financial and administrative concessions, but his efforts were undermined by the publication of Sir Francis Bond Head's instructions.

records.l: royal commission, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {44} CHAPTER VI THE ROYAL COMMISSION A general election followed soon after the passing of the Ninety-Two Resolutions and revealed the strength of Papineau's position in the country.
records.s: The royal commission was sent to investigate and, if possible, settle the questions in dispute in Canada. Its commissioners ultimately advised against responsible government and an elective Legislative Council and raised the possibility that suspending the constitution might be preferable to partial interference with it.

records.l: French Canadians, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {44} CHAPTER VI THE ROYAL COMMISSION A general election followed soon after the passing of the Ninety-Two Resolutions and revealed the strength of Papineau's position in the country.
records.s: French Canadians were the principal audience for Lord Gosford's conciliatory policy. Gosford promised that they would not face discrimination in appointments and that their native tongue would be guaranteed, but the publication of British instructions weakened the effect of these assurances.

records.l: Canada, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {44} CHAPTER VI THE ROYAL COMMISSION A general election followed soon after the passing of the Ninety-Two Resolutions and revealed the strength of Papineau's position in the country.
records.s: Canada was experiencing severe political conflict between the Assembly, the executive government, and British authorities. The dispute involved constitutional reform, control of revenues, relations between French and English inhabitants, and the withholding of supplies.

records.l: Lower Canada, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {44} CHAPTER VI THE ROYAL COMMISSION A general election followed soon after the passing of the Ninety-Two Resolutions and revealed the strength of Papineau's position in the country.
records.s: Lower Canada received Lord Gosford as governor and chief royal commissioner in 1835. Its Assembly rejected the proposed compromise over revenues and the civil list after learning that the British government opposed an elective Legislative Council.

records.l: Sir Francis Bond Head, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {44} CHAPTER VI THE ROYAL COMMISSION A general election followed soon after the passing of the Ninety-Two Resolutions and revealed the strength of Papineau's position in the country.
records.s: Sir Francis Bond Head, the lieutenant-governor of Upper Canada, disclosed his instructions from the Colonial Office to the legislature of Upper Canada. The disclosure revealed Britain's opposition to real constitutional changes and damaged Lord Gosford's conciliatory policy in Lower Canada.

records.l: Legislative Council, The 'Patriotes' of '37, {44} CHAPTER VI THE ROYAL COMMISSION A general election followed soon after the passing of the Ninety-Two Resolutions and revealed the strength of Papineau's position in the country.
records.s: The Legislative Council rejected the supply bill in 1836 after the Assembly refused to grant more than six months' supply. Its opposition contributed to the distress of public officials and their families.

records.s: The demand for an elective Legislative Council was not accepted by the British government. The royal commissioners later advised against introducing one.
